The voice wore the subtle roughness her daughter had developed in the months before Snap. Tiny affectations—gestures of breath and vowel—that Juno had catalogued in a fever of grief after the hospital call. There had been a recording, a custodian's message, a handful of volatile data that might have been corrupted in transit. She had kept it because each listening was a small victory against the cessation of the world. Each listening was a crime.

Ras's fingers ran through his hair. "How long did the Meridian have power downlink? This thing—could be an old emergency feed. A salvage trawler found their kid's shoe and—"

"It doesn't matter," Juno said. To say otherwise would be to say she was letting the past hold her like a hand on her neck. She told herself that is was only data. She told herself that she had sold and bought and recycled things enough to know there was no sanctity to an object. Then the shoe vibrated and a new sequence threaded underneath the lullaby, a low staccato that wasn't music but a grid of coordinates.

Ras looked at the HUD. The analyzer spit out text, then resolved it into an image: a map smear, a time stamp.

"Regression notation?" Ras asked, and his technical brain filled the silence with hypotheses as if building a ladder between him and the falling thing that was Juno.

"Notation," Juno echoed, eyes fixed on the string. The date was wrong. It was coded in a long-form temporal signature that traced out not a moment from the past but a moment that hadn't yet happened: 2439-10-12 02:13:07 UTC+0.

She would have thought it a corrupted timestamp. She would have wanted the tidy answer—a glitch, a backward fold, a misread registry. But the more rational parts of her mind—those she used for running profit margins and avoiding scars where she could—fumbled and tried to calculate what the literal output meant. A future-based release. A delayed activation. Somebody had made the shoe to speak not in the catastrophe but after its echo had had time to congeal.

"Delayed playback?" Ras suggested, less with the hope of correctness than with the need to do something. People will reach for procedure when the body wants to fall apart.

"Or a message sent from later, to then." Juno's voice tasted like iron. She had to fight to keep it steady. There were rules about temporal signatures. Laws. Warnings etched into neural net as if they were scripture—do not take things from the future, do not invest in echoes, do not be tempted by artifacts that promise corrections. You could trace a line from those rules to the people who had written them—governments, philosophers, the people who'd watched time burn itself and said, "No."

But the shoe didn’t care for rules. For the shoe, time was a place like any other, and the lattice sang it.

A second tone threaded through then, a human thing like a cough. A child's laugh, maybe, or the body's attempt at mimicry. Then a syllable that made Juno's stomach unclench with perilous recognition.

"Ma…" The word was a broken fragment, an incomplete offering. But it was connected to a name that Juno had not used in public for years, a name that existed in the private ledger of soft things and vanished birthdays.

Her breath left in a sound she did not know she had. The cabin was suddenly a small room full of too many people. The cutter's life-support systems clicked to warm the air. Outside, the Ring of Ash continued to be patient with its dead.

Some alarms began to tone faintly from the HUD—low-level background threads in the system noting the mismatched timestamp and flagging for a reporting sequence. Protocols wanted to know what to do with a possible future-origin artifact. Then a high-priority ping cut through the noise, a signal that the comm net had picked up a broadcast: a single carrier wave from the Meridian Sky, still registering in loop at the same coordinates they'd just harvested.

"This is impossible," Ras said, but his voice had the shape of the admission he had always refused to make.

It was impossible because the Meridian had been the first to burn. Its hull had been catalogued as a crater and a memorial. It was impossible because records said all alive people aboard had perished at 02:05, not 02:13. It was impossible because Juno had been standing in a harbor three days after that, with a body that was legally dead in another ledger.

But the ship transmitted again. The voice on the loop rang out that same lullaby and then, with a clarity that made the laboratory lights ring, the speaker said something new, and in that voice was a name that was not supposed to be alive.

"Juno?"

The cutter's lights went around the room as if the walls were breathing. Every rational node in Juno's head tried to file the moment under "malfunction." The left side of her jaw ticked. There were so many things that could unmake experience: signal bleed, correlated grief, the mind's ability to find pattern in static. And yet the tib of her knowledge—child things learned from a mother—began, inexorably, to answer.

She had not known which parent would speak first to call her back. She had not known the cadence of improper time. She had not known how small a voice could be to open the door.

"Who is the recipient?" the HUD demanded. Its voice was neutral and yet it felt like a question asked at the top of a cliff.

Juno's mouth moved before she had decided to move it. "Me," she said. The single syllable tasted like everything—the ledger, the rulebook, the places where people write out their obligations and failures. Behind it, the Ring hummed with a million small deaths, and the shoe on the analyzer sat like a fistful of signal ready to be unraveled.

In the radio, the word echoed, framed by a lullaby and the possibility of a future that might call for an answer.

The scrapyard doesn't have a bottom. You can tell a story about any piece of it—how a freighter lost its spine in a micrometeor shower, or how a leisure dome spun itself to dust in a honeymoon orbit—and the story will be true for a moment, then wrong forever after you drift past the next carcass. Out here everything is a rumor trying to be a fact: twisted metal telling its own history in the language of dents.

My suit hums like a tired insect. The hull is cold under my gloves. The Kestrel's outer skin flakes like sunburned paint; its name is still stenciled along an upper plaza in letters someone scrubbed off and failed to finish. I work the cutter along a seam where the plating bowed inwards. Sparks bloom, then spit away into black. For the thousandth time I remind myself not to think of what it's like inside when the cutter finds the hollow chest.

"Grip three engaged," Runa says in my ear, and the rig's voice folds around it—calm as a municipal announcement. The salvage rig is a floating belly of cranes and welders and auction cords, a thousand-ton convenience for anyone who can pay the docking fees. I am not that anyone. I wear the rig's name on my comm band because it's cheaper than pretending to be something I am not.

"You see anything of value?" Tom asks, his laugh small, a condensation held back by habit.

"Needs opening," I answer. "Maybe a life support array. Maybe a storage slug. Maybe a luxury cot with a TROPHY plaque that says 'FOR EVERYONE ELSE, WE SURVIVED.'"

Tom snorts; Runa doesn't. There's a tilt to her tone I can't place through the feed—alarm or boredom, I'm not sure. "Watch for containment," she says. "Kestrel's logs got wiped five times. Corporate wipe pattern."

"Good to know." I slice the cutter through a last seam and pry open a hatch that hasn't breathed in a decade. Light from the rig's flood spills into the cavity and paints the interior in clinical blue. Inside the Kestrel smells like old coffee and ozone and the metallic tang of people who once argued until someone slammed a door and then left.

There's a row of canisters lined along an inner wall, each one the size of a coffin. They are cryopods, the old kind—the vacuum-sealed, emergency-preserve models that more than half the stations still truck around for black-market exports and transport mishaps. Their faces are frosted opaque. I hover with the cutter idling, because opening a pod is like opening a mouth; you never know what it will say.

The first pod refuses. Its sensors are dead, a hard series of read errors that translates in salvage lingo to "do not touch." The second glows with a faint, steady pulse. The third—third's panel shows a registry imprint: MINERVA-EXTRACTION: PROTOCOL S— and then the letters flick like a broken heartbeat.

"Minerva?" Tom's voice is flat. "Thought that lab went offline when the Flood happened."

"They didn't—people always say they didn't," Runa says. "But you don't see Minerva seals on random junk. Unless—"

I have the universal gesture for 'unless' handy. I open the third pod's faceplate.

It's impossible before my brain finishes the word. It shouldn't be possible because the Kestrel launched ten years before the Flood and Minerva was not exactly a sanatorium for children. What slouches inside the pod is small, like a fist that learned to exist. The visor defrosts under my cutter's heat; breath clads the inside like a sheet. A face, small, with hair that clings in a shadow halo. The skin is dust-thin and luminous in the pod's wash, as if lit from within.

I expect a corpse. Instead, the chest under the glove-thin fabric of the suit rises; the infant inhales like someone measuring for a future.

"Contact," I say, and my voice shakes louder than I mean it to. "Biometrics positive. Heart on hold—low, but stable. It's a live human."

Tom swears softly. "Live pods are supposed to be registered. They're expensive. Whoever nuked the registry—"

"Nuked the registry to hide this," Runa supplies. "Or they were trying to hide whatever was inside from being catalogued in the first place."

I move to unlock the seal. My gloves tremble because it's a child's throat below them that will remember my touch. Ethical questions are luxuries in a salvage rig's manifest. Worth is a function of chain of custody, and chain of custody starts at the moment of recovery. If I bring a live pod out into the rig, the people who own it—or who think they do—will have lawyers with teeth and vectors. If I don't, a child could die because I counted credits over lungs.

"Bring it up slow," Tom says. "We don't need two dramas tonight."

The pod light flickers. There's a soft voice, nowhere but in my head, or in the humidity of the pod, or in the thing itself. It says a single syllable: "Mara."

My helmet is a bubble; my name is not a broadcast. The last person who called me that was my mother, and she hasn't called me that in ten years and a half and a sky of lies. I am very methodical on the outside. Inside I am a compass gone south.

"Did you hear—" Tom begins.

I cut him off with my comm. "All hands, stow. Lock containment. No boarders."

There's a protocol for live salvage when you think you have claim. It is also a protocol when the salvage contains an item stamped by a research house that one tends to avoid mentioning. We file forms, get signatures, call in a retrieval license. The corporations like paperwork because it smells like law. Law is a thing they can sell, but it is not a thing that will bring breath into a child.

I unseal the pod. Frost flakes away like old argument. The infant's eyes, the first thing that opens, are not ordinary. They are irises like maps—thin concentric rings and lines that shimmer with a faint bioluminescent trace in the low light. My helmet's HUD tries to catalog them and refuses, throwing up an error I've never seen: INVALID TEMPLATE. The eyes look up at me steady and mercilessly small.

"Hello, Mara," the child says, voice like a piano string plucked at the wrong time. Not my name again. Not words I used to think only dreamers and mothers could make.

Something in my chest folds open like an attic door. The memory that pushes through is not mine on the surface—the word comes not in the present but layered: a lullaby in a language my grandmother hummed while my mother braided hair. A pattern of consonants that attaches itself to the child's syllables like a lost key to a shuttered house. Two unrelated things fitting together and making a bell sound.

"Where—where did you get that name?" I ask because names are anchors and I have been unmoored for most of my life.

The child watches me. A tiny hand moves, slow, and presses to the visor. The palm leaves a smear that the rifters on my HUD try to parse into fingerprints and fail because the smear is wet and warm and impossibly human.

"You're late," the child says.

Somewhere on the rig an alarm chimes, statutory and unmerciful. My comm flashes with an encrypted ping. No caller ID—just a seal: the black triangle of Continuity.

"Unregistered live container," is the message. Followed by three directives: Contain, Transfer to Continuity, Non-disclosure until transfer complete.

"What are Continuity's vectors?" I ask Runa, even though I already know they're the vulture at the edge of anything that even whispers about old-world tech. The tag that flashes across my HUD is a stub of corporate vestigiality—so sharp it could cut a claim.

"Long and funded," Runa says. "They'll take it and read it like scripture. If Minerva's code is in there, they'll damn the sea for it."

"Then we take it," Tom says. "We bring it to auction. We get enough to pay the loan on your mother's suit and then…"

In my ear, the child's voice is a tide. "Don't let them read me."

Every training session I've ever had is a footnote now. Regulations say a live salvage that is flagged by Continuity is their jurisdiction. The legal department will call. A small, merciless part of me can imagine the numbers: bring in a live Minerva infant, sell to Continuity—payment enough for a decade. Another, sharper part recognizes the shape of the child's prison: a round of cold plastic that kept this thing from decay until someone wanted to drink whatever data its eyes could pour out.

My hands remember how to move in ways my brain doesn't intend. I transfer the pod from the crane to my harness. The rig's crew doesn't rise to stop me; they're all wolves in wheelchairs, their interest narrowed to their own margins. Runa's voice says, "You're stealing."

I say, "Then call me a thief. I'm tired of being owned."

The rig's outer lights dim as if the yard itself is holding its breath. I feel the tug of the rig's magnetic plates as I accumulate mass around a thing that smells like a future.

The pod is heavier than it looks. It is heavier because the child inside is light as a tissue and heavy with consequence. My suit reads my biometrics; it reads the pod's registry and flags up a suppressed hash that the Kestrel's scrape could not wholly hide. The hash is a string that pulls at the underside of memory—not mine necessarily, but a memory like a radio station that plays the same three notes whether anyone is listening or not. It calls up images that are not mine: a lab corridor with doors numbered for people who do not exist, a woman with my mother's hands opening a drawer and placing something inside, the girl—no, the child—hand being placed into a pod and the words "Protocol S" stitched across the inner lining like a brand.

"Where are you taking it?" Tom whispers.

"Nowhere they can get it quickly," I say.

We peel away from the Kestrel with no blessing, only a claim to chaos. The rig's cameras paint us a thin white line as we pass between hulks. The Earth hangs below, a blue coin, and above, a sky the pure black of everything that remembers the sun. My comm chirps repeatedly with Continuity's seal until I mute it. I set course for a place I haven't set course for in five years: an abandoned habitat the old boroughs used to call Anchor One, a place off the registry with a docking bay that is more rumor than concrete.

The child watches me the whole way. Its little fingers curl into a fist, then flex like a pilot learning the feel of a control stick. Once, my mother used to say you carry the things you can't fix. I have been carrying debt and whatever was left of my dignity for so long I forgot which of my burdens were chosen.

"Tell me your name," I say, because it's the only thing left to ask before the rest of the world arrives in the shape of lawyers and corporate grenades.

The child looks at me with those map-eyes and smiles like someone who knows entire star systems are waiting for the right footnote. "I remember," it says. "But I don't remember being mine."

We cross the teeth of the scrapyard and the Kestrel recedes into the darkness with the rest. Behind us, somewhere like a wound, a transistor sighs—and for a moment the noise of the vacuum seems loud enough to be a person sighing back.

A ceramic bell rings in my pocket—a relic, a keepsake—that my mother used to jangle when the nights were long. It has a sticker on its back: KEEP ME WARM. I press it out of habit, and it writes a small vibration I feel not with my nerves but with a place under them. The child looks at the bell, and its eyes, already maps, flare like beacons.

"Map-route locked," it tells me, and that's the last thing I understand before the engines sigh and whatever we've taken becomes a secret between us and the dark.

The first thing that dies in a memory is the smell.

It doesn't go like a switch. It's more like the lights in a theater dimming one row at a time until you forget there was ever color. When I spool the residue of someone else's life through my headset—my fingers steady on the micromill, my eyes on the visible fine-grain of synaptic graphite—the odor that should have been there is always first to thin and fall away. Burnt toast becomes an idea of toast. Rain becomes a formula: the angle of light on a slick surface. What remains is the architecture of feeling, the scaffolding of things that meant something.

I am a diver in that theater. They call us transcribers on the clinic bills, mnemosurgeons in the legal briefs. On the street they call us bone-listers and dream fencers. Officially, I extract and encode: last memories of the dead for the families who can afford them, forensic retrieval for the courts, the occasional archaeological pull for researchers who like to think of memory as a fossil bed. Unofficially, I'm an interpreter. People bring me memories without knowing what they're bringing.

The woman on the slab smells faintly of antiseptic and something caramelized—human skin under flame. Her name was Sindri Fer, forty-two, a cook at the market hub and, according to the registry, single. They brought her in with the head wound neat as a cut ribbon and the rest of her bones browned in a pattern that suggests she fought the fire awake. Her face is what I'm supposed to look at to ground myself—face, hairline, the light at the corner of the eyes. I do. I register the small technicals: neural clamp engaged, ionic hum steady, the read pairs aligned with the hippocampal ridge. Then, because I always do it, I press my thumb to the inside of her wrist to find a pulse that isn't there. Habit wants touch even when touch is empty.

I let the machines catch the flicker first. They are better at patience than I am—quantum nodes that listen at trillionth-second intervals and translate the mind's electrical whisper into something my headset can render. The memory arrives like a weather front: full, coherent, with depth that makes my teeth ache. It's a single burn—this woman's last minutes, compressed tight and raw.

At first it's ordinary: the pan, the oil spitting, the sound of the market's clarion alarm. My breath finds the rhythm of hers—someone frying spice on the third-floor veranda, someone humming without knowing a tune's name. Then the world tilts. The edges of the memory don't blur; they sharpen into a pattern that does not belong to a burnt kitchen.

It is a hallway that is not a hallway. It is long and impossible, the walls not quite parallel but draped in something like a skin of glass. Light moves across the glass in a slow, deliberate pulse—no natural light could do this. The floor is cold under bare feet. There are doors at intervals; each one is a mouth that opens before someone reaches it and then closes when they do, eating their shapes. Above everything moves a sound no instrument should be able to make: a low harmonic that digs into the molars and leaves a residue of metallic taste.

Sindri's point of view is close, uncomfortable. I feel pressure at the back of my skull, the muscle memory of turning, and then a name—not her name but another syllable threaded through her mouth like a swallowed foreign coin. "A-thal," she says in the memory, and the vowel is wrong. The syllable reverberates against the impossible walls and the doors respond with a ripple. When the doors open they do not reveal rooms but more corridors, folding inward like origami.

A child's laugh. Not Sindri's. Not a sound that should exist in a place like a hallway. The laugh is high and tuneless and then there is a plant suddenly on the floor—leafy, thick and wet with a dew that is not like any water I know. When the memory pans upward the plant isn't a plant at all but a cluster of bones curving into a shape like a small vertebra, and there, stitched to it, is a thing that looks like a coin made of blue light.

My own hands tighten on the micromill. Syllables we learned to avoid come to my tongue: artifact, implant, crossstack. Memory-evidence is a thing the regulators like to pretend doesn't exist. You can embed an image, a sensation, even a false thread of language into someone's synaptic lace if you have the right chips and the right old labs. It's called a graft in the trade, a filigree in the black markets. Some are harmless—advertising hooks, lullabies, old pop songs compressed into the hippocampus legible as nostalgia. Others are proof: proof of contact, proof of conspiracy, proof a corporation buried a death and stamped a new story into a corpse to cover the smell of its crime.

This is not a lullaby. The blue coin glows and folds and sheds a pattern that reads like coordinates in the language of glints. In my periphery the machines translate the pattern into numbers—it is a long string of delta-phase markers: a location between stars, a place they stopped naming after the fifth colony went dark and the maps began to hide things.

Danger, the clinic's interface warns in the corner of my vision. This memory is flagged. I freeze, which is not good practice. Machines like me are trained to maintain flow; the part of extracting that demands interruption is always a risk of corrupting the data. But the hum at the back of my skull is new and metallic, and the taste of blood on my tongue tells me that something other than a burnt cook's panic echo is in the feed.

I split the stream. I isolate the coordinates as my hands perform without my head's consent. They pop up like a flash watermark: Cassiopeia-7, Sector Slate, Bearing 2.4-Ohm. A location under provisional seal—public note: "Restricted research area; transit prohibited." Private note: "Anomalous event; do not interact." They put that in tiny gray letters so the average citizen would scroll past and the average official would nod. The other note, the one someone paid to keep, says nothing.

Because someone had implanted it in Sindri, I think. Or, thread more dangerous, Sindri had found it and carried it like an ember. I don't know which yet, and the not-knowing smells like cold metal. My training has a folder on how to proceed in these situations: extract-cleanse-encode-send. Report any illegal material per protocol. You don't keep evidence. You don't read further than the minimum.

But I had spent the last three months paying my sister's anti-fibro synth credits from salaries that barely covered the clinic's rent. I had been near broke long enough for my hands to learn where theft looked like survival. You tell a body you will follow the rules and your muscles won't always listen.

I thumb the softlock and save a copy to the chip hidden in the cuff of my sleeve. The clinic's interface pings me an authorization request, the sort of polite, corporate demand that wears caution like armor. "We will need a full extract, certified and scheduled," the chat reads. They have standard operating replies for grief-struck families, for probate courts, for kidnappings. They will want the whole feed. They will want to clear it. They will not look for the coordinate. They will not wonder why a cook at the hub had a hazard-sealed image of a sealed sector.

I finish the last of the extraction ceremoniously. Sindri's last thought is a child's hand in hers, and then the memory ends and her face goes placid, if placid is what we call the stillness after such a violent compression. The machines disengage with a little sigh of hydraulic air. I take the chip from my cuff and drop it into the bottom drawer of my console with the kind of care that says either I am hiding evidence or I'm making tea.

A shadow passes across the clinic's doorway. Yourselves is late and you know it—you only ever show up on time when you have something to hide. Captain Havel's face is a map of concern the way people's faces always become maps when they're trying to be official. He smells like star-ship oil and the inside of a uniform that hasn't seen sunlight in three weeks. He is, as his badge identifies him, legal compliance liaison for the station's management. In less official terms he is someone whose job is to close risky stories before they breathe too deeply.

"Kira," he says. He never says Ms. Eno in public unless he means to make me remember the one formal occasion we had. "We had a report. Sindri Fer. Fire origin nos. We will need your extract log."

"We're already logged," I say. My tone is smooth because I've rehearsed it. "Full protocol. Will be uploaded by cycle end."

He looks at the slab where Sindri lies blank as a screen. You could read a whole life in the way his jaw tightens; I could, if I wanted, make an argument that he didn't always have this job. Some men go into compliance to keep their hands clean. Some go in because they like the sound of authority. Havel's eyes are tired enough that they read as both.

"We can't have leaks," he says. "Precedent is expensive."

"We can have an extra check," I say. "If there's anything flagged as anomalous, it goes to Central. They can audit."

He studies me as if choosing a posture. "Deliver it to the dock block. An auditor will collect."

It is less an order than an expectation. I nod because nodding is a fine space to hide the things you intend to disobey. When he leaves he takes the clinic's poll of oxygen with him and I settle into the small ritual that helps me clear the residue of other people's deaths from my palate. It is never complete. We never leave the work clean. The machines breathe into the room and I scrub the rim of the micromill with the rag I keep in my pocket for the purpose. The rag picks up the faintest threads of light from the extraction chamber that aren't anywhere except in my eye's after-image.

The chip in the drawer under my hand vibrates. Not like the clinic's machine but like a heartbeat that doesn't belong to me. It is a soft coded tap: someone else's commstamp. The chip is old tech to avoid the system's sniffers; I buried it in a drawer that doesn't have a register. The message slides across its surface like a warbler. It is not an official tone. It is clipped and human and impossible to trace in the ways that matter.

We find you, it says in letters that are polite violence. Do not deliver the extract. Meet me at the third stairwell by the hydroponic sluice in ten minutes. Bring nothing.

My skin goes cold in the same place Sindri's memory pressed at the back of my skull. A blue coin folded in glass corridors and a note carved into a dead cook's final minutes. Someone else knew what that memory was worth. Someone else knew to look for it.

I could go to the dock block, file the mandatory reports, and sleep the way people sleep when the law draws a circle around their life and keeps them there. I could do what the clinic expects and become another node in the chain that keeps the station clean of dangerous knowledge. But the man who wants to meet me is not a server of protocol. He is a predator of secrets. He chose the third stairwell because it is where things desperate people go to trade favors and old bread.

I slide the chip out of the drawer and tuck it into the inner seam of my jacket. I leave the clinic door open with the air still on low and the machines singing like bees. Outside in the corridor the station is its usual mixture of commerce and compressed living: vendors selling quick protein pucks, a boy with a cracked faceplate arguing about a scraped coin, two maintenance drones doing their slow ballet along the rail. Overhead, the view of the city drops away into darkness and the little glitter of the orbital ring hangs like a promise.

The hydroponic sluice's third stairwell smells of wet algae and the kind of metal that softens in infinite vacuum. It is also warm because it's the living place of the station's plants, and plants hold secrets like people do. A figure is there when I arrive, half-shadow and the wrong kind of geometry under the floodlight. He is shorter than I expected and his coat is patched in a pattern of repairs that says he has been poor for a long time. His face is half-hidden by a hood and a scarf, and when he lifts the hood his eyes are the light teal of new growth.

"You have it?" he says.

I show him my empty hand and then the turned-in collar of my jacket where the chip waits. "Never keep evidence," I say. An old ethical joke. He doesn't smile.

He reaches for the jacket sleeve with delicate hands, the way someone who has taken apart many small machines might touch them—knowledgeable and careful. He feels for the chip and finds it like a diver finding a shell. He doesn't unwrap it. He doesn't have to.

"The coordinates are burned," he says softly. "Not the usual. Not a corporate seal. Some other signature."

"Not one I've seen," I lie. Truth is a currency here and I spend it sparingly.

He studies me for a long while like he's trying to decide whether to trust the hand that gave him the chip. "You know what happens when those get out," he says.

"Depends who opens them," I answer. "Depends on who reads the coin."

He nods slowly. "We were hoping to read the coin. But we don't have a diver. We don't have someone with your—capabilities."

And there it is: the ask. The word that means everything. We. We implies a group outside the legal framework, perhaps one with the reach to follow a set of coordinates into a place sealed by the state. We also implies consequence. We implies that the coin is a doorway to something else.

My life is small: a clinic, a sister on synth meds, rent that gets paid by the hour with the dead. But there are things in me that are not small. There is a stubborn itch I get when a secret is thrust into the light—a question that tastes like stolen fruit: what if?

"Why me?" I ask.

"Because you don't deliver everything you take," he says. "Because you salvage things. Because you owe people."

He is not perfect. He is not lying. There are many reasons the world keeps people like me in roles where we see the last things that others don't want to see. Some of us keep secrets and use them like money. Some of us break the seals and trade the consequences for a better life. I look at him and imagine the corridors in Sindri's memory folding inward like paper cranes. I remember the child's laugh. I remember the blue coin.

"I'll need a ship," I say before I know it. "And air. And a name to call if I'm caught."

He bobs his head the tiniest degree like someone who has listened to people volunteer their lives in exchange for nothing more than a place at the table. "We can get you a runner," he says. "We can get you an alias. We cannot get you the thing you will find once you cross the seal."

"Nobody can," I say. "Not if it's dangerous."

He smiles then—quick and real as a flash. "Good. You'll be company then."

The coin in my jacket thrums like a little heartbeat at my ribs, almost a sound I think I can hear if I press my ear to it. Someone put coordinates into the last moments of a cook who died in a fire. Someone wanted them to be found. Someone else wants to keep them from being found. I feel the cold slide under my skin again—the same cold that visited me when the memory parted like glass—and the shape of the decision forming.

For three months I have been counting how many hours I can shave off clinical shifting to afford my sister's medicines. For three months I have been living on the kind of tight arithmetic that forces your choices into two lanes: need and survival. Now there's a third lane opening like a fault in the city's crust: curiosity, which is a dangerous kind of hunger.

"Tell me about the coin," I say.

He tells me what little he knows. He tells me the coin isn't a currency but a marker used by old research runs—teams who sent probes into the region before the seals were put down. Those teams stopped reporting. Maps show black where light should have been. People stopped naming the place.

"Some of us think it's a machine," he says. "Some think it's a being. Some think it's both."

I smile, because when you keep the dead for a living you learn to read metaphors like how to read the weather. My smile is small but true. "Then we should be careful not to anthropomorphize whatever eats explorers," I say.

He lets the smile sit on his face like the right key in a lock. "Good," he says. "You'll leave at dusk."

I leave then, because the world demands I return to the clinic, to the paperwork, to the illusion of normal. I leave with the blue coin against my skin, the shape of its numbers folding through me like an ache. I am not the kind of person people bring into their plans when they want to stay safe. I am the kind they bring when they want someone who will not be afraid of what a dead cook might have seen.

As I walk back past the market, people look at me with the practiced neutrality of people who see displacement as water—something you push aside with your hands and keep moving. I keep my head down and the chip in my jacket. The station hums around me, lights pulsing as if in time with that little heartbeat at my ribs.

They say not all doors on station lead outward. Some doors are inward. Some doors are the places you hide secrets to keep them from dying. I do not know yet which side of the coin I'm on.

But tonight at dusk, I will get on a runner with a hooded man and cross a seal I have no business crossing. Tonight I will be, for the first time in years, on the kind of path that makes me feel like I am moving toward something that is not only survival. There will be risk. There will be people who come looking. There will be choices I cannot yet see the shape of.

There will also be, quietly and with the inevitability of tide, the possibility that something in the corridor of Sindri's last minutes has been waiting for anyone to notice the blue coin. And when anything waits, eventually something notices.

The first time Tamsin Vale found her own name folded into a drawer she hadn't opened in twenty years, she almost reported herself.

The Archive called them tokens—slim, palm-sized wafers of ceramic glass, etched with calligraphy that looked like handwriting and felt like weather. People sold names for rent, traded them like heirlooms, buried them under the official registry so their old selves could be exiled with dignity. The city kept the exiles where it could: below the Spires, where the light was only a memory and the humidity held every quiet thing like an echo.

Tamsin was supposed to catalog them, not touch them. Her job was to index the grief of the city and make it legible for the tax collectors. She ran the intake for Sector Twelve, which meant she listened to people whose faces were too young or too old for the names they carried. She scanned wafers, assigned lineage codes, and pushed the paperwork through the city's soft-systems so every erased past had a paper trail that couldn't bite back. An archivist's ethics were as sharp as any razor; the rules were written into the mnemos of everyone who ever trained under the Remnant Bureau. You do not possess what has been surrendered.

The wafer in her hand—if you could call it possession—had been tucked like a secret into a drawer labeled SECTION: TEMPORAL HOLD. The drawer was in the old Registrar's room, a place Tamsin only used when the new intake terminal hiccupped and forced her back into analogue. She'd opened it to retrieve a spool of archival tape and found a slip of white ceramic folded in half like a paper boat.

The script was small, cramped, looped in a child's hand: Penny.

Penny—an improper name for a grown woman, for an archivist with a Bureau badge and the right to order an orphaned file into oblivion. A nickname. An alias. An intimate thing.

For a fraction of a second Tamsin saw herself as something else: a child barefoot on a rooftop courtyard, scraping soot from the soles of her feet, laughing as the river of rainwater moved like a silver snake between panels of rust. She smelled orange oil and laundry boiling in a tin, a smell so immediate it made her throat tighten.

The memory didn't last. The Archive had a smell too—old polymer and ozone and the faint sweetness of countless stored regrets. She had been trained to separate memory from object. But a name folded like a secret is not an object; it is a hinge. It clicked, and a sliver of a life she did not own swung out. She pressed her thumb to it, felt the cool passive warmth of the ceramic, and the shape of the word under her skin like a footprint.

She should have slid the wafer back into the drawer, logged the misfiled token, and let a junior clerk explain the anomaly to the Board. People misfiled things all the time—old names migrated in the system like stray moths, caught in filters, reappearing where they oughtn't. But the wafer was not like other things. There was a curl in the capital P that matched the stroke on a child's drawing Tamsin remembered from a time that the Remnant Bureau had, in official policy, removed.

Officially, Tamsin Vale had no childhood. Her documentation began at nineteen, the age the Bureau assigned to adults who had been wiped, reissued, or otherwise realigned. Her face had a stamp of compliance: no formative attachments, no unsanctioned names. It was easier that way. Names infected. Memory contaminated. The city thrived on the separation between who people were and who they could be.

She slipped the wafer into the pocket of her coat instead.

It was a small rebellion—the kind you take when the only fight left is against the slow dullness of certainty. She told herself she would log it, submit it to the index, let the system reconcile itself. The Remnant Bureau's systems never reconciled anything; they only recorded how things had been excised. She was saying goodbye to this name the way people said goodbye to lovers, though people rarely said goodbye here; they traded it for silence.

"Vale?"

The voice hovered at the door, and Tamsin looked up. Mara Chen, her supervisor, stood framed by the corridor light. Mara's hair was the kind of gray that looked planned and therefore safe. Her badge caught the low lumens and threw a sanitised star across her cheek.

"This place still breathing?" Mara asked, scanning the room with the automatic politeness of someone who had learned to treat infrastructure as a person.

"Just the stored humidity," Tamsin lied, and the truth in that lie was the Archive's air. "The intake terminal reset. I was pulling a spool."

Mara's eyes flicked past the desk, to the drawer. "Don't leave 'em out," she said. "We have a quota on misfiled names this quarter—headcount's strangling us."

Tamsin closed the drawer. She felt the wafer like an extra heartbeat in her palm. "Noted," she said.

Mara studied her. For a thin, dangerous instant, Tamsin saw the way the older woman's gaze collected soft anomalies—an off braid, a loose sleeve—the way she had trained interns to notice friction. "You okay?" she asked.

Tamsin folded the question into the pocket where the name lay. "Fine."

Mara shrugged, accepted the answer, and moved on. When the door clicked shut, Tamsin realized her hands were trembling.

Name theft was a misdemeanor; unlawful retention of a surrendered token might be grounds for reassignment to the Outer Vaults. Names had legal weight: they were property that added personality to a ledger. Every wafer was coded, hashed, and timestamped. To possess a name you had once signed off without permission was malpractice and profound personal risk. But that was not what made her pockets sweat; the thing she feared was the memory that had slipped across her thoughts, a child's laugh like rain. The Bureau could execute a shame-quieting in minutes; archives had ways to freeze anomalies until they were numb. Tamsin had seen a senior clerk reduced to a smooth-eyed automaton because she refused to declare a spouse exiled. The city's excisions were precise and surgical.

She sat down at her desk and turned on the analog scanner. The intake terminal had an old-world interface that hummed like a living thing, honest in its failures. She fed the wafer into its slot even though she did not intend to register it. The machine dutifully traced the calligraphy, light scanning across the ceramic and reading the micro-etch. The green LED should have gone steady, a system acknowledgment. Instead, the lamp flickered, then pulsed an amber she didn't know the codes for.

"Diagnostic," she said to herself. Her voice sounded faraway. She checked the terminal's logs. Nothing under Penny. Nothing under any of the possible derivations. Not in the public registry, not in the exiles. The wafer had no lineage code. It had no timestamp. It had never been surrendered, which meant—she could feel the tiny gears of her mind aligning—that it had never, officially, existed.

She ran a deep query, a thing junior clerks were taught to fear because it pulled on context strings and sometimes brought down parts of the city's polite infrastructure. It was a net that gathered not only registry entries but peripheral mentions: hospital tags, adoption boards, private memos. The query returned pages of silence.

Her chest compacted as if someone had folded her heart. The name should not exist in the object she held. But the curl of the P, the angle of the y—it sat inside her like a tiny, stubborn shard.

The Archive's overhead hum changed. A pulse reverberated through the building: barely more than a hiccup in the city grid, but enough to make fluorescent panels stutter. On the other side of the wall, the Spire's maintenance channels threw up a warning plume of cooling fluid; somewhere, a relay had flicked.

Curiosity was an infectious thing in the Archive. Tamsin found herself routing a private request through the city's public terminal—one of the tasks she would normally log and hand off. She keyed the wafer's micro-etch into an isolated query and kept the channel open only to her eyes.

A reply came within the time the city considered polite. It was not from the registry. It was a message.

UNIDENTIFIED TOKEN: HOLD.

Sit with it, City protocols said. Mark it safe. Flag for Bureau review.

She would have closed the file. She would have done the right thing. She folded the wafer in her palm and heard, inside her head, a child's sentence: "Don't forget me."

The words were wrong. They belonged to a different voice—too small, too close—but they sat like dust on the sleeve of her memory. She had been trained to erase the echoes. The Bureau made its people clean. But some echoes clean back.

If she turned the wafer over she might find a serial number. If she drove it through the appropriate channels, the system would reveal its origin: a family file, a hospital shutdown, a surrendered identity. The machine would offer her a list—who had relinquished it, when, why. It would whisper the names of the living who had let this one go.

She imagined, for a moment, the map of her life overlayed with such whisperings. A grid of names connected by threads; people cutting threads; the city tending the severed pieces in the Archive. She imagined placing this name into that grid and watching it settle into its slot like dominos forming a figure she'd been promised did not exist. For twenty years she'd been moving between slots without looking at the shape she was forming. Perhaps that shape had been assembled for her.

Outside, the city made its habitual sounds—the soft droning of the hoverways, the distant clack of a market banner whipping. The lights of the Spires bled through the Archive's thin ceiling like a promising horizon. Tamsin slid a hand into her coat again and felt for the wafer. The ceramic was warm, as if it had been held by palms recently.

A notification blinked on the private terminal. ANONYMOUS DROP-OFF. RECORD UNTRACED. AUTHORIZATION REQUIRED.

There was a way to send a request to the Bureau for authorization, a bureaucratic act that carried the moral weight of self-incrimination. But to send it would mean revealing curiosity. The Bureau punished curiosity because curiosity led to context and context led to questions. She had survived the remapping at nineteen by not asking enough questions.

She made a choice she hadn't practiced in two decades: she went against procedure. She opened the Registry's terminal, routed a false log, and authorized a personal retrieval. It was a small lie, a skill she had sharpened over the years into a tool. The Archive would not notice at first. The protocol would chide itself. A junior system would sing the wrong note and a clerk would be reassigned. She could repair the damage and be none the worse for it.

She put the wafer under the scanner properly this time, as if to catalog it, and allowed the terminal to read every strain of its fiber. The light traveled across the ceramic, traced the letters, and for a second, when the machine pulsed, she saw the faintest ripple on the screen: an image that wasn't data—an instant of someone holding a child's hand over a canal with the sun at their shoulders.

The screen flickered black. The terminal threw an error she hadn't seen in years.

SECURITY BREACH: UNAUTHORIZED MEMORIALIZATION.

In the corridor beyond the door, a bang came—metal against metal, hard enough to make the Archive's shelves hum. Someone had tripped a mechanical alarm. Mara's footsteps, running.

Tamsin closed her hand over the wafer as if to hide it. Her fingers found the loop of the P again and the child's voice said, softer, "Don't forget me."

When the door burst open, Mara's eyes were wide. She did not look at the screen. She looked at Tamsin.

"Vale," Mara said. "What did you do?"

The wafer burned through the cotton of her palm dryly with the heat of things kept too long. Tamsin opened her mouth. The Archive wanted a confession and she almost gave one, because a confession would be neat and the Bureau preferred clean things. But the confession would also be a starting place for questions she did not want to summon across the city's measured calm.

"I found it misfiled," she said instead. "It has no record."

Mara's hand flew for the terminal. "Seal the room. Incident report," she snapped, and already the old protocols were beginning to roll out like tide—codewords, containment, the heavy imposition of compliance.

Tamsin had to decide on silence or speech. Both had costs. Both were roads whose ends she had practiced avoiding. She felt her life narrow to the width of a name.

She kept the wafer.

She slipped it into the inner pocket of her coat where thick glass could hide like a heartbeat. She did not voice the thought that had arisen with the child's laugh—she did not tell Mara that the curl of the P was a signature she had seen in a crayon drawing that, in the official story, did not exist. She didn't say she remembered being called Penny, once, when she had been smaller than the world and the river had been a glorious thing.

Mara's fingers tapped commands into the terminal. "Containment seal will hold until the Bureau reviews," she said. Her voice was all professional calm, and yet there was a tremor at the root of it, like something that knew better than to believe in certainty.

"Don't be in this room when they come," she added, meaning both the Bureau and the consequences.

Tamsin stood up. The Archive felt suddenly like the throat of something that could swallow her. Outside, the city kept humming. The Spire's lights steadied as if nothing had happened.

She tucked the name further into her pocket and left the Registrar's room with the quiet of someone who had decided to break the pattern. The corridor opened into a city that had rearranged itself to survive. People moved with the same practical gestures—coffee cups, paper wraps, the clack of shoes designed to make less noise on the new panels—but now Tamsin saw the way their eyes slid from face to face like plumb-lines testing for balance. Each person carried a wafer of some sort—some openly, some hidden in pockets, some as small tattoos at the jawline. Names were everywhere and no one admitted more than a curated version.

As she walked out into the dusk of the city, the wafer pressed like a pulse against her ribs. It was a thing that had been removed from her life by people with good intentions and sharp scalpels—people who believed in the virtue of a blank map. Perhaps there was a reason. Perhaps the city's silence about the past had preserved the peace.

But there was also a child in her head who asked not to be forgotten. And when you had been trained to forget, hearing someone else ask to be remembered was a dangerous seduction.

At the edge of the canal, where rust met neon and the river smelled faintly of copper and lilies, Tamsin paused. The city's lights reflected in the water like a galaxy that could be stepped into. She put her palm over the wafer as if blessing it, and the name seemed to lift under her hand.

She had one night, she told herself. One hour to reconcile a counterfeit past. One chance to decide whether to feed the city's architecture of forgetting—or to pull at the thread that might unravel something larger than herself. The Remnant Bureau would come in morning with its polite efficiency. In the meantime there were answers waiting in places the Archive did not want to look.

She walked toward the bridge and the river, the city's skin whispering with the sound of things being kept. The child's laugh came again, clearer this time, as if the name had given it permission. "Don't forget me," it said.

Tamsin tucked her chin into her collar, the wafer warm, and stepped onto the bridge toward a place where remembered things might still be alive. The city watched, patient and enormous, as one of its cautious citizens chose to fold her own past back into her hands.

Ana had always thought memories smelled like rain on concrete—sharp, metallic, with the faint sweetness of someone else's coffee gone cold. It was the smell of the Archive vents, of the sterilizing fog that rolled through the clinic every midnight and the beginning of every sale. It was the scent of her wages, the way her fingers remembered the weight of a sleeve-connector, the soft resistance of another person's past when she cued it up and unspooled it across the reader.

At eight minutes, twelve seconds into the harvest, the smell changed.

The donor's room was windowless and round, a pearl-shell cell in the Archive of Lumen. Light hovered in a steady ring above them, not bright but absolute, as if it insisted on clarity. The man on the cot had hands like two split geodes—knuckled, rimed with what might once have been paint or salt. He'd signed his consent in a scribble that had been both legalese and plea. His file read: Viktor Hale, Age 68, Former Dockwright, Class: Sinker. Credits owed: 12,400. Memories: assorted dockyard, mechanical repairs, one "Specialized Dive—nonrecallable" flagged by his last wife.

Ana clipped the sleeve to the temporal port at the base of his skull as she always did, watched for micro-microfissures in the gel before she engaged the transmitter. Her hands moved with the particular confidence of someone who had never been allowed to make a mistake. To be a junior mnemonist at the Archive was to be useful in ways the city could not measure: you chewed and spit out histories, making them palatable, marketable. You made yesterday into product. You could not afford to be sentimental.

"Calibrate to index three," Supervisor Liao's voice said in her earpiece, and Ana obeyed. Liao, who had the permanent odor of dust and coffee that the Archive cultivated like an official perfume, watched the monitors across the glass. Her face was a map of short-slept decisions. "We only want the workday sequences. Leave the personal index unless he volunteers it. No anomalies."

She eased the reader into Viktor's mind. For a second there was nothing but sensation: the sleeve's warmth, the coolness of the cot springs through tissue memory, the stutter of a heartbeat. Then the Archive foliage closed around the thread—a gray lattice of associative tags—and Ana threaded her way through it, the way one might step from branch to branch over a swamp. She tasted brine and iron and the exact angle of sun on a hull cleat. Viktor's dockyard, the tang of tar, the slap of tide against the pylons, folded into her like a cloak.

The procedure rendered memories into a holographic stream across the lab interface—a delicate tridimensional filigree of light that Ana could pluck through with the stylus. She guided the sequence, stripping out the harmful phantoms, tagging the mundane with market-friendly descriptors: "Repair—Econ," "Weather—Mild," "Tools—Named." She did this work with the kind of economy that earned her minutes for cigarette breaks and a correction of twelve credits per week.

At eight minutes, twelve seconds, the light shifted.

All the textures flattened into white. Sound withdrew like a held breath. Then something new sloped into the feed: a vision that held no harbor, no timber, no labor. It was not in Viktor's voice—memories were usually anchored in first person, and the voice carried with it a cadence that helped Ana triangulate ownership—but this was like seeing through a lens that had been rinsed in starlight.

She saw a roof of something that was not roof but membrane, stretched taut like a lung, lit not by sun but by thin, vertical shafts of color. The air in that memory had the taste of copper and salt, but it moved like slow music. The center of the scene was a column—a tall, living thing—whose surface was webbed with luminous veins, and along it climbed forms that wore the same skin as the column, sliding like fish up and down a living ladder. Their faces were not faces. They were maps of pressure and release; they had no mouths, and yet a sound threaded through the vision that she felt more than heard: a low, harmonic hum that made her fillings ache.

Ana's mouth filled with the same metallic tang of the Archive vents. Her stylus stuttered on the interface. Her training told her what to do—terminate, flag, extract the anomalous node and send it to Containment—but the memory was not a singular node. It spread, rooted like fungus into adjacent tags. If she cut it away, she would lose the sequence within sequence, and Liao would mark it as a ruined harvest. If she did not, it would be an unregistered anomaly, and the Archive had rules to treat such things with a careful, impersonal brutality.

She kept going.

Images batched themselves into syncopation: a narrow corridor filled with water up to the waist, and those faceless climbers moving like carp as if gravity were a suggestion; a sky that folded like a pleated fan and then opened again to reveal cold, white stars that parked themselves like neutral witnesses. In one beat she saw a child's hand—slender, webbed—reach for a thing that looked like a coin and dissolve into smoke when touched. The coin was stamped with a symbol that never resolved: a ring intersected by a slash of light. Every time it appeared she felt a tiny pinch in her sternum.

Then, impossibly, the vision turned inward and found her.

There was a flash—no larger than a spark from a lighter—and for the first time the scene chose an angle that she knew. For a sliver of a second she saw a narrow, long-ago street in the Quarter where she had grown up: a half-burned billboard advertising memory-loans, a stair that had been her first vantage point for watching the river, the exact scab on the inside of her elbow where she had tripped at seven. It was her street folded into the other place, and the hum that had been background swelled into the shape of a word.

Not a word in any language she knew, but a vibration on the back of her teeth that spelled something huge and small at once: Come.

Her fingers curled on the stylus. She felt as if someone had pressed their palm to the small of her back and nudged her forward. A flicker of something like recognition rose through her like warmth. Liao's voice in her ear went high, distracted. "Ana, isolate the harbor nodes."

The memory did not comply. It kept layering itself—images superimposed on images, like transparencies misaligned—until there was too much to hold. Ana felt the edge of nausea, a symptom she'd been taught to ignore. Instead she told herself she could contain it. She had done containment runs before; she had quarantined phantom sequences that were merely the residue of addictions, gendered recollections, the half-life debris of dream-hacks. This was something else.

The monitors flared the protocol: ALAR—Anomalous Lattice Response. A red strip crawled across the glass.

"Terminate," Liao said, her voice hard as a blade.

Ana's training curdled against the memory's insistence. For a crazy, thin instant she thought of her grandmother's cane and the day the city stopped manufacturing cane tips because synthetic clubs made better profits. She thought of all the little, identical trades she had made to keep herself breathing—consent forms signed for diets that were not hers, recollections sold so that rent could be paid. She had been a bodyguard for memories, letting them pass through her and into other's lives. Nobody had ever given one back to her.

The hum shifted into another tone—a chord that felt like a door opening.

She did the one thing she had no right to do.

She engaged a covert latch, the sort of benign corruption even the Archive tolerated in junior staff because it made them feel useful. An extra register that redirected a copy of the feed into a private slot. She fed the anomalous sequence into it, whole and raw, watched the duplicate ghost into a sealed node in her wrist-implant, where it glowed against her pulse like a second heartbeat.

"Extraction complete," she said aloud. Calm. Surgical. She wiped the sleeve, clipped it back into neutral, and the lights above the cot dimmed to the soft amber of aftercare.

Viktor's eyes were open and pale as the inside of a shell. He stared at her with that peculiar steady look you get when someone has sold their sleep and is now skimming the ledger of what remains. "Did it—" he began.

Ana did not tell him. She could not. Her thumb brushed the tiny ridge on her wrist where the private node resided and felt the memory there, black and vibrating. It tasted of copper and far water.

"Another day?" Viktor asked. He coughed, a dry bark, and the sound came out as if it had been measured against an old machine. He tried to smile. "For the boy with the bad wallet."

Ana nodded. She had been collecting other people's pasts to buy oxygen for her mother to sleep. She had known the arithmetic of grief since she had watched her father sell his lullaby to pay for Ana's first semester of mnemonics. Still—there was a sting to betrayal. The Archive's code required reporting anomalies; the code existed because the city needed people to trust what it remembered.

On her way out, Liao was waiting with the face she wore when she wanted to look like the thing that had never been young. "Observation," she said without preface. "There was a nonlinear sequence flagged. Viktor reported —"

"He had a specialized dive," Ana said. She held her voice steady, the way one does when lying about something small and saving something large. "Nonrecallable. He volunteered. It was all workday nodes, Supervisor. No personal recall."

Liao's eyes flicked to the monitor. Ana could see the tiny doubt like a fissure across lacquer. Then the supervisor nodded with the economy of someone who had traded too long in other people's regrets. "Good. Close the file. Second shift will pick up the contensions."

Ana signed the manifest and left the room, the memory in her wrist like a foreign body. Outside, the Archive's outer doors opened into Lumen, and the city exhaled its wet heat and neon into her face. Rain had started—an even, fine thread that turned the sky into someone else's smear. The canals were full and the river sang hard against its banks. Billboards towered in the fog: Buy Tomorrow's Smile. Rent a Memory. Relive Laughter. A child sold a laugh from a street cart and the sound sounded like a coin dropping.

On the tram back through the Quarter, the memory pulsed against her wrist with a rhythm that was half-seduction, half-warning. It spelled again that single, impossible thing: Come. And beneath that, in a voice that was not Viktor's—lilting, layered, as if several people sang out of a single throat—there was a syllable that she could not translate into her native phonemes. But when she pressed her palm to the node as the tram took a turn, the syllable translated itself into a map of pressure that corresponded, with needle-like precision, to a place she had known as a child: the Old Pier.

The Old Pier had been illegal to visit since the Flood Reclamation Act; it rotted at the city's edge where the river met the mouth, a lattice of skeletal pilings and algae and old gods' rust. When she was young the pier had been where she had watched fireworks and where thieves hid. Old men told stories that it led somewhere—downward, awash with light. Children dared each other to fetch a board to prove they were brave. For years the city had made it a clear line on maps: Exclusion Zone. No drivers. No drones. Do not go.

Ana finished her shift in a blur of paperwork and returns. Her hands moved on autopilot, but she felt the memory like a draft, like a second skin. Dinner in the kitchen was the grey stew of her apartment building—thin broth and two spoonfuls of protein made to look like meat. Her mother hummed a tuneless dirge and watched the window, eyes a little soft at the edges where sleep had been sold in entries and exits. Ana kept her other wrist turned inward so no one would catch the faint light beneath the skin.

"Everything all right?" her mother asked later, when Ana rose to the window to look at the river. The city was a black tooth in the rain, a smudge of lights. "You look like you've been given a secret," she said.

"A secret of the Archive," Ana said. She lied and told something small instead of everything large.

When she lay down, the node in her wrist hummed and the memory fed her in small doses—images she could not unsee, but that also did not fit inside the usual categories. They were not names and faces. They were movements, a community moving as one organism along a thing that might be grown or built. They had an economy that had nothing to do with credits: the trading of pressure, the transfer of salt-callus. There were no mouths in the memory, and yet there was language as old as tide.

Ana understood, in a place that had nothing to do with her reason and everything to do with her blood, that she had not merely taken a memory. She had taken a map. The Archive sold histories and comforts and the occasional dangerous recollection. This was neither. It was an invitation.

She sat up, then, in the small dark apartment, rain blurring the world into watercolor. The memory pulsed and the hum resolved into the shape of a single word that was clearer than anything she had heard all day.

Find.

Ana touched the spot where the implant's casing met her flesh. The node was warm against her palm like a small living thing. Beyond the sound the memory made against her teeth—tooth-hum, metal-tide—there was the knowledge that once you kept a thing, it kept you back. It rearranged where your footprints might lead.

Down in the Quarter, the city slept in the habitual ways it had learned to sleep: with one eye open, one digit on the ledger, always ready to sell or buy what made a life liveable. Ana thought of Viktor's hands folded like geodes and the ring-slashed coin she had seen in another world and the word that was no word but a rift.

She closed her eyes and let the hum fill her head until the room went thin and the edges of the apartment were only a suggestion. For the first time in her adult life, she imagined disobedience not as a sin but as a route. The Archive's rules were a fence and a promise. Beyond them, something older and maybe truer waited with a syntax she did not yet understand.

She would go to the Old Pier.

It was a small rebellion, a child's dare sewn into the shape of an adult decision. It would fit into the cracks of her life—one evening out of a thousand, one unauthorized walk, the kind of theft the city seldom punished harshly because it could be attributed to youth and sorrow.

But when she slipped the light coat over her shoulders and left the apartment, the rain had stopped. The city smelled once again of wet concrete and a sweetness she still could not name. The implant in her wrist pulsed like a compass, pointing not north but toward something that had not been recorded into the Archive's neat ledgers.

Ana kept her head down on the walk to the river, counting lampposts so she would not be tempted into larger thoughts. Past the third bridge a shadow detached itself from the underpass—an old woman in a coat that had once been finer, a paper bag of oranges at her elbow. The woman looked straight through Ana and mouthed the single syllable without sound, as if the city had become a place where even strangers knew enough signs to speak without words.

Come, she read on the woman's lip. Find.

Ana did not answer. She kept walking.

At the river's mouth, where the Old Pier waited like a broken promise, the city lights haloed the scene, and somewhere within the decay a faint, impossible luminescence breathed. It was small, like a distant biolume. It was also, when she closed her eyes, the exact pitch of the memory against her wrist.

Against all prudence and the tidy ethics of her profession, Ana unfolded the map in her head—the one threaded in light around her bones—and took her first real step into something that had been waiting to be found.

The first time I smelled vacuum, I thought it was rain.

It wasn't the cold, like everyone imagines when they read old space poetry. It was metallic — an iron tang under the skin — and it came through the port like a threat. You don't forget a smell that rearranges your insides. You either learn to work with it or you stop being useful.

I learned to work with it. I learned to move around the places other people were afraid to look. That's how I became a Remembrancer.

Officially, my ledger name is Naya Rooth, Remembrancer, license number stamped and barcoded and three stamps full of fines for late returns on client states. Unofficially, I'm the person you call when someone cleans a memory wrong and leaves a sliver sticking out like a burr. I'm the person who, for a fee and a long line of disclaimers, will take those burrs and pick them free.

The job is delicate because memories are not files you can back up and re-open. They're braided ropes of scent and muscle and the odd, stubborn lie. We use soft tech: mneme-lace, echo-needles, and the old, almost-gone science of touch-tracing. The lace is a fine polymer that grows into the synaptic gaps and hums at a frequency the brain recognizes as its own. The needle translates the hum into visuals; the touch-trace maps the micro-muscle memories you don't know you have. You have to be gentle. You have to be generous where the brain refuses to be honest. Most of all you have to be prepared for the things the world is built to forget.

My rent is paid in fragments. My studio — two rooms and a wall of plants grown under blue LED and a bed that is mostly sentimental — is where people come to reclaim themselves. Sometimes they come with a burned patch of night in their life, a missing year after a dive into the Pale. Sometimes they come with pieces stolen by corporations or cults. Sometimes they don't come at all, and their loved ones send what they can: a shirt, a app-scan of a laugh, a last blood test. You work with what you've been given.

The woman who came that morning carried her son folded in the lower crook of her arm like a package you might drop if you weren't careful. She smelled of cold coffee and peppermint and the Parliament Plaza's hopeless bureaucracy. She didn't sit down when I told her there'd be forms; she had already accepted the forms as a fact of grief.

"This is Jonah," she said. Her voice was raw in that chemical way people sound after no sleep. Jonah was nine, small for nine, with hair chopped unevenly as if by a pair of impatient teeth. He looked at me the way animals look at new things: curious and suspicious.

"How old?" I asked automatically.

"Nine," she said, and then, as if the number itself might have been mislaid, she added, "But he... he came back two months ago and he can't remember anything before the accident. He has names in his mouth that he can't explain. He keeps saying coordinates. He autistically repeats dates he can't place. The doctors say it's aftershock from the orbital collapse, but—" She stopped because there was nowhere to put the rest of the noise. She set a thin box on my desk.

I scanned it. The box contained a child's sweater, faint with mud and a smear of grease, and a small tin capsule with a paper inside: a drawing of a place that could have been a house if houses were made of bones and light. There was also a smudge of paint so bright it shouldn't have survived long near an atmosphere breach — opal-blue in streaks like a comet.

"Has he been through the clinic?" I asked. "Cortic cuts? Mneme-scrubs?"

"Yes. They cleared the big damage. The clinics do that. They take the noise down to two heartbeats and then resettle the patterns. They said he was safe. But he... when he talks, he says things that are not in his world. He names ships I've never heard of. He sings songs that were outlawed after the Quieting Acts."

That last line made a small bell ring in my chest that had nothing to do with the money I would make. Quieting Acts were older than me; they were the reason Remembrancers still existed. The Acts had been enacted after the first mass-loss event in the belts — something the government framed as necessary, the Reason for Erasures. People hadn't stopped asking why the belts ate people; they had simply been told it was safer to forget. You couldn't leave a child with a memory that told stories the law had decided were dangerous. It was easier to gut the past and sew something plain over the hole.

I asked the usual question: "What does Jonah know? Names, places, things he shouldn't—"

"He says the names like they are friends," the mother said. "He calls one of them 'Ikari'. He says Ikari showed him a room full of glass and told him how to listen with his teeth. He draws... this." She handed me Jonah's tin. "He drew this the night he came back."

The drawing had the awkward perspective of a child who had been taught to map sky to ground: a circle with teeth, marks like nails on the interior. There were coordinates written across the margin in a careful, adult hand — someone had traced over the child's trembling script. The coordinates weren't local. They referenced a sector on the ring outside the city, a stretch of the Null Belt people called the Sleeper's Spine.

I set the tin on the scan-reader and let the lace do its little humming thing. The lace wanted permission; so did Jonah. He watched it like you watch a stranger pick up your keys. He twitched when I ran the consent sequence and then, small as a cat, he looked at me and asked the thing that always comes before the work:

"Do you have a name?" he asked. He wasn't being charming. He wanted a label to place on the body across from him, and that vulnerability — the thing that says you are asking someone to enter your interior — makes some clients unable to look up.

"Naya," I said. "I'll do what I can."

He laced his fingers through his mother's and then, like a child testing the pressure of water, he held out his hand above the lace. Finger-prints tell us less about people than they used to; the lace reads the shadow-prints, the little echoes left on the skin from things you've touched. Jonah's shadow-print pulsed like a mollusk's shell under stress. It had been near energy. It had been near metal shaped by hands that didn't belong to the city. The lace purred at that, like a cat that smells tuna.

I threaded the needle.

Memory work is not cinema. It is not a flash, a superimposed image. It is a long, patient combing of thread through hair. You follow the pattern where it gives. Sometimes you follow it right into the mouth of things you do not want. You have to remind yourself that these are the client's memories, not yours. You must not fall asleep. You must not answer.

The first image came as acrylic cold: a ceiling not meant for eyes. Jonah shifted, and the needle traced the micro-movements of his knees. The ceiling held lines like ribs and a machine hung from it like a slow, patient thing. Light was not from any sun; it was from a lattice of bioluminescent rods which pulsed with a rhythm that made bones ache if you listened too long. Jonah's memory clung to the rods like mold.

He was in a corridor that smelled like battery acid and baked salt. Voices came as fragments: a name shouted, then a laugh that had teeth made of metal. The name repeated: Ikari. The sound meant nothing in my city; in other places it meant something like leader, or shipwright, or curse — the context was wrong.

I moved through the lace as one moves through a crowd with a purpose. The needle tugged at a set of images that didn't belong together: a child's hand held by a gloved adult hand then a flash of windscreen splintering like thought, then a part of a room I knew because I had once lived near its blueprint: a maintenance bay at Dock Twelve where my mother used to do contract wiring. The shape of a panel, the particular gouge at the third rivet. My chest went tight.

I told myself it was an associative slip. The mind stitches to what's known. The needle kept feeding me the rivet. It kept feeding Jonah's small thumbprint pressed into blue paint. The rivet had been chewed by tools that left a certain white filament — the filament I had once collected and kept in a glass vial no bigger than a fingernail. I had it in my cabinet, wrapped in a 3D-printed handkerchief, wrapped because it was foolish to keep anything that could be read as a breadcrumb.

I asked Jonah, reflexively, "Who was on the other side of the panel?"

He whispered something like a name and then, for the first time since the lace had attached itself, he said it slowly and like a man speaking through a mouthful of marbles: "Naya."

The room turned cold.

The mother made a small sound that might have been a cough. Jonah's eyes found mine. The lace hummed, obligingly, and the needle kept carving.

"That's not possible," she said. "You don't know—"

I did not answer. The word had been the wrong color, the wrong weight. It had slipped out of his mouth like a key and it fit a lock I had long told myself had no teeth left.

When the images finally surrendered, they were not the tidy linear things the clinics like to sell in their brochures. They were fractured, like the glass of a windshield you attempt to see through after a crash. I pieced them back together on my screen: Jonah standing in front of a panel, Jonah being lifted, Jonah's hand stained in blue paint, Jonah cupping something that glowed like a small sun. Then, in an angle the child couldn't have known, a darker flash I recognized by habit — a locket, old style, rimmed in brass, with the engraving of a spiral that I had seen on my own key.

I pressed my thumb to the drawer under my desk and felt the cold of my own keepsake against my skin. The room had three breaths now: my own, Jonah's, and the lace which purred like a satisfied animal.

"Why would Jonah remember you?" the mother asked. Her voice had gone from pleading to very, very small. "He was nine. You—"

"You shouldn't ask why," I told her, because I'm built to be blunt at the edges. "Memories don't owe us explanation. They are sediment."

She folded down like bad paper. "What does he remember? Will it hurt him to—"

"No." I said it because the clinic's scarring had been done. "But there are things he could tell us that the clinics cannot. The Quieting Acts didn't erase everything. They only eroded what was visible."

Jonah, who a moment before had been a child spooning attention like a warm soup, went very still. His eyes turned inward, and the lace shivered. The last image that came to me was not Jonah's; it was a room made of glass and light and a sound like teeth scraping against porcelain. In the center a machine hummed and a plate flashed coordinates. The coordinates were the same as the ones on the tin. They were for a stretch of the Sleeper's Spine, sector F-7, where ships go to die and sometimes don't die at all.

"Then—" the mother's voice went thin with an advantage that comes to people who think they've found a lever. "Then you can tell us where these coordinates lead. You can get him back what he lost."

There are many levers in this world. Most of them turn just enough to spill the same old water into the same old buckets. But there are other levers that turn and do not want to be turned. They open doors with hinges that have rusted for a reason.

I did not tell her I already knew the name of the ship recorded in the background of Jonah's memory. I did not tell her the spiral on my own key matched, by a measurement as precise as a lover's lie, the engraving on the ship's docking plate. I didn't tell her because the sentence that followed in my own head — a child I might have once been, a woman who had a name before names were stripped — was a shape I wasn't ready to hand over.

Instead I reached for the contract-slips and the one that warms my palm when I'm about to do something I might rue later. I set them between us and slid the tin into Jonah's waiting hands.

"Bring me everything he has," I said. "Leave me with what he touched. And don't tell anyone you came."

Jonah looked at me and smiled with a mouth that had teeth too clean for a child who'd been in the belts. "You have a key," he said finally, pointing, and it wasn't a question.

He was right. I did. I had a key that had lived longer than it should have in a city that forgot the reason for its existence. It fit doors I had never seen. It had been the sort of thing a child could mistake for an ordinary prize.
