When I reached under the desk and drew out the little brass spiral, Jonah's eyes narrowed with a knowledge that made the room tilt like a ship beginning to punch its nose into a storm. Outside the window the city was a smear of traffic and distant, impossible day. Inside we were a breath away from somewhere older than any law.

"Do you remember me?" Jonah asked, at last, in a voice that had the hardness of someone who has been given a blade to hold.

I put the key in my palm and felt its teeth, the cold, the perfect, impossible fit. It had been in my life longer than the city had allowed. It hummed, very faintly, like a lark just under hearing.

"Not yet," I said, because truth is a useful lie. "But I will.

"There's a place in the Spine," I added, the name slipping out before I could sheath it. "A ship called the Ikari. If Jonah can remember it, it's because something there remembers him. If something remembers him, then it might remember me."

Outside the window, the sky over the ring was a spare blue that had no patience for small people and smaller deals. Inside my studio, Jonah held my name like proof, like a breadcrumb pushed into a mouth that will not clean itself.

When the mother left — paperwork completed, her hand squeezed mine in an old, transactional comfort — she did not look at the key. Jonah watched me until the door was closed and the lock clicked, and then, from the center of the room, he said, as if to confirm something between us:

"Ikari doesn't forget."

I do not like being forgotten. For a lot of reasons that go back to my child's teeth and my mother's hands and a secret port where the metal is warm to touch, forgetting has been a luxury I've never been able to afford. I collect memories like a counterfeiter collects small bills: carefully, with an eye to the edges.

This job could buy food for a month. It could buy new plants to fill the empty corners of my studio. It could also open a door that had been shut for a very long time.

I put the key back in the drawer and closed the lid slowly, as if it were a coffin, as if it were a chest. Then I turned to Jonah and said what the contract needed and what I had not yet decided on.

"Bring me the sweater," I said. "And whatever else he's kept in his pockets. If Ikari doesn't forget, then maybe it remembers why you were taken. And if it remembers, then—"

My voice stopped where I didn't want it to. The lace hummed, and in that vibration there was a world of things I could no longer pretend not to know.

Outside, the Null Belt chewed on the edge of the city's reasonable light. Inside, a child with a mouth full of impossible names pressed his palm against the tin and watched the spiral on my key as if it were a sun about to rise.

They called it Shoreline because names had to sound ordinary to pass the scanners. The label was printed in a neat serif on the thin slate of data Anya held between thumb and forefinger—shoreline.mnem—and under it the Archive had stamped three approval bands: sanitized, non-hazardous, permitted for modification. She knew how those bands tasted: like lacquer and coin. She could feel the threads of them when she skimmed the surface with her gloves, the same way she could feel the pliability of a lie when she brushed against it.

Inside the tasting chair the studio smelled of ozone and lemon oil. Light bands slid under her skin and mapped her cortex in a language of levers and currents. The chair was older than the market it serviced; its cushioning had been replaced with someone’s memories of Japanese rice fields, but it still hummed with the same steady confidence as a man who has not yet learned to be afraid. Anya signed the consent with a breath and the chair took her in.

The client had paid in credit and quiet—enough to clear the last of Rian's injections and enough to buy a week without debt collectors breathing down her neck. That was what kept her fingers steady. Money made her amendments simple: strip the guilt, soften the edges, add a smell that made the lie believable. She made silhouettes of impossibilities into rooms where a rich man could tidy them away in the evening and sleep without nightmares.

She expected the Shoreline file to be a tidy job: coastal promenade, gulls, a first kiss on a pier. Instead, as the chair's filaments read and fed, the memory came into her—not as a scene but as a tide. It rolled across her mind with a pressure that made her teeth ache. It carried with it the metallic tang of something that was not sea but engine, the fizz of static like a radio tuned between stations. There was a child's laugh—too high, full of salt and fear—and then the sky folding.

There are some images human minds are not designed to hold. The sky folding was one of them. It was not the sky bursting into stars or a hole yawning open; it was a surface, a skin that crumpled like paper and creased, revealing a wrongness underneath: a lattice that glowed faintly with unhuman geometry, edges that hummed notes outside the scale. The memory narrated it in one clean motion—the city on a shore whose map did not exist, a tower like a blade, a light the color of lab-grown sapphires, and then the falling.

Anya snapped the tasting shut, and the studio light flooded back like someone blowing a match. She let the afterimages bleed out and sat, palms damp against the chair's fabric. The archivist on the other side of the glass—the one with the teeth-work smile they all wore as a uniform—leaned forward and asked, "How much of the shore do you want?" almost conversationally, like they were discussing wallpaper.

"I didn't extract it," she said. Her voice was steadier than she felt. "It came in already."

You were not supposed to taste without permission. To handle live artifacts—memories that contained nonhuman patterns or unidentified stimuli—was to gamble with contagion: the way certain images could cascade, the way a falsity could outbreed truth inside a mind. The Archive's rules were clear. If a file looked anomalous, you quarantined it, logged it, and handed it to the Bureau of Cognitive Safety. No one had the freedom to decide otherwise.

The archivist's hands hovered over the console. Her expression changed—the professional blank thinning into interest, then something sharper. "Run it through the filter stack," she said. "Anomaly profiles, novelty index, contamination scan. Tag it, Hash it, stamp it."

Anya watched the bands as the studio processed the memory: a green flare, then amber, then a red that made her stomach drop. Contamination: positive. Pattern: foreign lattice elements detected. Origins: undetermined. The system offered the usual mitigations—sterile excision, cognitive blots—but beneath the printed advice a secondary line pulsed, like a mosquito against the glass: ARCHIVE HAZARD ID: CLASS V. HANDLE WITH BUREAU.

Class V was a polite way of saying go home and forget you ever touched it.

But the memory had pressed against her in the chair; it had left smudges under her nails. She could still feel the residue of the child's laugh, like a shape that didn't belong in her hand. The studio tech filled out the forms with the deliberation of someone enacting bone surgery: correct, measured, not too curious. She turned to Anya, and when she smiled there was something almost like pity in it.

"You shouldn't have tasted it," she said.

"I didn't choose to." Anya's reply was thin as rem strips. "It was in the client's package."

The client's package was a sealed vault in the upper world where money and memory met. You only ever touched it if you had to. The person who paid for Shoreline had not wanted to be seen. His credits burned all the way to the ledger and left a trail of warm neglect—the way generosity looks when it's not about kindness. He had given no name. He had given an address anchored in the old quarter of the city, and the consent was signed by a voice that could have been a signal.

"Log everything," the tech said. "We forward to the Bureau." She paused, then, as if deciding whether to add something kind, murmured, "And don't scrub your own implants clean. Let them fade naturally. Always better that way."

Anya left with a copy of the incident file stamped with bureaucratic certainty and a mouth that tasted of iron. Outside the studio the wind on the archipelago moved as if it had not heard the sky fold. The city—Span—hung on great filaments above an ocean that was mostly corporate farms and dark water where old cables sank like ropes to the bottom of the world. Span pulsed with net-traffic and washing-machine light. Markets clung to the sides of the platforms like barnacles. Neon words promised everything from clean water to clean dreams.

She walked the walkways with her hands shoved in her jacket, the aroma of noodle steam and grease in her nose. A child in a red scarf chased a drone and laughed, the sound bright and greedy. An old man sold memory-scraps in a brazier—tiny vignettes burned onto resin beads like prayer tokens. It was an ordinary evening in an extraordinary city. But every so often, when the light struck the hair at the nape of her neck, she felt the folded-sky image prickle like static.

Rian was in the clinic two blocks from their flat, hooked to a slow-release pump that put his tremors at bay and his mind in a fog that kept the worst of his memories distant. He had been a cartographer before the tremors took his hands. Now the maps he drew were simple loops of the same three streets, the kind of art that can be folded into a napkin. Anya sent a message ahead: running late. The answer came: bring something nice.

She had nothing that bright. She had one of the old memory beads she had traded in for cash three weeks earlier. It was a simple thing—a market sunrise over the Jurek bridges—and it wouldn't mean anything to Rian. He liked bridges. He liked the idea of crossing.

At the corner an advertisement dissolved into a person. A woman stood on a platform selling cures in a voice like polished wood. Her suit reflected the city's levels—slowwealth, not so slowwealth, the top where light bent best. She was older than the spots of gray in her hair, the kind of person who had been allowed to forget what desperation smelled like. She moved across the walkway like an algorithm that knew exactly when to charm and when to withhold.

Anya let herself be charmed. She listened to the cure-seller's pitch about memory elegance—the scent of jasmine in a newly cleaned apartment, the hum of a lover's voice cut down to the right pitch. The woman smiled and reached for her and Anya thought about handing over the Shoreline file. It was a thought dangerous and bright, like a match in a hayloft. She shook it and shifted away.

Rian's apartment smelled like boiled cabbage and mint. The pump hissed; its lines were a little sticky with saline. He looked at her with an artist's poverty of statement: eyes that cataloged everything but told you nothing. He hadn't been able to keep a job after the tremors changed his     handwriting. He had lost his clearance for map reserves. He spent the day looking for lines in clouds and pretending they were useful.

"Did you bring something?" he asked. He had the pocket of his robe rolled down like a sympathetic magnet for stolen warmth.

"I brought a sunrise," Anya said, and she put the resin bead between his fingers.

He turned it and cried once, quietly, like someone who didn't want to train his breath into attention. "You shouldn't be taking those jobs," he said after a moment, more to the sound of the pump than to her.

"I don't choose them." She kept the studio's red stamp in her mind like a burn mark. "I didn't even want to taste it."

"You tasted something," he said.

"You don't know the difference between what you are given and what you keep."

Rian's laugh was small and rusty. "Yes I do," he said. "I keep you."

That used to have the effect on her it had on everyone else: a softening, a tired euphoria that smoothed the edges of worry. Tonight she felt the words inside a loop and they didn't come as warmth as they used to. The memory of the folding sky had set up a current in her that tugged at everything else. It wanted context. It wanted extension. It wanted to be looked at by more than a single set of human eyes.

She pulled up the client file on the pad in the gloom. The address had been an old node behind licensed corporeal units: a storage locker in Level B-17, sector of the old tech beneath the docks. The ledger listed a single, anonymous purchase, two hours ago, from a credit closed and reopened in under a minute. The signature was a composite key that resolved to a corporate subsidiary no one paid attention to anymore. The Archive's stamp glowed in the corner of the pad: FORWARDED TO BUREAU OF COGNITIVE SAFETY.

She should have let it go. She should have stayed the course. The law was a web you didn't poke from the edges. The Bureau didn't like piety from amateurs.

Instead she found herself standing on a ladder of decisions and reaching for one rung further. The map of the old docks was a relic on the net, a faded image that smelled like oil and salt and the worse days of the city's early growth. She copied the coordinates into a quiet channel and watched the pad pulse back at her, eager, like a ferret.

The truth: she had a file in her private bank that she hadn't registered. Not the client's file—something else. Right before the studio sealed the Shoreline they had offered an optional scrub: to remove the taste that sometimes lingered. Anya had declined. She had told them she didn't want the sterile forgetting. Out of habit, or bravado, or because part of her liked to keep a little of the world in sharpness. She had a copy—no, a sliver, a knot of data that slid like a stone into her private mesh. She had not told anyone. Not the archivist, not Rian.

On the pad, the dock's coordinates pulsed like a heart. She tapped the pad once. The path lit up: a walk through the old rail tunnels, a climb under a shipping crane, a gap walked over by people who had once been smugglers and still were, lyrically. The pad warned her: ADVISORY—UNREGISTERED ACCESS. The same old refrain. She clicked through anyway.

As she left Rian and climbed into the misting stair, she felt the memory's edges as if it were a cold draft under a door. The child laughed again, low and close. Above the city, the neon that spelled out promises blinked in conversation: REMEMBER THIS, REMEMBER THAT. For once they said nothing.

At the dock a single light glinted on a crate. Crates were the city's grammar for things people had decided to forget—things too heavy to carry, too precious to throw away. She wore her jacket with its inner pockets emptied of shame. The file in her hand was a weak star, a sliver. She fed it through her deck and watched it bloom on the pad: a tower, sharp as a spinning blade, reflected in water that shouldn't have been there; a child running along a boardwalk that was new to the map; a sky folding at the seam like a curtain being drawn.

You could keep a lie if you liked the feel of it. You could keep a memory because it fit a shape your life was missing. Or you could keep it because you believed it was true.

She walked closer to the crate. Someone had already fingered the latch recently; the metal was warm. She lifted the lid. Inside, packed with sponges and paper towels, lay a small, sealed cylinder of opaque material. It was not marked with a label and yet when she touched it with a gloved finger the cylinder hummed, like something recognizing her.

There are moments you watch like a scientist. There are moments you watch like a thief. Anya was both. She opened her palm and there, cold and vibrating like a tiny heart, was a bead. Not the market beads, with their naive scenes, but one that carried a sound: a low keening that didn't belong to human throatings. It had no author, no client, no stamped permission. Inside it curled an image like a fossil of the sky folding, waiting.

Behind her, the night flurried. Above, Span pulsed. And somewhere inside the city, the Archive filed its reports and the Bureau drew their nets. On Anya's pad a message blinked, anonymous: WE DREAMT AGAIN.

The writing in the message was not language so much as invitation. She could bring it to the Bureau and watch the sky die into reports and redacted pages. She could hand it to the studio and let them burn it until no one remembered the taste. Or she could listen to the child's laugh echo inside the bead and let it map a path for her that had nothing to do with rules.

Her fingers closed around the bead. For a moment she relied on the old thought that had pushed her into the tasting chair to begin with—that one person could smuggle a small truth into the city and set it loose like a seed. Rian's pump ticked in her memory, the way the world ticked when you were waiting for an answer. She slid the bead into her inner jacket pocket and felt the fabric warm with it.

Behind her, somewhere in the levels, a siren began to talk in the far-off language of enforcement—the gentle chitter of a security drone clearing its throat. She should have run. She did not run.

The first rule of living with forbidden things is you tell yourself you will be careful. The second rule is you quickly discover which forbidden things do not like being locked up.

As she turned to go, the bead's low keening threaded into her ear like a memory remembering itself. It sang the child's laugh and a phrase that made the hair at the base of her skull stand up: "We remember now."

And then the night tightened, like a lid. Footsteps came awake on the dock.

She reached for the ladder back into the city and did not look down.

The first time I heard my sister die, she was laughing.

It wasn't the kind of laugh that made you feel lighter. It filled the room like a sound with weight; it bent the light in the archive and left a taste of copper in my mouth. I had heard it a dozen times, cataloged it, indexed it under "Sera—vocalizations—minor hysteria—age 27." As an editor at the Atlas of Lived Things, I lived inside other people's memories the way some people live in apartments. You learn not to confuse the furniture—this laugh was in someone else's living room, a public lease of sensation I could check out and shelve.

And then, at three-fifteen, in a lab that smelled of solder and ozone, the laugh came out of a thread no one had checked in on for twenty years, stamped with a tag that should not exist: NULL/RELINQUISHED/UNCLAIMED.

I held the filament between two insulated prongs until the archive's interface registered the filament as real—light spilled through it like a private storm. Threads were fragile things, recorded on polymer lace and bound with volatile ions; they were the only way the dead kept speaking. The Guild said we were caretakers. The Board said we were archivists. When you worked in the fifth stack, you called yourself whatever you needed to say before sleep.

"Standard intake, Isha?" Mara, at the next console, asked without looking up. She had the same tired lids as the rest of us, etched with the same city-light scars. Outside the dome, New Alexandria's mesh of transit tethers stitched the dark into a lattice of commerce and weather. The city hummed in frequencies we learned to tune out; inside the archive, silence was a preservation policy.

"No id, no origin," I said. "Raw lace. Just one filament."

Mara's fingers hovered over her keys, the gentle cloud of her exhale catching in the console's air sensors. "Nulls are like rats. They breed a lot and leave nothing but bites."

I laughed, a short reflexive thing. "Then we'd better find bait."

The filament's signature was wrong in every way a filament could be wrong. Most threads came with provenance: a name, a date, a sanction—sometimes a court order or a death certificate. This was stamped with the old Legion code, a hasty Gothic script used before the Collapse, before the Charter that consolidated memory property into corporate vaults. Whoever had bound this thread wanted someone to find it and to hide it at the same time.

I ran the usual scans anyway: spectral, temporal, authenticity filters. The archive hummed with compliant algorithms; they slid over the lace and told me it was genuine. Genuine in the way someone could be when the thing that defined them had eroded—a fossil of feeling.

"Pull a passive preview," Mara suggested, fingers drumming. She liked knowing other people's endings. Maybe it made her feel less surprised by her own.

I engaged the preview module. The filament unwound as sound and smell and light. Memory threads were multisensory, and most editors preferred to sanitize them into two-dimensional records—words, timestamps, static descriptors. I didn't. I liked being the kind of person who let the ocean at the edge of a client's memory wash over me once or twice, just to test whether the tide had turned.

Sera's laugh unfurled first, exactly as I remembered: a loose, bright thing that always had a tear under it. The preview cut like a breath into an atmosphere I hadn't inhabited for seven years. The smell that came with it was salt and hot metal and the faint, impossible smell of ozone that only the frontier platforms ever made when their shielding failed.

"Sera," I whispered to myself. The name scraped like a file over a wound. My sister had been one of the missing people of the Breach, one of the tiny blips the city had learned to ignore. We had held a memorial with lights and a list of names and then we had sworn off looking for her in raw threads. The Guild's policies were clear: no living grief, no resurrection. Memories could be traded, archived, used for legal reconstruction—but not resurrected for private excavation. They were property.

But property was a polite word. My sister had been property to the Vaults long before I was born; she had been an intern at the Eidolon Program, an experimental platform that had promised to peel reality into sterile, useful layers and sell the layers back as discovery packages. Eidolon had been declared a loss when a containment failure scoured its core. The city had eaten the cost and moved on.

We all moved on, but some of us picked up pieces on the side.

The preview advanced. Suddenly the salt-lined laugh fell away into darkness and what came instead was a zeroing sound—the way gravity sounds when a machine forgets it's supposed to hold you. Then Sera's voice again, cut and raw. "Isha," she said. It was a whisper that rummaged through me like a hand.

I checked the overlays—the waveform, the harmonics, the micro-annotative stress markers we used to identify speakers. It matched. Sera's unique harmonic imprint was like a thumbprint in the archive: a particular tremor in the vocal cords that translated into a half-step at the end of her sentences. Whoever had recorded this had recorded her.

The dart of the memory landed.

"You okay?" Mara said. Her voice bridged the distance between us and the observation dome beyond, where the city glowed like a circuit in the dark. "You went pale."

"I—" I couldn't say it. Saying that Sera was alive in here would be the same as promising myself the impossible. "Log it. Tag it 'undetermined provenance' and file it for restricted review. We run that through Senior."

Mara raised an eyebrow. I saw the moment she calculated the risk—if this was an error, reporting it would send auditors and lawyers and procedural disinfectors into the stack. If it wasn't, they would take it away. The Board loved tidy solutions.

"Your call," she said. She meant the real thing: the ocean-sensed moment where you chose to follow a thread or to cut it and pretend you hadn't seen its light.

This time, I did not put it in a file. I disengaged the audit trace and pulled the whole filament in—my hands moving before my brain finished an argument with itself. The filament wound around my fingers like a pulse. Pulling an unregistered thread from the stack without authorization was a felony. You didn't lose your career for that, you lost the map to your city-subsistence. But I had lost something else, too: a small person who had been the center of my careful little orbit.

I slotted the filament into my jacket's inner pocket and felt the warmth of it against my ribs. It answered me like a small animal under my skin, like a secret about the shape of the world that only I had been offered.

"You're burning the reel," Mara said softly. "If the detectors pick that up—"

"My sister is in there, Mara."

Sera's face inhaled into me again. The memory had a scene that the preview had refused to show: a corridor with a ceiling like ribs, lights running like stitches. There were hands—Sera's hands, thin and callused from the tools she favored—and a slate screen with characters scrolling that no longer existed in our modern alphabets. Sera's mouth formed words I couldn't understand. Then she said a thing in plain language, a line that detonated the air around me:

"Remember the hollow star."

She spoke it twice, as if to make sure someone would remember once the rest disintegrated.

Memory threads were fragile against compression and translation. All sorts of noise and interference could fold into them—old encryption, collapsed metadata, even foreign agency interference. But that phrase had no artifact around it. It had been recorded clean, emphasized in the waveform like someone had put a hand around the mic and pressed hard to make the syllables clear.

Hollow star. The phrase made my mouth close on a dozen impossible associations. Eidolon was named for a ghost, an echo. There were stars that hollowed themselves into Dyson remnants and planets stripped to fractions; there were also the small private stars the wealthy carved out in superstructure rings—places you could exile a secret to and let it fester in silence. None of those was supposed to speak to me.

Because Sera had been noted as lost in the Breach seven years ago. Corpse unknown. Vault closed. And yet here she was, in my hands, like a fact that had rearranged itself.

I checked the archive's window; the city outside had finally become awake in some parts, the morning tethers flaring. The dome dimmed for a second, a sigh as the grid rebalanced to meet demand. The archive's internal AI, Archivist, was a good listener and an obedient cat. It sniffed anomalies and left them curled by the storerooms in pairs. I had never actually been admonished by it; the reprimands in the archive were usually human and contained fewer circuits.

Someone else was paying attention to my interface.

A notification flashed at the corner of my peripheral HUD. Quick, bright. Unscheduled: Access attempt—stack 5—thread ID: NULL/RELINQUISHED/UNCLAIMED. Suspicion: elevated.

I should have erased my fingerprints from the console, should have reseated the filament back into the slot and re-locked the transfer lock. I didn't. Part of me was a wiring diagram of stubborn circuits: if you give me a place with loose screws, I will unscrew them until something interesting happens.

"You're about to get hauled into Committee," Mara said.

"Then add it to my file," I muttered. "Maybe I'm due."

There are things you do for grief that are not rational. You follow drip lines in basements. You open boxes you promised not to. You unscrew light fittings in spaces that used to hold other people's hair. Some grief is a practical, domestic thing: you scrape in the corners until the thing that bit you, or the absence of the thing, has to reveal itself. Today, grief had an interface and a law.

I was halfway down the central stair into the stack when the dome's external speakers crackled and a voice—flat, high, corporate—called our section number. "Attention, Atlas Fifth. Please prepare for scheduled audit. All active clients to be logged."

People's shoulders went small, like animals under attack. Mosaic lights in the stack cooled into inspection blue. The Archivist started to hum a note of compliance. If they came now, they would find the filament missing. They might trace the missing signature to my console. They might open my file. They might ask about the day Sera disappeared in ways I did not want to answer.

I kept walking anyway.

My feet took me past storage bays I knew by the patterns of dust on their handles, past a mural someone had painted years ago—an abstract of hands and wires that older archivists insisted was a good luck charm. The stack's air tasted of old paper and new rubber. The door at the back of the fifth was a maintenance exit that opened onto the city's underside: conduits and service platforms that smelled like hot grease and colder stars. People used it to smuggle things, to meet in the hidden hours when the overseers slept.

I had one contact in the underside, a woman named Kade who owed me a favor for reasons I didn't care to remember. Kade had a small ship with a name you could fit a fist around—The Bargain. She trafficked in small risks and, more importantly, in routes. People like me learned to value routes above names. Names could be bought; routes could be trusted.

The stairs dropped me into the underside's light. Ahead, a plasma cart hummed by with a load of blue-cold storage canisters. The tunnel curved. There was an unremarkable door painted matte black—Kade's mark. I should have hesitated. I didn't. Habit had a weight and it kept me moving.

The Bargain smelled of engine oil and rosemary. Kade was smaller in person than I expected, as if she had spent her youth trying to compress herself into a space the world would find more convenient to accept. She looked at the filament in my hand like someone who had been offered the wrong end of a deal and was trying to be polite about it.

"You brought an old ghost to my berth," she said. "You got a death wish or a plan?"

"A plan," I said. I set the filament between us like a pawn on a table. It glowed faintly, as if remembering the light.

Kade examined it with a lens that made the lace look larger than God. Her fingers tapped the edge of my palm.

"Null-coded," she murmured. "That's... not a common thing to pick up loose. People don't leave ghost tags around here unless they want someone to find them. People who plant Nulls usually are trying to be found."

"Including me," I said.

Kade's face smoothed. "So you want Eidolon."

The word landed like a key. Kade's eyes flicked away then came back, the way a survivor checks a map and then looks up to see if the ceiling matches the map's legend. Eidolon was a dead program, but dead things have ways of moving through history. "There are rumors," she said. "There are always rumors. The Board closed the accounts, but rumors are not in their ledger to close. You know what this costs?"

"Everything," I said. It was the honest answer.

She smiled, small and sharp. "Then we have our terms."

We hammered out the terms the only way cities like ours knew how: currency and favors and the faint smell of mutual desperation. The Bargain would take me to a vector outside the system's mapped transit flows, beyond the sanctified lanes. The cost was a stash of my saved hours—time credits I'd been hoarding against a future I had not allowed myself to imagine. Kade wanted those, in part because the economy loved time the way the faithful love ritual.

I sealed the trade. There was a moment as the pact signed itself across the Bargain's ledger that felt like the hinge of a door opening. If I had closed my eyes, I would have heard a whisper: do not.

But the filament in my pocket was warm against my ribs and pulsed like a tether. Sera's voice had said remember, not forget. I had always been a person who practiced remembering for other people. Today I practiced it for myself.

When I left Kade's berth, the city had pulled a sheet over its night and was starting the slow ritual of waking. The tethers flashed like eyelids, and a tram peeled away, carrying whole families to markets and to offices that would never know they had been touched by the hollow star's shadow. In my pocket the thread answered with a small, steady pulse—like a heart, like a compass.

Someone had put a memory into a place where no rules could find it. Whoever had done that wanted someone to pull it out. The someone I had become was not a person built for surrender.

On the tram, I cupped the filament with my free hand and let the city's light make it glow. Sera's laugh unspooled in my head again, and beneath it the words that had planted the seed of everything: remember the hollow star.

I watched New Alexandria pass by in the window like a city on a turning wheel. People moved in and out of the frame, lovers and thieves and children, all of them with their private perforations of memory, none of them with access to the thing I held. I was not supposed to go looking. The Board wanted neat archives and tidy grief. The Board wanted the missing to stay missing. I had always known that. I had also known how to break rules without becoming a cautionary tale.

The tram slid into the station, and the city took my breath away with its ordinances. I fitted my jacket tighter. I thought of a hollow star and of the way something could be hollow and still draw you inward. My hands tightened around the filament like a promise.

Behind me, the archive's hush was still active. The craft of forgetting is delicate. But some objects—a laugh, a phrase, a laced filament bearing the ghost of a sister—refused the neatness of forgetting.

Sera said remember. I had always been the kind who listened.

I stepped off the tram and into the morning. Somewhere in the meshes of orbit and time, a place named Eidolon waited with a shape like an empty promise. The filament hummed. The city kept its rules. I kept my hands. I kept walking toward the place where the hollow star might burn its light through the dark—or swallow us whole trying.

Either way, I had already heard her die. It was time I heard her tell me why.

They traffic in other people's yesterdays and call it medicine.

When my client dies on the table, the machines keep humming as if nothing changed. The room smells the way all extraction rooms do—ozone and lemon oil and the kind of antiseptic scent that pretends sterilization can put out a life like a candle. Outside, the city arches up into a permanent twilight of neon and cloud; inside, under the soft wash of the loom's light, a man had just stopped being a man.

He was ninety-three, if the forms were to be believed. He'd been propped in the chair like an exhibit piece: thick-lensed spectacles, a silk tie knotted with care, half the town's tax credits wired into a trust somewhere in a vault that wouldn't feel his absence until the auditors finished kvetching. They brought him to me because his daughter couldn't stand the thought of his worst memory being left in the family vault. She wanted it gone, like a stain you scrub from a shirt before sale. "A clean ledger," she told me. Clean in her mouth sounded like virtue.

I told her the procedure would take nine hours. She paid seven. She left me the balance in a paper envelope that smelled faintly of her perfume and guilt.

Weavers are supposed to be professionals. We are trained to tell the difference between grief and hazard, between the normal abrasiveness of human memory and the kind that chews through a mind if handled badly. We have disclaimers that look like old prayers and insurance policies that sit like bricks under the clinic desk. We stitch memories out with a loom—an optic ring the size of a coin and a spool of filament made from chromatene threads and scraped dreams. You put the ring to the temple and you listen until the thread catches something worth unspooling.

This one had a catch right away. The old man's pupil shadowed at the edge of the loom's readout, a tiny surging spike I could see in the waveform and feel like a tremor against my teeth. He wasn't having a single memory; he had an old knot of them, braided with something like...affection? No. Something more precise. A map. I can usually tell when I'm in over my head; this pulled at one of my older knots—something professional and electric—and I told myself, Good, be careful. That's the sound of competence.

Then the heart monitor stopped.

It wasn't dramatic. No great flatline wail, no emergency lights. One keen little beep and the other instruments went slack. His chest lay still under the hospital blanket, like a road emptied of traffic. His daughter made a sound—not a sob, not a scream, but a long single inhale that held too much air. She clutched at the back of a chair as if she could brace the room. I kept my hands on the loom.

Protocol says: if the subject dies during an extraction, you stop and seal. You log. You call the clinic director. You make notes. You don't keep going. People read the policy and sign them in a neat, calming hand. Practically, however, you park your ethics next to your livelihood. In nine years I had stopped counting how often policy and survival had parted ways. I did my job for the fee, for rent, for my sister's oxygen tabs. So I palmed the loom to the old man's temple and told myself I would be careful.

When he died, something else woke up in his head.

It started like the way light spills through blinds at dawn, only colder—wet and metallic. A wind with the smell of salt, but not ocean salt; something older and acid-bright. The memory bled through the loom and it wasn't one image but a stadium of them—faces that weren't faces, a skyline of vertical light that refracted like splintered glass, a humming architecture that moved like a living animal. A child's laugh, high and full, braided through the sound of distant bells. The loom readout lit up in a way I have learned to fear: a neat ladder of spikes ascending into a pattern I knew from warnings and classified training slides. There was a symbol in the upper quadrant, one I'd seen carved into drift-scrap in a museum once, a ring with three axes like a skewer through a fruit. The symbol felt like a key; the memory felt like a locked door suddenly pressing open.

"Stop," his daughter said.

I did not. I had my hand on a half-finished extraction and a spool full of creditor names. There is also another thing—curiosity, and the way it can smell of need. Memories are addictive the way sugar and danger are: they taste like salvation. I threaded the spool with the loom and coaxed the memory outward. Images arranged themselves on the loom's ocular, hesitant at first and then with the merciless clarity of someone who hasn't used filters. The child's voice named a place the old man's tongue couldn't hold: "Lumen," it said, and the name folded into the skyline like a house into a street of houses.

You learn over time that other people's memories are not entertainment. They are freight. They weigh. This one was freight with a cargo hold door open.

The loom sang—a note low enough to sit behind the ribs—and I felt the room slide sideways. For a heartbeat I was not in the clinic but under a sky with a sun so pure it made the air taste like copper. I was somewhere that had weather like the inside of a machine and water that did not know it wanted to be sea. There were buildings like the inside of clocks and people with skin like paper-thin metal. A child held out a hand and a thread of light slid into the palm, and the child winked with an eye like a camera and said, "Come."

My hand tightened on the loom because the single, irresistible fact of the memory was: it was not a private thing. It carried coordinates—of a sort. Looms don't generally carry coordinates. They carry textures and scent cues and emotion markers. This thing had a lattice of angle and measure beneath the human veneer, the geometry of place, and when the geometry folded itself around my spinal column it looked, absurdly, like a map of the Ring.

The Ring: a sliver of infrastructure that circled our system like a cheap halo. Mostly myth, mostly salvage and half-legal settlements, the Ring was a scattering of habitats and shards of industry and dead elevators. People said it was a silver chain left by the Ancients, a tool, a trap, a fortune-teller's pulley. The old man's memory folded into that shape like a glove. When it did, some three-degrees-of-separation thing in me woke.

"You can't keep that," his daughter said.

She meant the money I hadn't yet taken. I turned and saw the urgency in her face; she looked younger, less like the person who had signed the consent forms and more like someone who'd been reached, at last, by the shadow of private grief. She came forward like she might snatch the loom from me. Her breath was small and hot and human in a room that had been hearing the wrong kind of futures.

"I'll log it," I said. I was lying. Nobody logs the sort of thing that eats you like that. The company doesn't want the bad press, and there are regulatory holes big enough to bury a city in. You cook the books, you hide the oddities, you sleep with your head on a pillow full of quiet.

She didn't argue. She left without the envelope. She pressed her palm to the old man's shirt and looked like she might kiss him. Then she left, and the door slid shut behind her. The clinic fell back into a quiet that was, perversely, heavier for the human absence.

I eased the loom's spool to the receiving cradle. The readouts weren't a coherent narrative so much as a braid of impressions. Nodes. Bridges. A child's name. A ring. An instruction—faint, like a child's whisper caught in a stormwind: Don't take it to the light.

"What does that even mean?" I asked aloud, which is stupid because memories don't answer back.

The loom answered anyway. Not in words, not with a voice, but with a depth-of-field image that sat in my head like a second sight: a room with a window, beyond which the Ring hung like a constellation and, set against its arc, a light that was too bright and wrong. A machine, maybe. Or a consequence. The old man, younger now, stood before it like a pilgrim who'd reached a shrine and couldn't decide whether to kneel or to run.

And then the heart monitor recorded a sharp little artifact—an electrical ripple the likes of which I hadn't seen on an extraction in years—and the loom stuttered. A sound at the clinic door, too soft to be a footfall but too regular to be a rat. My scalp prickled. I cut the loom feed and the world snapped back with the sting of having been dunked in cold water.

The loom spit the spool into the cradle like it had decided on its own that this transaction was over. The spool held a memory like a core sample—tight and wrung and humming with something. You can erase most memories back in the labs. You can bleach and burn and stretch until the image becomes a rumor. This one resisted. I tried the standard process: decomposition, sentiment filter, an acid I use like a carpenter uses a chisel. The memory kept folding back into itself. It refused to become less. It wasn't just resilient; it was organized.

That's when the door opened.

He stood in the doorway with his hands empty and his head tilted in a manner of evaluating a theft he hadn't yet decided whether to commit. Black, all of him—black coat, black hair, a smile that sat wrong on his face like a borrowed thing. He smelled of old copper and motor oil, and he had the look of someone who'd lived two lives and been impatient with both. He shut the door behind him carefully, like locking a note into a safe.

"You shouldn't have seen that," he said.

There are things you expect to hear when someone confronts you about a theft. "Hand it over." "Do you know what you have?" "Do you know what you took?" But "You shouldn't have seen that" was intimate in the wrong way. It suggested the man on the doorstep knew whatever the memory contained and had an interest in it staying secret.

I kept my hands on the loom like an animal that wants to appear still, not because I was afraid of him—though I was—but because the spool in the cradle hummed against my palm like a heart with bad news. "Who are you?" I asked. The question sounded worse than the answer would have been.

He smiled again and took a step into the room like someone entering a house he'd paid off to forget him. He didn't answer in a way that soothed. He answered by setting his palm on the clinic counter and saying, "You don't know how lucky you are, Weaver."

Lucky is not how I felt. Lucky feels like coins clinking. Luck feels like a hand you can take. This felt like a door slipping closed behind me, and on the other side, the Ring hummed, and something like a child's voice promised things that would make blood ill. The man in black leaned in, his face close enough that I could see two tiny scars at the corner of his right eye, like the chevrons of someone who'd been assigned ranks he never earned.

"If you keep that," he said, "people will come."

There are quiet threats and loud ones. This was the quiet kind, the suffocating sort that doesn't bother with noise. People will come. He didn't need to enumerate which people. In a city that runs on other people's histories, there is always someone whose whole life is built on retrieving what another person has accidentally found.

Outside, the city continued to glow as if the night didn't care which dangers walked its streets. Inside, the spool hummed, and somewhere inside the old man's head a child laughed and a ring held a light that shouldn't be, and I had just decided—unwillingly or not—that I was part of whatever map that made.

I don't sell the past. I rent it, one perfect hour at a time.

People come to me when they've had enough of owning the future. They want the ache of a mother's hands for an afternoon, the exact warmth of a first kiss, the way a harbor looked before the tides learned to glow. They tuck those hours into their implants for a night or a week, then give them back, clean as a returned dress. My cut is the work of making the borrowed feel like home. I splice. I smooth. I remove the loose threads that would give the lender nightmares.

Helix Station looks like a tangle of thoughts: a ring of living quarters, a fractal of labs, and at its center the Palimpsest—a thing that eats names and coughs up other people's yesterdays. People trust the Palimpsest to remember what they ask it to, and when it hiccups it throws the whole orbital court into a scandal. Which means opportunities for someone like me.

I have a storefront three levels down from a hydrofarm and two doors past a clinic that still bills in analogue. My neon sign is honest in the only way small signs ever are: a single word, burned clean into polymer, MEND. It's a lie half the time. "Mend" suggests repair. I alter. I rearrange. Repair implies consent.

This morning the rain on Helix smells of copper and old wire. We don't get clouds anymore; what falls from the sky is condensation from the cooling loops, and it takes a city to extract the romantic out of that. A courier left a case on my threshold, an ugly black thing that ticks like a heart in a jumping suit. The courier had no name on his patch. I paged his carrier and left the box on the counter where glass and metal could keep it calm.

Inside the case there was a single thread spool, a thing of woven light you'd mistake for fog if you couldn't see the intervals. The spool hummed with an undercurrent, rich and patient. When I touch a thread I feel the person who stitched it: expertise or clumsy fingers, hands that knew instrument or hands that knew only knives. This one felt...old in a way my instruments couldn't index. Like the memory had been waiting in a dark place for someone to find the right song.

Clients sometimes want something richly ordinary—laughter in a kitchen from a culture that's been eaten by years, the grit of sand that used to have no microplastics. Those are worth a pittance. Rare are the threads that are forbidden, wrong, or impossible. Forbidden is usually flagged by the Palimpsest itself; wrong is what happens when someone forges a past. Impossible—that's what you keep quietly if you want to eat well and sleep at an angle.

I coaxed the spool into the cradle, let it unwind across the luminous field, and set the relay to safety. I wear a tether when I do this, a thing that straps the back of my skull to the chair and tells the Palimpsest where my cortex ends and where the borrowed memory begins. The tether is habit, not law—the law is the Palimpsest, and the Palimpsest is a bureaucracy with teeth.

The memory opened like a room already dressed for guests.

A child runs on the bank of a river I don't know. The water is a slow, glassy thing; the banks are wide and every stone holds sun like a tiny kept coin. And the air—God—this air carries the smell of fruit I had thought extinct, orange and green and wet, the smell of something alive enough to peel itself clean. Someone is laughing, high and small. The voice says a name I have not heard aloud since the wars that erased personal registries: Mara.

My chair forgets gravity for a fraction of a second. I clamp the tether tighter because panic is exactly the wrong tool with a foreign past coiling in your synapses. The name is not my legal name; I do not even use it among colleagues. But it is mine in the way thieves keep cursed things: possession by the lightest of touches.

I back the spool up. Memory stitching has rules, ritual. You wind, you map, you listen. You never, ever let a fragment touch the wrong cells without a fuse in your hand. The sensations remain, floating at the edge of me like fish just behind glass—too close to be comfortable.

Data readings come next. Every thread has metadata: origin node, custody chain, timestamp, a trail of where it has been. I expect a clean string: Helix-Palimpsest-ClientID. What blinks at me is a gap—the origin is labeled Archive-17, Dead Sector. Archive-17 hasn't been in the registry since the Kessan Riots when the Palimpsest flattened a quarantined wing for reasons still classified. Dead Sector means "do not touch" in every policy I've ever read.

The spool carries a signature too, a glyph like a thumbprint not in any script I know. It looks like a map of a spiral with a dot nested in one of its coils, the kind of thing kids scribble when they try to draw forever. I run the glyph through my private lexicon; nothing. I cross-check Helix network logs. Anomalies like that have a habit of lighting up like suns; this one is dim, like a star behind a cloud.

"Where did this come from?" I ask the room, because talking to empty shops is cheaper than calling a lawyer.

A small text pings on the side of my display, a scrubbed packet with no signature. It might be a prank. The message is two words and a time code: do you remember? 0724.

I don't answer. You don't answer strange messages when you have an impossible memory in your cradle. You do nothing until you know what the nothing will cost.

I play the thread again, slower. The child by the river is older in the second pass; shoes on the wrong feet, hair in the sun like a living halo. There's another voice now, low, an adult's, saying something in a language the Palimpsest flags as extinct. The translation shows up on my periphery like a post-it: "Mara—do not go to the city when the lights fall."

The warning tastes like iron in my mouth. It doesn't belong to me, but the syllables align against my teeth as if they'd been waiting there since before my birth.

Threads like this fetch fortunes on the black market. Memory brokers pay for "true" impossibilities: a child's claim to life on a non-existent planet, a soldier's recollection of a battle that never occurred, a love affair with someone who famously never left cryostasis. Collectors want relics. Corporations want leverage. Governments want leverage plus the trust of a populace that believes their past hasn't been propertized. The Palimpsest pretends it can keep those lines clear. The Palimpsest lies with the best of us.

I should have sealed the spool, logged it, and handed it over to the Palimpsest's compliance node. That is the story I'd tell my counsel. Instead I did what I always do when the world hands me a secret: I read it until it told me more.

Behind the child's laughter there is a sound like a ship's bell, metallic and slow in a place made for wind. The adult voice hums a lullaby I don't know and then hums another, layering them like a locksmith adding tumblers. At one point the child sings my name as if it were a coin they can spend to open a door. I can feel, absurdly, the texture of the name: it is rough as rope, warm as a palm.

Then the memory shudders. The child's hand reaches toward something off-camera, toward a light just out of frame, and the memory fractures into static. I yank the spool away like a hand burned by coals. The tether tastes of ozone.

You can be a thief of memories for a long time before you learn one brutal truth: the past is not always inert. Sometimes, if you listen carefully, it has a mouth and a plan.

The courier's case is still on the counter, its timer reset. No return address. No payment recorded. A small smudge of rust on the latch, as if the case had been in a place with seawater and old metal—my hands go cold at that texture. Helix is above sea now, floating in vacuum. Rust speaks of ships and places like that no longer exist.

I strip the spool into the station's sandbox, a dark mode for things you do not let into the public net. The sandbox is a ring of analog processors and a single handful of sanctioned neural shields. No outside access. No Palimpsest logging. You put things there when you intend to keep them un-lost.

The message pings again.

This time it's voice. The voice is small and untrained; it breaks often, like a signal from a transmitter on a failing battery. "Do you remember the river?" it asks. There is static under the question, an undertone like someone listening through a wall.

"Who are you?" I say, because I have to sound casual, because the last time someone asked me that question in the middle of a quiet shop it ended with a warrant and a fine.

"Do you remember?" The voice answers. "Your hands—did you forget what held the spoon? Did you forget the name I taught you, Mara? Did they make you forget?"

The voice knows my name. It knows the name that is not on my registry but sits in a drawer behind everything else. Panic claws. I should call Palimpsest. I should call the station's security. Instead I ask the only question that seems to exist between us.

"Why me?"

There is a pause long enough for dust to settle in the empty shelves. When the voice comes back it's almost a whisper. "Because you are the only one who will listen without cleaning it."

That answer is both a threat and an invitation. I have listened to a lot of pasts. I have polished a thousand hours until they glittered. To be told I am the one who won't "clean it" is to be accused in a language I speak: I imagine the speaker has memory surgery in mind, the slow removal of rough edges, the erasure of contradictions.

I put the spool into a locker and lock it to a code only I know. I write two things down on a physical pad because numbers on pads are contracts and because there is safety in old rituals: Archive-17; the child's voice; message at 07:24. My handwriting looks immediately traitorous to me. I fold the pad and shove it behind the coffee grinder where rats don't go.

Outside, the station hums in the lightless way machines do when they are pretending to be lived-in. You can never be sure whether Helix is an organism or a cemetery with a soundtrack. People move like strangers in the corridors, faces bright as ship's stickers, hair that reflects the failed suns above. Names are sticky here; some people change them like gloves.

I should have welcomed the interruption. Instead it arrives like the first cold that tells you a fever is coming. The hull under my feet thrums—a low, bone-deep shudder that has nothing to do with the gears or with the rain. The lights in my shop flicker. For a sliver of a second the holographic shelves go out and my neon sign gutter-mutters like a living thing breathing its last.

Every alarm system on Helix is tied to something called the Palimpsest Watch, and the Palimpsest Watch hates anomalies more than anything. For a beat the station forgets to be polite about its fear.

The door to the alley outside my shop clatters. That sound is small but it carries all afternoon's promises in it. I touch the locker where I hid the spool and find my hand shaking.

Two choices publish themselves in the dim: turn the spool over, let the Palimpsest clean it and close the wound, or follow the child's voice into a part of Helix that, by right and registration, should not exist anymore.

When you make a living on memories, the right choice is usually the safe one. People will tell you the brave choice is the other. I don't know which I've made until the door swings inward and someone who ought not to be here steps under my sign.

They are small, wrapped in a coat that has seen better weeks, with a head too big for their body and eyes that catch light like coins. They don't look like they belong to an Archive-17. They don't look like much of anything except determination.

They say, without prelude, "They are coming for the river," and the name Mara rolls off their tongue like a stone fleeing a child's hand.

Outside, Helix Station remembers how to be a place under threat. Inside, my shop remembers me as someone who makes bargains. I remember the spool in its locker, the voice on the line, and a past that might be mine, or might be someone making mine because it is the only name left that fits.

On the countertop, the black case ticks like a heart. I don't open it. I don't have to. The world already is starting to decide between forgetting and being remembered. Somewhere in the Palimpsest a dead archive watches with a patience that could break us all.

I slide the coat off the child and let them take the stool by the counter. They fold their hands like a person with rules, and when they look at me, I see a map of a river in their pupils.

"Tell me the name of the river," I say. It is the only thing I can think to ask.

They close their eyes and say, simply, "Litha."

That is not a name I know. It will not be the last impossible piece that walks into my shop today. But for the first time in a long time I feel a hunger that is not for money.

Outside, Helix groans as if settling into a dream. Inside, a child called me by a name I buried. Between us, the spool in the locker hums like a promise. The Palimpsest will not let such a song go unanswered. Neither will I.

The rain in Meridian never learned how to be polite. It came down in sheets of silver ash that smelled faintly of ozone and old copper, as if the city itself were copperwired to some dying engine and exhaling its last, useful ions. Neon lighthouses—advertisements, mostly—flickered through the wet and turned the puddles into suggestions of other worlds. People moved like they were carrying invisible baggage, shoulders tight, eyes narrowed against something they did not want to be reminded of.

I like the rain, which is a small complicity. It rubs soft the edges of memory. That matters when your job is to touch other people's staying—when you are paid to be the place where lives end up, to stitch them into records and sell them back in pieces.

My name is Nara Voss. I work at the Archive, Level Forty-Four, on the wind-lean side of the city tower. We keep what the city throws away: moments, quarrels, the last breath of a lover, a child's first steps, a banker's guilt at bankruptcy, the texture of a winter morning in a skyline five centuries old. The rich come to us to order custom nostalgia—freshly clipped memories to taste like dessert. The poor come to sell, to trade a year of a child's laughter for a week of heat in an apartment. I don't care about the morality of it. Memory is a commodity, and I am a good broker.

Today, my desk smelled like ozone and corroded coffee. My gloves still smelled like the back of a consignment crate. The Archive's floor lights hid the seams of weighty cases and the labels that mattered—Authorization, Chain, Quarantine. We were a bank of people with bad songbird voices and better lies: we promised to preserve, but we also pruned. The most interesting things are marked Quarantine.

"Morning, Voss." Arlo's voice had the oily warmth of someone who'd been promoted from technician to middle management and forgot his original cynicism. He moved like he had a hand on two futures at once. "Got a sealed shard for you. From a private seizure."

"Seized by who?" I asked. The seizures were either government—rare and procedural—or private and very messy.

"Obscure. No packet trace. No owner ID. Label says 'personal – do not release.' They didn't want it on any register. Cash-only recovery. They flagged it for anomalies."

"Anomalies means 'it crawled out of the vault and sang to the night-shift guards,'" I said. Arlo smiled like he'd enjoyed the metaphor and spun the crate toward me.

The shard was small—a sliver of crystalline lattice no bigger than my palm but dense as bone. It held its own dull light, as if the thing had been put out in a room that remembered sunlight. Someone had wrapped it in a rusting paper band, the ink smeared into something like a fingerprint. The band read: ECHO 041 / SEAL: TEMPORAL / SUBJ: NARA VOSS / DATE: 15.IX.29—THREE WEEKS.

Time in Meridian was a ledger with margins; it didn't flinch at annotations. A memory marked with a future date was a malpractice without a license. The Archive had a quiet, airtight policy on future-imprinted shards: quarantine, notify the Bureau, and do not, under any circumstances, interact with the fragment until it had been scanned and its provenance confirmed. The policy existed for good reasons. People used futures for manipulation—blackmail, market speculation, worse.

Arlo's smile didn’t reach his eyes. "Private sector didn't want to wait for the Bureau."

I felt the air go cold, though the room hummed with climate-controlled warmth. 'Nara Voss' was printed on the band, unmistakable. Someone had put my name on the seal. Contractual sense or not, it uncoiled an unprofessional prickle along my spine.

"Where did it come from, officially?" I asked.

"A drop in Dock Five. Runner claims they'd found it in a container with other--contraband? No manifest for that container. They sold it to a handler who sold it under the table to a collector. Collector panicked and moved it to us. Said they couldn't keep it because—quote— 'It was speaking of her as if it were there.'" Arlo shrugged. "That's the part I'm supposed to forget."

"You're not supposed to have told me any of that."

"You're the only one who'd actually look at it without phoning the Bureau and watching them hand it back to the city." Arlo's smell of coffee sharpened into concern. "Nara, if this is some kind of temporal imprint—"

"If it's a time-leak, the Bureau makes it disappear and we all get better jobs," I said, because bluster was the old woman's coin where I came from. But my fingers were already warming to the shard. It hummed against my glove, a quiet thing that looked like a trapped night.

I hooked it up. The Archive's sync cradle accepts shards like vervain accepts sunlight; it tastes the lattice and opens with a slow, obedient nuzzle. The cradle read its seal: unauthorized, temporal data, cross-referenced with a dead signature. We had instruments to tease out when a memory was recorded—neural drift patterns, encoding fingerprints native to particular synth-kits. This one had none of the hallmarks.

"You're going in," Arlo said. He put his hand on the lid of the cradle as if to bless it. "Don't—"

I had never been one to obey 'don't' when it was a mechanical noun. We are all collectors of small rebellions. I strapped in. The Archive's public suite smelled suddenly like lemon and ozone, and the world narrowed to the hum and the cradle and the lattice.

The imprint didn't wait. It unfurled like a slick ribbon, not a memory like a recorded song but like an organism sitting to be observed. I felt the first wash in my teeth—metal and sea brine—and then the corridor of a ship opened in my eyes. Not Meridian's corrugated steel and neon, but something scaled differently: corridors that angled like a thinking animal, dark panels stitched with light that troubled to be soft. There were no windows. The air in the memory was heavy, perfumed with the sharpness of cold engines and the wet slap of suits.

Someone running—boots like soft thunder. "Nara," they whispered. The voice in the memory was my voice and not my voice: lilting, cracked, older by hard things, and perfectly intimate in the wrong way. I could have sworn the voice was mine for reasons that made my mouth fill with a tiny, truthful hurt.

"Do not turn," the voice said again, and it sounded like prayer.

I did not turn, because the memory told me not to. That's the virtue and the vice of the Archive: we experience others' compulsion as our own. Ahead of me, in the memory, another body crashed into the corridor wall and bled a copper rain down the seam. The lighting stuttered. I was in that body, in the same breath that the body was in me. The sense of presence was granular—a hiss of someone else’s breathing mapped against my cheek.

A figure at the corridor's end turned a blade that caught the light like a confession. The blade held shapes, and in its reflection I saw a face that might have been mine in another life—lank hair plastered to a sweating forehead, eyes too dark, pupils pinched with pain. The figure did not look directly at me but at something beyond me, a viewer the memory could not share. Behind them, on a bulkhead, a projection flickered: ARGO-ORPHEUS / DISTRESS.

The memory tightened then, like a fist. The person in me stumbled, and every sensation was a sentence I had not written. "Nara," someone whispered at my ear in the imprint, and the whisper was so intimate that I flinched awake inside the thing. "They'll come for it. Remember the lullaby, remember the window."

I had not the faintest idea what a lullaby could be in a starship corridor, and if something had taught me to remember windows in a place built to be blind, I had no recollection. The imprint presented the lullaby anyway: a lilting sequence of notes like a child's toy dying. The lullaby made my hands move as if from memory: I reached for a seam in the corridor, unlatched, and opened a compartment that revealed a small, crying child curled inside like contraband.

The child did not look at me. It looked at something outside the memory and then at me, and in its eyes I saw a figure in black robes. The figure leaned close to the child and whispered a string of numbers. Then the memory burst with a sound that felt like the ocean breaking over damp glass. My senses reeled.

I ripped down from the imprint and hit the release. The cradle's lights blinked and steadied. My back burned where the harness had been. Arlo was there, always a little too quickly. "You okay?" He asked the question as a professional courtesy, but his face was pale in a way that made me know he'd seen something that had cost him sleep.

I had a taste in my mouth like iron. "Who sealed it?" I asked.

"No owner listed," Arlo said again, quieter, now with the kind of detail that erodes people. "No manifest. The future-stamp is an anomaly. The child's image—"

"Child?" The word left like a small grenade.

The band on the shard said my name. The imprint had said my name. It had said the date three weeks hence. There are many ways to die in Meridian; memory shows some of them off like a trained animal. But a memory written from the future into the now—targeted at me—was a kind of map. Maps are dangerous. They had a habit of being followed.

I thought of the month I couldn't account for last year. I had two days that were blank—erased, eaten—marked only by a scar the shape of a crescent on the underside of my skull. I had woken with a debt and a whisper of guilt that tasted wrong. The Archive had replaced the missing time with ten shifts of overtime and the same repetition of lies. I had told myself I was lucky to still have a job. It hadn't been enough of a consolation. When memories left gaps in people, they tended to take something back in return.

"Who dropped it off?" I asked Arlo.

"Cash drop. Anonymous. He didn't want the Bureau involved. Said it wasn't his problem." He hesitated. "Nara, you should log this. Seal it. The protocol—"

"Oblige the Bureau to bury me?" I said. "No. I want a copy."

The Archive frowned upon unauthorized duplicates. We were the keepers, not the bootleggers. But half the job was understanding when a policy needed bending. You learn that if you want to survive the business. I asked Arlo for a discrete imprint and he fed the cradle a quiet pulse of energy. The shard let me take a copy—a sliver of the sequence, only the corridor, only the whisper of the voice. I tucked it behind my ribcage in the form of a small, illicit token—a mental breadcrumb—and felt like a thief of fate.

"You shouldn't," Arlo said for the third time. He didn't say that he might lose his job for the transgression. He said it because he had seen things like this bend people to iron. He had once told me about a man who had watched a future memory and then spent the rest of his life living backwards to avoid it. He had ended up in a hospice that smelled like disinfectant and failure.

I told Arlo I understood. It was a lie that had become my professional creed.

After work, the city felt thinner, as if the rain had stolen the color and left the skeleton. I walked home through alleys that smelled like fried algae and neon, the shard's echo thudding against my ribs like a pulse. My apartment was a box in a building of boxes, horizontal lives stacked like the Archive's cases. I should have gone to sleep. I should have done the sane thing: report, hand over, awake early to a more lawful sun.

Instead I went to Dock Five.

There are places in Meridian you go when you're trying to find the past or to be a little nearer to the things that make no promises. Dock Five is one of them, where containers sit like sleeping whales and the fog hovers with the resignation of a bad apology. The runners there sell cigarette memories, the cheap kind: yesterday's arguments, someone’s love at first sight for a few coins.

I found the container the runner had mentioned. It was sealed with a manufacturer's stamp I could read without trying: ARGOS SHIPPING, manifest scratched off with a blunt tool. The container smelled of different things: salt, oil, the ghost of human laughter. My shard was small but the imprint behind my ribs felt like a key.

When I put my palm to the cold metal of the container, the metal answered with a hum. Underneath the corroded seal, someone had scrawled a number in a shaky hand: 15.09.29.

A date three weeks away. A whisper already being kept alive.

Before I could do anything with the number, the air behind me moved. I heard boots—no, shuffled feet, the softness of something that wants to be heard and not seen. I turned. There was a woman in a coat, her hair braided with wire, eyes sharp. She was Fourier—a memory smuggler I'd met once and preferred not to again.

“You shouldn't be poking around, Nara,” Fourier said. Her voice had the particular boredom of someone who had made a lot of bad decisions and made them faster than most.

"Who dropped the shard?" I asked. In my mouth the words tasted of carbon.

She smiled like a rusted hinge. "That isn't safe to ask, not for you. But you already know there's a date. Everyone knows about sealed future shards. They carry obligations. It will attract the collectors."

"Why did you come here?"

"I came because you have something they want," she said. "Because you are a name on a shard and names are hungry. Because perhaps you remember less than you think." Fourier’s eyes flicked at the container. "Be careful, Nara. The future is a pattern and sometimes the pattern wants to be rewritten."

I wanted to tell her to go eat someone else's prophecy. Instead, I put my hand over my heart where the duplicate lay, feeling like a criminal of time. Something in the pocket of my jacket—something I hadn't known I'd been carrying—banged against the shard's echo. It was small and wrapped in oil-slick cloth and it hummed with the lullaby from the imprint. The notes found me like a key in a lock, and for a second, my mouth remembered the cadence of a voice I didn't have the right to know.

Fourier's face went still. "You don't remember, do you?" she said. It wasn't a question.

I thought of my crescent scar, of two days missing from my life, of the way the memory had whispered my name like a summons. I thought of the child on the ship and the number scrawled on the container.

"No," I said. "I don't."

She nodded like someone closing the book on a story they'd known since they were a child. "Then the ledger is balancing, one way or another. Keep that shard hidden. If the collectors come, they'll think they have a way to change things. They do not."

"But what if—" I began.

She interrupted by turning and walking back toward the fog. "What if is for people who like to drown in possibilities," she said. "Do one thing well, Nara: remember this. Whoever wrote your name on a shard knows the ending. That means they're planning for it. Planning is always crueler than chance."

When her boots vanished into the mist, I felt the shard in my pocket like a small, terrible planet. I had a name on a future, a child's eyes like a window, a date that ticked like an insect in the walls. The Archive's rules were suddenly less comforting and more like a cage with one wire already clipped.

I had always told myself that memory was a trade I could control. That dayfolded shards proved otherwise. Some things wanted to be found. Some names were bait.

I walked home beneath the neon advertisements and the ash rain thinking about lullabies and numbers and the way the voice in the memory had whispered my name like a verdict. The city hummed overhead in its sleep like an animal in a cage. Somewhere, in the lattice of things people kept and sold, someone had placed a bead with my name on it and attempted to stitch it into a pattern I had not volunteered for.

When I opened my door, the apartment smelled of old lemon cake and the new thing that had followed me home: the shard's echo. In the small, silent mirror above the sink, my face looked like someone who'd been interrupted mid-sentence by a forecast of doom. I reached up, feeling the crescent scar—pale, under the hairline—and the skin there felt like an answered question.

The lullaby began to sing behind my teeth, carried in memory. It was not my voice, but it was placed in my mouth like a coin. I found myself singing along without meaning to, the notes falling into the apartment like rain.

The phone in my pocket, which I had not expected to ring at midnight, blinked with a call. No number. No identification. Just the single word: AUTHORSHIP.

I answered.

"Nara Voss," said a voice that was both mine and not, like the memory had learned to speak outside its skin. "You have been asked to remember. Remember well."

The line went dead and the apartment's lights flickered. Outside the city kept its rain-stitching. Inside, I held the shard like a living thing and the future sat up in my chest and began to breathe.

Three weeks, the band said. The rest of it was waiting to arrive.

The universe remembered less and less of them.

It wasn't that the stars blinked out. The sky still kept its indifferent archive of light. It was the small things—names, recipes, jokes, the cadence of a lullaby—that slipped like sand through some cosmic sieve. Whole neighborhoods of memory—family dinners, examinations, arguments that had dragged through the night—collapsed into single, untranslatable images. Governments blamed time flux and the patchwork errors from when the continents of data had been rerouted. Priests blamed the lack of worship. Corporations blamed everyone else and charged more to stitch things back together.

Mara Voss stitched for the poor.

She had learned to earn in the liminal places: the drifting graveyards of hardware, the shiver fields where fragmented minds clung to the last things they'd thought. People who could not afford licensed restorations gave her the scraps: old photo shards, hair held in resin locket, bits of nonfunctional interface that still hummed with a particular someone's laugh. She repaired, or rather, she learned to coax the memory back into a shape that could be shared and traded. It was dangerous, sometimes illegal, and it left her feeling less whole than the things she mended. But it paid in spares, in favor notes, and most importantly, in the trust of a neighborhood that had been cut adrift from the official archives.

The Gull pulled itself through the wreck field like a tired animal, its hull a patchwork of plates scavenged over a dozen contracts. Mara liked being alone with the ship because the Gull had only the faintest ghost of a personality—an auxiliary weave that kept the lights from flickering and the recycler from clogging. The ship's interface was an old syntax, warm and low-policed. It did not ask why, only when.

"Tenebrae drift at eighty-seven markers and closing," the Gull said. Its voice was a bell heard with gloves on—metallic, without judgment. "Sensor horizon: three wreck clusters. One active signature. Heat variable."

Mara rubbed the bridge of her nose and watched the field through the cabin window. The space was cold in a way that made breath come out in steamy ribbons that caught the cabin light. The drift lay like a smashed city wrapped around an intact spine of a station: Tenebrae. Once Tenebrae had been a research hub, then a transit node, then a casualty to something the archives had labeled only "Event 39-B." Now it was a carcass with one way left in it—a hangar that still opened.

She thought about the job: a council from Sector Seven had sent a small package of credits and a list of coordinates. "Recover sample C," the message had said. "No questions. No delays. High discretion." Discretion was often a euphemism for "someone rich would rather not be caught with what they hid." Mara liked paying her own bills more than she liked dealing with rich secrets. But the money was good, and she had too many little hands to feed: a sister learning to code with borrowed hardware, a father whose arthritis had started to eat the days, a street of neighbors who'd helped when her own mother became a no-name fragment in an archive purge.

She sealed the suit and cleared the comm, letting the Gull stage the airlock. The hangar's mouth less than a kilometer out yawed like an open ribcage, caught on debris strings and the hulk of a cargo-packet they had once used to transport living things. There were silhouettes in the field: supplies, exosuits, a child's toy wheel still spinning on its axis. The field loved to keep ghosts because ghosts don't take up much space.

When Mara's boots left the Gull, the metagravity dragged the fabric of her suit like a careful hand. Outside, the dark made details sharp. Tenebrae's outer mesh pulsed with the old kind of power—a slow, tired heartbeat. It felt like crawling into a memory that had been left alone for too long.

"Active signature approaching," the Gull said. "Unknown vessel."
