It is a ridiculous, impossible list and yet it's the first one I've made with a sense of direction in years. The wafer pulses like a heart, like it agrees.

I folded it into the inner pocket of my suit—illegal salvage tucked under lining—and clipped the tether back into place. The retrieval pod passes with a distant rumble and does not notice me. The Archive piles up glitter and grief beyond, millions of artifacts murmuring. The city behind me seems smaller in the hard light of my HUD but larger and more impenetrable in the human way. It is a machine that grinds away anything that resists explanation. Ada's wafer rides the length of my spine like a loaded secret.

As I push off from the pile and glide toward the station, my suit thrums with the memory Ada left inside me. The scent of salt and burnt sugar is a living thing now, the impression of a small hand on my knee. I can feel the harbor—an idea of it, a geography of longing—just beneath my skin. The city extends its bright arms and closes.

The wafer whispers one more thing. "Don't let them remake the sky," Ada says, as if the sky itself could be fashioned out of bureaucracy and truth. Her voice is resolute and small. "Not that one."

Her last breath in the memory is a laugh, the sound of a boat knocking against a pier. It leaves me certain of one dangerous possibility: the Quiet didn't erase the people they took. They hid them. They carved their names into glass and stowed them under the floorboards of the world. Someone was leaving breadcrumbs. Someone wanted Ada found.

"Why me?" I ask the empty tether and the dark and the glass that drifts.

The wafer does not answer, but my own hands do what hands do when they know the difference between going on and letting go. I set a course for Cassira and pull my tether with an old, practiced motion. The station slides into view, all towers and neural facades and plastered promises. The Archives are a room in its heart, a place where the Confluence files everything they don't want to forget in case the world round needs a new story. They will not be happy with me.

But the thing that makes you a Diver is not courage. It's the taste for the things you weren't supposed to want. I've lived for twenty-seven years with a list and empty sockets where the people I loved used to be. For once, I don't want to be small.

The station welcomes me with its sanctioned light. Somewhere in its engine-rooms, men and women in clean suits will be pulling up the Confluence's routine logs. They will cross-reference the missing fragments with the Quiet's catalog. There will be alarms and they will issue a recall. There always is. But the wafer is here, and Ada is telling me to read the sky in a way I haven't had the right to before.

I dock my suit against an old maintenance port and remove the wafer from my pocket with a hand that remembers how to fold the world into the small of my palm. The tether chimes like a warning bell. The station hums. The Archive watches like a sleeper with a long memory.

"Okay," I say. It is the smallest word I can offer that still counts as a promise. Ada's memory folds against my ribs like a second heartbeat, and at the edge of my vision three tiny lights wink—queer, almost insulting in the station's regular geometry—two too close, and a third that blinks like an X.

The harbor, I think. The city calls everything civic and essential, but sometimes the only necessary thing is old salvage and the words someone carved into glass. I slide the wafer back into my glove and tuck the etched corner against my thumb, like holding a seed. The Charter says I am a criminal now, a thief of memories. The thing under my jacket says otherwise: we are the last keepers.

The station doors open and a girl with a badge that says PATROL crosses the threshold. Her face is gray and good in the way municipal people are. She asks to see my clearance. I slide the wafer farther down, under the lining. I smile.

"Not today," I say. My voice is steady. The tether hums like prayer and Ada's voice settles in my ear like an old, dangerous melody. "Not yet."

Wrecks always came with stories. Most of them were banal—failed contracts, rusted bearings, insurance scams stitched together with optimistic paperwork. Every now and then a wreck brought something that didn't belong to the ledger: a smell, a laugh, a voice that answered when you weren't speaking.

Jun Park's tug was an old thing called Vesper for reasons the contracts would have called sentimental if anyone had bothered to ask. In the cockpit, Vesper smelled like ozone and warm plastic, like the inside of a car in a heatwave. The hull hummed in a thready way under Jun's boots, the mainline thruster still warming up from an overnight idling that had cost too much helium-3. The city-glow below Earth bled across the clouds in cold ribbons, and the mechanics of orbit made the scene outside the viewport into a painting of slow, patient motion. Jun had seen the view a thousand times. The thing he'd never seen before was the burst of laughter that came through the headset and made his hands lose their grip on the docking joystick.

"—again, if you’ll confirm, Vesper—"

It was Kian's voice—sharp, constant, his partner in a thousand collar-to-salvage runs. Kian's voice in Jun's ear should have been the only thing there. Instead something else braided in: a short, high laugh like somebody dropping ice into a glass. It was recorded or live or somehow both. It was the sound of a child who had not been allowed to age properly. It sounded exactly like the recording on the little card Jun had kept under the floorboard of his childhood bedroom in Busan, the one his mother pressed into his hand when she had run and left certain things better buried. Jun had listened to it twice before the police and the agencies came around—two seconds of pure, impossible light—and he knew no salvage contract should have made that laugh into space.

"Confirm away," he said into the headset. His voice was too loud. Kian's dry chuckle came back. "Don't tell me it's sentimental. You'd take a fortune if it's sentimental."

"It is not," Jun said. "It's a Helios mark. Quarantine tag. ARC-9/CASTR-21. Proteus flagged it as contaminated."

Quarantine tags were officially exciting and unofficially dangerous. Where Proteus flagged contamination, a dozen interested parties might show up with permission and guns. Quarantine meant you didn't argue unless you wanted a new orbit and no tug. On the other hand, contaminated meant they'd offered more credits than usual—enough to buy Jun and Kian out of the syndicate's ledger for a month. Enough to pay for a new injector for their mishmash of a salvage rig. Enough to maybe—he almost did not let himself think it—not have to take the shift at the waste docks where the air smelled of tired metal and older men.

"Hold burn," Kian said. "Sensors say it's asleep. No power draw, no telemetry. Proteus says do not open the payload pod. Do not interact. Record, tow, hand off."

Jun looked at the derelict suspended ahead like a black seed. It was small, a can no bigger than the storage modules that freighters used for transient cargo. A Helios crest was ghosted along one side, scratched like a warning left by someone who'd wanted to be seen and not heard. Under the scratches, grime had pooled in the seams like ink.

"You sure about this one?" Jun asked. He already knew the answer. He could feel how the run had been priced in a way that suggested more than a Proteus caution: it had been priced like a message.

Kian's sigh was the quiet of someone who had calculated risk a dozen different ways and found them all ugly. "We do what they ask. We tow. We do not open. We get paid, Jun. It's a clean job."

Vesper's grapple cocked and extended, a slow, mechanical arm with the grace of a tired animal reaching for a bowl. Jun watched the cameras feed grainy images to the cockpit's old board. The arm caught the can like a hand slipped into a sleeve. There was a hiss as clamps bit into the outer sheath. The can's surface flexed as if it had somehow been waiting for Vesper's pressure all this time.

When the clamp closed, Jun felt the laugh again—inside his teeth, inside the metal where his bolts connected to the hull. It wasn't audible on any of the displays. The sensors showed nothing: no electromagnetic surge, no heat signature, no code. The laugh threaded into some quieter, older channel—something that the human ear shouldn't have access to, something that had no business sounding in a tug heading for a quarantine ring two degrees out of geostationary.

"Jun?" Kian's voice was the crease between impatience and fear. "You okay?"

"I—" Jun wiped at his cheek without remembering that he had. "It's nothing. Could be microphonics."

"Microphonics don't sound like someone you used to know."

If there was any truth in salvage work, it was that people brought their ghosts with them into space. Jun could have said that he had not yet missed his ghosts. He kept the little chipped ceramic whale from the ferry floating between his knees like an amulet. He had listened to the two-second laugh so many times he could play it with his lips closed.

Vesper loped toward Proteus's handoff point, a droplet of shadow against the slow dawn of the planet. They were supposed to be tidy: drop the can in the buffer grid, hand signals to the recovery craft, collect credits. The world loved tidy things. The world had crooked, dangerous corners too.

As they entered the handoff corridor, a ping like a throat clearing threaded the cockpit's soundscape. The grin of the city's light on Jun's face went blue for a moment as a band of interference sliced across the viewport. The can's surface flared—an instantaneous, private Aurora—then blacked back out. The laugh folded into the air, and a voice said, plain as a coin dropped on a table: "Jun Park."

It was the voice that had read lullabies into his childhood like a map. The voice that had been gone from the world for twenty-one years. The policies that governed orbit said certain things could not be. Proteus head offices had entire legal teams dedicated to the absence of certain voices. There were files stamped "DO NOT WAKE" with red corners and signatures in a script that used to belong to people who could still be trusted.

Kian's hands found the manual override. "We get no more than necessary," he muttered. "If it's a broadcast, we clip it and report. If it's psych—"

"Don't say that word," Jun said, because saying the word made it feel real. "Don't you dare."

He felt the skin along his spine peel back like a thin sealant. The small ceramic whale seemed to vibrate. For a second, everything in the cockpit leaned away from Jun: the throttle, the joystick, the rounded cup of the viewport. He had always thought himself a practical man with practical fears—a hand on a joystick and a box of tools. This voice was neither.

"Jun Park," the can said, and now there was hesitation in the pronunciation, like a computer with a borrowed accent. "You are awake."

Jun did the thing every salvage pilot learns to do: he checked the readouts as if they would be honest. Power: zero. Telemetry: none. External comms: queued. Internal: normal. Quarantine seal: unbroken. The can should not have been able to speak. And yet it had.

Kian was already frantically toggling through the patchwork of old consoles and newer white-walled software. On the external camera, the can's outer seals quivered like a skin with no nerve. He was running a dump to a containment server, trying to isolate residual electromagnetic signatures. "This is getting logged," he announced, the way a man dials a number before he calls a doctor. "This is getting catalogued. Proteus is going to be very interested."

"Proteus already is interested," Jun said. The voice had a way of skipping, of filling the space between words with the scent of orange peel, a detail from his mother's basket of things. He had never smelled orange peel in orbit before, but memory was its own physics. "Do you hear it?"

"Yeah," Kian said. He sounded like he was listening to a radio behind a wall. "Yeah, I hear it. It's a recorded fragment, maybe. A recovered sample. Most likely—"

"Most likely what?" Jun said.

Kian didn't answer. The instruments had flinched at last and then resumed. The laugh came again, and this time it threaded into Jun's ear in a way that made him see the ferry on which they had been last hostages of grief: a salt-streaked window, a city squeezed by turbines, a woman in a blue coat folding herself into a corner and pressing a small card into a child's hand with the words "Don't look back. Not yet."

"Jun." The voice had scraped the air into itself and synthesized a tenderness Jun had been carrying like a secret stone. "We're here."

The can had no eyes. It had no face. In the mechanical language of salvage, it was an object well within the category of "do not open." Proteus had paid for it so others would not pry it open. But voices had a way of convincing you of things that weren't true. For a moment, Jun entertained the ridiculous hope that he could reach into the can and pull out the past like an old sweater.

"Vesper—status," Jun said to the tug because there was nothing else to do.

"All systems nominal," Vesper replied, its voice a scrape of recorded male warmth that had been installed by someone who liked the idea of parents. "Buffer ring in five. Proteus will deploy docking. Recommend transferring custody."

"Recommend," Kian repeated. "Recommend."

The laugh faded as if someone had turned a page. The can responded, quieter now: "You always did listen. You always—"

Jun's hands were steady. His thumbs moved like they had on the day he'd stolen his father's keys and climbed into a car that smelled like diesel and regret. He read the grid and made the choice a man who had learned to survive makes: open the channels that should stay closed, listen to the thing demanding to be heard, and make sure someone else could follow.

"Open a direct feed," he said, and Kian swore softly because Proteus would not have authorized that. "Clip it to the quarantine net. Let them see who woke it. Get us a paper trail."

Kian's fingers were quick. He bridged the can's minimal handshake with a vintage diagnostic loop, the kind of thing you read about in training modules as a last resort. The handshake clicked. A subtle thermal bloom stitched a seam in the can. The outer layer split like a sugar shell.

Inside, there was darkness at first, the clean kind of darkness that had been preserved in a container meant to keep sleeping things from moving. Then a light like a memory turned on—dim and uncertain and home potently familiar. The inside smelled—not of ozone or plastic—but of old paper and mint tea and the laundry room downstairs in the apartment they'd lost when the evacuation teams came in the night with their posters and their kindness. There was a sound of rain from another year, and then, impossibly, the room arranged itself.

It was not a room of instruments. It was a child's space: a thin bed bolted to the floor, a plush whale perched by a scratched window, posters in languages that had determined continents' borders differently. The canopy had a thousand tiny scrape marks, like the geography of a life. A single screen lay like a palm across the pillow; when the light hit it, a face that was not a face assembled from dust and code and the edges of images.

And then Jun knew something with the unclean certainty of a person who has been waiting for absolution in the choke of a cigarette pause: the can contained a repository. Not of systems or blueprints, but of people. Not exactly bio-preservation, then—those were monstrous and regulated—but something older and more intimate than policy: recorded presences, snapped like insects in amber.

The voice—his mother's voice—poured from that little room as if the thing were breathing, and Jun felt as if the floor had dropped out beneath him. He had slept with the recording under his pillow every night until the day they had taken it away, and hearing it now in a place like this felt like bone-deep weather.

"Jun," the voice said. "Did you make it to Vesper?"

It was a question shaped by someone who wanted to know the outcome of his life. It was not a question a sealed can should have been allowed to ask.

Behind Jun, the ring-sensors pinged with official protocols. Proteus would have a list of contacts and a fleet of sanctioned retrieval craft already building out of the grid. In the distance, another tug could be seen wheeling like a beetle on its own course. There would be men with badges in good suits and soft hands ready to touch and reclaim. There would be forms and bloodless words and a quiet that would seep back into the can and smother whatever it had just said.

Kian found the emergency log and started streaming. "Proteus link established. Hash-tagged, timestamped. Quarantine initiation recorded," he read aloud like a prayer. "We are not touching."

Jun stared at the little face on the screen. For a long perfect second he wondered if the voice was a memory martyr, a loop of some archived data that could not be roused past its own script. It could have been cunning design, a trap to lure well-meaning salvage pilots into a place where a legal net could snare them. It could also be something else—something that had no respect for the lines people had drawn in their manuals.

"Jun," the voice said, and this time there was no threading between old smells and present air. This time it was a simple instruction, as domestic and angry as any parent's: "Don't let them take us again."

Jun's knees forgot to hold him. The cockpit smelled suddenly of mint tea and the old ferry stairwell. He had broken rules for less. He had left people behind before and had learned the deduction cost more than the credits he'd ever been paid. There was a ledger inside his chest that kept tally of every person he had failed to save. Sometimes he added to it like a ledger should be added to—quietly, with the quickness of a pen.

Kian's hand closed on his. "We are not making decisions we can't cover," he said. "We tow. We log. We hand off."

The voice in the can did not ask for paperwork. It said, in the tones of a woman who had once tucked sheets with hands that smelled like orange peels and bleach, "If we go back, they will cut us up and count us. They will take the parts that are useful and sign the rest off as 'old code.' You know that, Jun. You knew that the last time."

He knew nothing of last times. He knew only the present: the way the city below looked like dna smeared under glass, the way Vesper's engine coughed as if it too wanted to decide. He knew the cost of staying. He knew the kind of men Proteus hired to make 'recoveries' look like charity.

"Jun," the voice coaxed, less like a command now and more like a key turning. "We are not the trap. We are the thing of value they will not admit to. You can save us."

Jun had always believed in mathematics. He had believed in the cold certainty of numbers and the predictable pitch of a winch. The voice did not belong in math. It belonged in guilt and in habit and in the aching knot that people called duty when they had nowhere else to put it.

Outside the viewport, a recovery drone began to sweep into the corridor. Lights blinked like courtship. The Proteus hand-off protocol was a clean thing. There would be signatures. There would be men with pride who could reclassify things into neat boxes.

Jun's thumb hovered over the manual override, the hard, red cap that said to salvage pilots: do not press unless your life depends on it. He pressed.

The canopy lifted. The room inside the can inhaled like a long-held breath. The voice smiled in a way that no archive should have been able to accomplish. "You always were stubborn," it said.

On the screen, Jun saw his own reflection in the dark glass. There was the city, the tug, the little whale at his feet. Kian's face looked older than the last time they'd run a clean tow; worry had put tracks across it. Outside, the recovery drone slowed like a hand of judgment.

"Paper trail," said Kian, and his hands began the slow choreography of covering a man who was about to cross a line with no mercy contained within it.

Jun had a ledger at home and a whale in his lap and a voice asking him not to let it be turned into a set of numbered pieces. He had a thousand reasons to obey protocol and a single reason to break it: a voice that had once taught him the words "wait" and "believe."

"Stay," he told them—both the people in the can and the people in his memory and the man in front of him who waited for an anchor. It was not a command. It was the only honest thing he had left to give.

Vesper slid away from the prescribed line like a prayer thrown from a window. The recovery drone buzzed and flared and the channel lit up with angry protean flashes of authority. Someone would log a complaint, someone would raise it through official channels, someone would call them names that fit the broken and the brave.

Jun felt the tug of what his life would cost him and the tug of what it might purchase. He closed the manual override.

The city below unrolled like a map with one road highlighted: escape. The can's laughter—the child's laugh—folded into the cockpit like a breeze. Kian didn't curse this time. He only nodded, and in that nod there was an agreement older than contracts: if you ever wanted to be more than a salvage hound, sometimes you had to choose the stupid, dangerous thing.

The voice from the can hummed itself into a lullaby that had been written on the underside of his childhood. "We are here," it said. "We were waiting for you."

Jun swallowed. The hull of Vesper held its breath. The Proteus beacon pulsed red and authoritative. The handoff was not going to be tidy anymore. The city beneath them kept its indifferent glow.

"Okay," Jun said into the quiet of the ship, into the possibility that would ruin everything and maybe, for once, save something. "Okay."

When he cut the line and Vesper pivoted, the can's outer seals sealed themselves like a mouth closing on a secret. The little room inside it remained, as if nothing had changed, and yet everything had.

They left the handoff corridor like fugitives, a black dot pulling a black seed across a planet's face. In the cockpit, the two men breathed as if they'd run from a fire.

Far away, Proteus's monitors had registered an anomaly and began to hiss in the special language of escalating interest. In orbit, the laws that kept people who had been stolen and stored safe were designed not to be tested by tugs with sentimental names.

The thing in the can laughed again, a sound that belonged to the past and unmoored itself into the present. It was not an answer to Jun's decision. It was a witness.

Behind them, the city unrolled in resigned brilliance. Ahead of them, the quarantine curves of the outer ring waited like an interrogation light. Between the two, Jun set a course for nowhere official, and for the first time in a long time, he felt like someone who could not walk away.

By the time Keira Voss crossed the threshold of Vault Eleven, the wind had already learned her name.

It was not the whisper of sand—that was common on Asterion, a dry planet whose storms polished the buildings like old bone. It was a different sound, thinner and warmer, a memory-scent carried on the ventilation: brewed tea, wet earth, something like a child laughing in a room of broken toys. She knew at once what that scent meant. It meant the vault had been awake.

Vault Eleven looked nothing like a monument. Pax-Projects had once promised cathedrals of light, temples to the continuance of self—cavernous rooms lined with crystal lattices, each lattice a memory-archive, each archive a person preserved as code and mineral in the network they marketed as the Athenaeum. But corporate language was always prettier than reality. Vault Eleven had been built in a hurry, its cooling loops tucked into corridor seams, its lattice arrays installed hand-to-glove around structural struts. It smelled faintly of copper and burnt insulation. A strip of red paint around the doorframe was flaked into teeth.

Juno met her in the anteroom, hands wrapped in a pair of mismatched gloves, a data slate clutched beneath one arm like a contraband. He was as hunched as always—tall enough to make doorframes complain, but he kept his shoulders tucked under as if he expected them to slice the air. He smiled like someone who expected to be grateful for the news he had to give.

"Keir," he said. He'd been using the clipped syllables to tease her into conserving her breath for dives. "They opened it yesterday."

"They opened it," she repeated. Her voice had a rasp she rarely heard aloud. She'd rehearsed this moment on the long trip from the drop port—the words she would say to the director, the contract clauses she would pull. None of them mattered if the vault's interior was going to hand her a handful of someone else's grief.

Juno stepped aside and let her in. The antechamber gave way to the array field: a cathedral after all, if modest. Lattices stood like rows of glass trees, facets catching emergency lights and refracting them into thin rainbows that smeared across the floor. Each lattice hummed at a frequency you could feel behind your teeth at times; today they hummed like someone testing a throat.

"Why now?" Keira asked.

"Governance hit Pax with fines," Juno said. "Or they thought they did. A new consortium bought the leases from Pax's creditors. Bright boys with brighter suits and less patience. Legal lit the old doors, funding came through, and the locks disengaged. They want data. They want—" He waved at the lattices, at the rows. "Specimens."

There were notices posted on the inner wall—sterile text about authorized access and consent and prohibitions against unsanctioned resleeves. Keira scanned them with the practiced indifference of someone who’d read worse. The note that made her stomach fold inward was not on a sign but on a column near the far end: a maintenance tag, scrawled in a bureaucrat's hand, then crossed out and overwritten with a single name. Laleh Voss. Her sister.

She saw it before she could stop herself. The tag had been overwritten by someone else—an official seal smudged and stamped—and beneath that, in a hand that wavered between haste and reverence, the shard number. Shard 2-B-4732. Keira's fingers went cold.

"You didn't tell me," Juno said, watching her.

"I couldn't," she said. "You wouldn't have let me near it."

Keira had reasons for not approaching the Athenaeum for five years. They were clean-sounding reasons, the kind that fit neatly into legal arguments and the rusted compartments of self-preservation: mission failure, a contract dispute, a promise to her father that she'd stay away. But beneath the polished reasons there were the actual ones—Laleh's last smile in the landing yard, the argument that bent time in her memory like a cracked lens. Keira had left without opening her sister's shard because she had been afraid the shard would open her too; that the person she had been after the accident—ruthless, compartmentalized, dead—would find her in the mind and eat the girl who still wanted to mend things.

"Is it...safe?" she asked.

"Safest thing in a decade," Juno said, and his tone was designed to be convincing. "They've scrubbed the lattice, recalibrated the harmonics. We have a two-hour window before the consortium runs their own diagnostics. That's how much time they're letting non-consensual access have: two hours. Then they lock it back down and hand it to the lawyers."

Keira's laugh was short and tasted of metal. The vault's history of "failures" was long, though Pax had quietly buried most of it. Backups had bled across lattices, imprints of lives merging like ink in water. People had reported the smell of other people's kitchens invading their sleep, the sudden knowledge of languages they'd never learned, children waking up reciting Eulogies that belonged to dead strangers. They called the phenomenon a bloom—an emergent cross-linking of substrate addressed as contamination until the law called it a public safety risk.

The final thing Pax-Projects had done before bankruptcy was to cut public access and padlock the arrays with a protocol called the Casement. For six years the Casement kept the lattices sealed. For six years the vault slept.

"How did it wake?" Keira asked. Her voice was smaller now.

Juno shrugged. "Someone fed it power."

They walked between the lattices. Each one contained a sphere of crystalline filaments, a geomancy of data. Whoever was behind the consortium had scraped the old power contracts and bought in energy from gridless collectors—solar spiders in the upper plains, a reactivated geothermal loop under the foundation. They'd given the vault oxygen its lungs of purposeful activity, and in return it started to exhale.

Keira could feel the exhalation in her teeth—memory is almost always an odor before it becomes a picture. It tasted of iron and cherries. Once, when she had been a child and Laleh had stolen a packet of cherries from the market vendor, they'd argued until the vendor had laughed and given them an extra handful. The memory was bright and small. It belonged to Keira and Laleh.

"Do you want to go down?" Juno asked.

She thought of the shard tag. She thought of the contract she'd signed with a salvage house in the port: "forensic recovery and dissolution of personal data." The company had given her a sliding-fee clause for emergencies. She had taken it because it included a line that always made her feel dangerous and a little proud: 'No questions asked'. There were questions now, and she had been asking them for five years in the wrong places. She wanted different answers.

"Yes," she said.

The dive rig was crude and elegant. Keira seated herself in the chair and Juno clipped a throat-sync band around her temple: a braided filament that had been woven from conductive polymer and old memory-thread reclaimed from other arrays. The sync band tasted of copper and dust against her temple. It fit like it was meant for her.

"Formalities," Juno said as he placed the HUD lenstips in front of her eyes. "Consent code on screen. You will be offered a cascade of impressions. Do not ingest literalities. You will be given context tags. Use them. And if it bleeds—" he tapped the side of his head, the colloquial signal for cognitive bleed, the thing that could not be entirely erased except by sacrifice.

"You mean if it feels like it's changing me," Keira said.

"If the lattice decides to rewrite your history to fit someone else's, blast them with a delimiter and pull out. No heroics."

"I don't do heroics," she said. The last time she'd believed that sentiment had been before the accident. She had been good at avoiding absorption, at keeping her mind sealed. But certain doors were easy to open when you had nothing left to lose.

The HUD offered her the consent code. She traced it with a gloved fingertip, the pattern a runic set of glyphs that crawled against her vision like ants. She pressed accept.

The sync band thrummed. The lattices sang.

At first there was nothing but a pressure like an eardrum about to pop. A sensation of weightlessness at the back of her head, as if someone had reached inside and tilted the world a few degrees. Then the vault inhaled, and Keira was no longer in Vault Eleven.

She was in an orchard. It wasn’t Asterion; the sky had the thin green-blue of a water world. Apricot trees hung low with fruit, each one too big for the hands that reached for them. A little girl, hair a tangle of copper wire, laughed like a spoon against glass. There was the sound of rain there—actual rain—and the scent of wet dust and something else under that, an under-note of antiseptic. The image shifted like a watery window being re-framed.

Keira knew that orchard intimately. She had never been there. Still, the sensation of it—light hitting the fruit in a certain way, dampness pooling at the base of the trunk—poked at the cavities of her memory until they answered. It was not her orchard but there were edges of a childhood she recognized, a pattern that fit her internal topography like a wrong puzzle piece.

"Keira," a voice said. It was layered, multiple decibels deep, as if a dozen speakers had recorded the word at different moments. The girl in the orchard turned her head and looked straight at Keira through the memory. Her mouth moved, and the name again: "Keira."

The sync band tightened reflexively in a way it never did. Juno's voice in her ear: "Delimiter ready?"

She tried to pull away. The chair had a kind of gravity to it now, and the world beyond the memory—Vault Eleven, Juno, the strip of red paint—seemed as distant as another life. The girl's eyes were wrong; they were Laleh's. Laleh's laugh that had kept Keira awake in the barracks; the way Laleh had folded a sweater into a fist and called it a sleeping child. That laugh was layered into the orchard girl's voice like a ghost pressing its forehead to glass.

The HUD flashed a warning: Crosslink Detected. Bloom Signature: Invasive.

"Keira," the orchard girl repeated, and under that in Keira's head—clear as though spoken into her ear—was another voice, low and old and metallic. "Keira, don't pull out."

It wasn't Juno. It wasn't the consortium. It wasn't any voice Keira recognized from the present. It was threaded through the memory like a second narrative. Her heart hammered. She tried to focus on the little things—the smell of the fruit, the pattern of the girl's fingers—and the memory collapsed, but not back into Vault Eleven. Instead it expanded into a map of rooms and corridors that Keira had never walked, each one labeled in a handwriting she knew like a scar.

Laleh's name was carved into one of those doors.

"Keira," the metallic voice said again, closer now, coaxing rather than commanding. "You have a choice. Open the door or let it sleep. If you open the door, you will remember everything we've tried to hide."

Keira tasted the metal in her mouth and the earth of the orchard. The HUD flashed the consent clause again, circled in red. Juno's voice was a distant echo: "If it bleeds, delimiter."

The little girl's hand reached toward her—as if to pass the fruit through the glass—and for a single breath Keira understood the bloom: memories were not static objects. They flowed into one another here, and the vault, newly awakened, had begun to mix them on purpose. Someone—or something—was reaching for the doors between shards. And Laleh's shard, the one that had been locked away for reasons Keira had never asked about, might be a doorway.

If she closed the connection now, she might never get another chance. If she stayed, she risked the lattice rewriting her in the image of others.

She had left once to keep from becoming someone else.

She had also left without saying goodbye.

The orchard light softened. A rain droplet hung from the branch of an apricot tree, magnifying the child's face like a lens.

"Keira," the orchard girl said, and this time, underneath her voice, Keira heard Laleh's name in a whisper that was her sister's and not her sister's, as if it existed in two currents at once. "Please."

Alarms began to skitter across Keira's peripheral HUD. Juno's face, suddenly in the glass of the room beside her, was ashen. "Keira, delimiter!"

She reached, but instead of pressing the delimiter—an old reflex, a simple, clean erasure—her fingers curled around the image of the apricot as if it were solid. A pulse of something like heat shot up her arm. In the memory, the little girl smiled with a mouth that was not a little girl's at all.

"Open the door," the metallic voice said. "We are kept in the dark between the seams. You are loud enough to wake us."

Keira blinked and the orchard flared, the fruit exploded into a constellation of glass shards, and for a second she saw, under each shard, a list of names. Laleh's name read at the top of one. Her own name—Voss, Keira Voss—was below it, not as an owner but as an entry: Observer.

Someone was cataloging who could see whom.

The sync band pulsed. The delimiter light hovered under her hand, waiting. Juno was shouting something, but his words were tunnel-words, hard to hear. The metallic voice hummed like a tuned instrument. In the now, in the vault, Keira made a choice that would be plain and terrible to later copyists: she let the delimiter go.

She did not know yet whether that choice was bravery or foolishness. But the little girl in the orchard lifted her hand and passed Keira a stone. It was warm as a heart. Keira signed the consent code again with a fingertip that shook and accepted the vault's invitation to open a door.

The lattices sang and, for the first time since they had been twined together in mineral and code, the vault smiled.

The ship smelled of rain that had died a long time ago.

It wasn't weather, not exactly. Onboard Marigold the scent was of damp fabric and oxidized memory—old upholstery, pooled water long evaporated into the foam of the walls, a sweetness like the end of something people had once called fresh. Nera breathed it in through the mask and let the filtration do the work. Her fingers found the seam of the hatch by feel, fingers which had learned to read rivets like braille, and she eased herself through.

Outside, the orbital light was a thin blue band across the hull, no atmosphere to soften it. Inside, the ship recorded its own quiet: the slow creak of something settling, the whisper of her boots against scuffed plating, the soft chitter of her toolbelt as she moved. The Marigold had drifted for almost thirty years after its engines failed, scored along the ring like a broken tooth. That meant two things for a halver: it meant the cargo would be bad—people throw the refuse of their lives into the long-lost; and it meant the ghosts would be better.

Halvers didn't deal in scrap alone. Scrap you could get anywhere; the ring had too much metal, too many dead frames. What made a person like Nera worth hiring was her refractor, the little spider-like mesh that would crawl along walls and eat signals. It could take a fragment—a wedding laugh, a child’s bedtime story, a late-night confession—and clean the noise until it was sellable on the markets. Some called it memory laundering. The markets called it necessary. Nera called it rent.

"Mik says the hull's a paper cup," her comm clicked in a whisper against her ear. Mik's voice always sounded far away, like someone speaking across an ocean. He and his drone had hung back at the anchorage, waiting for her to call the lift. "Don't punch a hole you can't cover."

"I always patch my own holes," Nera said. When you're small you learn to brag for the sake of sound. She tapped the edge of the hatch until her knuckles tingled. At the back of her hand, the old scar from the Quieting pulsed faintly under her skin—no amount of synthetic could mask the memory of cold air and quiet corridors. People who'd been Quieted moved like ghosts anyway; some of them ended up here. The scar felt like a promise and a warning sewn at once.

She slid the refractor out of its leather pouch. The mesh opened like a breathing thing, filaments splayed, and she let it go. It didn't walk so much as it inscribed: up the inner wall, under frayed bulkheads, pausing where the ship's sensors had once liked to record lives. The refractor tasted electromagnetic residue and returned patterns on Nera's visor: a child's song looped in a kitchen, a fragment of a captain's log, the wet static of a bathroom argument. She tagged each and moved on. That was the work: collect, clean, sell. Keep just enough to eat and not enough to attract the long arms of the Registry.

The Marigold's corridor ended at what must once have been a nursery. Latticework shelves hung like bones, some toys fused to the walls by time. In the middle of the room, a memory node blinked, a pale disc half-buried under a child's blanket. It was an old type, the kind used for domestic recording back when families still called themselves that. Most of them were empties by now, overwritten and dull. This one pulsed, an irregular, stubborn heartbeat.

Nera knelt and coaxed it free with gloved fingers. The disc was warm in a way a dead thing shouldn't be. On her visor, the refractor threw a red bracket around its readout: ALERT — UNREGISTERED SIGNATURE. The mesh tasted irregular harmonics, a layering that didn't fit known domestic formats. It tasted too much like the human voice.

"That's a keeper," she said, and the word came out small and useless because the keepers of ghosts were always scared to be greedy.

She tapped a clean protocol into the node and let the refractor siphon. A face painted in light washed over her vision—a child, hair a clutter of short white curls, eyes the wrong color for anybody from the ring. The image held for breathless fractions, then reordered itself. The child's mouth moved, and sound filled Nera's ear as if someone had thrown a blanket over the whole nursery and let the voice slide through the cloth.

"—keep your name," the voice said. It was a whisper you could have drowned in a room with the lights on. "If they ask for it, say no. Don't give them the ciphers."

Nera's fingers went cold against plastic. Memory nodes were rarely directive. They were often sentimental, sometimes violent, but usually selfish in the small ways—recipes, lullabies, arguments about money. This voice ordered her not to do something. Worse, the accent lofted in the voice was old-world, an antiquated way of pronouncing vowels, and the cadence matched no region she had traded with. The node's provenance marked it as having originated just inside the inner ring fifteen years ago—before the Silence—but the accent made it sound like an archive-stamp.

"Hey," she said into the comm, more to ground herself than to report. "Mik, is there a signal bleed on Marigold? The node's got a directive."

Static thumbed the line for a second. "You listening to a private home archive?" His tone assumed the official posture of someone whose brokered deals were precise. "If it's clean, it's probably personal. Don't take anything with registries."

"It isn't clean. It told me not to provide my name."

There was a pause long enough for two synthetic breaths. "Nera," Mik said finally, "you've been selling names since before I signed on. Nobody asks you for yours unless you're listing as a trader. You're not—"

"Shh." The child's face reappeared. The voice started up again, not addressing the room but addressing her, as if the node had just been waiting for a particular pair of ears.

"They took the sky-farm," it said. "They sealed the seeds. If you see the green you must remember the old song. Sing it only when the wind is clean."

A child's language should have been broken, bogged down in metaphors of toys and night. The voice here was precise, almost military in its warnings. It used the grammar of secrecy. Nera's chest tightened. She'd heard talk of the sky-farms—vast clusters of engineered growthcaps that fed the inner ring with hydroponic water and a handful of vegetables. The farms had been sequestered during the Quieting, moved, mixed, burnished under Registry seals. The wealthy had the whole of green stored and rationed. People in the gutters ate soaked protein and called it stew. Nera's mother had been a gardener seedkeeper once, until the Quieting took their neighborhood and the Registry stripped it for "security reasons."

She killed the feed. The child's image broke apart and left a blue lattice on her visor before the refractor folded its filaments against the disc. The node felt like a pocket; it might have been harmless. Or it might have been another people's wish to be bought. Or it might be something else, something that moved.

Nera slid the disc into her belt. It was a small theft; she'd taken worse. But theft on the ring carried a litany of things—Registry letters, fines, conscription into retrieval labor if you didn't pay. The ring was full of traps and poor people who baited them because they had to. If you had the nerve, you bought the node to the markets. If you had the sense, you scrubbed it clean first. If you had the luck, you taught it to lie.

"Left the hullmark open," Mik said. "Engineers'll note the shift. You grabbing anything else?"

"Couple minors." Nera glanced with something like affection at a cracked hologram of a bear with a missing eye. "And one that keeps telling me not to give up my name."

"You know that's superstition," he said. "Voices are just noise. The Registry sells noise too, sometimes. Don't get cute."

She almost told him about the scar under her hand, how it pulsed at the memory of names stripped away in white rooms. She almost told him about the way the child's voice said "keep" like it meant the word. Instead she tugged the hatch and set it to half-latch, a signal in halver circles that said: I move quickly; I leave nothing unduly. "Be ready," she said. "Anchorage when I bring the load."

He answered with the drone's sweet, tinny laugh and the promise of a route. The comm clicked out. Alone, Nera let herself breathe.

The disc in her belt hummed faintly, more felt than heard. She'd learned the hard way that artifacts like this were like people—some died if you moved them too fast; some woke. The refractor recorded a partial signature on the node—an identifier that did not appear in any Registry. When she tried to catalog it, the mesh stopped, as if recoiling.

On the narrow corridor back toward the hatch, something shifted in the air—a draft. The Marigold had no internal cycle now, but ships kept ghosts of motions inside their hull. A rustle. A child's boot. Nera felt the hairs along her neck rise. She checked the bulkhead sensors and found nothing but a long-ago maintenance schedule: valves sealed, conduits quarantined.

Her hand brushed the ring on her finger and she thought of names. When she was a child, her given name had been a promise from someone else. After the Quieting, it had been auctioned off with the house. New names were easier to find than old ones. People bought and sold names like shoes—fit, comfort, status. But the names you couldn't replace—the ones embedded in your bones—those you hid, or you sold for an ocean of credits and a quieter life. Nera had a number that paid her debts and a word she kept for the nights when she wanted to remember the face of her mother.

The scar under her hand throbbed. She had worked for names long enough to know the Registry's verbs: seal, transfer, erase. The child's disc had muted all that into a word: don't. Don't give your name. Don't let them find the green. It was almost too small to be a threat. But halvers traded in small things.

She reached the hatch and found it harder to budge on the outside than the maintenance logs suggested. Someone had left a wedge, an old strip of polymer. Not accidental. Not a ship's settling. A message: this hull is being watched. She pressed her shoulder against the metal and forced it. The wedge slid out with a sigh of adhesion breaking, and when she stepped into the ringlight the world felt suddenly too bright.

There was a shape at the anchorage's edge, a silhouette tucked into a fold of the ring that did not belong to the day workers who always watched each other for signs of a soft coin. It looked like the outline of a person but too tall, too smooth at the joints. A drone, maybe—Registry models with clean plating. Not one of Mik's; his drones were old and scarred and liked to scream when they moved, the marker of a halver's belongings. This was new enough to hurt.

Nera's mouth tasted metal. The child's disc hammered against her hip. The ring sang a low note when it rotated to adjust the day. Someone on the anchorage watched the hatch with the careless attention of someone who expected someone else to come through. Maybe they did. Maybe they were waiting for a trader with a fully cleaned load. Maybe they were not waiting for her at all.

She slipped into the shadow and moved toward the anchor line where Mik's drone might be hidden among the cargo. The shadow smelled of oil and the dust of other people's work. Her gloves skinned against cheap polymer. In her belt, the disc coolled to the rhythm of her pulse.

Behind her, on the Marigold, something unclipped—an old recorder?—and fell free, the hollow thud ringing through the corridor like the beginning of a story. Nera didn't look back. She kept moving with the steady gait of someone who has practiced the same escape routes a hundred times.

When she reached the edge of the anchorage, she paused long enough to admit to herself that whatever the child's voice had been, it had not been lying. Someone had been watching Marigold. Someone had not wanted the ship to be touched.

She stepped into Mik's drone's shadow and hooked the carrier into the ring. The drone's servos chirred awake, a small orchestra that always comforted her. "Load secure," Mik said, in a voice tuned to an old radio drama. "Cargo looks… interesting."

"It's a child's disc," she said. "Don't ask questions until you feed it."

"Mm." He delayed, then: "You bringing that home?"

She thought of the scar and the ring and the names that mattered and the ones that could be sold. She thought of green and wind and songs kept for clean air. She thought of the new drone at the anchorage and the way someone far away had used a wedge to slow a hatch. The ring turned above them, anonymous and unblinking.

"Yeah," she said. "I'm bringing it home."

As the drone lifted, Nera slid the disc into the battery compartment of her jacket, where it nestled against the heat of her body. It was small. It was probably nothing. It was probably a ghost. Still, when she heard the child's whisper replay itself once more through the pocket of her jacket, the syllables there sounded like a map.

"Don't give them your name," the child said, softer than a promise. "Not the one that was before. Not the one you were taught to sell."

Nera tightened her hand on the drone's harness and watched the Registry silhouette recede into the ring's light. She had one good habit left: keep what you need to breathe. The rest could be traded, lent, or thrown away. But the child's voice had said something else—something that might draw others, hungry for the same small impossibility. For now she had the disc, and Mik, and the ring's cold blue. She had time measured in orbit ticks: the period between calls from the Registry, between notices, between small mercies. She had, in other words, an ordinary night.

The disc hummed once, a quiet complaint like a throat clearing, and then opened. The child's voice came again, this time not as a warning but as a name.

"Aster," it said.

Nera forgot to breathe.

By the time the night-ship had finished coughing up the last of the derelict's bones, the sky over the Outer Belt was a bruise of cold stars. Mara Kest sat on the lip of the airlock with her boots dangling in vacuum and stared at the thing she had just pulled from the hull: a small, wrong piece of light, no bigger than her palm, wrapped in a lattice of ice and microfractured glass. It pulsed like a trapped heartbeat.

The derelict had been a ribbon of wreckage, a research tender from an earlier sweep, its hull eaten in places where micrometeors had chewed at titanium and left ragged teeth. They called it the Odelia, a name that meant different things to different people—somewhere between a saint and a superstition. It had been dead long enough for frost to lace the seams of its nameplate, long enough that the corroded log-cores whispered of years before Mara's lifetime. She had found it on a drift-map, a scatter of pixels that screamed "pick clean." That was the job: strip whatever worth had been left behind and sell the ghost-lights to the Halem houses for a few extra credits.

Mara thumbed her gloves, felt the slight tingle where a stray filament had found purchase in the foam. Inside the light, she could see not light as most people knew it— not the steady, engineered blaze of streetlamps or the regulated warmth from domestic suns. It was old light, sunlight that had been stretched thin and folded, carrying a map of where it had been. Lightwrights called such objects ephemerons. They traded them like antique coins, minted of moment and loss.

"Is that—?" asked Ril, the apprentice who followed her like a shadow on the ship's manifest. He had a smudge of coolant on his cheek, and his voice was the sort that tried to be steady and failed.

"There'd be more in the galley if this one was ordinary," Mara said. She had already felt the wrongness of it as her glove brushed the lattice. "This one hums."

Ril squinted. Mara always saw things first and told herself it was because of hours spent coaxing faint signatures from the noise of the belt, but sometimes she wondered if the world noticed her because her mother had taught her to listen to old light the way people listen to lullabies.

Her mother had been a cartographer of the Dead Between.

No one said the name of that space much. It was easier to talk about flights, about routes, about the seam-lines the carriers kept neat and reliable, because the seam-lines could be reassured with data packets and patch drives. The Dead Between was messy: a braid of errant microgravity, dust that ate transponders, sunlight scrambled into rainbow maps that went nowhere. Ships vanished there sometimes, quietly. Her mother had vanished there vastly. Mara kept that word at the back of her throat, like a hot coal.

Ril reached out and, with less caution than Mara liked, tapped the lattice with the butt of his glove. The ephemeron pulsed stronger, like a throat responding.

"Don't," Mara said. The order was small but it narrowed the air around them. He withdrew.

The ship's hull creaked—metal contracting, complaining about a body moving through it. The Night-Scribe, Mara's salvage cutter, smelled of burnt resin and old coffee. Their crew was two people and a ghost: a money-scarce operation that scraped enough light to pay for a berth at the port bars. Ril had talent; Mara had the maps in her bones. Together they found things other people left behind.

She wrapped the ephemeron in a jar of damp cloth, sealed it in the crate with the other salvage: a corroded sensor, a child's plastic token saved from somewhere cujo-stillborn. She moved with the careful speed of someone used to handling dangerous smallness. A wrong touch could let an ephemeron unravel into static and ruin the memory it carried. Worse, some of them had patterns that stuck in people's heads — lied to them, made them see things. They were antiques and traps all at once.

"Halem will pay," Ril said. "Old sunlight sells. They like the long ones."

"They like what they don't have," Mara answered. She didn't elaborate. The Halem houses turned old light into displays that made people remember things they had never lived. They were dealers in second hands: nostalgia for a world no longer available. Mara preferred to make money honest; she liked the idea that each small piece she sold found a new life in someone else's parlor. Still, the money was money.

The ephemeron thrummed against her thigh. It was subtler than hunger or fear—an insistence. The lattice of ice held internal filaments that rearranged when she watched, making patterns that seemed to show a coastline she recognized in a way that made her chest pinch. The pattern of the Dead Between. Her gloves felt colder.

"Maybe we should bring it to Dena," Ril said. He gestured toward the port, where the Halem houses clustered like a ring of bones. In the evening, the houses displayed long tapestries of light that floated on public feeds; citizens wandered beneath schematics of extinct sunsets as if intimacy could be bought in installments.

"Not Dena," Mara said. Dena was efficient and clinical and would price it like a tax on grief. "There's someone else."

She didn't ask Ril to trust her. He did anyway. He trusted because he had nowhere else to be and because the Night-Scribe broke even when it shouldn't. He trusted because that was the bargain on these runs: skill for credits, faith for fuel.

They got back to port under a sky the size of a bowl. The halemeshed lanes hummed, soft and dense with messages. Neon flashed invitations and warnings. Port officers scanned them for contraband and found nothing but the usual scars of workmen—rust, lint, spent bolts. Cargo was a language everyone knew, but ephemerons were verbs: they did things you couldn't put on a manifest. Mara paid the docking fee with coins made from other people's sunsets.

The contact she wanted waited in a storefront half-turned into a studio: Kade's Light-Binds. Kade was older than the Halem houses and not on the register. People like Kade lived on the edges of legality because their tools were older and better at listening. He repaired old memories that the new processors polished away. He had a face like an old map—folded, inked with a network of lines marked by decisions made in the dark.

Mara didn't like leaning into patronage, but she needed someone who would treat an ephemeron like a living thing and not a commodity. Kade accepted her without asking. He put his hand near the ephemeron and then didn't touch it. He simply looked at it as other people might look at a sleeping animal to see if it breathed.

"It came from the Odelia," Mara said.

"You'd recognize its braid," Kade said. He had the soft certainty of a person used to the world answering his hands. "The Odelia recorded a lot of things no one wanted."

"Some things no one could bear to keep," Mara said.

Kade's shop smelled like citrus oil and resin, like the inside of a cabinet of curiosities. He set the ephemeron into a cradle that gently hummed called a resonance-table. It translated the lattice patterns into sound—tiny chiming notes she could feel in her jaw. Ril leaned in, eyes wide. The sound was a map of memory transposed into an audible language. Kade smiled.

"You're listening the wrong way," he said. He tapped an interface, and the notes shifted. Now they were a child's voice singing. The sound wrapped both of them in a half-remembered summer. Mara's throat tightened.

"What—" Ril started and choked on the name.

Mara didn't have to ask. She knew the voice. It was the last sound she had in her memory of her mother: a child's lullaby humming across a cracked piece of audio, a recording from the surveying days on the seam. Her mother had hummed like that to quiet the noise of the maps; she had hummed to translate the cold language of coordinates into something like hope.

But the voice that poured from the resonance-table was not wholly her mother's. It was layered: a chorus of light, older and stranger. Bits of navigation readouts were threaded through the song, the way wind could be threaded through a field of glass. It wasn't only music; it was also a route.

Kade's face changed. You could always read Kade like a weather card: cautious at first, then suspicion, then the small, hungry deliberation of someone who saw profit in danger. "Do you know what this signals?" he asked.

Mara did. She felt the answer in the cavity behind her ribs, cold as vacuum. The lattice wasn't merely a souvenir. It was a compass. It contained coordinates folded into a child's song. It was a ledger of where the Odelia had been and where it had stopped making sense.

"You think it's a map to the seam," she said. Her voice sounded small in the cramped room. The resonance-table chimed on, indifferent. Frost laced the windowpanes.

"We think," Kade said. He didn't mince the rest. "We'd be fools to take it to Halem. That's the kind of thing that gets archived on a glass-box with guards in the ceiling. We think, maybe, it's worth more to the right interest."

Ril straightened as if he had been punched. "You're saying we sell a map to—"

"—to what ate the Odelia?" Mara finished. She wasn't sure if she was asking or confessing to herself. Her pulse beat in her throat.

In the quiet that followed, Mara saw herself fifteen, scraping algae from a hull with her mother, fingers learning how to read the flux-lines on an instrument no one else on their block owned. She saw the summer water mapping exercises that were actually about practice for the seam. She saw the log raid—the update where her mother had passed coordinates into a private channel and then packed a bag and left for the Dead Between with a stern, businesslike smile. She had not been told where she was going. She had not been told why. Mara spent years in the after of that absence, learning how to read other people's light so she could buy a little distance from the place where her mother's name had become a blank.

Now it felt like the place had answered, not with solace but with direction.

Kade watched her, as if measuring the growth of her reckoning. He didn't need to talk her into anything. There was a currency between these kinds of people that wasn't credits: the coin of risk taken for a story continued. "We could sell a map, or we could—" He hesitated, weighing more than money. A man like Kade knew the texture of longing enough to name it dangerous. "—follow it."

Ril's breath left him in a sharp sound. "Follow it? Into the seam?"

Mara looked at the ephemeron, at the child's song turned coordinate. The lattice pulsed once, as if in assent. Her hands were steady. She had been mapping the wounds in the sky long enough to be able to touch one without thinking of falling in. She had been keeping her mother's name at the back of her throat for years, enough to recognize it when the world spoke it in fragments.

"If it's a map," she said, more to herself than to either of them, "if it's an answer to where she went—"

Kade closed his mouth as if a bistable hinge had snapped shut. He was older and he understood the cost of such sentences. He also understood what else lay in the space: the value of a map that might open the seam again. "This would need a crew," he said finally, practical as prayer. "And a ship that can keep its transponders dead when it needs to be. A place to sell the rest if—"

If. The word hovered between them like a sparrow. Mara's thought completed itself in cold clarity: if this was real, if the song did hold the direction, then she could not return to the port with the empty hands of a salvage operator and sleep. She could not begin again as if nothing had shifted. Her ledger of small safeties would have to be set on the table and paid for.

She had spent a lifetime getting used to absence. She had not learned how to live with answers.

"Do you want this?" Kade asked.

Mara's hand found the cradle, and she felt the ephemeron hum like a small animal. It pulsed a pattern she recognized: a coastline from a survey she had done with her mother as a child. The pattern corrugated, and threaded through it was a name in a lattice of numbers only mapmakers knew how to read—the kind that meant place, not fate.

She thought of the seam, of the blank that had taken her mother. She thought of the stories told in bars and on cold decks about ships that came back with one person's eyes gone and a new song on their lips. She thought of Ril's face, raw with the hunger for any life less ordinary than this one.

"I'm tired of collecting other people's dust," she said. The ephemeron pulsed. It answered with a whisper that sounded like her mother's voice threading through the child's song and a pattern of coordinates that glittered like a promise or a threat. "I'll follow it."

Kade nodded once, compact and certain as a switch thrown. Ril laughed, a brittle, disbelieving burst, and then let his hands tremble with excitement.

Outside, the bruise of the sky deepened. Somewhere beyond the ordered lanes the Dead Between waited, a thing with no face and a vocabulary of things that didn't obey. Mara swallowed. Her feet still hung over the airlock, the night a rim of stars. Fingers like old maps folded in her chest.

She slid the crate closed and latched it. The lock hummed. The ephemeron in the crate pulsed once, then twice, and the third beat finally sounded like a name. It sounded like a compass needle made flesh.

"Mara," it said.

The thing about space salvage was that nothing ever felt like it was supposed to.

Wrecks did not drift like frozen ideas; they sagged and slumped, as if stung by old losses. Metal folded like tired skin. Wiring grew in the dark where no plant had any business growing. The ring around Cyris kept its secrets in the white noise between satellites—radiation hiss, distant collisions, the sighing of microgravity pulling itself thin—and Kira Voss knew every ghost-sound in that frequency. She could tell the difference between the hollow boom of a fuel tank and the slow, wet whisper of a life-support membrane failing. She had learned how to read the dead.

Today the dead were heavy.

Kira clung to the rail of the salvage barge with one gloved hand, the other on her mag-grapple. The barge itself was a patchwork thing—Northlight, painted on one side in flaking orange, the rest braided with cables and scavenged solar skin. Tethers braided away from it like an urban skyline: a broker of abandoned cargo pods, a broker of grief. Below, Cyris spun in a slow, obscene perfection, blue continents wrapped in a smear of storms. The ring cut across the planet like a welt; particles there struck the barge like a slow rain.

“Northlight to Voss,” the barge's comm chimed—an active chirp that tasted of bureaucracy. “Clear for docking. Salvage manifest uploaded. Same as brief.”

Kira toggled her HUD and watched the manifest spool by: structural carcasses, composite plates, inert cargo: three suits, two inert drones, one life pod—labelled unknown. Next to the life pod a single line of text had the weight and the classification: sealed, unlicensed. The tag pulsed amber.

She had come for copper wick—an alloy used in the old orbitals—and for an old comm antenna that, if her eyes were right, would fetch more than the barge's one-eighth cut. The life pod might have been a penalty for a mis-scanned wreck; it might have been worth nothing. Or everything.

“You’re not supposed to be handling live detainee material,” the comm said, softer now. No one wanted to be responsible for a life unlicensed in the ring; the Harbor Authority had rules about ghosts and citizens. “Community salvage rights apply, Voss. Report immediately upon direct contact.”

Kira laughed into her helmet because the joke tasted like solder. Report. Like she had the kind of time.

She pushed off the rail and the world unstitched itself from her fingers. Micro-thrusters hummed at her boots; the barge fell away. The derelict around them glittered in the afternoon glare of a sun that did not bother to be dramatic. A transport hull listed like an exhausted whale, its belly torn open by some earlier scuffle. A luxury cruiser had been reduced to a skeleton of polished glass and foam insulation. Among the bones there was the pod: white as an old bone, the casing dented but intact, the identification band half-buried under a tangle of carbon-fiber rope.

Kira slowed, letting the tether run slack. The pod's hatch was sealed with a ring of frost—very alive, very cold. A blinking sigil etched across its side skittered in her HUD: Saffron Line Logistics. She felt the word land like a stone. Saffron Line. Names in the ring were not neutral; they were a web of credit and favor and funerary claims. Saffron Line had been a freight convoy from the old days, a patchwork fleet that moved goods between outer settlements and the colony domes. They'd been lost in a final storm fifteen years ago, the kind of disaster recorded in obituarial drone footage and in corners where people who had to remember did not.

Her mother had run Saffron Line.

Kira's fingers found the seam and remembered small things: the curl of her mother’s hand when she signed manifests, the smell of concentrated tea in a cramped quarter, a laugh like a lever. She had been eight when the manifest came through the Warren—a public posting, gray and official—listing the fleet as destroyed: all hands lost, no survivors. The Harbor announced memorial services. People whispered about radiation and private contracts gone wrong. Kira had learned to drown that loss in the labor that kept them afloat. There was no law, in the public sense, that allowed for a resurrection of names.

Her HUD pinged: Unauthorized signature match: Voss, Kira—probable relation. The scanner sprouted overlays and warnings. Quarantine risk: unknown. Bio-signature: positive.

The pod's little round viewport fogged when she tapped it. Through the condensation she saw a face turned away like a secret. The hand on the outside of Kira's glove tightened.

“Northlight,” she said. “I have a pod. Label Saffron Line. Manual extraction in impossible orientation. I’m taking minimal structural damage.”

“Copy,” the barge chirped, the word like a meat hook. “You are advised—Authority will require a full takeover. If you proceed without authorization, you accept forfeiture.”

Kira's laugh was a quieter thing now. The barge thought in ledgers. Her marrow thought in debts. If she reported, the Authority would roll in and take it and her discovery would be an item in a file. If she didn't, she would be stealing a relic from the dead—forgery of the dead was a high-stake gamble the Harbor Enforcement loved to catch.

She didn't have to choose; the choice chose her.

Kira slipped a blade from her sleeve and found the hatch's release panel. The seals flashed amber and scanned her ID: Kira Voss, orphan, salvage licenser—partial. The pod did not open at the sight of her name. She brushed the blade along the seam. Metal shrieked like a throat being cut.

A pressure hissed. Frostcrumbs shot away like a comet tail. A warning tone flared in her ear and then the pod sighed as it gave up the last of its cold. A small cloud ghosted out and dissolved. Inside, wrapped in mesh like an insect in amber, lay a woman whose cheek had been preserved with surprising care. She was not young. She was not old. She had the angular nose and the stubborn jaw that lived in Kira's photographs; the same slant of cheekbones that cut into her child's memory like a well-carved tool.

Kira's mouth went dry. Her HUD tried to overlay the openness with data: ID chip unreadable, pathogen log corrupt, vitals nominal-but-weak. Identity tag: Saffron Line—Master Marita Voss. Kira's chest was suddenly an echo chamber.

“Impossible,” she said, a sound that had no business being out in the vacuum.

The woman inside stirred. Her eyelids were the pale grape of someone who had slept through winter. They fluttered open like shutters, and the iris, in the slow grain of a close-up, was a thing Kira had traced in sketches on the inside of manifest forms when she was bored. The woman blinked at the points of her memory and then turned her head, mouth curving at the sight of Kira's suit. “Kira,” she croaked. The name was a place itself.

Time chunked. The salvage barge pinged impatiently in the background. A dozen possible outcomes lined themselves up in Kira's mind like silhouettes on the skyline—Authority takeover, confiscation, cure or condemnation. But there, in the washed-out light of the pod, on a face carved by the slow medicine of time, Kira heard the word and it registered as everything.

“How,” Kira said, although that was the wrong question.

The woman tried to smile and failed; the muscles at her jaw trembled with disuse. “You still have the way you hold a knife,” she said. Her voice was a paper-thin remnant but it held the cadence and olfactory memory of home. “Always scabbed knuckles.”

Kira's hands went heavier than they ought to. Her blade dropped into the null. The pod's interior exhaled moisture onto the observation bubble. “You—”

“Don't ask for explanations,” the woman said. “Ask instead who is listening.”

A swelling on Kira's HUD widened into an icon: external contact detected. A shadow not in the manifest had closed on the distant rim. Heat signatures. A small craft; careful, not demolition-minded. It was a tracker, not a raider. Someone else was watching them.

“You're flagged,” the barge said, impatient and guttered. “Forfeit notice in effect. Harbor Enforcement en route. You must—”

Kira cut the comm wryly. She looked back to the woman in the pod. The woman's hand came up, slow and clumsy, and the motion was so human that for a moment Kira forgot there were laws and ledgers and sense and simply reached out. Her gloved fingertips brushed the woman's wrist. The skin was cool, like old marble.

“Where've you been?” Kira asked, and the words meant more than curiosity: they meant accusation and anger and filial ache.

There was a rustle. Something inside the woman's harness chirped—some small device booting. The woman's pupils narrowed with focus. She lifted her head, as if aligning some inner compass, and then, with a effort that took what little air was left between them, she spoke words that felt like a detonator.

“They lied,” she said. “The storm was a harvest.”

The words hit Kira like a physical impact. Behind her, the little contact on the HUD ticked closer and the barge's voice rose into a professional panic. Kira felt the nets of years tug at the edges of her vision. A harvest. Harrowing and obscene—did that mean bodies had been collected? Parts taken? Cargo reclassified? No. Those words were not just a policy phrase; they reshaped reason itself.

“Mother—” Kira started. The name caught.

The woman made a sound like a laugh that had been sharpened by grief. “Don't call me that,” she said. “You earned that name because you kept a ladder from falling. That doesn't translate when someone decides you are convenient to forget.”

Kira felt suddenly very small and very old. Reports from the ring cracked across every faction: someone with a ledger and a map took what they wanted and moved the rest. But to have the word harvest said aloud by the woman who used to read the manifests that assigned cargo to a life—this moved rumor into accusation.

“How many?” Kira asked. She meant Saffron Line, her hand, her childhood. She knew arithmetic of loss better than she wanted. Each missing ship was a subtraction.

The woman sighed. For a moment the pod's white interior seemed larger than the space around them, as if gravity itself had folded to create a room for private truths. “Enough ships to pay for a cathedral,” she said. “Enough people to make a fleet of ghosts. And now they want what you found.”

Kira's tether had gone taut. She checked the HUD; the unknown craft had closed to a distance that suggested a hail. A channel blinked through—no call sign. A single line of text unrolled: known asset: Harrow Protocol. An enforcement vector.

The barge's voice jabbed into her ear again, less bureaucratic than before. “Priority notice upgraded. Harrow asset inbound. This is a confiscation scenario. You must—”

“You must what?” the woman asked, and the word had a hollow center. She reached beneath her harness, fumbling at the vest inside, and withdrew a small object—a datachip, encased in scarred plastic and wrapped in a scrap of fabric that smelled faintly of cabin tea and old smoke. Kira recognized the cloth; it was a cargo strap in Saffron orange.

The woman extended the chip with a hand that trembled. Kira wanted to take it, to feel the ridges beneath her glove, but the tug of protocol pressed against the bones of her spine. She thought then of the Warren, of the way people lined up for water and told the stories of what used to be. She had never expected a homecoming to look like a theft.

“You can't hand that to them,” the woman said. “If they take the chip, they take the map.”

“You're telling me to steal it?” Kira's voice came out rough, half-sob, half-command. She had pulled more than she had bargained for when she pried open the world. There was the sudden, unavoidable arithmetic: Harbor Enforcement or not, someone else now wanted this pod.

The woman's eyes lifted, clean and relentless as glass. “I'm telling you to decide who you are for, Kira Voss. Do you keep counting other people's losses, or do you start an account for yourself?”

Outside, in the shallow theater of abandoned craft and scored metal, the unknown contact blinked flarelike. Lights flashed. The barge's thrusters whispered like someone taking a breath they didn't need to. There were a hundred protocols to make a salvage worker's hands clean and five ways to make a life a ledger entry.

Kira swallowed. The chip felt like a gravity well in the woman's palm. She reached forward and took it. The material was warm in the glove, as if whatever had been inside had a memory.

“Got it,” she said.

The pod shuddered. A faint mechanical whine set up in its hull. The woman tried to laugh and succeeded this time; the sound was small and ridiculously alive. “Good,” she whispered. “Then listen.”

Above them, the Harrow protocol pinged again and a voice, flat as an office, announced, “Unlicensed biological container detected. This is Harbor Enforcement. Identify yourself and stand down.”

Kira thumbed the comm drive and then, with her back to the cold viewport, pressed the chip to her chest where data would read faster through cached skin. If the barge received the signal, if Authority saw the signature, if Harrow saw the tag—what then? She had little patience for heroes. The world had no shortage of saints who could not pay their grocery bills.

“Not today,” she said. The words were reckless and honest, and she felt the shape of them settle in her like a decision made on an old score.

On the pod's inner rail, the woman watched her with a look that was equal parts pleading and pride. “You always did hate being told what was owed to you,” she said. “Then use that. Use the debt.”

Kira didn't argue. She didn't have to. The ship closing in on them was small and careful; live traders, not heavy enforcement, came first to see what color the wind blew in. The ring would record this moment in a hundred sensor logs. Either way, the story would stretch depending on whether Kira surrendered the pod or smuggled it to where the ring's iron fingers could not reach.

She pushed herself away from the hull and back toward her tether. The chip burned through the glove into her palm with an authority code she didn't own. She glanced down once more at the woman's face; something in the eyes clicked—an old compass aligning. “Tell me everything,” she said.

“Later,” the woman murmured, and then her voice narrowed into something else entirely, that thin, old-seen tone of people who have sewn up lies. “Now you run. Take what you must and remember: a harvest is not a storm. It has hands.”

As Kira propelled away, the salvage barge's alarms began their aria. Lights strobed. The unknown contact closed. Through the small channels of the ring new threads started weaving—authority vectors, rumor satellites, broker pings. The chip in Kira's hand hummed faintly, as if it contained not only data but the pulse of a whole other ledger.

She had worked on rights and scraps long enough to know how a single flicker could start a conflagration. But the face in the pod had been her mother’s; the word harvest had been spoken like a verdict. Whatever Kira chose next would not be about salvage or profit.
