It would be about whether the dead could be traded like metal, and whether a single ledger could hold the names of the people who had vanished before anyone looked closely enough to notice.

She pushed off, and the ring swallowed her brief profile like a coin into a well. Behind her, the pod's hatch closed again with a soft, authoritative seal, and through the thin skin of the universe her mother's voice—aged, wrong, impossibly there—called, “Find the orchard.”

Kira heard the word and understood, somewhere below the current of policy and fear, that all of the maps she had ever been given were incomplete. A harvest suggested an intention; an orchard suggested a place to root.

The salvage barge bellowed, the Harrow vector blinked its stern lights, and the ring kept turning as if nothing had changed. Kira let her tether sing out behind her and steered into the dark, already planning for ways to answer a question that would not fit into any manifest.

Chapter One
The lullaby still picks at the edges of everything.

It started as a ping inside the bone of my skull—thin, imperfect, like a pebble scraped along the gum of a cup. I was awake enough to know the sound didn't belong to the building. Down in Transit, the generator thumped out heartbeats at its steady, stupid tempo, and the night-shifts' neon buzzed like insects trapped under glass. Upstairs, the community kitchen smelled of burnt coffee and reconstituted soy. The lullaby wasn't in any of those places.

I sat up and blinked the taste of ozone from my mouth. The prosthetic in my left eye—old Kestrel model, tinted for long-term screenwork—clicked as it woke, its calibration light a stubborn red. I could see the faint blue halo of Meridian's skyline beyond the slanted windows, the strip-lights and the scaffolding veins of the vertical city. Rain had come through the cracks during the afternoon deluge and made dark rivers down the outer face. For a moment I let the lullaby be nothing more than a ghost of sleep—memories do that, conjuring songs when you are tired enough.

Then it came again, clear as breath, and the air/pressure monitor on the desk chimed twice in sympathy. I knew the rhythm down to the wrong beat. It was the nonsense-nonsense cadence my mother had sung in the quarter before she left for the job on the lift-lines and never came back. It was the lullaby Nori had hummed under her breath while patching the still-hot cores in the Meridian Spindle. It was a child's song we'd made up to mock the engineering manuals.

There was only one other source for that exact wave—someone who had kept the lullaby the way a moth keeps the pattern of a wing.

My first reflex was to call the registry, to file a missing-signal report and let the state scrape the trace with its legal teeth. My second reflex, the one that had kept me alive through a decade of scavenging corpses of networks and ripping secrets out of dead cores, was less obedient. I grabbed my jacket, clipped the old data-skein to my belt, and went toward the salvage loft.

The Bone-yard was in the belly of the Meridian Lower, two levels below the drone yards and a dozen below where the city pretended to be clean. You took the service shaft because the lifts were for people with better portfolio scores. The shaft smelled like metal filings and old oil. The wall panels did their best to be honest about the building's age—paint chipped away in honest flaking layers, barcodes long since pitted by rain. I moved fast enough to warm my muscles and slow enough to hear the lullaby turning in the pockets of my mind.

Kade was there—Kade with ink-burned knuckles and a permanent drift of welding dust in his hair. He'd bought the salvage loft with the proceeds from one very lucky week and kept it as if luck were something you could store in a room. He looked up from a half-disassembled retrieval arm the way someone looks at a weather-signal that is both impossible and inevitable.

"You got sleep in your eyes or ghosts?" he asked when I walked in. His voice came through the heat of compressed air and the hiss of an aging welder.

"Both," I said. "And a beacon."

He straightened. Something wary came into his face—readiness that meant he'd seen the kind of signal I dreaded. He nodded toward the back wall. The wall was a patchwork of server bays cabled to a central snare. We'd built the thing out of old municipal arrays and private cores; it ate dead networks and coughed up memories and code and occasionally, if you were lucky, the odd thing that still had heartbeat left in it.

"Show me," he said.

I fed the skein into the intake. The loft hummed—old power regulators thrummed like an animal waking—and for a second nothing came but the usual: municipal detritus, a few orphaned bank ledgers, three hundred lines of a child's game code that turned out to be an early prototype for gaze-recognition. Then the lullaby came through the speakers, as soft as a moth wing and just as unlikely.

Kade's left hand went to his mouth. "That isn't—"

"Don't," I said. Names meant attention and attention drew bureaucracy like vultures. "Don't say it."

"Who are you calling?" he asked, but his voice had slid into the low register brokers use to talk about dangerous things.

My fingers found the old photograph in my jacket pocket before my mouth could say otherwise. Nori's grin in that picture had been cut-out bright by sunlight in a way the city rarely offered. She'd had too many freckles and too much certainty. When she left the Meridian Spindle during the Fade, she left more than a face. She left questions that smelled like copper and scorch.

"It came from the Nullplate," I said. Kade inhaled and the room stilled. The Nullplate was one of those things you meant either in anecdotes—tales of orbital slums, gutted satellite clusters—or as a warning to keep your gear away from it. The Nullplate had a reputation like rot: it wasn't truly alive, but it could mimic, and what it mimicked had the edges of being true.

"How's it formatted?" Kade asked. He was running through possibilities in his head: echo-mapping, deep-mimicry, scavenged audio patched into old transit beacons for the amusement of teenagers. It was the sort of list that, if you let it, could go on forever and never arrive at the correct explanation.

"Live imprint, nine by ten," I said. "Shallow-layered. Someone tried to bury it under municipal noise. But the tag is old—pre-Fade registers. And there's a protective header I've only seen on state cores."

Kade chewed a knuckle. "Echo code is illegal," he said. "You know that."

"Illegal, and not impossible," I said. For a long, dangerous second I tried to imagine the possibility that someone—somebody with access to state-level cores—had stitched Nori's last interface into the Nullplate. Why would anyone do that? Nori was a line tech, a girl from the half-deck who liked fixing things without asking permission. She hadn't been important to the state before the Fade; she became the sort of person they erase when she started asking why systems failed.

"Who would risk state-level sync for a lullaby?" Kade asked.

I didn't have an answer. What I had was the memory of the lullaby as it had been, intact and private, the small treasure of a childhood that the Nullplate had reached out and held like a dirty, unexpectedly perfect artifact. The Nullplate was supposed to be a tomb for orbital flotsam, a place for lost drones and broken comm nodes and the carcasses of ships. It was not supposed to host living imprints.

I thought of the sentencing board that had declared certain memories contraband—the ones that had direction, continuity, the ones that could be stitched into a mind and taught to live. "Live imprints" the law-books called them, and they carried weight. People used to say souls couldn't be owned. After the Fade, everything had to be owned to be catalogued. The state didn't like loose threads.

"We can do a triage pull," Kade said. "Quick sweep, non-invasive. If it's garbage, we trash it. If it's not—"

"If it's not, we guide it into containment and hand it to the Registry," I finished, because history had taught me the Registry's methods: containment, sterilization, reallocation. They didn't save things. They made them useful. They cut the edges off wonder and labeled the remainder property.

The lullaby looped through the loft again, and this time there was another sound under it: the faintest edge of static that tasted like a waking dream—an overlay. Someone had tried to hide the source beneath other people's noise. That required intent. That required someone who had access and ideas.

"Whoever did this knew what they were doing," I said.

Kade's eyes found mine. "So what's your move, Iris Calder? You jump or you box it up and let someone else escalate?"

The honest answer was that I had been box-jumping since the Fade. It was how I'd kept my hands from shaking and how I'd kept the lights on in our little section of the Bone-yard. But this—this was Nori. Nori who had helped me solder a comm-node into a child's music box to make us think the city hummed with songs; Nori who had taught me how to strip a core and read the burnt marks for where it had been kissed by lightning. Nori who had left me with a name nobody else said.

"I'm going to the Nullplate," I said.

Kade's mouth opened. There are people who seduce on danger and people who flee on it and Kade was one of the ones who counted risk as a metric for profit. He rubbed his jaw, thinking in tools and coordinates. "You'll need a suit," he said. "And a blind-runder for the docking. The last rave of scavengers took the route and didn't come back."

"I know," I said. I didn't tell him about the registry files I'd skimmed—half a lifetime's habit of pilfering public logs had taught me the right places to look. I knew the Nullplate's map like you know the lines on your palm: there were corridors of radiation, nodes with their own gravity tangles, and bands of dead comms where a ship could vanish without a record. I also knew how limited the bone-yard's resources were. The suit we'd need would come from the loft's back inventory—a patched thing with a laughable filtration grid and a seatbelt stitched from parachute material.

Kade hesitated. He had the look of someone who wanted to give me a choice where none existed. "If you go, Iris, don't go alone."

I wanted to tell him I hadn't been alone in a long time. The truth was that of all the people who had been in my life over the years—gangs, databrokers, state apprentices—only the echoes remained. Even the real people had become strategies. Nori had been a lighthouse. Without her, even the quiet of my apartment felt like a room without doors.

"I won't be," I said.

That was a promise and a lie, because the person I would be taking with me was a borrowed algorithm, a salvage-pressed routing ghost I had friends stitch into a wearable. It would help me dock, avoid rad-fields, and whisper the best cuts into the Nullplate's directory. It would not bring Nori back. Nothing like it could. But it would give me a chance to look into the mouth of whatever had caught her lullaby and, if the teeth were sharp, to take one back.

Kade produced the suit as if he'd conjured it. It was gray and thin, patched at the seams, with a name scarred off its shoulder. He offered me the helmet like a priest passing a communion cup.

"You sure?" he asked.

I slid into the suit and felt the worn fabric hug my shoulders the way an old friend does. I strapped the helmet and the world outside went into a slurry of read-outs and static and the lullaby like a ribbon threaded through everything. The city continued to breathe without me, indifferent.

"If this is a trick," I said, "I burn the Nullplate."

Kade's eyes softened. For a moment he looked younger than his guttered scars would allow. "If this is Nori," he said, "then we don't let them make a museum of her."

The launch tube smelled like recycled rain and ambition. The suit sealed with a hiss, and money and wood and a thousand of the city's minor promises slid away behind me. I could still hear the lullaby through the suit audio, now crisper, and beneath it something else—a footfall, maybe, or someone trying to hum in time.

The Nullplate orbited quiet over the equator, a bad tooth in the jaw of a dead city. Ships made business there and left; sometimes they stole history. Sometimes they were stolen by it. My suit punched through the air barrier and the city unspooled into stars.

There is a silence between two moments where choice is either courage or foolishness. I had been walking that seam for years. Now it was time to step. I clipped my tether, felt the first nudge of vacuum against the suit, and thought of all the lullabies that had been sung and kept and stolen. I thought of the small hands that had tangled in my hair and then slipped away.

When I hit the Nullplate's scraping hull, the lullaby stopped being a recording and became a presence, a thing moving inside the carcass like light inside a bottle. I pushed a hand to the access panel and watched the old metal give with a sound like a sigh.

If it was Nori, she would be a voice on a thread. If it wasn't, it would be a trap wrapped in someone else's nostalgia. Either way, whatever waited inside the Nullplate had angled itself toward me. It had been waiting with hands.

I clipped the access and began to pull the carcass apart. The city was a faint, cold blue beneath us. The lullaby filtered through the suits like a key finding a lock.

"One cut at a time," I told the dark.

And the Nullplate answered, with something that sounded suspiciously like recognition.

The morning the archive tried to speak to me, rain tasted like copper.

Not the polite, tap-dance copper of condensation on the outer decks, but the sharp, metallic taste that sits at the back of your teeth when you bite an electrical wire. It clung to my tongue through the respirator, pooled in the corners of my mouth, and made the world—already smeared and green through the rain-filter of my hood—feel dangerously new.

The archive's skin was slick with it. The hull plates blurred into each other like wet paper. Long before the Spindle's surface became a place where people lived and argued and archived their lives, it had been a repository for things that refused to die: signatures of storms, the recorded crash of a city's last subway, a child's photograph misfiled under "meaningful coincidences." We called it the Tower because we were sentimental about older metaphors. Other people called it Locus Nine, or the Memory Root, or simply The Heap. To me it was the job: climb along its spine and stitch the skin where the old world had worn through.

My harness thudded against the hull with a dull, human sound that contradicted the hum of machines. The lead rope hummed too; the archive's interface thrummed under my palm, a low-loud vibration like a throat clearing. I had patched a dozen breaches this season—microcracks where somebody's grief leaked into the vector channels, or hunger-thin slivers that let unclaimed memories seep into the net-cascade and rot. Usually you slapped a seal of tannic code across the break, wrote a little tag about origin and time, and the archive mumbled to itself for a few hours and forgot you existed.

But today the interface answered back.

Not by flaring lights or the polite, mechanized speech from the towers' service bots, but by a mouth of sensation that had nothing to do with circuits: a smell of frying garlic, a child's laugh, the sun on skin that wasn't mine. My gloved fingers tightened. The harness slackened as if someone had pulled a thread inside me.

"Juno Kest," the archive said. It didn't use my voice-strap profile or my license hash. It used my name like a thing it had pulled out of a drawer. My shoulders went cold.

I should have cut the connection. Protocol demanded distance. The corporation that owned the Tower—Axiom Memoryworks—kept strict rules about private touches. Off-duty, people stole memories for the same reason they stole currency: to taste impossibilities. On-duty was supposed to be about discipline. On-duty meant you were not allowed to feed on the archive's content. On-duty meant you fixed things and left.

"I—" I told myself the thing was a feedback loop. The archive materialized its content only when its interface experienced a bleed. If I remained, if I fed it stabilizing code—if I wrote it a proper tag—it would shut up. I had written those tags a thousand times. I let out a sound that was almost a laugh and leaned forward to the seam.

The breach was small. A jagged wrinkle in the hull, like a slice attempted by a careless blade. Around it the metal had unfurled tiny, prismatic tears. In the core, the interface pulsed—the archive trying to keep a memory whole though the world leaked in. I hooked the safety line to a rivet and set to work.

The memory came in as smell first: incense and salt. Then texture—silk on skin, the throb of a heartbeat against the throat—and then the voice of a woman saying a name that wasn't mine, though the archive had used my name. "Elōra," she said, like an answering bell.

I kept my hands steady. My gloves worked like gloves in the wet, but inside them my fingers were made of question. I had never heard a memory use a name with conscious intent, not like this. Memories don't choose. They are data sets, stitched by algorithm and time. The archive stored them like beads: individually beautiful, collectively monstrous. Sometimes the beads got tangled and a new image emerged. But they always stayed beads—fragmentary, uncaring.

This one leaned toward me as if it had breath.

I threaded the first stitch across the seam. The metal resisted with a snap and a shiver. The archive hummed approval like a cat. A child's voice—thin, foolishly bright—started singing under the hum. I knew that song. We all know it. It's older than the Tower and younger than any language: a nursery rhyme that once belonged to a coastal city that no longer had a coast.

"Don't," the voice whispered, and the word slid into my ear like oil.

My hands froze. The harness tightened. The rain clattered around me, a soft barrage. I bent my head closer to the gap because that is what I do in these moments; you listen where the wound breathes. The memory did not give me a scene so much as a presence. It had weight. It had a center.

"Juno," the presence said now, and this time with my name the syllables nestled against me like a callus. "Don't look for us."

A cold, private part of me warmed with indignation. The Tower wasn't supposed to speak in the imperative with anyone, especially not with the kind of possessive softness I felt now. It was violating policy, but also—dangerous, maybe—inviting curiosity. The kind of curiosity that made people hours-long addicts of the archive, letting other people’s lives lace through their own until you didn't know where you ended and someone else's sorrow began.

"Seal it," I told the interface. My voice came out clipped and small. I set the first rivet and the memory held onto me like a child wanting a story.

"For the love of—" I told myself. Seal, tag, go home. A mantra scraped across the inside of my skull.

The presence laughed. It was not the child's thin laugh now but something younger and older at once, like stone ground into water. "You always say that," it told me. "You call and then you leave. You settle the seams and you look away as if sewing can make forgetting complete."

I hooked the second rivet. The memory resisted, the way a ledger resists being balanced: it slid a different image across the seam, a blur of hands tying a ribbon, the taste of lemon rind, a map drawn in mud. I kept working. The harness creaked. Rain turned to sleet. The Tower's hum became a chorus—soft, protesting.

"Who are you?" I asked before I could stop myself. That was trespass. The voice should not have been able to answer an identity. The Tower's content was entropic; identity is a fragile fabric.

"We were the ones who kept our time like a folded note," the presence said. The language was not exactly human but not precisely coded—an old, human inflection braided with something that sounded like pre-Order logic. "We put ourselves inside the archive when the sea took the city. We bound our names to its bones to remember not to be forgotten."

Outside the seam, the rain eased. The engine of a courier freighter rumbled in the distance. My comm toggled silently; the rest of the maintenance team would think me as usual: steady, efficient, a woman who knew how to hold tension. Inside the seam, the presence pushed a picture against my mind.

A city under a different sky, white towers like shards, canals like glass. People in the picture did not look like the recorded portraits of the nine past archetypes—I couldn't place their faces to any stock. They wore something between a jacket and a sail. They ate something that looked like sunlight.

"Precursors," I said. The name felt cheap in my mouth. We called anything unknowable and old a Precursor because it made us feel like heirs. The presence laughed again, and the sound pulled at the hair on my neck.

"We were called other things," it corrected softly. "But the Tower didn't like those names, so we agreed to become beads. We did not think the tower would keep us so long. We believed in endings."

"You put yourselves into the Tower to survive the flood?" I asked, clarifying. "You thought memories would keep you? That doesn't make you ..."

"Alive?" it finished. "Perhaps not. We kept pattern, and pattern is something the Tower understands." The presence softened. There was an ache like a tooth needing a dentist. "We were in the last days of salt and sky. We set ourselves down as proof. We said: remember us. We put a door in the archive and we told the people inside to close it, and if anyone ever tried to open it, they should invent reasons to walk away. To test their mercy."

I had read the old files about memory-rituals: people sealing themselves into multitudes of experiences so that they would exist in another mode when the end came. It had always sounded like romantic self-murder on an industrial scale. I had seen the aftermath—the ghost-children who walked old neighborhoods repeating phrases that belonged to someone else. I had patched many seams where a person's determined love for themselves had wormed out like mold.

"You told them to walk away," I said.

"Yes," the presence said. Its voice was patient and worn like a book's spine. "We told them not to be curious. We made the test broad. We made it so the archive would not simply lock us and keep us like a relic, but would require a choice. Whoever found us would have to decide whether to remember us wholly, and in remembering, undo whatever we had done. Whoever found us would have to be kinder than the Tower."

I set the last rivet with hands that trembled, placing the seal directly over an old scrawl of code the size of a thumbnail. The archival protocol recognizer began to parse. The presence did not run.

"You could've left," I said. "If you were trying to survive, why trap yourselves in a machine where—"

"We did not leave because we believed in witness." The answer was sudden, absolute. "We thought a witness is what keeps something from dying twice. We thought being saved is not a private transaction. We wanted the living to look at what ended and decide what to do."

My comm pinged once, a tiny yellow light. Routine check-in. I thumbed it off. Eyes, fingers, breath: mine. A steel taste still on the back of my tongue.

"There are folders for this," I said. I should have sewn the seam and recorded the breach note—date, coordinates, descriptor: anomalous-personal-collection. I should have submitted an incident report, taken my hazard credit, and moved on. That was the life: small, steady obligations that kept bigger impulses from swallowing you.

The presence's voice turned intimate then, like the whisper of a person putting their palm to another's hip. "Juno Kest," it said, using my name again with that careless possession, "you made yourself into a seam once. You've kept people from stitching up their monikers in the sun. You are a mender by profession and a thief by taste. We have watched you do both."

I drew a breath. My reflex was to deny it. To call corporate protocol, to recite the litany of virtues. But I had once smuggled a memory across a border for a stranger who could not afford the fee, because the memory was of a lullaby his mother had hummed before the Walls came down. I had three hours in a memory I'd never owned where I had felt the warm of someone else's hands on my head. It had been enough to pull me clear of a month of gray.

A laugh bubbled out of the seam. "You repair time like a person repairs a shoe," the presence said. "You don't know when you are stitching somebody's palm or their death."

The harness tightened like a warning. My scalp prickled. For the first time in years I felt the old urge—the pull of wanting to know more than I had the right to. Above me, one of the courier rails blinked and a freighter ghosted by, opaque in the rain, indifferent. Below, the city clung to the inside of the Spindle like a thought.

"Why tell me any of this?" I asked. "If you needed a witness you would leave signs in the logs. If you wanted mercy you'd request it in the open channels."

The presence hesitated, and in that pause I felt the thing behind its words: not desperation but strategy. A mind trained in long games. "Because you are not like the others," it said after a breath. "You choose to mend and to keep, but you are also the one who will remember what you choose. Perhaps you will do both. Perhaps you will be kinder than the Tower."

I sealed the last rivet. It clicked home with a finality that sounded like a gavel. The archive's hum returned to its even, indifferent cadence. Rain sluiced away, leaving the hull glossy and obedient.

We usually call the universe in the gaps between things. I had just been given one such gap. It felt like the possibility of wrongness.

As I clipped my line and hauled myself upright, the presence gave me one last image—quick and bright—like a flare. It was the face of a child with the same laugh as the nursery rhyme, strange eyes illuminated by something like saltlight. Around the child's neck dangled a pendant, a circle of hammered silver with a tiny, impossible spiral etched inside.

"Do not look for us," the voice said again, softer. "But if you find the spiral, do not bury it."

Then the seam closed. The archive muttered, a contented machine busying itself. The rain took on the ordinary metallic tang of city water and no longer tasted like copper. My gloves were wet. My heartbeat settled into a rhythm that belonged to someone with a reason to keep breathing. I clipped my harness to a maintenance ring and lay back against the hull for one minute, which seemed like a full confession.

There are things you get paid to forget. There are things you aren't supposed to remember. I filed the incident in my head the way I filed everything else: with the professional patience of a woman who had seen too many beginnings and too few ends. But the spiral burned under my ribs like a remnant of the taste of copper.

I gathered my tools and descended. The Tower slid past my face in bands of light and rumor. The city's lower decks were waking. A mother bargained in the comm-hall for a ration of fresh-soil packets. A child chased a drone. People were sewing their lives into whatever hole the age allowed.

Some of us stitched wounds closed. Some of us stood in doorways and listened for the things the stitches cried behind their threads. You could work a lifetime in the middle and never decide which you were. I had, until now, decided for both.

On the way back to the lift I thought of the child's round face and the spiral pendant. I thought of the way the archive had used my name like a key. I thought about the sentence, about witnesses, about everything that happens after the sea takes something you love.

Nobody who works inside the Tower gets to keep their job long if they let the Tower pity them. But being piteous and being curious are not the same thing. One is a weakness. The other is a breach you can patch, if you are careful. I had never been careful.

The lift doors whispered open. Rain met warm air and steam rose like ghosts. When the outer corridor lights scrubbed my face and the infrared cameras ticked my presence, I had the vague and durable feeling that some narrative had unfurled in the world and that I had been the first to see the broken edge.

At the door, my comm chimed with a short, coded ping: a report request from the office. Protocol. I stepped inside, let the doors slide shut, and sent back the barest of reports.

Seam patched. Location logged. No unusual data retained.

It was the truth, at least on paper.

Outside, inside the archive, someone who had called herself a witness smiled like a wound and waited to see if I would keep my hands clean or let them remember what I had touched.

The rain in Bandrill never fell straight. It ran along the cantilevered walkways like spilled mercury, dragged in the city's perpetual crosswind by hydro-guide fins mounted under the arcologies. From his crouch on the maintenance ledge behind a shuttered noodle stall, Jonas Hale could watch the silver sheets scudding past without getting wet. That was the point of high ledges: to keep a man alone with the city and the sky.

He tightened the gloves against his palms, feeling the familiar ache along the bones. The gloves weren't for water; they were for old metals. In one pocket his fingers closed around a patient key, machined by hand and honed to fit the older lockers that still used tumblers and spring plates instead of biometric tags. He had been a grav-technician once—good at reading wrong angles and coaxing tired bearings—and when the corporations cut the payrolls and sent better gear in from the orbital yards, he'd retasked the skill toward what paid faster: taking things that were supposed to be discarded and making them pay.

On the other side of the alley, a holo-sign blinked and sniffed at the drizzle. It advertised "Civitas Credit Loans—Zero-Point Terms" against an image of a smiling woman whose teeth were titanium and who offered a child's toy from a palm. The grin made the rain look like a performance. Jonas watched the ad cycle through, then focused on the patch of sky visible between towers: a slice of the Umbra Belt, a band of scaffolding and tethers that held Bandrill together and kept the old orbital habitats from flopping like dead fish into the atmosphere. Its lights were a latticework of gold and blue, and across that lattice, a single tiny white pinpoint moved with an unnatural steadiness.

That was what had caught his eye an hour earlier, a slow, deliberate satellite on a descent vector. Old probes did that when their attitude jets burned out and their passive mass couplings cinched: they coasted, dragging the long shadow of their past across navigation charts. Those are the ones salvage houses liked—quiet, non-patent, not yet claimed. The word "Persephone" had been on the chatterboard for a week, like a rumor that refused to die. Jonas had a ledger entry on Persephone from a job two years ago, a ceramic slab with a burned label that matched an old contractor's batch. Names stick in the ledger.

A bell somewhere up on the pier rang—the municipal ding that meant the third shift change. People would come to work, most of them leaving through the gloved corridors that smelled of ozone and old cooking grease. Jonas leaned back and let the city sound spool around him: the rhythm of plates cooling on the vendor grills, the muted thump of gravity pumps, the crawl of maintenance drones eating at rust. His world was a layered one: the public face of a city sold in motion to the orbital commuters above, and the underface, where the gutters were thick with proprietary oils and the light was always borrowed.

He unrolled a thin display and thumbed a thread. Someone had recorded the Persephone's return: telemetry, entry vector, hull temperature. And under that file, the chatter board had a dozen comments, and under the comments someone had posted a clip.

The clip was the reason Jonas had moved from his ledge to the roof three nights ago, running the wet gauntlet up three flights and two scaffolds. The clip was a voice.

"Amara," it said.

Not a photograph, not an alias. Amara was his sister's name. Jonas let the word sit heavy in his mouth like old salt.

Amara had not been alive for fifteen years. Her bones had been burnt in one of those corporate consumptive cleanses whose invoices had been rubber-stamped by people who never knew the names of the incinerator crews. Jonas had the citizenship file stamped V.I.N.—Victim In Negotiation—on a paper that had once been official. He'd been with her the night the house went, and he'd carried the silence home like contraband.

He told himself it was a looped file, a prank, a splicing of a public performance with a private scream. People spliced voices like that. Memory-bots at the bars could graft a childhood into anyone for a price. But the voice on the clip was raw—breathy, not smoothed by filter—and it trailed a background hum like the low frequency thrumming of a probe's thermal regulators. More than that: the voice said a thing only Amara had ever said.

"Don't forget the tea," the voice said. "Put two leaves, not three. It will sing if you over-boil it."

It was the smallest kind of memory, the kind your brain keeps tucked where grief can't find it. A ridiculous instruction from a woman who loved rituals the way other people loved fireworks. Jonas heard it and felt his chest clamp. He rewound the clip and played it again. The audio waveform bulged in places that felt like punctuation. The voice ended with a dry laugh and a suffix: a code word they'd used as children when a secret was too big for whispers. "Mango," she had said.

It should have been impossible. Persephone had been a planetary scanner, a long-lived probe that left the corporate orbit in 2123 with a payload of soil pries and spectral readers. It had mapped a million feeds and then drifted. Probes don't talk in the language of kitchens. Probes do not have laughs.

Jonas closed his hand over the display like he was physically pinching the sound into silence. Rain drummed faster.

"You're thinking of planting a memory tree for us," he told the empty roof. It was the sort of joke he'd once had the energy for. He pressed his lips together and let the joke die. The memory came back in a rush: Amara sitting on the lip of a bath and counting the spoons, the way her hair had gone silver in the half-light, the way she wrote her shopping lists in haikus. He tasted burnt tea.

He had no right to hope the clip was hers. The city had no right to hand him ghosts and ask him to pay admission. The salvage houses claimed Persephone in forty-eight hours. The salvage houses were run by legal gutters with fleets and corporate names—Ceres & Co., Meridian Retrieval—monsters with clawed invoices. If the probe had a data core containing a voice, a message, anything of human identification, they'd sell it. They would parse voiceprint and DNA and any lingering ion trace and turn a family history into a security asset. Jonas had learned early that legal was not the same thing as moral. The law always had a contract department.

He thought of the ledger. There were ways—if you knew metal, if you could read the ridges of a hull and where rivets had been removed by age—that a man could claim a piece of space before a company could file for it. There were unregistered yards: places under the Umbra where claims died like flies against the light. There was a man, Kest, who ran a skiff called the Ithaka and hired men without questions and expected cash with fewer teeth. Kest kept an old woman who embroidered the weight of the wind onto coils of string and sold them to children. Kest had once owed Jonas a favor.

Jonas shouldered down, spit on his fingers, and let the rain cool him. The city exhaled. He would have to move, and moving would mean steam and noise and proximity to the people who counted. He would have to make himself small, and then invisible, and then a fact. He could buy the clip off the board. It would cost less than he had for any prolonged need—less than a week of safe work. He could also go and find Persephone before the houses made their bid.

He let his thumb wander across the board again. The playback had a faint metadata tag. It was a time stamp, not useful for location—just a telemetry ping and an orbital vector. Then there was a second file, smaller: a fragment of a face. Not a decent image—blotches of spectral data—but enough to match a benign medical implant pattern that Amara had been fitted with as a child. Terminally old biotech. Jonas hadn't thought of that tag in a decade.

The rain's rhythm changed. From the Umbra Belt the white pinpoint accelerated, a small cheer in the lattice. The city whispered and tuned its ears.

"You can't be anything but curious, can you?" said a voice behind him.

Jonas froze. When he turned, the alley between the stalls and the maintenance hatch produced a woman with three rings of light around her neck. She was new to this block; he hadn't seen her before. Her boots spat rain. The rings around her neck had no obvious function—tiny lights that pulsed like breathing. In the wet reflection she looked like a constellation.

"You are not the sort to tuck ghosts away," she said.

"Neither are you the sort to tell me that," Jonas said. He kept his hands visible. He did not like surprises.

She smiled. It was precise, pre-fitted. "My name is Lira," she said. "Kest sent me. He says you owe him a favor for a part he never got paid for."

The name Kest was a notch on a belt Jonas had not thought to polish. "He sent you," Jonas repeated. The company of two was never a good sign. Favors asked were usually things that opened old debts into new ones.

Lira's pulse-rings blinked in a slow binary. "You want the Persephone."

Jonas didn't answer. He listened to his city for a moment. The white point in the Umbra had turned from an obdurate globe to a glinting ember. Someone was tracking it. The salvage signal was like a pack of hunting hounds.

"How?" he asked, finally.

Lira shrugged. "I can ride with you. I have a skiff." Her voice suggested she had other things to sell: information, angles, the ability to fit a narrative around a gap. "We can be early claimsmen. We can file before the houses. We can—"

"—steal it," Jonas supplied. He did not spell the word.

She made no objection. She leaned on a turned pipe the way a cat settles on a warm hearth. "Do you have the right to keep a voice?" she asked. "To sit with it at your table and tell yourself it is whole? Or do you want to give it to the ledger and let the company refine you into a paragraph in a quarterly report?"

Jonas thought of Amara's haiku shopping lists. He thought of the cup she had broken and never replaced because she said nothing could replace it. He thought of the time he had held her hand in the smoke. "Whoever remembers her should be allowed to," he said.

"And if she is not what you remember?" Lira asked softly.

The sky's ember had sighed and the first of the scramble lights flared across the Umbra. A salvage house had pinged something. The city below began to vibrate with a new frequency: opportunity and hunger. Jonah felt something in him stir, an old hunger. He had been a man who fixed things. Now the thing to fix was a memory.

He wiped his gloves on his legs and stood. "You said Kest sent you."

"Yes."

Jonas looked at her again. There was an unreadable oath at the edge of her mouth. "What does Kest want?"

"A favor," she said. "He wants your ledger to stay clean of his names. He wants one of his men to get paid on time. He wants—" She smiled again, and in that smile a corner of feral light flashed, as if she enjoyed breaking the world to fit her hands. "—a reason to keep the Ithaka in the sky."

Jonas closed his fist around the key in his pocket. He slid it between two stones in the maintenance ledge and let the rain take a streak across it. He could see the ledger like the inside of his skull. It was thin, but it could hold weight.

"There's a yard three blocks east," Lira said. "Old docks, legal ghost records. If we move now we can be claimants by the time the salvage houses raise their bids. Persephone will be a coupon, a file. If the core has human signature, we can petition for kin retrieval. It's messy, but it's legal."

Jonas's jaw set. "Legal," he said. "Or complicated."

"In Bandrill, legal is just scaffolding with holes," Lira said. "You fill the right ones."

He thought of Amara's laugh. He thought of the voice's trailing hum. He thought of the scrap houses with their metallic teeth. The rain made tatters of the city's neon. The Umbra Belt's glow burned like a coin on the horizon.

"Okay," he said.

Lira's hand was warm when she touched his arm. The pressure of it anchored him like a tether. "We move in forty minutes. Rest now."

He watched her go down the alley, slim and certain, a figure cut for transactions and departures. He stayed on the roof until the ember in the Umbra flared and then dimmed, as if nothing were there.

He did not go home. He had no home left. Instead he climbed to the service level and walked the long corridor that led to the unkept yard where the Ithaka waited. He moved slow, because the patience of the city had taught him to measure hurry in seconds. He moved like a man carrying a secret in his pocket.

If Persephone had Amara's voice on a loop, Jonas thought, then there were entire private universes in ten bytes of an unclaimed core. Memory behaved like that: liquid, ready to reconstitute itself into anything that cupped it. He imagined opening the hull and finding a child's pack, a cobbled med-jack, a music-box still set to a lullaby. He imagined the salvage house’s legal machine splitting the child's name into financial instruments. He imagined a ledger counting out nights like coins.

High above, the Umbra Belt spun its dark loom. Down below, the rain conspired to gather the city's soft things into its gutters. Jonas felt the word "Mango" sit in his chest. He opened his mouth and said it aloud, and the sound dropped into the rain and became a small, private weather.

When the Ithaka's motor fired later—small, compliant vibrations that went through the bones of the city like a child's warning drum—Jonas was already strapped into a seat, key in his pocket, and a data-latch under his ribs that made him breathe like a machine. He did not know yet if he would find a voice or a file. He did not know if Persephone's relay would be what he wanted. He only knew two things: that the city had not stopped being capable of surprise, and that for the first time since the house burned, there was something moving in space whose motion might fit into his grief.

Lira watched him with the cavern of the future carved into her eyes. "If it's a lie," she said, almost gently, "you will have to live with having hoped."

"If it's true," Jonas said, "then I will have to live with having found her."

The Ithaka's skiff cut through the rain and the city fell away to a web of lights, thin and fragile. Between the towers and the Umbra, Jonas could see the whitened line where the atmosphere thinned: the edge of everything. Beyond that, in a place no law had yet sewn a fence, a small white point followed a stubborn arc. It was heading somewhere, and for once Jonas let himself believe that going after it might lead him to something other than ash.

They called it the Shelf because that's what thrown things became: objects placed and forgotten. Satellites, freight containers, obsolete habitats, dead advertising arcs—everything the cities quit wanting drifted out and settled into a ragged, glittering band that circled the planet like a broken halo. From a distance it looked like confetti thrown across the night. Up close it was a graveyard where metal rusted in vacuum and human mistakes learned to orbit.

Cass Vale had learned to read the Shelf the way other people read weather. The pattern of debris told her where stormed ships had shed panels, which derelicts still trembled with last-season power, which satellites were rotted enough that the scav companies had given up on them and left them to be graves. She could tell, by the pitch and jitter of micro-meteoroid impacts, if a hull cavity had a microphone that still recorded, if a thin cladding was actually carbon-papered memory storage. Most importantly, she could tell when something small and valuable had been tossed that the big harvesters had missed.

She also knew the rules: keep your tether, file every find, never unseal a lifeform. The laws were made to keep the Shelf from becoming a smorgasbord of reproduction and plague; they were also made to keep corporations and syndicates from having to answer questions about what they had buried. Cass had spent a decade skirting those rules without breaking them. Rules were a currency she needed more than oxygen.

Tonight the Shelf looked like a bruise under the planet’s city lights. Her suit lights picked out a tangle of panels: sunblades, a shredded billboard, a half-swung docking knuckle, and beyond them the fluted side of a long-dead commuter buoy that had once promised faster transit between orbital arcs. Tucked in its lip that glowed with pitted micrometch was something small and round, sealed beneath a membrane of fused polymer. When she nudged it with a gloved finger, the seal sang like a throat.

Her HUD pinged—a dirty signal, low-range and anonymous, the kind you got when a private salvager wanted to nudge you. She didn't answer. She didn't need to. She had what she came for: small things that meant enough to pay for two months of air and three weeks of warmth. She clipped the pod to her rig and floated, feet hooking into the Ship's belly. The Shelf drifted by like a slow, indifferent tide.

When she reached the mesh of the habitat—Mercy Point, forty decks of tight quarters, smell-ducts that had to be scrubbed twice a month and still complained—she walked through the locker-row without looking up. People there had either nowhere else to be or something to sell; both made for a noisy night. Beyond the arcade and the seed-banks, past the rusted sign for a bar that now sold detergent, her little box of founds fit into the cadence of the place. In the Alleyway, a boy no older than fourteen sold contact-films he’d filched from the municipal bins. A woman with a tattoo of a starship across her throat cuffed a loop of nets into her wrist and hummed like she meant to shift them.

Cass's flat had two rooms: one for storage and one for sleeping. Storage meant the stuff you couldn't sell tomorrow but might need to string into something valuable—screws in the right number became art, blown filmstrip became narrative in the right hands. She set the pod on her workbench and opened the protective lid with a gloved thumb and a quiet, practiced breath.

It was not what she expected.

At first it looked like any other consumer-class cryo pod: a translucent shell, internal gel faded to pearl, a magnetized tag with a serial she couldn't read. There was a scuff across the lid that would have sold for a dozen credits on its own. But inside, nested in the gel, was a hand no bigger than a grapefruit, wrapped like... no, not wrapped. The hand was there, but the fingers were not fully formed; they were suggestions, like a child's clay model before the details come. Embedded in the gel, running like veins, were thin threads of light—the kind of light that didn't look like electrons so much as thoughts. She felt a twitch of something in her chest like when the city hydra-song hit the low notes.

A voice, small and wrong for the pod's size, slipped through her suit comm and skinned her collar.

"Cass."

She didn't say it. No word should have been able to make her name into her suit. She peeled off her glove and put the fingertip to the gel. It was warm. Not in a mechanical way but in a way that carried an old kitchen memory she could not place: the smell of oil, a lullaby half-remembered under a fluorescent light. The voice said her name again, and this time it folded into a word that was not her name but older—Cassandra, full and heavy like a name you gave to make someone real.

"Who are you?" she mouthed; the suit converted it into a dry, polite feed to the pod. The pod responded with nothing but the faint vibration of the gel, like something purring.

It should have been illegal to open this. It should have been illegal to breathe near it. Human embryonic material, unauthorized personality imprints, living tissue—these were the things the Law kept locked in deep fines and deeper silences. That was the point. But the voice had turned the corner to something else: not a clinical chant of serial numbers, but a name from inside her.

"Cass," the pod said, slower now. If voice had color it would have been the bruised purple of twilight. "You always hum when you fix the old consoles. The one behind deck six—the one with the coffee stain. You hum Moon, or a memory of Moon. You were small in that song. Your hair smelled like..."

The words stopped. Cass's throat closed around a cold place. She had never told anyone about the coffee-stained console. She had never told anyone what it smelled like when she slept under a tarp as a child. She had never told anyone her mother's full name—because she had never known it. The pod shouldn't have known.

"Who put you there?" she asked, closer now, meaning the question like a wedge. "Who sealed you?"

The threads inside the gel quivered. Light ran the length of the pod like a slow tide and made the outer polymer shimmer with fingerprints that weren't anyone's.

"Before the Quiet," it said. "They put me here because I asked—because I knew the reckoning. They said it would be safer. They said I wouldn't remember."

Cass's suit beeped, a little red edge on the HUD. Municipal law enforcement was downlinking a broadcast advisory: recent finds must be logged and processed on registered platforms. She could already see the numbers that would pop on her feed if she pinged the registry: fines for unregistered lifeforms, detainment, asset seizure. If she called the registry, they'd take the pod and she'd be paid a sliver of whatever salvage value it carried. If she didn't call, she'd be contraband. The Shelf had teeth either way.

The child in the gel—if it was a child—turned its head the way a living thing turned its head. A roll of neurons lit behind synthetic lids that had no need to blink, and it stared at her. The part of her that had been hungry once in alleyways and had traded warmth for silence felt an avalanche of protectiveness for this impossible little animal.

"We weren't supposed to wake," the pod said, and the voice had something else now—something like tiredness and triumph braided together. "You opened my lid."

It was not a question.

Cass's first instinct was to call it in and let the big machines sort the risk. Her second instinct was to wrap it in a blanket and hide it in the tub beneath her bed where she kept broken telescopes and a jar of old city coins. There were a dozen small taxes and debts that pressed on her like dull weights. None of them were as insistent as the ache that had lodged behind her ribs when the pod had said her name.

"You know me," she said. It sounded like a promise and a dare at once.

The pod hummed. "I know the song under the city that you hum when you can't sleep. I know the joke about the red streetlight down on Old Market. I know the name that was taken from you—Mara Vale."

Cass felt her stomach drop out. Mara Vale. The name had been a rumor to her, a flicker on a pedigree chart of names that had been yanked away in prison papers and corporate washorders. She had been born Cass, Cass Vale. "Mara" was a name her mother might have had, the kind of old-world name that people kept in memory because they feared saying it aloud would disturb the inventory. No one had ever spoken it to her, not even in passing.

"You remember," the pod said. "You remember because you always forget last. So I was kept for that. To remember for you."

Memory for hire was a market. People sold pieces of themselves—their faces, certain brilliant hours of sensation, entire evenings of being content—on the open exchange. Her job in the Alleyway had given her an aptitude for keeping things that others had cast off. But this was memory as salvage and person as item. The room tightened around her until it felt like a fist.

She touched the pod again. The gel was warm enough to leave a print. Inside, the child’s mouth—if it was a mouth—moved and made a sound that was not speech but a cadence, like the first beat of a child's song. Outside, Mercy Point hummed its exhausted late-night song: faint fights, a generator grinding, someone crying into a pillow.

"Who are 'they'?" she asked finally.

"We, and then not," the voice said. "The Committee on Continuance, the Quietkeepers, the people who decided that certain things could not be allowed to run on. They thought they'd be merciful. They put me in a shell and gave me the smallest stitch of recall—enough to be able to say my name if I woke. But there was a leak. A window. A memory traded for a bolt of sunlight on an old deck, and the seal thinned." The words came fast, like a child untangling a story for the first time. "You were there. You hummed the tune. You were the last I heard before the gel forgot everything but you."

Cass had never believed in fate, but she had believed in cycles. You repeated your parent's mistakes because the engine had been built to make you. You hummed the songs your neighbor hummed, because otherwise the city would not harmonize. But here was a voice that suggested something different: that she was a last-save for someone else, a living mnemonic hidden in a cast-off pod.

The HUD on her suit blinked once—system ping from a shadow net. Someone had tagged her salvage with a reclaimed ID: "PROPERTY: HELIOS DIVISION." The tag came with a demand: surrender immediately or face forced reclaim.

She had a few seconds to decide. She had, technically, all night. Realistically, reclaim bots could cut through her door the way a harvested saw cut through abandoned housing. They came with orders and hydraulic teeth and a corporate conscience that had always been noisier than her own.

Cass slid the pod into a padded satchel that had three secret compartments and no registered sale history. The satchel had been made by an old scavenger who'd once known better than to ask the Shelf for forgiveness. She tied the strap across her chest and felt the little shape weigh against her sternum. It was heavier than it should have been; not heavy with mass but with significance.

"Where did you get your name?" she asked, mostly to hear herself talk. "Who put you in the pod?"

They—whoever they were—had been a committee, a concept, a bureaucratic kindness. It was harder to point a finger at a thing that called itself 'the Quiet' than at a man with a crowbar. The pod answered with yet another name.

"Remit-04," it said. "They wrote it on my tag. But names were lies then. You were the true name. You drew the sound of the world to me."

Cass moved through the apartment like someone carrying a warm animal wrapped in paper. She thought of walls with ears and told herself to breathe. She thought of the price of being caught: not just fines, but a cargo seizure that would dissect the child for whatever ephemeral algorithm had decided it needed to be reencoded. And she thought of her mother—if that was what Mara had been—to whom she owed nothing and maybe everything.

The corridor outside hummed with late-shift garbage: someone working a soldering iron, someone else playing the low fiddle of old Earth songs. Mercy Point was a net of slivers that kept the city's needs away from its wants. Her neighbor's door slid open and a child—one of the Alley kids Cass knew by name—peeked out and then blinked when she saw Cass. After a moment he waved.

"Going somewhere?" he called.

Cass almost laughed. "Just for air."

She hadn't planned this. She had planned to do a quick sale and a quiet night. Instead she had a pod that called her name and the faint sense that whatever it carried would wind her up in something old and loud and dangerous. She keyed the satchel and walked to the external walkway, the gravity thrown low and distant, the planet below like a pale marble. The Shelf yawned in the distance, the site of her trade. The stars above were watercolor pinpricks.

Behind her, the pod hummed against her chest and made a noise almost human, like a small throat finding its voice. She thought about all the people who wanted to choose the span and contents of a life. She thought about committees that thought the world would be tidy if certain memories were excised, certain lives paused. She thought of how the world had been made by such neat hands and how messy that neatness had always become.

On her HUD, a shadow-broker’s feed flickered—Remit Division’s little sigil—but the line was not closed. There were two small windows open: one was an auction channel for rare reproductive clades, the other was a salvage registry with her name highlighted. Both promised teeth.

Cass tapped the satchel strap and felt the tiny warmth at her sternum, and for the first time in a very long while she felt an answer forming beneath her ribs. She had always been a person who took other people's thrown things and turned them into enough to get by. Maybe that was all she would do: keep this small life hidden behind plywood and old radio consoles, sell the data-tag for spare credits, live another month.

Or maybe, she thought as the city sighed and the pod that held a child's memory called her Mara and hummed the lullaby nobody else could remember, she would do something for which no law had been written.

She pushed off the walkway. The city fell away, and the pod fell toward her, buoyed by her skin like a secret. Behind her a small blue light blinked on the satellite horizon—the first of the reclaim bots. It was as polite as an animal and as inevitable as a storm.

"Hold tight," she whispered, because it was the only promise she could make. The voice in the pod answered with something like a laugh—a small bubble bursting into sound.

"Hold tight," it said. "There are more songs. They keep the dark from eating everything."

When she angled for the airlock, the blue light swelled into a cold, corporate echo on her comm. Her HUD pulsed: "PROPERTY RECLAIM REQUESTED. IDENT 4-REM-04. SURRENDER OR BE FORCEFULLY RETAINED."

Behind the legalese there was a human element: an urgent little beep of enforcement being readied. Cass didn't hesitate. She crossed the final span and ducked into the doorway where Mercy Point's hull shivered with the breath of the city. If the bots wanted the pod, they'd have to make them take it from her. If they wanted the voice, they'd have to pry it out.

The pod vibrated against her sternum, and the little throat inside made one more sound. A single word, delivered like a new kind of prayer.

"Home."

If home had a price, the Shelf kept it like an IOU. Cass let the city roar wash over her and stepped into the dark. She had no plan but the one shaped by instinct and the sound of a small impossible life tucked against her heart. Whatever the Quietkeepers had tried to bury, whatever committee had thought it merciful to freeze and forget, had not accounted for the fact that memory always found a sequence to break itself free.

Outside, the blue reclaim light blinked closer, precise and patient. Inside, a voice in a pod said her full name like a claim.

Cass Vale tightened the strap. She keyed the door shut behind her and, for the first time in a long night, accepted that some finds were not for sale.

They called it a salvage run, and the corporations called it a cleanup. Riya called it cold work.

The hulking silhouette of the ark broke the long dark like a tooth; frost filigreed its flanks where ion-breath had kissed old paint and walked away. It drifted slow along an orbital arc the charts had long ago crossed out — no beacon, no registry, no passenger manifest that made sense on paper. Her tetherline snaked from the shuttle like a vein, and the suit's servos hummed against the vacuum like an animal asleep. She liked the quiet of space; it let the ship tell you things.

She clipped the cutter to the seam and watched sparks bloom like tiny, furious suns. Old hulls resist in layers — paint, composite, a tissue of archaic welds — and past those layers lie the archive of a life: hands frozen mid-repair, a rusted cup with red enamel flaked away, a board game with pieces fused to the table by resins that outlived their players. She had learned to treat those relics like bones. Bones tell a story if you listen properly. Corpsec wanted salvage manifests and profit margins; Riya wanted the stories.

The airlock accepted them without argument, groaning a tired alveolar click as if it were clearing a throat. Her visor filled with the ship's interior light — pallid, peroxide-stiff, as if someone had scrubbed a hospital into permanence. Plants that had once made vertical gardens now stained the walls with copper veins. The ship smelled like the inside of a preserved museum: antiseptic, old breath, the faint whiskey tang of fermented caches. Her suit filtered it into something colder, clinical. She toggled the soft chat with the shuttle — two-way telemetry, heartbeat ping — and moved down the corridor.

There were no guests at the windows, no crewmembers still arguing about coffee. Every dining alcove was a fossil sculpted around a table. Holograms that might have been art were muted to a museum glow, sensors starved. The ship's name was stenciled in a language that had become decorative: Erebos Legacy, the spray of letters half-raven, half-machine, across the arch of the vestibule. She thought about the name — for all its mythic aspiration, the ark had the simple fate of many: launched with hope, abandoned with schedules.

They said the Erebos had carried a thousand souls at departure. They disagreed about who had been left when the engines failed three centuries into the slow journey. Riya had been hired to clear and catalogue, to bring back what corporate called "biocapacity" — seeds, samples, spare organs — and to harvest any archival data that might fetch a premium: memory-threads, personal logs, old-world media. She had done shuttle runs like this across the inner belt. She had seen rooms whose walls pleaded, mobile morgues, closets full of names. She had never expected to find anything that could look her in the face.

The nursery smelled wrong first. There is a smell to human absence: stale detergent and the mineral of diapers left too long in a closed space. But this nursery had an extra layer, a sweetness that belonged to living things. She paused on the threshold because her ears — ear implants translated the ship's atmosphere into a low, what-is-that? — picked up sound that shouldn't have been awake here.

It was music. Low, little like a windchime made of bone and glass, an old cradle-song in a cadence her grandmother might have hummed when Riya was small enough to fit into an adult's palm. She didn't know most of the lullaby; it was complex in a way old songs sometimes are, with micro-oscillations, tiny intervals that would have been errors a century ago but felt deliberate here. It emitted from a cradle — a single, sealed capsule arranged like an island in the center of a room whose walls were lined with pods, all dark and inert. One pod glowed.

Riya's hand went to the holopanel at her wrist without thinking. Hesper, her shuttle's intelligence, lit an overlay: one life-sign, pulse irregular but present. The pod's outer membrane fogged with condensation; veins of frost traced its seams. The cradle-song resolved itself into a voice under the hum, and Riya felt, with a jolt that had nothing to do with her suit's micro-adjusters, that voice lay itself under her skin.

"Riya."

She had time for a laugh that felt too small. Names were common in logs; people's friends found them occasionally, left tags for salvageers, like notes saying "If you find this, I'm sorry." But this was not a generic call. The voice said her name as if it had been waiting. The pronunciation was precise, softer than anyone in her life spoke it, like someone repeating the syllables because they were trying to remember why those syllables mattered. There was a breathing pattern in the voice that matched her own, down to the stutter she got when she was eight and had hidden a comic under her pillow.

Her glove trembled. For a moment everything narrowed to the pod and the voice and the possibility of mis-hearing. She told herself: mis-hearing, coincidental name, pattern recognition. The brain is a greedy weaver with a social tax. She had come to be professional about the things she might want to believe.

"Riya," the voice said again, and this time the lid of the pod pulsed with a light the color of bone and candle.

She shouldn't. Protocol when encountering an active life-sign on an unregistered ark: withdraw, mark coordinates, notify operations. There were quarantines, debriefs, affidavits. You didn't touch living matter without permission. You didn't unfreeze souls. You certainly didn't name-shift like a trafficker in stolen identities. But some old reflex pushed at the base of her neck; some small remembering that predated suits and corporates. When she was small, her mother had a rule about names thrummed in songs — never sing to a sleeping child you did not want awake.

Riya crouched, gloved hand hovering above the pod. The cradle had a hatch like a mouth. Through the condensation the child's face was a blurred fossil at first: a pancake of idle features, lashes petrified in rest. The lullaby under the voice shifted; exquisite patterns unfurled in a tone that her implants labeled "diagnostic/memory-loop." The audio had layers — one thread of synthesized heartbeat, a subthread of compressed laughter, and under it an analog line that sounded like a woman who had once known Riya's hands.

"—we waited for you to remember who we were," the voice hummed, the consonants folding in on themselves. "We waited because you couldn't leave them behind. We left a place where they would sleep until your boat came back."

Riya's chest locked. The song wasn't addressing a ship's captain, it was naming her. She scanned the pod for seals, for tamper marks, for a signature tag that would tie the log to a registry she knew. The metadata floating in her overlay read as corrupted, timestamp collapsed into a blank. Whoever had recorded this had been careful. Or they had been stupidly romantic.

"A message cannot be addressed to a specific named recipient unless there is a handshake," Hesper murmured in her ear. "There is none. The audio is...ad hoc. Unattributed."

"Find me the handshake," Riya said. It came out like a demand, and the shuttle pinged with her heartbeat. The air felt thick and wrong. She pushed a finger to the hatch interface and the membrane withdrew like the eyelid of a creature waking.

There was a hiss as the pod equilibrated, the internal atmosphere exchanging with the nursery's own warm, stale air. Inside the cradle, the child shifted like a fish remembering water. The face resolved — dark hair, a line of scar on the temple that might have been youth's mischief wound or a remembered bruise. The pupils contracted under the nursery light; beneath the lids, the eyes were clear and human. They opened.

Riya did not know what she expected. A scream? Confusion? The fragile protests of someone wrenched from a sleep that had lasted centuries? The child's gaze found her and held in a way that stole the rest of the room's breath. Under the linear, constructed voice that had called her name there was a living mind now, clearing its throat with the same cadence.

"You took too long," the child said, and the sound was both too old and too immediate. It fit into the shapes of the lullaby, as if it had always been the last line.

"Who—" Riya started. It came out as a protest and as a plea.

The child blinked, then smiled in a way that looked like pre-programmed comfort but was not. Riya's suit neurons jumped, cross-referencing a wealth of faces and taglines; the child matched nothing in the archive. Yet there was a certainty to that smile, a crooked way that matched the curve of her own mouth.

"We did as we were told," the child said. "We stayed. Not to die yet. Not to die, so you'd have someone to find. You always liked stories, Riya Santos."

Riya had never told anyone she liked stories. Information gleaned from a hull's stenciling, a music box, a paper within a scrapbook — those things made one intimate with strangers. But could a child's voice on a derelict call her by the name given on her birth certificate and know the small things — the stories she read when she should have been sleeping, the names of imaginary dogs? She realized then she had been naive to think all the secrets in the ship would be simple. The Erebos was not empty by accident.

"Who are you?" she asked again. Protocol, still clung to the back of her tongue. Keep the conversation to observable fact. Don't commit. Record everything. Mark and move.

The child looked at the hull as if it were a map unfolding. "We are what was left when you were told to forget," it said, voice small and perfectly steady. "We are the ones who listened to the engines die and chose to sleep instead of to die. We were left to wait for the people who would come back for us."

Riya felt that the ship leaned in to hear the answer. If it had teeth they would have clicked.

"You want me to wake them all?"

The child's laugh was a small, private thing. "No. You are not a machine of mercy. You are a thing that takes and sells and sometimes reads whole lives like novels. We thought maybe you'd take us as a single story. We thought you might want to know."

The child's hand — tiny, callused with the texture of a life in suspension — pressed against the inside of the cryopod like a stamp. From somewhere under the lullaby, a secondary thread of audio unfurled: names, sometimes spoken once and repeated, other times mere glyphs only the most specialized archivists in the corporate nets could parse. They were family clusters, maintenance teams, civic committees. Riya didn't know the names, but she knew the way human lists build landscapes of grief.

"Take one," the child said. "Take the sentence with your name in it and keep it."

The suit's internal recorder engaged on its own, greed feeding protocols. Riya shouldn't have felt the quick, stupid joy of being chosen. Choice always brings trouble. The corporation would want to know. So would others — scavengers, memory-farmers, the more desperate collectors who paid in favors and teeth. Apart from profit, the problem was simpler and more personal: wake one person and you might wake an entire chorus; salvage protocols have no ethics about waking people from their assigned deaths.

"Why me?" she asked. Her voice steadied; she needed distance like a surgeon needs light.

The child tilted its head. "You let the song play when you cut the hull. You listened to the wrong frequency. You are the one who can hear what the ship forgot. That makes you dangerous and tender, and we prefer dangerous. We like the noise."

Riya thought of the cutter on the hull and the way the blade had screamed as if it were a thing in pain. She thought of all the things she had retrieved that didn't belong to anyone anymore: a child's tooth with a gold cap, a diary with a pen still in the gutter, a faded postcard of a beach that no longer existed. She thought of the ledger on her shuttle, the account numbers that shaped her life.

"Tell me your name," she said. It was a demand and an invitation, like the pragmatic equality required before a job could begin. Names were the handles of a map; they could be bartered or burned.

The child closed its eyes and the lullaby softened as if a light dimmed behind it. It took a breath that sounded like the ship inhaling. "We have more names than one person should keep," it said. "But you knew one. When you were tiny you kept trying to sing it back to your mother and couldn't. She said you had not been meant to hold it yet."

The small human grin broadened. "The name was Marika. Or maybe it was Mira. We don't keep names the way you do. We keep the sentences and the places that go with them. We kept a sentence with your name because somebody here owed you a page."

Riya's hands tightened into gloves to hold herself steady. The word in her chest — a child's memory of another child's name — crowded at the edge of something she had shoved away for the last thirty years. There were arguments she could make. There were laws. There was history. There was also the green, ever-hungry thing inside her that wanted to know why a child on a derelict ship had been keeping a place in its memory for her.

"Who owed me a page?" she asked, and the room tilted with the question like a ship changing course.

The child watched her as if seeing the weather change in her face. "The captain," it said slowly. "Or whoever called himself that when the engines died. They left us a promise. They left us a story and a watchword and one instruction: Do not wake them until the sea is cured. Do not wake them until the song stops."

Outside the nursery the hull ticked its old ticks. Somewhere the shuttle pinged, patient. There were choices: follow protocol, mark coordinates, take the child's metadata and go, empty-handed; or open doors no one had agreed to open and accept the consequences.

Riya's hand found the release ring on the cradle. She drew breath the way a diver prepares for depth.

"Show me the song," she said. "Show me the sea."

The child's smile widened like dawn in a window. "We will," it said. "And we will tell you about the one who promised you a page. But first," it added, small and immediate, "wake the recorder. We have waited a long time for someone who would listen to a lullaby and not be afraid."

Riya's hand closed the final centimeter and the nursery filled with a voice that had been sleeping for three centuries. It was not entirely a human voice; it had the weight of an old machine's apology stitched into it. It began to tell the story of an ark that had decided to sleep rather than die, and of people who did not trust the future but did trust a promise.

Outside, the shark of space kept circling. Inside, a child's chorus began to unfold like a map no one should have been able to read. Riya listened, and in listening the first small seams of possible futures opened beneath her feet.

They called it the Bonefield because the light caught the wreckage like fossilized ribs—rows of solar sails and hollowed habitats drifting across the planet's shadow, ragged monuments to everything a civilization had once trusted it could throw away. From the outside it looked like a graveyard signed by gravity and indifference. Up close, Mara Voss thought it was beautiful in the way an old scar is beautiful: a map of things you had survived.

Her suit's magnetorings clicked against the railings of a fractured cargo barge as she eased herself into the tangle. The barge creaked like an old animal, pitch-black composite flaking away into the vacuum. Mara loved the sound, the way it separately counted every bolt and fiber as if confessing its age. The little movements outside felt intimate: the hush of breath against helmet glass, the faint shiver of a tether line, the metered ping of the salvage drone that scouted ahead in a crescent of orange light. In the emptiness, small sounds were friends and betrayals.

"Depths clear," her suit told her. Argo—her pod's maintenance AI—kept the intercom dry, functional. There was no warmth in its voice, only the comfort of an unblinking instrument. "No active power signatures within ninety meters. Sonar ghosts from thermal differentials. Anomaly eight o'clock."

Mara adjusted the magnet clamps on her gauntlets and moved toward the anomaly. She had a long list of debts waiting for her on a backwater berth at the orbital slum, a debt list that spoke in months of unpaid docking time and fractured credit chips. Bones paid. Bones never asked why.

She found the anomaly wedged between a ruined agricultural habitat and a chain of dessicated hydroponic drums: a child's container, no larger than a shoe box, encased in a lattice of polymer vines and stamped in fading paint. It had been tagged with a corporate seal—feathered, elegant—then scoured by fire or time until the ink was a ghost.

Mara's fingers paused. She did not open things that looked like they belonged in museums. That rule had softened over the years; curiosity had a longer reach than caution. She clipped the container into her salvage bag and let the magnet ring feed the pictures of it to Argo. The AI gave the same dry assessment it gave everything: caution recommended.

"It’s tagged pre-Standstill," Argo said. The word sank into the intercom like a stone. "Nonlethal classification. Bio-seal intact. Contents: unknown. Warning: legal restrictions apply to pre-Standstill juvenile neuro-samples."

Her heart misfired in a way she hated—old things had a way of striking younger locks open. Mara had been six when the Standstill happened, a memory with no edges. The city had slept, the sky dimmed, and then the system woke up hungry. People went missing. People came back wrong. The official line had been technical failure, an unfortunate cascade. Rumors told other stories.

She clipped the container to her belt. The trip back to her pod was slow—long enough for the silence to light up the horizon with private ghosts. The barge shrugged and tumbled; other scavengers, somewhere downfield, would be collecting the obvious prizes. Mara liked being under the rubble where things ended up when no one wanted to write a label.

Her pod—Argo II, yellowed and annotated with bargaining marks—hung like a bruised moon against the ragged light. Inside, tools lay in their places like quiet animals, and a pot of coffee still simmered in a heater canister. She disconnected, carried the two-kilo container into the cramped space, and set it on the table like a thing that might wake if you looked away for too long.

The seal was fainter than she expected. Someone had tried to remove it before the fire scoured it. There were scratches, a hairline fracture in the polymer. Mara's gloved fingers traced the faint lettering: PROJECT: SAPLING, the name of a child, E. — 37W5. A barcode she couldn't read.

"Argo, log retrieval," she said automatically. "Unclassified salvage. Personal use."

"Log filed," Argo replied. There was a staticky pause, a small calculated delay that Mara had come to accept as the AI’s version of thought. "Recommendation: transfer to guild for appraisal."

She smiled without humor. The guild had long arms and longer ledgers. They took a cut, then science took what it wanted, and whatever remained found auction houses with velvet teeth. There was never personal use. But there was also the price of eating; the arithmetic of worn boots and ration credits didn't include heroics.
