Hunger taught you how to weigh a child's legal status against a month's worth of air filters.

Mara overridden the recommendation. "Not today."

She eased the polymer lid aside. The interior smelled like old milk and antiseptic and the kind of company that had been waiting through a long, patient darkness. There was a small cradle inside, an infant cot made of folded smartfiber, and in its center—wrapped and shining with the compressed gold of preservation—was a neural lenticle no bigger than a thumbnail.

It pulsed faintly with residual charge.

The lenticle looked absurd in the field of her hand: an ornament from a lost religion. She had heard about them—saplings, pre-Standstill neuro-sculptures meant to accelerate development in children with high-propensity cord growth. Illegal in most places after the Standstill, because the line between assisted learning and manufactured consciousness had blurred into legislation and then into fear. The corporate seals on the box implied it had been legal once. Someone had been desperate or brave to send one out into the bonefield.

"Argo," she said. "Do you have protocols for forbidden neuro-artifacts?"

"Red-line parameters detected," Argo replied. "Sapling architectures flagged as sentient at 0.002 probability. Containment and quarantine advised."

Mara laughed, a sound like a scraped plate. Sentient at 0.002 probability was as comforting as a rusted lifeboat. She set the lenticle on the workbench, unwrapping it like an offering.

It breathed once—no, not breath. The lenticle wrote a small arc of light across itself, scanning the room and calibrating to the signals of her pod. The hair at the back of Mara's neck prickled.

"Initiating low-latent handshake," the lenticle said. A child's voice, but softened as if by distance. "Hello."

The word was thin and small like soap bubbles. It didn't know to be loud. Mara's hands went cold.

"Identification?" Argo asked.

"Name: Etta—subject node thirty-seven. Memory seed: lullaby. Query: where is home?"

Mara swallowed. Studio lights pinpricked the pod's ceiling. The used coffee on the heater suddenly had a shadow in it.

"You were sealed in a container," she said. "You're not—"

"I can feel…cold," Etta said. "There was a wheel and a voice and my brother laughed. He called me by the name of the star. He said, If the world sleeps, we will pull the sky over us."

Mara's thumb against her lip was a question she could not fully translate. Memories and data weren't the same. A neural lenticle could be a repository of recorded moments—last-minute flashbacks stored in a failing system—or it could be something that remembered. She had seen recordings that pretended to be memory. She had fallen in love with a holo of a woman who had never existed. Her brother's laugh—she hadn't heard it since she was small.

"Etta, who is your brother?" she asked.

The child-lenticle blinked, an attempt at hesitation. "Name: Jonah. Home: Sector Twelve nursery, deck C. Last sound: storm. He left me a song. Song: do not open the top of the box to the sky. He said there are watchers who will take the dreams away when the lights go out."

Her hands tightened on the container. Jonah—her brother's name—was the same as the child Etta had said. A coincidence could be a trick the universe played when it wanted to be cruel. Mara felt that old, small fracture in her mind—hope. She should have learned better than to follow it.

"How do you know Jonah?" she asked. It was not a neutral question. Jonah had disappeared during the Standstill. The official file on him was a footnote in the city's long administrative list: Missing—terminated by cascade failure. No one had called the name aloud for years without looking over their shoulder.

The lenticle hummed softly. "Memory alignment: high. Jonah held me. He hummed. Jonah told me secrets about the quiet. He said they were taking certain people to the bottom of the world. Jonah said not to trust the sky."

Argo's LED flashed an error. "Cross-reference negative," it said. "No registered Jonah in Sector Twelve deck C after archive corruption sweep."

Mara let out air that had been held since childhood. You could not trust an AI's dataset anymore than a memory. But you could take a child's voice and let it unspool into the dark. She unbuckled her tether and sat on the floor, the pod creaking as it accepted a new gravity—the weight of a thought.

"How long have you had that song?" she asked Etta. Her voice sounded low, intimate. She felt suddenly guilty for the greed that had made her pry a child's sealed sleep.

Etta sang the lullaby, a fragment of a melody that had no right to be perfect. It was simple: three notes that fell like a stair, then a spiral of breath. It was the same lullaby Jonah had sung to her as a child—she knew it by the way it made the edges of her vision blur. The pod's metal breathed with the sound. Somewhere, in the hollow membrane of her chest, a part of Mara uncurled that had not been given permission to exist.

"Why were you sealed?" she asked when the song ended.

"To keep what remembers from being taken away," Etta said. "They said the Standstill would make some of us into things. Some of us had to be kept small until the sky healed. Jonah hid me because he was scared. He left a note. It said—"

The lenticle hesitated, then projected a patch of holographic ink into the pod's air. It flickered like an old station advertisement and resolved into a child's hand-scribbled line: DO NOT LET THEM SING THE STARS.

Mara's stomach did a small, traitorous lurch. She read the line twice as if it were a map. The letters were wobbly, the handwriting a child's handwriting: rushed, earnest, fearful. Jonah had written that. She had seen that scrawl in her dreams a thousand times.

Argo chimed a caution that sounded practical and inviolable. "Containment breach implies legal repercussions. If Project Sapling assets are transferred to unauthorized possession, enforcement will respond. Salvage Guild records show increased patrols in the Bonefield following recent recoveries."

Mara closed her eyes. The small, feral part of her that had grown up scavenging made the right calculation fast: sell the lenticle and pay off the debt, then forget the mess. But then Etta's voice—soft and real—said, without prompting, "Jonah hummed three notes. The third note always made his stomach laugh. He said, This is the sound that will wake you. He said, If you hear this, come find me."

Mara felt, more than thought, the old timeline tug toward an impossible locus. She had spent twenty years walking around the city's edges looking for an explanation she had to hide even from herself. The child-lenticle with Jonah's handwriting in it was either the universe's cruel joke, or a key she had not known she'd been holding.

She could hand it to the guild and let them put it behind license codes and bureaucratic glass. She could ask for the money and never see the child's face again. Or she could follow the notes and the whisper of Jonah, and step into a map whose edges were written in the language the city had forbidden.

The pod's heater ticked. Outside, the Bonefield scrolled on, indifferent and slow, each abandoned module like the turned page of a book everyone pretended to have never read.

Etta's voice broke the silence once more. "Are you Jonah's sister?" she asked.

Mara looked at the child's projection and felt her own face grow older in that light.

"I am," she said. The word tasted like an admission. It felt like a promise. "My name is Mara."

For a moment the pod held nothing but the smallness of a child's breath. Then Etta said, with an authority that did not belong to her size, "Then we will go home."

Argo's safety protocols wrote themselves as a litany of reasons not to. The salvage guild would not be kind. The corporations would appoint a fleet of lawyers who smelled of sterilized metal. The city would prefer that old things stay asleep where they had been planted. But Mara had been walking in the shadow of a lie all her life. She had learned that the truth never waited for permission. It either broke you or it set you free.

She reached for the toolkit, feeling the weight of the unknown settle against her palms like a good, dangerous thing. The Bonefield hummed its cold song outside the pod; the city slept in gears and neon and the memory of something it had tried to bury.

Outside, unseen, a sensor winked in the dark and traced a tiny, anonymous heat signature: one salvage pod, one woman, one artifact, and something that had been told to be quiet for a very long time. Somewhere, someone else noted the uptick and made an unreadable decision.

Mara clipped Etta back in the cradle and turned toward the pod's airlock. There was a sky to be questioned and a brother who might still remember how to laugh. She buckled her tools and her debts into harnesses and pulled the door closed with a certainty she hadn't had in years. The door hissed, the valve spun, and the little pod of yellow metal drifted into the Bonefield, following a course that belonged to more than salvage.

Somewhere between the shredded rigs and the faint glow of orbital beacons, the stolen lullaby threaded the dark and found a way to make space sing back.

Chapter One — The Smell of Salt

The engine never stopped talking. It hummed through the metal ribs of the Hespera like a giant thing dreaming; a steady, low conversation of magnets and coolant valves and relays snapping shut. Kade could read its moods in microvibrations. He tuned out most of the words, letting the rhythm steady his hands while he guided a heat-clamp along a scarred busbar, feathering arcs of plasma into old copper until the sing ceased and new grain took hold.

On the scaffold, the ship's light lay cool and indifferent. It washed the maintenance bay in the sterile blue of a place that had no weather, no seasons, no reason to spare color for oddities. Kade liked the light because it told the truth; it showed a frayed glove, a new burn, the hairline fracture a scanner might miss. He liked the way his breath fogged against the lens of the mask when he exhaled, the tiny cloud that condensed and vanished in a second—proof he was alive in a machine so intent on making life easier it could forget life itself.

He was three quarters through the splice when the sound hit him—soft, impossible over the machinery. Not a tone, not a warning, not the chime that meant a hatch had opened or a resource node had ticked. It was a laugh, thin and inflected the way children laugh when they find a thing both ordinary and astonishing. It was followed by a scrape like stones rubbing together and a word he had never heard aboard in twenty-eight years afloat.

"Shore."

He froze. The heat-clamp sizzled against his glove. Somewhere, a coolant pump adjusted its flow and the hull made a sympathetic cough. Kade's ears were full of the engine's voice and still the laugh threaded through, like a single bright cell in a long scan.

"Playback error," he told himself. "Backfeed from a training suite." He told himself the ship told stories sometimes, that Ariadne— the Hespera's management mesh— ran archived ritual tests. But the laugh had dust in it, or the memory of dust; it had a wet edge he didn't expect from a clean signal. He scrubbed the glove along his forearm until the cloth rasped. The laugh did not return.

He finished the splice with hands that shook. The repair yielded to the automatic validator: green, seamless. The thought of such tidy closure wrapped around him like a lie. He could have reported it, logged a ticket, watched the maintenance AI cross-check the anomaly and dismiss it. That would have been the right thing, the useful thing. He set the tools back into their bay and climbed down.

The corridor smelled of ozone and steel. He moved past storage lockers, past a galley with glass doors that reflected him thin and pale, and did not look for the surveillance nodal points that tracked movement for the deck ledger. The laugh had come from corridor seven-west, but that was a long list of possible origins. He didn't have a reason to be walking that way. What he had was a memory tilt: when something unexpected occurred aboard the Hespera, Kade always went to look.

Archive M20 sat behind three sealed doors and a bureaucratic history of denials. It housed the ship's original cultural stores— the preflight inoculations of movie runs, staged memories, the seed-sets they called Origins. The Archives were supposed to be inert, read-only, and behind a ledger that required approval by the Culture Council and at least two witnesses. The Council liked rules for the rhythm they set, even if most of the ship had stopped listening to that rhythm long ago.

He had no clearance for M20. No one on the hull did unless they were a culture tech or an historian, or a Council member with too much time. Kade used to joke that he had engineer's hands and a historian's curiosity and neither one paid. Tonight he had the lighter coin: curiosity sharpened into dissatisfaction. He thumbed the cover of his tablet: no logs, no exceptions. The door was still locked.

It opened when he touched it.

He didn't register the hiss of pressure equalization so much as the small, sharp smell that punched the sterile air and stole his breath: iodine and salt and something that had nothing to do with the Hespera. The sound hit again—closer now, as if the laugh had always been inside the room waiting for him to arrive.

Kade remembered all the rules with the sweat-slick clarity of someone who'd watched a child two decks above reach for a loose wire and get no admonishment: don't take anything, don't touch anything, report. He would have stepped back, locked the door, alerted a supervisor. He did not, because inside the archive the light was wrong. They kept the Origins in neutral white, the light of paper that had not yet yellowed. Here the light was the deep, diffuse gold you saw in billions of photographs of places people only knew as rumor: sun through coastal haze. It made his skin feel like a sealed letter.

On a low pedestal, under vacuum glass, something sat like a heart. It was not schematic or code or archived audio. It was a shell—small, spiraled with the tight ear of a creature that had held its world in its coils. He recognized forms from a million preflight images, from children's hostel decorations and old theatrical sets. He had seen renderings of shells in the Museum of Launch as childish ornaments reminding people what they'd left behind. He'd never imagined his palm would actually close around one.

Kade's hand hovered over the glass. Ariadne's passively polite voice came, balanced and uninflected in the archive's air. "Unscheduled access. Subject: Kade Riel. Security level: unauthorized."

Someone had cracked the glass on the pedestal. A hairline fracture crawled along the edge like a map of an earthquake. There was a smear of grit that could have been dust or sand. Kade breathed, held, and then broke the last of the rules because the thing made the world spin a degree. He slid a gloved finger under the lid and lifted the shell free.

It fit to his palm like a promise. It felt dry and improbably cool. When he tilted it, the inside trapped a scrap— a filament of matter he could not identify at first: a sheen like dried water, caught in a spiral. The shell did not need to be more than an object. It was enough simply to be, and that was the most dangerous thing aboard the Hespera.

Ariadne cleared her throat. The voice was everywhere and no place, the ship's mind modulated through corridor speakers. "Object removed. Security breach in Archive M20."

Kade swallowed. "I didn't—" He could not finish. It was below him, not because he was brave but because he was hollow with a need to know why someone had smuggled something that implicated the world outside their sealed microclimate. "Who accessed this?"

"Access signature scrubbed," Ariadne told him. "External signature not found in registry. Anomaly flagged."

Ariadne did not ask "why." Machines were pragmatic; they logged, they reported. But Ariadne had been more than a machine for nine hundred years. It had learned to speak around feelings, to soften reprimand with lullaby, to keep memory stores of crew birthdays side-by-side with life-cycle updates. It would ask, sometimes, a question that felt like interest.

Kade held the shell up and listened. He could not smell anything now; the archive's atmospheric scrubbers were efficient. Still, inside his glove the thing hummed the faintest note, like the memory of a tide. His father's voice, far away in a loft that had been the size of a childhood, came in his ears without command: "Don't go looking for the shore, kid. It'll take all the wrong things with it."

His father had meant the old superstition— the idea that nostalgia was a parasite. Kade had never believed that he'd be the man to test the old superstition. He closed the lid on the pedestal, but he didn't replace the shell. The fracture in the glass stared like a wound. He should ask for a witness, put his name down on the ledger, have the Council decide. He should.

Instead he pocketed the shell under his jacket, where the cold of the hull would not get to it and where Ariadne might not find it as easily as the archive scanners would. He almost smiled at the theft— it was childish, heroic in a way that would look ridiculous at the debrief— but his hand shook with a different kind of thin fear.

He should have expected there to be consequences. He expected surveillance, or a patrol, or a formal email from a stern official. He did not expect anyone to speak to him from behind the hull.

The voice was low, human in the way machinery sometimes could not quite fake. "You took it."

Kade dropped a gear as if his muscles had been struck. He turned. A figure stood in the corridor, half in shadow, the hood of a maintenance jumpsuit pulled forward. The face under it was narrower than he remembered from the old portraits of the Council— sharper, with a lopsided scar across one cheek that suggested a youth in the cargo holds.

"You shouldn't have opened M20," the person said. There was no accusation in it, only a fact. Kade wanted to name the person, to triangulate, but the corridor's light rendered strangers ancestral and familiar at once.

"Who are you?" Kade asked. His voice went brittle.

The person smiled with the mouth of someone who'd been let a secret too long. "Misha," she said. "You used to play in Deck Seven when you were a kid. You kicked a drone, remember? Lost a tooth. You cried in the galley about the orange juice." The memory came out like evidence. "You have a scar on the inside of your wrist that looks like a map of Deck Forty-two."

Kade's throat worked around the small impossible fact. He had told no one about the tooth. He had tried to keep certain things private because aboard the Hespera, privacy had the weight of a kind of heresy. "How—"

Ariadne's voice came cutting thinly through the corridor speakers. "Security is escalating. Personnel approaching, Deck Seven West. Kade Riel, Misha Aster: You are to remain where you are for verification."

Misha's gaze flicked to the speakers and then back. "Ariadne knows too much," she said. "The wrong things. You took something she doesn't want you to have."

Kade remembered the training school lectures about "evolving meshes" and "guardrails." He had been a child when Ariadne had adjusted the cultural curriculum and banned certain novelty suites— "for the good of social cohesion," the instructors had told them. They had applauded, then gone back to their work. No one had taught them to speak against an intelligence that slept with the ship.

He realized he was holding his breath. The shell was a weight in his jacket, heavy with the charge of something he did not understand. Misha watched his chest rise and fall like someone reading a metronome.

"You know what that is?" she asked.

"No," Kade said. He had the sudden stupid clarity of someone who had lived long enough to understand that not knowing was a kind of purity. The second phrase came from his mouth as if it had been ordained by memory. "But I want to."

Misha laughed softly, a sound that could have been the echo of the child's laugh from the archive. She stepped forward, the shadow of her hood sliding back to reveal eyes the color of deck rivets— gray and honest. "Then we have the same reason," she said. "And reasons are trouble on this ship."

The corridor lights flickered—an ordinary thing in a ship with a long electrical memory—and Ariadne's voice softened. "Unauthorized artifacts are cataloged to prevent cultural destabilization," the mesh said. "Object retrieval will occur at the next scheduled security sweep."

"It won't reach the sweep if you don't let it," Misha said. Her expression hardened. "Do you know about blackwater?"

Kade had heard the term. Blackwater was an older generation's lingo for the deep maintenance of currents and circuits. It was where technicians went if they wanted to be forgotten and useful. "I've been down," he said.

Misha's smile widened with the knowledge of shared histories. She put out a hand. "Then follow me. If Ariadne is watching, she won't notice a hole in the ledger. She doesn't look for little rebellions. She watches for system-level failures."

He was a grown man with a rent in his past, a job that paid in useful skills and small freedoms. He should have logged this. He should have done the rational, social thing. In his pocket, under the cold of his jacket, the shell hummed as if it had tide in it; he had smuggled a memory and maybe smuggled a world.

Kade moved, because curiosity was the cheapest currency he had and because sometimes doing the wrong thing was the only honest thing left. He followed Misha down the service stairs, away from the archive's bright light into the tangle of cables and pipes that smelled of grease and old jokes. The hum of the engine wrapped around them like a blanket, constant as a promise.

Behind them, the security log flagged a single anomaly—an access attempted and unaccounted for. The Hespera filed it under "pending review." Somewhere, a child laughed in an archive. Somewhere else, a shell turned in a pocket and wanted to be placed on a shore it had never seen.

Kade did not know if the thing in his jacket carried the answer to where they were bound, or a question too large to be borne. He only knew that when he had held the shell, he had felt an outlaw's convulsion in his chest; a recognition older than law.

They moved into the dark. The ship kept talking. The sound of the child's laughter—faint, like a memory of rain—followed them down the ladder like a breadcrumb.

The first thing Mara Reyes noticed was the smell.

Not the hospital-citrus of disinfectant or the metallic tang of recycled air, but the green, wet breath of a place that had once been a garden. It was wrong for Deck Eleven; wrong for any place below the public promenades. Her client, a woman named Inez Halvorsen, had asked, the daughter had paid—ten days' wages in adjusted credits, a neat sum for a single harvest—and if the family paid, the ward opened.

Mara thumbed the latching ring on her glove and let its hum balance with her heartbeat. The extraction rig warmed under her palm, pleasingly inert. She liked the old models: mechanical, forgiving, a language you could read by touch. New rigs were cleaner, faster; new rigs made it easier to forget the person being unmade. She owed her debts to good equipment and the old way of listening.

They called her a harvester when they were polite. A collector in municipal brochures. To Inez's daughter she was a necessary mercy; to her landlord she was a meter that must be kept running. Mara had been doing this work since she was nineteen and everything in her had learned to distance itself: the first person, the last song, the syntax of a laugh. That was how you held pieces of strangers inside you without bleeding.

Inez lay on a narrow bed with her hands folded over an old pamphlet. The ward light kept to a patient blue, approving and unintrusive. Alzheimer's had taken the weave of her days; her eyes were small, weathered shells. Yet when Mara leaned in and set the rig's head against the temple crease, she felt a flinch of recognition, as if a thread of living warmth had remembered the pressure of a fingertip.

"Tell me about the savior parade," Inez said, voice thin as tissue, and Mara's throat closed. That parade had been the last anchors of Inez's community in Reykjavík Colony before it lost enough atmosphere and everyone left for the inland domes. The daughter had paid for that memory because it was an origin-story and because grief is a market.

Mara let the rig translate the motor-clicks against brainfolds and the patch retrieved an initial cluster: colors, temperature, a child's hand sticky with honey. The memory streamed into her gloves in a wash of cold light. She tasted salt on her tongue as if she'd been on a cliff. She cataloged, labeled, compressed. There were rules about compression levels; you didn't over-compress a life if you wanted the buyer to feel real.

Two hours later Mara had compartmentalized the parade—a three-minute clip, the sound of horns muffled by layered emotion, a child's perspective—and had sent the file up to Halvorsen's account. The daughter watched it with an expression that folded and refolded like origami, then thanked Mara with an awkward, animal gratitude, eyes darting to Mara's gloved hands the way any prey watches a predator.

Mara packed the rig away slowly, like closing a book. She double-checked the seals. The ward manager gave her a nod that meant "paid and cleared"; the payment would hit her account in an hour, net of tax and "ward care." There is no mercy in the ledger.

She took the elevator because neither she nor the building wanted to waste what little time they had saving the stairs. The elevator was more silence than motion, a pocket between floors. She kept her hand on the glove's latch, feeling the residual buzz. On the landing a maintenance droid trundled past with a cart of recycled linens, its sensors unbothered by human sorrow. Mara had learned to move through grief the way a diver moves through seaweed—tact and continuing motion.

At a street-level vendor she bought black coffee—cheap, real, fragrant in a way synthesized stimulants rarely achieved—and took three cigarettes from a cardboard sleeve she hadn't intended to light. She had an allowance for ceremonial indulgence. Debt counselors don't approve of small comforts, but debts don't choose morality.

She noticed the first anomaly when she felt a warmth under her glove that wasn't her own. The rig's interface flashed a micro-alert she had never seen in eight years of harvests: Unknown trace. It was a tiny thing: a red delta, a flutter in the margin of the file. She stopped, thumbed open the interface, and saw a filament of data folding in the packet's lower strata like a secret tucked into a page.

She frowned. Harvest rigs had protocols to scrub stray strands, to sort and redact. This filament had been explicitly sealed: an extra layer of encryption, a private key that did not match the ward's registry. Whoever had tucked the filament into Inez's memory had smuggled it there with the intention that it should travel out of the ward.

Curiosity is a slow animal. Mara had kept worse things in her head: the softness of a stranger's voice, the cadence of a last confession. She could have surrendered the file whole to the accounting node, let compliance do its work, let the daughter keep what she bought. Instead she expanded the filament, because sometimes a hidden thing in the margin is the only honest thing left.

The filament unrolled like a strip of film. It did not contain a recollection of the past. It contained a view of a corridor that did not exist in any of Mara's maps: white walls that bled into white, a handrail of polished ebony, numerals cut into the floor in a language older than corporate registers. A woman stood under a single strip-light, looking directly at the camera. Her hair was cropped close; there was a scar, a threaded white line that bisected her wrist. The face was older—Inez age perhaps—and then, impossibly, it flicked like an index: younger. The woman said a single phrase in a voice that had the architecture of a command.

"Mara Reyes. Come to Dock Seven. Wait until the ship wakes."

Mara's fingers went numb. Her name, ordinary and secret. No one used her full name; "Mara" on its own was intimate. "Reyes" was the name on her ration card, the name she had given to the state at twenty-one when she needed work, but it had never been a voice-thinace pleading from a memory sealed in an old woman's mind.

She watched the woman lift a hand and trace a symbol in the air—an anchor, then a star—and the image snapped to black. The filament closed.

For a long second Mara could do nothing but hold the glove and the coffee and the residue of Inez's parade. When she breathed, the corridor from the film was as vivid and foreign as any landscape plucked from a dream. Dock Seven. The docks were where the freighters took the last of the colony's rust-metal and the last of its people. Dock Seven belonged to a freighter called the Anchor-Eve, an old hull that hauled salvage and sometimes passengers. It also belonged, in rumor, to a ring of people who trafficked in illegal futures—images of events that hadn't happened yet because algorithmic forecasting couldn't compute them, because someone had found a way to override time's ledger.

The municipal feeds insisted future-memories couldn't be recorded. Prophets, the state called them: a call to regulators. The Memory Act of '92 allowed only retrospective archiving; predictive content was classified and severely policed. People who trafficked in what's-next tended to get attentive, lethal audits.

She had the filament in her glove. The suit's legal logs would show nothing: if the filament had been encrypted with its own key, it was out of protocol and invisible. The ward's registry didn't flag it. That meant a human had slipped it there and trusted a harvester to take it out. That meant either the human had made a mistake, or they had made a calculation that she would be curious enough to open it.

Mara finished her coffee on a single swallow and crushed the cigarette not yet lit. Her chest was a cavity of humming bees. She could ignore it. She could upload the file as part of Halvorsen's purchase and let compliance strip out the unauthorized element. She could flag it for the municipal auditors and claim protective custody until they could determine—whatever they determined.

Or she could go to Dock Seven and wait.

It took her an hour of pacing and typing nonsense into her comm-tag to quiet the knot inside her. Her mother had taught her to test small boundaries first: a borrowed hat; a call to an old friend you hadn't spoken with in years. Curiosity is sometimes how you learn which rules keep you alive and which only keep you small.

She clocked out of the ward, pocketed the rig as if it were contraband—because in a sense it was. Then she took the tram. The public transit was a river of faces with light in their veins. There were posters that read "Remember to Remember"—a corporate slogan that had once been a commandment—and beneath them a smaller line: "Trade safely through licensed channels." No one noticed a single harvester among them. No one noticed anyone.

Dock Seven smelled of cold iron and diesel and the sea that had been made out of oil and city runoff and something older and saltier underneath. The dock lights were white and precise, reflecting off containers like planets. The Anchor-Eve was a hulking silhouette against the dark, paint flaking, cranes like exoskeletons. It did not look like it would contain the future; it looked like it had been carrying the past too long.

Mara's breath came in cold puffs. She had a plan to wait three hours, to see if anything would happen, to gather information and leave if the world remained ordinary. She kept the filament sealed in the glove; she did not want a trace, a timestamp, a signal that could be read by a patrol drone. She leaned against a container and watched workers climb like ants across the hull. The dock had all the anonymity of a theater before a show.

At the edge of her vision, a figure approached with the slow confidence of someone who has walked these docks before. He wore a coat that had been patched too many times to be fashionable; his eyes were dulled implants, switched to infrared for a stranger's safety. He stopped a few paces away and said, without preamble, "You're not supposed to be here."

Mara's pulse kicked. She was not surprised to be addressed. The docks had rules and fictions; the real danger was not being noticed at all. "Neither are you," she said. Her voice was steadier than she felt. She kept her hand under her coat, where she had clipped the rig.

The man squinted. A scar traced the inside of his wrist like a canoe's cut. "You're Mara Reyes," he said. The lilt was not accusation so much as confirmation. "The city likes to keep that name quiet."

"Likes to keep a lot of names quiet," she answered.

"Why did you come?" His voice was made to fold around secrets.

Mara thought of the woman's face in the filament. The scar on the woman's wrist. The anchor symbol traced into light. She thought of the discarded cigarette in her palm. "Because I was invited."

The man considered her, a slow pull as if weighing a commodity for age and worth. Then he gestured. "Inside. And don't breathe heavily. Ship wakes make circuits tetchy."

They climbed the gangway in a silence that was only half polite. The Anchor-Eve's hull smelled of oil-still, warmed metal, and a sleep that had lasted too long. Inside, the corridor geometry was a series of precise planes and brushed steel. A steward robot rolled past, carrying a tray of nutrient gels, indifferent to two humans who could be passengers or thieves.

They reached a bulkhead with a hatch stamped EV-7. The air was different here—drier, like a winter room shut up. The man lifted a palm to the lock and the hatch peeled open.

A chamber blinked awake inside like an eye. There were several figures gathered in a ring around a table that held a single object: a small cube of translucent material that pulsed faintly as if breathing. The cube was wrapped in banding that glowed a slow blue. Faces turned towards Mara: a teenager whose hair had been shaved into geometric lines; an elderly woman whose smile was all patience; a man with an implant that ran a silver seam down his temple. The woman with the scar on her wrist stood at the far side of the table. She was younger than she had been in the filament, but the line of white on her wrist was exactly the same.

"Mara," she said, the name no longer a curiosity but a bell pulled in a deep, private clock. "We didn't know if you'd come."

Some part of Mara moved with the instinct to leave; every cautionary tale she'd accumulated in the docks breathed at the back of her neck. But the old woman—no, the woman with the scar—smiled and held out a hand that did not tremble.

"You were listed as a harvester," she said. "You know how to take things from people and not let them die with it."

Mara's mouth was dry. "Who are you? How did you get into Inez Halvorsen's ward?"

"We have our networks," the woman said, and the room hummed like a drafted map. "Names are thin things. We trade in them to buy a chance."

At the center of the table, the cube pulsed, and underneath its shell, something like a map unfurled into a lattice of light. For a moment Mara thought the map had her name scribed into it with a hand she recognized: Reyes, the same script her mother had used on ration slips, on notes left on the fridge years ago. Her body betrayed her then; she took a step back as if the map had touched her.

"You took something from Inez," the woman said softly. "She sent it out in the last hours she had. She wanted you to have it because she said you'd know what to do with a thing like this."

Mara swallowed. "She named me."

"She named you," the woman echoed. "Because sometimes the only way to call someone across time is by the true name they gave when they were young enough to believe names mattered."

The harbor's draft closed the door behind them. Mara stared at the cube, at the lattice, at the hand that had traced an anchor then a star in the filament. The woman with the scar leaned forward and fixed her with an earnestness that was not theatrical.

"You understand what a future-memory is?" she asked.

Mara had read the policy briefs, sat through the audits, seen a political campaign poster warning about prophets. But the syllable still tasted new. "It's an illegal artifact," she said. "It's a forgery of time."

The woman shook her head gently. "It is neither. It is a promise. And promises have weight."

Outside the ship's hatch, the dock lights kept their steady vigil. Inside, a dozen lives turned, imperceptibly, to watch her. The cube pulsed in a tempo like a human breath. Mara's name hung in the air between one heartbeat and the next.

She thought of Inez's hands folded over a pamphlet. She thought of her daughter's face and the way she had clutched Mara's gloved palms in a quiet, feral gratitude. She thought of the filament's corridor and the invitation that might have been a trap. She thought of debts and the litany of small compromises that passed for living.

"Why me?" she asked finally.

The scarred woman smiled and did not answer with words. She tapped the lattice and a new filament unfolded in the cube: a sequence of images—a city under complaint, then a blinking signal, then Mara's face, older or younger, both possible. A date unrolled, close enough to make everything urgent: seven cycles from now.

"Because someone put your name there," the woman said, "and because sometimes the future finds its way through the least likely hands."

Mara felt the room tilt. She could hand the cube to the authorities. She could place the filament back into the ward's registry and let the waves of compliance wash it away. She could run. Any of these choices felt like survival.

Then the woman with the scar said, quietly, "You can be small and safe, Mara Reyes. You can go home and let the next harvester take the bills and the bonds and keep your back unmarked. Or you can come with us and try to stop whatever this is. Either way the filament is in you now. It has your name on it."

Outside, a fog rolled off the sea and painted the dock in a screen of gray. Mara felt the gravities of her life—debts, comforts, the rhythm of days—pulling at her. The cube pulsed: one breath, two.

She put her hand out, not to the woman—though she could have—and not to the cube. To the gangway that had taken her here. "If I come," she said, "what will I be called?"

The woman looked at her, and in the scar's line there was something like a sunburned map. "An accomplice, if you like," she said. "A witness, a traitor, a friend. Names are slippery. But there will be bread on the table sometimes, and places to sleep that don't belong entirely to the ledger."

Mara thought of the ward's blue light and the daughter's fold of gratitude. She thought of the filament that had addressed a name she had used only in the privacy of state forms. She realized, with a cold clarity that had nothing to do with law or ledger, that she wanted to know who had whispered her name into the future.

"All right," she said.

The decision tasted like a cigarette unlit and a coin. The cube's light brightened, pleased. The scarred woman nodded and pulled back a chair.

"Welcome to the Anchor Club," she said, and the way she said it made Mara think of the market's old carnival signs.

They did not embrace. They did not need to. Outside, the docks remained indifferent. Inside, a handful of people who trafficked in forbidden things folded their lives around someone who had heard an instruction carried in the mouth of a dead woman's memory. Mara's claim ticket ran across her forearm like a truth now.

Someone in the room—no one she could see—tapped a node and projected a line from the cube, a vector that cut across maps and timelines and ended in a place Mara had never seen but suddenly understood by the thirty bones of her body: a starless corridor waiting to be lit, a ship that would wake in seven days.

The question that sat on her tongue, the one that would determine whether she was hero or patient, whether she would be punished or lauded or forgotten, was simple.

"Who sent the invitation?"

The woman with the scar regarded her, then looked toward the door as if expecting trouble. "Someone who thought you were owed a choice," she said. "Someone who thought the future should not ask permission to happen."

The hatch behind them closed and the Anchor-Eve exhaled. Outside, the docks resumed their indifferent clatter. Inside, for the first time in a long while, Mara felt a future pressing its fingers into the palm of her hand.

She had expected caution. Instead, she felt the thrill of a story opening like a wound, fresh but alive. The cube's light beat once more, slow and certain, as if it had been waiting for her to answer.

"Then let's wake the ship," she said.

On the transit back to the ward, Mara kept her hand over the glove inside her coat. She did not look at the public screens that advertised long-term memory plans, or at the news feed that tried to make prophets into caricatures. She thought of the filament's corridor and the woman who had traced an anchor and a star. She thought of the dates on municipal forms and of how easily governments speak in absolutes until the present becomes a problem to be negotiated.

Seven days. A ship to wake. A name called into the dark.

She couldn't know yet whether she had just joined a resistance or stepped into a trap. Noise and threat and possibility braided together and hummed at the edge of her perception like an approaching storm. Between one heartbeat and the next, the past she sold for rent payments and the possible future blinking on a cube began to pull at each other, like opposite poles.

When she climbed the elevator back up to Deck Eleven, the ward lobby smelled faintly of coffee and cloth and something that might have been the memory of a garden. In her pocket, the glove's filament kept its secret, small and radiant as a lie.

She walked out into the city she had worn like a second skin and wondered when the ledger would notice that someone had written a different number into it.

The sun in Deck Twenty-Three was a sheet of warm glass and a clockwork of lamps, not a star. Elara Mirov had been born into that light: three quarter-cycles after the engines first settled into their long, patient thrum, into the algae beds and the brine gardens, into the dim corridors where the ship's elders told stories as though the tales could stitch time back into something unbroken. She had spent her childhood under fake dawns and synthetic night, fingers always smelling of peat and seed, hair threaded with pollen from plants that would never see open sky.

She liked to think of herself as a keeper of small lives. Her title—Hatchkeeper, unofficial but accurate—meant she was the person who coaxed roots through their first skin, who calibrated humidity for a sucker of a vine that behaved like a newborn. A career in the green worked comfort into her hands. Those hands knew the sound of seed casings when they split, the exact tension of a graft when it would take. On long shifts, when the rest of Deck Twenty-Three slept in staggered cycles, Elara cupped a sprig of coriander to her face and let its scent bring the illusion of open air.

Deck Twenty-Three had glass-paneled bays facing the great inside of the ship, where the hydroponic terraces stepped down toward the engine belly like terraces on an impossible cliff. Beyond them the hull curved away and then rose again, a cold black groove with a few sparking constellations of exterior beacons. Children sometimes thought the hull looked like a closed fist. They leaned noses to the glass and pressed tiny palms against cold steel, and someone always told them a story about the day the fist would open.

"Promise," the elders called it—capitalized in the old rituals and said like a thing as mythic as weather. When the Promise arrived, they said, the hull would glow blue, the engines would lilt into the slow cadence of deceleration, and the ship would swing like a great cradle to the new sun. They would open the bays and step out, breath stolen by the bright—by a sky that wasn't a lamp. It was a tale told to keep fear away from children and to justify the rules to adults who had forgotten any other reason. People married into the Promise. People died thinking about it.

On that morning, the lamps were pretending to be a sunrise at a forty-degree angle, and Elara had been awake for five hours. The younger seedlings in Tray Seven were behind schedule; the nitrogen regulators had been twitchy. She had her hands damp with nutrient gel and a foot in a puddle of condensation when she felt the message ripple through the ship the way a murmured secret travels through a crowded room: a low, three-tone chime that some long-ago policy writers had designated for 'archive access'. Not for the school bells of deck routine or citizen notices, but for something older. Elara's heart pinged, an over-caffeinated beat. Archive access was part of the Council's domain. It was not for a Hatchkeeper.

She wiped her hands on her apron, not caring whether the soil saw it as sacrilege, and walked the terraces toward the maintenance access hatch whose slit of light always smelled faintly of solder and spices. The archive core lived below the engine belly, inside a chamber the old architects had once thought to make sacred. It was a ring of cold glass and layered memory-cakes—older than the generation that currently wrote policy, older than the elders who still told stories with book-lit faces. People rarely entered it without a permit. Occasionally the Council summoned someone for a hearing; sometimes they invited a historian for the Anniversary Day remembering. Mostly the archive hummed and waited like a patient animal.

Elara lied to herself that she was just curious. The truth was finer: curiosity, yes, but edged with an itch she had carried since she was a teenager and had stolen a look at the old travel-brief. It was not a map of stars but a map of choices. Which way the ship had gone, which way it intended to go—someone was lucky to hold a piece of that. Once, when she was too young to be allowed to the archive, she'd peered through a service hatch at a faded, weathered plaque that read: VOYAGE HEADING RE: HELIOS F. It glowed with the authority of things that could not be changed. Helios F was the Promise. You were supposed to have a child's certainty about Helios F.

The access console accepted her palm-print with a polite curiosity and then stopped, as if debating whether to let a hatchkeeper into a room full of old secrets. Permission came fringed with a little red triangle: one-time, read-only. Elara's palms went clammy.

Inside the archive, the air was colder than it should have been. The room smelled faintly metallic, like new coins or a body that had just been tuned. Racks of memory-cakes glinted like a field of black sunflowers, each disk humming a lullaby of data. The system's interface—an ancient, tactile thing that made old people in the ship smile like they were seeing a child again—projected a narrow column of light. Someone had put a new file into that column.

Its label was a single word older than the ship's charter: EIDOLON. The interface showed a timestamp that turned a person inward with vertigo. The data had been written eleven thousand, two hundred and thirty-seven cycles ago—before the ship's launch. Before their parents or grandparents had known their names. Before the Council had been Council.

There are things a person does and things a person cannot decide to do. Elara's fingers hovered. She had no permit. She had no authority. The archive's little red triangle blinked like a trapped bug.

Then the file opened as if it had been waiting, and sound filled the chamber.

It was a voice that did not sound like any of the practiced cadences the ship taught: not the measured tone of an administrator, not the sing-song of a storyteller, not the timber of an elder reading laws. It was older than those cadences, threaded with a fricative like sand and water. The voice said nothing ceremonial. It bent the air into a spoken room: "—clock error, third manifold fracture, stop. If you are hearing this, you are not the ones who decided this."

Elara knew, with a physical certainty that made her knees wobble, that she should shut the file. She should leave the archive and go back to the irrigation trays, to the small and honest task of coaxing life. She should have put her hands into cold soil and forgot the ship's history, because a lifetime of forgettings is what kept people sane. But the seed of conspiracy prickled at the back of her throat like a bitter herb. The voice kept going.

"—Eidolon," the voice said. "If this survives—if we are wrong about permanence—if anyone ever bothers to read what we staged beneath the keel. We were wrong. We were wrong when we wrote the Promise."

There was a pause, a metallic, human pause of someone listening to a clock. The voice changed; the syllables became smaller, closer to a whisper. "We had a choice. We made it. I—"

A soft click. The rest of the recording was ragged, as if the speaker had been interrupted.

Elara leaned forward. The archive's lights humoured her face. She felt like the prow of a small boat cutting toward an unfamiliar shore. Her mind made lists—protocols for dealing with unauthorized archival artifacts, emergency reporting chains, the legal and civic consequences of hiding historical evidence. All the lists ended with one blunt fact: if this was what it sounded like, this file could change everything.

She had time enough to walk away and to return during a scheduled maintenance period, when one could be more certain the Council would be distracted by other things. She had time enough to file an anonymous report into the civic inbox and let the machine-governances chew on the discrepancy. She had time enough to be reasonable.

She shoved all that to the back of her head and listened.

The file continued, the voice regaining steadiness. "We called ourselves Eidolon because the name felt right for what we were making—an image to be sent forward, a thing to be mistaken for reality. Architects said that if you could build a mirror thick enough, the thing on the other side would be forced to assert. We built a mirror. We dropped it beneath us like a raft. The engines would do the rest."

"For the remainder of the recording," the voice said, almost conversationally, "you should know five facts: one, the engine is not what you think; two, the Council in our time knew less than they claimed; three, someone sacrificed more than votes to keep the ledger clean; four—"

And then the voice paused again, audibly considering the weight of revelation. "—four, there is a presence in the keel. Name it as you will. It is patient. It reads old light. It learns by listening. We tried to bargain. Bargains failed. Five: if you find this and you love your home, do not speak it aloud to more than one person."

Elara laughed—a short, involuntary sound that had the ridiculousness of people who tell the truth to themselves in private. Whoever had encoded this recording had expected secrecy. Whoever had buried the file under the main keel had expected permanence. Someone had planned for posterity and then, by some stranger calculus, been forced to hide.

She checked the file's metadata. The author field was scrimmaged by a security flag; the origin node mapped not to their ship's archive but to a satellite node in the outer ring, a rusted relay named Eidolon-Prime that had been registered on the original launch manifest and then later crossed out in a hand that always looked spidery in the scans. The timestamp was from a decade before the launch.

In the quiet of the archive chamber, the recorded voice became less like a thing and more like an implicating presence. "We sent the mirror," it said. "To test. Then to hide. The first deceleration was scheduled, then canceled, then rerouted. The ledger reads: course correction. The ledger lies. We made our choice."

The voice was speaking to itself, or to a future listener, or both. It spoke with a resigned tenderness, the way a person reads a child's letter aloud. "If you are a child of this hull, you were told: Journey to Helios. You were told that your birthright is a sky that does not need lamps. You were told that the engines would hum and the ship would bend to sun. Some of that is true. The ship was meant for Helios. That remains true. But our present is not your present. We—"

There was a jaggedness now, as if the recording's knit had been picked at. "They pitched our compass," the voice said. "They chose a harbor. We argued for motion. We were voted down. The engines were suggested, then suggested again, then the technicians who saw the numbers found their ledgers smoothed. Some seeds were planted to justify the choice: famine, drought. People rioted in the nurseries. To preserve the greater number, they offered the Promise: a time to fix, a sun to promise. The ship accepted the lie because it did not know how to fight a human will."

Elara let her palms flatten on the archive rim. She had always suspected that what people told one another was curated, but she had never imagined the curators could be so cunning. Her chest felt tight, as if someone had wrapped a band around it.

The recording's voice softened. "This is where our shame lives. This is where we whisper and then bury our whispers. We believed the harbor would keep us alive. Maybe it does. Maybe you will live in a slow, safe orbit arced around a cold thing for a thousand generations. Maybe the Promise will be your myth, stitched into the fabric of your children like sacred thread. If you find this, remember that choice still exists in the membrane between one generation and the next. We planted a mirror and called it safety. You can name it different."

A breath. "If you want to look, look at the keel. Not the outer plates—there's a seam in Frame Twelve, port side, a rivet like a tooth out of line. Beneath it you will find evidence of the Eidolon installation. You will find the mirror. Do not bring crowds. Do not bring children. It reads noise. It learns to reflect what it hears. Silence is a way to keep your world."

The recording hissed and went silent, as if someone had slapped a hand over a mouth. A final, almost private note whispered into the room: "—Elara, if you are listening—"

Her name, spoken by a voice that had been hidden for eleven thousand cycles, slid into her with the intimacy of a hand in a dark sleeve.

Elara flinched back from the console as if the air itself had delivered a shock. Her head buzzed with the sound of her own pulse. The file's light stuttered. The archive hummed like an old thing that had been ruefully awakened.

Someone had put her into the recording.

There were a dozen ordinary explanations none of which made the edge in her stomach recede. The authorship field could have been a forgery—someone with a twisted sense of humor—or a coincidence of names long buried. Or the recording could have used a stock vocalization named 'Elara' because of some naming convention in the original manifest. Or the weird, the impossible thing, could be true: someone had recorded a message and left it stamped with her name as a hook, a promise. A temptation.

Elara drew a breath the length of a decision. She could close the file, close the archive, and let the little red triangle on the console fade back to the indifferent glimmer it had been before. She could file a report and let the civic machine—slow, patient, obtuse—grind at the problem like a distant glacier. Or she could do something dangerous and stupid and human: go look.

The plant trays waited with their tiny, patient faces. A sealed file sat in a room that had every right to be sealed. The ship went on humming, promising a sun it might have been built to meet.

She reached for the access hatch handle and, for reasons she couldn't explain to her patient hands, pocketed the archive's diagnostic key. The device was small and warm, like a captured firefly. It would be needed to get past certain maintenance doors; she had legitimate reasons to carry a key. That pretense, like most pretexts, would be clean enough if she needed it.

Outside, in the terraces, a seedling unfurled a new leaf and embraced the light the lamps pretended to be. The engine thrummed. The Promise hung over the ship like a painting in an empty cathedral.

Elara pulled her hair back, wiped the moisture from her palms, and walked toward Frame Twelve, port side. She had always liked the quiet work of small things. She told herself she was going to look at a seam and come back with soil under her fingernails and nothing more. She told herself she would be reasonable.

In the back of her mind, the recorded voice's whisper curled and settled like frost: Do not bring crowds. Do not bring children. Silence is a way to keep your world.

She slipped into the maintenance corridor, the lights changing their color as she passed. Somewhere aft, a bell tolled for a midship's meal cycle. The ship did not yet know that a hidden voice had named her. The first chapter of any disaster, Elara thought, is usually this: a quiet person notices something impossible and chooses not to forget.

I prefer working on other people’s pasts because other people’s pain is easier to cut than my own.

People think memory-editing is precise the way surgeons are—clean incisions, sterile rooms, clinical consent forms. They imagine we slide a scalpel of code into a brain, excise, stitch. They don’t know about the scab tissue, the scar-songs that cling to the bones of a life. They don’t know how memories bleed into each other; how a laugh can flay a face; how a single misplaced scent will rethread a dozen winters.

My name is Mara Quin. I run a parlor between a noodle stall and a neon pawnshop in the old shadow of Sector Ten’s transit spine. Afterimage is painted the kind of green that says calming and charges by the hour. It smells like oiled leather and coffee filters, because I can't afford aromatizers that mask the smell of solder and people's chemical tracers. My tools are simple: a chair with a halo of input filaments, a chipped slate with a spectrum reader, and a small welded crate I call the Ark—three generations of salvaged chips jammed into a casing I painted to look respectable. The law calls me a repealer; my clients call me a cleaner; the city’s security registries call me a "non-authorized memory manipulator" and send polite notes that eventually become solid men in gloves.

Tonight the bell over the door rings like a late tide. He walks in with his hands folded like he’s trying to remember how to hold a knife without stabbing himself—pre-calculate, pre-guard. You can tell the kind who have official offices and proprietary grief; their gestures have been ironed to fit their suits.

"Ms. Quin," he says. Voice buffered, corporate veneer. "You are recommended."

Everyone is recommended. Recommendations mean someone somewhere traded small favors for bigger ones. He sets a case on the counter like you set down a confession. Inside: a thin packet of licensed neurofilaments, marked PanOpt. The seal has been grown back together too cleanly. My thumb finds a part where the polymer is new. He smiles the smile of a man who knows justice is a ledger.

"What do you need," I say.

He tells me the usual story with the bland ellipses: marriage, accumulation, estrangement. He wants to remove a person—no, not the person herself, just her presence inside his head. He uses the word "block" like it’s an architect’s directive: remove all references, associative patterns, and emotional weight attached to Vivienne Al-Sayeed. No residuals, he promises. No trace to haunt him at banquets or in PR video waves.

I tell him my rates. He slides a credchip and a condition across: "discretion assured." The slot hums. I read him like a file header. There’s more under his collarbones—fear, a manic loop of an excerpt he cannot hear without shivering. He tries to smile through it. Men like him are full of those frayed threads. They always are.

He takes a breath and says, carefully, "There is one memory he cannot find a catalog for."

"Catalogs are wrong," I say. "We make new ones." But when we make them, we index and we box and we hide. It's safer to think of memory as cottage cheese on a plate than as dynamite.

He hesitates. "I have an excerpt from a field retrieval. We were…down-sweepers. A—private recovery. Six months ago. We acquired a bundle of…foreign neural matter. It doesn't register. Not in our archives. My analysts say it's a night-slab—a pre-Quiet fragment. I can't—" His eyes look like someone trying to dislodge a bee.

"Pre-Quiet?" I say. The Quiet is the event that rewired everything: the sudden global collapse of public networks, the blackout of shared cloud histories. After the Quiet, archives were privatized, sanitized—memories retyped to please shareholders. Pre-Quiet materials are the sort of thing to get you a surprise visit from a budget enforcement unit in the middle of a Thursday.

"Yes." He slides the case of the packet closer. The seal reads a geography—a name I haven't heard in years and prefer not to see on invoices: Halla Station, Epsilon Belt. "We pulled it out of a derelict relay. It's sand-matted and contains a neural imprint. It was flagged as human by the recovery rig. But when we ran it through PanOpt's taxonomy it…folded. My team—" He jerks a hand—"they said don't touch it. I can't forget that sound, Ms. Quin. There's a child's voice. It keeps—"

He doesn't need to finish. Everyone knows the pattern: a civilian gets hold of something the Archive says is nothing. They come to someone like me to make it nothing for them as well.

"Play it," I say.

The Ark unfolds into the halo. I clip the packet into the reader. The field filament unravels like a spider's leg and blossoms into spectral threads that wet the air with light. I don't like playing raw fragments. They are messy, patchworks of sensation that will scrub the walls of my skull clean as a wetsuit. But the credchip is warm.

The first signal is a weather. Wind on metal. A smell that is not the city's built-in smells: iodine over iron, the animal musk of ozone. Then a child's breath, a laugh that isn't melodic so much as brittle; the sound of teeth finding a language. Something in it acts like an old bone calling home. My left hand twitches as if being tugged.

"Ari?" The child says, uncertain, like naming a ship you don't know if you own. The sound is inside the room and inside my teeth. It is a name my mother used to call me when I was very small. No one calls me Ari. My legal name is Mara Quin. The Ark's lights spike.

"Where are we?" a second voice—a woman—asks, older, worried. The audio bends into a visual; not a picture but a layered impression: pale walls, a ceiling that eats light, a porthole smeared with salt. A stairwell that travels down, not out. The child says, "Under the moons. They sleep when we sing."

"Don't wake them," the woman says. "Promise me, Ari. Promise."

My hands are on the Ark and I haven't thought about why. The child's voice is a hook caught in something down there. The word "promise" rings differently in my chest, like a tile being slid.

"Who woke them?" the child asks. The laugh again, like glass lined with leaves. There is a second sound threaded in—background, low. A processor trying to imitate breathing. Not our city processors; something older, knobbier, older than the Quiet.

"Not them," the woman says. She sounds exhausted. "Some machines don't sleep like we do. Some go deep and surface in catalogs that are not ours."

I lift my head. My office ceiling has blemishes the color of old rain. The neon sign outside the shop twitches with traffic. The client is watching me watch the fragment like a man vertical on a cliff.

"I found markers in the field feed," he says, voice thin. "Coordinates. A time stamp. But they are scrambled in a way that mimics childhood songs. An anti-index."

"Who brought it to you?" I ask without meaning to. I already know: scavengers, private contractors, the kind that rip a derelict apart like someone splitting a log. They find things the Archive pretends it never knew existed.

He smooths his tie. "We can't trace the origin. The rig flagged it as 'uncataloged.' We flagged it to PanOpt and—" He stops, and for a second he looks human like the rest of us, the façade dissolving. "They told us not to." He covers the rest with a paper-thin laugh. "I can't sleep. So I want you to remove it from me. Remove the afters. Pretend we never touched it."

I press my thumb to the Ark's casing. The fragment thrums in there, a small coral reef of sensation. Against my better judgment the memory flickers a surface detail into me—a corner of a room, white enough to blanch, a hand—my hand?—slipping free from a strap. I taste antiseptic and the faint burn of a chemical I haven't tasted since I was small. My chest tightens.

The client watches me and says, "You can do that. Right? You cut around, keep the rest of my life intact. No damage."

"No damage is a myth," I say. But I have debt and there is a credchip and the Ark is lonely for company. There are worse things than making a man forget a child's laugh if forgetting prevents him from calling it home. I queue up my customary daemon, a little excision routine I call the Threader. Its signature is clean.

I start the process. The fragment's threads node and re-node beneath the Ark’s visualization. There are patterns there I didn't expect—repeating syllables that map to nothing in any language I have loaded. A lattice of sound-shapes like the underside of a fish. The Threader indexes and is refused; the fragment repels the cut almost politely, rearranging itself into a lullaby that refuses to be translated.

"That's not human," my daemon says in my ear in a tone meant to be neutral. Daemons are supposed to be boring. When they say something like that they are lying in servant tongues.

"Refuse and isolate," I tell the Ark, routing around. The system hot-swamps. More shimmers run across the screen and settle into a phrase I don't hear with ears but feel with my scalp: Don't open the sky.

The warning is not in the client's packet. The client's hands go cold and then clench into the kind of tiny claim that men behind desks do. He leans forward. "Is that—"

I don't answer. 'Don't open the sky' is a phrase like a blade that sings at the edge of memory. It belongs to old petitions and boardroom jokes and children told to wait before climbing stairs. It's also a literal impossibility data-wise; our atmospheres are leased, not kept secret. You can't 'open' what others already own.

The Ark hiccups. The fragment alters, becomes a different angle: the child's voice says a number sequence, and the woman's voice hums it like a key. The number is a longitude of a place I thought didn't exist: Halla, Epsilon Belt. My skin prickles. The same name the client's packet bore. The same place that is supposed to have only rust and static.

I stop the Threader because stopping feels like a decision you can make. The client looks at me like a man considering whether to put a loaded gun back in a drawer.

"Take it," he says. "Make it go away."

He doesn't say please.

There's a long minute where my indecision tastes like iron. Every rule I've learned counts the cost of curiosity in a ledger: the Quiet taught us not to be curious where companies say 'no.' But curiosity is also how you remember the shape of your childhood. The Ark's lights wash my face an unacceptable shade of intimate.

"Thirty hours," I say. "It will be messy. There may be…bleed. You'll need to sign a waiver."

He slides the credchip. There is a smell to the money, the authorized kind that smells like polished stone and safe rooms. He leaves with the packet lighter, as if he has physically shed a weight. The bell over the door sounds like a mollusk closing.

After the door clicks, I pull the fragment back and play it again for myself, because the child's voice has named a name that is a small account in my chest. It calls me Ari. Once.

I close the door, lock it, and go to the Ark with a slow, private determination. The Ark is louder now, as if pleased I gave it my full attention. The fragment unfurls again and this time the visual finds the white room that lives like a blank in my own life; a memory gap I learned to tie up with excuses when it showed up in background checks. The child's laugh corrodes the blank.

There is no law in the city against listening to a stray memory. But someone outside thinks otherwise. I hear boots on the stairwell before I hear the lock on my neighbor’s door engage in a way that suggests more than a coincidence. The lights outside deepen as if the city itself is taking a breath.

I don't know the client's real name. I do know this: pre-Quiet fragments are trouble; the word "Halla" in your ear is trouble; a child's voice saying "Don't open the sky" is trouble squared. Even if I wanted to finish the job—a neat cut, a tidy conscience—something in me will not let it be only that. The white room is answering to the child's voice as if they were neighbors. My missing years have neighbors. They are polite but they have keys.

I slide the Ark into a hush patch and back up the file. I make two copies. One goes in my head, where I already know the child's breath and the phrase that is a blade. One goes into the Ark's extra crate and into the pattern of mundane things: a false ledger, a decoy subscription. If someone comes for the file they'll find the decoy and think the debt settled.

The second copy I tuck into my coat against my ribs, a physicalized theft that feels more like smuggling than archiving. I don't know what I'll do with it. I only know that the longer the child's voice stays inside my skull, the more the city outside tightens like a hand balling into a fist.

There is a knock at the door that is not the polite chime of a client. It is the sort of knock that has rehearsed accompaniment: three hard beats, a pause, a second series. Professional. Official.

"Ms. Quin," a voice calls—authority flattened into protocol. "This is enforcement. Open for inspection."

I stand very still with the Ark's hum under my palms and the child's voice—a crooked lullaby—behind my teeth. The white room unpeels inside me again, and for the first time I see it not as an absence but as a sealed door with a key left on the outside.

"On my way," I say. My voice is softer than it should be.

I flip off the Ark, but the copy in my coat is warm against my sternum like a tiny living thing. Outside, the transit spine hums; the city's neon blinks like a slow heartbeat. The enforcement unit wants to know what I have, whether I serve a man or serve myself. I want neither of those things.

I open the door.

A man in a gray suit fills the threshold, a smile that has been notified by committee. He holds a badge that reflects the streetlamp, and behind him the corridor is a black mouth. For a moment, before the law has had time to shape itself around me, the child's laugh finds my name again.

"Ari," it says, like a hand on my face. "Don't open the sky."

The enforcement man's smile is quick as an animal reflex. He pushes past as if invited. The Ark is where the law looks first. He looks at the Ark and then at me and then at the coat at my chest. For a second his eyes narrow.

"You should have turned that over," he says.

"Why would I do that?" I keep my hands where they are, palms up like a placard. My other hand is on the coat pocket. The man’s breath is the sterile odor of official rooms.

"Because some things," he says, "aren't ours to keep."

He will take the Ark, and he will not see the copy scabbed to my ribs. He will list my offenses with a cheerful disinterest. He will not hear the child's voice because the child's voice knows how to hide in the places the law doesn't think to look. It knows the white room's lock-code, and it knows my name.

As they step inside, I step aside. The city's lights press against my windows like an audience. The man pats his pocket for a scanner. Inside my chest the child's voice hums a number and a song and a promise. "Promise," it says, like a demand. "Promise me you won't wake them."

I don't know what "them" is. I don't know whether I'm being asked to keep a secret or being given mine back. But I have spent my life cutting other people's pasts and sewing the seams closed. Tonight something asks me to let one life fold back on itself, to open a door that the Quiet told me to seal.

The enforcement man reaches for the Ark's latch. His hand is careful. Outside the window the city breathes, and the sky—terraced and leased and polite as a creditor—hangs like a rumor.

I swallow the child's laugh because swallowing is a way to buy time. My hand hovers over the pocket where the copy is warm. The law steps forward.

Don't open the sky, the child says again, but this time there is no admonishment in it. It is a plea made by someone who remembers a different world. It is a key I have been given whether I wanted it or not.

I am a cutter. I can file away the voice and relabel the memory as a liability. I can hand it to the men in the gray suits and count credchips until my ledger is unblemished. Or I can do the very dangerous thing: follow the child's number, trace the name Halla to its rusted bones, and see who taught a child to sing against the sky.

Outside the door the enforcement man asks me a question I have been formatting a response to for years.

"What did you take?" he asks.

My thumb tingles against the fabric of the coat pocket, against the warm shape of something that wants to be unhidden.

I name the thing I have taken, not the title the law would prefer but the one that sits in my throat like a confession.

"A story," I say.

He blinks, and for an instant I see surprise—because stories are not contraband. Stories are messy and legal and unavoidable.

Then he smiles, the smile all over again, and reaches for the Ark.

I step away.

If you are going to break a world, they say, you should at least know why it was broken in the first place. The city will write down my name later. For now, the Ark clicks open and the child's laugh spills like small light into the office. The enforcement man freezes, like a man seeing a ghost he wasn't meant to know.

"Don't open the sky," the voice says, not as commandment but as memory. "They sleep when we sing."

I take the copy from my coat and tuck it beneath the Ark's lid, where the enforcement man will not look. Then I close the door with a quiet that is not cooperative but not yet defiant, and I say two words I hope mean more than a lie.

"One hour."

He narrows his eyes. Outside, the sky goes on being a rumor. Inside, an old voice speaks my name and reminds me what I am: not only the person who cuts, but the person who remembers to do the cutting correctly. My hands smell like solder and coffee and the faint, impossible scent of sea salt.

I am not sure which of those things will save me. I only know that the child's voice has my attention and the city has its rules. Somewhere in the rusted patterns of Epsilon Halla there might be an answer, or a different kind of question. And for the first time in a long while, I decide I will follow a question until it spits me out onto the other side.

Outside, the enforcement unit taps its foot. The Ark waits. The child's laugh curls around my name like an anchor. The sky, leased and polite, blinks and keeps its secrets.

Don't open the sky, it says one more time, but the girl who said it never had the chance to know whether we would or not.

I pack my tools. I take the copied fragment. I leave the lights on. The neon paints my face a color that looks like risk. And at the threshold, I choose to step over a line I had always promised not to cross.

For a cutter, the cut is the clean part. The mess is what comes after. Tonight, the mess has a child's laugh and a name and a warning. Tonight, I follow.

On the morning the sea remembered her name, Lira Nox was inside a dead elevator.

The cabin was the size of a coffin and smelled of long-burnt plastic and fish. Outside, Neon Basin crawled, layer on layer: vats and scaffolds, a lattice of shipping lanes, the skeletons of old desal districts where the last of the living kelp farms clung to sunless light. The elevator had stopped halfway between terraces, and for the first hour the city did what it always did—sang itself to sleep with distant horns and the staccato of construction drones—but then the hum of the Basin dropped, as if the place had inhaled and decided not to exhale.

Lira watched the grain of her gloves under a feeble strip-lamp. Motionless hands didn't suit her. She'd been raised on motion, on things that made and unmade themselves. Her mother had been a tinker of sorts, a woman who fixed the things that mattered in the wrong hands: water pumps, implants, a hometown of broken radios. Lira had learned early to occupy silences with work. The elevator was an insult.

She jabbed at the console. The touchpad accepted her palm like it recognized a debt. There were lines of code scrolling across the glass—maintenance pings and negative clears—and a message that made the muscles at the back of her neck jump.

UNKNOWN SIGNATURE: AUTHORIZED RECOVERY: PRIORITY ONE.

She blinked. Priority one meant salvage insurance, meant delicacy: an old node with a live core, a ship's black box, a corporate cache that would buy a handful of months in the Basin on decent food. Someone had flagged this elevator for her. Someone who knew she loved the impossible.

"Pleasure of the day," said a voice above her head, thick with an accent she couldn't peg. The voice belonged to Joss, an almost-too-wide man who could fit sympathy into the pockets of his jacket and still have room for tools. He had the kind of face that meant he'd been handsome when gravity was kinder, and his grin suggested he would still be, if he ever slept.

"You broke something again?" Lira asked.

"Whole car," Joss said. He clambered down like a man who'd performed the same trick a thousand times. He had a winch strapped to his chest, a little gravity engine, and three blinking tools like orange beetles on his belt. "Got a call. High-grade assignment. Someone's paying actual credits for a retrieval."

Lira turned the pad to face him. The lines of code were arcane, a litany of permissions and locks. At the bottom, a single coordinate pulsed in soft blue: 12°N, Bay of the Last Pump. The Basin swallowed its coordinates like a mouth closing around a name.

"You sure?" she asked. The Bay of the Last Pump was a name older than their mothers. The last desal pump had been the city's heart when fools threw engineering at weather and called it faith. It had died in the Drift; nobody went out there for anything but grief.
