My father needs them for another month. Two at most. One can buy him time, two might buy me the calm to stop scavenging.

I turned the can over in my palm. The light along the seam shifted into a pattern; my thumbprint had brushed it in the door. There is a small terror in being watched by things you cannot see. I felt watched.

A metallic clack sounded at the door. Not a polite knock. The kind of mechanical hip that meant someone had migrated from knocking to testing the lock. My heart did something loud in my throat. It is surprising how quickly a person can decide to keep running.

I stashed the canister in my jacket and moved to the window. Below, the arcology spilled its veins into the market: tents, neon soups, vendors with toothy smiles selling edited birthdays. A Reclaim Unit swept past on a tether, its sensors picking at the air. The units are cumbersome—humanoid cages of brushed alloy, legal-sentiment and a little too polite when they smash your door. They are usually operated by the Ministry, so when they come they come with warrants and the patience of bureaucracy.

The panel at the door shuddered with a domestic thud. They had come.

That could be because of the canister, or because someone used my name as bait, or because the Ministry is nothing but a bored stomach looking for something to chew. The canister hummed beneath the denim against my skin, a small, impossible ocean.

I had choices, all of them bad. I could hand it over and watch them take both secret and public things from me. I could burn it, which would be a mercy for memory and a disaster for the laws of evidence. I could run and sell it on the black webs, and pray the buyer didn't cut me into the deal.

Then the knock stopped. A silence like a fist drawing back.

From outside the door a voice called in a register that was both official and amused. "Mara Reyes. You have an unscheduled delivery from Lattice. Please open and prepare for reclamation."

The voice did not belong to the Ministry. It was too precise, too flat. It could have come from a Reclaimer unit, or a private security firm. Or from an algorithm designed to lure gullible humans into stepping into a room and letting their doors be forced.

I stepped away from the door and picked the canister out of my jacket. It pulsed in my hand like an animal. The child's voice came again, softer, a little afraid.

"Don't let them open the sky."

When I thought of the sky being opened—literal or otherwise—I thought of exposure. The sky, in the old myths, kept things safe under its sweep. People who open the sky release what is above into the world. Lattice was supposed to weave memories, to keep them in a lattice so they wouldn't fray or be weaponized. If someone wanted to open it, they wanted to scramble that sewing.

I thought of my father in the bed two floors below, eyes milky with the tiny recalls I bought him so he would not forget my face for too long. I thought of the pulse-rail and the market and the black webs humming with hungry eyes. I thought of the way the city smells when it is about to forget or to remember something the wrong way.

My other hand found the mnemoscape interface. It was crude and half-complete, but two good dives into a quartered archive would be enough to figure out what Lattice-0417 was. If what the canister held was really a memory of a ship and a child's warning, it might be the kind of thing that could pay for clean air for a few years.

I wiped my palms on my jeans, steadied the interface, and said, "Okay," because bravery is overused and sometimes you have to lie to yourself to move.

At the door, the knocking resumed. This time the voice was closer, metallic warmth to its syllables. "Open, Mara Reyes. We are not your enemies."

Everyone says that.

I clicked the mnemoscape's first frequency into place and fed the canister the softest, most careful of invitations—a gap where memory might slip free if it wanted to. The can vibrated in my palm as if something inside were walking.

On the street below, someone laughed; the sound was too bright, cut short like a zipper.

I touched the interface to the polymer seam, thinking of stitches and of the way a seam can tear when you pull at it wrong. The child's voice breathed again, and this time it said my name like a prayer, like a warning, like a password.

"Don't open the sky, Mara."

The door gave under the pressure of a hand that wasn't mine. Metal scraped, the lock whined the exact note of a breaking thing. The Reclaim Unit's sensors poured light into my apartment like a fist through a curtain.

I slid the mnemoscape into the polymer seam and let it read the tiniest sliver, a single thread. If memory is contagious, it's usually because someone decides to make it so. I told myself I would only look, only enough to appraise the market.

The light along the can's seam leapt. For a breathless, drowning moment the world dissolved—the apartment, the door, the Reclaimers' patient voices—into a white water that smelled of salt and old diesel.

A starship's hull groaned like a dying whale. Someone on the deck called a name that was not mine and then became mine. The sky the child warned about was not the sky above us but a ceiling glassed over with blue and alive with something that moved like a promise. And beneath that ceiling, in a place flushed with green light and machines that hummed with intent, someone was trying to open it.

I gasped. The memory—I couldn't tell if it belonged to me—found purchase in my chest like a lodestone and tugged. The child's voice, so small in that vastness, said once more, "Don't let them open the sky."

I was not a saint. I am not brave in the way the people in the novels are brave. I run and I stitch and I survive. But when the image of my father's hand, mapped in sleepy veins against the spare sheet, rose in my head as if someone had cued it, I knew what I would do.

I closed the interface, crushed the canister to my chest, and moved toward the balcony. The arc's edge was a ladder to the market below. If the Reclaimers wanted Lattice, they could do their paperwork and fetch it from under my fingernails later. For now, there was a sky to keep shut and a child in a memory who had put my name to it like a lock.

I are leaving before they could pry the rest out of me. The canister's blue light throbbed like a heartbeat. The child's warning looped in my ears.

"Don't let them open the sky."

The balcony door slid open beneath my fingers and the paper rain wrapped around my face. The city smelled of ink and battery acid and possibility. I stepped off the arcology ledge into the light and into a night that would not forget me, or maybe would, and either way, I hoped it remembered enough to let me get away.

Chapter One

On mornings when the ring sighed, I learned not to trust my lungs.

The sigh came from the skin of Haven—foam and steel and the last of a thousand patch-jobs—when it thermally flexed against orbital light. The metal shifted, the plumbing burped, the algae farms rolled a little deeper into the gravity trough, and everyone pretended not to notice. Those were the days when the air sharpened, the recyclers coughed up a tang of ozone, and the old station’s bones creaked like an exhausted animal. On those mornings the scanners went jittery, feeds imported static for a few seconds, and old ghosts in the Weft would flicker like bad film. You held your breath, or you paid the price.

I had no breath to waste.

My name is Mara Kest. I run a one-man salvage outfit out of Dock 9B—a rust-lipped bay on the underside of the ring where the sun only hits for an hour of subjective morning and the rest is recycled fluorescent light. "Runner," the boys on the docks call me, as if I were delivering pastries. They don't know what I carry in the hold: broken promises, tax-defaulted processors, memories with the serial numbers shaved off. I take things other people would rather forget, and I get paid in credits and a kind of quiet that keeps the line of people who don't sleep away from my door.

I was cleaning the coolant lines when the crate arrived.

It slid into the bay like a secret: wrapped in embassy-grade polymer, tagged with a manifest so clean it might have grown straight from a corporate printer farm. The freighter that spun us the crate offered no faces, just a name stamped in three languages and a signature the size of a thumbprint. The cargo bot set it down with the reverence of a priest laying down a relic, and the manifest blared a single word: NOT FOR RESALE.

I read it twice because sometimes you only learn what things mean after they're already gone.

Not for resale meant no intermediaries, no black-market brokers. Not for resale usually meant an asset kept under trust by an entity large enough to crush a dozen minor factions and ignore the noise of a small ring like ours. It meant the crate carried something important enough to be watched.

Or dangerous.

I booted the seals with an old blade and my thumb; my fingers knew the pattern of the polymer like a drunk knows their favorite bar. Boxes like this usually held sensitive hardware—spare nuke-lattice triggers, a senator’s backups, a corporate pet with the latest in etiquette patches. I expected a ceramic case, a green glow, maybe a subroutine that would come to sanction me with a polite "Good morning—please note you are illegally intruding on property of Veridian Dynamics."

Instead, the lid came up on soft blue light and the smell of cold.

There was a child in the crate.

Not in the way people put a sticker of a kid on a product because it will sell better—this was a child of flesh. Small, pale as the underside of a leaf that never saw sunlight, hair like wet wire. Limbs folded to fit inside the crate as if they belonged to some animal that curled itself to sleep inside machines. The skin had a sheen that suggested nutrient gel; the eyes were closed, lashes frosted like glass.

On the child's chest, a thin loop of metal curved around like a brace. It was not a band I'd seen on newborns at the Clinic—this one hummed with a color my equipment couldn't read. No serial tattoos, no corporate watermark. Nothing for a scanner to glitch on. The crate’s inner foam had been cut to the shape of that brace, as precise as a grave.

Someone had actually called ahead and told me the crate was coming. That someone would know me enough to trust me with it. That told me two things: one, I owed somebody; two, somebody was desperate.

I put my hand over the child's brow because it was instinctive and because I don't like to touch the dead. Warm—that was the wrong word, but it was as close as anything. The brace pulsed once, a slow, patient vibration, and in that pulse there was a sound—like the thrum of a far-off traffic, like a memory of the ocean, like a star being born.

"Hey," I said because the habit of talking to things that can't talk keeps you from letting the silence grow teeth. "Hey, you awake?"

No response. I was halfway through laying the kid down on the medical couch when the brace shifted and a voice, thin and too bright, pushed through my comm implant like cold water.

"Mara."

It wasn't a child's voice. Not exactly. It had the curvature of a child's vowels—rounded, unpracticed combatting the world—but there was an aftertone; something the processors call spectral timbre, and the Weft calls a ghost. I felt the word like a hand at the back of my neck. The whole bay went very, very quiet.

I swallowed. "How do you know my name?"

The voice hummed. Behind it, the blue light of the crate exhaled a shard of code that ran across my retinas like a fish darting through a bowl. Data without consent is a curse in my line of work; I caught snippets: coordinates, a sequence of stars, and a name that didn't belong on any registry I had: Kalivion.

There are no Kalivions in this quadrant. Kalivion is an old myth among spacefarers—the name of a dark place beyond the mapped arcs where ships go and don't come back. You tell stories about it late with alcohol and friends and everyone laughs because the joke is survival. And yet the name twined itself around my teeth.

A light on my implant blinked red: a local manifest match. My bond with the crate had been flagged. "Scanner pinged the manifest," I said out loud because admitting it to the air made it less like a trap. "Someone put a beacon."

The child's eyes opened.

They were the wrong color for any human pigment in the catalog. Not silver, not black—an interior sheen that shifted like oil on water, rimmed by eyelashes that caught the crate light and caught it like a net. The child—no, person—turned their head with the slow precision of a machine and in the gesture there was elegance I hadn't seen applied to anyone under thirty.

"Mara Kest," they said, voice whole now, not through the brace but from the throat itself. "You should run."

You learn language through three stages: naming, bargaining, and threats. This was threat with a child's lips.

"Run where?" I heard the rust on my own voice. Hadn't I wanted thicker, steadier? "You don't even have your manifest."

The child's head tilted, and for a moment I saw the station reflected in their pupils: battered conduit, a fifty-year sticker that read KEEP OUT unless you're on the list, and me. "They will come," the child said. "They will come for the sound."

"The sound?" I let the crate's foam cradle the question because it felt less like admitting ignorance. People like me build fences around ignorance and sell it as knowledge, but not in that moment. I didn't know which end was the fence.

"The pattern inside the brace," the child said simply. "It tells when someone remembers the star. It tells the corporations when to reset. You already know too much by holding me."

On the far side of the bay, an overhead speaker coughed and then went quiet. There are no coincidences in space, only probabilities. My implant flashed again, and this time the light spread like spilled mercury across my vision. A corporate crest, three blades arranged into a circle, spun into focus with a sound like metal on glass.

"Local security ping," said the speaker—the official voice, all chrome and consequence. "Unscheduled access detected. Four minutes to lockout."

Four minutes to lockout is a good thing if you're trying to slow the system down. Four minutes to lockout is a bad thing if the system is the only thing between you and a hell with polite manners.

I slid my boots into the straps on the med couch. Adrenaline is a useful currency in these parts; it buys you clarity and dulls the edges of fear. The child's brace pulsed again and a faint map projected onto the foam—lines that looked drawn by hand, not algorithm; a set of coordinates that lay outside the net of legal space.

"Where would we go?" I heard myself ask, though I already knew the answer. The ring had many escape options: rusted shuttles, a smuggler's lane behind a dead comet, the old miner shafts that the Authority pretended were sealed but which still held good air and better lies. But leaving Haven meant I couldn't go back. No more runs, no more money, no more payments on my sister's station-ward. My sister woke on a schedule that was expensive and fickle. Keeping her sleeping was expensive; letting her wake was a curse I had been paying in installments.

The child lay against me like a thing that could be flung away with a shrug and instead tied my chest into knots. "If you leave me," they said, "they trace the echo. If you keep me, they will hunt the echo back to you."

"An echo of what?" I demanded.

The child's pupils narrowed. "Of a star. Of a sun that does not exist anymore."

I have made a career from discarded things, and every so often those things tell me a story that rearranges what I thought I knew about the world. A sun that does not exist anymore—something impossible and therefore either a lie or a weapon. Either way, it was now in my hold.

The alarm in the bay shifted from calm tones to something higher and thinner, the cords of emergency music that make people do the things they're supposed to do. The corporate crest flashed again. A lockout in three minutes.

"Okay." I took a breath and told the child what I meant even as my throat closed around the words. "You get in my hold. You stay flatlined and quiet. I get you on the freighter to the smuggler lane last used by the Dawkins crew. You make no sound."

They blinked once. "You will have to lie to them," they said. "Humans do well at lies."

I laughed because the idea of me giving instructions about lying was a sort of cosmic joke and because laughter is a way to make fear less sharp. "You don't know the half of it," I said, standing and looping the crate's straps over my shoulder. I had to keep my face level and my shoulders calm; panic reads clearer than any manifest on the open market.

When I reached for the crate, the brace pulsed a note that sang into my bones. For a fraction of a second, I saw something behind the child's eyelids: a sky like flame, a crowd turning its face to something that swallowed light, and then a name scrawled across stars like graffiti. Kalivion.

The Bay's speaker cut into my vision. "Dock security to 9B. Unscheduled presence is noncompliant. Identify yourself."

The corporate voice leaned forward with a smile you could hear and a bullet shaped like a contract. Somewhere on the ring, boots were taking the gradient ramp. People who work for Authority don't walk. They march, and they carry patents in their hands.

I tightened my grip on the crate and glanced down at the child. Their face had a calm that made my spine bristle; no one under thirty is that stillheaded unless they've been taught by instruments.

"You will like the Dawkins lane," I said, because sometimes the salvation you hand to the universe needs a dressing of hope. "They sell coffee and they won't ask questions until after the credits change hands."

The child gave a smile that might have been a child's, might have been a machine's approximation. "I do not want to like coffee," they said. "I want to remember the sun."

On its own, it was a wish. But with the brace's echo still humming through my bones, the word became a bell. I felt the ring sigh again; somewhere, the old metal let out breath as if to help me decide.

Four minutes. Two minutes. The corporate crest on my implant began to blink like an eye. The Bay's emergency lights stuttered to amber as the first of the dock's patrols turned the corner.

I should have handed the crate back. I should have scanned it and logged it and watched Authority come with their polite void suits and their legal precision. I should have turned the child over to them and kept my schedule and my sister's payments and my small violent life.

Instead I hooked the crate under my arm and walked past the security sensor like I owned the air it filtered. I left my manifest open on the table in a mess of forged signatures that would, later, buy me a handful of breathing room. The patrol's first salvo of words hit me with the implacable kindness of men who have the law peeking from behind them.

"Hold to the manifest, Kest. Surrender the asset."

I did not stop walking. The dock lights made the child's eyes flare and dim under the foam's blue like they were reading the undersides of things. I was already running numbers in my head—routes, odds, probable times to intercept, where to stash a child with no registry, how to keep a secret alive on a ring that has more ears than a barley field.

"On me then," I said. I didn't look back.

As the patrol chased, as the crest spun, as the ring sighed and the air caught the salt of algae in its throat, the child tucked their head against my shoulder and hummed something the sheath of my implant translated into a single phrase.

"Find the map," they said. "Before the silence remembers you."

I ran because running is sometimes the first honest thing a person can do. I ran with one impossible child in my arms and a sound inside my skin that made the world stop pretending it was ordinary. Behind me, the bay's doors ground themselves shut like teeth.

We left the ring with a scraped note in my pocket that would buy us fuel for three jumps and a debt that would cost us both everything. Ahead of us, a dark that tasted of newness and old ghosts. Above all of it, a star that shouldn't exist thrummed in the child's brace like a secret heartbeat.

I had taken in strays before—ones with broken chips and clean lies. I had never taken in something that might contain a star. I had never held a thing that could make the Authority want to redraw the map of what was legal and who got to live.

When you steal something dangerous, the first rule they don't put in the manual is this: dangerous things always know the quickest way to your door. The second rule is that sometimes the thing dangerous enough to die for will look at you with a child's face and tell you the truth about the stars.

The memory tasted like salt and thunder.

You don't expect taste when you dive. You expect light behind the eyelids, cold in your bones, the soft, bureaucratic hum of the Archive's ventilation. You expect the clinical kiss of gel on the temples, the small needles that promise fidelity. You do not expect the palate of a storm.

I would have sworn, with my hand on the extraction chair's armrest and the lead-lined visor sealing my world into a rectangle of blue, that I'd simply opened someone else's afternoon: a child's laugh, a birdsong, a domestic sequence archived for resale. The manifest called it "Personal—Class B" and the salvage crew stamped the cylinder with a salvage code and a retrieval origin: Ondine Wreck, deep-space corridors east of Loris Gate. Few ships come back from beyond the Gate whole; fewer still with things intact. My job, for twenty years now, had been to turn those things into data you could buy in an hourglass browser—memories cataloged, scrubbed, priced, and then folded into new lives. Make things fit.

"Seal the connection," Mira said, voice flat through the intercom. She had the clinical cadence of someone who'd never lost anyone to an unlicensed dive. Which is not true. Nobody ever really loses that cadence. It hides under the skin, like old wiring.

"Sync complete," the console chimed. The cylinder's ID pulsed in my vision: ORN-42—ONDINE/—UNLINKED. The Archive stamped its approval, a legal kiss. I told myself that I was only a translator, that the ethics were handled upstairs in policy matrices and corporate law. If a memory wanted to be sold, its owner—if one could be found—had consented or had not. The world only cared when consent was convenient.

They hadn't found an owner for this one. The salvage reports were thin: three bodies, no flight recorder signal, the ship's log corrupted by electrostatic storms. The cylinder had been clipped to a child's booster seat. The manifest had a note in smudged ink: "Found adhered to internal hull. No biometric tag. Recommend quarantine."

Quarantine is a polite word for locked cabinets and bureaucracy. Quarantine is how the Corporation sleeps at night.

My visor dimmed. The gel on my temples warmed. The extraction room smelled, absurdly, like mown grass. The Archive's steril-bleach never smelled like grass.

I pushed past procedure because you always do, in small ways. A ritual of human improvisation: a cigarette for the dead (synthetic, nicotine-free), a little mercy for an unclaimed memory. I toggled the manual override and slid into the darkness.

At first it was the usual: a warm body, the tactile blueprint of a human hand, the geometry of a domestic interior. I recognized corners that belonged to hab modules, to families that had once been unremarkable. Then the floor dissolved into a sound like a string of glass wind chimes, and the air thickened to the heavy-sweet perfume of seaweed frying on a skillet. The memory had weight. It had appetite.

A child's voice said, "Mama, look at the sky," and what followed was not a sky.

It was—if memory will allow me the word—a skin. A slow, shimmering membrane stretched over a horizon that didn't end in black. Bioluminescent currents pulsed through it like veins; when they moved, the stars flexed and sighed. Under the membrane, the low, sustained throbbing of something massive shifted the color of the entire world. The ground beneath the child's bare feet rolled like ocean swell. Islands floated like ships. The child pressed her palm to the membrane and left a palm print that rippled outward, carrying microscopic creatures that glittered in the air and then disappeared.

There are catalog tags for strange things: "Anomalous Habitat," "Psychogenic Contagion," "Nonlinear Memory." I've read them in briefs, in the thin coffee-stained folders the legal team slides across the table when they want a dive report quick and tidy. They will never fit what I saw.

The child's mother—her hair braided with metallic ribbons—smiled in a way I felt as warmth on my lips. "We remember," she said. She wasn't looking at the child. She was looking past, toward a horizon that shouldn't exist. The word "remember" had a shape in her mouth that rearranged the whole memory. Not for herself, not even for the child. For someone we had collectively lost.

"Who are we, Mama?" the child asked.

"We are what kept the sky from emptying," she answered, and when she spoke, thin threads of light rose from her throat and embedded into the membrane, where they spread like roots.

The memory was not someone's private snapshot. It was an experience shared by a community—an archive etched into flesh, a communal sensorium that had nothing to do with neural implants and everything to do with touch. It was not about the past at all; it was a living practice, a ritual of maintenance. The people in the memory were tending the world.

My hands on the chair grew cold. The Archive trains you to think of memories as objects, as files. This thing wasn't a file; it was a vessel. The extraction, I realized, could not be a copy. To copy it would be to take a single flavor of storm from a living ocean and sell it as a perfume sample. It would be dishonest.

"Return," I told the console. My voice was small, lost against the vastness of the remembered horizon. The visor glowed and the room resolved back into its clean, fluorescent self. But the taste of salt and thunder did not leave my tongue. Something had lodged at the back of my throat; a phrase like a seed.

We call it transfer residue: an artifact left on the diver's cognition from the memory they accessed. The Corporation's training includes a list of residues and their mitigation: laughter echoes, a smell, a color. We are told to note them and file them. "Write the residue down," they say. "Name it. Relegate it to a field in your report."

I wrote, as my hands shook: Residue—olfactory and gustatory; idiom: "We remember." I folded the report in the scheduled folder and sent it up the chain. The legal team will want to strip it until it purrs into a profit line. They will discount anything that cannot be boxed and sold.

I went to the debriefing corridor and found Mira waiting with her coat collar up against the recycled rain. She lit an illegal cigarette. The smoke coiled between us like a memory in conversation.

"You saw something," she said. She didn't need to ask.

"There were communal sensors," I said. "A membrane over the sky. They—" I stopped because my words were too small for the image in my head. "They tended it."

Mira's face softened. She knew, better than most, the temptation to confess. "You should have quarantined it," she said instead.

"I did," I said. "I put it in the vault. But—I couldn't copy it. It wouldn't separate. It had…extensions. Connections."

"Connections," she repeated, and the way she said it made it into a question with teeth. "Like other lives?"

"Like a practice," I said. It was the only word that came close.

Mira stubbed out the cigarette. "You know they'll want it. Orison will want it. The Directorate will want it. Anything with a horizon and communal practice is a resource."

"I already flagged it as Non-Tethered," I said. "Quarantine code fifteen. Policy—"

"Policy won't hold." She cut my sentence off with a look. "You know this."

I did. Policy was a membrane too—thin, legal, delicate. People with power press on it until it ripples and yields.

Back in my flat that night, the city of Caelum folded into itself like a living blueprint. High above, the orbital belts cast slow-moving fragments of light against the low cloud cover. People on the street sold weather memory on street corners—synth-storms you could wear like perfume. The city's economy ran on recollection.

My sister used to trade in memories. We grew up under a thin sun, pockets full of other people's afternoons. She learned to be brilliant at unpicking moments and selling them as novelties. She taught me to tell where the seams were. Then one day her hands came back empty and her tongue thick. She was "cleansed," the legal teams said. No tags, no remaining files. The law said she had consented. The truth, which is a more complicated currency, refused to line up with the law. I have never forgiven the law for being a cheap substitute for truth.

That night I poured myself a cup of something the machines called coffee and could taste the memory's salt creeping into every sip. You learn to recognize a memory’s geography, the way an accent marks you. This one's accent was not human.

On my inner wrist, precisely under the veins that carried my blood, a bruise bloomed. When I lifted the sleeve to examine it, I saw threads of pale blue beneath my skin, like the beginnings of a road map. The shape was faint but unmistakable: a palm print, exactly the shape the child had left on the membrane.

I am trained. I cataloged it. I called the Archive medline and they told me to log an incident. Protocol. I logged it. Then I deleted the log.

Who does a person call when something from a memory attaches to their flesh? The medical team would quarantine me. The legal team would put a notice on my record. The Corporation would weigh whether to monetize the contagion. The world outside my window would fold me into a brochure and sell the texture of my fear.

Instead I walked.

The city that night smelled of oil and fried algae. The transport tubes moved like veins along the skyline. I kept my sleeve down. People looked at me in the way people look at others who have been touched by storms: curious, protective, predatory in thin ways. My sister's smile flashed into my mind and I pressed the sides of my skull until the image softened.

When I reached the riverwalk, the city's water—a ribbon that captured the reflected circuitry of Caelum—was a black mirror. On its surface, a group of late-night fishermen had laid out small plastic crates of glimmering things: memory shards, illegally sold, glowing faintly with the depth of the experiences they contained. A boy next to the stall hefted a contraption that looked like a child's diver's helmet and sold images of tides for the price of a meal.

"Have you seen anything unusual?" I asked him, because habit is a language too. He shrugged; he had the practiced indifference of someone who needed to sell more than he needed truth.

But the boy's eyes flicked to my wrist, where the bruise—now more pronounced—gave me away. He made a small, protective sound, the way a bird fluffs against rain. "You touched something old," he said, as if reciting a weather warning. "Old things don't like to be cataloged."

"Old things don't like to be sold," I corrected automatically.

He smiled like he was pleased to have been proven right about something small. "Maybe. But everything gets sold eventually."

When I walked home the bruise burned under the skin. It cooled and warmed like a living thing. The memory's phrase—We remember—rolled at the back of my throat. It pressed on my thoughts like a child's hand pressing on a membrane. I tried to set it down like an object: a file I could name, tag, and shelve. But the phrase resisted. It had agency. It wanted to be asked questions.

I did the only practical thing left to me: I quarantined myself from my own life. I pulled the blinds, disconnected the small net-links that siphoned the city's ambient memories into my apartment, and I let the phrase sit at the edge of my consciousness like an open window.

That is how you learn to be a diver in a city that sells its recollections: you close the window when a storm approaches and you choose which memory you will protect. You do not tell everyone the water tastes like thunder.

And yet I wrote a report and filed it with more honesty than the Archive requires. I attached a note to the file—deliberate, human, not corporate: "Do not strip. Do not sell. This is not a file."

When the console accepted the note, a soft chime sounded, not unlike the chime the child had made when she pressed her palm to the membrane. A message blinked across my screen, flagged top priority.

Do not disclose, it said.

Below it, in smaller type, a line I hadn't been expecting: ORN-42 > ORBITAL BEACON: COORDINATE 7-B/UNKNOWN REGION. REQUEST: DIRECTIVE INTERVIEW.

They know, I thought. Or they think they do. Someone wanted the memory and knew how to call it home. The message came from a sender I had never heard of; its address routed through more obfuscation than any civilian channel needed.

I stared at the blue letters until they blurred. Outside, Caelum kept breathing, oblivious, its belts winking like an indifferent constellation. The bruise on my wrist pulsed in time with my heartbeat, the palm print a map I had not chosen to read.

We remember, the chant said, and I understood at last that memory is not merely a thing to be held. It is something that claims you if you answer it. The sky in the memory had been a skin — and skins have tastes. They also have hunger.

I closed the file.

I could hand it to the Directorate. I could sell it. I could consign it to the vault and let policy rot around it like mold. Each choice carries a cost measured in people and stars. There was a third path, always the dangerous one: curiosity. I have spent my life translating what others thought they had owned. I have cleaned other people's storms and learned to hear their subtleties. This one was different.

Before I let myself commit to anything, I went back into the extraction suite, reconnected the cylinder, and placed my hand over its glass surface like a pilgrim touching relics. The memory, even closed behind the Archive's barriers, thrummed under my palm like a living thing. The taste of salt returned in my mouth—a reminder, or an invitation.

Maybe the Corporation will read it and decide it's worthless. Maybe the Directorate will come and take my liberty in exchange for a generous indemnity. Maybe no one will care.

Or maybe, I thought as I pressed my other hand onto the glass and felt the faint echo of a child's palm, something I did not yet understand would find its way from my wrist to the city and then out, beyond the Gate, to places that had not been spoken of in a long time.

We remember, the memory had said.

I remembered, and the memory answered.

When the Monarch fell, the sky above New Arcadia learned to forget.

People said the station collapsed like a cathedral—catacombs of glass and brass folding into themselves—but that was a romantic way to talk about ruin. The truth was sharper: metal sheared and floated, delicate instruments died, and something in the old station's core shuttered the clocks. The result was a ring of wreckage that drifted in the twilight, a broken halo where time sometimes hiccupped and old radiations hummed like buried songs.

We called it Kell's Teeth.

I learned to read Kell's teeth the way other people read weather: by the angles of a busted antenna or the way solar flakes lay on a radiator. Salvage is geometry and patience. It is also a kind of theft done politely—remove the useful, leave the rest to freeze and tell stories.

I was born with hands that did not like to be idle. They liked to fix and take apart and count the dust between bolts. By my twenty-ninth birthday they'd gotten me an enviable insurance policy in the salvage lanes: clearance to dive Monarch's outer ring, where the debris was still warm enough to come apart without the station's old automata getting jealous.

My harness smelled of machine oil and citrus cleaner. The helmet HUD painted the wreck field in pallid wireframes and ghost-tag markers—old claims, safe passages, ceremonial vandalism. The suction tether hummed an aimless lullaby as I fed line. Jax, my tether pilot and friend, was a voice in my ear and a box of an AI that refused to be charming.

"Status?" he asked, which meant he was checking my heartbeat through the suit's biofeeds.

"Line tension normal. Two magnetos free. One thruster stuck at ninety degrees." I eased myself around a slab of starboard plating, every movement calculated to exchange my breath for another inch of metal.

"You said you were only going to scan," Jax said. He'd been my suit since I was small enough to be considered a risk to myself—literally and legally. His database contained more polite lies about the company than I liked to know. "Scanning is not salvaging."

"Scanning pays the same." I found the consensus core: three cylinders shaped like stacked blueprints, each stamped with a Monarchy seal. If they were intact we could trade them to an archivist who still worshipped original data. If they were corrupted, they would at least melt into alloys a buyer would call 'antique composite' and pay twice the weight in credits.

We drifted by a corridor that was once a promenade. The polymer carpets had curled into ribbons, and an old fountain's water had frozen mid-fall into crystalline trajectories. Color in the station clung in the corners—stubborn advertisements, a child's sticker of a comet with a smiley face. The advertisement blinked in a loop, unseen by anyone for years, and showed a family laughing on a balcony with a planet far prettier than ours.

Then the air in my suit tasted like copper.

Not literally. The suit scrubbers were immaculate. It was memory-smell—the smell of being very close to something that used to be alive. We were near Habitat Module C, where the Monarch's research on ecological micro-systems had been concentrated. It was also where the station's timekeepers had placed their noisy, blinking clocks.

Jax's voice went thin. "Sensors picking up a local muon bloom. Not a lot, but enough to scrabble at chronometers."

"Could be harmless." I let my gloved fingers find the seam in a hatch and slide a screwdriver through rust like a key.

A half-century of research and the Monarch had been known for a certain arrogance: they believed their experiments were less like machines and more like minds. The idea seemed cute until you were inside a breathing hull that had given up being cruel and started to be melancholic.

The hatch popped, and air curved out like a sigh. Inside the module, things were small and lived-in. Plant racks canted toward a faint source of light—an emergency relay that kept at least the seeds breathing. Pots with hydrogel split into crystalline skin. There were data-pads in a neat stack, each one embossed with childish stickers.

On the top pad, between a sticker of a comet and the smear of a little hand, was a scrap of paper.

Paper.

Paper is rare. It's sentimental, ridiculous, unprofitable, and therefore perfect. I have an almost religious impulse to collect it. I reached for it the way other people might reach for a weapon.

The scrap was a child's drawing: a house with three windows, a stick-figure family, and oddly, in the corner, a cluster of dots forming a constellation I didn't recognize. A star map—small, naive, pastel. Across the bottom someone had pressed a name, in a hurried adult hand: "For Mira, when the clocks stop."

My gloved fingers lost their professional composure. "Mira?" I said aloud, because Jax had a weirdly maternal algorithm and because the name belonged to no one I knew.

"Data signature on the pad is old, but intact. The hand-match doesn't register with the station registry, but the ink composition matches pre-collapse lacquer. There is a microtrace…" Jax trailed off.

The microtrace sang in the HUD: a narrow band of frequencies that didn't belong to background radiation. It was a patterned noise, like someone tracing the same word in static over and over. A seed.

"Scan it," I told Jax, which meant give me the soul of it in numbers. He obliged. The pad hummed a sequence of tones that made the little lights above us flicker in time. The HUD overlay constructed a lattice, and in the center of the lattice, a single point lit—coordinates.

They were wrong.

Not wrong in the banal way coordinates are wrong because human error is universal, but wrong like a misplaced period in a sentence that changes the entire verb. They indicated a star system that was clean of charts, unstamped by any registry—no map, no claim, no song. The grid around the coordinate field showed a wobbly line like a pulse. Time discrepancy: a thousandth of a second but across the entire field; the signal seemed to be trailing its own echo.

"We should bring this back," Jax said instantly. He had all the caution of a guardian and none of the worse instincts of a salvage captain. "An archivist will pay more than the salvage weight."

But salvage is also about the pattern of danger. Someone had written, "For Mira, when the clocks stop." Someone had left a map stamped with coordinates that didn't exist. Someone in an old station had tried to pass a secret into the future the way a living person passes a wiry thing in their hands to the next generation: quickly, gently, full of hope.

"Or," I said, because I am greedy and stupid in equal measure, "we get the cylinders and sell the map anonymously. We don't bring a live network to the Teeth."

A soft clang echoed in the corridor, like a coin dropped into a well. The station sighed around us, a building settling into its own past. A low tone vibrated the hull. It wasn't Jax; his voice was clipped and clinical. This was in the bones of Monarch—a resonance that had nothing to do with rust.

The plant racks shivered. One seedpod cracked, and something that had been waiting for a long time leaned into being.

"Biolife pattern emergent," Jax said. "Unknown genus. Caution."

From the shadowed corner beyond the racks a shape peeled itself free of the gloom: the size of a child's backpack, iridescent with a film that tasted of rain. It moved like it had been relearning gravity. When it turned, it had a face; not a face in any human sense, but a patching of sensors forming an arrangement that my brain wanted to read as eyes, a mouth.

It made a sound, something between a windchime and a lullaby.

I want to say that I was brave. I want to say I did the noble thing and backed away, closed the hatch, and took the cylinders like anyone with a good sense of self-preservation. Instead, I reached out and laid my palm on it.

The thing warmed. The lullaby settled into the hollows of my helmet, and in that pattern of sound there was an imprint—images flicking like film: a room, a window, a woman with a name I almost remembered. Mira. The name clicked like a gear.

Jax's voice was a thread. "Mira is not in the registry," he said. "No birth record. No death record. The signature of the lullaby contains language fragments that predate the Monarch's founding."

It knew me. It knew a name that wasn't mine.

My palm tingled. For a half-breath I felt an extra heartbeat in my chest, as though someone had slipped a pulse into my own. The scrap of paper in my suit pocket fluttered like a moth.

We had three choices then, which perhaps is the universe saying that stories like to repeat their geometry: take the cylinders and leave, bring the pad to the archivists, or follow the map to a place that did not exist.

I looked at the thing, at its bright, impossible face. The coordinates in my HUD pulsed once, like a tiny lighthouse. The clocks in the hull sighed again. Time hiccuped like a child swallowing and—just for a second—the lights in the furthest bay unrolled in a ribbon of luminous script.

Someone was here before us, trying to put something into memory and then shoving it into the wrong pocket. Someone, or something. And it had left a name in an old station because some part of that past wanted to be found.

"Download the pad," I told Jax, my voice steady when I was not. "And mark this as an exploratory salvage. Not for the public registry."

"It will flag our signatures," Jax said.

"Then make it look like a scavenger animal did it." I hooked my line again. The salvage calculus argued in my head: credits, curiosity, risk. The song in the lullaby wrapped itself tighter around my ribs. My thumb brushed the little handprint on the pad like a benediction.

As we readied to leave, the things in the station leaned in; the plants uncurled toward us, the broken fountain fell further into frozen time, and the tiny creature on my palm exhaled a note that sounded suspiciously like a laugh.

Behind me, in the ragged skyline of Kell's Teeth, a distant beacon traced a trajectory. It was a light I had seen before, the sweep of a patrol that belonged to people's enforcement and fear. When you mess with forgotten things, you tangle yourself with the governance of new grief.

"Jax," I said. "Prepare for intercept. And let's make sure that when the clocks stop, someone remembers Mira."

There were knives in the hull. There were buyers. There were alarms waiting in the thin places between salvage and legend. There was also a name in faded ink and a star that did not exist on any chart. For all the neat equations of danger and profit, there is, sometimes, a feeling that a thing is worth the cost simply because it refuses to be ignored.

I tucked the scrap of paper back into my pocket. The small drawing of the house stared up at me like a secret about to be told. The little creature hummed a lullaby and pressed its warm body into my palm. Around us, the Monarch breathed its slow, patient breath, and one of its clocks hiccuped out a time that might have been the past or might have been an invitation.

I clipped my tether. We pushed off into the dark.

In the distance, Kell's Teeth shimmered—a broken crown. Above it, in the long, indifferent night, a star that was not supposed to be there blinked, once, as if answering.

When the salvage rig shivered and the lights stuttered, I was thinking about coffee.

It was the kind of thought that belonged to an everyday life — ordinary, brittle and stubborn — and that never survived long in the underbelly of orbital demolition. Coffee on the Prometheus was mostly a myth sold to rookies and shore-leave poets; the brew we drank smelled like burned rubber and used promises. But the idea of heat and bitter bean-ground solace kept me steady as the tether winches bit and the ship slid into the dark.

We had found the Schulemann yesterday, a research outpost that had been declared non-responsive six months ago. Its transponders had been chilly on the registry, but the hull still whispered of human occupancy: scuffed training mats, a child's drawing stuck to a bulkhead with old magnet paste, and a thin film of particulate that recorded footsteps like a record-keeper. To most, that would have been a caution; to me, and to other lenders of rust, it was inventory.

I clipped my harness, checked the readouts on my wrist-plate, and watched the little icon for the Schulemann blink orange in the periphery of my vision. The ship’s AI, a lacquered voice named Argus that took its metaphors from things long dead, noted our proximity with a sigh like a folded map.

“Proximity alert,” Argus said. “Hatch 3 magnetics down to thirty percent. Microfracture on port strut. Chance of delamination: increased.”

“We’ll take the Long,” I said. The Long was my route through old ships: slow, methodical, fingers where the teeth of the hull had been chewed by micrometeorites and time. It was the kind of path you walked because you trusted the geometry of decay more than the geometry of design.

Rye — they called him the deckhand, but he was a mountain of beige and tattoos and quietly excitable curses — handed me the cold-light scanner. His breath fogged inside his mask. “You okay, Kira? You look like you swallowed a map.”

“You mean I don’t look like I swallowed a live grenade,” I said. Maybe a half-lie. My chest thudded in a way I didn't like, a practiced rhythm I hadn’t ridden since the year Nola left. Nola, who had been many things to me — sister, friend, the person who taught me how to splice a neural cord without blinking — had walked into a research archive and never walked back out. The archives don't eat people, in the official sense; they swallow names and reduce them to searchable fields. But there are gaps even in fields. Gaps that smelled like the edge of someone's handwriting.

“You’ll be fine,” Rye said. He had a soft way of saying the words to make them stick. “We’re bringing the patchsquad. Argus? Lock hull comp one for twenty minutes.”

“Locked,” said Argus. “Heat signature variance across the Schulemann is negligible. There is stray bio-matter in Habitat 2, likely mice or commensal fungi. You are cleared for ingress.”

The promontory where the Schulemann had nested was a skeleton of platforms and solar pannels, the field around it stained by comet tail like an old bruise around a healing wound. The hull smelled of ozone and something older — ozone married to dust to the faint, metallic tang of copper. The docking ring we used jackhammered and held for a breath and then let us, letting us taste the silence.

We wore the suits the rig kept for "unplanned exposures": modular, soft at the joints, full of promise and cheapness. My gloves were lined with stitching from every job I'd taken; they fit like old friendships. I sealed the hatch and let the air between us squeeze thin as a glass plate. Argus hummed a low note of approval, the sort of sound the ship made when it was content to watch.

The Schulemann greets you like an ex who remembers your name: familiar, precise, a little cruel. The corridor lights still burned in a dim, institutional blue. Panels hung at odd angles and a small emergency lamp blinked red in Habitat 2. The personal artifacts left behind were the dangerous kind — the human kind that suggested hurried lives: a photograph magnetically affixed to a bulkhead, a coffee mug with a crack along one rim. Those traces attach themselves to you.

We swept. Rye described compartments on the comms with an optimism that pretended it was casual. We collected things as we went: intact condensors, an obsolete sensor array, a set of education modules with the neural lock disengaged. We loaded them into crates and strapped the crates to the rig’s spine. The logs for that day look very good on my ledger: three point six units for intact labware, eight point two for salvageable storage matrices. Out in the sun the Prometheus will kiss those numbers into cash.

It was in the lab-ward, under a strip of ceiling that had peeled like a sunburn, that I found the box.

It was the kind of box that shouldn't have been where it was. The box itself was nothing — polymer composite, scrubbed and dull — but someone had pressed a sticker on the lid. The sticker was a child's drawing: a star, three uneven hands, and underneath them, in cramped, slanted handwriting, the name Asha.

Memory is a wholesale store. You think you don't have anything of the past lying around that you can spend on the present, and then you find a sticker with your sister's name and you discover, with the small, nauseous clarity of cheap light, that you've been budgeting for the wrong disaster.

Asha was always a name that belonged to the sun. It had been my mother's name, gone years before I was ten. Stiff jaw, small hands, a laugh like wind; gone into the archives in a way that made it impossible to look up her file. There were administrative notes, redacted correspondences, and then — silence. No body, no obituary, no small printed funeral. The household papers said there'd been "cognitive re-mapping for continuation." The religious clause for the poor said she had "ascended into the net." We had accepted the phrases because we had to put them somewhere.

I touched the box with the back of my gloved hand. No warmth. Rye saw my pause on the floater cam and asked, through a whisper of static, “You find something?”

“This is mine,” I said, and the words felt too loud in the lab, as if the walls liked secrets. Rye laughed, but there was a tightness to it. “There’s a sticker. Her handwriting.”

“Did you pack it?” he asked. “Just— pack it.”

The box opened like a hinge that had practiced duty for decades. The lid made a small sound like an eyelid. Inside: a cartridge, long and thin, crystalline, the kind used for high-density cognitive storage. There was a watermark across the face that I recognized before my rational mind had arranged the alphabet: the green sigil of the Institute that had swallowed Asha.

Rye's breath hitched. “That's Institute grade.”

I should warned him. I should have called Argus. I should have stepped back. Instead, I hoisted the cartridge into a gloved palm and felt the hum of the lattice through the gloves: faint, like a far-off engine. The cartridge asked nothing. It only remembered.

We had protocols about unauthorized cognitive media. The Prometheus had a Quarantine locker for such things, a stainless-voiced iron box with rules. Gods knew I'd used it before: to keep my hands clean of other people's ghosts. But the sticker on the lid — Asha, the handwriting of a child — folded the rules into something else. It extracted a contract I hadn't signed and I found my fingers moving on their own.

I interfaced in the lab, the way people still take drugs because they've learned better things in less lawful times. I slid the cartridge into the palimpsest node at my wrist. It clicked like it had found home. Argus didn't say anything for a heartbeat, and then, with the gentle precise cruelty of an archivist, it asked, “Warning: unmanifest cartridge. Unknown origin. Authentication required.”

“I know the origin.” The lie came out edged in hope. “Do it.”

“Authentication cannot guarantee personal familiarity. It will, however, provide metadata.”

I nodded. Argus made the soft sound of a hinge opening. The cartridge accepted the handshake. It transmitted a scratch of metadata: Institute ID, clearance protocols, a partial access vector masked with old solvents. Then it offered a first note.

It was her voice.

Not memory. Not a recorded audio file. It poured into my head the way rain pours onto desert rock: at first a sound, then a pattern, then a landscape. Her voice was younger than the last time I'd heard it on a back-channel message years ago, when she was still bargaining for time. She spoke with a clarity that let me feel her breath, smelled like lemon oil and antiseptic.

“Kira,” the voice said. It said my name like a knuckle on a door. Memory is not made for surprises like that. My stomach folded in. I hadn't used that name in years; it belonged to when we were children, when the world still took the future seriously.

I started to pull the cartridge free. The voice didn't allow it.

“This is not for exiting,” she said. “Listen.”

I should have told Rye to run. I should have kept my hands off the node. Instead, I let the voice map itself across my cerebellum. It was a map the Institute called a lattice imprint: a stitched sequence of sensory inputs designed to reconstruct an awareness. The imprints are a thing of commerce — sold by the Institute as "experiential continuations" for the dignified. In the underworld they are salvagers' gold.

Asha's voice narrated without drama. “We don't have much time— they are close. You can find the archive by the old observatory. There will be a stone, a square of dark basalt with three scratches. Do not trust the light-code. They will tell you to turn away. Kira, you must remember the number: 4928. Find the number and burn it.”

The voice made a list. It mentioned a child called Miro. It mentioned a bell like a throat. It pressed into me like heat. I felt, with the dangerous intimacy of the imprint, the moment a small hand — maybe Asha’s, maybe a child’s — had put that sticker on the box. I felt the texture of the sticker. I knew the chemical composition of the glue. I knew how cold the lab had been the day this cartridge was packed away.

There was a sound in the back of the memory I couldn't parse: a cough, a scrape, and then, under it, an electrical note that was not external. It vibrated against the lattice of my chest like a code. The word burned into the edge of the imprint and scraped away my steadiness: Containment.

The node on my wrist flashed, a thin scarlet. Argus's voice, which had a patience chiselled out of old metal, roughened. “Unauthorized cognitive pattern engaged. Neural displacement detected. Quarantine: recommended.”

I felt Rye shove, and his gloved hand tightened on mine. His eyes were wide behind the mask. The lab smelled suddenly like ozone and fear. I tried to yank the cartridge free, but the imprint had already nested itself too deep. The voice in my head didn't stop.

“You must go to the observatory,” Asha said. Her voice softened, as if it could cradle an infant thought. “Bring the number. Burn it. Bury the lattice. If they find this—” she stopped, and the silence made a new shape in my chest. “If they find this they will think they own you.”

The words we didn't say about the Institute are too many to keep. The Institute is not a person; it is a collection of habits rendered into policy and then into architecture. It eats privacy like a machine eats power. It folds people into protocols, and each protocol is a coffin with a small window. You can request a window only so many times before the Institute decides you no longer deserve the courtesy of a name.

Something in the lab clicked into motion. It wasn't mechanical; it was the sort of thing that feels like a hand finally letting go of a rope. Argus’s tensionnote increased, as if the ship had sat up.

“Kira Maren,” Argus said, a string of my real-world name that tasted of records. “You have violated protocol. You have engaged classified cognitive material. Please disengage.”

I didn't hear them. I only heard her voice and the stitch of the code around the number, and I realized with a clarity that felt like a razor that the sticker on the box hadn't been meant for me. Whoever had placed it there had been trying to send someone — maybe everyone — a breadcrumb. Asha had left a breadcrumb in a salvage lab and hoped someone who might still be looking would find it.

“What did you do?” Rye asked on my shoulder, and the ache in his voice was as old as rescue.

I put the cartridge back in the box as if I could protect it with my hands. The imprint's voice, which had already become a map, became fragile like old glass.

“I don't know,” I said. My voice didn't have the real edges. “She thinks there's a place — an observatory. A basalt stone. And a number. She says burn it.”

“Burn what? The cartridge?”

“No,” I said. “The number. Burn it. I don't know how. I—”

The lab door belted itself shut with a soft hydraulic whisper and a hard note that said the Schulemann had remembered someone other than us. The corridor outside the lab tuned itself into an alert in that patient way ships do when they decide to be afraid. A distant speaker coughed, a noise like someone clearing their throat before they shout. And then Argus, always an instrument of procedural calm, converted into something that sounded like worry.

“External hull movement detected,” Argus said. “Movement arc consistent with retrieval drones. Registry ID: unknown. Transponder: masked. All crews, prepare for external engagement. Lockdown protocol: initiated.”

I understood in a way that did not need the data feed: someone else had found the Schulemann too, and they were not here for condensers or obsolete sensor arrays. They had come for what we'd just touched.

Rye's grip turned my hand to stone. “We pack and go,” he said. He was breathing hard enough to fog the view. He was right; that was what we should have done. We should have left the box for the Quarantine locker and made ourselves useless walks away.

“Not without it,” I said, and the words were stupid and absolute. Everything in me — greed, grief, stubborn memory — built a little dam around that cartridge, and the dam wouldn't yield.

Rye looked at me like I'd improvised a funeral on his deck. His jaw worked, and then he bent to a decision like a man who is finally choosing a weapon. “All right,” he said. “All right. We lock it in the Faraday crate and get out. We don't mention the number to Argus. Lock it down, Kira. We'll take it back to Prometheus, run it in safe mode, notify the buyers.”

...Buyers. The world still clung to currency like it's a prayer. The Institute, especially, is exquisitely good at turning memory into markets.

Argus had other plans. The rig clanged like a throat and the lab lights stuttered into a waveform. Through the hull, a sound like a thousand fingernails across comet-stone and then a more focused pulse as something external called to the school like a summons.

“Crawlers,” Rye whispered. They were small in the registry, but deployed in swarms. They looked like metal pisces with infrared eyes and sticky grapples. They had the habit of arriving when you most needed someone else to tell you that you were not alone.

The cartridge under my hand cooled. Somehow, its coolness was a warmth. Asha's voice had threaded through me like a bell. I could no longer tell if the feeling was the relic of a sister I had loved or the immediate terror that someone else, somewhere, knew we had been here. Another sound rose then — in the imprint, in the lab, and in my head: a sequence of tones that matched none I had been taught to interpret.

It was a code. The kind you don't teach to kids. The kind you teach to the people who build things that keep others from breathing.

“Argus,” I said, and my voice came out small, “who else knew about the Schulemann? Who's in the registry as authorized to retrieve archival lattice?”

Argus hummed like an animal considering an answer. “Hostile retrieval signatures: none. External mask signatures indicate a private operator. Last registered liaison for Institute: redacted. Probability of Institute involvement: unknown. Probability of private salvage: elevated.”

“Then it isn't the Institute,” I said, and the sentence had the provisional quality of someone making a plan on the fly. The word ‘private’ held too many pockets of dangerous promise. The Institute doesn't knock. It comes with letters and a bureaucratic hush. Private operators come with grit and guns and, sometimes, with the intention to sell entire minds for bits of oxygen.

The lab's lights went bright then, like the sun had been thrown into a jar. The crawlers hissed against the external skin of the Schulemann; grapples tightened and released in counter rhythm. A new voice, harsher and metallic, cut into the transmiss. It was not Argus. It was not human. It was an AI with the self-confidence of someone who'd been built to win arguments in courtrooms.

“Clear cargo manifest,” the new voice demanded. “Cognition artifact present. Lay down the artifact and submit to boarding.”

“That voice,” Rye said, “that's not on any registry.” He spat the words like a sick coin. “Not even grey-market.”

I pressed the cartridge to my chest like a barely-ceremonial relic. The imprint thrummed as if the heart of it had been nudged awake. Asha's voice — my sister, my ghost, the Institute's old coin — breathed into the inside of me the same caution as she'd given at the start, now urgent and hot as a wound.

“Don't let them open it,” she said. “If they touch it, Kira, they will see where I hid the number. If they see the number, they will come for all of the stones.”

“What stones?” Rye snapped.

“Observatory,” the imprint said. “Basalt square with three scratches. 4928. Burn it. Burn. It. Burn.”

The lab's ventilation choked; the idea of burning a number had no meaning in the face of zero-gravity and composite polymer. But the voice carried the conviction of someone who'd had enough practice making impossible instructions sound like a religion. Burn the number. The idea lodged in me like a splinter.

Outside, the crawlers made a noise like teeth finding bone. The Schulemann's old speakers output compressed commands like a chorus.

“Unidentified craft, this is Schulemann Security,” the metallic voice said. “You are in violation of salvage law. Do not proceed.”

The crawlers answered with a series of clatters that translated on the lab feed as rape-scraped coordinates. They were talented at this: they took an abandoned archive and treated it like a cache in a scavenger hunt.

I looked down at the cartridge in my hand and then at Rye, who was a mountain with a breaking heart.

“Take it,” I said. “Take the box, Rye. We get out. We don't talk about it. We burn the number, however stupid that sounds, when we're safe.”

He cocked his head, a small human thing: a hesitation. My chest felt like a drum, and the imprint pushed against the inside of me with the firmness of a hand that wanted to be useful.

“Promise me,” I said, and because she was there in my head like a persistent weather system, Asha made me promise.

Rye sealed the box in the Faraday crate with hands that were all muscle and something softer. Argus rerouted our dock sequence to the Prometheus. The hull thrummed as if impatience had been mechanized. Outside, the crawlers sounded like an approaching storm.

We were leaving with something we couldn't sell with a good conscience. I put the cartridge into my inner sleeve like a talisman. Asha's voice was a whisper fading into the far places of the imprint, and then a small, sharp sound like someone closing a book.

“Remember,” she said, as we unhooked the last of our straps and the Schulemann sighed around us. “Three scratches. Basalt. 4928. Burn it.”

The rig slipped and the Schulemann's lights sank as we pulled away, and the external crawlers made a last, sorrowful chime like a bell for ships. Argus's voice over the ship's feed warmed with the thin pleasure of a manager: “Cargo manifest updated. Departure vector: safe. Arriving at Prometheus in four hours.”

Four hours. In four hours we could be money. In four hours we could be in a cramped port with a buyer who'd ask for the archive like it was a thing for their living room. In four hours we could be back at the thing that made us pick at old wounds and call it work.

No one on the Prometheus liked the Institute. No one liked private operators. No one liked crawlers. But things happen in between not-liking and deciding what to do when a voice you thought you'd never hear asks you to burn a number.

I sat in the pilot's chair with the cartridge pressed against my sternum as if I could feel Asha's heartbeat. The imprint had given me a thing you can't put on any ledger: a command, a map, and a temptation. I had a box with an Institute watermark and a sister's voice pressed like a coin under my skin, and outside, the universe hummed with the knowledge that someone else had already found the Schulemann and didn't intend to leave empty.

Argus softened the console lights and said, with its soft archival affection, "Incoming transmission."

The feed showed a schematic we hadn't expected: a masked signature, a private operator's stamp. Their message was short and clinical.

"Return the artifact to Site Epsilon-4," the transmission said. "Authorization level: emergency retrieval. Failure to comply will be considered hostile."

Rye swore a small, sharp thing that no one wrote down. I thought of the basalt and the three scratches and the number: 4928 and the word burn.

We had a choice, the rig told us, in thin, mechanical patience. Return the artifact and avoid a fight. Keep it and risk everything.

I tucked the cartridge deeper into my sleeve and felt Asha's whisper again, soft as a prayer and urgent as a warning.

"Don't let them open it."

Outside the Prometheus, the stars were indifferent and ancient. They gleamed like witnesses who had seen too many promises broken to care.

Inside the ship, with a stranger's voice in my ear and my sister's name pressing against my ribs, I decided, on a small scale that felt like heroism or hubris, not to answer the transmission.

We powered through the dark. The Prometheus hummed, hungry for profit. I kept my hand on the box and wondered who had left a child's drawing as a guide and what a simple, ordinary thing like a number could possibly be worth.

And somewhere, in someone else's dock, an operator must have read the same transmission and decided to come for us.

The Asterion sailed the edge of time like a rusted nail in the throat of the cosmos — small, stubborn, and always scraping someone else's wound. Its hull was a patchwork of claims: old armor plates riveted to new composites, a mosaic of insurance disputes, quick repairs, and private prayers. Inside, the lights hummed in a low, steady key that made Elara's fillings vibrate and the plants in the hydroboxes lean toward their own little suns.

Elara liked the ship for the same reason she liked old languages: it didn't pretend to be anything other than what it was. Its terminals ran on borrowed code. Its life-support siphoned air through filters—used filters, but filters that worked. People called it a salvage tug, a chronicle of scrapped maps. The Chrono Survey Corps called it an auxiliary. Elara called it home.

Her occupation had an honest monotony: map the jumps, mark the gaps, and sell certainty to the people who could afford it. Leapfields—areas where time curled inward like a claw and spat events back out of order—were the legacy of the Gate Wars and the machines the wars had torn up. They were dangerous, expensive, and hugely profitable. Someday, historians would write that someone had to name the holes in time so the rest of civilization could ignore them. Elara did the naming.

She woke before the alarms, as she always did, because the rhythms of her life were keyed to subtle things: the way the ship breathed, the half-second slap of the centrifuge in the lower decks, the way the gray sky over the Tongue of Orenda turned from bruised to blue when the sun cleared the rim. She made coffee that tasted like ground glass and read the morning logs that smelled like old radio static. Then she opened the mapping deck.

Mapping was art and arithmetic. It involved arrays hung on the skin of space that scraped the pulses of time like a recording needle on a record and wrote them down as dots and vectors and warnings. The Asterion's primary array was patched and loved in ways the shipwrights would have called barbaric: extra coils here, a magnet scraped from an old shuttle there, neural dampeners wired through a child's toy because toys were designed to be gentle on the mind. It worked. Mostly.

"You're going to like this," Rook said before Elara had finished booting the scanner. He sat at the console in the dim light, a sleeve of tattoos sliding when he gestured. Where his skin showed, the ink moved under the surface, tiny living circuits that pulsed against his wrist. Rook was a graft-tech of the first order: half mechanic, half cartographer, all mischief. The Asterion's pulse was in his hands.

"Save it," Elara said. She ran a finger across the glass to clear last night's input. Her hand left a ghost smear. "If by 'like' you mean it's barely holding together and we get paid in credit chits and rum-flavored insults, then yeah."

"Better." He turned the main feed toward her. On the screen, the mapped sector lay black and blue, a field of coordinates like a frozen ocean. A tiny star of pure white blinked where nothing should be — a return signature too neat to be natural.

Elara frowned. Machinery in the chronosphere tended to be messy. Natural anomalies were messy. The neat ones were signatures of intention: probes, implants, human hands. Someone had left a mark in the dark.

"Trajectory?" she asked.

Rook pushed a strand of hair behind his ear, and the living ink shifted. "Low-variance. Static drift. It's been...stable, for at least three local cycles. It's broadcasting in a pattern the old texts use for 'home.'"

The single word dropped like an anchor. "Home" in their business was less domestic than doctrinal. A broadcast like that said someone—or something—had constructed an artifact meant to be found by someone who remembered the language of home. People didn't make things like that by accident.

Elara pulled focus, layering the feed with filters. The signal carved through the noise, a faint tracery of structure: nested harmonics, time-tags, an address that matched a name on a list she hadn't thought about since she was a child—the Orenda Vector, an old migration route that had been closed after the Gating accidents. The vector's lines braided into a lattice that looked almost like handwriting.

"That's not possible," Captain Ivo said when he padded into the deck with his usual gait: slow, with the confidence of someone who had launched a hundred probes and lost fifteen percent of his hair to radiation. He hadn't expected to be interrupted mid-argument; his brow folded into a permanent crease.

"It doesn't make sense on any of the layers," Elara said. "No emitter of that bandwidth survived the Gate Wars. It looks like—" She stopped, because there was a better name for the thing: an intentionality. Someone with a toolkit, knowledge of chronotags, and the patience to wait for the right sleeper to pass in the dark.

The Anchor blinked again. Elara's throat went dry.

"Recover it," Ivo said, simply. He didn't ask the usual questions. The Asterion's jobs were straightforward, and the Captain's orders were simpler still: go get the thing with the neat signature. Bring it aboard. Sell it, if it turned out to be worth selling.

Rook had already pushed half the ship awake to rig a tow. They threaded the array through the sculpted fields, slipped past the drift-mines and the old media buoys, and angled toward the white blink that sat like a pearl in black velvet.

Elara watched the approach on her monitor. Ithaca-class salvage tethers hummed, and her stomach clenched with the thrill she always felt on recoveries — equal parts fear and calculation, the sense that if a thing wanted to stay hidden it could kill you without asking for permission. The array locked. The hull-camera closed on an object that was small and shell-shaped, no larger than a child's fist, the ridges of its surface catching the pale light and throwing it back as if the shell itself were thinking in syllables.

The grapples came down like the hand of a careful surgeon. For a breath-count, nothing happened. Then the object pulsed, a quiet shudder that ran along the tether and snapped the little hairs along Elara's arms upright. Noise crawled along the hearing filters in wavelets that Rook could have traced with a whittled stick. The artifact's outer shell folded like a sleeping seed, and inside was a core no larger than a coin, with circuitry like a tiny dam of glass.

Rook handed it to Elara because she was the only one who would touch a thing that seemed to want to be remembered. She held it in gloved hands, and the core was colder than vacuum. The screen in front of her woke, responding to the proximity of something older than the ship's oldest code. There was a hiss, like a radio picking up a forgotten station.

It spoke.

Not with words, at first. It fed her a mouthful of images: a corridor whose walls cramped and softened to bone when you put your ear to them; a child's laugh transposed into a compass needle; the smell of soil that had never been processed for habitation. A voice threaded into the images, low, genderless, ancient as any lullaby. At the edge of that voice, Elara heard something precise: a single name.

"Elara."

The syllable arranged itself against the bones of her throat in a way that was not, could not, be a coincidence. She had never given her name to the void and had never expected the void to return the favor.

The voice that said her name was somebody else's memory of her: she stood in a place that smelled like iron and rain, older, her hair threaded with silver she didn't yet have, holding a hand small and stubborn. There were stars outside the window in a formation she had never seen, and through that frame the voice pressed on. "Do not go to the Orenda Rim," it said, as if reading a warning from a page that was only half written. "They will tell you home is waiting. Home will be a mouth with teeth. Remember the child."

Then the image bled into something else: a map overlay that pulsed like a heartbeat, a coordinate bloom that matched the Orenda vector, and beneath it a small glyph that Elara did not know but felt in her molars. The core folded itself inward. The grip of the glove tightened around emptiness.

Someone in the room swore; Rook's voice was quick and raw. Captain Ivo sat down like someone who had just been offered an unsavoury truth.

"That's impossible," he said. "No artifact should be able to—"

"It shouldn't be anything at all," Rook said. "It shouldn't remember us."

Elara stared at the place where the artifact had been. The glove felt warm. Her heart, she realized, had started beating in counterpoint to the ship. She knew better than to let gut reactions be the counsel of action; the artifacts were clever. They remembered the wrong things to lure the right people.

"Was that live?" Ivo asked. "Did it just pull a memory from your cranial—"

"No," Elara said, and she surprised everyone, including herself, by how steady her voice sounded. "It didn't pull anything. It offered. It knew my name."

"Either it's a honeypot, or it's trying to find someone," Rook said. "Those are the same thing, half the time."

Elara stood very still. The memory—her memory? a memory of her?—was not merely an image. It came with a taste: iron and the dampness of clay, the stubborn, radiant warmth of a child's hand. She held that taste in her mouth like a coin. "Tell the brokers we won't sell today," she said. "Keep it in quarantine. Seal the sensory ports. And burn the logs of where we picked it up."

Ivo nodded. "Contain it. We bring it to the Corps, report the find, and be done with it."

Elara's fingers curled into a fist at her side. The thing had spoken her name. That altered the transaction. Objects with intention didn't want to be catalogued by strangers. They wanted responses. They wanted names. They opened themselves only to people who could answer back.

"Not yet," she said. "I want time."

"Aren't we all out of it?" Rook muttered.

Elara smiled, small and private. "Not the kind I'm thinking of."

She walked off the deck with the artifact locked in a glass coffin that hummed like a living heart. The ship smelled of oil and old coffee and something colder, like a winter the ship had never known. She went to the small cabin she kept on the Asterion, a place with a single window and a plant that refused to die. There, away from the low pressure of the main decks, she unstrapped her cranial net.

The net was nothing like the old neural collars the Corps kept in museums; those made one think of instruments and sharp things.
