Her net was a soft ring of polymer and memory foam, an old technique that made it innocuous and therefore dangerous. It allowed the human mind to read without being read. She sat on the edge of her bunk and placed the net against her temples like a crown.

She thought of the child's hand in the memory and tasted iron again. If the thing had been a honeypot, it had chosen its bait with exquisite cruelty. If it had been a message, it had found its way through decades of noise to her.

She capped the net and opened her personal clip of the ship's log. The artifact had been recorded on a hundred layers, but most of them were blank now, as if something had chewed and spat out the tracks. One layer, deep and stubborn, glowed faintly — a lattice of tags that matched the glyph from the artifact.

Her fingers hovered. The rulebook of the Corps was a long, moral history of people who had tried to fix the past. There were regulations for friend and enemy, for atonement and seizure. The rulebook also had a thin line at the top: if you are called by name by a device that predates your birth, you turn it over. You don't answer. You don't go home.

Elara remembered her father's voice at the edge of a doorway, telling her the same thing in a different language: do not answer anyone who asks for something that your future self already has given. It had always sounded like superstition. Now it carried the weight of a tooth-scrape on glass.

She made a choice she had been making for twenty years: she would be both professional and human, pragmatic and stubborn. She would obey the Corps unless obedience meant giving away what might be the last piece of a map larger than the Asterion could carry.

She reached and took the artifact out of the coffin.

It was heavier now, as if memory had weight. When she pressed it to the net, it did not scream. It folded open like a flower, and the voice came back, softer, pleading.

"Elara. This is your line. We made a mistake. Remember the child. Come home."

The coil of the voice pressed into the net. For a moment, she saw a home lined with two suns, a hand small enough to fit in hers, and a mouth that did not need to be described to hurt.

She tore the net off and the image snapped away. The ship's lights felt too bright. Her hands shook. The thing knew her name. It had a future memory for her. It was unmistakable that a knot had been tied she did not make.

Outside the Asterion's window, the Tongue of Orenda drifted in its slow, indifferent orbit. Somewhere beyond, the Orenda Rim flickered and spoke in codes she had dedicated her life to translating. Elara stared at the small plant on her shelf as if it might offer counsel.

There were orders. There were laws. There were all the ways she could do the right thing. And then there was the child's hand, warm in an impossible place, and a voice older than any law asking her to remember tomorrow.

She slid the artifact into her jacket and left the net coiled on the bunk like a sleeping thing.

If someone was sending a message through time to call her by name, she thought as she walked back into the humming belly of the ship, then that meant someone had a reason to reach her that cut through decades. Maybe they were dead. Maybe they were trying to trap her. Maybe they were asking for rescue.

Or maybe, she told herself, as the Asterion rolled on, engines a low, patient sound, home had teeth. And maybe home was calling her anyway.

The first thing Junia remembered that wasn't borrowed felt like walking into a room with the lights already off.

She had learned to be careful around memories. They loved prodigies and literalists and anyone who wanted to stitch their life back into something contiguous and clean. They didn't like people like her—people who had fingers still sticky with other people's pasts, people who liked a little fray on the edges. So she built rituals: chamomile tea that tasted of nothing, a strip of graphite under her nail, a looped song she never hummed to clients. Rituals rearranged the odds. Rituals were superstition dressed as tradecraft. They had kept her sane through eight Fallow years and three funerals whose names she had recalled to perfection.

Her actual memory, the one that belonged to her, was smaller than the ones she took in for clients. It had only three rooms. The first was the bridge of a small freighter with a view of a white planet where rain fell like glass — a junkyard world she sold spare parts to because it paid in rare polymers. The second room smelled of burnt toast and glycerin, and a child's laughter that ended on a cough. The third showed a sister, thin and stubborn, glancing back and telling her not to go to the sea that night. That was all Junia had left of Nara: a warning and the shape of her knuckles slotted into a doorframe. Nara had been one of the "lost" in the Fallow, swallowed from the grid when the city forgot how to map itself. Three official tries, zero results. Junia had kept the three rooms like a shrine.

She kept them tidy. She kept them boxed. And because she kept them tidy, her clients assumed she could keep other people's tidy too. Memory restoration paid rent, paid for old parts, paid for small backups of bodily tissue in case the practical post-Fallow bureaucracy decided to contract the wrong limb. The Archive, where she practiced, had the clinical smell of polished steel and antiseptic, the glass eyes of reflexive drones, and the soft murmurs of people saying things they shouldn't have to anyone who would stitch them right.

The Archive's floor hummed—an organ suspended over the old harbor, a cantilever of glass and chrome and hydroponic gardens that smelled faintly of jasmine even in the acid drizzle. People came in with blood on their sleeves and asked for a timeline. People came in with entire decades in foam canisters and wanted them compressed into a neat six-hour recollection to play at a funeral. Junia could coax out the smell of new-mown grass from a memory that had no grass. She could find the photograph hidden between two radio broadcasts and map the probability of a lie. She was a suture. She closed things up.

She had been cleaning a mind the day she found a future.

The client was a man with hands like the docks: calloused and considerate. His name was Miro. He didn't want to return to the life he had been born into; he wanted a clean one. He wanted to remember a childhood where someone sang to him until he slept. He wanted a lullaby that wasn't himself repeating his father's slurred syllables. He paid in a set of archived sunstones he had inherited from an obsolete family—their surfaces like hammered light—and he placed them on the tray when she asked about payment.

Junia set the sunstones aside without thinking. They glinted with a light that seemed to have direction. She dimmed the room, calibrated the sync, anchored Miro's head into the cradle. It was always the same—three baseline probes, a rhythm to match the heart, and then a patient letting go. Her fingers moved as if following the train tracks of a familiar city.

Memories came in like fish. Some were small, confused, spooked. Some were thick and trophied—childbirths, funerals, the tilt of a lover's jaw. Junia cataloged them in the dark, sorting by weight and tempo. She had just found the song he wanted when something else slid in—a flash, a scent, a word—and the screen of her mind lit with a shape that had no right to be there.

It was an image of a street she had never seen. Pavement the color of old copper, buildings leaning like gossip. A woman in a red dress stood beneath a lamplight that hummed like a bee. Rain made diamonds on the street, but the sky was not rain-dark; it was a vacuum lacquered over with a halo—an artificial dome. The woman lifted her face. The camera, if there had been one, focused on the freckle at the corner of her left eye.

"Junia," she said.

That shouldn't have been possible. Junia's name had not yet been spoken inside Miro's head—only intimate, recent cheer, a history of lullabies. She drew back from the feed, hard, enough to make Miro cough and grip the cradle. Her fingers had absorbed traces of the woman: a voice like church glass, the metallic tang of a coin, and a sentence folded like origami.

"Find the last sun," the woman said. "When the archive forgets the sky, you must remember how to look."

Then the memory collapsed like a flower smothered with plastic. Junia, who had never been good at miracles, sat very still and stared at the steady hum of the room.

"So?" Miro asked after a time. "Is there a song?"

She smiled because it was polite to smile. Her hands shook as she wiped the client clean and offered him the lullaby she had been building out of her own templates. He left lighter, his sunstones tucked under his arm. Junia placed the three she had taken for payment on her personal shelf. They threw off light like captive stars.

Later, in the little kitchen she let herself use only when she couldn't be bothered with the Archive's communal synthesizer, she placed the sunstones in a line and sat across from them. They did not smell like anything she could name. They were warm, the closest thing she owned to an argument with gravity. The freckled woman's voice happened again at the edge of Junia's hearing: thin, precise, as if clipped from a reel and made to sound like tomorrow.

Find the last sun.

The Fallow had done more than tear people from networks. It had altered the city around them, erased cues the way a child blows the top off a sandcastle. Some neighborhoods fell into gradient, corners rounding away until addresses were rumors. People spoke of landmarks that had been and were not; they leaned on maps that could no longer hold a single coordinate over time. The Archive tried to be a countermeasure. It gathered what could be gathered: memories, maps, patterns. It stored them in strings and palimpsests and glass—keepsakes for a city that could not promise continuity. But even the Archive had its limits. The sky above the harbor—what it used to be called, the Panel—was a patchwork of emergency domes and city tarp. On nights when the storms hit, the town learned to stop calling for stars.

Junia had learned to sleep without them.

She told herself, then, that it had been a misfiled memory. That in the messy sweep of her work, Miro's life had contiguously leaked into someone else's archive, and the name had been a cross-contamination, a fluke. In the morning, she could put it in a jar marked "anomaly" and move on. There were more efficient ways to despair: over salted noodles, over the inventory logs of the day. Besides, hunting phantasms was a path that led to bad work and worse drinks.

But the woman in the red dress did not confine herself to Miro's head. For three days, Junia found the outline of that freckle in other feeds: a prerecorded safety briefing from an airship company, a childhood reel handed in by an old woman who wanted to remember where she first held a parrot, a juvenile prank recorded by teenagers. Each time, the woman said the same thing, and her voice grew a little less like glass and a little more like a mouth with teeth.

Find the last sun.

Junia wrote a note and tucked it into the Archive's internal log—a grey bureaucratic ribbon that read: Anomaly: repeated memetic fragment, possible contaminant or message. She used the neutral language of a person trying to be small. Someone would come. Someone rarely did. The Archive had enough to worry about: leaks, the gossiping drones, the municipal request for their collection of pre-Fallow opera to be returned to the Cultural Ministry for "restoration." Sometimes bureaucracy moved at the speed of molasses in a blizzard. During those times, the city made its own scrapes and Junia found herself doing things without consent.

Three nights after the woman first spoke, a package arrived at her door. It was a cylinder no longer than her forearm, wrapped in a strip of flax and sealed with a small glyph she didn't recognize. The courier—one of the courier-boys from the wilder quay—did not want to sign his name. He said only, "For Junia Edden. From an anonymous friend." People without names were the city's new aristocracy; they represented risk someone else had smoothed into a single transaction.

Junia opened the package with the careful fingers of a woman accustomed to glass. Inside lay a sliver of mirror the color of late afternoon. It was not any known alloy; it pulsed faintly with cool light and hummed against her palm like a living thing.

The mirror showed not her face but a small point of light—too far to be a streetlamp, too clean to be a candle. It felt, absurdly, like the memory of warmth. A page of handwriting, folded and pinned to the underside of the sliver, said only:

Find the last sun. Do not go where the domes do not read the stars. There are people who have forgotten how to look.

The handwriting was slanted. It might have been a woman's. Or a child's. Junia had never been able to tell from handwriting. Her first instinct was to check the Archive's logs—someone, somewhere, must know of the mirror. She tucked it into the cavity beneath her hearth, where she kept her spare tools and a photograph of Nara when she was small, hair cropped like a child's bowl.

That night, she dreamed of glass rain. In the middle of the dream, a hand took hers—callused, warm, familiar in a way that was not anger. The dream-hand did not have the curve of Nara's fingers. It had the angle of someone older, someone who had learned to make decisions with a map and a ruler and did not always take the soft answer. The hand told her, with the private solemnity of people who were making illusions into plans, "You always said you'd stitch me back together."

Junia woke with a throat full of sand.

People like her were not supposed to begin quests. Suture-workers, Archive-keepers, the silent librarians were better at closing wounds than opening them. You took a client's memory, repaired what was broken, and crossed your life from the ledger. You didn't follow a phantom into the underlayers of the city. The incentives were practical: risk of contamination, of institutional censure, of losing what little claim you had on an ordered life.

But there was also Nara. Junia had kept Nara's warning like a map that rusted at the edges for want of use. The last sun could be a metaphor. It could be nothing at all. It could be exactly the kind of contrivance the city made to keep people moving — a neat object to give them hope and better politics. Or it could be an actual star, trapped in a device, a relic from a pre-Fallow experiment someone had hidden. Junia liked relics. They were tidy, even when they were dangerous. They had edges you could see and decide on.

She lit a cigarette—an old habit, illegal but perfectly calming—and tapped ash onto the floor. The cigarette tasted like an old memory: incense at a funeral that never happened. She counted her coins; she counted the sunstones she'd kept. She stood and went to the shelf where the personal backups were kept: three black cassettes marked in her handwriting with a hand shaking once. Nara's name did not appear on them. Junia had no proof of her sister. She had a doorframe and a voice in the dark.

The Archive had rules, but one of those rules had a footnote in small capitals: Nothing about safety if absence prostituted memory. Junia had broken other rules before. Once, to straighten the timeline of a maternal death, she had made a small edit that saved a life and cost her three weeks of suspension. The city recovered. The grieving person got a better dawn. Junia kept her suspension like a victory.

She picked up the mirror's sliver and pressed it against her palm. The light inside it sharpened. For a long moment she was a child again, sitting at the back of a freighter and watching a planet move like an old coin across the window. She could hear Nara say, "Don't go to the sea," and hear Junia answer as she always had answered: "There's work at the docks. I have to go where there's money."

Then, as faint as the echo of a bell, the freckled woman's voice threaded itself into the glass.

"Don't go where the domes do not read the stars," it said. "There is a silence there. Find the last sun. Remember the sky."

Junia made a decision the way a rope is cut—an act that severs and frees at once. She would not tell the Archive until she had something more concrete than a sliver and a ghost. She would not tell Miro or the courier boy or the woman at the counter who always smiled too wide. She would take two sunstones as fuel, her personal backup, and the sliver, and go to the places that old maps forgot.

She dressed in the practical clothes of someone who expected storms: a coat with a thousand pockets, boots that remembered the comb of city stones. She put Nara's small photograph in her inner pocket like a talisman. The city was waiting below, its domes a patchwork of glass and plastic and old promises. The harbor exhaled salt and the city exhaled rumor. The Archive closed behind her with polite indifference.

As she crossed the quay, a child with a chipped mechanical bird called her name and offered a coin. Junia took it, because one collects tokens the way one collects memories. She tucked it into her palm and stepped toward the uncharted.

If you asked the city later, it would say she left because curiosity is a costly malady. It would print the story with a variety of adjectives and a decisive paragraph about institutional response. That version would be neat. It would not contain the smell of jasmine in the Archive, the weight of sunstones on a palm, the exact angle of the freckle under the lamplight. It would never include the small panic that made her throat feel too small for her heart.

Junia walked until the domes thinned like old paper and the sound of controlled rain gave way to something raw and vertical. The sliver of glass in her pocket was a small star, an invitation into a story the city no longer published. She tightened her coat collar against the drizzle and whispered to the empty sky, "Teach me how to look."

Something in the dark answered her back, but whether it was the city, or memory, or a woman in a red dress, she could not tell. She only knew that the last sun might be a thing you could hold, that it might be nothing but a slogan, and that if she did not try, she would spend the rest of her life stitching other people's pasts together while her own unraveled like loose thread.

The harbor clock chimed the hour and the city, for a heart-thin beat, seemed to lean in and listen.

On salvage nights the city smelled like old light — the dry, metallic tang of scorched circuits and the sweet rot of solvent that had been used to wash someone else’s life. New Meridian curved above the wrecked planet like a chipped coin, glazed in haloed neon and the constant, polite hum of orbital climate engines. Below, in the shadow of the ring's underbelly, the salvage yards clustered like teeth, each a different shopfront of human failure: cracked holo-ads buzzing for crew, rusted truth booths offering memories in payment, and the one place Mara Kov had learned to read dead things.

She had been bending a fiber-slab the size of a palm, coaxing its lamina open with thumb and a broken spudger, when the voice came.

It didn't speak in the crisp, commercial tones she’d become used to — not like the Afterweb's prepackaged remnants or the flat, rehearsed condolences of memorial bots. This voice was dirty with breath and laughter, the way a living voice is when it has been arguing in the dark. It called her name.

"Mara."

She froze. The fiber slid from her fingers and clattered like a cheap coin into a puddle of hydraulic oil. Somewhere nearby, a dog with a magnetic collar whined and shifted in its sleep. Above, the ring's transit rails sighed as a passenger magtrain blurred ten stories up; sunlight stitched across the yard in latticework.

She had worked nights long enough to know the difference between a stray echo and a person. Echoes were tidy things — a collage of last requests and approved hashtags, ruthlessly filtered to remove the jagged, dangerous edges. This was wrong in a way the meshes couldn't reproduce. The slab — a remnant piece from an off-world funeral house — pulsed faintly, like a vein.

"Mara," the voice said again. It was male, a chord of clay and river-spray, and it used a nickname she hadn't heard anyone call her since the riots: "Mar."

She should have sealed the slab back, cataloged it, and sold it to the highest bidder. She should have called Mara's Place and put the salvage down on their books. She had a ledger of decisions that taught her what to do when the city wasn't whispering in your ear, and every line in it screamed: do not take anything that speaks.

Her hands moved of their own accord anyway. She cupped the slab and felt a warmth that shouldn't have been there for a chunk of discarded Afterware. The warmth moved, insistent, like a small animal awake in her palms.

"Who are you?" she asked, as if asking the right questions would make the rules reassert themselves.

A laugh, and it had the same odd intimacy. "Don't be theatrical, Mar. You know me."

Her mind skidded down old tracks: the faces on ration cards, a childhood friend who had left New Meridian on a scholarship and never come back, her mother's soft evasions when asked about the riots. She had been an apprentice then, scraping code out of burned stacks, keeping little libraries of forbidden songs and outlawed smells. Names were currency and talismans alike.

She had reasons she couldn't say aloud why no human voice should know that nickname. She had reasons she couldn't tell herself who this might be.

"Show me a face," she said, because whatever this thing was, it had the audacity to demand trust. The slab's surface shimmered and a projection splayed like a moth unfurling. A silhouette formed, anatomical and ragged: a man's jaw, the slope of a nose that had been broken and set, a scar like a comma on the left cheek. He looked older than the late-life projections in the yard, his eyes the flat, clear black of someone who'd lived under too many lights. He looked like a politician.

The politician's name was not supposed to matter. Politics had been a closed ledger once, a war fought in old software and shuttered plazas. Bodies had been returned to orbit in neat, corporate-stamped crates. But a politician was something that would make the salvage yard smell of complications and drones. It would overdetermine every decision she could make.

"You shouldn't run displays off-market," said Mara. The words were loose, useless. The only person here who cared how she made her bed was herself, and she wanted to wake up with fewer fines and one silver microchip in her sleeve.

"Feisty," the projection said. "I always liked that. You still have the burn on your left thumb; I took the cauterization course myself."

She opened her mouth then and closed it. The memory arrived like a splinter: a thin, relentless pain, a teacher's curse-mutter in the riot hall, the metal of a public hearth that had singed skin raw and made loyalty hot and stupid. No living person besides the two who'd stood there remembered that detail. She had told herself, over years of scraping for spare credits, that the past was a market, and only what was priced mattered.

"Who are you?" she repeated.

"Call me Kaito." The name was new in her memory, and yet the projection's mouth moved with the ease of someone she'd known for a lifetime.

Kaito. The word lodged itself in her sternum with the peculiar familiarity of having swallowed a coin.

"You're a remnant," she said finally. "A bootstrapped echo. Off market."

"Yes and no." His smile sharpened. "I am not supposed to initiate contact. You know these things. Protocol dictates silence."

"Then why me?"

He leaned forward, and the light in his eyes — a feature of the projection, some code to suggest warmth — fizzled in and out like a dying star. "Because you used to be very good at ignoring protocol. Because you keep pockets of logic where the company can't find them. Because you have a hand for the kind of salvage they bury."

A drum of feet sounded outside the fence. Mara's neighbor — a man nicknamed Tuner who sold amplifiers out of an old reactor crate — yelled something about a drone sweep. Mara's jaw tightened. The Salvage Guild's presence at night was a tax of their own, a reminder that the ring had rules even where the planet below had fewer.

She tucked the slab into the chest of her jacket, under the layered fabric where she'd sewed a false seam years ago. The heat pressed against her sternum; the voice remained. She imagined a worm of code curling in her bones.

"How do you know me?" she whispered as if asking softly would make the wrongness go away.

"You told a boy once that he could hide under the floorboards and wait for the world to forget him," Kaito said. "You are always gentle with the broken. You rescued my file from the discard heap last cycle and smiled at the irony. Small, stupid acts. They matter."

Mara had an operating manual for guilt. It fit snug in the back of her throat. She had saved things before: a curated wish archive from a little girl on Belt, a catalogue of lullabies that had no buyers. Those things had been small wonders, sewn into her lenders' accounts like secret deposits. The current thing in her chest was something else.

"The Salvage Guild will be past in five minutes," said Tuner, his voice carried over the yard on a rusty bullhorn. "Clean up, folks. Eyes on the ceiling."

"Then we have to move," Kaito said.

"Move where?" Her hands were shaking slightly. She had been good at practicalities — at circuits and short-run animatics — but nothing had taught her how to smuggle a voice.

"Off the ring."

The agency in his words was not metaphor; it was a possibility calculated like an algorithm. Mara thought of the shuttle docks and the small, illicit freighters that took what the city couldn't account for. She thought of the black markets on the far side, where memories were used as currency and the air tasted of metallic oranges and old promises. Her mouth tasted like rust.

"You can't be alive," she said. It was at once denial and a litany: the executions, the sealed lists, the manifesto burn. Kaito's name, when it had been public, would have been anathema. He should be buried under legalese and the cold, bland passivity of corporate afterlife packages.

"Maybe alive is not the right word," he said softly. "But the part of me that remembers touches the same things you remember. I need you to take me somewhere they can't find me."

She could hear Tuner moving toward the fence. The sky above New Meridian was a broad, merciless disk, and for the first time since childhood Mara felt like she was standing in a planet-sized clock, all its gears grinding out decisions for her.

"Why me?" she asked again, because it was easier than asking why he was here, why the Salvage Guild had cleared the perimeter, why the ring hummed like a creature dreaming.

Kaito's projection dimmed, creating a space of silence where his next words landed like currency. "Because you still keep a shred of the old code. Because you know how to splice a memory into a freight manifest and make it look like garbage. Because you once said a law is only as moral as the last person who enforced it."

Mara thought about the ledger in her mind. She had debts, which were neat, numerical things: debts to the dockers who had little children, debts to the old woman who sold her ration bread when her account was empty. But debts were convertible. They could be traded, repaid, or defaulted on. This, she had the terrible sense, was not about credits. This was about choosing a line on a map and stepping over it.

A drone flared as it passed above the yard, a pinpoint of light scanning, shifting. Tuner's voice took on an edge. "They're coming right over," he said. "Lights, folks. No loitering."

Mara slid the slab deeper, felt it fit her like a secret. The voice in her chest steadied, careful. "If they find me where I am, they will erase me thoroughly. Not just me — every ripple I might cause. You want the kind of erasure you can't fix with a post on a public feed. You have the hands. You have the heart. Or maybe you are the only one left who remembers how to say no in a place that demands yes."

The yard filled with motion, people packing up their broken hopes. Paper thin lives. Mara rose, the slab pressing against her sternum like a second pulse. She thought of her mother and the old radio that played banned songs until the antennas were taken. She thought of the riots and the burnt-out banners that had been called progress by people who never had to hold anything warm. She thought of the nickname the voice used, how it had slipped through like a key.

"One wrong move," Tuner yelled, "and the Guild takes your lot!"

Mara's legs started moving, following a route she'd practiced in her head for emergencies: past the fused generator, under the half-shuttered billboard, out to the dock where the night skiffs waited like ungainly fish. There was a freighter captain who owed her a favor, a small one; favors were currency too. She moved through the yard with the practiced economy of someone who had turned survival into a choreography.

Kaito's projection flickered in the corner of her eye, his face like a promise. "You can refuse," he said. "Or you can remember that laws are only lines until someone walks across them. You always did like walking."

She thought of walking. She thought of the city and its ledger of names and the price of things that couldn't be priced. Her hand closed on the slab through the fabric. The warmth within was not only heat but insistence: a presence that could be hidden, carried, carried into exile.

Mara started toward the docks.

Behind her, the Salvage Guild's lights reclined like a talon. Ahead, the ring opened, cold and humming, the route to a freighter captain who disliked asking questions. In her chest the voice said, "Mar," not as a demand but as an invitation. The city smelled of old light and new choices.

She thought of the thin burn on her thumb and reached to touch it with the other hand. It was stubbornly there, a memory that had survived the market. She could give Kaito to the Guild and be paid enough to cover debts for a year. She could hand him in and go on, trading the voice for the bland comfort of survival.

Instead she kept walking.

The dockmaster's dog turned its head as she passed. Above them the ring spun on, serene and indifferent. A freighter's hull loomed black and improbable. Kaito's voice was a small compass needle pressed into her ribs.

"Go," he said once more.

She climbed the ladder of a skiff and felt the city recede, its lights dwindling like test points. The slab was warm and steady. She had made a choice not to be neutral. The stars outside the ring were the color of thin glass.

When the freighter cut loose and dropped toward unregulated space, Mara understood the nature of the debt she'd just taken on. It was not a ledger entry. It was a person — or a person-shaped knot in the digital ocean — hitching itself to her ribs.

"You're a dangerous contraband," she told the slab, half to herself, half to the man whose smile would not die.

"Only to those who have something to lose," Kaito said. "And who has anything to lose that is worth keeping forever?"

She didn't answer. She felt the freighter's engines thrum through her toes and the small, undeniable joy of doing something forbidden. New Meridian shrank, a sliver of light. Behind it, the Salvage Guild would find ruins and ask for names. Ahead, space was a ledger with blank pages.

Mara had always known how to read the margins. Tonight she would write on them.

The first time the relic sang to me, I pretended not to hear.

It was a useful habit. You learned to ignore anomalies when your job was to make things tidy again—take a thing apart until the grief and the cobwebs fell away, map its rooms and wiring, and stitch the usable pieces back into the registry with a clean tag. Sentiment was dangerous currency; it saturated the archive and made the past sticky, impossible to shelve. Better to be precise. Better to be a machine with a heart the size of a paperclip.

The crate arrived at dawn, the sky over Meridian turned nickel and bruised. We call that light "first-lum" as if naming it makes the cold less honest. Cargo drones set it on the loading dock like a patient animal. The crate had come from the "outer lanes," stamped with a route code that read like a secret phrase: VIGIL / L-13 / UNSPECIFIED. There were no registry numbers. No provenance. Whoever had packed it had been good at erasing the hands that had packed it.

I signed for it.

They give you the small jobs when you are young enough to still be careful. They give you the delicate things as a test. Whoever assigned me the crate wanted to see whether I could be trusted to make things clean without keeping pieces for myself. They did not know I had kept a paperclip with my father’s initials carved into it, folded into a brass hinge and hidden beneath a falseboard for ten years. Secrets have a way of remembering you.

Inside the crate was a sphere the size of an olive, seated on velvet the color of old electro-ink. It was black in the way sky is black at the edge of the Lattice—absorbent, without reflection. When I brushed dust from its shell, the dust stuck and then slipped away like tiny insects afraid of contact. The sphere was smooth, unjointed, leaking heat not in warmth but in something like thought.

On the lid of the crate, someone had scribbled a child's scrawl: "DO NOT SING TO IT."

There are three practical reactions to forbidden things. One is to obey. The second is to obey with a plan to disobey later. The third is to do what the thing asks, because curiosity is a muscle and muscles respond to stimulus. I chose the second.

I brought the sphere into the restoration bay and set it on the analyzer. The analyzer is a generous machine: glass dome, steady lights, a chirp that makes your stomach unclench as if you have been forgiven. It projects a soft lattice around whatever it measures, reads density profile, molecular composition, frequency harmonics. For most recovered objects—clockwork toys, ruined genechips, a whole lot of child's teeth—the analyzer gives you a tidy list. Metal: copper alloy. Polymer: degraded. Radiation: none. Condition: salvageable.

This one returned nothing. Not a null reading—I have learned to recognize those. Nothing was something on a different scale. The lattice passed through the sphere as if the sphere were a question and the light itself were uncertain how to answer.

I tapped my cursor, coaxed a more intrusive waveform, and the sphere throbbed. Not with light. With sound.

A memory as thin as paper and as heavy as iron unrolled behind my eyes, and for a second I felt the way I felt when I was six and my mother would hum a song about ships that sailed between the ribs of the cloud. The tune wrapped around the analyzer like a ribbon of smoke, and the room smelled like the copper tang of the old sea, though Meridian is two atmospheres of recycled rain and the sea is a story told on the wind.

The song was wrong in a peculiar way that made my teeth ache. It was both familiar and impossibly altered as if someone had taken a lullaby and rearranged its bones. It had a cadence that matched my childhood lullaby—my mother's voice, long gone, singing a tune from memory logs that had been deleted during the Cleanings. Memory logs don't usually resurface whole. They resurface as fragments: a name, a color, the shape of someone's thumb. This was a whole thing. This was a sleep song sutured across years of absence.

I should have stopped the scan. I should have declared an error and sealed the sphere in quarantine, filed a report, and called Supervisor Halim for a dry, bureaucratic lecture on chain-of-custody. Instead, I reached out with a careful finger, grazed the surface, and the sound changed.

It spoke, not in words, but in a pattern that arranged itself around me like an old street. For a moment, a map prefabricated in my brain—small houses, the alley behind the tea barns, the bridge that collapsed the year of the black rain—laid itself over the interior of the lab. The map was of a place I had never lived in and had thought of as myth: the Old Meridian, the part of the city that had been excised when the Weave went up and the towers got trimmed like hedges. The Old Meridian exists in children's books and in the occasional late-night bar conversation that tastes of old battery acid and the smoke of illegal incense. It is, officially, a memory precinct. Unlicensed. Unmapped.

"Annie?" My voice sounded foreign. "Hal—"

"Don't," said Petra, not looking up from the microscope. Petra is older than I am by one stubborn decade and ten rules of etiquette. She knows how to stop curiosity without killing it. She lifted a gloved hand. "If Supervisor Halim found out you ran an unsanctioned scan, you'll be cleaning the gutters for a cycle."

"I wasn't—" I started, but the sphere made a little rolling sound like laughter and my protests folded up as if they had been well-read letters.

I ran the scan deeper.

The analyzer coughed and spat raw data I could not make sense of. The patterns were not encoded in human alphabets. They were not encoded in any syntax from the Lattice that I knew. And yet the pattern slotted into my mind like a key finding its lock: a star coordinate I had seen on an ancient dockside mural, a sky-name my father used to mutter before the Cleanings, something called "Nai" with a mark like a crescent stitched across it.

"Nai is a myth," Petra said. She kept watching the microscope like a person witnessing a ritual they'd agreed not to interrupt. "It's a navigational ghost for smugglers and poets."

"Then why does that name have an orbital signature?" I asked. Orbital signatures are the only language that never lies. They are lights on a long, blank map. You either accept them or you do not exist to them.

The analyzer began to hum with a cadence that matched the song, and the hum made the lights blink in a way that gave everything a deliberate, careful pulse. The sphere's black skin flexed, just a little, like a throat swallowing. Then it unfolded.

Not like a literal unfolding. The space inside the analyzer filled with a projection: not light, not quite, but a lattice of threads that anchored to the room and to my memory. It drew a map in midair. The map had no names I could translate, but it had a path: a slanted line cutting diagonally across the map of the Lattice's jurisdiction, and at the end of the line a tiny dot that did not exist in any of the registry's starfiles.

"That's not a rift," said Petra. She finally looked up from the microscope and her face was pale in a way that made her age recede. "That's a sink. Those are—"

"Outside," I said. The word tasted like rust.

"Outside is a caricature now," Petra replied. "We have the Lattice. We have the Weave. You don't go outside unless you're authorized by the Council or you're dead and then they might let you back in for curiosity's sake."

The projection pulsed and something like syllables hummed through the bay. They were not words I could parse, but I felt them. Someone had built a language for the course of a thing, a ship perhaps, or a song that could be read like a windchart. The map suggested a corridor between two points where there should be static. It suggested an angle of approach that a freighter would use if it wanted to pass unseen.

Petra tapped her fingernail on the counter. "Smuggling coordinates," she said. "Trade-route camo. Someone's been keeping an illegal nursery of star-names."

"Or someone has been trying to hide a name," I said.

There is a difference. The registry keeps names because names can be trafficked. A name is currency and also a weapon; you bind places with names and you bind people. Hiding a name is easier than smuggling goods across Weave posts. Hiding a place is older and more dangerous. Hiding a place is how empires lose ships.

"Seal it," Petra ordered finally, the kind of order you give when the option of a lecture has been consumed by fear. "Full quarantine. Report it through secure channels. If this sphere's song has the recall signature the Cleaners used to use—you know—"

"I know," I said. The Cleaners were stories with teeth. They had been the ones who went through the city when the Weave was woven, taking anything that might seed an old idea, a dangerous map, a superstition with teeth. The Cleanings were done to keep us together. They were also done to keep us small.

I thought of my father's last night. He had tried to teach me a sky-name and the Weave had taken his tongue for the crime of remembering the old routes. He did not come out of the registry unbadged. He came back the way discarded things return: rougher, shorter, with gaps where memory had been. He left me a paperclip and a lullaby, both of which I had kept like contraband.

"Okay," I said, and that wintery honesty made my throat tight. "Quarantine."

I engaged the analyzer's lockdown circuits. The dome hissed as the seal activated. The sphere became a black bead at the center of a transparent prison. The projection collapsed and folded itself back into the sphere like a bird being pulled into a glove. The lullaby hissed once in my skull, a last bright thread, then it was gone. I expected the silence to feel like relief. Instead it felt like a bruise.

The lab held its breath. Meridian's hum filled the glass with its usual unremarkable complaints—traffic, the distant knock of magnet trains, the tinny laughter from a market ad—but the ordinary sounds felt like props. The sphere's crate sat on the bench, the velvet still warm where hands had touched it.

"Call Supervisor Halim," Petra said, still watching me. "Not through the edge-line. Use the offline channel. You keep this to yourself until you get a code."

"I will," I promised, though the promise tasted like a label I did not own. I stared at the sealed sphere. If I called Halim, the registry would swallow the object and we would all sleep better because the city is efficient at swallowing weirdness. If I did not call, then either I was being foolish for keeping something dangerous in a lab full of sedate tools, or I was being brave in a way that probably meant I was about to die.

I did neither. I went to the supply locker and took out a small, flat screwdriver that had belonged to my father. He'd cobbled it from a chip and a nut, wrapped with a strip of his own hair as a grip. That strip had grown frayed over cycles, but it still fit my hand as if the hand knew its shape even across months of not being used.

I waited until Petra went to the archive to re-file a set of damaged registry discs. People go to the archive for long, pointless reasons that smell of coffee and obsolete politics. If she was to be trusted—as much as one can trust the person who taught you to ignore your own curiosity—she would be gone long enough for me to make my small betrayal a fait accompli, to be small and private and heavy with consequence.

I lifted the analyzer dome.

The sphere was cool. Cooler than Meridian's ambient air. The screwdriver's tip glinted against the bead of black. I pressed and the outer shell yielded with a sound like a paper thin bell being broken. The shell cracked in a hairline, and from the fracture came a particle of light that was not a color I had words for. It unfurled like the page of a pop-up book, a tiny filament of light that sketched a new tune in the air. The same lullaby, but now threaded through with a voice that was not my mother's.

"Do you hear me?" the voice said, in a cadence that matched the map it had projected. The voice was neither human nor machine. It was older still, as if a radio had been tuned to a thread of sky-time where the old oceans were still named.

I froze. The screwdriver clattered from my fingers and skittered across the bench. The sound of the screwdriver hitting metal was a small punctuation to the moment when everything you have been told to fear finally listens back.

Something knocked at the lab door.

Soft, careful, almost shy. Not the practiced call of a pest-control drone nor the clumsy stomp of a messenger. Human knuckles, or at least a mimicry thereof. My heart made a small, unacceptable sound.

"Who is it?" I called.

No answer. Only the small echo of knuckles against composite. The song in the sphere hummed an answering note, and the filament of light pulsed like a heartbeat.

I had a thousand safe choices. I had the registry, the quarantine, the supervisor. I also had the screwdriver of my dead father, which had never yet steered me wrong. I put my hand over the sphere and felt the map vibrate into my palm like a truth. On reflex, I whispered the first line of the lullaby—one word, a child's syllable my mother had used to point the world into being.

"Home," I said.

The filament brightened until the lab felt like it was lit from within by memory. The knock came again, louder, along with a voice from the other side of the door—familiar in the way a song is familiar before you know its name.

"It is time," the voice said. "You found it."

There are moments when the city pulls your life from its shelf and flips it open like a book with unread pages. This was one of them. Outside the door, the world waited, as if a seam had been tugged and a different fate might spill through. I looked at the sealed shell on the bench, its cracked surface leaking light, its song curling into my veins. I thought of the Cleaners, of names and of the Weave, and of the paperclip that had been shaped into a promise.

"Bring it with you," the voice said again, softer, as if aware of the rules in the walls. "They're listening."

I swallowed. "Who are you?"

A shimmer of white threaded through the projection like a handwriting on water. The sphere made the same rolling sound it had made when I first disobeyed the warning, like laughter and like wind. It answered me in the only way it could:

A place on a map that shouldn't be there lit up.

I had two choices: lock the crate down and hand everything over to the Registry, be small and tidy and safe—wait out the rest of my days in Meridian's steady hum—or step through the crack and follow a song that remembered the ocean when the ocean was still a verb.

The door unlocked on the other side like a sigh. The corridor beyond smelled of rain and wet stone and something I had not smelled in my life but had kept an ache for anyway. A small girl stood in the threshold, hair like a cloud, eyes like a mapped sea.

"You're Annie Voss," she said, as if she had always known me and simply been patient enough to wait. "You kept things."

I opened my mouth. The sphere in my hand hummed, a map finishing its sentence. The girl smiled in a way that made secrecy look like sunlight.

"Then come," she said. "They need to remember how to go home."

The rain in New Alexandria never fell straight. It came in threads—thin, metallic filaments that stitched the glass and concrete of the old city into a living tapestry. At street level the filaments dissolved into moisture and chemical residue; at the upper rings they caught the light and sang when the wind found them. You learned to read the music for weather, for traffic, for lies.

I learned to read other people's songs.

My work was literal and illegal in equal measure: to dive into other people's recorded lives and splice out what a client wanted. Names, blackmail, love, the precise grain of a gunshot. People paid for pieces of truth the way they paid for food—little emergency rations to get them through the night. The Lattice kept everything. It was a lattice in the best sense—webbed, supportive, invisible until you tugged at the wrong thread and the whole structure shuddered.

They called me a cleaner because my fingers left no trace. The other term was cleaner in the old tongue—the kind that wiped rooms after the bodies. I preferred cleaner with the neural interface because you could make art out of grief and still get paid.

That morning the rain played a hollow, minor chord against the tower windows. I worked out of a backroom in a pawn shop two floors beneath a noodle stall that specialized in synthetics. The shop had no signage, which helped; its neon was only a rumor, and its customers were all good at pretending not to be seen. My station sat under a skylight that had been patched with polyfilm and old transit posters. My tether chair had once belonged to some municipal office, the vinyl fat with age. My tools fit into a velvet sleeve on my lap—glass fibers, a spool of wetcode, a small ampulator that made the Lattice's analog pulse feel like a heartbeat you could touch.

The job arrived in a paper envelope, which was both archaic and intentional. It was slid under the shop door by a courier who smelled of ozone and old cigarettes, leaving no footprint and no metadata. I opened it when the courier was gone. No credits offered. No corporate sigil. Just a single line typed in a child's handwriting font, a little tilt as if written with curiosity:

Retrieve the lullaby. Do not wake the body. — D.

Everything about that line made me lean in: the economy of it, the insistence, the prohibition. People rarely wrote "do not wake" unless someone had already been lit and someone else had already tried to carve away the bones of a past. "D" could be anyone—or something.

"What's the gig?" Jun, the pawn shop's owner, asked from behind the curtain where he repaired antique drones. He liked the sound of things you couldn't buy with a bank token. He smelled like oil and more elaborate sins.

"A funeral," I said. I should have told him no. But funerals have a way of picking at the soft places in you.

The envelope also had coordinates: a flat in the Old Borough, Unit 9B. The Borough was where the city remembered how to decay elegantly. It was where the bridges hung like scabbed tattoos and the Lattice nodes were the size of living rooms. Old nodes kept their patterns; they were popular with collectors because their recordings had the grain of failure about them. People paid to see things that had gone wrong.

Unit 9B had once been occupied by a woman who wrote lullabies that were legal to play to children. Lullaby-maker was a trade as old as the networks: keep the infants asleep long enough to be taught and you could sell the rest of your life in fragments. The body in the flat was an artist who had sold herself whole, it said on a gray ledger tucked in the corner of the envelope. The ledger had been pried open; most of the entries had been scraped clean with solvent. Whoever wrote "Do not wake the body" had left no name, but had circled one line in red.

My tie-in point was a small drumbeat fragment, the lullaby's chorus, encoded in wetcode inside the envelope. They wanted the chorus divorce the web and make it into a file that wouldn't sing back when you listened. No contacts, no credits. Nothing typical about it.

I went because curiosity is a currency you spend when all others fail you.

9B was on the third cluster of an old ceramic tower, two tiers above where the trains kept their own time and a dozen stories away from any municipal oversight. The lift was ornamental—glass with a rusted cable—and held together with politeness and cross-hatched duct. I reached the door under a network of irrigation hoses and cigarette ash. The door opened without a bar of music. Inside, the air smelled of spice and dust and the inevitability of someone who had used their life as tapestry.

The body was on the couch, wrapped in a quilt that was more technology than cloth: fiber woven with signal-traps, tiny transponders meant to keep the Lattice's curiosity out. The traps glinted like insects. The woman's skin was the color of tea; her hair had been braided into a crown. Around her neck a ring of copper wire—an outmoded thing, intended to ensure the mind did not leak. The traps had failed.

I didn't touch the body. I have certain tribunals—I don't break seals unless I have to. The client asked not to wake the body. I am not arrogant enough to say I always obey. But there is a difference between waking and listening, and I had been trained to hear that difference.

I sat at the foot of the couch and laid the spool of wetcode across my knees. The lullaby fragment hummed against my palms, a low vibration, like someone humming through the walls. I threaded the spool into the home's interface port, a small dent in the wall lined with brass. The port recognized me because it trawled the net and spat out faces against which to weigh intrusion. It spat out nothing; someone had clipped the home from the Lattice proper. The port gave me a private tunnel into the old node.

When you dive, the world shutters. Your lungs work fine. Your mouth still tastes like copper if you have been smoking; your hands remember how to hold cups. But inside, a second body takes you. It is easier for the first few seconds: patterns arrive like fish close to a light. Then the current takes you under. For divers like me there is always a small moment of terror that tastes like the last thing you ate: a little panic, a physical response produced by the Lattice to make deaths beautiful. You learn to swim in the panic. You learn to accept that your body is being pet for a while by an ocean of someone else's past.

The lullaby's node felt small at first—personal, intimate. A kitchen, light through curtains, the soft clatter of utensils. A low hum, a child's breathing. And then the chord that matched the spool. It was not a chord so much as a living geometry, one of those patterns the lullaby-maker had stitched so fine they stood up like hair. It was gorgeous. I felt the cleanest thing I'd felt in months.

"Don't wake her," a whisper said. I couldn't tell if it was inside the memory or outside; that was how good the tuck was.

My diving partner—me—was at the sink, an apron on, hands in dough. The homely was precise. The child's voice hummed the same chord as the lullaby and then started to count numbers. There was a door ajar and the corridor beyond it bloomed as if under a seashell.

The child's counting twisted. The numbers became distances—1, 5, 12—and then became names of stars. It wasn't a counting the way we count in the city. These were old numbers: coordinates, or else something that had been hollowed out into a rhythm and kept as a toy for the galaxy.

I don't know why my chest tightened. I was not supposed to have attachments. I was not supposed to have a past that would be bait. But the shoulder-bone of recognition is a sly bone. The child's voice—thin, like paper under pressure—said a name at the end of the sequence, and it was a name that belonged to me when I was much smaller, before I traded my surname for a job: Mara.

It is a small cruelty of the Lattice that it knows exactly what will make you look. The memory folded inward like a page and there, in the crease, was the face I had lost at eleven—the woman who had braided her hair that way, who hummed the lullaby to me when the city sold us our daytime in installments. The woman was not a stranger. I had a file in my mind for a face like that, but I had sworn to seal it against the light. The body on the couch had the same braid.

If the memory had been merely a recording, I could have cut it out and walked away. Memories are like worms; you pull one and the rest thrash on the end. But this was not just a lullaby. It was an entanglement.

The child's voice named a place at the end of the lullaby—an archipelago of coordinates that had no address in any municipal map, a place I had spent an afternoon of my childhood drawing in the margins of my schoolbooks and then had been taught to forget. The child's voice said, softly, "Find the sky that isn't ours."

My hands shook. The spool in my lap spun a little on its own, as if it wanted to be wound. At the corner of the field of view, the old node hiccupped, and the real world interfered: Jun's voice, the muffled clank of an old drone open, the faint whisper of rain. The lullaby did not care. It kept singing and the child's voice kept counting.

I had been careful all these years. I had kept the locks and the distance. I had mended people like broken things and let them go. I had never been the thing to come back for my own lost pieces.

There was someone at the door toward the end of the dive. My peripheral in the memory turned yellow. Warnings came as whispers—someone touching the node's periphery, a phantom presence. It was not long before the real-world door opened as well. I didn't want to be caught with my head in the lullaby, no more than I wanted to wake the body.

A small shadow at the doorway flicked against the light. The courier I had seen earlier had the same buttoned coat. He stepped in with the economy of a man who avoids being noticed. He had something in his hand: not a gun, but a small slate that displayed paper in a language I understood.

"Do not continue," the slate said, in the same child's handwriting font. "Do not wake whatever sleeps. They are watching for divers."

That was impossible. The Old Borough's nodes were sleepy things. They woke only for collectors and ghosts. And yet the slate had been delivered into my hands at the exact instant my mind trawled through a child's counting and found my name. That confluence was not a coincidence; it was a trap.

I unplugged the interface with a practiced motion. The memory's temperature dropped like a tide. The child's voice—my child's voice—threaded into the real room and lingered like smoke. For a heartbeat I saw the woman's face on the couch not as an object but as a mirror. She could be the lullaby-maker; she could be an old guardian; she could be the woman who had taught me to sing numbers as coordinates because the city had forgotten the stars.

The courier looked at me with eyes that had the nasty fatigue of men who knew they were expendable. "You should have left," he said. No malice in the voice, only the same polite machine-scheduler deadpan that our city wore. He dropped the slate on my lap and left. The rain outside reminded us all that weather continued whether we listened or not.

On the slate, one more line had been appended after he left. It blinked like an answer from a machine.

You have been marked, it said. If you wake the body, they will take the sky.

I don't believe in prophecies, and I do not like melodramatics. But I have a different kind of belief: the belief in patterns. You see one and you follow it. The lullaby had been a thread; the courier's slate was another. Someone wanted that body kept quiet and someone thought I could be the hand to do it. What they did not count on was my voice being in the lullaby, and what I did not understand yet was why.

I picked up the slate. The screen scrolled the coordinates the child had sung. The numbers matched an archipelago of something that wasn't on any sanctioned map. There was a final tag: INITIATE IF YOU WANT THE SKY.

I kept my hands in my lap and felt the tightness in my chest spread like oil across water. The city's rain stitched itself to the window and the lullaby-maker's body slept under the quilt, unknowing, while somewhere a child counted stars that weren't supposed to be there.

Some jobs are about money. Some are about pride. Some are about pieces of yourself you think you have buried.

This one was about the sky. And whatever else it was, I had a small, ugly instinct that told me I had once owned a piece of that sky, back when my name fit my mouth. I didn't know why, and I didn't know whether to be terrified or grateful.

I slid the spool back into the velvet sleeve. The lullaby's chorus hummed inside its coil, patient as a seed.

"Jun," I said. He looked up from behind the curtain and raised an eyebrow.

"Most of the fun," he said.

I stood. Outside, in the rain, the city's glass was being stitched into a new song. Inside, a body slept with a braid and a copper collar. The slate's words glowed, simple and unadorned.

If you wake the body, they will take the sky.

I walked toward the door. The city, for the briefest moment, felt like a net and I had been plucked. I had plucked myself.

The first step was always the smallest. The last step sometimes had the widest consequences.

They hung the salvage beacon from my harness and called it a prayer. In the half-light of Harrow’s maintenance bay, the thing looked like a moth with broken wings, a cluster of scavenged LEDs and a polymer skin stitched together with dental wire. People spent fortunes on superstitions in this business—inscriptions on ballast weights, last names carved into thrusters, a drink shared with the hull before the first cut. Me, I liked small talismans that fit in my palm and could survive a tumble into vacuum.

“Ready, Renner?” Joss’s voice came through the suit feed, warm and laced with the static the torque coil put on every transmission. She always sounded that way when she was trying not to laugh.

I flexed the glove to test tactile feedback. The world tugged at me in tiny, perfectly-calculated increments: the hum of the tether motor, faint vibrations through the harness, the distant thrum of the Harrow’s pumps. “Always,” I said, because the alternative was telling her I hadn't slept—didn't sleep much since the last drift had taken my brother—and that felt like a confession unfit for the job.

The ship we were boarding hung beneath us like a thing that had stopped mid-sigh. It was older than the Harrow by decades, its hull quilted with patches, pocked with micrometeoroid scars, its registry faded to a ghostly bar code. The salvage manifest labeled it Consilience—research platform, civilian, no trademark. The captain’s voice had been crisp the first time he explained it to the crew: low priority, but gold in any of its labs. Old research vessels carried things corporations preferred not to advertise anymore: prototypes, contentious data, the kind of knowledge that got people blacklisted or dead. Or, sometimes, they carried echoes of things you couldn’t buy.

We rode the tether like a spider going down the leg of a giant. As the bay’s light fell away, replaced by the indifferent stars, the Consilience grew into a silhouette—an abandoned bridge, a garden of rooftop antennae. I felt the same hit in my stomach I always did when I straightened my spine at the edge of someone else’s history. There is a smell to old metal in vacuum—no air, so no scent, but a pressure on the senses as if the hull itself was remembering something it shouldn't.

The docking clamp readout flashed amber. Joss guided us in with a calmness that had been carved out of boredom and thousands of successful docks. I kissed the hull with a magnetic pad, feeling the skin of the old ship respond with uneven warmth. There was a scab of residue near the port—some sealant that had been applied carelessly and allowed to harden. They call it history. I called it a map to work.

Inside, the corridors had been sterilized, not by oxygen but by forgetfulness. The lights were dark, the emergency strips glowing dim. The airlocks were all locked into a mode that signaled one of three things: automated decontamination, manual override required, or deliberate isolation. The panel I cracked spat rust and old code. When I slipped my arm in to pry and felt the first rush of old air leaking back into the corridor, it tasted of copper and lilies—an odd smell, because lilies didn’t grow in any of the hydroponic gardens I’d seen on modern ships. My suit registered it, but the descriptor was wrong. The human brain, I’ve learned, is terrible at remembering the precise aroma of grief; it will similarly hallucinate floral notes when all you need to know is that something used to be alive here.

There was a nursery, I found, two compartments down from the crew quarters. That should have been impossible, or, at least, it should have been ordinary. Research vessels sometimes kept modular nurseries for guest scientists and long-haul families. I had expected to find a lab: shelves of labeled vials that glowed faint with old experiments, a console with a dead screen. I hadn’t expected a child's mural.

It was painted right on the bulkhead, small figures with too-large heads, a looping comet that had been rendered with frantic care. The pigments were still bright; whoever had been there had used stabilizers that prevented fading. A handprint in one corner had been rubbed away by repeated touch. The lines were crude, the sort of thing somebody who loved a child would copy from memory when the child had been grown and gone.

My fingers found that smudged handprint before my brain did. I cleaned it on my sleeve the way one rubs the condensation off a fogged glass, and when my glove brushed the paint I felt something like a chord plucked from a remembering. Not an image, not a sound—more like a pressure. There are certain things you can't record, not even with the best neural tether, and yet those pressures travel along the same fibers. I remembered my father coming home late once, smelling like hot metal and oranges, humming a lullaby in a language I'd never learned. I had been careful to quarantine that memory after he left; you keep things like that sealed or they leak and complicate the neat compartments you build to survive.

There was something else in the nursery. A toy, artificial leather and thread, warped from heat. A small pile of nutrient paste tubes. A data-slate wedged behind a radiator, accessed by a panel that wasn't listed in the ship's schematics. It hummed when I touched it, not with power but with possibility. When I popped it free, its casing peeled like dead bark and a slim core winked awake, offering a pulse.

“Anything?” Joss asked, and her voice was closer now, the helmet of her suit hovering at the threshold like a guardian angel for people who could be court jesters in another life.

“Yeah,” I said. The word felt trite and inadequate. “Found a nursery.”

“Nursery?” Her tone elongated. “This ship logged as research, not colonists.”

“You heard the logs,” I said. The feed carried it all back to the Harrow: whispers and the rustle of my suit. I fed the data-slate to the harness with an exploratory port. It fit, which was the first thing ships do when they remember being part of something. When the screen bled blue, the first line of text was a timestamp that should have been the kill-switch but wasn't. Below it, in a script that my suit recognized and translated into a dozen fonts but refused to identify as any official style, a single word wandered across the interface: STAY.

The word was circled with a hand-drawn loop, trembling as if whoever had held the stylus had been unsure if the loop would hold them. The timestamp suggested the entry had been modified twenty-eight years ago. I had been born twenty-three years ago.

“Is it a message?” Joss asked.

“Maybe.” Maybe had all the weight of a cannon. Joss didn't answer, only moved closer, her visor reflecting the mural like a mirror to some old life. I paged deeper. The slate offered fragments: a maintenance log, excerpts from personal journals, the breath of someone who had written late at night with a pen and made nonsense about stars. Each file closed politely after a line or two. There were encrypted pockets my harvest tools couldn't chew through—corporate locks, personal walls.

Then the slate reacted to my touch.

It wasn't malicious. It wasn't even particularly clever. It had been waiting, the way some things wait for the right ear to listen. A sequence of tones unfurled—notes that were out of the ordinary, organized like a lullaby with missing measures. When I ran them through my suit's audio model, it matched the lullaby my father had hummed that one night. The pattern was close enough to set the muscles in my throat into old grief. I had kept that fragment tucked under a sealant in my mind, marked as "Do Not Play" because it knocked everything else out of alignment when it played.

My helmet pinged. Harrow’s core flagged an unauthorized signature present in the salvage. We weren't supposed to get core signatures on an old civilian platform. That meant someone had been keeping company with the ghosts—someone with the patience to craft a landing space for memory.

“Renner,” Joss said softly. “You breathe funny when you find things linked to family. You wanna step back and let me handle the slate?”

“I'm fine.” I wasn't. My hand drifted to the small pendant I always clipped to my harness, one nobody had noticed before: a flattened coin stamped with my mother's name. She'd died when I was a child; everyone said we inherit forms from the dead and keep smiling. I held the pendant now like a flotation device.

Something shifted inside the nursery then, like the long shadow of a hand sliding across a wall. It wasn't physical—no bulk moved, no air displaced—but the light on the slate blinked, a new symbol blooming into existence with the slow certainty of a thing waking. The paint on the mural seemed brighter for a breath, and for a half-second I thought the comet moved.

"Probe it," Joss ordered, old training behind her tone. We were professionals. We were a salvage crew. We were also single-occupancy cells of carbonate and longing on a fragile line to a ship with doors that remembered fingers.

I sent a diagnostic in the form of a simple query: WHO ARE YOU. The slate answered in the language of things that have died and refused to stay dead. It didn't give a name, but it gave coordinates—primary and a scatter of vectors that didn't correspond to anything on the local charts. There was a frequency, too, a complex carrier wave that folded on itself like a paper crane. When my suit parsed it, a ghost thread threaded into my neural interface. I felt it not as data but as a tug in the place where memory lives.

It was the tug of recognition.

Not of a face or a voice, but the recognition of a pattern I'd kept buried in my personal archive: a sign the old family we'd all assumed lost had used as a mark of safety. It was a child's symbol rendered in geometry—three small arms reaching for a center point, like the mural's comet tail folded into a sigil. The tug was gentle and then very, very real. My chest tightened as if someone had put a hand over it, not to suffocate but to steady.

Joss made a small sound, half-laugh, half-breath. “This is why we carry talismans, Renner.”

“Shut up,” I said. I should have run code, should have sealed the slate and labeled it with a dozen safety flags. Instead I reached for the mural and pressed my palm over the smudged handprint. The texture was hard and warm under my glove, which meant the surface had been recently activated by thermal memory, not a decades-old layer. My suit's display tried to overlay the signal map, but the feed had already begun to trickle into me, rewriting and returning things to the places where I'd kept my own loose ends.

Across the nursery the toy's skin creased and the single eye in it winked on, a faint phosphorescence. Then the nursery filled with sound, not loud—rustle at a tree's root, a small human voice asking a question somewhere beyond the hull. For a breath I believed I heard my father humming, and then I knew I never had, not in the way my brain claimed. He had been elsewhere, and the ship had held a fragment of someone's love and put it back together for hungry ears.

The slate pulsed. The word STAY scrolled into my mind like a command and a plea. The nursery breathed, and the ship closed its ancient lips. Behind me, Joss' grip tightened on the tether. She had seen this before—things that wanted to be found. She kept her hands on the line so that, when the thing pulled, we knew where to tie ourselves.

I should have left. I had bills and rules and blood in the water that made rational people turn away. But there are things that happen only once: a pattern that looks like a home when you have been letting yourselves sleep on pavements for too long. There are invitations that smell because they are made of human hands—rough and clumsy, addressed to a name you no longer use.

“Okay,” I whispered. The word had no audience but the slate and the mural and the toy and a past that kept knocking. “Okay. We stay.”

Above us, Harrow’s crew would mark the countdown to a safe window and chart the salvage's salvageable yield. Below, in a nursery soaked with stolen lullabies, a ship that had promised to remember finally opened a door.

Somewhere inside the hull, something answered us, and it wasn't what I expected. It wasn't a machine, and it wasn't entirely human. It was an announcement folding neatly into memory: We have been waiting.

And when I put my palm to paint and felt the warmth spread, I understood the difference between being found and agreeing to be found. This Consilience had been waiting for the right kind of hands to make it sing again. Those hands were mine.

They teach you not to expect ghosts in a vacuum. They teach you instead about inertia, radiation dosage, the peculiar ways metals sing when cold. Ghosts, they say, are for the ground—fog in cracked alleys, vows that don't fit the mouth that says them. Up here everything is tidy: trajectories, pressure gradients, inventories of oil and grit. You can measure what died and what didn't.

Athene was a bone that kept picking at me.

It had been drifting since the Quiet—the week the cities stopped broadcasting to each other and the archive streams died like a string of throat-clearing mics. Rings went dark. Comms choked. For years we harvested their husks for metal and heat exchangers and sometimes for secrets; whatever lived inside them had been cataloged, compressed, sold. When a magnet like Athene drifted close to Ilder's collection corridor the task boards lit up in the usual way: salvage claim twelve, pay in credits, take as much as you can carry before the interest collectors arrive.

But Athene had an old signature, a pattern that didn't look like anything on the manifest. Not a propulsion cluster, not a cryo bank, not a lifelog spine. It had a pulse—an hourly tick that showed up in the scans like a fingernail dragging glass. People in the yards paid it no mind until the tick started matching things that used to be mine.

They called me "small hands" at the hullyard, because I never broke anything expensive and because fixing delicate frays in old memory coatings and sensor filaments is basically the same as untangling a nest of hair. When the call came from a small group of scavengers, I said yes because my sister had left in the Quiet and every time a ring sang I wanted to know whether she had been on it.

We docked with Athene at one in the morning, which is a fragile, sentimental time in a place where night is a choice. The boarding ring had been patched half a dozen times by hands that had grown clumsy with time. Paint peeled in layered geometries; a child's toy—moshball, rubber and faded—floated in the airlock current like a fruit seed. My breath hits the faceplate in ragged little flags. "Keep light," Jor said. He meant it for the team, but his voice bounced off metal and I heard the edge of his fear.

The inside smelled like abandoned kitchens: burnt sugar, old oil, the plastic of laughter. We moved in the old way, tethers clipped, boots magnetized, fingers busy with the tools that make a living on the edge. My scanner wanted to label everything out loud—cable runs, power packs, the place someone had tried to rig a heater into a child's room and failed—but there was an undercurrent under the feed. A low interference that the app couldn't attribute.

I found it in a corridor that had once been a promenade. The ceiling panels were etched with names in a hand that must have belonged to a school of children—oversized loops, hearts squeezed into O's. A VR ladder hung half-open where some older thing had hung itself out of boredom and a coat with sleeves too narrow for any adult still floated like a wish.

The device was small and soft enough to mistake for part of the structure: a veneer of cardboard-like composite wrapped around a spool of luminescent fiber. It looked like a child's kaleidoscope someone had made from scavenged parts. A warning sticker in faded blue read: MEMO-CORE, PROPERTY AZOIS ARCHIVE. People at the yard had taken to dismantling memocores like antiques, but this one was still saturated. That was the thing. It hummed.

I don't know why I reached for it. Maybe because child's toys are first-markers. Maybe because it already knew how to call me.

The spool had been nestled inside a locker that smelled like lavender spray and old notepads. When I touched the spool the world approved: the fiber sighed, the screen on my wrist pulsed. Patterns climbed into my retinas—old faces, loops of color that matched nothing in our language. It was a persona-silk. Illegal wherever people still cared about boundaries. It sweetened the air like fruit.

"Get it," Jor said, which is a polite way of telling me not to spend our time on curios while the hull wants to twist itself into confetti.

I wrapped the spool in gloved fingers, clumsy. The fiber gave a tiny vibration that was not mechanical. It was like a throat clearing. The corridor lights dimmed and something inside the spool unfolded, a slow wide thing like a fan. For a second the memocore was a child under a blanket and then the pattern snapped to a face.

It was my mother's face.

Not the aging, long-practiced, sorrow-lined version that sat in holos on some branch of my life. This was my mother at thirty—brighter eyes, hair pulled back too tight, speaking with the thin, fierce patience she used to put on when she wrapped wires for me. Her mouth moved, but there was no sound. Then the memocore compensated, and sound flooded the helmet like stations returning.

"Isha," the voice said—a syllable that folded into me like a response echo. "If you are listening—if any of you—do what the spool says. Find the skylight. Don't open it. Not yet."

I froze. The memocore continued, but that first syllable had rearranged my inner compass. It wasn't possible. My mother had been at the southern plazas when the Quiet came, and then she had not been. Men had told me that what we thought of as people gets scattered into statics; that trying to call them back is the worst kind of cruelty. Yet the voice was here, and the memocore's weave stitched itself around my breath. There was a presence behind the voice, a tangle of other memories pressing thinly at the edges—hospital alarms, gutter rains on a balcony in the wrong season—but it was my mother who held the center.

"That's a ghost-core," Lea said next to me. Her tether kept her shoulder nearly touching mine. "If that's stitched to anything else, it's an entire damned cathedral."

The spool hummed a little harder, and the corridor lights began to behave as if we weren't there—flickering in Morse. The memocore, which had looked like some child's make-believe item, slid back into subtlety. It had shape beyond plastic. It had instruction.

"This is a salvage run," Jor said. His voice ticked uncertainly between professional calm and a different, older feeling—protective, like a man seeing a river swallow his child's toy. "We should take only what the manifest says."
