We took it anyway. People who occupy the edges of a dying substrate take chances. We bagged the spool, clipped it into a backpack set with a soft quadrant to cradle contraband signals, and moved on.

Athene didn't give up much else. A few gardens in sealed bays had been coaxed into life, little green units that had their own weather and knew nothing of the Quiet. There were bodies in their storage racks; the usual ethical unreadable. The promenade loops were better than some—someone had painted murals of other worlds. Old love notes flaked from their plaster like dried oranges. But the ring itself had no pilot. Its engines chewed at the thinness of the corridor and spat out cod pieces of time.

Our prize fit in a knapsack and weighed nothing. Back on Ilder, the spool went into a private room I had learned to rent on the cheap. The room was a patchwork of borrowed comforts: a cracked sink, a curtain that never caught the right sun. I set the memocore on my workbench, peeled off my gloves, and for the first time since the boarding ring held half a promise and half a ruin, let myself listen.

It started with the lullaby—I knew it before I recognized my mother's face. She had sang it when we were smaller, the tune stitched from one of those pre-Disconnect holofilms that got played in our apartment to drown silence. The memocore threaded the lullaby into something new; it added a counter-melody that belonged to a child's voice—a child's voice that said my name between the measures in a whisper like wind in old teeth.

And then the memory changed.

It was sudden and wrong in ways that rearranged the furniture in my head. The memocore showed an image I had not had the right to possess: a map of empty space with a single bright node in a sector long thought sealed. There was a coordinate pulse, a string of numbers like teeth. Under the numbers, woven into the pattern of the voice like punctuation, was a phrase I did not anticipate because my mother would never have used it: Come home.

My hands went cold. I had to sit. Every trinket in my room—staples of my life—stared at me with the calm indifference of the habitual. The memocore's light painted wavering shadows across the cracked sink.

It is the malleable thing about memory-lanes: they can lie to you in the softest of ways. They can offer you someone you want back and cloak a vendor's prices in the same breath. I told myself all manner of cautions. The spool could be laced with manipulative suggestion, an old program meant to bait the hungry and the sentimental. The coordinates could be a dead trap. This world had enough of both traps and the bodies who laid them.

There was also a truth that tipped me like a coin. The voice on the thread—my mother's, my sister's, whatever ghost the memocore had chosen to stitch into its center—had said my name. It had aligned with where I had kept hope like a prayer in my pocket. That alignment mattered. It was why I wasn't an archivist, or a planner, or a clean-room operator. It was why I was small hands and why small hands reach for whatever vibrates.

I unlocked my emergency kit and sealed the spool in a film that would hide its signature from yard scanners. I tucked it under the mattress with the rest of the things I couldn't bear to catalog as merchandise: a child's sock left at a hostel, a holo of a balcony in better weather, a photograph of a pair of eyes I had thought mine.

Outside, Ilder spun as it had for thirty-seven years, a lean collection of panels, markets, and a dozen different leagues of broken promises. People still traded in salvage and memory, in futures you could sort by color. The world below us was a dome of clouds and the neon of other people's joys. There were markets where memocores were legal and markets where they weren't. There were jobs where you never touched them and jobs where you rebelled around them like a mad artist. I had enough credits to buy me another month and not enough courage to match whatever the spool suggested.

A sound came from the spool through the mattress. It wasn't the voice; it was a slow smoothing noise, like breath leaving a small animal. Then there were words again—soft, urgent.

"If you are listening," the voice said, and it folded the world in half, "this is the first. They will come looking for it. Keep it small. Keep it hidden. There is a skylight. Do not open it until you have the key."

My chest tightened in a way the Quiet never did. The memocore finished with one last line that did not sound like my mother at all. It sounded like someone who had been doing arithmetic in a language of old nav-scripts.

"Grid 7-2. Bring the spool to the anchor. Remember: the anchor remembers us."

The spool went quiet. I lay on my back and looked at the ceiling, the worn pattern of a cheap plaster tile. The room was dim and smelled of old coffee and a hundred forgotten tiny coffees like it. The memocore hummed in the underlayer of things, like a tide under a frozen shore.

It would have been easy to hand it over—to Jor, to the salvage yard, to the men who liked to put things in bright, legal boxes and sell them back to the desperate. It would have been easy because easy is the thing people praise. But I had the spool. I had the name. I had a coordinate that was not on our charts. I had a voice in a familiar tone telling me to keep it from being opened.

I stood up. My hands were steady. There were noises outside the wall—cars, or the orbital equivalents thereof, small lives grinding against each other. There was a world of rules that said don't dig into forbidden memory, don't follow ghosts, don't make market-disturbing waves. There were also people who had affairs with rules every day. My sister had been one of them once, before she left.

I wrapped the memocore in a blanket, slipped it into my bag, and walked out into the hallway.

Sometimes the Quiet gives you an invitation, and sometimes it gives you a test. Sometimes the first chapter of a story is only the moment where you decide whether you pick up the thing that calls your name.

I picked it up.

Chapter One

On harvest nights the city smelled like two things: ozone and citrus. The ozone cut through the trapped heat of the tower-block canyons; the citrus came from the artificial groves that ringed the lower rings, their scent pumped like a placebo for anyone who'd never seen a real lemon tree. Up on the fifth mezzanine the air tasted metallic and old, like a memory you can't quite place.

They called the ritual a "cleansing." The municipal vaults purged every quarter, siphoning trauma and clutter from the tenements, the towers, the company enclaves. People walked into collection booths, pressed their foreheads to frosted glass, and let the city take the parts of them it preferred not to keep. For most it was relief. For some it was a shifting market commodity: curated nostalgia to sell, curated sorrow to be studied. For people like me it was a job.

I called it scavenging.

My suit came up to my waist in scarred carbon weave, the sort of thing you bought used when you didn't have the license to buy new. The glove-hands were lined with microresonators—little silver teeth that sang the memory-signature back to the net. I calibrated them with a flick of my thumb, listening for the right pitch the way other people listened for rain. The harvest line hummed along the ceiling like a sleeping thing; the reservoir itself—an old river basin retrofitted and sealed into a biocage—gleamed beneath.

"You don't look like you're built for it," said Tilo from somewhere in the dark, voice ricocheting off the metal. He always hid behind jokes. He was good at it; good enough for now.

"I'm built for money," I said. I shouldered my pack. We'd split whatever I could pull—minus what the broker took, minus what the vault auto-deducted for "processing." You could live on the cut if you kept your head down. Tilo could do that if it weren't for the gray list that had been tacked onto his name like a malarial shadow: medical debt, expired credits, a lease sublet that had gone poof when the landlord decided he wanted a real tenant.

He hummed, low. "Just be quick. Aram wants that synth-laughter sample before dawn. She says she has a buyer—a couple of executives with more nostalgia than sense."

The harvest line let us in without asking who we were. The custodians made a show of checks, of beads and signatures on a tablet that meant you had permission to be near the Reservoir, but permission didn't mean you owned the memories. Nobody owned them; the city merely kept them on a ledger until an algorithm matched them to demand. Traders bought, psychs analyzed, funerary houses restored ghosts to the living. The value of a memory depended on context and condition—pure joy in saturated color fetched more than slurred grief; memories with multiple avatars, unadulterated, drew collectors, and whole sequences where someone's death hadn't been fully offloaded could be sold to medical teams for a fortune.

The surface rippled, a memory-lake breathing in our mesh lantern light. Offscapes—detached incidents that the vault couldn't stitch back into owners—moved like jellyfish, phosphorescent and slow. They responded to touch. You knew how to coax them, how to let your resonators trace their threads without ripping the head off the sequence. The wrong move and a memory would implode, a billion delicate little things snapping into static. Those were the things that paid less, because they'd been damaged, and the things you wanted were the clean ones—new, bright, unsullied by municipal bronze.

A bright thing answered tonight. It was small, like a child's breath caught in a bottle: a bead of white-blue light with a tail of silver. I felt the resonance in my palm before I saw the shape, fingers tightening like desperation. The tail licked out like a fish's fin, and the thing pulsed.

"Careful," Tilo said. He always said that. He'd said it the time I opened the wrong crate and watched a memory rattle out at us shrieking in somebody else's voice. He'd said it when the night-guard found them sleeping face to face with their past and decided they liked it there.

I set the glove to harvest and let the skein drift. The bead attached to the net with a little pop that no one in the world would call a pleasant sound. We pulled. There was always pressure; memories resist being taken. Some of them didn't want to be catalogued. We coaxed it. It filled my visor with a tasteless color—pale lemon—then it shifted.

I remember to breathe when the past is right here, inside the palm of my hand. The old training made every image sharp, like glass. The bead unfolded into a room I knew before I knew the name of it: low ceiling, a window that was more letterbox than window, a linoleum floor, sunlight dusted with sawdust. A child's hand reached in—small, chubby—and there was the smell of oil and lemon from the grocer on the corner.

The child's face resolved. My chest went cold. It was my face, three years ago. Not older—smaller: the familiar scar along the left brow not yet a puckered line, my hair shorter, my eyes the same stubborn green. I blinked into the visor and the old voice, all tiles and little rain, said, "Don't tell them about the sky."

It was my voice because I had said those words at five, tucked in a blanket, explaining why thunder hurt. I recognized the cadence that came from my mother's lullaby. My hand tightened—too tight. Memory jittered; the image snapped. Where I had expected a child's kitchen, the perspective shifted outward and suddenly I wasn't in the memory with the child; I was above the city, looking down, looking at a ribbon of light that wasn't a road or a train. It was a seam—an incision—across the sky, and above it stars were falling like sifted ash.

I don't know how long we stood floating over the city. My throat started to ache, the kind of ache you get when you cry in a language your parents won't translate. The net hummed again, not in accompaniment but in warning. "Anomaly detected," the suit intoned in a voice that had all the warmth of a bank alarm. "Unsigned signature. Timestamp mismatch."

Timestamp mismatch. The little digital line across the corner of my visor—where the vault normally stamped everything with date and owner and extraction hash—flared a clinical white.

2039-04-17 02:11:04 ZUL.

My fingers went numb. The current date—my present, my hard, stubborn existence—read 2039-04-14. Three days in the past, or three days before what? I stared until the world thinned into a smear. Three days ago would make no sense. Three days ahead, even smaller.

The memory did something I couldn't control. It pivoted, and this time the view wasn't of the child; the camera—whatever had captured this scene—turned on me. In the bead I watched a woman older than me, hair streaked with silver, a long scar that ran from temple to jawline. She had my eyes. She didn't smile.

"Mara Voss," she said. My name was a thing you'd say once, when the words had weight. The sound of it in her mouth did something like a stitch. "You don't get to forget this."

The memory cut like a snapped chord, a blip of static and then silence in my ears. The bead stayed quiet, but it vibrated in my palm with a pressure that was more like intent than anything the vault usually held.

"That's not legal," Tilo said, but his voice was small now, thin. The suit's automated systems were chirping blue warnings—"Violation: Unauthorized Retention"—and a server pinged somewhere across the Vault. You could argue the legalities until your teeth fell out into your soup. By then someone had marked you for a retroactive audit. Retroactive audits involved visits. They involved needles. They involved the Custodians.

Aram would kill us if she found out we'd kept it meant for catalog. She paid well, but she had procedures: nothing with unauthorized signatures; zero-timestamp anomalies; and nothing that could be cross-referenced with a flagged identity. That the bead had my face in it made it worth more than we'd dreamed. That the bead had my voice and a date in the future made it lethal.

I could have dumped it. I should have. I moved my hand toward the disposal chute—a simple circular mouth in the ceiling where undesirables were meant to vanish—but my fingers refused. The memory thrummed in my palm as if it were breathing.

"You'll be fucked, Mara," Tilo said. The joke had teeth now; it wasn't humorous. "If that's a flagged thing—"

"If?" I said, and the word tasted like granite. You don't get to say it lightly when the thing in your hand says your name three days from now.

The net pulsed. There was a soft clank from the conduits—someone up top had heard the warning and pushed a manual override. The hatch to the mezzanine sighed and little lights along the rail flickered red. People moved above us in the sleeping towers, silhouettes—neighbors who'd sold parts of themselves for rent. If the Custodians came they would not come with sirens and courtesy. They would come with scanners and a list and a blade for memory.

"Lock it," Tilo said. He swallowed and the glove near my earark clicked. He always did the sensible, slow thing first: hide the evidence. He'd expected me to. But I'm not sensible; I'm stupid and I remember things I don't mean to.

I tucked the bead into my pack with the well-practiced motion of thieves and fixers all over the city. The pack closed over it like a coffin lid. The moment it sealed, the suit registered an unauthorized retention and spat out a local diagnostic: "CUSTODIAN WATCH: High Priority. Trace: Engaged."

Lights flared out on the wall: blue, then hot, then the cold white of a will. Someone else had already logged the anomaly: a remote audit node, voice attempting to override. The vault's net runners were at their keyboards, sleep-masked and expensive, eyes like hunters.

If I left with that memory on me I would be a target. If I handed it back, I would be handing a future at least partially carved of my face. Either way, the city would make a tidy little coffin for the choice and slide me into it.

Tilo made a movement toward the chute again, as if to do the sensible thing for me. His fingers trembled; the light on his face made him look younger than he was. We had just enough time to make the decision that would decide which of us lived to see breakfast.

"Run," I heard myself say, as if the word had been folded into my mouth by someone else. There were other words I might have said—let's get a lawyer, let's sell it for enough cred to clear his debts, let's turn it over to Aram and hope she buys the story that we didn't see the signature—but run was the simplest, the most useless, and the most honest.

Tilo didn't ask why. He moved. We left the way thieves always leave: with our boots silent against metal, with our faces set, with the vault behind us like a grave under glass.

When the external hatch closed behind us and the towers swallowed the city-light, the world seemed too loud. Somewhere above, a Custodian's boot would have touched down against metal. Somewhere below, someone would be selling synth-laughter to some person who wanted to remember what they never had. The Pack hummed dumbly at my hip, the bead sequestered like a heart. The city pulsed around us, and in a pocket of warm dark I felt my name turning like a key in the lock.

"Tomorrow," Tilo whispered. "How are we supposed to—what are we thinking?"

"We're not thinking," I said. "We're moving." I could feel the memory thrumming as if it were a thing of its own, a living small animal that didn't like being contained. It tasted of lemon and oil and the particular cold of a child's forgotten secret.

I didn't know what it meant for a memory to carry a future date, but I did know this: whatever the woman had said—whatever my older voice had ordered—someone with more power than any broker wanted the past to be tidy. Someone had threaded the city with a stitch it hadn't had in years. And here, at the mouth of the harvest, with a piece of the future in my hand, I had a choice. The city would not be gentle about the next one.

We ran.

They told me once that the city remembers you before you remember yourself.

It was raining then, the kind of rain that lessons off the neon and leaves the walls sweating, the smell of copper and old battery acid rising like incense from the gutters. I sat on the fire escape of a third-floor flat that hadn't seen a fire in fifty years and tied the fiber braid into my temple the way other people tie their shoes. The braid hummed when it found the old scar there — a thin white crescent like a moon map someone had drawn across my skull — and for a moment the rain filled with tiny, impossible sounds: laughter threaded through static, the bark of a dog that had been dead since before I was born, a child's voice giving directions in a language I didn't know I knew.

That half-second of wrong memory is the thing that makes clients pay more.

"You're sure you can pull it?" asked the man who'd hired me. He sat across from me in his kitchenette like he could ordain the answer by staring. His apartment was a museum of things that had been forbidden by taste: a chipped ceramic bird under a jar, three postcards from continents that no longer existed, and a photograph of a woman whose face the light in the room kept trying to pixelate away.

He was small, with hands that trembled around a cup of tea he didn't seem to wish to drink. His eyes were the color of a drained battery — the kind of gray that made the insides of your eyelids feel like they'd been scraped. "It's only a laugh," he said. "My daughter's laugh." He said the words as if saying them might jiggle something loose inside his chest.

Memory jobs are never "only." They are burglaries, excavations, transplants. The thing people ask for most is the easy part — a scent, a day — but anyone who deals in the Stream knows that memories are stacked like city blocks, with alleys and cellars and foundations. You pry at one brick and you won't always like what you topple.

"Last I checked," I said, flat, adjusting the braid, "you want her laugh from June Vandik, age six. Last afternoon before she—"

"Before she went," he corrected.

"Before she left," I said. Leaving was how people say death now, and leaving could mean the hospital, the desert docks, the transfer rigs where permanent uploads were bought and sold before the net tightened its teeth on the trade. It could mean the river that swallowed most of New Eido when the northern levee gave. It could mean nothing at all. The Stream won't tell you which.

He pushed a thin plastic key across the table. My reflection in its surface looked older than my face. It was a memory key — a cheap thing, not the corporate-grade blocks the wealthy use to preserve entire personalities. This one was for a single node: June Vandik, home node, address marker three-eighteen, the little laugh marker nested inside an audio residue. He'd gotten it from someone who claimed to have been there the last day June was seen. That was usually how it went. Someone had seen something. Someone had a key. Someone wanted to forget and passed that forgetting to me in exchange for a ledger number and the smell of tea.

"They can give you access," he said. "They can give you permission—"

"Permission doesn't mean anything," I told him. "The Stream doesn't keep the door labeled 'Permission.' It keeps the door that has the key. Keys don't know what they open."

He fumbled for a breath. "Do it."

It is absurd to be brave when you have a lock on your throat and a payment in your hand. So I went.

My studio was two rooms inside an architectural ruin that used to be a bank, the kind of place you stop noticing the architecture of because the city wants you to. I stripped down to the braid, felt it cool against my skin, felt the anchor settle along the base of my skull. The duplex node in my apartment was years out of date — not with old out-of-date, but with a kind of exile that made corporate nets whisper behind their teeth. The braid clicked into the socket and my apartment punched the small, private hole the key offered. I always left my stove on when I dove. Not because of superstition — because I liked the idea of something continuing to burn in the little part of the world I had left sitting on a table in the exact place I'd left it.

The first thing that hit my mind when I put the key in was a smell that wasn't a smell. It moved through me like a chord: a pitcher of lemonade on a wooden porch, sunlight that kept its outline, the funny way a collar chafes a child's neck. Then the laugh — small, high, surprised and delighted and nothing of guilt in it. It exploded into me and I could feel it in my ribcage the way you feel a song. I held onto it like a net. The laugh didn't belong to me, but it fit like a glove. That is what clients pay for: the right shape.

You are not allowed to keep anything you take. Everyone knows that, and everyone breaks that rule in half and keeps the smaller edges — a scent in a locket, a sound in a bone behind the ear, a tiny slice of a face tattooed somewhere no one can find. The police call it "unlicensed retention." The Stream calls it survival.

I took the laugh and kept an extra breath, just until the key's return relay asked for it back.

Something else slid past my net.

It was like stepping out of a clean room into a ruin. The laugh was a bright room with a single open window; what followed was a corridor of gray that smelled of oil and iron and was full of names strung on wire like laundry. Names I shouldn't have been able to reach. The memory key had the laugh keyed clean; it did not have the corridor. Whoever had packaged the key had done something to squeeze a portion of a node into a smaller box and left a seam. The seam was open and something watched from inside it.

I could have retracted. I could have told the client that the laugh had been corrupted, that the node had been burned, that sometimes the Stream throws a stone into your face and you bleed. That would have bought me a smaller fee and a better night of sleep. But I have always been bad with things that look like knife handles.

There was a flash — not of light but of geometry. A pattern of points that did not obey Euclid, a small sky mapped into brass and tarnish, and at its center a ring the size of a coin. Something in my lumbar spine pinged as if they had looped a cable around it and given it a tug. The names on the wire rearranged themselves into a date.

Nadir's Comet.

I had heard Nadir's Comet on late radio transmissions like a ghost story. Pilots telling jokes in the dark. Dock-boys saying it was good luck if you saw it. My mother once told me that she had seen it when she was young, and that everything had changed for three whole days afterward. No one kept good records of small celestial phenomena anymore; governments charted things more useful than bad omens. Nadir was folklore. Nadir was a name you use when the wind keeps you awake.

The corridor tightened. I saw faces — not faces like photographs on a wall but module faces, system identifiers that had been painted with paint that peeled into images. Children in raincoats lined up like trophies. Rituals of people leaving their homes with big jars. A dock I had never heard of. A solder seam around a satellite plate big as a school bus.

And then, as if in answer to something I had not spoken, a voice slipped across the back of my teeth.

"If you take that, we'll know."

It wasn't a voice that wanted to be private. It was thick with static and it sounded like concrete settling. A watcher. Stream police are a thing some cities have and some don't. New Eido had a network we called the Gray — private enforcers, corporate contractors, municipal ghosts dressed up as law. They are expensive and they are thorough. But their pronunciation of threats rarely takes the form of direct speech in your head. Warnings in the Stream are usually a directory slam, a weight at your temple, the brief recall of a sensation. This was a voice with intention and teeth.

I could have let go. That word "let" is slippery unless you have tried it on a live system. You let them take the laugh and everything else you had in your hands and you take a ledger number and go home and spend the rest of your life making sure you never have to be cornered by your memory. But the corridor was a canyon and the pattern at the center of the sky didn't look like anything I'd ever seen — which, in my line of work, means it might be treasure.

And I had a daughter's laugh in my chest.

I snapped the braid.

When you snap out of the Stream prematurely, it feels like a body surfing on air that collapses. My apartment filled with the immediate roar of my stove, the rattle of a neighbor's music a floor away, the small mechanical sob of the duplex trying to compensate for a bypassed relay. My heart thundered. The laugh was in my mouth like a coin. Adrenaline leaked into the blood and made everything raw. I tasted lemon and metal at once.

You do not want to be jolted out of the Stream with anything extra. The net keeps track of impulses in and out. Unauthorized residues call attention. I clawed at my temple as if the world might hand me back the braid like a lost hat, but the socket was empty and the key sat inert on my table like a thing that had been knifed.

There are tiny rituals you perform when you come up wrong. You drink water fast. You look at the light to ground yourself. You run a diagnostics on your hardware so that when the Gray comes — and the Gray comes faster than any of us want — you can tell them exactly what was supposed to happen and what, if anything, they caught you doing.

I did the rituals. My diagnostics reported a minor scrape where a node had been closed improperly, a small corrupt trail that had been flagged and then anonymized by my own firewall. That last bit was comforting. My firewall was old and it had saved my life twice. It also had a small, wide-open door between two registry spaces. A place where something could rest.

There was a knock at my door.

We always think the knock will be long and low, that it will be the Gray in their coats. Those are the knocks you remember in film. The knock that came for me was three soft taps, as if someone would rather awaken me than rattle bones. The intercom flashed. Someone outside said, "Mara Voss? This is corporate compliance. We have a matter regarding illegal access to a municipal node."

"Come in," I said, because saying anything else would be either cruel or stupid. The door slid open and light from the stairwell painted the hallway the color of old milk. A man in a uniform that wasn't quite Gray — a different gray that read as a municipal ghost hired out — came in. He wore the standard expression of a stranger who has been told they will have to do unpleasant things but don't get to say which ones. Behind him, the stairwell hinted that someone else waited: a shadow like a pressed flower.

"May we?" he asked.

"Coffee?" I offered, because it's impolite to make people come into your home if you host no hospitality.

He declined. He did not come in with a weapon visible. That is part of their performance. The shadow behind him had one hand tucked into something hard inside its coat.

"You're in violation," he said. "There's a registry. We—"

"Cut to it," I said. My voice had a flavor I neither liked nor trusted. The laugh in my throat had turned into a small axe.

"We have a log," he said. He placed a tablet on my table and turned it, small lights pricking its surface. "Unauthorized decryption on the Vandik home node. Anomaly flagged. Corporate compliance would like to ask you a few questions."

He was methodical. People under orders always are. The shadow stepped forward. Silver in its palm was a device the size of a matchbox: a harvest scrapper. It shone like a single tooth drawn from a skull.

"I'm an independent," I said. "You're not municipal, not Gray. So what are you doing with a compliance box?"

The man did not answer. He didn't need to; the thing in the shadow's hand answered for him. The scrapper was for detecting leftovers. For following a breadcrumb when someone had tried to hide a scent. For finding things in the place where you shouldn't have left them.

The laugh in my chest was suddenly much too heavy.

"When we take the official sample," the man said gently, "it will be standard procedure to remove any residual contaminants. If you have nothing illegal, you will have nothing to fear. But if you have something we want..."

"I was hired," I said. "You can ask the client. He paid in cash and in fear and he gave me a key."

"Which client?" the man asked. He moved the tablet's display so I could see the registry numbers. The key the man had delivered looked like any other small, cheap thing, but the registry embedded within it glowed for a second like a little sun.

I could see why they were here and who had called them. Somewhere my face had been older than it was, and a photograph in someone else's file had connected dots. Corruption tends to make itself look like an answer.

I could have told the truth. The problem with truth is that it is often the first thing the Stream eats.

Instead I thought of the corridor. The comet. The ring the size of a coin. I thought of the children's raincoats on wire. The man watched me like a ledger waiting to be balanced. The shadow moved the scrapper closer and the little blade inside it tuned like a tongue.

My hands, for once, did not tremble. I set the memory key on the table and slid it into the man's reach. I gestured to the couch as if offering seating to an unwelcome judge.

"If you'll take the laugh and be done," I said, "I'll cooperate."

The man's face was calm as a sluice gate. He took the key with two fingers and, without ceremony, slid the scrapper along the edge of my skull where the scar creased like an old river. It clicked. It hummed. The device read nothing until it read everything.

When it sang — a sound like a small animal screaming through electrical wire — the shadow's jaw tightened.

"You're carrying a foreign residue," the man said. "This will complicate matters."

"Do what you must," I said, because there was nothing left to bargain with, and because it is a useful thing to say when your life is a scale and someone else is touching the other pan.

But the thing on my table wasn't a small scrap of matter. It was a silvery thread of geometry the scrubber had pulled out of me and placed carefully on the tablet. It was not much: a thin strip no longer than a coin, wound tight as a watch spring. The device had named it for me as it cooed: Nadir.

The city, somewhere outside the four walls of my stale apartment, remembered Nadir and had put a gentle, hungry face on it and sent me a knock to see if I would answer.

I felt the laugh recoil inside my chest like a trapped animal. I thought of the child's face in the photograph on the old man's table. I thought of the comet that had no place in our sky and yet came here like a letter not meant for us.

"We will need to take you in for questioning," the man said, careful as a man who hurts people for a living but has not yet chosen his favorite instrument.

"Your compliance will be... generous?" I asked, because sometimes generosity can be bought and sometimes it can be traded for silence.

He smiled a small, professional smile. The smile of someone who has not yet been offered the right coin.

"I think you'll find," he said, "that the matter of a foreign Nadir residue is not the kind of case municipal locksmiths handle for petty fees."

Outside, the rain stopped like someone snapped a glass. For a moment the city held its breath and the neon flickered to a blue I hadn't seen since childhood, the kind of blue that says something is being written and we don't get to read the sentence.

They led me out in cuffs that weren't metal. Little bands of light that pinched the tendon at the wrist and tasted like steel. The thing they removed from me — the thread the scrubber had pried out — they bagged with reverent hands and slid into a container with a label that smelled like sulfur and regret.

As the door shut behind me and the stairwell ate the sound of my boots, I could hear, faintly, underneath it all, a child's small laugh, echoing from somewhere it shouldn't have reached me.

The rain remembered me before I had my coffee. It folded along the glass of my window in old arcs, tracing gutters and gutters where city drains had, for decades, given up any pretence of carrying anything but stories. When the first drop landed on the sill it sounded like a hand tapping Morse code: come in, come in. I let it, and for a few minutes the sound was a patient thing that had nothing to demand of me.

I am a restorer at the Fifth Archive, which is a polite way of saying I put other people's pasts back together so they can sell them, study them, or, sometimes, forgive them. We don't make memories; we unpick the threads that keep them from unravelling. People call what we do resurrection if they're romantic, or clairvoyance if they're drunk, but mostly it's just seam work. We deal in mneme: crystalline nodes that hold the pattern of a life, or a snippet of one. Some of the mneme are full suits—years of a life. Most are fragments, fuzzy like the edges of a dream. The ones that come to me are those the rest of the Archive can't trust with their microscopes.

On a gray morning like this one, the work can be a mercy. You put the node in the cradle, pull the loom out, and listen as someone else's music fills the room. Sometimes the music is a lullaby and a life goes quiet. Sometimes it's a handful of laughter and you feel like you know what warm looks like for a single breath. Today's node had been in Storage for three decades. Its carrier had been logged as "Bridge—Victim ID 2741." The Bridge had a thousand logs; the official report had been "catastrophic structural failure." The State liked tidy things.

The client was small in ankle boots and decisive scarves. She called herself Mira Hal. She did not come from the part of the city that gets to leave the Archive's waiting room often—her eyes said that. She spoke like someone reading from a script older than her life. She wanted "just the voice," she said. "Just a warm sound to put a cup under."

I put the node in the cradle and it hummed like a trapped insect. The loom unpacked the pattern slowly, like a book with brittle pages. I knew the object's history before I saw the face because the Bridge ones always began the same way: wind, a wrong angle, someone's radio feed cut to static. Then a translation, then a shout.

The face belonged to a man named Oren Hal, or at least the file said so. His voice when it came through—rough timber, the kind of voice that made you imagine hands that could steady a ladder—filled the room and immediate things happened to my body. You would think that being a restorer would make you sterile to other people's grief; it doesn't. My chest clenched the way it does before a storm. Mira took it like a practiced actor taking a bow. She put her hands over her ears and curled like a prey animal savoring a sound too cruel to last.

The first minute was the expected litany: alarms, the low mechanical purr of the Bridge, a child's voice in the far background. Then it shifted. The feed jumped; the image in my display—thin, skeletal, a ghost map of the remembered scene—tore vertically like a page ripped wrong. That was a sign someone had tried to excise a frame. It's my job to sew it back.

I widened the archive's window, brought up the splice tools, and began to look for the cut. In most of these cases, the excision is literal: a rectangle of missing time, a clean burn. You rebuild it from what surrounds it, from the overlapping sensory cues—pressure changes, haptic echoes, cross-referenced nodes. But this cut wasn't clean. It pulsed faintly with a signature I had only seen once before: a dying watermark, layered by quantum obfuscation, the kind the State applied to memories they wanted to make "unequivocal." I felt my scalp tighten. Whoever had handled this node had found something the Archive had been told to forget.

I worked the weave like a surgeon. The loom spat up audio, static, a smell like fried copper. The Bridge's metal sang under the memory's hands. Voices overlapped, one man counting, someone else cursing, then a voice I didn't expect—hers, younger and laughing. A camera feed ducked from the underside of a girder, eyes of machines looking where human sensors couldn't. The frame I had built, grainy and dusky, showed a corridor of blue-lit trusses. A shadow moved, quick and small, then a hand reached into view and turned something no one had supposed could be turned.

A key? A ratchet? The angle was merciless; whoever watched this after the fact would have thought it was a random hand, something technical. But the hand wore a bracelet with a thin braided band—three strands of silver and copper. I sucked in air and my fingers began to tremble.

We forbade personal attachments into the Archive. It's a rule written to keep the rest of us honest. I kept it anyway, tucked tight and secret. The bracelet in the frame had been worn by a boy the city once printed photos of in the paper corner, the hungry-sallet kid they'd turned into a cautionary tale after he ran with the wrong crew. The boy's name, on the grainy face of those old public notices, had been Luca Mendi. Luca Mendi had disappeared the week the Bridge collapsed. My brother had been six when he took Luca's side at recess. People forget small things like that; you carry them or you don't.

I did not know how to reconcile my chest's sudden sieve with the professional calm I owed Mira. I kept my hands steady enough to keep the weave. Mira's mouth moved when the voice said her name; she smiled like a woman holding breath to keep from sobbing. The man in the memory—Oren Hal—called a name too, but not Mira's. He called "Luca." The audio, brittle as moth wings, had that cadence people keep when they talk to children: low and coaxing, the vowels drawn soft to make the world seem smaller and safer.

"Replay that last half-minute," Mira whispered. For her, the voice was medicine. For me, it was a map to a place the city had put a fence around.

I pushed the replay. The missing frames refused to hold. The watermark bled; the image stuttered and then collapsed into silence, as if someone had pulled the plug on the Loom itself. I swore under my breath and dove back into the splice. There are salvage tools in the Fifth Archive the State doesn't even admit exist, old scripts and pirate patches left by restorers who learned to resist the official erasers. I fed one to the node: a thin, patient piece of code called a "ghost stitch." It crawled through the pattern like a parasite, copying fragments from neighboring signals and reconstituting them. For a breath I saw a face: young, scrape-of-green eyes, hair in an unruly sweep. He looked at the camera and smiled like someone who believed in laughing at the wrong time.

Then the image went black. The audio bled into an undecipherable whisper and nothing in my workbench could get it back.

Mira's hands trembled on her knees. "They cut it," she said. It wasn't really a question.

"Officially," I said. "They cut anything that contradicts the final report. But we can rescue pieces."

"I need the voice, Miss Ril," she said. Her index finger reached, as if to touch the air where the man had been. "Only that. If more is there—if you happen to see anything else—you know what to do."

I did. I had my own ledger of what to do when a memory came alive and started pointing at the city's soft spots: you lock it down, you file it under a numbered case, you either send it up the chain to the Directorate or you bury it where it can't harm anyone. I had buried things before. The Archive's code is full of graves.

But there was something in the way Oren Hal's lips crinkled when he said "Luca." It wasn't the professional neatness of someone consoling strangers. It was private. And when memories get private, they become dangerous.

I finished the restoration we had agreed to: voice only, compressed to a clarity like a single bell. Mira cried into it. The bell was all she needed. She kissed my knuckles with a thank-you that smelled of rosemary and hard water and left with the node sealed in a case that made it look like a relic rather than a piece of her heart.

After she left, the office hummed and the rain remembered. I should have catalogued the stitch, filed the node back to Storage, and moved on. Instead I opened the node again and pulled the file's metadata. There, buried under three layers of obfuscation, was a string I hadn't expected: a call tag. It wasn't the Archive's. It wasn't departmental. It looked like a private thread.

My mouth dried. I didn't know how to feel that my own brain, that repository where memory is both job and bane, should make me feel so treacherous. I could erase the call tag, normalize the file. But someone's attempt at censoring it had been unjust and clumsy. I liked mice that were cleverer than the traps they fell into. I ran the thread.

The thread wasn't a message. It was an address.

It led not to another Archive node but to a location in the old industrial quarter, a place the State had given up after the DarkGrid reallocation. People called it the Underlayer—a tangle of basements and narrow alleys where signal benders and data-brokers live like rotgut kings. You could buy anything under the right light there: forged certificates, old memories, a future you could afford if you were willing to rob your own past.

A flare went off in my chest. There is a rule: never follow a thread that points to someone you care about. Another rule: never go into the Underlayer alone. I held both rules like two fragile coins and slid them into my palm.

I did not have long to decide. The Archive's main door clicked and someone stamped up the steps; a pair of boots in the corridor told me they were Directorate. They didn't come to the Fifth unless they wanted to make a point. The door opened and an official stepped in—tall, with the precise shoulders of someone used to being obeyed. He had the Directorate's lacquered pin, the kind that used to be made of silver and truth but now was plated with warnings. He glanced around the room as if testing whether it had been tidy enough for a raid.

"Ms. Ril?" he said. His voice had the flat quality of a man who has said "Ms." too many times to mean anything in particular.

"That's me," I said. I wiped my hands on my trousers, more to give them something to do than to make them clean. I kept my eyes level. There are small performances you perform for the Directorate: the steady gaze, the measured voice. They like to feel a virtue unfolding in front of them.

He nodded and produced a thin card the color of late rain. A seal I didn't recognize glinted at its corner. "You have a client this morning who requested voice-only," he said. "We need you to secure any anomalous output in Node 2741."

"I already did," I said. I didn't mention the stitch or the call tag. The man inclined his head, like he expected a modesty but not a lie. "File's clean."

His lips pressed thinly. "We received a report of an unauthorized recovery attempt on Archive property last night," he said. "Someone tried to retrieve frames from Node 2741. That is a criminal action. Ms. Ril—have you been approached by anyone about this node?"

The question slid between us like a knife. My answer lived in the space of air I had exhaled. I gave him the professional decency of restraint. "No, sir."

His eyes sharpened. "We'll be conducting an internal audit, then. Please make sure your workbench logs are available."

Logs. The Archive keeps logs for a reason: to know who had their hands on what. I smiled the kind of smile that keeps a face from being taken. "Of course."

He left no other instructions. The card in his hand hummed—an aftertouch that told me what he wanted done. They wanted visibility, which is how the Directorate controls memory: by watching, by cataloguing, by smothering oddness in official light until even oddness feels tired. He'd left and the room sighed.

The rain slowed. I thought of Luca's bracelet and of my brother's smudged school picture stuck to my childhood wall. I thought about fences and whether you could step around them without setting off alarms. The Underlayer calls to some small, unpatriotic part of me. The part that knew what it was to lose someone and not have a neat paragraph in the public chronicle to point to. The part that would go to any length to fix a piece of someone, even if they were not legally mine to rescue.

I had once believed my trade was about consolation. Today it was a fault line.

I powered down the Loom and slid the node's metadata into a private cache. If anyone wanted to audit me, they'd find what they expected: a voice file, a completed restoration, a neat invoice. If they dug deeper and moved with the discretion of someone who believed in ghosts more than in uniforms, they would find the ghost stitch and the last stuttering frame. If they followed the call tag they'd end up where I was thinking of going.

I made a list the way some people make a grocery list. Coat. Wallet. Tools. A charm my mother once sewed into my collar—useless superstition. I wrote it down because making lists turns indecision into motion.

When I slid my boots on, the rain remembered one more thing: the city has a dozen ways to tell you to stay inside. Sirens are one. Another is the feeling in the back of the throat that says your name in a voice you don't recognize, the way a future sometimes speaks to you like a warning. I shut the Archive's door behind me and the city folded me into its wet palms. I walked down corridors I had never walked before, toward a place the Directorate claimed belonged to the forgotten, and toward a face the State had stamped out of its official photograph.

I told myself I was going to find Luca Mendi, or at least the man who had worn his bracelet. I told myself I would go alone, that I would return with nothing but knowledge and a schedule marked "resolved." The truth is smaller and sharper: I was going because once, when I was six, my brother had shown me a secret crack in the world. You climb a little hole like that, you always want to see what's on the other side.

Rain kept mumbling against the city. It had been telling me something for hours. I had only just remembered to listen.

Chapter One — The Quiet Between Things

They called the Graveyard "the Quiet" because when you drifted inside it the world fell away and all the industry of people—engines, advertisements, arguments—slipped into a vacuum silence so absolute you could hear your own skull. Kira Nadeem liked that kind of silence. It made the ghosts easier to lift.

Her cutter was a patched scrim of scavenged composites and jury-rigged thrusters, the sort of little ship insurance companies wrote off in polite memos. It had a name on the hull—PHOENIX Q-3—hand-painted by someone who'd lost fingers and still wanted poetry. Kira had no illusions about poetry. She had a sister on ventilators in a high-rise in Lathis and three months of unpaid synth-plasma payments and a hole in the pocket of her jumpsuit where she kept a faded photograph of a girl who used to have hair that caught starlight.

The Graveyard hung around Lathis like a bad memory. It was the thin ring of dead satellites, burnt-out freighters, and corporate trophies that had missed their deorbiting window during the wars. It glittered—sharp, beautiful, dangerous. Artists called it stained-glass orbit. Insurance adjusters called it a hazard, and the Salvage Guild called it free money. Kira called it a job.

She threaded the cutter between a lattice of antennae and a torn solar sail that fluttered like a flag frozen mid-salute. Her gloved hands moved without thinking: tertiary thruster, two ticks port, counterspin zero. The cutter breathed slowly, a warm mechanical sigh. Her visor readouts chirped trivia—composition readings, micro-debris cloud density—numbers that meant profit when you could read them.

She wasn't looking for anything special. You never started out looking for special. Special rattled the way some people rattled loose teeth, unpredictable and painful. She was looking for panels, power cells, circuit arrays—things you could sell to the brokers who still trafficked in the old technologies. She was looking to make a run that would pay for one more month of respirator filters for Mina. She was looking to be careful.

The call was small, a whisper against the static of scanners: a localized thermal bloom the size of a child's palm inside the belly of a freighter hull. Heat was a promise in the Graveyard. Heat in an object that should have been cold for decades was a promise of life, of power, and of danger. Kira tagged it and followed.

The freighter's hull had been stripped by scavengers years before, peeled like an orange and left with an exposed ribcage. Inside, the light from her lamps fell on scrap that told a story of hurried abandonment: food dispensers with their doors gaping, a row of empty bunks bristling with dust, one wall still lacquered with a propaganda mural that had faded into a child's mural. In the center of the hold, half buried under wire and cloth and a scatter of children’s toys sealed in amber, something hummed.

Kira anchored her cutter and clipped her bobline. The tether felt lighter in zero-g than it did at home in Lathis, where gravity pulled like a question you couldn't answer. She wished for a cigarette she couldn't smoke, then clipped the hull ladder and drifted forward, a small, stubborn planet in flight.

The thing that hummed was round and patched and sealed with an old cargo seal. It was the size of a baby and had finger-smudges in the polymer where someone had pressed against it from the inside. Kira's gloved hand hovered a breath's width away. Her suit readout told her it was warm—warm enough to have been on within the last fifteen minutes. That shouldn't be possible. No power, no life-support, no passengers. The freighter had two dozen abandoned modules catalogued by the Guild. None of them were supposed to hold a heart.

"Come on," she said aloud, because even solitude needed confirmation. Her voice came out tinny through the comm. She pried the cargo seal ring with a flathead, old habits from being taught to steal a living. When the ring came free it screamed once, metallic and high, then stopped.

The round module's lid was translucent with crimps of frost on its inside. When she brushed it with the glove, condensation beaded and formed the shape of a small face for a second—no more than outlines—and then it was gone. The module sensored her. An identity flicker ran across her visor: UNREGISTERED OBJECT — BIO-ECHO CORE — UNKNOWN ORIGIN.

"Unknown origin" meant good money. It also meant trouble if anyone from Cicada Systems—one of the consortiums that still owned half the bureaucracy of salvage—decided to come by and declare it theirs. Kira didn't like the word "unknown." Unknown took the shape of possibilities that ate living things.

She broke the lid.

Inside lay something that shouldn't have been inside anything dead. A child's fist curled around a strip of hair like a sailor clutching a rope. It was bio-printed skin, not quite the same as a real body—there was a seam along the left temple, a place where the synthetic epidermis met the inner composite—but the breath it exhaled fogged the module's lip and tangled with the frozen dust like someone shaking a blanket.

"Hey," Kira heard herself say. There was no answer. The child's hand flexed. The module projected a holo line—HELENA-Passenger 4: PERSONA HYBRID —STATUS: ACTIVE —SIGNAL: MUTED.

The name struck her like a thrown stone. Helena. She'd seen that name in old manifests when her sister Mina had been younger—someone once had indexed the ark ships, had scribbled the names of old passenger lines with a handwriting that looked like both grief and instruction. The Helena had been one of the vessels that disappeared in the Southern Firedrift, a route that had taken refugees into the smaller colonies and never returned. Everyone assumed the Helena had burned, or been eaten by micro-asteroid storms, or been folded into politics. No one who mattered knew what had become of passengers.

The child's eyes opened, blue and wet with the small, fierce clarity of someone who had just decided they were awake. For a breath Kira forgot everything—gravity, bills, the way the cutter's engine coughed in low thrust. The child was only three at most, maybe less. It stared at her like an accusation.

"Can you talk?" Kira asked. The child cocked its head and made a noise that wasn't speech—more like a sequence of notes, a pattern that interfaced directly with Kira's suit. Her visor translated, slow and rough:

—Is this Hel— / Is this home?

The voice's phonemes were stitched. There was a familiar echo inside them; older than the child's supposed age. The module might be a "persona hybrid"—a legally sanctioned entertainment unit, a child's companion with layers of inherited memory. Those were supposed to be sterile toys. Not alive. Not warm. Not looking like the child was looking at her now.

"Not home," Kira said. "Not yet."

The child squinted. Its lashes were dusted with metallic flakes. "Where is the sky?"

Kira's chest went tight. People born in orbit had a way of naming things that made the world tilt. The sky had been replaced for them by the ring, by the glare from the city, by the advertisement smears that made the stars into a chart. She thought of Mina's last lucid night, when she had whispered about a sky that used to bleed colors people forgot. She thought of the picture in Kira's pocket. She thought of everything she didn't have a language for.

"Outside," she said finally. "Outside and bright. But it's far."

The module began a quiet sequence of diagnostic pings. Kira pulled out a scanner pad and bailed fragments of the stored matrix. The recorded memory overlay flicked on and off—images too fast to be called a memory and yet too specific to be randomly generated: rows of passengers sleeping, a stewardess with a sleeve badge shaped like a compass, a child whose face mirrored this one laughing with a woman whose hair fell like falling stars. Then it hiccuped into a holoslice of a sky with the kind of auroral bands that didn't happen in the Lathis system and an echoing voice that said a name Kira's grandmother used to curse under her breath.

"They called it Aster," the recording whispered. The child's mouth shaped the syllables and then it cried out—not in pain, but like a bell rung by an empty hand.

"Is it—" Kira began. Her fingers were cold inside the gloves. "Is that why you're…"

The child, because the module's language was both mechanical and dangerously intimate, repeated the name in a way that felt like a hand on Kira's chest. "Aster. Home-saying. Remember. Don't let them take the sky."

The Skin on Kira's arms went slow gooseflesh. "Who'll take our sky?" she asked, knowing already where the answer would lead. The Graveyard had rules. Cicada Systems and its enforcement arm, the Quiet Registry, patrolled salvage claims and made sure no unauthorized revivals were performed. Persona hybrids were the easiest way to smuggle data—sensory memories, illicit maps, the blueprints of things that had been hidden. If the Registry found a stolen persona, they'd either take it and destroy the contents or take the people who had it and make them disappear.

"Not them," the child said, and for the first time its voice did something like sorrow. "They are hungry. They go where stars sleep."

Kira swallowed. She had money needs, not moral ones, but trebles were what made her good. Selling off a hybrid to a broker in Dock Ten would pay for Mina's filters for six months. Keeping it would be a gamble—if the Quiet Registry found it, they'd lock it in a vault and her face would go on their watch lists. But the child's insistence—Aster, don't let them take the sky—flashed behind Kira's ribs like a dare.

She pulled at the module's diagnostic. Under the persona overlays, in a layer labeled PRIVATE, there was a file with a code the Salvage Guild didn't archive: ASTRAL-ANCHOR — PROTECTION KEY: UNKNOWN —ORIGIN: HELENA-EXODUS-THREE.

"Exodus-three," Kira breathed. The Helena had been part of an exodus convoy. Nobody on Lathis talked about exoduses without smearing the conversation with old grief and legal silence. There were privileges to forgetting and power in keeping things buried.

Behind her, in the hold, some thin vibration hummed across the metal—an approaching engine, gentle at first. She wasn't alone in the Graveyard. She never was. Other graverunners threaded the bones of ships like needlework, and sometimes the Quiet stalked the Rift, its cutters like black knives making sure order was kept.

Kira sealed the module back up and clutched it to her chest like contraband. The child curled into the crook of her arm and went silent. Her cutter reported a fast-moving contact on the outer sensors—far enough not to matter, close enough to be worried about.

Her hands shook when she strapped the bobline. "Stay quiet," she told the child. The child might have puffed a laugh if its lungs had been made for that. Instead it hummed a line of music like someone trying to remember a lullaby, and for a moment the hold was filled with a sound that almost had a name. The name, Kira realized, matched the picture in the pocket of the faded photograph: a woman with hair that caught starlight. Her name had been Aster too.

The cutter coughed when she fired the thrusters. She pushed off with a grace that came from years of similar little betrayals against gravity and caution. She had hauled home houseplants of other people's lives before, and the knowledge that the Quiet's contact would be scanning every transponder in the field made every move a bet.

Out of the corner of her visor a chime blinked. A beacon pinged her cutter, a formal tone that meant business: UNAPPROVED RECOVERY — REPORT TO REGISTRY — HOVER FOR IDENTIFICATION.

Kira toggled the comm, voice steady. "This is Phoenix Q-3. Local salvage. Manual claim. Visual on cargo module: bio-hatch. Offline elsewhere."

The Registry's reply was flat as ice. "Hold position. Registry vessel designated Cicada-Six en route. Await inspection."

She looked down at the child's face, which had gone small and trustful. The child's palm found her sleeve and clung. Kira's mouth made a line. She could wait. She could hand the thing over. She could sign the papers and walk back to a life where the worst risk was more late fees and a fluorescent machine.

"Or," she said, very quietly, and without looking to see if the child understood, "we could go."

The child opened its mouth and made that pattern of notes again. It wasn't assent; it wasn't refusal. It was some kind of recognition, the way a person recognizes a city they were born in when they smell the sea.

Outside, a star flared like a bell rung by someone who had learned to sleep underwater. The Quiet Register's cutter burned closer, black and poised like a question. Kira tightened the straps on her harness and hit the release.

The Graveyard unrolled beneath her like a story, and she was beginning to write a new line. The sky above Lathis looked small in the distance, a ribbon of light stretched thin by city glow. The child's pulse against her arm was steady. It whispered, in a voice that still carried the edges of other minds, a single careful phrase that sank into Kira's bones.

"Don't let them take the sky."

She tucked the module against her chest and pushed her cutter's throttle. The Graveyard would scold her with drifting scraps and sharp metal, but the Quiet would scold her worse. Kira had always been good at holding scoldings off until she could pay them. This time the credit line might be different.

She didn't know then if she'd made the right choice. She didn't know the Helena's ghosts could find rooms inside living things, or that Aster—if that's what the child would allow herself to be named—knew maps of skyways no one had drawn in a century. She didn't know the Registry's cutters would call in a net of enforcement, or that someone in the Registry kept an old ledger with a face that looked an awful lot like Kira's mother.

She only knew, as she fired the cutter and the graveyard slid around them like a slow tide, that the Quiet had been broken. Something had stirred that wanted the sky. And she was the kind of small, stubborn person who didn't do well with things that wanted to be kept.

Behind her, the Graveyard hummed its ancient lullaby. Ahead of her, the city shone crooked and bright. The child in her arms uncurled a finger and, somewhere behind the seam of its synthetic wrist, a constellation blinked awake.

The first time Meridian forgot someone, a dog kept vigil at an empty doorstep for six hours. People noticed the dog—its ribs and the scar along its left flank—because the rest of the block did not. Crosswalks hummed, coffee vendors called out names, the tramblades sang on their rails, and no one else saw the absence. The dog stood and refused to move until a child from three floors up came to the street and asked, without surprise, “Where’s Mr. Loma?” as if he were asking the dog where he'd left his bone. The dog padded away, satisfied, and a Sunday went on.

For Naima Sayeed, remembering the dog meant restarting a machine.

She lived on the fifty-seventh tier of Meridian’s lattice, which was close enough to the sky to be cold and far enough from the ground to know the smell of engines better than earth. Her apartment was a boxed-in negotiation: walls of adaptive fabric, a window that could reject light or surrender to it, and a kitchen whose appliances argued about utensils. Her most human possessions were a paper notebook, whose edges were ragged as the corners of a life, and a small lithophyte plant that buzzed faintly to signal the city’s thermal cycles. It had survived what the city tried to forget.

Naima worked for Continuity at the Institute of Urban Memory—not because she liked continuity, which sounded like an ode to bureaucracy, but because the job was the only place that paid people to listen to what had been erased. The official title, she liked even less: inverse cartographer. They mapped the negative spaces of Meridian, tracing holes in the city's story and sewing in stabilizers so that commerce and commute and governance could proceed uninterrupted. Continuity made sure the tram schedule didn't collapse into a black patch where trains never left the depot. In exchange, the city let them keep the bother of knowing how much of the world could be unmade with a bureaucratic signature and a carefully targeted Rewrite.

Sometimes erasures were accidents: a line of code corrupted a school registrar, and two hundred children's names glitched into "Unknown." Sometimes they were repairs: a colleague patched a failing transit ringhole and the name of the contractor vanished with the ring. Sometimes, very occasionally and with goddess-like discretion, Meridian's Directorate sanctioned a clean cut—an erasure to wipe away an inconvenient memory so that politics could keep moving.

Then there were the erasures no one sanctioned. Those left freckles on the registry—references to dead things that were not dead, or to births that never took place—and sets of fingerprints that, when fed into the databases, gave back only the smell of static.

Naima had learned to follow the smell.

She was at her desk—more a slab of worn composite with two heat rings where people used to lay their elbows—when the package arrived. It was a simple cylinder, maybe eight centimeters long, wrapped in gray unmarked banding through which the Institute's pest-control algorithms should have flagged an anomaly. No one had flagged it. Naima recognized the serif of ignorance: someone had intentionally made it seem ordinary.

She turned the band slowly. Paper shivered open, and inside, pinned to the cork of a lid, was a photograph. Someone had obeyed an antiquated script and left her a thing that could not be rewritten by a patch. The photo was small—polaroid-sized—creased along the corners as if someone had carried it in their mouth. A child sat on a doorstep in a dress the color of bruises and held a stuffed thing that could have been a rabbit if rabbits weren't extinct. The child looked directly at the camera and smiled in a way that was both trusting and accusatory. On the back in looped blue ink, someone had written, in a hand Naima recognized and did not: Ori Sayeed.

The name hit like a draft through a seam.

Naima’s first reaction was private muscle memory—she drew the fingers of her right hand to the inside of her left wrist automatically and found nothing there. She had lived long enough that her wrists had been checked by every department; they were blank of registry numerals and of the common Continuity seals that reinforced identity. But the name was smudged into the paper like a fossil. She did what she always did in the face of such fossils: she opened the echo-loom.

The echo-loom was not officially hers. The Institute had a fleet of looms—surgical, tall machines used to trace the vector of an erasure and coax echoes back into present tense. The loom Naima pulled from beneath her desk was smaller, an illicit thing soldered from expired parts, still warm from the last time she'd used it to pull the ghost of a lost library into readable air. It hungered for calibration.

She fed the photograph into the loom's receptor and thought of that smile. There were protocols for this: tag the object, record the feed, run an initial pass to check for bleeds. She did them, because Continuity had rules and she liked the ritual of order. The loom sighed—an almost animal sound—and spat a filament of light, a hair of memory. It showed her a faint smear at the edge of the child's cheek, a shape like a shadow that shouldn't have been. Where its edges bled into the rest of the image, the light trailed off into a pattern of static: not a deletion, but a ghost.

Naima leaned forward until the loom's hum vibrated against her sternum. She listened to the smear. Memory had a music if you were trained to hear it; it could be the scrape of a chair against a floor, the timbre of someone's laughter, the way a city filled with footsteps at dawn. The photograph's smear sang a single note and then fell silent. Beneath that note a voice, lapping like a child at the edge of a tide, said one word: "Naima."

Her name in someone else's mouth was a kind of temperature check. People said other people's names as an ordinary economy. But to hear it from an echo—especially one attached to a name that, in all her records, had never existed—was an odd inflation of urgency.

She reported the package. She did not report the echo itself.

Reporting was bureaucratic honesty. The package logged into the system within the hour, a small entry of "Found artifact: suspected unauthorized residue." A compliance agent pinged her terminal and asked a series of rote questions: chain of custody, point of discovery, whether the object had been exposed to lacunal ionization. Naima answered them because she had to; she could not write the part about the name. The compliance agent sent a return ping with a single phrase: "Exercise caution. Directorate involvement possible."

Caution was the Institute's polite word for submission. The Directorate liked things neat. They liked small squares of space where the city narrative ran uninterrupted. An unsanctioned artifact could mean a breach in the net that tethered Meridian’s past to its present. The Directorate's penalties on breaches were seldom applied to objects, more to people who kept them and to the curiosity that refused to let go.

It would be easier, everyone said, to hand the object over.

Naima put the photograph into a drawer with other small rebellions: a fossil ticket stub, a child's name carved on a tree-bench that no longer existed. The drawer had a lock whose circuitry she had rewired when she had been young and certain. She had not been careful then about the risks of memory. She had been certain that fidelity mattered more than comfort.

Outside, Meridian adjusted itself. The acoustic canopy, a lattice of metallic windbursts and light, rearranged shade to maintain a comfortable morning; the market clouds above redistributed their particulate to keep the optical skyline pleasing. The city acted like an animal that loved when it could be certain of its own story, and the Directorate was the veterinarian administering sedatives.

Naima left for a field job two hours later. Field jobs were where the true music happened: there were more contradictions in one street block than in an entire archive. Today she had to assess a lane where apartment doors had been flickering—light and then absence, as if rooms were blinking. The residents reported nothing; the logs showed three minutes of null, and the repair crew had sent back a cogwheel with teeth scorched in a pattern no gear should burn.

When she drove out, Meridian wore the weather of a city that wants to be believed. The tramways ran on time. A mural along the main boulevard advertised the Directorate's new "Continuity Gratitude" program: an infant smiling into sunlight, with the slogan, "Remember to Remember." It was glossy in a way propaganda often was: sincerity rubbed flat by too much care.

At the lane there were yellow ribbons—the kind Continuity put up when anomalies had been identified—and a person standing on the sidewalk who should have not been there. The person was a child in a bruise-colored dress, the same dress as the child in the polaroid. In the child's hand was a stuffed rabbit with one eye.

Naima's breath halted in her throat, a quiet arrest. The child looked at Naima and did not look away.

"You left me a photo," the child said in a voice like paper. "You told me to wait."

Naima stared at the child because there are moments when professional caution is not enough. She would have radioed for a sweep, but the child did not wait for the machinery of the Bureau to come and make sense of them. Instead, she leaned toward the rabbit—naïve curiosity—and pulled from its stuffing a small, rusted tin that had been sewn into its belly: a tin that was warm with an old current. It clicked when she set it on the pavement and unfolded into a mouth-speaker, and out of it there came a thin, unpolished lullaby in a language that seemed to be carved from the scratch of a coin.

The lullaby wrapped around the lane. A man from across the street came out of a doorway and, for a moment, looked as if he'd been turned down to a lower volume; then he blinked, shrugged, and went back in with a grocery bag. Continuity volunteers arrived within four minutes, as though they'd been waiting. They came with their own panels and their own solemnity.

Naima held the photograph in one hand and listened to the lullaby through both the child's eyes and the tin's shivering speakers. The song kept repeating one line in the same voice that had said her name in the echo: "Sing the seam, Naima." The children's mouth sang the line but the tune came from somewhere else, below the layered street, like a canal humming in the dark.

"Who are you?" she asked finally, but the child only smiled.

"Ori," the child answered.

It was a name, and Naima's head felt as if someone had slipped a key inside. The name had sutured itself to the photograph; it had been stitched into the hollow of her day. Ori Sayeed, meaning a strange twin of a name she had carried every step of her life—Sayeed—and yet she had never had to pronounce or explain this other half. The child—Ori—looked harmless in the way of impossible things: a kid on a pavement, a small thing that might be a mistake.

A Continuity agent in a pale coat arrived and extended a device like a detector. It beamed the child's heat signature, molecular print, and a series of registry tags. The device returned a soft mechanical apology. "No record."

"No record," said the agent, and their voice held the practiced neutrality of someone who'd accepted a small way in which the world ceased to be reliable.

The child tilted her head. "You don't remember me," she said. The lullaby paused for a breath. "That means it's working."

"We—" Naima began, but she stopped. Something in the choice of pronouns made her stomach go cold. The phrase "it's working" matched a different kind of arithmetic: a working mechanism that preferred absence. She had fixed things, not set them in motion.

"Who told you to leave the photo?" asked the agent.

Ori touched the picture with one small finger and smiled, which was not the same as the smile in the photo but matched it in intention. "You did," she said simply. "And you said I'd be safe if I waited."

Naima thought of the dog at the first forgetting. She thought of drift and hole and the dog’s patient geometry. The city had trained her to be a seamstress, a person to mend the ragged edges of stories. But a seamstress who carried an unstitched half of a person in a photograph had to ask a different question: what happens when the stitch is from the wrong hand?

The Continuity agent took Ori by the elbow. "We have an ambulance—"

"Don't touch me," Ori said quietly. The lullaby rose again, not loud but authoritative, and the agent's fingers melted away, like heat off metal.

Naima stepped forward then, because some kind of responsibility unhooked from her ribs and fell into her hands. "Let her come with me," she said. It was not a request. She heard herself speak into a habit that had once been hers: the habit of taking people who didn't fit their place and teaching them where to be safe.

The agent hesitated, then signed it into the rolling tablet: "Field assessment. Escort with certified inverse cartographer."

As they walked away, Ori's eyes found Naima's wrist. "You kept a promise," the child said. "You promised me you'd see."

Naima's right hand went to her wrist again. This time, when she curled her fingers around the place where the inner skin met the bone, she found coolness and ink: a faded tattoo under the fold of skin that she had never remembered getting. It said, in the same looped blue script as on the back of the photograph, Ori.

The animal part of the city thinned. A tram slammed by three lanes over and the hiss of its brakes sounded like a question. Naima felt the city watching to see if she would obey.

"Where did you come from?" she asked.

Ori shrugged, small and untroubled. "From the other side of the seam," she said, as if that were an address.

Naima had catalogues for seams. There were the municipal seams—scheduled closures, cultural edits, vendor-specific deletions. There were lacunal seams—places where memory sloughed off into a dark taxonomy that the Institute only spoke of in the metaphor of cavities. There were also, rarely, unauthorized seams, surgical cuts without signatures. Those were dangerous because they were creative: their erasure erased not only people but the reasons why the world had kept them. They were holes that dissolved proofs of existence so well that even the mind could not hold the shape of a missing thing.

"Who made it?" she pressed.

Ori leaned in and whispered the lullaby again, the one in the tin and in the child's mouth and in the smear on the polaroid. This time, as the line settled, it carried with it a new echo, a thin superimposed voice like metal underneath silk: "When you forget us, sing us home."

The lullaby was both instruction and confession.

Naima looked down at her hand, at the blue loops that spelled a name she did not know how she had earned. There are jobs where knowing can be chosen, where one can decide how much to shoulder. Naima had been choosing for a long time not to look too far under the city. This time she had not chosen. There was a child's name pressed into her wrist and a child's voice that knew her and a photograph that had no authority to exist but did.

She could give Ori to the Directorate and return to the Institute and write her field report, and the city would do what cities do: wash its face and keep ordering time into tidy lines. Or she could let the line break.

There are people who stay neat. There are other people who pry at the seams because they feel something like a moral itch—a belief that when something is remembered wrong, you mend it, even if mendings cause storms.

Naima slid her index finger along the margin of the photograph where the paper had been rubbed thin from years of someone holding it. The ink bled faintly under her glove.

"Tell me everything," she said finally.

Ori's mouth opened with the patience of a thing that had been asked serious questions before. "Not everything," she said. "Only the parts you forgot."

Naima thought of the dog and the empty doorstep and Meridian that liked to be believed. She thought of the name that had been there like a coal under a pillow, small and hot. The lullaby's line knifed through her: Sing the seam.

"Okay," she said. "Then let's go sing."

They crossed Meridian toward where the lattice loosened and the city's story thinned. The Institute's volunteers watched them go with the cautious interest of people who police possibilities. Continuity could not afford too many of those.
