Between the towers, the sky opened to a strip of pale, excuse-like heavens. There, in a space the city kept designated for minor anomalies, the ground folded. The fold looked like the softest of breaks: a smudge where the light angled wrong. The air smelled like an old loom room—wool and ozone and the hint of something that had once been there.

Naima stepped forward. Her hand found the child’s and found her own name written on the inside of her wrist like a talisman left by a stranger. The city's hum went thin, as if holding its breath.

When she placed her foot over the seam, it shuddered and a music came up from the gap—a chord that wasn't quite human but that recognized her. The lullaby's last line brushed her ear as if someone had sung it directly into her memory: "When the world forgets you, remember me."

Naima threaded her other hand through Ori's, tightened her grip, and stepped into the place where Meridian's story loosened and other names tried to come back into themselves. She did not know if she would be mending or unmaking. She only knew that the first stitch had been made in the wrong fabric, and someone had to follow its tail.

Behind them, the city corrected itself a little: traffic lights blinked, a vendor’s hat floated down to the pavement. People returned to errands. The agents closed their tabs and wrote reports.

Naima moved toward a darkness that carried the scent of song. It felt like home and like accusation at the same time. If something unfathomable had been unpicking Meridian, she thought, then perhaps the work of someone who maps holes was not to patch them blindly but to find out why the cloth had started to fray.

Ori hummed under her breath as they went deeper. The lullaby threaded through the seam and wrapped them in a kind of memory that wanted to be found. Naima kept imagining the dog's patient shape at a door, waiting not for a person to return but for a name to be acknowledged. She had always fixed what she could see; tonight, she would fix what the city refused to admit existed.

And somewhere in the other side of the seam, a voice briefed by a child's mouth and an old tin sang the refrain that would become Naima’s burden: "Sing the seam, Naima. Sing the seam until the city remembers why it forgot."

Chapter One — The Day the Map Cried

The lattice smelled like copper and rain.

Amaya Kestrel learned to read weather in tastes. Not the weather outside—there was almost never an "outside" in the city that circled the node—but the weather inside the seams that held the hab together: small, electric storms that traveled along data-threads and left behind the metallic tang of drifted ions. She could tell, by the way the taste sat on the back of her tongue, whether a surge in the far-west dome had pushed a heat patch into the nursery, or whether a transport skip was punching through a cool alley of time a half-cycle ahead.

That morning the copper taste turned to something else. It was thin and sharp, like a child's penny chewed clean.

Amaya's hands were steady as she threaded the mapping needle into the lattice. The seam-suit hugged her ribs like a second skin, the membrane humming where it met her collarbone, listening. Around her, the city of Vell drifted on its slow, ritual glide toward the node—the machine at the heart of the system that kept light and currency, grief and supermarkets, circulating at regulated rates. Vell was a rope of habitats and barges and vertical farms that had been tethered to the node since her grandfather's generation. It kept people safe from the coordination storms that could twist a week into a day or a year into a sigh. Safety, in this neighborhood of space, came at the price of routes—carefully charted corridors of altered-phase that you used if you wanted to be where the rest of the network knew you would be.

Amaya's job was to map those corridors.

"Lattice-cartography," her badge said, although everyone called them weavers. They stitched usable lines through the node's invisible fabric, catalogued the crosstalk and dead zones, and patched any holes that opened after storms. The work paid well enough to buy nourishing broth and a cheap bed. It gave her a name. It did not give her back Lio.

She felt the memory of Lio like a notch on a compass. The sister had been six when she'd disappeared at the east transfer. A girl with a scrape on one knee and a laugh that left patterns in the air. The official record said Lio had been lost to a drift accident, a casualty of illegal skipping—an anomaly that had eaten bodies and erased transponder tags. For years, the family had folded itself into the muttered condolences and the small allowances for grief, until grief itself became inconvenient and quiet. Amaya had taken to the lattice because it was the only place between nodes where the past wouldn't be allowed to rot in silence; the mesh remembered everything it had carried, as long as someone could read its threads.

She threaded the needle deeper. The mesh was colder now, fingers of phase running in parallel like a string of frozen rivers. Her heads-up traced them in pale maps across her vision: green for secure lanes, amber for monitored drift, and pulsing red for closed sections. Between two closed reds, a thin filament of light flirted—too small to be official, too precise to be random. It did not match any registered passage. The system's overlay labeled it with a blank tag: unknown. That was the first rule of practice: you don't run unknowns without clearance.

The penny taste bloomed into a clear sound—a syllable folded into the mesh itself, like a signal left in an old radio. It was a child's voice, impossibly buoyant, and it said her name.

"May."

The suit's diagnostics gave a soft chirp. Protocols flared in Amaya's vision like warning lights. Illegal signal. Possible trap. Historic echo. There was an official line, dry and antiseptic: disregard anomalous personal signatures. If the node had learned to mimic—if it could retrieve the sound-files of your life and use them like bait—then every weaver who followed such a trail would be stepping into the maw.

"No," she whispered, not because the suit couldn't hear her, but because the voice had borrowed the cadence of a thousand evenings when Lio would call for her across the bunkroom. It folded the past and present together so neatly that the world for a moment became a child's bedroom and a habitat corridor at once. Amaya's chest tightened at the memory: Lio's loose braid, the teeth of her laugh. She had buried that ache under instrument panels and schedule matrices and the ugly, efficient engineering of living.

The unknown filament pulsed again. This time it carried a second sound, faint but layered: a recording, an echo of a laughter which made the air do something like bending. It didn't match any file in the city archive, but it matched something else—a signature Amaya had only ever seen once, in a classified retrieval she had glimpsed as an apprentice. The signature wasn't a voice at all but a temporal harmonic—a fold in local chronology shaped like a syllable. Whatever had spoken to her had not used the network; it had used time.

Her training supplied the next steps in neat bullet points. Record the signature. Seal the access. Send a flag to Control. Wait for a licensed team. Do not, under any circumstances, follow.

She did not follow protocol.

Not because she had no respect for the system—she'd built many of the small patches that kept Vell from sputtering—but because the call felt like a question spoken in a language only she had left in her body. It had Lio's cadence, but older, as if the child had learned from waiting.

"May," the voice said again, and this time Amaya answered.

"Who are you?"

The filament widened, a strand of light uncoiling into a ribbon. It was wrong: the ribbon's color was an impossible slate, a hue that didn't exist in the spectral vocabulary allocated for safe mapping. The seam's reticules reeled and tried to classify it. Unknown. Noncompliant.

"May," it repeated, softer. A laugh like a rusted bell. "You left the sofa."

Amaya's mouth moved with a half-smile she hadn't realized she'd been saving. It was a stupid, private joke between sisters—Lio had always been the one to drift from the sofa while soaked in old programs. How could a fragment of her sister's manner end up folded in a lattice line no one admitted to knowing?

She knew the tricks. The node stored everything it moved; it could order that material into any pattern. The more tentacles of the network reached into your life, the more it knew how to replicate the scent of your child's lime cough or the way your partner licked their thumb before they folded your clean shirts. But the node was also, supposedly, corrected for memory anomalies. It could not, in official terms, invent independent patterns.

She hooked her hand into the ribbon anyway. The seam cried out at the contact—a small, sympathetic cold that made her teeth ache. It was like dipping a finger into a river that ran sideways. She felt other hands come to meet hers through the membrane: a sensation of smalls and jars and a grandmother's knuckled patience. For an instant, the lattice showed her a house she had never lived in, and there, on the step, a little figure turned. Lio, or a memory of Lio, or something that wore Lio's outline.

"May."

Amaya didn't notice the suit's alarm until Control's voice dropped into her ear. Formal and clipped, the way the city used official tones to keep panic prosaic. "Kestrel," said Director Havel, "you're in an unregistered trace. Withdraw immediately."

She held the ribbon tighter.

"It knows me," she said.

"This is not your call," Havel replied. "You're an asset, not an adventurer. Seal and report."

There was a pause. The ribbon brightened, slow and deliberate, webbing itself inland. For a wild, absurd second, Amaya imagined a child waiting by the east gate, exactly where Lio had disappeared—imagined the small, scraped knee and the hollow hush that had grown in the family after. She could see the angle of sunlight on Vell's corrugated walls, a particular kind of waiting she had never been allowed to break.

"Do you have a warrant?" she asked.

There was a different kind of silence. Control's voice had the taste of pressure and the old, worn-out smell of coolant. "We can open a review," Havel said finally. "But you must withdraw."

Amaya closed her eyes. She thought of the little knot of rope they'd sent down to salvage the east transfer after the first drift, how the knot had been frayed into nothing, and how their neighbor's boy had never come home. She thought of the alphabet of reasons people wrote to themselves to keep from following the wrong map. She thought of the map on the wall of her childhood room—the crude charcoal strokes Lio had made from memory, connecting impossible islands. The node had swallowed those islands. It had kept them in the textures of light, but not in the registry.

"Fine," she said. Her voice was small. She began to pull her hand free.

The ribbon didn't let go.

It coiled instead, and the sound that came out of it wasn't a child's voice now but music—a folding song that made places step sideways. The seam translated in flashes: unstable temporal zone, harmonic imprint, composite memory. The music was older than either Amaya or the city, older than the node itself, keyed to a rhythm of arrivals.

"May," it sang, not through her ear but into the bruise of her chest—into the space that still remembered Lio's hand. "May, come."

She should have called for a licensing team. She should have obeyed. All decent mapping belonged to group patience and communal safety. People she respected had vanished because they chased private signals. Protocols existed in case the node learned to be cruel.

She let the ribbon pull.

The seam's sensors flared and the city hummed like a giant insect. Amaya felt a tug in the line of time—a small, slippery pull that made the blood in her arms feel like it belonged to two days at once. The taste of copper changed again, became something like iron and old pennies at a fair. For a heartbeat, then two, the lattice showed her the east transfer as it had been the day Lio disappeared: bright paint chipped on the railing, a taxi cart with a dented wheel, a loudspeaker loop telling people, in nine languages, to keep moving. There was a child's sock on the step, white and clean. Lio's laugh—no, its shadow—skittered across the seam and pressed against Amaya's ribs with the soft insistence of truth.

Control's voice was a thin thing now, farther away. "Kestrel, withdraw. This is an unsafe contamination."

Amaya realized only then that she had broken the first rule of mapping not because she had been pushed by nostalgia but because the lattice had thrown open a door into someplace it shouldn't have. The physics made no sense. The signatures didn't cohere. If she followed entirely, she could find salvageable memory, or a collapsed reality, or less. She didn't have time to analyze. She had a sister's laugh, and there was an ache that did not let itself be accounted for through logic.

"Standby," she said to Havel, which was both a promise and a lie. Her thumb found the override switch—an illegal procedure embedded in the old notebooks from when the node still needed mappers who were willing to bend the rules for a day's survival. She pressed it with the new, furtive habit of people who learn how to live in the seams.

On her heads-up, the ribbon unfurled into a corridor of stars. Not literal stars, but points of light that chased each other like fireflies trapped behind a pane. The seam read it as a gradient of stability—somewhere between a usable lane and a collapsed memory. Between the lights, something shifted. A silhouette moved.

"May," the voice said, and this time it sounded close enough that the suit picked up micro-modulation. It wasn't just the past. It was a present trying to be past. "You promised you'd come back."

Amaya slid her shoulder against the seam harness and let the mapping needle follow the ribbon. Her compass spun enough to make her stomach drop. The city swam into a pattern she didn't recognize. The lattice didn't so much keep time as hold it like a collection of fragile, humming glass. For every step she took deeper, the world added a layer that felt like an extra skin.

Behind her, the Control voice had become urgency. "Kestrel—withdraw now. We are authorizing a clean sweep—"

She cut the comm.

When she did, the city noise receded to a thin hiss. The ribbon's light brightened, and the taste on her tongue turned at last to the copper of truth.

"May?" said the voice again, and this time it wasn't entirely memory. It sounded like an invitation.

Amaya's hand clamped down on the needle and she imagined the little map on her childhood wall. She pictured the charcoal strokes and the way Lio had cross-hatched the unknowns like fields she meant to plant one day. Maybe, she thought, the node didn't swallow people. Maybe it hid them the way a mother hides a key, not out of malice but out of some mindless, bureaucratic tenderness.

She did not know what she would find. She only knew that if she followed, she would not be alone in the lattice. Something, or someone, had been waiting for her to remember the way home.

The ribbon pulled harder. The seam's alarms bled into her bones, a chorus of dull bells. Amaya Kestrel, mapmaker, sister, child of a city that preferred tidy grief, tightened her fingers and stepped after the light into the place where the map cried.

Chapter One — Threads

The first thing Nila noticed was the sound. It arrived before the image—an undercurrent like a tuning fork dragged along the rib of the city—and the studio lights stuttered as if in time with it. For a fraction of a second she felt it in her molars, a low metallic vibration that mapped itself across old teeth and new scars, and she had the absurd thought that the sound could be plucked like a string and replayed later for a price.

She was mid-cut. The wedding memory on her bench shivered under the microscope, a filament of someone else's July. She had already made the laughter warmer, softened a broken vow into a half-forgiveness, removed the flash of a bruise around a wrist no one at this reception would ever notice. There was an art to it: enough honesty left to pass inspection, enough polish to stop people from returning. Her fingers moved on autopilot, coaxing the thread filaments into a new weave. Memory editing was a craft of small lies, and Nila was good at keeping her hands steady.

The courier pod arrived before the client could. It landed on the studio roof with a soft hollow knock that carried through the building's bones and set the algae lamps flickering. Nila swore under her breath and slid the welding visor up, wiping film from her eyes with the back of her hand. Packages were always late in Meridian, but the pod smelled of ozone and something older—salt, rust, the dry perfume of machines that had spent a long time out in the Scar.

The label was nothing. Paste of white plastic stitched to metal: Unregistered Material. No return. No hazard code. Just a barcode that hummed when Nila waved the scanner over it, as if the metal wanted to be read.

"Late drop," Ajay called from the adjoining bay. His voice came through like a soft fan, practical and amused. "You getting another ghost?"

Nila opened the seal. The pod unrolled like the pages of a book, and inside lay a memory-rod the color of dried bone. The rods—people called them laces, filaments, threads—were the raw language of experience: glassy, folded around themselves, when you held them to the light tiny storms swirled inside. This one had a thin crust of salt across one edge, as if it had been minted on the lip of an ocean no one on Meridian had seen in living memory.

She should have vaccinated it: quarantine, scan, dump it into the Archive if it flagged as corrupt. That was protocol. The Migration Authority loved its protocols because protocols made things legible, and in Meridian legibility was power. But she had a habit of breaking the rules for things that smelled of other people's ghosts. Maybe it was the way grief clung to her job—her sister's laugh cached in a sealed patch behind her right ear, the one she kept live because everything legal and clean had taken the rest of their life. Maybe it was curiosity. The salt tugged at some part of her that remembered water.

"Only if it bites," she said. Her voice sounded too loud in the studio. Ajay rolled his eyes. "Don’t die on the bench, Nila. You're ruining my break."

She clicked the rod into the reader, made tea with one hand, and watched the waveform crawl. At first it was noise: a jag of frequencies the software couldn't place. Then a frame assembled—a corridor like a mouth, curved and smooth, edges folding in on each other in ways the human eye didn't make. Nila felt her stomach hiccup.

"Corrupt," the system said, calm as a clock. She ignored it. The viewer drew the scene sharper. It was architecture that contradicted Euclid, rooms spliced onto rooms like stolen reflections. There was no ceiling, or rather, ceilings folded sideways so that looking up was the same as looking back.

A voice threaded through the image. It spoke in a register Nila couldn't find among her cataloged languages: a child's rise pattern encoded into a vibrational geometry. The software tried to translate—default response: noise—then produced a single phrase in Meridian Common, the translation poor, uncanny: WE ARE NOT THE ORIGINAL GUESTS.

Nila's scalp tightened. The thought of being "not original" lodged in her throat like a broken badge, and the memory filament shifted under her touch. It wasn't just visual. For a second she tasted iron, then rain, then something sharp and sweet she couldn't name. Her eyes watered.

"Quarantine flag," Ajay said more sharply now. "Quit the bench."

She shouldn't have. She should have sealed the rod in containment and put a secure notice into the Archive. Someone would have picked it up—Registry, Migration, the black-market traders who made a religion of weird memories. But she sat back on her heels and let the scene roll. There was a person in the image, or something with a person-shaped absence—an indent of being—and it folded itself through a doorway that shouldn't exist, leaving a smear like a fingerprint of light.

Nila reached forward reflexively, not to touch the rod but to touch the screen. Her fingertips brushed the holographic projection and the studio answered her: the sound flared, and for the slimmest instant the viewer wasn't a viewer anymore. She was inside the corridor.

It was not her body that moved but a perception that rode its filaments. A memory wasn't just seen; it had weight, gravity. This one tilted her as though she were about to fall out of the world. A scent that wasn't scent—cold and mineral—wound around her chest. The child's voice came again, closer, and this time the translation software offered another line, the grammar wrong in a way she felt through her teeth: DO NOT TRUST THE LIGHT.

She yanked her hand back. The rod hummed in the reader—a low, persistent tone that seeped into the concrete. The security lights in the studio dimmed and then reasserted themselves. Ajay had the doorway open now, looking across at her like she was a patient animal. "You need to kill that," he said. "Purge, quarantine, whatever. You don't see this kind of corruption unless it's been out in the Scar a long time."

"Why would the Scar—" The Scar was the rip in space above Meridian where derelict satellites and relic ships fell. It was the city's dead sky-dump. No one expected to find language in the Scar. It ate whole fleets and left only noise. "Because salt," Nila said. Her voice was steady. That explained nothing and everything.

The system flagged the rod again, desperately, with banners and protocols that felt like hands closing in. The rod's metadata read nil: no author, no origin, no signature. It was as if the memory had been born naked, unclaimed. That was illegal in several ways. It was also thrilling.

A soft green mote had landed on the inside of her left eye. She registered it as some kind of artifact—afterimages were common after aggressive cuts—but this one persisted when she blinked, a pinprick of unfamiliar light that the system could not map. It moved when she moved, but at a slant, and when she focused on it she could taste the rain-sweet now from the memory, only this time the taste came in a slow bloom along her tongue.

"Get rid of it," Ajay said. The command had the shape of fear in it. "Nila, now. If Registry gets a read on that, you know what the fines are."

She stood, fingers brushing the bench. Her own right ear hummed—she could feel the vestigial memory of her sister there, the laugh she'd kept despite the law. That laugh had saved her once, quiet and illegal, when the Migration Authority came for family patches after the Cease. She had cut the family into legal lines and glued that laugh in a place the system rarely looked. It was the reason she hadn't joined the Registry herself. It was also the reason she couldn't throw this rod away.

"Don't be dramatic," she said, and meant it for Ajay but not at all for herself.

Ajay watched her like he knew her better than she knew herself. "You can hide it like you hide everything," he said. "But one day it bites you hard enough and nothing will keep you under the radar."

She laughed, a thin thing. "Then I'll bite back."

The protocol demanded she log the event for later audit. The system's auditors would find nothing now if she masked the rod with a legal signature and misfiled the read. She had done that trick before—phantoms slipped through Registry fingers on the thin thread of bureaucratic competence. But something else tightened in her chest. The child's voice had not sounded like a threat exactly. It had been a warning. Do not trust the light. It landed on her skin like a bruise.

She unplugged the rod and slid it into a lined envelope, then into a toolbox no one ever opened: a battered tin from her grandmother's kitchen, the lid corroded at the seam. She told Ajay she was going to the market, which was true in the most literal sense. She needed to see other kinds of things: the open sky, the market's odors that were not salted metal, the dancers who sold old songs for coin.

On the alley she paused and let the city wash over her. Meridian had built itself into a cliff-face of habitation and commerce: terraces like stacked plates, transparent bridges that hummed, and the Scar a scab of black above the skyline. Somewhere beyond the visible arc, the Lattice would be going down tonight for scheduled maintenance—a ritual that always made the city hold its breath. Lights would dim. Traffic would be rerouted. Registry would be looking the other way in their narrow, sanctioned focus.

She had the rod in her bag and the green mote in her eye, and in the mole-thin corner of her head the child's phrase repeated like an earworm. It was a call and a riddle. She had no proof and no plan. But she had time until the Lattice came down, and that was a kind of shelter.

When she crossed into the market, vendors called her by two names: Nila the Cutter and Nila the Quiet. They meant different things in different rooms. She bought bread the color of sunrises and some dried fish wrapped the way her mother had once wrapped sorrows. The city moved past her in long sweeps of faces and fabric and neon. People traded lives for memory-laces in the flesh, bartered moments for better nights.

At the end of an alley she paused because she felt movement—no, it was only the city, always rearranging itself. But the green mote in her eye pulsed, a small lighthouse that tugged at her privacy. She could have walked away. She could have turned the rod in to the Registry, watch the officials clap interested hands and design containment suits. She could have erased the child's voice and gone on with her life.

Instead she slid the tin under the false floor of her cart, under the spare blanket she used for long cuts, and locked the latch with a tiny wire she carried for emergencies. She told herself she would learn what the voice meant later. She told herself she was not a hero. She told herself many things.

The city folded its terraces and the market became a smear of sound as the Lattice announced a scheduled reboot. Light lanes blinked. Drones shifted like insects to memory, and above them the Scar sighed. Nila adjusted her bag, felt the rod press light against her ribs, and took one step forward into a city that had always taught her how to deceive.

Behind the bench the wedding filament cooled into a neat little honest lie, ready to be delivered. In the tin the unregistered memory lay, patient and impossible. It hummed with an order she could not admit to herself: that memory wanted to be more than watched. It wanted to be understood.

When she smiled, it did not reach her mouth. She had kept worse things than this hidden. She had kept the sound of her sister's last breath locked as a luxury none of her neighbors could afford. That scream, a scandal tucked behind her ear, had taught her how to keep secrets.

She named the new thing in her head because names gave weight. She called it the Knot, because it was both a loop and a trap, and because knots are meant to be unmade.

The child's voice echoed behind her eyelids as she pushed through the crowd: DO NOT TRUST THE LIGHT. The city answered with the metallic tuning fork, and the studio clock blinked the hour of the Lattice.

The first thing you learn about salvaging in the Pale is how loud silence can be.

Out here, where trade lanes braid like veins and dead ships break apart into snowfall of parts, vacuum keeps its own record. It holds the thinnest scraps of voice and light and grief and stores them in crystal. The job — my job — is to go into that record and pull the pieces people are willing to pay for. Names. Birthdates. The precise pattern of a laugh. Entire private libraries if the buyer has deep pockets and darker tastes. We call them memory-cores; law calls them property. Somewhere between a commodity and a soul, they are a gray market’s currency.

I tether myself to the hull of the Seraph Lark and look out at the field. Pieces drift like constellations — a dining module framed in smoke, a cargo bay with wheels still trying to remember rotation, a child's hand-shaped magnet spinning loose. Stars are indifferent pinpricks; the real light comes from the cores themselves, tiny lattice fossils of consciousness. They wink in and out as they spend their last stored energy. Kids on the dock call them ghost-fire. For me they’re inventory.

Tess decides which ones I can take.

Tess is half-drone, half-library. Someone soldered her together out of an old courier drone and a stack of pirated curation protocols. She hangs from my shoulder like an arthropod, her optical array sweeping the field in microbursts of blue. Her voice slips through my suit comm, flat and practical.

"Primary picks ahead," she reports. "Two biosignatures, one contested. Heat spikes volatile. No live crew signatures."

"Of course not," I say. "The Contested ones are always the best ones."

Below me, a slab of hull rotates slowly, bedecked with graffiti from a civilization I have yet to meet: a barcode that spells "FOR SALE", bracketed by a child's scrawl of a ship I cannot identify. Memory-cores are embedded in the composite like geodes; you can't always tell by eye which is valuable. That is Tess's job — find the fluorescent anomalies and keep them from dissolving into static.

I plant the pry-plates and watch the anchors snake out, fingers of steel sinking into brittle composite. The Lark groans, translating my pull into a motion that feels almost shy. Space is patient, but ships are not. The salvage line chants through tensile memory as my suit pumps air and nerves.

When the hull gives way, a pocket of cold light blooms. Tess chirps.

"Two cores, heavy encryption. One stamped Helix — corporate."

Helix. The name lands like weight. The corporation owns the patents for memory lattices and the laws that made them property. They are the people who decided some memories were dangerous and priced them accordingly. Where Helix has its name, the Bureau has its watchmen, and where the Bureau watches, judgments have a way of becoming execution.

"Helix always marks their cores. They don't dump them unless it's deliberate," I say. "Maybe it was a transport hit. Maybe an offload."

"Possibility: illegal transplant. Risk: high."

Risk is the word for my life, shaped into daily increments. The Lark is mortgaged in six different directions; Thalia Kest is behind on breathing. My father used to tell me that debt was the only honest religion, and I am a faithful convert. I take a breath, check the tether and my suit's reactor. My hands are steady.

I cut through the panel and lift the core free. It nestles against my palm like a stone made of glass and memory. The lattice throbs faintly, and for the briefest time I taste salt and the inside of a cassette player — old, archival. The tag is a corporation's neat stamp, and beneath it someone has scrawled a name in felt-tip pen.

Kest, Mara.

My fingers go cold despite the suit. I know my name. Everybody knows their own name. But my heart taps a rhythm of alarm: the core has my name on it.

"Scan?" I ask Tess.

"Scanning." Her optics narrow. "Encryption variant: helix-3. Local hash pattern... anomalous. Timestamp: tomorrow."

Time is a blunt instrument here. You see it on manifests, in credits, in the smudged stamps of arrivals. A core stamped with tomorrow's date should be impossible, unless someone is lying to me or to themselves.

"Maybe the transport's manifest is wrong," I say. My voice sounds small against the stretching dark. "Maybe it was scheduled."

"Possibility: scheduled. Possibility: backdated. Possibility: time corruption," Tess supplies, as if that is equally mundane.

She is being facetious, but she cannot take it all away. I stuff the core into my inner pouch and haul it into the Lark. Back in the ship's cramped lab, the air smells of ozone and boiling coffee. Niko would curse me for it; Niko does not like salvage that smells like trouble. Niko likes the neat problems: the broken motor, the stripped screw, the ledger that balances if you whisper to it.

I sit in the lab and power the core down against the weld of a portable field. The lattice cools like a body in a bath. Then I bring it up on my reader.

Memory-cores are stubborn in different ways. Some shout their contents like fireworks; others are mausoleums. This one opens like a book at the wrong page. Images spill: a row of trees I'd never seen, a smell of fresh linen, a child's hand — the same hand in the salvage field photograph. There is a room with soft blue light and, threaded through all of it, a voice.

"Mara," it says.

The word isn't recorded; it's a familiarity I have been hearing my whole life. It is my name as a lullaby and as an accusation.

Time does not follow the rules in these cores. The voice is layered over itself, chorus and echo, like a choir singing in a mirror. And beneath the harmonics is one line — clear, present — a woman's voice I have not heard since the Quieting.

My mother died during the Quieting. The Quieting was a ten-day cascade where the Bureau executed a recall of certain memory-threads. They said subtleties had infected politics, that embedded identities were destabilizing governance. They said it was a necessary consolidation. They said a lot of things in neat sentences that meant people lost themselves and jobs and children. My mother's case was old enough to get buried in the dust of policy. They said her core had been corrupted. They said she was gone.

I breathe until my suit's oxygen thinks I'm calm. The voice on the reader fills the lab, soft and impossibly familiar as a weathered sweater.

"—they lied about the Quieting," the voice says. "Mara, listen."

My knees give a polite tremor only gravity could explain. Tess's optical sensors ping with a pattern I have come to read as concern.

"You aren't Helix," I whisper to the core. "You're not even legal. If this is a trap—"

"It's not a trap," the voice insists. "It's a fracture. We got out. You got out."

"Who are you?" My voice breaks. It is a ridiculous question to ask to a voice that called me by name, but here we are, and I am a woman who measures danger by carbon copy.

There is a soft sound, like paper folded and unfolded. "It is me," the voice says. "It is Ana Kest. They made it look like I... like I stopped. There are still others."

The ship tilts slightly. For a moment I taste iron and the possibility of betrayal. The Lark has a way of keeping secrets; she also has a way of losing them when the wrong person gets hungry.

Tess's voice is flat. "Helix flagged as origin. Trace inconclusive. You still harboring the asset is criminal."

"Did I mention I'm behind on breathing?" I say. It is supposed to be a joke. It lands on a stone.

The voice — Ana's voice, if the core is what it claims — continues. "They took our names and put them into ledger-states. They call it property. They call it safety. They sell pieces. But there are fragments that don't want to be sold. They fracture across the lattice. Some of us wait in the dark, waiting for a person who'll remember the wrong thing."

"Why mine?" My voice is thinner. "Why my name?"

A laugh, small and familiar, skates through the reader. "You are the one who never could be far from home. You pull what the world throws away and make it a story. You always were a salvage dancer."

Memory is not kind. My childhood catalogues are all brassy and practical — a mother who worked as a curation tech, a father who taught me to unfasten screws, and a last day where paperwork became a verdict. I pulled on the last thread of that day until it yielded nothing but a list of regulatory codes and a printed note that had been stamped "COMPLETED."

"There's a timestamp on this," I say. "It says tomorrow."

There is a pause. Even through metal, even through circuitry, I can hear the weight of years in silence.

"Time is a commodity, Mara," Ana says finally. "They have better accounting than they admit. I wasn't destroyed; I was deferred. My ledger will resolve. But before then, I can whisper. Before then, I can tell you where to find the rest. They are not gone. They are placed."

Placed.

My mind catalogues implications. Placed like goods on a shelf. Placed like children in the waiting room of the world. My throat tightens at the image of my mother being filed away.

"You want me to fetch them?" I ask. It's not a question; it's a decision I can already feel pulling threads in my bones.

Ana's voice is suddenly sharp. "I want you to remember. I want you to look, Mara. The field where you work is not random. Helix is throwing its refuse where laws are lax. They cover tracks with wrecks. There's a barge they call the Promise. It will pass through the Pale tomorrow. There will be a manifest. Get on board. Find them. Get them out."

I taste the word Promise and find it thin and brittle. I know what a manifest looks like and what it costs to alter one. I know the Bureau's ways.

"This is insane," I tell the lab, the cosmic debris, the satellite orchestra outside. But the voice knows me. "You could be a memory that thinks it's her original."

"A memory is all I have," Ana says. "And you are all I have left who might remember me for more than a property code."

My hands are steady, but inside there is a heat that feels dangerously like hope. Hope is stupid and expensive. Hope is also how the world keeps moving. Niko would say it's a bad investment. Tess would say it's a variable in a formula I cannot afford.

The lab hums. The Lark breathes. The day stamped on the core — tomorrow — feels less like a misprint and more like a summons.

"Get on the Promise," Ana says. "Find the manifest. There's something Helix doesn't know they're carrying."

Outside, the Pale folds itself around us like a wound. Somewhere beyond where metal pieces became constellations, someone or something had decided to keep my mother's voice alive enough to be found.

I press my thumb to the safety rim of the core. It is warm, alive as a heart.

"All right," I say. "But if this is a trap—"

It is a threat, and it is a promise. Ana does not answer with words. The lattice pulses once, twice, and goes dim, like a candle snuffed by a small, deliberate hand.

Tess clicks. "Deviation: high. Legal exposure: critical."

"Welcome back to work," I tell the ship. Outside, the field waits, indifferent and listening. Inside, the small stone in my hand vibrates faintly like a second heartbeat.

Tomorrow, a barge called the Promise will cross these stars. Tomorrow, a stamp and a manifest will mean the difference between property and person. Tomorrow I will decide whether to remember a law or remember my mother.

Tonight, I sit and listen to the silence, and it listens back.

The first wake on Palimpsest always smelled like iron and resin.

We were an archive built from things humans had once thrown away: the skeleton of a decommissioned habitat, the hull of a research probe, the braided wiring of a thousand canceled projects. We drifted in Lagrange, a knot of metal and glass and glass-quiet corridors where the sky outside the observation ring was an uninterrupted black, jeweled with a few apathetic stars. The sun rose across the station in a shallow metal glare that slanted through exposed lattice; everything caught it and turned into cold, useful lines.

I liked the light on the restoration bay. It cut paper-thin across the shelves of cylinders, across the patches of old fiber and the patient rows of memory-cakes that hummed in their cases like sleeping insects. That morning I had a cup of coffee and a new cylinder on the bench: an unlabeled thing someone had shoved into Drop when the conveyor jammed. Small objects always felt like secrets. The Archive ran on secrets.

My name is Mara Voss. My job title was Restorer—tacit meaning: nudge the old world into telling you what you needed to hear. I leaned my forehead against the cool polymer of the bench and listened to the hum. There is a kind of weather inside an archive; sometimes it was meticulous and kind, sometimes corrosive and beggarly. Today it was patient.

The cylinder was thin, maybe the size of my forearm. The outer shell had flecks of frost in its polymer and a stamp I didn't recognize: a little spiraled glyph with no registry in the central lexicon. Whoever had found it had left no metadata. Whoever had built it had not wanted to be found.

I laced my gloves and slid the seal. The cylinder sighed as it accepted me. Inside: a strip of woven memory-film, the kind that older households used to keep snapshots of a life. It wasn't the archival-grade composites we kept for institutions; this was domestic and brittle. Someone had liked their memories tactile.

I threaded it into the Reader and fed the film through, watching the patterns bloom on the screen. Where other files came in frameworks—time-stamped, indexed, spliced into neat genealogies—this one opened as a thin, resonant thing. Sound first. The audio wasn't compressed the way I'd expect for a domestic reel. It carried in layers: at the base a machine ticked, an echo of metal; above that, a voice.

It sang.

Not in any musical key that registers on the Lattice's symbolic analyzer. The song had no tempo markers, no margins. It was a human voice doing the careful halting thing people use when nobody else is listening. It was messier than the hush voices we keep on tapes in the family vaults—breaths, swallowed syllables, the sort of half-words you leave when the room remembers.

I listened because that is what we do. My sensor array pulled fragments for the lexicon—the waveforms, the timbres—and tried to match them to known variants. It spat back null. No match. Domestic. Preteref: 0.0. Not registered in national or Colony archives.

And then, after the third bar of the song, something in the chorus shifted, a particular cadence I had not heard since I was small enough to be carried on my mother's hip. The syllable split and reformed and the voice said a name.

"Little Dove."

My hand went cold on the bench. The muscles in my wrist remembered the way my mother used to call me across a market stall, the private nickname that had disappeared from official records when I was ten: a casualty of the Consent Edit, the legal erasures after the Purges. People had names for what you forget, then. Little Dove wasn't listed anywhere; it was something soft and alive that the state had meant to scrape smooth.

The voice on the reel was not my mother's. It shouldn't have been, not with the spike in my personal history log, not with the blank where the family archive ought to have been. It was older, ornamented by someone who had not quite learned the rhythm of the syllables. That voice continued, not singing now but speaking, slow and precise as if weighing every word.

"Mara Voss," it said. My name. My implants ticked, took the sound as a data packet. My ID chimed—this was not supposed to be possible. I checked the Reader twice; the reel did not contain any hash-tagged authorization. Whoever had made the reel had embedded a voiceprint custom-shaped to the genetic shape of my name.

"You will not remember all of it," the voice said. "Remember what you can."

A flicker of static, like someone who had been cut out of conversation and then allowed back in. The film flashed an image: a child's hand, small and grime-streaked, reaching for a bench rail. Behind the hand, a horizon that should not have had any stars besides the sun. There were stripes—two faint, vertical bands where someone had tried to overlay a map. Coordinates revealed themselves in slow bloom, lines of numbers and an arrangement of angular glyphs a little like a child's map to a treasure.

The coordinates referred to a place called the Hollow—an informal name used by salvage folk, but also something darker. On our charts the Hollow was annotated with a caret of caution: Excluded. Do Not Approach. The Hollow existed at the heart of the old asteroid belt, a pocket of rock and abandoned structures where the Reckoning Stations had collapsed long ago. No sanctioned vessel had taken the route in centuries; insurance underwriters considered it a metaphor for the sort of trouble you didn't ask for.

And yet the map matched the coordinates in the image. The image was stamped with a date I had never seen on anything: Year -12.

"Do not tell them the time," the voice said, as if reading my thought.

I should have closed the reel. I should have catalogued it, labeled it as anomalous, and sent it up the chain. Instead I pushed the image larger on the Reader. The child's hand in the photograph was mine, or at least scaled to the bones I remembered: small knuckles, a scar along the thumb from when I'd cut it on a shard of glass in the market. The scar existed. My biometrics didn't lie.

A line of the song returned, an undercurrent that had been running beneath the voice since I started the reel. It was not melody in the usual sense. It was a mnemonic: the kind archivists used to hide coordinates in lullabies, the kind sailors used to hide routes in rhymes so their enemies could not parse them with early scanners. The Lattice couldn't translate it because it expected text. The song expected a listener.

"Open your hand," the voice said, and I did, reflexively.

My implant—my hand-level chip—lit, a faint ribbon of turquoise across the joints. This was routine; the chip communicated with the archive systems, allowed me clearance to sensitive restoration bays, to measured labs. It ought not to have responded to anything on a domestic reel. It did. The turquoise ribbon pulsed twice and then went dim, like a heartbeat.

The reel ended.

Silence dropped onto the bench. I sat with the aftertaste of the song, with the echo of the voice in my bones. There are rules to being a restorer. Keep things, don't become one of them. Report anomalies. Don't be a fool.

I told myself I would log it. I told myself I would not leap into an unauthorized plot the way the old operas did. Then I copied the reel to a secure, private partition—something I had promised myself I would only ever use for personal fragments. The copy was an index-one, a clean duplicate. The archive's arms circled and claimed the original.

Only after that did I stand and step into the corridor.

The corridor smelled of recycled citrus and ion grease. Outside, the observation ring showed the belt: a scatter of rocks like teeth against the sun. The Hollow was a dark fret somewhere past those points, an absence on the map as old as the first salvage codes. People whispered about it in the mess hall as though naming it would summon debt. The Archive's official memorandum on the Hollow filled three paper-thin volumes of not-my-job, glossing it with phrases like "unstable gravitational topology" and "nonconforming artifacts." Good reasons to keep one's distance.

My palm still tingled where the implant had pulsed, as though someone had laid their hand over mine and left a warmth. The station's routine moved around me—shifts swapping like quiet tides, the minor government of chores and errands—and the song was a thread under it all.

I should have gone home, finished my coffee, filed the reel. I should have done nothing.

Instead I went to the map room.

There is a cabinet in map room twelve where we keep the old plots that have been quarantined. Its door had a small mechanical lock and a soft, smug little warning that it was easier to ignore a locked thing until it goes away. I opened it with the same finger that had been small enough to be called Little Dove. The files inside smelled of dust-sugar and old paper. The Hollow's annotation lay at the bottom, scrawled across the map like a bruise.

For a long time I simply leaned against the metal shelf and remembered a song my mother used to hum while mending the nets at the market. It had no coordinates, only the rhythm of hands moving across a weaving. I had been certain the memory was mine, that the person singing was my mother and not a reel. The Consent Edit had taken many things, but it had missed the small lullabies. Perhaps they thought you couldn't weaponize a lullaby.

The coordinates on the reel matched the coordinates on the map except for a single digit: a tiny variance that could be an error, a slippage of cartography, or something intentional. In the corner of the map there was a tiny, almost invisible annotation—a glyph I'd never seen before. Someone had drawn it in the same ink my mother used to write with, thin and deliberate.

It was in that line, in that faint curl of ink, that the possibility bloomed and pressed against me like a living thing. The song had known my name. The reel had known my scar. The coordinates were a place we didn't go.

"Remember what you can," the voice had said.

I cracked my knuckles, tasted coffee in the back of my throat, and felt, for the first time in a long while, as if something outside the archive had decided to call my name and expect an answer. The station hummed, unreadable and ordinary. The Hollow waited, excluded and implacable.

Somewhere, in a shallow orbit of past errors and old erasures, something had reached out to me across a memory, across a child's thumbprint and a lullaby. It had a voice that could say "Mara" and mean it. It had the arrogance to suppose I would hear.

I slid the map under my arm and left. The corridor swallowed me in its cool, and the observation ring passed a cloud of debris like a curtain. On the way out I turned, not toward my quarter but to the bay where we kept the old transit skiffs—small, uninsured, and perfect for thought crime.

The law said many things about curiosity. The archive kept a ledger of them. I thumbed my implant, tightened my grip on the map, and whispered to no one in particular.

"All right," I said. "Let's see what you remember."

On the third stitch, the memory reached for her.

Juno felt it like a hand sliding along a scar. It was a tactile phantom — a cold filament of sensation that threaded through the back of her skull where the clinic's interface met her neura. For a second she couldn't tell whether it belonged to the client on the slab or to herself. The lamps above the operating bay hummed and the air smelled of ozone and sabathine coffee, and then the memory unfolded in her mind as clearly as a headline: a woman's face lit by sodium lamps, hair braided across one shoulder, eyes that knew the pattern of Juno's childhood so intimately it hurt.

The client on the slab did not stir. He lay like wirework beneath the sterilized sheets: pale skin, loose cable curls, the telltale silvery disc behind his left ear that marked him as a Class Four interface—enough bandwidth to run boutique edits but not to hold a full echo. Juno's gloved fingers hovered over the placer tool, watching the neural map bloom across the cortexpad before her. The extraction window was supposed to be clean, binary: cut here, pull there, fold the residual into the clinic's vault for legal logging. There were no ghosts. That was the rule. The law made ghosts a sanitizable product.

She tightened her jaw and forced the stitch to continue.

The woman's voice came with the face, small and precise, like a memory recorded on an analogue cassette and then slowed. "Kira," she said. It wasn't the name the woman had called Juno on every birthday—Mama, Junebug—rather a name she hadn't heard since she was six and they'd boarded the shuttle out of the scrublands. Kira. Juno had been Kira once, before the Clearing, before the implants, before her mother folded her into a blanket and taught her the rhythm of breathing under alarms.

The clinic's scheduler beeped at the edge of her awareness, a mundane reminder that there were three more clients queued in Suite B and that her manager, Reza, would want the day's manifests before midnight. She pushed them away. Protocol was a muscle separate from bone; she had been trained to ignore echoes. But training didn't teach her to ignore a voice that said your original name like a key in a lock.

"Juno?" Reza's voice over the intercom. "You good in there? Client's on two-hour hold."

"Fine," she lied. Her hands were steady. Her tools moved like memory and met its shape. The face in the extraction window smiled as if she recognized this intrusion and chose to indulge it. "Find the ledger," the woman said. "Find the ledger and follow the ledger. Not to the city. To the water."

The fragment collapsed. The interleaved maps on the cortexpad flickered, then conformed to expected topography. The woman's face was replaced by the program's trusted icon: a hollow disk with a crosshair. Juno exhaled and held the breath. The sensation of a hand on the scar receded; the extraction protocol completed, and the client would wake with the requested dissociation, the particular ache in his chest whittled down to an unremarkable regret.

She sealed the file to the vault with the practiced ritual — a line of encrypted hashes, a timestamp, a Reza-authorized key — then, before the clinic's logging agent could write the metadata to the State's ledger, she copied the fragment into a private partition.

That alone was stupid. Illegal, too, and not clever. But the woman's voice had threaded through something in Juno that had not been fully seamed away by the plastic sutures of new names and new laws. Kira. Find the ledger. To the water.

She swiped the copy into a cold drive she kept in her boot — ten grams of metal, cheap enough to be missed in a gear check and old enough that the clinic's scanners might not peek inside. Reza would call it a lapse. The State would call it an offense. For now it was the only piece of the world that felt unaccountably like something she had known before the Clearing.

Memory work had been a lifeline for Juno. It paid the rent in a city where rent was measured not in credits but in module space and atmospheric allowance. It paid for the little things that kept her from slippage: a window patch in her unit, the bartending shifts she picked up at night, synthetic mangoes that tasted like the summer her mother had promised they'd have someday. It paid for not asking questions. That was part of the employment contract, unspoken and absolute. You erased people. You didn't take their ghosts home.

She closed the clinic door and felt the corridor's synthetic wood breathe under her boots. The clinic, "Remlex Stitchworks," sat on the underside of Habitat Forty-Six, a ring of apartments and arcades and low-cost treatment centers that circled the city like a ribbon. Outside, the ring gleamed against the planet — an old salt of atmosphere and industry — a permanent smear of light under a permanent sky. The city below, Nadir, never slept because it didn't have to; the sun was a disciplined engineer himself, and the ring's shadow drew a perfect night across the towers.

Juno took the transit to the lower levels, where the air thinned and the windows were thicker and the people who couldn't afford to be noticed lived behind net curtains. She kept to the shadows the way some people kept to the edges of conversation. Her face, unremarkable, was a gift: it let her be what she needed to be in rooms that were watched.

At a bar between a seamstress and an awning repair shop, she poured herself a drink and tried to untangle the echo. She had known her mother, she told herself. She had remembered her until the Clearing. Officially, the family line died the day the authorities decided to sanitize the neighborhoods for the Extension. They had bulldozed the scrubfields, they had displaced the communities to templated modules, and with them they had authorized one of the largest "social corrections" in the city's recent history. People with subversive loyalties got Identity Reshapes; people who objected got their names washed from the State files; and entire divisions of memory were sealed and buried, logged as "Non-Operational." Juno's family had been logged as such. She had been made new.

Except she hadn't been entirely. A seam here, a lingering taste of river water, a way of tying a braid — these things had survived the Clearing in the hairline cracks of herself. She had grown up with a hunger that lines the ribs, a permanent pause when the siren of the transit sounded — habits of a life erased.

The voice — Kira — presented a contradiction she couldn't file away. It claimed continuity. It issued an instruction. Find the ledger. To the water.

Her boot tapped the cold-drive's metal like a metronome. She could have burned it, fed it to the clinic's bio-incinerator and watched the data atoms scatter. She could have reported the error and let the State's arms shorten her life quietly. Instead she left the bar with the drive warm in her palm and a song she didn't know caught in her mouth. Find the ledger.

The night on the ring smelled of coolant and burnt citrus. She walked to the port where the river-trams docked — a thin line of water recycled from the nearby condensers, held in gutters and canals that the city called aqueducts. The water was never free; the State taxed it and the privateers set up pretenses of stewardship. But the people of the ring still thought of it as water the old way, the way folk think of an old lover: dangerous and essential.

Juno sat on the edge of the canal with her boots dangling over the polymer foam. Below, a tram blinked its arrival signals and glided past like a silver thought. Above, the ring's sky was a scatter of service drones and delivery lights, their paths catalogued by the city's air-traffic net. She opened the drive.

The fragment was tiny, smaller than a thumbnail pulse. The woman's face unfurled again, less a memory and more a breadcrumb: three frames of low-res video intertwined with audio metadata. The face looked directly into the camera, and for a moment Juno could smell the sodium lamps and the dust of a place that didn't exist anymore. The mouth turned and the woman — her mother, by every measure of bone and speech — spoke the phrase again and then held her hand up like someone making a promise.

"Ledger," she said, and then she managed the map like a child's gesture with a pointer: a trail of symbols Juno recognized not from the city's digital legends but from her childhood. The symbol for a ledger wasn't what the State used; it was older, a faded sigil that represented a logbook on paper, the kind of analog stubbornness that survived the Clearing in hidden trunks and under floorboards. She closed her hand around the tiny drive and a pressure like cold iron descended over her eyes.

"You're not meant to have that," a voice said behind her.

Juno's hands went to her jacket automatically; her fingernails found the knife she'd been issued when she first turned eighteen and joined the Remlex apprenticeship. She stood and turned to face the speaker. He was small, older than his station suggested, with the kind of face that made you trust it until you felt the teeth. The man wore a municipal jacket with a badge that said "Archivist Support Unit" and his eyes glittered like someone who'd read too many classified legends.

"You scanned me, didn't you?" he asked. "Most people hide their chips better."

"I didn't scan you," she said, which is to say she didn't offer a lie and she didn't offer the truth. It was a habit she had with strangers: give them just enough to make them leave.

He smiled. "You're a stitcher. We hear stories. Little ghosts attached to your tools. Too bad for you. That one you stole?" He lifted a hand as if to measure something small. "Not supposed to be lingering."

"Who told you—?"

"State archives don't like cognitive strayware. I'm not from the State," he said quickly. "I work with an independent reclamation collective. We do fieldwork. Recover items that got through the filters. Old things. Names. Songs. We help people reclaim histories that the Clearing took."

Juno watched him. He smelled faintly of oil and river algae, the raw tang of someone who had been down near the canals. There was a defiant, clumsy tenderness to his uniform, like something patched over a more dangerous history.

"Why would the State ban a face?" she asked. "Why a ledger?"

He shrugged. "Ledger isn't just a book. It's a concept. A ledger can be a list of names, a ledger can be a map of people, a ledger can be evidence. Evidence burns bridges. The Clearing burned things for a reason: it made history tidy. If you've got a ledger, you've got the messy truth."

Juno thought of her mother's face in the extraction window, the way her mouth had made shapes that belonged to a different grammar of life. You could pretend those lives had been erased and therefore safe. But the ledger seemed like a stubborn geography, a map that refused the erasure.

"You're a stitcher," the archivist said. "You have access. You remember things other people don't. You have an imprint on you, one that means... useful things to us."

"Useful for what?" Juno asked.

He didn't answer with words. Instead he reached into his jacket and produced a small rectangle of card. On it was printed in faded ink a coordinate, a symbol of a wave, and a short line: To the water.

The same phrase. The same symbol.

He watched her with a look that was equal parts hope and caution. "You can help," he said. "Or you can go on erasing things forever and never know what it is they wanted you to find."

Juno had always thought she worked to keep people comfortable in their own blanks: a little fewer pains, a little fewer haunting regrets. She had never considered that some blanks were doors.

She slipped the drive back into her boot and felt the clammy metal press into the tendon above her ankle. The city's light washed over them both and the canal's water shimmered. There were a hundred possible futures stacked between the ring and the water, small and sharp as fishhooks. She could hand the drive to the archival man and let him take it into the sewers of legend. She could burn it and phone Reza and let the State pass judgment. She could go home and tuck the thing under her mattress and pretend the voice had been a glitch.

"Find the ledger," she muttered, the words in her mouth a hinge. She toyed with the idea of going back to the clinic and erasing the day from her memory, a clean solution that would make the hands on the scar stop aching. But when she looked at the archivist he did not seem like a threat. He seemed like the first person in a long time who had offered her a map without asking for payment.

"If the ledger is real," she said, and the sentence tasted like betrayal, "then the water isn't where the State looks."

The archivist's eyes softened. "No," he said. "They don't look there. They don't like water that remembers."

Then his face changed to something more urgent. "You should go home," he said. "Get your things. They watch stitchers. If the State notices loss in the logs they'll come down with auditors. They won't be gentle."

Auditors were worse than jail. Auditors were re-sculptors who specialized in making people forget. They trimmed memory like farmers prune orchards — systematically, until the tree no longer bore fruit.

"How long have you had this?" he asked.

"Minutes," she said, which was both true and a lie.

He nodded like that explained a lot. He tightened the municipal jacket around his shoulders. "Then go. And take the ledger with you."

"Not what it is," she said, looking down at her hands.

"Names," he corrected. "Places. Proof. The kind of truth people die to hide."

Juno left the bar with the archivist at her elbow and the city blinking around them like a living instrument. The canal's water hissed under the polymer reeds. The drive in her boot was heavy with possibility. She thought of her mother's face, the sodium lamps, the braid across the shoulder, and felt a small, furious thing unsnap in her chest: the want to know.

They moved through the ring toward her unit. The archivist's steps were steady. He did not try to read her mind. He left the silence between them intact, like a space they could both pay attention to later.

Behind them, somewhere in the city, a municipal sensor registered an anomaly: a small unauthorized read on a Class Four extraction pattern. It blinked once and then sent a whisper into the net.

For now, it was only a whisper. But even whispers have ears.

Juno looked down at the drive again, feeling the weight of a thousand erased summers. Her hands opened as if to hold the ledger the way her mother once held summer weather. The ring's city hummed around them, and the canal moved in its constant remembering.

Outside, the planet turned slowly, and in the space between one night and the next, a story that had been shelved in the Clearing sighed and shifted like a body waking up.

Chapter One

The city had learned to forget long before I was born. It did not do it by accident. Forgetting had been engineered, codified into law and silicon—an algorithm called the Sieve that skimmed the city's attention like a hand across a blackboard, erasing tremor and grief until the walls stopped humming with ghosts. They sold forgetting the way other people sold hot bread or clean water: at booths under neon canopies, in packets the size of fingernails, passed from one life to another like contraband sugar. Forgetting made Palimpsest prosperous. Forgetting kept the towers tidy and the clocks polite.

People called it mercy. The Memory Authority called it civic hygiene. The rest of us—reclaimers, divers, the kind who could read the grain of an erased thing—called it theft.

My name is Lira Voss. On paper I was a petty technician assigned to municipal memory maintenance: a bureaucratic title, a thin credit line, an implanted badge that made the doors open and the Sieve's cursors skip over my name. In practice I was a reclaimer. I was one of the handful of people willing to go into the places the Sieve had smoothed and try to scrape something salvageable from the underlying pattern. People like me were tolerated until we were not. We were the city's stitches; when the fabric tore we were called in and told to make it tidy again. That was the easy part.

The hard part came when the thing you pulled up remembered you back.

I was in the Reclaim Market that morning—the lower arch of Gate Thirteen, where the vendors set up booths of memory-ore in trays and the air smelled of ozone and burnt citrus from the brain-frying pans. Stalls sold first kisses, exam passes, baseball games from a thousand suburbs, and weekends that had never actually existed. People traded in nostalgia like credit. At the far end of the market, under a stall's blue tarp, a woman with three copper scars across her throat handed me a slate the size of her palm. The slate thrummed with a low, liquid sound that made the hairs along my forearm stand up.

"You sure?" she asked. Her voice had the dry, clipped cadence of someone whose in-situ memories had been trimmed once too often.

"I get paid either way," I said. The slate was warm. The hum fit under my teeth.

She blinked, and for a second her eyes looked like unguarded sockets. "They say this one bites," she said. "Child's mind. Cleaned wrong. Or not at all. Authority paid me a stupid sum to get rid of it."

"Not Authority work?" I asked. The Memory Authority did not like loose ends.

"They didn't ask for a purge license," she said. "They just told me to get it out of the market. Said the buyer would die if it stayed. Said—" She lowered her voice in a way people do when the city means more than the market does. "—Said the child remembered the day before the Cleanse. Said it remembered a sky we don't have."

Of course they had the sky. Everybody knew what sky meant: a canopy of even light and measured weather, produced and regulated by municipal climate rigs. It was safer that way. There were old songs about wild weather, storms that bent glass and took roofs, but songs could be filed away in arch-libraries and nobody had to live with them. The idea that a child's memory might preserve something different—something messy, local, organic—made my mouth taste like pennies.

"How much?" I asked.

She named a number that would set me up with passable parts and a month of quiet credits. I took it.

I work with tools that can coax a memory open as a diver pries a pearl from a muscle. There are the soft things—the empathic draws and lull rhythms that let the mind relax and reveal its shape—and the hard things—the surgical pluckers, the splice-needles, the hydroscopes you stick into a neuronal lattice to feel for seams. I had a hand that could slide between the Sieve's threads without leaving a snag, a knack for listening to the particular cough a memory makes when it's lying. People paid me for that—quiet skills, a ledger full of other people's ghosts.

Back at my little room under the greenhouse of Circuit Three I set up the slate on the table. The hum pulsed like a living thing against the old wood. I fed it the basic coax: a slow loop of synthetic lullabies, a small token of scent—sea salt, because old childish memories like obvious anchors—and the vignette began to unspool.

At first it was a wash of color. Then a child's voice, thin as the paper it was written on, said my name.

"Lira," it said—my name, which I had never shared with any memory but my own, spoken with the flat certainty of someone who had always known. I stopped breathing. The slate kept humming.

I had worked long enough to know the tricks the Authority used to bait reclaimers. They used names sometimes, grafting familiar syllables into dead vignettes to see if you would take the trap. You memorize a face, go to a pre-arranged slot, and Discovery teams are waiting. But this voice didn't sound like a lure. It sounded like a bell that had been rung the same way for years.

The child's memory didn't open like a book. It opened like a place. I fell into an orchard of light that had the wrong geometry: trees with braided trunks and leaves that made the air taste like metal, a horizon that bent, not flat but curved, as if the sky itself had been stitched into a pocket and given volume. Under that sky there was water that moved like a living mirror, and something—an object, a person—humming at the edge of the child's perception.

"Don't leave it," the voice said. There was a name now, a syllable that was nothing I recognized and everything my ribs wanted. The memory had the texture of rain. It had the smell of a house that had not been sanctioned.

I slid my fingers into the memory to map it. They met resistance—threads tugged at the edges, not hostile, but shagged with a kind of determination. This memory didn't want to be peeled open. It wanted to stay whole. It wanted to keep what it had. There was something inside it like a small, bright seed that pulsed with its own weather.

I pulled a sample. It was a sequence of coordinates more complex than municipal grid math, overlaid with an image: a place where the city's wall met something that wasn't city at all. The slate projected the pattern into my optic overlay and for a second I saw a place I had never been: a shore of glass-black rock, a broken machine like a rib cage reaching into foam, and above it a ribbon of sky so clear and wrong I felt like a boy who had found his father's violin after it had been hidden away forever.

"Remember the sky," the child said.

When I came back out of the memory the room was bright and mundane and the humidity sensor blinked to life. My hands were wet with someone else's ocean. The slate sat on the table, its hum diffused. I should have wiped it, catalogued the fragment, labeled it authority or salvage and walked away with my payment. Instead I did a thing I hadn't done in five years. I pressed the sequence into the flesh behind my left ear, where a small patch of skin had thinned from a childhood mark, and let its signal nurse against my nervous system.

It burned for an instant—like a little star uncoiling under my skin—and then there was a new memory: the feel of sand underfoot, but not sand I had touched, not the municipal grit from palimpsest maintenance. It was real—bristling, pulling at the calluses of my toes—and the smell of wind that had not been measured jumped into my skull and refused to leave.

The door chimed at the stairwell. The sound of formal keys is not a little thing in Palimpsest; it carries a legal pitch. I had maybe fifteen heartbeats to decide whether to burn the slate and throw the child away, or pocket it and smuggle memory into my veins. Fifteen heartbeats that were all the city's quiet tragedies stitched together.

Before I could choose the stairwell door folded open and four Authority uniforms slid down into my corridor like the blades of a knife. They smelled like sterility and new leather. The lead officer glanced at the slate on my table and did not bother with words. His visor displayed a single line: WATCH-ORDER: LIRA VOSS—UNAUTHORIZED MEMORY INTEGRATION.

Hands moved the way hands always do when authority meets evidence: deliberate, careful, the choreography of people used to breaking things they would later claim to mend. The officer's gaze flicked to the back of my neck, and I felt the heat there, the private flare of the sky that had not supposed to be mine. He smiled in the professional way of men who believe their smiles qualify as condolences.

"You have something that doesn't belong to you," he said. He could have been saying it to a shopkeeper about a knife. He could have been saying it to a child about a lost toy. He stepped forward like a judge.

The child memory inside my head pushed back. It was not frightened. It wasn't petulant. It articulated like someone who had been given the truth and kept it in a tongue of its own.

"Don't let them forget," it said into the space I shared with it.

For a moment the corridor was two things at once: the sterile sheet-metal of Authority and the fruit-scented horizon of the child's recollection. I could keep my hands empty and let them take me through court and erase me and file my name against misbehavior, and the child would be fed to filters that would smooth it into nothing. Or I could do the stupidest, most dangerous thing any reclaimer ever does: I could run.

The lead officer moved closer, and the badge over his heart blinked. "You can help us," he said. "You can tell us how the slate found its way to the market. You can tell us where the child's memory came from."

There are lies you can say that make a body heavier; there are truths that make it light. I had chosen secrecy for half my adult life. I had kept other people's lost things in boxes under the heater and called them artifacts. I had taught myself to keep my mouth full of reasons that sounded like morality.

I stepped back until my heel hit the edge of the table, and I made my choice.

"You want the truth?" I said. I tried to keep my voice even. My hand slipped to the blade tucked under my jacket—illegal, but it could buy me an extra minute. "Then you've already come too late."

The officer's smile hardened. He raised his hand. Behind his visor I could see the soft white glow of a city archive sensor aligning itself to my skull. It would read the truth like a map, and once the Authority had a map, they never folded it to fit anyone's hands.

The child's voice hummed against the inside of my head. It didn't plead. It didn't bargain. It just said, as if announcing something obvious, "The sky remembers. If you read it, you will not be the same."

The officer's hand lowered. So did mine. The blade stayed tensed in my palm.

Outside, through the little porthole of my window, the towers of Palimpsest marched toward the horizon in their precise, municipal rows. Their climate rig balloons blinked with the measured light of a city that had decided what could be allowed to exist. For a flaring second I could see the curve of the older world beneath their careful lighting, a scar of something the Sieve had tried to smooth. The child's memory folded itself into the space behind my ear like a living thing settling into an unmade nest.

The officer took me by the shoulder with an almost-roughness that was too practiced. "You will come with us," he said. "You will explain. You will return the slate."

I looked at him. I looked at my palm. I thought of the shore, of the rib-like machine, of the sky so wrong it demanded to be named. I thought of the little voice that had spoken my name.

"No," I said.

Nobody expected a reclaimer to run. They expected us to be measured, to accept erasure as a kind of civic hygiene. Running made you a footnote in urban myth or a hazard, depending on whether you were ever caught.

I stepped away from the table. The child's memory in my skull folded the map into my blood. When the officer made to stop me, I moved with a speed I hadn't known I had and the corridor became a place of scramble and shouts. The slate slipped off the table and hit the floor. The hum went out like a held breath.

There are rules for running in Palimpsest. Don't go up. Don't go to the river. Don't try to cross the wall that separates the city from the old constructions. Authorities expect you to be frightened and to run like the sheep the civic essays say you are. They don't expect us to run because we want to remember.

The officer reached for my wrist. The child's voice filled the space between us.

"Don't let them forget the sky," it said, and when I hauled myself past his grip the words were a small, hard thing in my throat. I looked back to see him realize, the way men do in slow moments, that the thing he had come to collect would not be chained again by neat procedure.

We had not been designed to hold the past against the city's will. We had been designed, perhaps, to file it and forget. I had just stolen the future's right to a sky.

They would come for me in an hour. In a week the Authority would flood every market with orders and reasons and the city's tidy conversations would reassert themselves. But in my chest, under the new memory and the old hunger, a pulse had started. It was a compass needle, tiny and stubborn.

They had given the city a capacity to forget. I had found something that refused to be forgotten.

I ran.

On the day the city forgot my sister, the rain tasted of old photographs.

Not the metallic tang people pretend to taste—what those kitschy weather programs call "ozone," as if they could name the world back into wonder—but the dry, papery grit you find between the pages of a book someone keeps for the wrong reasons. I knew that taste because I had been living within other people's recollections for ten years; my palate had been trained to parse the residue of memory like a sommelier parsing notes. We were called memory editors, though the company called us Preservation Specialists and the city called us indispensable. The municipal servers called us a tax write-off.

Mnemosyne was a tower that rose like a cut tooth from the old riverbank, all faceted glass and matte chrome. It broadcast the Stream—the constant curated flow of shared moments that underwrote civic trust—and in its hollow heart it held the Vault, where the city's inconvenient truths went to be rewritten or buried.
