That was my floor: nineteen, the gray slab between creative and compliance. We trimmed, smoothed, excised. We took the jagged edges of grief and made them neat. We took rage and put a soft seam down the middle so people could live on without remembering why they had been angry in the first place.

You could live in a city like that and tell yourself you were helping. You could tell yourself you were saving people from the way a bad memory can calcify into a life. You could go home and sleep and not think about how easy it is to be wrong.

I was late the morning the clip arrived because I had tried to outrun a memory.

Lira had been gone seven years. The disappearance didn't have a neat timestamp because the Stream eats details, but I kept my own fragments secret in the locked place beneath my skull where the company could not reach. Everyone's neural profiles had a routine: open, verify, encode. Most people liked being easy to read. Lira never liked being catalogued. She told me once, years before she vanished, that there were whole kinds of personhood that refused to be archived. "The last thing we should do is put ourselves into boxes," she said, and she tightened her fingers around the little brass gear she wore on a chain. She called it her compass. I think she thought the compass could find directions the maps had lost.

I had that chain on the shelf by the sink—a superstition—and every now and then I’d take it down and turn it between my fingers just to remind myself that people sometimes disappear without stacking up neat dossiers. I never asked Mnemosyne for the official files on Lira. There was a directive, a legal block, and a lot of persuasive corporate language about privacy and protection. I assumed she had grown tired of the city. I tried to be fine with that.

The clip landed in my queue like a paper plane folded through the sky.

It was untagged. No creator, no timestamp, no metadata. The file name was a single character: 0. The system threw it up on my console with a little warning chevron and the polite, corporate question you get when a door opens at night: Are you sure you want to proceed?

I told the system yes because I didn't want to hear the polite question. When a memory plays in an editor's room, sound is muted and visual unprocessed until you authorize the neural mesh to map the electrical signature. We don't smell or taste in the room because those senses complicate the feed. We are trained to be clinical.

The image hit me like a boot in a chest.

A hallway I recognized from holiday postcards: the old underpass by Dock Five, the murals of sea creatures painted by people who were young before smartphones. The light in the clip wasn't the city's even wash. It was the narrow, angled light of a late sun. There were two figures—a child sitting cross-legged on the concrete, holding a tin airplane, and a woman with her hair in a looped knot, who stooped and pressed something into the child's palm. The child’s face was tucked under the rim of a cap. The woman's face was turned. For a beat I thought I would not know her, that grief had dressed the face into fiction. Then the woman turned fully.

She had my mouth. She had Lira's stubborn chin.

My hands started to itch, the old nervous behavior I had suppressed with hands-free protocols. The studio's hum shrank into the hum in my ears. The classifier tagged the clip as anomalous; its predictive models couldn't lane it into a present category. The trust guard triaged it away from the Stream, threw a temporary bubble of quarantine around it. The console asked the polite questions again.

Who authorized upload?

No one, said the log.

Who owns the file?

No owner.

The feed smudged. The child in the clip looked up. He—or she—was not a child I knew. And yet the voice that spoke when the woman said, Keep your left hand empty when they come, was Lira's voice in my bones. I had heard that phrase in a dream years before. I had said it to myself in the bathroom mirror like an incantation, testing whether it fit that void where the files had been wiped.

"Patch the location retro," I said into the room because procedure demanded it. See if there's an exfil. Find out where it came from and when. Mnemosyne's job was to trace, to sanitize, to make sure that anything that might destabilize the Stream never touched public perception.

The system told me it could not trace.

I tried to play the clip again—slow, single-frame—watching the woman's fingers close around the child's hand. The camera shift wasn't consistent with consumer devices. This was a recorder designed to be invisible, or clandestine. There was something else in the frame, too, at the periphery: a flash of brass like a gear catching light. I did not need the system to tell me what that meant. I felt it fill the room like cold glass.

I pocketed the reflex that wanted to call security. The City Security Protocols were a separate branch. They had a habit of sealing things up. I had learned, painfully, that some things you ask Security to look into never come back the same.

"Are you okay, Juno?" Mara from compliance was at my shoulder. She had been with Mnemosyne since the first public streams went live. Mara's eyes lived on thin film displays; she always wore extra memory—like jewelry—so she could whisper corrections to the feed with a blink.

"I'm fine," I said.

"You're sweating."

I shouldn't have been. I wasn't allowed to be private at the console: the edit timestamp, my respiratory rate, the mic data—everything was logged. So I lied, because sometimes lying was the only small act of rebellion left to us.

"I ran a small patch to cohere the audio," I said, and watched Mara's eyebrows flatten. "There's a line at the end. It might be an instruction."

We had long since learned that instructions embedded in private feeds were the most dangerous thing you could find. To be told by a memory how to act, especially when the actor's identity was known to you, that was an invitation—if not to action, then at least to the risk of knowledge. Mnemosyne had lived long enough to learn that knowledge could corrupt systems.

"Put it back in quarantine," Mara said.

"No," I said. Saying no was a more dangerous act than anything else in the building. People treated it like a weather event. You said no and the building rearranged itself around your refusal.

"We have protocol," she said.

"We also have the clause about employees accessing personal files," I said. Lira's legal block was still on my local, but not the corporate vault. I had a tiny backdoor, the sort of thing people with long memories accumulate. It meant nothing to anyone but me. "I want to run the clip through my personal filter."

Mara looked at me the way people look at someone deciding to stand on a cliff. "You don't want to do that."

I wanted to tell her a hundred things at once: that I had always wondered why Lira's chain had been taken as evidence and never catalogued; that the files about her were blanked out of the Stream the same week the city's water pipeline revisions went through; that there were noises in my dreams—gears clicking, like the compass—when I was trying to sleep. I wanted to tell Mara I had kept the compass, that the brass gear had been in a bowl in my apartment and that some nights I would lay awake and feel as if the gear remembered more than I did. I wanted to tell her I had spent ten years making other people forget, and every redaction had taken a piece of my face with it until I did not recognize my reflection.

I said none of that. I said, "I have to be careful."

Mara let the issue be care. She left, and I clicked the authorization through my own key. You are allowed the one private safety edit, the policy said, the clause intended to keep employees from going completely feral under the constant gaze. It meant you could play your own memory one last time unaudited. It did not mean you could open anomalies that had no owner.

The clip played. My throat dried against the taste of old photographs. When the woman's hand released the child's, a small brass gear slid into view, catching the light. The camera focused on it. There was an inscription: an angular glyph I didn't recognize at first, and then it flexed in my chest like a muscle remembering the feel of cold iron.

It was the mark Lira had traced in the dust at the edge of our grandmother's attic when we were nine. She'd told me not to ask. She had called it a direction marker and then closed her palm over the dust and said Don't trust the maps if the maps are made to keep people in lanes. The memory had been soft, so soft my hands often reached for it in the dark.

The clip finished with a line I did not expect: the child's voice—thin, oddly robotized—said, "They are not taking what they want. They are taking what we will give."

Then a static, like a soft machine cough. And the image went black.

My system threw a soft error. Someone had attempted to overwrite the clip mid-archive. The trace showed a half-second of code the filters did not know how to route: an algorithm designed to excise itself from detection—clever, almost affectionate.

I had a detail: the gear, the glyph, the phrase. I had a memory of Lira's mouth forming a clause I had ached to remember. I had nothing else but that taste of photos and the way my chest contracted.

It would have been the end of it. I could have done the thing proper people do: close my console, press the little paper-brown button that eased the day back into its smooth lines, and step into lunch like nothing had happened.

Instead, because I had the kind of curiosity that had gotten me into trouble my entire life, I walked down to Dock Five.

Mnemosyne had more rooms than an old palace. People joked that the building contained more ghosts than the old riverfront combined. The Vault had layers of security, but docks were porous: you could always find someone unloading something, and people who unload also gossip. I carried my official badge, which let me pass through the security gates because the badge did not judge your motives only your clearance. I also carried a pocketknife and a handful of coins.

The underpass smelled like river and rust. Spray paint flowered across the concrete in the mural's place, bright things that declared in block letters: REMEMBER. A child had stuck a paper airplane in the seam of the mural. I picked it out. It was hollow inside, and in the hollow, folded like a secret, was a sliver of brass.

Not the chain, not the compass, but a splinter—half a gear the size of a coin. The same glyph was stamped into it, small as a sigh. My fingertips went numb. I wanted to laugh. I wanted to cry. The rain began again—soft, the sort that only shows up on the cameras a city like ours trusts—and the drops made small craters on the brass.

I could have gone to the police then. I could have put the gear in an evidence locker and let someone else make the call. Instead I smuggled it into my palm and walked back to the building, the brass pressuring the base of my fingers like a heartbeat.

Back at nineteen the fluorescent lights had an honest buzz. My console blinked the way it had when I left it. I set the gear on the desk like a sacrament. I felt exposed and ridiculous and true. The system registered the object as contamination; any random input was flagged as hazard. There were cameras in the ceiling that liked to declare your indecisions.

I could have run it through procedure: submit to analysis, have a chemical and metallurgical scan, and wait the long humane time until some analyst wrote an oblique memo about it. I did not do that either. Instead I plugged the gear into the private mesh.

It should not have worked. The device looked primitive, archaic: a cog with teeth and a stamped rune. It should not have sung at me, but the mesh has always been a listening thing, looking for patterns where human eyes saw junk. I thought the company calibrated me to be the one to resist whims. I was calibrated wrong.

The gear warmed like a human palm where it sat against the nanofiber plate. The room smelled of paper and ozone. For a second the hum in the ceiling and the hum in my veins matched pitch. I thought I would faint. Something in the mesh attached to the glyph and opened subtly, like a pair of eyes blinking against dust.

A scrape of sound: a child's voice again, distant, singing a tune I didn't know. My vision flared, but not from the clip. This was memory bleeding in a way I'd read about in case reviews—two memories wrong in the same room can couple like misaligned teeth. You get an emergent pattern. You get moments.

I heard Lira's laugh as a thread. I saw a series of frames that were not in the clip: Lira at the river, Lira burying the brass gear beneath a line of river stones so she could find it again. Lira handing the gear to a man with a face I did not know, their shoulders touching like two halves of something folded. Lira whispering, "Promise me you will always leave me free."

Then the flash that made the room go white: Lira turned and looked directly at me. Her eyes were not Lira's from memory or the clip; they were a different kind of seeing. She mouthed a word and the mesh translated it into warmth behind my ribs: Run.

Then the interface snapped down, like someone folding a curtain. I was left with the metal in my palm and the smell of rain and photos. My console chimed with a dozen protocol pings I had nowhere near authority to answer. Somebody had tried to dump an overload into my local logging buffer. A benign corporate flourish—the system's way of protecting itself—had moved surveillance into overdrive. The stairwell's cameras shifted vectors as if someone had taken offense at my thoughts.

I had, technically, committed a series of small crimes. I had, very probably, broken several company clauses and a municipal ordinance. The part of me trained in compliance wanted to sign right now and let the machine do its work.

The other part—the part that had kept Lira's compass in a bowl and listened for her voice in rain and had learned the taste of old photographs—stood up straight and stuffed the brass into my pocket.

You never put a compass back on the shelf after someone you love instructs you to run. You do the opposite. You take the direction you're given and you move.

I turned off my console. The lights hummed. The city streamed on, unknowingly clean. On my way past the door to the Vault, a custodial bot hummed. It looked at me with a sensor like an unblinking eye. I thought, briefly, of the child in the clip and the line about giving. We were a city that had learned to give its own past away. It was possible someone had taught us, piece by piece, to offer our histories as currency to the machines that would value them best.

Outside, the rain drew silver threads across the glass. People moved with umbrellas like small islands. The Stream above the promenade shifted into a new commercial: a family camping in simulation-sky, laughing in a pre-formed key. Text scrolled at the bottom: MEMORIES MADE SMOOTH.

I placed my hand against the wall of the tower and felt the building breathe in a manner peculiar to the long-lived. I had 0 on my personal file. No owner. No timestamp. A brass gear. A phrase I had whispered in the dark because I feared the sound of it like a prayer.

I walked into the rain tasting of old photographs and did not call Security. I walked instead toward the river where someone might be waiting with a map no one had seen in years. I walked because I had always promised myself—if ever anything from Lira returned—it would be returned to me by my own two hands.

You can spend your life excising other people's memories and still be unequipped for a memory that returns to claim you.

The water was high, and the underpass hummed with life. My left hand was empty when they came. My right hand, in my pocket, held the compass. I didn't know yet whether that would be salvation or indictment. I only knew that the city had started to forget, and that forgetting had teeth.

I kept walking.

The first thing I remembered was the taste of steel and an old song I couldn’t name. The second thing was that the song hurt.

The cryo pod opened on a soft hiss; cold fog clung to my lashes like breath. For a moment the world was a single bright point of light and then it blurred into hands—callused, blood-smudged hands—and a voice that was too patient for the pitch it used.

"Don't sit up," the voice said. "Not yet."

I did it anyway. Muscle remembered angles my head didn't. The ship—Pelican, the scratched stencil on the bulkhead told me that—smelled of ozone and fryer oil and the iron tang of old blood. Someone had left a pot of something black on the stove; it burned beneath a thin film of dust. A half-empty bottle rolled against my boot when I moved, making a sound like a tiny metronome. Light from a single viewport painted the deck in the sickly green of salvage yards: fluorescent, unforgiving, suspended between two suns and no rain to wash it.

"Name?" the voice asked.

My tongue felt thick; my mouth was an engine of questions I couldn't quite start. A tablet floated up on a magnetic rail: bio-profile, last deployment, a photograph of a younger me with hair cropped close and eyes that had been persuaded—by too many years and a thousand narrow choices—into certainty. My name was Ilya Kest, the tablet said, and my rank—Junior Reconmod—under it, crossed out by a line of red script.

"Memory wipe," the medic said. She held a vial between finger and thumb; it smelled like mint and hospital. Her right cheek was streaked with grease. This ship did not have room for both a clinic and pride.

"Why?" I asked. The word scraped out like a key that didn't fit.

"Because your last run kissed a core," she said. "You came back singing and we had to—" She waved a flat apology. "Safe for you, safe for everyone."

"Who authorized it?"

"No one's that professional aboard the Pelican," said the mechanic, who had been watching me from between a tangle of cables and the skeleton of a servo-arm. He was shorter than his roles suggested and wore a respirator like a talisman. "We did what we could. You woke up breathing."

That was something. Breath. The rest of me felt like borrowed machinery.

I swung my feet over the pod lip and stood on a deck that remembered too many repairs. A chart smeared across the bulkhead showed the margin where the civilized lanes thinned into the Grey—labeled on my own tablet earlier as "Fold-9." Beyond Fold-9 were derelict arrays, failed habitats, discarded machine-habitat caskets; the kind of things that paid well because they were dangerous, and because the risk came with old things that still held old secrets.

Pelican's crew—three too many for a salvage barge and one less than a funeral—clustered around the mess table. There was Marek, the mechanic, who had once been a deckhand on a grain scow and now patched servo-motors with prayers; Tamsin, the medic, part-surgeon and always-something-less-than-human, who had polished teeth from an old world; and a small, scarred synth named Locke with a chipped porcelain face that had been painted soft and hollow. Locke's voice broke into a laugh like glass tapping.

"You look like you swallowed a sun," he said.

I pressed a thumb to the inside of my wrist and felt for the mesh-bandes there, the little ports that read when the neural net hiccuped. They hummed faintly. The song in my chest tightened like a stuck fly.

"Brief me," I said. Brevity felt like an ally when logic fled.

Marek produced a holomap and projected it over the table. Between the stuttering stars and projected junk, a pale lattice shimmered: A structure-bone of something the Ancients had left behind. They called these ruins by many names. On the Pelican's map it had a single practical label: ARIADNE-7. "Sits in the old loop," Marek said. "We drifted across a beacon—bits of signal bouncing off the hull. Old-array tone. Could be nothing. Could be—" He stopped. The word didn't need finishing.

"Could be a gold core?" Locke supplied. The synth's voice had a tone that always worried between appetite and reverence. "Data-keys. Biofilings. A human signature."

My chest compressed until I felt I might cough up the fog itself. Human signatures were currency older than credits in the black. They were keys to places people had tried to shut—vaults where pre-Quiet labs stored the little things they thought would make immortality manageable: embryo tanks, seed-banks, live code fragments, and sometimes a thing called a 'keepspark'—a tiny neural core containing the fragmented consciousness of someone considered vital enough to ship forward, to keep, to trade.

"That extinguisher we're carrying isn't worth the lift," Tamsin said. "If it's a core, it'll have a guard. Ariadne's bells don't ring unless they want to."

"Then we'll be careful," I said. I felt absurd arranging plans with a muscle set that didn't know its own movement. Yet the plan settled edges down in me like an old map.

"There's more," Marek said. He tapped the lattice and the projection rippled, focusing on a cluster of glyphs that shivered against the array like minnows. "Signal tag keyed to a persona."

"Persona?" Tamsin frowned. "Like a public ID?"

"Like a signature," Marek said slowly. "ID-tagged to a Kest."

My skin went thin. The word made the song spike. Kest—my family name; small rural line, lost to the migrations in a decade they now sanitized. On the tablet my face stared back at me, and under the photograph, older, an emblem I had never seen: a stylized ring of light with a notch, branded in rust.

Marek's finger hovered over the pulse. "It isn't wrong; it's not recent." He scrolled. "A marker, old encryption. Looks like someone seeded something—left it behind with a tag only Kest-line access could open."

Locke's head cocked. "Wouldn't that mean...?"

"If it hasn't gone dead," I said. The thought hit me with the force of a remembered fall. Wiping my memory had been custom for scaldrun survivors whose neuro-cores hummed with forbidden contact. We erased to keep ourselves small, to keep the noise muffled. Someone—somewhere—had left a breadcrumb keyed to me.

"Or keyed to your prints," Marek said. "We can piggy-back. We can try."

Sometimes the technical term people used on the Fold, when they meant little and betrayed hope—they said "trying was easy." Trying, in the battered calculus of salvage, involved a vacuum suit, a salvage lift, a payment ledger, and the kind of courage that didn't know it should be fear. I found myself nodding, because nodding was something that sat behind all immediate decisions: machine memory drove action while brain worked the rest.

Pelican re-burned its primary drive for the first time in months. The engines sighed as if relieved to be useful. The viewport filled with the skein of debris fields, their ragged edges combed with flares from distant impacts. Space here had the intimate cruelty of a rusted shipyard. Bits of habitat glass drifted like snow.

We set a course.

Approach to Ariadne-7 was slow and ceremonial. My hands remembered the motions of docking and line-throw like a liturgy. I stood at the loading bay with a suit clipped at my hip that smelled of scalded rubber and solder. Tamsin slotted a thin strip into the port at my neck and the feel of it was like being read aloud.

"Are you sure?" she said. She did not use my name. I understood why. Names made it real.

"No," I said, because if you were honest in the Fold you always tried that. "But I'm present."

The salvage harness hummed, a familiar vibration that sat in the bones and spoke a language of systems and tolerances. Tamsin's fingers brushed mine. "Don't let the old things sing to you, Ilya," she said, softer this time. "Half the crews we've seen who've come back don't know which worries were real. And the other half don't know when they stop."

Her last words were a reprimand and a promise.

The hatch sealed behind us. Pelican's airlock spat us into the white noise between structures. Ariadne's skin was scored like an old ship's hull, pitted with the micro-impacts of a thousand small collisions. The beacon tugged us in with an insistence that felt less like a call and more like a remembered whisper. As our tether feed locked, my mesh-band lit at my wrist with a pulse of code that made my teeth ache.

We cut a panel with a buzzing saw and the air inside the wreck came alive—dry and old like a book left in sun. The corridor was a cathedral of frost; temperature regulators long dead had left breath in the air that belonged to other decades. I walked with the ghost of a dozen memories underfoot. My steps made shadows like hands.

"Signal's stronger," Marek murmured. "Close."

A door that shouldn't have opened for any of us slid sideways with the effortless smoothness of a thing not meant to be idle. Inside was a room no lithographer would market as salvage: clean lines, surfaces that remembered detail, and in the center of the floor a seating that might have been a cradle and might have been a throne. At the base of it, a cube of glass hummed and within the glass there was something no redeemable salvage would object to preserving: a small sleeping form.

They were small enough to fit in an adult's arms. The body inside the cube had the pellucid, sickly quality of cryo, but when the hatch's light went across a face it had the sharpness of living bone. Dark hair in a ragged clump. Closed eyelids fret with a will to open. Around the cube looped a ribbon of metal whose etchings matched the emblem I had seen in my tablet photo. The ring with the notch. Kest. My lungs caved like a man in cold water.

"That's—" Marek started.

"That's a child," Tamsin said. Her voice had a tremor in it I couldn't make sense of.

The pediatric cryo was old, a model the historians called 'pre-Quiet.' My fingers went to my neck, where a token hung on a chain. I had not known why I had kept it through whatever had erased me; relics tend to find their way into hands that need an anchor. The token was stamped with the notch-ring. My thumb had shaped it until it fit like a palm.

The cube's indicator flared, then a single line of script flowed across the glass. Too old for the Pelican's oldest drives but simple enough for a farmer on the old coasts to read: ACCESS: KEST-LINE.

My chest moved with a speed my lungs did not expect. The old song returned as a loop in my head; it carried no words I could find, only a cadence of waiting. The mesh band at my wrist registered bio-authenticity. It clicked. Systems in the room sighed and in the hum of ancient power a voice—digitized and softened by decades—spoke.

"Welcome home, Ilya Kest."

It wasn't the child's voice. It was the architecture's, the voice of the ruin. But the words folded like a key and something inside me shifted, like a lock turning that I had thought irreparable. A blot of memory—sharp as the cut of a saw—pricked the skin behind my eyes: a beach with black glass, a promise spoken to hands that fit tiny as seeds. A lullaby I didn't know the words of but that had been used to measure time.

I could have stepped back. I could have closed my eyes and let the warning Tamsin had given me keep me safe aboard the Pelican. Instead I kept moving forward. The team followed like a procession.

The child stirred. Eyelids cracked open to reveal irises like wet stone. The cry, when it came, was not a newborn's bullish wail but a small, practiced sound that had been stored and preserved. Its lips formed a syllable that had been washed in a hundred different seas and heard as different names.

"Mama," the voice said.

It was a single word, old as a lie and new as an engine. For a second the world kept only that syllable and the way it lodged inside my chest like a splinter.

I did not know whether the person behind the word had meant me. I did not know if my name belonged in the child's mouth. But the ruin had said it, and the token at my neck had worn the same notch and my tablet had shown the same face from a decade before inviting questions I had not asked.

"Strap in," Marek said, though he was as unsure as I was. "We don't take it out yet. There could be more—contingencies. Protocol—"

There would be, because there always are. There would be nodes that registered my presence and remembered who I had been and who I might become again; there would be shadowed markets that would take the child's core as tribute and sell it to the highest ghost; there would be a Quiet law that told us that some things, once opened, were not meant to be.

Some decisions were made by engines that spat sparks and some by small hands that fit inside the palm and made everything else shrink to a point. I picked the child up. Cryo gel cold around my palms. The token lay heavy at my throat, a notch aligning with a ring in the child's mouth that fell like a completion of a circle.

Locke's voice squeaked. "You're sure this is—"

I looked down. The child's eyes were like the old song made visible. I found my name on my tongue and let it fall out like an anchor.

"If it's not mine," I said, more to myself than anyone else, "we'll make it ours."

The ruin hummed. Somewhere in the lattice of Ariadne a panel slid closed as if it had been waiting for an answer. The beacon's pulse on our deck flared, then steadied into a rhythm that matched the beating of my own heart. The token warmed against my skin.

We had come to salvage a thing and, by an accident of tags and old loyalties, we had been found to be the ones who would carry it forward. Outside, the Fold ate the trailing tail of our wake and the stars watched without blinking. Inside, a child blinked again and the sound of their breath synchronized with a song I didn't remember learning.

"Record it," Marek said softly. "For the ledger. For whoever comes after."

Locke flicked his wrist. A red dot floated over the recording panel. We were living a moment that the ledger would not understand. It would try, in numbers and timestamps and credits. Its arithmetic would be blunt and inaccurate.

I strapped the child against my chest. Old lullabies are not always about comfort; they are also calculations, measures of debt. The song in my head broke into a sharper pattern. Somewhere, out in the architecture, something that had been waiting for me woke up and recognized the sound of my heartbeat.

"Home," the child said again, and this time the syllable fell like an invitation.

I wanted to tell them no, that home was a line on a map and a ledger entry and a bed with a mattress so thin it was a plan. But the token at my throat compressed like a memory finding room.

"We'll find out what that means," I said. The rest of the world held its breath at my words. The Pelican hummed under us like a patient thing.

The ruin's voice spoke again, the intonation full of old power. "Access granted. Initiating retrieval protocol: Kest-Line."

Outside, the Fold shifted, and a storm of light began to build at the edges of the lattice. The ship's sensors flared and a single, clean transmission reached the Pelican's comms, a ping like a bird in the quiet of an old room. Whoever had sent it had the kind of patience that made empires. The message was simple; the language was older than the credits that hummed in the ship's belly.

WE KEPT OUR PROMISE, it said, in a hand that might have been kind or might have been a chain. FOLLOW.

I looked down at the child and felt the song in my chest become a map. A map that could either lead me home or lead home to me as something else entirely.

There are moments when the world sets before you two doors and calls the one you pick brave. I had time only for the sound of the child's breathing and the cold pad of their small hand pressed against my collarbone. The token was warm. The beacon pulsed. The ship needed a decision.

"Set course," I said. Not brave. Not courageous. Just a sentence for existing in the present tense.

Locke smiled, porcelain cracking by a hair. "Then let's go find whatever 'home' is."

Some promises are old enough to wear rings. Some are dangerous enough to call themselves home. We crossed the threshold and left the ruin's light behind like a compass point. The Fold closed in around our wake, and between the stars something shifted its weight as if someone had moved an old thing a half inch and everything recalibrated.

The song sharpened into a single phrase and then a hole opened in the map that had never been there before. I put the child's head against my chest and listened to my own pulse. The name at my throat felt like a hinge.

If the past wanted me back, it had sent a child in a box with my family mark and an architecture's voice. If the past wanted a reckoning, it had chosen the Pelican's crew to carry its first step. Whatever waited beyond the Fold would not let us be small.

I tightened the straps. We pushed. The engines burned. The ship answered, and in the seam between one beat and the next the world shifted, and a voice older than law said very plainly, for the first time since I could not remember when: "Welcome home, Ilya Kest."

I wanted to believe it meant only a place. The child in my arms wanted me to believe it meant a person. Outside, the Fold waited like a mouth.

We crossed the threshold.

The sound woke Mira before her eyes did.

It wasn't the alarm on her wrist—the soft, sequence-clocked ping that marked the beginning of her shift at the Harmonics — it was lower, older, threaded through the city like a piano string someone had forgotten to mute. It was a note that lived between other notes, something the city's public chorus should not have been singing. It hung in the air of her small flat, braided through the machine-scent and the remainders of last night's stew, and when Mira reached up her hand brushed the glass and the rippled dreamline above the district shivered as if in answer.

She sat up, the blanket falling away, and for a beat she let herself pretend it was a dream. The world had taught her not to trust those. You could lose a person to a dream—lose them to a drift and never know whether they had walked out into a different fold of the lattice or simply never returned. Her brother had been one of the lucky ones: they found his body on the riverbank, two years gone when they finally cut the line on the old transmitter on his roof. Luck was how the city defined survival; it was a currency Mira could not afford.

She swung her legs over the bed and flexed the joints of her foot. The city was still—too still. The municipal Dreamlines pulsed on a schedule that hummed under every step, a low frequency that kept people anchored to a shared narrative. People argued that those lines were what made civilization possible: the same bedrock myths, the same timed lullabies, the same curated dreams. Others called them chains. Whatever the name, no one lived without them.

Mira worked where the lines were knotted and mended. The Harmonics department was built of people who understood pitch and fixings, the ones the city sent up on maintenance cycles to stitch the weave when a node frayed. Her hands were the city’s seamstresses—except they used tools that could fracture minds if slipped. Most maintenance calls were routine: a microfracture here, a phase-shift there, a lazy overlap that made half a block hum in the wrong key. Routine, and yet never the same.

She tapped the panel beside her bed. The alarm acknowledged her with a soft biolume flare. On the display, the shift manifest sorted itself: Sector B6 night sweep, two nodes: Dovetail-7 and Anchor-3. She had been on the list for Dovetail-7 before the note. She frowned; the map's feed had a small red triangle blinking under Dovetail—an anomaly flagged by a neighbor's DreamLens. Invisible censorship scanned in real time, but a neighbor kept their lens on manual, on old instincts, and something had slipped past municipal filters.

Mira dressed quickly—pants with reinforced seams, a jacket with pockets used more for tools than belonging—fishing out the harness she had learned to prefer. She didn't bother with the little station near the building elevator; both public and private lifts in her block were set to maintenance lockdown until dawn. She took the stairs instead, a narrow spiral that opened onto the walkways above the tram artery. The city at two in the morning was a different thing: the neon ribbon of the transit line made a pale river below, the lattice threads folding overhead like strings of a harp, their glimmering threads crossing at intersections that hummed with soft municipal law.

At street level, people slept with the public lullaby tuned low; their DreamScreens were set to autoproduce for them, tiny theatres of branded memories and state-approved peace. From a distance they looked like islands of blue light. Up here, among the maintenance walkways, Mira could see the lines at their seams, the moment where a public dream became private reverie. It was thin work; you had to place your ear close and listen.

The note pulsed again, just once, and this time it was clearer. So clear it hurt.

It was a lullaby—old, the kind her grandmother used to hum in dialect long gone from the city's playlists. The lullaby had a fault in it, a missing bar that made the rest of the lines shudder; it reminded Mira of a language with half of its consonants removed. She hadn't heard it sung outside of the antique recordings before the Event, and it should not have existed in public memory. The municipal archives suppressed songs like that because they were linked to an experiment in communal dreaming gone wrong. People remembered too much or too little; they changed.

"You're late," Jonah said from the walkway. He was not late by clock—he gathered the team with the efficiency of an autopilot—but his breath came in small clouds that fogged the Fal-glass. His apprentice eyes were bright and raw. Jonah had been assigned to her this cycle; he was the kind of young man that asked questions out loud to strangers. She liked him for that.

"There's a flagged anomaly at Dovetail. But listen—" She closed her eyes and sent a quiet line into the nearest node. The Dreamlines hummed to her, not as data points but as texture. She could feel the threads as if her palms were blunted instruments: a steady bass of coordinated lullaby strings, a higher register of ambient advertising, the micro-sounds of private fantasies folded into the public chorus. And threaded just under the surface, the note, thin and metallic, like a child's spoon tapping a bowl.

Jonah cocked his head, then frowned. "That's not supposed to be there," he said.

"No." She was already starting the preflight check. Dovetail-7 sat at the corner of the prudence gardens and the old riverwalk. It was one of the city's earlier nodes, retrofitted with a reticulation mesh to keep it stable during tidal flows of thought. Mira loaded the maintenance kit—stitch-sutures, a resonant calibrator, a spool of doped filament—and clipped the harness at her hip. "We go in soft. Manual, no auto-inject. Something's been embedded."

"Embedded by who? The old kids?"

"The old kids don't sing lullabies anymore. They sing manifestos." Her voice was lighter than she felt. The Harmonics liked to pretend itself a science; sometimes that made the work sound like surgery and not like magic. "This is older than the War. We don't know how people got it back."

They moved out along the walkway. Below them, Dovetail-7 made a halo of sound that shimmered in the air and painted shadows on Mira's face. At the approach the note stabilized, came into color. She felt a weight in her chest, a small electric pressure that had nothing to do with fear and everything to do with recognition. Her hands went cold.

"That's—" Jonah started.

An old woman's voice answered on the wind, a whisper that seemed to come from the weave itself. "—hush now—"

Mira remembered the room from the recording—hazy film, a grandmother with too-large hands humming over a wooden cradle. The lullaby's missing bar was a place where a child's name should fit. Mira thought, stupidly, of her brother's small hands around her finger. She had been careful to keep the city at arm's length, but the city kept remembering for her.

They descended to the public space around Dovetail-7. The node was at the center of a small plaza, hollowed at the middle to allow the lines to converge and pulse without interference. Citizens rarely lingered there after curfew. Tonight, a couple of runaways slept beneath the soft wash of municipal lullabies, their faces lit by the same blue glow as the tram's underside. The municipal nodes were ringed with fencing, but the Harmonics had access codes that let them step inside without tripping the crowd-quality sensors.

Dovetail's access hatch sighed open. Mira stepped into the hollow and felt the note sharpen into a distinct sequence. It wasn't simply a lullaby; it had been folded into something else, a function layered beneath song: a pattern that caused a delay in the shared dream, a pause that could let a private memory slip between public frames. Whoever had put it there had wanted someone to remember something unsanctioned.

She set to work. Her calibrator hummed against her palm; she placed it on the edge of the node, feeling for the micro-resonances. The city's dreamlines were not magic so much as a complicated set of harmonics engineered to prevent that's-what-you-thought. The calibrator picklocked into the lattice and began to translate the note into a waveform she could test. The lullaby's missing bar was an insertion, a malicious bit, and as soon as the machine isolated it the plaza stuttered: the runaways twitched in their sleep, an advert cut off mid-frame, a street vendor down the line jerked as if remembering a dream he shouldn't have had.

"Careful," Jonah said. "That's a memory anchor. If you cut—"

She didn't answer. Cutting felt dangerous and necessary in the same way surgery might. If she didn't remove the insertion, the node would propagate it the way a cough propagates a virus. If she did remove it, she might unseat whatever had been buried there—someone's grief, someone's crime—into the open. The city preferred the buried.

Mira's hand trembled as she adjusted the filament's length. Her thumb was in the exact place it had been years ago when she had turned the same kind of wrench on the pump at her father's factory. She thought of the river, of washing machines and the sound of her brother singing off-key in the dark. She thought of not keeping secrets. Her breath became a metronome.

The profiler on her kit threw up an overlay. The insertion's origin trace was... strange. It was ancient code, pre-Net, threaded with a signature she couldn't quite place: an old family cipher, a personal watermark that most people used for trivial things—bread recipes, personal logs. This one was different. The watermark was a name.

Mira's mouth went dry.

The name matched none of the municipal registries. It should have been impossible to track. She ran it backward through the archive like a diver reading a tide table in reverse. The more she pushed the data, the more the city's surfaces looked inaccurate, as if the web of municipal memory had a damp spot in it. The water-logic of the lines pooled around the insertion and refused to return a straight readout.

"That's not a municipal sig," Jonah said in a whisper, the breath fogging the air between them. "That's personal."

Personal signatures were supposed to be private. Unless you left them attached to something public.

Mira made the cut. The resonant hum of the calibrator modulated, smoothing the lullaby's bar back into municipal frequency. For a second everything aligned. The runaways slept on, the street vendor's hands stilled on the cart, the advertising streams went back to puffing their prescribed joys. The city yawned the way a living thing will after being pricked.

Only the note remained.

Mira stepped back, suddenly hollowed. She had expected the lullaby to go away and for the plaza to resume its low, friendly uniform. Instead the air quivered, and a small, translucent image materialized above the node. It was the size and clarity of a child's polaroid: a face, smudged but alive. The image was not driven through municipal projection arrays. It had come out of the weave itself, like a bubble of memory that had been trapped and suddenly released.

It was a child's face, curls pinned back with a scrap of fabric. The eyes were old, too old for such a small face; they looked out of time. The child smiled, but behind the smile there was a shadow. Mira's breath hitched.

"Do you see it?" Jonah asked. His voice had an edge of something like a prayer.

Mira did see it. She saw a locket around the child's neck, a small metallic thing with engraving she could not make out. The locket seemed to pulse with the same low note she'd heard, and then—like a final hiccup of static—the image flickered, and for one stolen second the child's mouth moved.

"We remember," it mouthed. Then it dissolved into the lattice like mist.

Mira's hands fell from the calibrator. The tool chimed a clean note to indicate it was unburdened. Somewhere above them the Dreamlines harmonized. The plaza resumed the rhythm the city expected. A security bot glided past at the edge of the plaza, its sensors scanning for anomalies. It did not pause.

"You took the sig," Jonah said, as if accusing her.

"I didn't take anything. I cut the insertion." She could feel the taste of adrenaline in her mouth. "That face—"

"Wasn't really there," Jonah finished for her, but his voice carried a doubt that slid between his words. He had seen faces in the weave before; everyone had. The city scaffolded such illusions for the sake of nostalgia. The municipal playlists fed the populace curated memory to keep continuity. But those illusions were shallow, manufactured, and anonymous. This had been something else.

Mira's hand moved to the pocket where she kept a small, discarded thing: a child's badge from before the War, metallic and scratched at the edges. She had kept it because it had been hers once, not because it meant anything in the city's present. Her thumb brushed the insignia, then came away with a wad of lint. She had a sudden urge to know who the child had been. The urge felt like hunger.

"Report?" Jonah said finally.

Mira looked up at the sky. The dreamlines there had whole constellations—lullaby arcs and advertisement loops, the municipal safe dreams. A message flashed across them now, a simple system ping asking for a log of their intervention. She could make the municipal feed read as if everything had been routine. She could claim a routine calibration and be done with the paperwork.

She did not log it. Instead she sent a private ping to an archive address she knew by heart: an old hidden archive, something she'd been promised access to on a bet she had with her mother long ago. It was a stupid, brazen act that had more to do with a child's stubbornness than with professional procedure. Putting the anomaly into municipal hands would bury the face again; no one in the city would want to keep a memory that didn't fit.

The message left her hands in digital silence. The relay acknowledged with a single flicker, then went dark. Someone had read it.

A second later the plaza's ambient sound shifted. This was not municipal correction but a human voice folded very small. "Mira Thanh," it said.

The name landed like a pebble in a glass. Mira's stomach dropped. She had not put her name on the log. Only a few people still used full names in public. Her full name belonged to family records, to old grievances, to the kind of files you only accessed if you were trying to prove you had existed before the city began to write everyone into itself.

She turned to Jonah. His mouth was a thin line. He shook his head. "We didn't flag this," he said.

"No," Mira said. She felt small, reckless. The city's harmonics suddenly felt like a net rather than a cloak. "We didn't flag this. But someone else did."

They left Dovetail-7 the way they had come, the note now a memory in the city's bone. Outside, the morning light was a gray-washed thing that suggested dawn and asked people to rise. The lullaby receded into ordinary playlist fare. Travelers boarded trams and the city resumed its usual patina of half-consciousness.

Mira kept her hands in her pockets to stop them from trembling. She thought of the child's face and the locket, of the mouth that mouthed "We remember." She thought of the prewar lullabies, of her brother's twinned laugh, of the moment he had wandered and never quite come back. She had always known the Harmonics could open old wounds if they were careless. She had always told herself she would be careful.

Now she had an image and a name and an archive ping that had been read. Her actions had set something in motion. She could feel it like a current tugging at the hem of the city's dreamtime.

"You realize this isn't a routine job anymore," Jonah said quietly. "You sent that to the old archive."

"I didn't send the child's face to anyone," she said. "I didn't have to. It left on its own."

"Then someone is fishing," he said, and his hand went to the strap of his toolbag as if to make sure the calibrator was still there. "And if they're fishing for names…"

They both knew the implication. Fishing for names in the city's weave was one thing. Fishing for people was another.

Mira looked up at the lattice above the plaza. Threads crossed and recrossed like the bones of the city. The harmonics would adjust and bury the insertion again. People would sleep. The municipal queues would take the incident as a blip and file it under "anomaly." Corporations would log the metrics, and no one would sing that lullaby again.

Unless someone coaxed it back.

She had, in a cut that was supposed to be routine.

She had seen a child's face saying a thing no child should have to say to the city.

We remember.

The thought settled like a stone at the bottom of her chest. It filled her with a terrible and simple certainty: ghosts in the weave were not all dead things. Sometimes they were signals sent forward, small survival messages in a future that had tried to erase their past.

Mira tightened the harness around her waist and left the plaza by the maintenance ramp. There were forms to fill, reports the city would expect. She would write none of them as they instructed. Her badge would show a routine calibration. The city would close the file. But the thing in her hands—a single insertion, a child's image—had been set loose. It had the potential to spread like a rumor in a crowded room. It had the potential to start a chain.

On the walkway, the Dreamlines hummed clean and untroubled. Above them, the dawn threaded its first shard of light through the lattice. Mira stepped into the morning, feeling the secret like a pressure in her throat, tasting the iron of everything she had not yet done.

She walked toward the old river, toward the place where the lines were thinnest and where memory had once overflowed into water. The city's harmonics would come for the log eventually; people who read the archives would send messages she couldn't anticipate. She had a name in her head and a child's mouth on the edge of impossible things. She had a small, private war to begin.

We remember, the child's mouth had said.

Mira whispered back to the empty sky, because no other answer occurred to her. "So do I."

They called the place the Falling City because once it had fallen. Once it had been a city — glass towers, gardens braided through its ribs, a cathedral that had learned to reflect the star like a jewel. They had made it fall deliberately, an act of salvage and penance both: a habitat that wouldn't wake again was pushed into the planet that had birthed it, dressed itself in reentry fire, and promised its bones back to the world below. The rest of the system kept the myth alive; children played with models of its skyline, drunkers swore they could feel its pull on the tides. To Mara Kestrel, who had dived three hundred meters through the debris ring and lived to tell the tale, the Falling City was only a scatter of metal and memory.

Metal and memory were profitable.

The field was a slow machine of collisions and quiet radiation. Thickness of cloudlets would compress and swell with microimpacts until they resembled the weather in a glass jar. Mara watched the shrapnel drift past — a dented water tank, a half-melted escalator, a wing flayed open with ribbon wiring like exposed veins — and kept her suit's cutter from snagging. Her breath in the helmet was a metronome. Around her the lights of distant salvage ships blinked like faint, patient eyes.

"Grid three," Jalen said over the comm. His voice came from behind the hull of the Fagin, a cubic salvage tug that smelled of oil and coffee and old smoke. "You're clear to approach the module. I have the grappler on standby."

"Copy," Mara answered. Her voice sounded thin in the visor, too high for the forty-year-old woman who had been telling herself she would stop chasing ghosts. The suit's thrusters nudged her forward; metal murmured beneath gloved fingers as she worked a caliper clamp onto a fractal of twisted alloy. Her gloves smelled like burnt copper. Everything smelled like other people's decisions.

The module was mostly intact: a cylinder the color of river stones, etched with a childlike bloom of star-petals in faded lacquer. Someone had painted a name along one seam in a shaky hand. SAFFI. The letters had been scratched into the lacquer afterwards — a desperate, patient addition. The Fagin's scanners had flagged it as late-generation polymer, and its tag made out as civilian registration. There were other things to take before anyone noticed this, but Mara had a soft tooth for names.

She eased the clamp on and felt the soft give under the alloy, like putting fingers to a sleeping person's throat. Inside, packed against impact foam, was a small sphere the size of a child's skull. It was glass but thicker than glass, an opal die where light did not so much reflect as remember, casting back a field of cold colors. Little frost blooms skittered across the surface when she moved. When she lifted it, the suit's sensors hummed, and a tremor of static shaped itself into speech in her ear.

"—home... Ma—"

Mara's hand tightened. The word did not complete. The sphere had exhaled the beginning of a syllable and then gone mute, as if embarrassed at being heard. The flight of brittle air on the module's surface made a tiny bell of sound. Behind the sound, old circuits within Mara's skull — earlier, more dangerous installation — pinged an alert. She had been trained to notice names like live mines.

"Got a signature," she said, switching to Jalen's private channel. "It contains a mneme capsule. Low-frequency polymer acting as an affinity coupler. Looks pre-war. Handle with caution."

"On our books?" His question was a mutter. The Fagin's scanners had a thousand ghosts in their logs; most were claims and counterclaims, registry numbers that meant nothing until someone with enough cred signed them. "If it's a citizen remnant we could hand it through corporate channels. Better money that way."

"I don't give corporate channels to anything that says someone's name," Mara said. She heard a humorless bark of laughter somewhere in her past and turned it down.

The sphere warmed against her gloved hand. The opal surface breathed again, and this time the word was whole.

"Marisol."

The name struck like a hand against Mara's ribs. It was the name her mother had used on the better days before the sea took her grandfather and left a hollow where both joy and forgiveness should have been. It was the name her sister Aya used when she wanted to make Mara stop laughing and remember things. Mara had not been called Marisol in twenty-one years. Mara had answered only to Kestrel, to the job, to debt, to the hollow knot of habits that kept her afloat. She had left home young and left the name with the doorframe.

"That's impossible," she whispered. The suit recorded it. The Fagin recorded it. Out in the debris cloud, old screws spun in indifferent arcs, their trajectories forgotten by everything but gravity.

A sound, shaped like breathing on glass, pushed through the sphere. It didn't speak in words so much as in weather patterns — a memory of rain on tin, a child's palm tracing the seam of a toy boat. Images came then, not to her eyes but to some part of her that remembered what it was to be small.

A plaza: glass lawns, a fountain that hummed, a mother threading sun through her daughter's hair. A hand: small, sticky with syrup. A command: don't go into the water. The final frame clipped off with a hiss.

Mara dragged the sphere close, finger pressed to the crown of the opal. The surface was neither warm nor cold. It held a taste of ozone, and at the edge of it the memory wanted, quietly and insistently, to be continued.

"Do we have identification?" Jalen asked. "Could be a mnemonic for a child's memorial. Corporates like those thing—"

"Wouldn't be in the Falling City if it was just decorative," Mara said. "Someone brought it here for a reason. Someone who knew where to hide it."

"Or it's contagion." He was always the one to pitch the worst angle, and that made him useful. "There are mneme viruses that piggyback on cores. They...rewrite. Could be illegal-level bio."

"They call them mneme viruses and you call them art," Mara said. In another life, she might have teased him for thinking in hazard matrices. In this life, it was why they paid him.

The sphere pulsed, and for a moment a child's laugh skittered through the comms like broken glass. Mara's throat closed. She did not tell Jalen that the laugh belonged to a child who had shaved hair like river reeds and eyes too smart for the world. She did not tell him that the laugh had once belonged to Aya.

"Get it aboard," she said finally. "No one else gets a look."

The Fagin's grappler closed with a series of soft, hungry whines. A tether threaded down like a hand and wrapped the cylinder. Metal groaned. The module was lifted slow, the kind of slow that tried to be careful because the debris field had no mercy for hurry. Mara watched the sphere's opal skin through the tiny sliver of hull between her helmet and the module. It made the light do something that reminded her of the mosaic windows in the church near home — the ones Aya used to dare her to climb when they were girls, to see how much of the sky you could hold in your chest before it swallowed you.

"Hey," Jalen said on a flat laugh. "Claim on the manifest just came in."

A name and a code lined the overhead. Ownership code 7-Delta: a contractor for private memorials — those businesses that digitized and embodied people's final words and then fenced them into vaults. It was a small piece of law in an unregulated sea.

"How small is the profit split?" Mara asked.

"You'd get X if you auction. Ten percent if you hand it over now. They'll take it to a registry, run a match, and tell you nothing."

Mara's gloved finger closed around the opal sphere and she felt a resistance as if something in the sphere didn't want to be moved. It didn't speak. It waited, like someone holding their breath as a letter was read. In the quiet she had a clear, sharp memory of Aya's knuckles pressing the name Marisol into her palm on their last night together.

"Whatever tax code they show," Mara said, "store it under my rig. Run the paper. We'll decide once we're back."

She had not intended the words to be a lie. She had not intended anything more than to have time. Time was currency here in the rings. With time came choices, and with choices came the possibility, however small, of undoing things worn too thin by gravity and habit.

The module clattered aboard the Fagin with a sound like distant thunder. Inside the cargo bay the air smelled of old metal and the faint, almost-kitsch scent of someone else's substitute pine. Mara unstrapped and padded in zero-g, the sphere cradled in her arms like a creature. The Fagin's crew moved around her — short, efficient motions, conversations rendered down to essential vibrations.

"Let me see it," Jalen said. He reached, and his fingers hovered near the opal as if he were respecting a prayer.

Mara handed it over. The sphere did not feel fragile; it felt watchful.

As Jalen ran a diagnostic, the sphere flared, and a map unfolded inside Mara's head — a place that was not on any of her charts. It was a sliver of coastline with glass like teeth, a pier collapsing into water that did not reflect but swallowed. On the map, a tiny beacon pulsed in pulsing slow. Text labeled it in a language Mara's navigational brain didn't translate, but she understood the grammar: this was a place of last significance. A command: come here.

She blinked and the map snapped like a screen saver. Her throat burned.

"Translate?" she asked.

Jalen's face had taken a hard line. He had started to understand patterns long before him. "It's old polymer. Language overlay is corrupted. There's a coordinate stamp, though. If it matches our charts, someone pulled a location off-grid. That means someone wanted it secret."

"Or someone wanted it safe." The sphere hummed between them, patient as a heartbeat. "It came from the Falling City."

Jalen looked at her. For a moment — a fraction of a fraction — she could read the math in his face: profit versus risk, memory versus law. Then he said, "You alright?"

She almost lied. Everyone she had ever loved was either dead or better off being so. There was a long list of good reasons to ignore a child's recorded voice floating alone in a decommissioned city field. There was a longer list of reasons the sphere should be cataloged and sent to the vault and left to be munched on by committees.

Marisol — Aya — the syllable of her childhood — curled on the back of Mara's tongue like a small bone she wasn't sure how to let go.

"Yeah," she said, and the single-syllable was a decision. "Keep it under my claim for now. And Jalen? Promise me you don't register it until we check this coordinate."

There was a pause, the kind that held debts. Jalen's answer was not a promise so much as an admission. "I owe you one."

Mara let herself believe that was enough. She let herself believe it as the Fagin pushed away from the ring and the debris field and a little of the Falling City's former light fell out of the engine wake. The sphere lay in the cargo like a heart.

As the grav drives eased the tug toward the private lanes between salvage zones, the Fagin's older antenna — a stick of wire wrapped in a thousand apologies — pinged alert. The ship's interface flashed a color Mara had learned to mistrust: legal-hold. A corporate crest glowed. Messages arrived stacked like bills. Someone had noticed the remove from the field. Someone had traced the cylinder's tag through a half-broken registry and had issued a claim.

"We've got contested rights on that module," the broadcast said. "In the name of the Ministry of Heritage, commonwealth claim number 9972-Delta. Return for archival custody. Or face seizure."

Mara held the sphere closer, like a child with a secret. The voice that had whispered her name moved in the opal, patient as a tide. It wanted to be followed. It wanted to be found by someone who would go where the Falling City had been told not to go.

"No," she said, the word a thin line of sound. "No, we don't return it."

The tug's course corrected. Engines sighed and then held. Out in the dark galaxy, past the ring where rules were written by people in suits and bleach, the Falling City's bones turned in the slow dark, and the opal's light mapped, somewhere inside Mara, the first of a path back to a place her life had sworn to forget.

The sea kept secrets because it had nowhere else to put them.

Lira thought that as the water closed around the broken tunnel, as if the city outside had been swallowed by a mouth and the mouth had been politely holding its breath until she arrived. Her suit's lights slit through the black and found a grove of glass and concrete, storefront facades hung on ribs of exposed rebar like bones. A slow bloom of silt swept past, carrying with it hair and fabric and the fluted lids of toys gone pale with salt. It tasted like iron and cold electricity in the back of her throat. She tried not to think about what that meant for the people on the other side of the glass.

Her HUD blinked: DEPTH 83m. SUIT INTEGRITY 97%. CLAIM QUEUE: 3. TITLE: UNREGISTERED.

She touched the side of her helmet to mute the feed; corporate comms would want updates, but the collectors preferred quiet when they were alone with the dead. In the quiet she could hear the sea making its old patient sounds—pings of shifting debris, the slow creak of a structure still remembering its last living weight. It was a sound she knew better than her mother's voice.

"Pull left," said Mara's voice in her ear. The barge overhead hummed; Mara's breath fogged the microphone. Mara was her partner and the only person on the Harvest who still called her by the childhood nickname that had stuck like a burr. "There's a bank of sinkers down the tube."

"Copy," Lira answered, though she could see the tube in her lights. The sinkers were small cylinders—two inches of ceramic and silver and a coil of memory fiber—designed to be the last cooperative gasp of the dying. You screwed it into the temporal node at the base of the skull, or into the ruined neural lattice left after floodstroke; you pulled the coil free and it came alive with a literal last. The affluent had their lasts smoothed, scrubbed, packaged into high-fidelity suites. The rest—those who couldn't afford the after—were left in the sea. That was how the business was balanced: the ocean housed humanity's forgotten hours while the market sold eternity to a few.

Lira had done this for eight years. She could harvest a sinker in the dark with one hand while keeping the other braced against shifting masonry. She liked the order of it, the mechanical ritual that made death into inventory. Her own lasts were banked in account subfolders with dull names—snippets for later bargaining, emotion samples to trade for food. There were no lasts for escape.

She turned the beam. There, wedged between a collapsed turnstile and a child's bicycle, a black cylinder blinked like an unblinking eye. Unregistered. She recognized the make: old stock, pre-Harvest reforms, the type that didn't submit to automatic claim flags. You could sell those on a dozen markets and no one would ask who had licit title.

She freed it with a practiced motion, her gloved fingers scraping across something—paper, maybe, folded and fossilized by salt. It slid free with the gentle finality of something that had been waiting to be found. The coil unspooled when she cracked the seal; for a breathless second the water around her thrilled with the recorded echo of someone's last senses.

It wasn't always like the simul-suites, neat playback that could be sampled like a song. Sinkers gripped raw, unedited minutes: the heat of the person's final breath, the snap of air in teeth, the rush of blood, and always the smell—always some phantom, an impossible fidelity that made the living step back. The Harvesters learned to treat them like living creatures. You boxed them or you took on a ghost.

Lira saw, through the fragment's stuttering feed in the corner of her HUD, the underside of a skylight. A sun that wasn't the sun: a shallow, green-tinged disc like a bruise, hanging in a blue sky. Buildings grew downward from the rim of something incomprehensible—like stalactites reaching for a cavern floor that didn't exist. The camera angle swam, as if the recorder had been upside down. Someone laughed then, a thin bright sound that had no business being there at the end of a life. It might have been a child's laugh if the voice weren't the grain of a stranger older than the sea itself.

"Hey." Mara's voice pitched, metallic with worry. "Flag's changing. You're sitting on something, Edden."

Lira tightened her grip. Up close the feed smeared into color, a swath of fabric that looked handwoven, a ring of silver that might have been jewelry, a hand that cupped nothing but air. The laughter became syllables, then words that rippled undersea like sunlight. "—Lira."

She froze. It wasn't possible; sinkers couldn't know names. They captured sensory closure, not addresses. Her mouth went dry behind the helmet's membrane. Her whole life had been a ledger of names—debts, tags, corporate IDs stamped into the palms of workers. Her own name had been used and sold until the edges were ragged. She had not expected to hear it from the past of someone she did not know.

"Lira," the recording said again, but this time it curved around the bones of the tunnel and struck her forehead like a deliberate tap. It was not where she had left her name. It was in the register of things claimed: intimate, private. Her throat ached with a memory that wasn't hers—her mother singing a wordless lullaby in a language Lira couldn't place.

Her HUD began to flash warnings. QUARANTINE WARNING: UNREGISTERED SENSORY PACKAGE. TITLE DISPUTE RISK. CORPORATE HOLD PENDING. Mara muttered something into the mic—an apology and a curse and a calculation. They were not supposed to pick up unregistered lasts without running them through the barge's autopScanner, which would plasma-burn the unclaimed signature and fingerprint the core for corporate ownership. That process cost credits. So did silence.

Lira hesitated. For a fraction of a second the sea narrowed to the thickness between two fingers and she thought about what owning a last meant: a permanent claim on the minute that other people most wanted to forget or keep forever; a final thing you could sell to buy freedom. She thought, too, of the small ledger she kept in the soft light of the bunks—payments due, interest accruing like mold. The Harvest's debts were larger than the Sea. People like Mara had called for austerity and thrift and had then bought hymn-suites and "clean sleeps" to remember their own good deaths. For Lira, a single, unregistered last could buy an extra term of arrears, or medicine for her sister, or a bus ticket out of New Shanghai.

But the voice had said her name.

She swam the coil into her inventory pouch and sealed it. Her suit reacted, a cold chattering alarm across its internal mesh. In the corner of her HUD a faint pulse began that did not belong to the sinker feed—a signature that resonated with the name. It wasn't the barge's system. It couldn't reach this deep.

"Lira, get back," Mara said. "We've got currents coming. Don't carry—"

"Shut the hold," Lira said, and then softer: "Don't mute the feed." She had no idea why she wanted that. She knew, with the stubborn certainty of habit, that a Harvest few things were sacred: the sound of a last unpackaged, the quiet between the sea and the barge, the way the sinker still warmed under gloved fingers. She wanted to keep the naming alive, to hear it once more without any corporate scanner unspooling it into a serial number.

She swam up the tube. The city outside bled bits of light through the broken glass—little flats of neon and the odd flicker of a rogue bulb clinging to an unclaimed mast. Her gloves grazed a sign for a noodle house, half-ruined, its letters glowing like bruises. The barge's lights were a golden smear above; Mara's silhouette looked too small and precise against the membrane of the hull.

"What's the tag?" Mara asked the second she breached the lighter water and followed her toward the hull. "Any biometric signature? Age? Language?"

"Unregistered," Lira said. "No claims." She paused. The coil in the pouch seemed to thrum faintly against her ribs, as if it were alive in the way sinkers weren't supposed to be alive. "It said—"

"What? Say it."

"Lira."

The word landed and then spread across the deck like spilled oil. Mara's hand hovered above the webbing where Lira had sealed the pouch. Her face, when she turned, was all small hard questions. She was older than Lira by one generation of worry—scars at her temple and an old company tattoo that had faded to a map. "You're sure?"

"Yes." Lira could feel the name like a charge in her chest. "It said my name."

Mara's mouth thinned. She looked out past the barge at the dark city folding in on itself, at the line where the sea met the smog. "Unregistered sinkers appear from the ruins all the time. Lots of folks talk to them in the hush and hear their dead answer back. You heard yourself."

The harvest crew were a pragmatic tribe; superstition was a liability you could not afford when your suit's integrity depended on your paying close attention to physics. But there was a look in Mara's eyes that she had seen once before—after the storm that had taken her father's shoreline house, when she had stood stamping her boots and trying not to cry. That look said: we have rules but we are people; we keep our dead like wet fire.

"Do not let anyone else see it until we run it through the scanner," Mara said. "I'll seal the hold. We'll run it full-spectrum and then claim if it's ours. If it isn't—" She let the sentence hang like a blade.

Lira nodded. The barge's crew tightened their routine like a muscle memory: plots, seals, signatures. They were professional, practical, the kind of people who turned grief into work. But as the hold sealed and the air scrubbers hummed on the deck, Lira could not shake the feeling that the coil was not a thing to be bartered. That under the ceramic and silver lay not an ownership to be tagged but a message aimed like a stone.

She thought of another time, a year and a half ago, when she'd climbed a rusted elevator shaft to get a better signal—a stupid job that had earned her three days of rations and a quiet lecture from Mara. At the top she'd looked out over the city and seen, very faintly, a sky like a bruise and the suggestion of twin moons. She had laughed then and told herself she was tired. She had told herself the city made phantoms out of everything: light, hunger, longing. Yet here, under the barge's soft hum, the same impossible sky unfolded in a last-minute playback of a stranger.

Lira thought of her sister Tamsin, asleep in the lower bunks with a fever that refused to break. She thought of the ledger with its red columns. She thought, too, of why the name had the weight it did. Names here were not casual. You were tagged at birth and then laced with a dozen other names: employer, account number, debt interest. For the sea to know "Lira" and not "Idra Edden 349-12" was a personal claim.

"Run the scan," she told Mara.

Mara tapped the barge's console. The hold released with a whisper. A scanner arm folded and reached into the pouch where the sinker lay. The arm emitted soft ultraviolet that smelled faintly like ozone. The coil opened as if relieved to be free. For a moment the feed blossomed across the barge's screen: the same underside-sky, the same laughter, the same hand.

Then the feed went dark. The screen blinked its corporate error sign: EXTERNAL SIGNAL CORRUPTING. There was a new overlay now, one none of them had seen before: a lattice of nodes that threaded the feed like a scar. It pulsed in complex rhythms that the scanner tried to interpret and failed. The corporate scanner spat out a truncated log: PROTOCOL VIOLATION. POTENTIAL CROSS-TIME SIGNATURE DETECTED.

Mara swore softly. "What the—"

A voice spoke from the coil then, speaking not through the barge's speakers but through the space right behind Lira's sternum where everyone kept their private playlists and old lovers' recordings. It said, slowly, as if testing a word for the first time: "Lira. Do not be afraid."

She felt the room tilt. Time felt as if it had taken a breath and stretched until the seams of it showed. Across the deck of the Harvest, a dozen hands—callused, nervous—reached toward controls that made no answer. The crew looked at one another, not yet daring to name what had just happened.

Lira's own hands went cold around the insulated edge of the console. "Who are you?" she asked, because there was that hope that the living voice would be a person who could be bargained with.

The voice did not answer with a name. Instead it produced a sound that Lira recognized in the marrow of her bones: a pattern of numbers, then a map, then a phrase in a language she could not place. It said, finally, and with a clarity that was not of this place: "This is not your sea."

Above them, the city breathed. Below them, the dark held its secrets like teeth. Lira remembered the first rule of the Harvest: nothing that looks like a personal claim belongs to you until the scanner says so. She also remembered the second, quieter rule: if something calls you by name, it will not let you sell it. It will want you.

She reached for the pouch and felt the coil thrum like a heartbeat. Her choices spread before her like an ocean; each one was fractal, each one yielded a hundred other endings. For a long minute she only looked at the name on the HUD and listened to a voice that had no right to know it.

"Run another scan," she told Mara, though she wasn't sure if she meant the scan for the barge or the one inside her ribs that had begun opening like a lock. "And someone call dispatch."

Mara's jaw moved. She tapped the console with the economy of someone who had balanced a hundred lives worth of risk and benefit before breakfast. She called dispatch.

The barge hummed. The coil hummed back.

And somewhere in the multitudes of ruin that had once been New Shanghai, a dead city's last laugh echoed, and the world, for a breath, curved away from what Lira had known into something very old and very recent and not yet explained.

The Meridian thrummed like a thing alive.

Juno felt it through the soles of her boots, a dull, perpetual vibration that rose from the metal lattice and settled into her bones. It had been a lullaby and a threat for as long as she could remember; older people said the ring sang differently when storms came. Tonight it was steady, a low, patient purr beneath the scaffolds and the two dozen lights that marked the maintenance corridor she was crawling along. A thousand kilometers of engineered sky and Juno had been given three meters of it to call hers for the night.

Her gloved hand brushed a bead of condensation that had collected on the seam of a service hatch. The air here tasted of ozone and cold iron and the oil-sweetness of composite resins; she liked the smell. It meant things were holding. It meant the world at the center of the Meridian—the luminous, false star that the ring siphoned and folded into usable heat—was still doing what it was built to do.

She was there to thread a new splice into the thermal gird, to guide a filament into place, to make sure the heat bled where it ought to. Routine. The job would take less than an hour if the cranes didn't hesitate and if the tether drones behaved. If Commander Havel's schedule held, coffee would be waiting at Sector Nine's galley by 0300. The pay would go straight into the ledger, which meant rent, which meant that for another month she could pretend the old debts were just that—ledgers, not teeth.

Her headlamp caught something at the edge of the walkway. It was small, brown, caked with the dust of ten thousand air exchanges, lodged in the lip of an intake vent. For a breath she thought it was a nut, or a rat's pelt. She reached with the tip of a gloved finger and drew it free.

It was a shoe.
