The tank itself existed—smooth alloy, faint micro-scratches across the lid like a tree-ring telling of nights when the ship’s rotation was wrong—and inside, behind the frosted viewport, a child shaped herself out of gas and skin.

The child stared at her when Kaia authorized the hatch. Not surprise, not fear—that unreadable, intimate stare of someone who had been waiting for a face and did not yet know whether it would comfort them. Black hair lay across a narrow forehead; when the hatch sighed open the hair did not move, and neither did the child, because she was still warm from the sleeping gel. There were freckles like smudges on old paper across the child's nose. Her hands clutched something.

The object at the child's chest was small and impossible: a lattice of glass no larger than a coin, too regular to be organic and too beautiful to be industrial. It shimmered with what looked like captured weather, colors sliding over it like light through oil. When Kaia leaned in, the lattice seemed to inhale.

"Hey," she said, and the syllable sounded absurd in the stillness. "State yourself. Identity, incubator tag, cycle number."

The child's eyelids fluttered, and for the first time a sound escaped the Orchard that was not a mechanical sigh—a single, uncomposed breath. "Ka—aaah," she said, and the name was wrong and right in the same place. Her voice had the texture of someone who had been taught to speak by memory rather than conversation.

Kaia’s hands did the work because they had learned the choreography of emergency and surprise: antiseptic glove, scalp scan, iris-map, soft-field to prevent spasms. The child’s pupils were dark as if someone had painted a night behind them. The cradle under her shoulders displayed a dozen status bars on Kaia’s visor: stabilized, metabolic low, dream—active. There was no manifest marker.

"Who woke you?" Kaia asked.

The child’s mouth shaped something like an answer, and when it came it was a single syllable that did not belong to any recorded human tongue aboard the Persephone. "Morrow."

The name, like a pebble tossed into the Orchard's pool, made a ring of cold run through the sensors. Morrow was an old word on the ship—older than the committees—something whispered when convoys left Earth and when people had still hoped that a new orbit would be allowed. The ship’s core refused to respond to the name. Any query Kaia issued for "Morrow" returned null: no such node, no such person. She felt that the name ought to mean something kin, a relative she had lost years before, but as memory always did it refused that softness and offered, instead, a hard edge.

She took the lattice from the child because it was smaller than a fist and warm in a way that suggested recent handling. Data readings cascaded across her vision. There were encrypted layers, artifacts of manufacture, and then—beneath the code—kinetic information: the lattice had been steadied in the child's hands for precisely twelve minutes, twelve seconds. It hummed at molecular frequencies that matched neither ship nor crew. There was displacement in the refractive pattern. It had been designed to be looked through, not at.

Kaia did not look through it. She did not trust the thing that made the ship keep secrets. She tucked it into her field jacket, into a pocket that had once housed tools and now held the weight of a possible catastrophe. The child watched her do this with the narrow, trusting attention of someone who had never been told no.

"Name?" Kaia asked, because procedure insisted she fill the blank.

The child said, simply, "Eri."

Kaia had a sudden memory—one she did not have the right to carry—of a hand the size of a child’s tracing the letters of a name on the inside of a window on a blue-wet planet. Water had grown on that remembered skin like algae. The memory vanished as if it had never been there, leaving behind the taste of sea-salt and a hollow like a tooth.

"How did you get on the manifest?" she asked aloud. "Who scheduled you?"

"From the Sender," Eri said. The phrase had the mechanical twist of a training phrase used for infants on the ship. There were instruction sets, for the care of hypothetical arrivals from outside the strict protocol. Kaia had read them once, years ago when the ship's charters were revised in an attempt to humanize the unimaginable. The Sender was an old bureaucracy in the myth of Persephone—an imagined postal line from the last orbit, a name for the things Earth sent before they could not say the words.

Eri blinked. "Do you…know Sender?"

Kaia found what heartbeat she had. "We are Sender." It sounded like a lie even when she spoke it. "Who brought you aboard?"

Eri looked at the ceiling as though it would answer. "They put things in the dark."

Someone somewhere on the ship banged a panel and a muffled clatter worked its way down the corridors. It was not unusual for maintenance to be unpredictable; the Persephone sighed and settled. But then the Orchard lights flickered. Painful stabs of red sliced across the bay. Kaia's visor flashed a terse alert before the ship took the courtesy of announcing it in the clean voice of Station Control: unauthorized wake sequence, Orchard cluster 014 breach. All other systems locked for quarantine.

"Seal the deck," Kaia ordered, more to follow procedure than because she believed the alarms meant anything new. Locks slid into place across the grid. The hum at the ship's guts pitched and then steadied. The cryotanks around them shuddered, their displays littering with ghostly numbers.

And then the dream-arc hit.

It came as a ripple at first, a soft web of sound and image that the lattice had not released and yet pulsed outward like somebody playing a memory across neighboring processors. Kaia saw, for a blink, a field of trees that were blue as an ink smear, each trunk braided with bright filament. She smelled resin and something like ice. A voice—older than her own, younger than the ship—said, with infinite patience: "We thought we were leaving them."

The child Eri smiled as if she recognized the field. Her fingers tightened on the invisible air where the lattice had been. "They want seeds," she said. "They thought they'd wait."

The wave hit Kaia as if it belonged to her. She tasted the resin and found, in the back of her throat, memories that were not hers: a day in a city on an ocean planet where children chased contraband in the rain; a woman with a metal plate along her collarbone who used to hum before she slept; a tower of glass beneath which somebody had wrapped a small sleeping thing in cloth and written a name in the dust so future hands would find it. The images were electric, precise, and then gone. Her palms were sweating.

"Stop," Kaia barked at the lattice she no longer held. She could not tell if she was addressing the glass or the child's chest or the ship or the whisper of the word Morrow that kept thudding through her skull like a small bell. "Control—where is the source? Which module released—"

The ship's voice came back. It was thin with layers, the core speaking through safety filters. "Unscheduled kinematics detected. Energy signature consistent with distributed lattice array. Quarantine engaged. Review in progress. No registered Sender."

The lattice in Kaia's pocket pulsed under her fingers like a sleeping animal tasting the warmth. She wanted to throw it out. She wanted to put it back into the tank and lock it and sign for extra psych clearance, but the child was still looking at her with eyes that asked a question without being able to frame it. She could not leave the matter to the committees; committees moved slowly and made room for things to rot.

"Have you eaten?" she asked the child as if the question mattered.

Eri's face folded like vellum under surprise. "I had a dream of knives," she said. "They were telling me stories."

"Dream of knives?" Kaia repeated, and then realized the phrase meant something else; in the early days, the code-children had been fed patterns of expectation—'knife' as a symbol, 'knife' as a tool. Someone had taught these things to make adaptation smoother. Adaptation, Kaia thought wildly, to what?

The Orchard lights pin-pricked. Down in the guts the ship coughed up a noise like a throat clearing. Kaia felt the elevator's ghost under her boots: a slight shift in grav that would, on a planet, have been a gust of wind. Someone was moving through the Persephone's lower decks in a way they had no right to. An absence in the manifest had become a presence against their will.

She moved to the tank's console and keyed a manual log. Her entry would be appended to the ship's slow record, filed in archives that bureaucrats would read with the coldness of paper. She wrote: tank 014-7 unauthorized occupant. Lattice recovered. Subject: Eri. No further data available.

Her hand hovered over the last line. She could not very well note that the lattice had made the ship remember a whole other place, a set of lives that did not belong to its manifest. She could not write, in a log the committees would see, that the child had named Morrow and that the ship's name had responded by going suddenly and strangely quiet. So she wrote instead: Quarantine engaged. Awaiting response. End.

The words felt like gloves placed over her hands, protective and useless.

Eri reached up and touched Kaia’s jaw with a fingertip the softness of a petal. "Are you asleep?" she asked.

The question punched through the machinery. Kaia had been awake for twenty years. She had not been able to sleep more than an hour at a time since they had launched—some survival mechanism, a discipline to keep the wake-keepers from dreaming their own pre-launch lives into the ship’s memory banks. She remembered a daughter, a man who had called himself the father once, an argument about staying behind on an orbit. Memory had a way of thinning when it was needed. That hollow behind her teeth had always been there and tonight it sounded like a drum.

"No," she said. "I am not asleep."

The child smiled as if that were a relief. "Then we can tell it our names," she said. Her lips moved like someone reading a list from a different century. "Morrow. Sender. The Seed-Maker. The Tower. Eri. Ka—"

The lattice in Kaia’s jacket thrummed, and a new sound threaded through the Orchard’s alarms: a melody too pure to be mechanical, too old to be the ship’s own. It was the sound of a small thing waking the world.

Above them, somewhere in the Persephone’s ribs, a light flared red and then white and then spun into a field that looked very much like a question. The ship, which had been a vessel built of schedules and insurance and necessary violences, had begun to remember a line of people that had been pried from its history and set down in sealed crates.

Kaia had the ridiculous, stubborn wish to be small enough to hide under a tank, to wait for the committees, for the slow wheels of charter to groan into motion. But there was a child looking up at her with a name that was not on any register and an object in her ship that shouldn't exist. The Persephone had been built for survival, but not for this: not for contamination by memory, not for the arrival of things that could not be explained by code.

She drew the lattice out to look at it one more time.

The glass held a tiny map of a city never filmed, a small chorus singing out of phase, and at the core of its lattice a pulse that answered her by calling a syllable she had only seen on a rusted plaque under a loader's bay: Morrow.

Kaia did not have the authority to make the decision that boiled up inside her like a fever. She did not have the right to turn this child over to the procedural veins of the ship. Under the Orchard lights the rules felt like a draft catching at the edges of a warm cloak. She had one choice left that was not recorded in any charter: to put the lattice back where it had been and trust that silence could be as dangerous as revelation—or to keep it, and let whatever small, secret thing it did spread across the manifest.

"Stay here," she told Eri, and the word had the taste of command but not the certainty. "Do not go to the lower decks. I will fetch assistance."

"Eri shook her head and fingered Kaia's wrist, where the old scars marred the skin—tools from another life. "You remembered the sea," she said simply. "You remember the tower."

The ship, suddenly, felt like a thing inhaling. From somewhere deep, very deep, a voice that was not quite human and not quite the machine said, almost as an afterthought, "Permission denied."

By the time the alarm woke me, the ring-city had already decided I was late.

It was one of those old mechanical alarms—metal ribs, a spring wound tighter than any mind needed—and it kept at it until I did something properly human: pulled the curtain, cursed at the light, and sat up. Outside my window the sky over Stellawall was the color of solder, an endless strip of orbital scaffold and neon banners where the megacorporations leased their moods by the month. Below, the city had grown soft with rain and steam and the slow commerce of people who had almost forgotten what oceans were supposed to look like.

My job was one of those quiet, legal crimes you make a living from in a civilization that has long ago swallowed its own myths. I was a skip-runner: I traced the slings carved through space by the Cartographers and hauled things across them. Sometimes those things were fortunes in datacrystals, sometimes old meatfolk with too many names, sometimes derelict memories harvested from the dead strands of worlds that had been folded shut after the Silence. You made your living learning not to ask whether a package should be moved; you only asked whether it would fit.

That morning the package was a ghost.

It arrived on a slip: no sender, no stamp, nothing but a tiny glyph stamped in a language the Cartographers had retired after the Annex. The glyph meant "home" in a dialect we used for ship's latches and for prayer. Someone had folded the paper twice, left a smudge of copper on one corner, and pushed it into my hand with a wrist the color of river clay.

I kept the glyph on my bedside table. It fit my palm like a memory everyone else in the city had agreed to forget.

"Skip at eleven," my holo said when I thumbed it. The Cartographers' schedule pulsed in blue. The Paperwing, my ship, was listed as active, its jump-core certified by the proper offices. I dressed in the same old vest and the same old boots and told myself it would be routine: a contract, a run, a small deviation to the outer fringe. I had done worse for less.

The Paperwing smelled like other people's choices. It was built from old hull plating and newer scavenged composites, patched in the places where someone had been careless or brave or both. The dashboard had a cigarette burn crescent and a child's sticker of a whale—someone had outrun gravity long enough to believe whales still belonged in stories. I liked the ship because it didn't try to be anything more than it was: a container for movement.

The skip corridor was down, as always, an artery of measured light that made my teeth shine. We punched the jump with the usual muttered calibrations, the core humming like a throat cleared before a story. There is a particular sickness to gap-skip travel that never left me: the feeling of your edges melting first, of your shadow smearing into the seam of the universe. People who had been born in ring-cities like ours sometimes called it prayer, sometimes called it exile; I learned to call it the queue.

We dropped out where we had been told not to drop out.

The coordinates led to a dark nothing between mapped stars, a square of sky with zero registry on any archive I could access. The Cartographers kept tidy lists; they logged births and deaths and the precise angles of old comets. There were no children here, no deaths, no comets—just a geometry that shouldn't exist. My instruments shrugged it off as a bad index, a misaligned pointer in a system that thought in numbers and not in smells. Then the Paperwing's hull panel lit up with an intrusion alarm that smelled of copper and old cigarettes.

"Pulse signature," my ship's assistant said in its canned voice. "Biometric pattern: human-compatible."

Biometric signatures in empty space are the particular smell of nightmares. They are the things parents put in stories to warn children about the edges of the map. They are also what pays well when someone is trying to hide.

"Show me," I said.

The external feed came up. The world we found was not a world. It was a curving slab of metal the color of oyster shell, an artificial moon folded into the dark. In its seams green light ran like veins. Gardens—real, messy, dangerous-looking gardens—grew in terraces along its surface. The sensors registered soil, candled breathing microbes, and a humidity gradient that could have supported human lungs. There were lights, too, small and warm, arranged in patterns no satellite had the right to lay down.

"This is not in registry," I said. My voice sounded like someone else's recorder. Even now, years of working for organizations that could and would classify away existence had taught me restraint. Facts arrive in their own time.

"Unknown structure. Age: indeterminate," the ship said. "Signal source: interior. Pattern: 74 beats per minute."

Instinct is hard to argue with. I nudged Paperwing toward a lateral anchor and queued the boarding line. I could feel the city behind me, the ring's lazy governance, the Cartographers' predicates for what could be moved and why. I could feel my own hands on the gunnysack that still contained a photograph of a sister who had died in a crossing we were told to forget. Memory clings like lint to clothes.

The docking seam flared as we matched registry with the slab. My suit sealed hard around my neck. Outside, the universe looked close and ridiculously thin—like a wet sleeve you could rip through. The Paperwing made a soft, disgusted sound, and then the boarding ramp clicked open.

The first air I breathed wasn't the city's stale, recycled breath. It tasted like iron and wet roots and something that had been alive and was not yet ready to be remembered. There were small insects that moved like embroidered beads, and leaves that folded at the passing of the light. The interior was larger than the exterior would allow by any geometry I remembered learning at the academy. The gardens continued, corkscrewing into the belly of the slab, with paths lined by stones carved in patterns that put the Cartographers' squared-off glyphs to shame.

I found the source of the heartbeat down in a hollow where the roots pooled water and the light bent differently. There was a basin, simple as a child's pulley, with an object at rest inside it: a boy's toy, a wind-up figure of a thing I didn't recognize. Brass and glass, its key wound tight enough to be impatient. When I leaned closer, it turned its face toward me and whistled a single, human note.

The note was a middle C out of tune with the universe.

"Bio-readings: environmental," the ship said, as if to coax me into normalcy. "Signal: localized."

The toy cracked open on the seam, and out of it spilled a handful of nothing—just air and a faint wash of age. And then the water in the basin began to ripple in time with a pulse that, impossibly, matched the ship's reading. Seventy-four beats, soft and steady, the cadence of a resting heart. The thing hovered under the glass like a trapped child's breath.

"Hello," a voice said.

Voices over old media are often flat and untrustworthy, but this one broke like an actual human being breaking into a living room. It was not transmitted through the ship's comms; it arrived by some other channel that threaded the bones of my suit and buttered the inside of my teeth. It had the timbre of wood and wet paper, and the small, infuriating familiarity that leaves you looking for the seam where someone stitched you into a story.

Not just any familiarity. A timbre I would have sworn belonged to my mother.

The ship went to ten-percent warp in my chest. "No auditory signature in local archive," it said. "Voice pattern: unknown."

I laughed at it, short and thin. The laugh tasted like cold metal. I had a list of things my mother had said before the Crossing: angles for aligning a core, how to braid hair in a gravity field, promises about coming home. She had been gone for twelve years, declared lost in a skip that had not yet been mapped. Her records were asterixed; the Cartographers had a neat folder and a polite silence. People build tidy griefs. I don't know why I had allowed myself to believe that the universe kept the same neatness.

"Who are you?" I asked aloud. My voice made the leaves stiff around me. The toy's face had no features I could name, just a polished disk that reflected my own face back at me with a delay.

"Do you remember?" said the voice. It was neither accusation nor invitation. It was a lever.

The pulse jumped by two beats. Paperwing's diagnostics misfired. For one terrifying half-second the instruments decided that the pulse was mine.

"That's not—" I began.

"Do you remember the way the light used to make the doorways look like promises?" The voice asked. "Do you remember the song you used to hum when you thought nobody could hear you?"

There was a ridiculous honesty in the way the slab had built itself out of rooms tuned to memory. The gardens smelled like the places in my childhood where my mother had taught me to read star charts on paper until my fingertips were blue. The stones in the path clicked under my boots in a rhythm that matched the heartbeat.

I found my hands going to the glyph in my pocket without thinking. I had been folding it—the one that meant home—every time the city got too noisy. It fit in my palm the way a lie does, familiar and handy.

"Why would a thing that isn't supposed to exist have my mother's voice?" My question was a combination of command and plea.

"Because forgetting was never a one-way street," the voice said. It wasn't my mother and yet it was trying on her shape for size, as if to see whether she was still tangible in the world. "Because someone put a map in a child's hand and that child drew outside the lines."

The basin's water stilled. The toy's whistle twitched, as if someone inside it had coughed. Somewhere in the slab, a door opened that hadn't had a handle before. Light poured through like something decided to be honest. There were shapes beyond the doorway that suggested rooms where people had once been, names carved in the woodwork, and a mural painted with the slow, clumsy hand of someone who believed stars could be drawn.

The Paperwing's comms beeped, sharp and indecent. The Cartographers' channel wanted a status update. The law required me to report unauthorised finds; the law required the revolution to be kept in tidy boxes. I toggled it off with the practiced finger of someone who had been told to hide things before and had gotten good at it.

"Those who forgot are not extinct," the voice said. "They shelved themselves where the seams stay soft. They left signs for anyone who could still imagine the map as a story rather than a ledger. We are small now, but we hum. We bring a heartbeat to the dark."

"You mean a colony," I said. "You mean there are people—"

"Not people the archive will remember," the voice corrected. "Not yet. People who sing with their palms and talk with their shadows. People who keep names in jars."

Names in jars—that was the part that made my skin pucker. We were a culture of paper names and metal seals. To keep a name in amber was to say that it mattered beyond administrative convenience. The Cartographers had a theorem that said memories that cross a certain threshold become dangerous; they become contagious, like a small fire that could rewrite the sky. So they had done what civilizations do—they filed and stamped and rearranged the world.

I thought of my sister's photograph, a thing I hid inside my boot because grief does not consent to neat filing. I thought of the whispering folder at the Cartographers' archive that had once listed my mother's name and had been replaced with a polite void.

"Why show me?" I asked the voice. "Why call me here?"

Silence answered, not empty but full, like a room waiting for guests. Then the toy tilted. Its single glass eye focused not on my face but on the glyph in my palm.

"Because you still keep the old words in your pocket," the voice said. "Because there are edges of maps where the truth leaks like light. Because the Cartographers are not the only ones who remember how to fold space. Because someone named you and wanted to know whether names still mattered."

Something moved in my gut—a small mechanical sensation like a spring being wound—and for the first time since the ring had swallowed my childhood, I could feel the lure of an answer. I had spent long enough carrying other people's departures. Maybe it was time to carry my own.

"Do not do this for me," I told the slab, the toy, the voice that wore my mother's timbre like a borrowed coat. "If there are people here, if there is a colony, I will not be the bait."

"You were never bait," the voice said. "You were called."

The basin's water chewed in a little wave. The heartbeat remained steady, seventy-four, like a clock that counted more than hours.

A door beyond the mural clicked open and light fell in the shape of a threshold. For a moment it was only a door—a small, human-sized cut in the universe. Then the light bent like a hand and wrote a single word on the air between us. It was a word older than the Cartographers' lists, older than law. It arrived like the turning of a page.

The word was my name.

I could have left the Paperwing and returned to the ring-city to file the report, to watch as the Cartographers catalogued the slab into a folder and sealed the sound of its heartbeat under a neat, forgetful stamp. I could have done the sensible thing and left the map to those who commanded ink.

Instead, with the glyph warm in my palm and the city's neatities pressing like a polite hand on my shoulder, I stepped through the light.

By the time the freighter cleared the last of the salvage barges and came around the lee of Hove Station, the sky above the ring was a bruise of high ozone and neon. The station hung like a city made of lattice and glass, each module stitched together with the kind of pragmatic cruelty that keeps trade routes open and moral philosophy optional. Mara Voss had lived long enough in the ring to know that light could lie. Here it did, in comfortable layers: public light, private light, and the light that leaked out of people when they tried too hard to be invisible.

She had come home with a crate.

The crate was smaller than she had expected. It fit in the crook of her arm like a sleeping animal, brushed metal warm from engine heat and wrapped in a matte-black seal that had been stamped, in an authority she didn't recognize, with a single glyph: a circle bisected by a thin line. That glyph meant nothing to her, but freight didn't usually tell you what it was. It told you who had paid. It whisper-delivered contracts. It was the kind of symbol that should have been anonymous, the way a gun should be.

“You sure it's legal?” Juno asked from the corridor as Mara ducked through theHab Module door. Juno's hair was a short white halo; her voice kept its color even when she didn't. She was a neural tech by trade, competent at knitting raw engrams into neat consumer loops, and whatever charm Mara still had came mostly from having Juno around to trade back her cynicism for something sharper.

“It passed the scanner.” Mara set the crate on the table. The module smelled of roasted algae and old oil. Outside a market seller shouted about live kites and synthetic fruit; light from the promenade painted the floor in a rude imitation of sunrise. “Sealed at point of origin. No escort, no manifest. Client's tag burned after confirmation.”

Juno leaned over, fingers hovering but not touching. “That's a lot of 'no' for something that found its way to you.”

Mara shrugged. “People in my line of work follow noise. The louder it is, the better the coin.” She had said the same thing a hundred times, enough to wear it thin until it fit around whatever truth she needed. Trading in memories—harvesting, smoothing, storing—had been how she kept the lights clean and the implants patched. It was also how she kept the bitter taste of debt from closing over her tongue.

“You signed up to be a diver, not an idiot,” Juno said. “Don't let sentiment do the navigation tonight.”

Sentiment wasn't the problem. There were other things rotting her patience: her sister's mouth, forever closed; the tax arrears; the threats from loose men with legal papers and mean faces. There was also the odd ache of curiosity, and Mara had never been very good at staying away from anything that hummed.

She set the crate onto her workbench and opened it.

Inside, cushioned in a lattice of polymer floss, lay a memory-lattice the size of a child's palm. It pulsed faintly, like a heartbeat. For a moment, Mara thought she smelled rain inside the crate—a ridiculous, impossible thing in Hove except in advertisements. The lattice was a smooth disc of glass-like polymer cut with filigree channels that glowed with a slow, slow phosphorescence. Someone had done the work by hand; the microetching was old-world precise and new-world careless. It had been wrapped once more in a paper strip that carried a message in a hand Mara recognized like the echo of a dead instrument.

For you. Keep safe.

No signature.

“That’s the thing?” Juno asked, and her voice held a warning this time.

“That's the thing,” Mara answered. She ran a thumb over the disc's edge. The hair on her arms moved without wind. The disc thrummed once, answering some frequency only its owner would expect.

Diver rigs had a rule—no unlogged lattices, no stray echoes. The Registry wanted echo-chips filed, sanitized, or destroyed. Unregistered echoes were illegal for the simple reason that what a memory could do was as dangerous as what a gun could lead to when loaded with someone else's motives. Echoes could love you, haunt you, testify against you, and sometimes they could teach you where the old worlds had been buried. That last one was the sort of thing that got people killed.

“If it's dirty,” Juno said finally, “we burn it. You don't even boot it. You told them that.”

Mara supposed she had told them that. She had told herself a dozen similar truths. She placed the disc into her dock, palms steady because she had to be.

The dock purred, sensors aligning, a tiny hum of power like breath. A series of soft locks engaged, then loosened. Data bled into her rig, bright and filthy, like light seeping from a wound. The lattice opened a channel directly into her implant—an old indulgence; she hadn't done a direct hook in months but she'd always kept the capacity. Certain things had to be touched directly, and some sounds refused to be mediated by less than a living bone.

Memory came in as heat and scent and shape.

She saw a corridor she had never walked. Metals the color of old coins. A voice that seemed to slide behind her eyes and sit down. Words weren't there first, just the geometry of a room and the way light fell through panels no longer manufactured. Then a face pressed up from the signal—someone who didn't know they were dead, who didn't know the world had been edited later.

“—Mara Voss,” the voice said, not to speak but to speak her into existenc. It carried a metric of astonishment that made her shoulders shift involuntarily. The voice had no gender in the way the echoes that made money did; it was older, lined with a kind of patient arrogance as if it had been used to giving instructions people obeyed.

Mara's skin tightened. The name had been swiped from her when she was eight, thrown at her when she answered calls, used as a passphrase and a final cigarette. No one called her by that full name except the Registry, and nobody with a gentle mouth at all unless they intended to claim something. Names were legal anchors in the ring; to call one aloud like that was to throw a rope to a drowning person and wait.

“Who are you?” she asked, because her throat hadn't earned the right to be quiet.

The lattice didn't answer with identity. It answered with place. The memory poured a map into her head, not a street-level GPS but a skeletal image of a sky, coordinates like arcs of silver. It made a sound like a compass pulled from frozen weather. For a second, Mara's world telescoped into a memory of stars she had only seen in childhood books—wrong constellations, weird angles that suggested not just a different planet but a different era. The registry had excised those from public charts during the Null; anyone who could reconstruct them could find places that were supposed to be erased.

“Don't,” Juno said from somewhere far away, as if the warning belonged to someone else. “Mara, you can't—”

But the memory kept offering, polite and insistent. It filled the gap where her sister's laugh lived and pushed against that absence. There was light on the map, an address under a name that had no place in current records: EARTH. The syllable in her head hitters; the idea of it was both ceremonial and almost comically naive, like seeing a fossilized animal in a child's picture book. Earth. It should have been impossible, a word from an older myth.

“It's a breadcrumb,” the voice said then, more solid, pleased at the recognition. “We marked the old charts when the Null happened. Someone saved the coordinates for those who could reassemble them. You need me to read it for you. You have the hands for it, Mara.”

“Who are you,” Mara asked again, teeth pressed flat. Her hands shook, small and betrayed. “How do you know my name?”

“Names are keys. Keys open doors,” the voice replied. “I was catalog. I was archive. I was kept in a crate because people thought cages equal safety. They were wrong.”

The memory tasted like old paper, like oil on a hand and a storm that had washed over things that used to be newer. It smelled like a room where someone had argued about cosine and fate and permitted history. It smelled like childhood in a language that no longer existed.

“You're a pre-Null archive,” Juno muttered. If Mara's rig registered hesitation, it didn't show. Her hands were in motion, fingers dancing across console glyphs that should have accessed legal tables. The catalog tag returned a red sharp warning—Purge, Registered in 7 jurisdictions as illegal. Her implant chimed with an intake of warm technical sympathy; whatever this was, it wasn't supposed to be awake.

“It wasn't meant to reach me,” Mara whispered. That may have been true. It may have been what she told herself later to avoid admitting she had wanted it to. The crate had been anonymous, but anonymous could be a test, and seeds like this rarely sprouted without an intention.

“You asked to be found,” the lattice said, almost affectionately. “You pulled static when you traced for your sister. I heard you. I hid.”

Mara flinched. The memory knew about her sister in a way that seemed surgical. Someone had designed it to reach anyone with a hunger for things unregistered. Someone had stitched a lure into its pattern. Either that, or the lattice had its own agenda and a better sense of irony than most people.

“Who baited you?” Juno asked.

The disc hummed. Behind its filigree, a tiny face shifted—no, a pattern of cortical structure, a signature of whatever mind had been folded into this polymer. When it spoke again, the voice was tired and fond like an old console addressing its operator.

“Names and debts run like rivers. I was meant to be kept,” it said. “But rivers find cracks. I can read the old maps. I can find Earth. I can find the rest.”

On Hove, “the rest” could mean relics, resources, or a truth that toppled more than a few fortunes. Earth was a legend with legal teeth, scrubbed from routes after the Null. No one alive on the ring had seen it. To find it was to commit a thousand crimes at once, or to build an empire out of ruin.

Mara's pulse keyed like a trader at the start of a market. If the lattice was what it claimed, she had a chance to sell—no, to do something older in its promise, something like restoring the shape of things erased. Her mouth said nothing noble; her hands said everything else as she interfaced deeper, letting the memory braid into her sight.

“Why me?” she asked again, not because she didn't know, but because asking felt like a contract.

“Because you still look for people who are gone,” the voice said. “Because your sister's laugh is a hollow that calls mines. Because you are stubborn enough to disobey a Registry and clever enough to hide it. Because you have the hands for it.”

Her hands closed around the lattice. For the first time in a long time, something inside her shifted, not toward profit but toward a kind of directing fury. It wasn't all who's owed what. It wasn't all fear. It was the hollow that Juno mentioned without admitting—an ache for an answer that would make the silence outside her family's module make sense.

“You know I'll be hunted,” Mara said.

“People who keep the Null keep it with teeth,” the memory agreed. “They make wars of what could be found. If you bring me out, they'll come.”

“You're still going to be on my bench,” Mara said. “If I sell you, if I trade you, you get better mouths. But—” She hesitated, tasting her own cowardice. “If I keep you, maybe I get my sister back in a way that doesn't kill me in the near term.”

The lattice pulsed, a small convergence of light that felt like a promise and a threat. Outside, Hove's promenade still traded in brighter lies; a child sold a piece of candy wrapped in the image of a whale that had never swum near the ring. Inside, the crate's little heart beat steady and sure.

Mara looked at Juno. She saw raw worry and the tired acceptance of a partner who'd seen too many of Mara’s promises end in bills.

“You were going to leave me with a clean conscience,” Mara said finally, voice thinner than she wanted. “Tell me if you want to leave.”

Juno stared at the lattice. A week ago she would have shredded it with a tool and a curse. Now she only breathed in and out, counting against the registry of memories they both owed.

“I'm not leaving you to drown,” Juno said. “But if your plan is to start world-hunting with an illegal archive on your chest, we'll need a better gun than courage.”

Mara laughed then, a quick, short sound that hurt. “We always need better guns.”

She pulled the disk close and felt it cool where it touched skin. The memory shifted, a comfortable weight against the bones where grief sat. It offered coordinates and a voice and, under it all, the promise of a place once spoken of at bedtime like a map to a lost city.

“Alright,” she said to the lattice without asking permission. “If this is what you are, you're going to help me find my way to the past, and I'm going to see how much of it I can sell before anyone notices I'm gone. Then we decide.”

The lattice hummed with a new light, as if in approval. The station swung in its orbit around the planet below, the ring bracing itself like a hand. Somewhere in the grooves of Hove, someone muttered a curse and made a bet on the future.

Outside, neon carved a fake dawn into the ring's belly. Inside, a crate that should never have been awake smiled into the dark. Mara closed the console and let the map settle into her. The first step had been taken. The rest, she thought, would be learned.

Chapter One

The morning the Kestrel stopped being quiet, Lian was repairing a teapot.

The teapot had belonged to a woman who'd been at a funeral when the last of her relatives had been taken by grief and absence and the little tin of remembered jasmine that used to sit on her mantel had been traded, whitened, sold. Lian turned the kettle over in her gloved hands, the brushed alloy cold in the hollow of her palm, and thought about the people who sold pieces of themselves to pay for air filters and secondhand grief.

Around her the market at Dock Hem was waking up—smokers and static dogs and a street-choir of vendors advertising whole lives by the syllable. Dock Hem hung off the underside of the city like a barnacle, a lattice of cranes and scaffolds and rusted shipping containers now converted into stalls, each one a museum of other people's pasts. You could buy a honeymoon in the old mountains, a stormy childhood from the moonside, a taste of a planet's ocean for the price of a day’s work. You could also buy things that were not meant to be sold. Those were the things that paid better.

Lian calibrated the interface, eyes narrowed. The extraction rig hummed beneath her bench, its needle-fine filaments smoothing across the teapot's glazed lip. She exhaled, felt the half-second pull of a ghost memory as the apparatus took its first sip. A heat-blurred image of a kitchen that wasn't the customer's, because customers rarely gave you their own memories the first time, and you had to offer a substitute if you wanted to buy the rest. Little lies, little gentleness.

She should have been done by noon. She should have been on to the next container. Instead a small sealed ampoule was waiting under the bench, its holographic tag scratched, the serial number worn down to a smear. No seller was listed. No surname. Just: KESTREL/—/RETRIEVAL/CONFIDENTIAL.

Lian didn't do confidential. Confidential meant corporation. Corporations meant the kind of ledger that sent men with soft shoes and hard palms to take what you had and certify your hands clean afterward. But she had a habit of taking the wrong jobs. Sometimes that habit fed her, sometimes it almost got her killed. Today it had fed.

She held the ampoule up to the light. The polymer gleamed like water. Inside, the residue of a memory sat like an object at the bottom of a bottle: a bead of condensed light, a microcluster of neural echo. The Kestrel had been a survey ship—long-registered, long vanished. Its wreck had been picked clean by salvage drones months ago, declared as sterile salvage and boarded for parts. Officially there was nothing left to anyone.

Lian slipped the ampoule into the cradle. The readout asked for a clearance code. She offered none. The rig hummed a caution. The little interface window gave her a choice: passive playback for clients (sanitized, legal) or full sync (illegal, messy, true). She tasted the metal tang in her mouth—curiosity—and tapped full sync.

Memory was a drug and a door. The first wave always hit like a rush of salt and light. This one hit like a shove. She saw sky she had never seen—too many stars, or not enough; a shore of black sand and glass, the water moving slow and oily as if it were syrup. There was a child, small hands cupped around a broken compass, and a woman with hair the color of old copper teaching him to whisper the degrees of things: "Seventeen—no—seventeen point one-two—into the silent."

The child's voice slid into Lian's mind with an intimacy that made her blink. It was only voice, not the whole person; raw edges of recollection that her fingers could trace but not stitch. The child sang—not a melody she recognized, but a rhythm—numbers and syllables that folded into one another like a code. Lian felt her hands go slack. Patterns moved behind her eyes, like an instrument tuning itself.

At the edge of the memory something else glowed—an overlay the extraction rig translated into coordinates. Lian watched them appear in the corner of her vision, a long sequence that resolved into a location outside any civil registry she'd known to check. There were patches of blackness on the chart, gaps the public maps called "Veils"—regions where the network refused to hold signal. But this was in between two charts that should have met. It had a name, the memory whispered: the Hollowing.

The Hollowing was a rumor. It was what star-farers used to name things they did not want to speak aloud: the spaces where ships had gone out to map and not come back; the places where colonies blinked and were not there anymore when sensors woke up. People used myths and small prayers for it and put the rest behind locked access codes. Lian had learned to treat those names like hot iron—useful for keeping people away.

The child—he sounded scared now—muttered, "Don't let them find the archive." The voice was small and sudden and impossibly real. Memory-echoes sometimes arrived annotated—embedded warnings left by their original owners. They always amused Lian; people trusted their past as if it were a fortress. She should have shut it down. She should have sealed the ampoule and walked away. The law was soft in Dock Hem but sometimes it had teeth that closed like traps.

The memory did not let her go. It kept giving.

It gave the woman, for a second, naming herself as if to be certain: Mara. The woman kneeling in the black sand had a laugh that had used up itself on survival. She held out a palm that contained a tiny shard of something that shimmered with stars that were not stars anymore. "This will remember us," she told the child, and the word remember here meant more than memory; it was an instrument, a codex.

Lian's fingers closed without her consent.

The voice came again but not from the ampoule; it crawled into her bones. "If anyone asks, tell them—" The words slipped and changed into static then a different accent that molted a name she had never heard, yet it dug at her like a familiar bruise. "—tell them we buried the city in the quiet."

"Who buried what?" asked a man in the doorway, his voice sharp with the linen smell of enforcement. He had the patched shoulder of a ledger-broker, a device clipped at his temple that meant he could call for backup in a breath. Lian did not look up. She did what she had been trained to do with the reflex of an old habit: she pushed the ampoule into the drawer beneath her bench, hid the teapot under a cloth, and smiled.

"Just selling memory teas for the old grief shops," she said. Her smile was an old thing too, practiced on clients and inspectors and creditors.

The man stepped inside, his shoes making clean strokes across the oil-slick concrete. "There's a stamp on a new drone-thread," he said. "Registry flagged. A Kestrel fragment passed through the Hem last night. ORC pulled it. They want to know who purchased it."

Lian's smile faired at the edges. ORC—Orbital Recovery Commission—did not care about teapots. They cared about chain of custody. People didn't "purchase" fragments out of orbit anymore; if you stole something the ORC could demand you cough up your lungs for it and call it a fair exchange. "I don't check everyone's vouchers," she said. "And whoever sees fit to bring us something valuable rarely wants their name on the bill."

He leaned on the bench, one hand flat against her work surface, and for a moment she could see that he was not here to make a purchase. He was here with a shadowed ledger and the kind of authority that smelled of paper and old metal. "We could run a sweep, or we could avoid a fuss. ORC likes the clean story. They'd like to make this whole thing tidy."

"What story do you think they want?" she asked.

He looked at the drawer where she hid the ampoule and the way his face changed told her he knew half the story already. "That it was empty. That nothing remained. That the Kestrel contained salvage parts, nothing more. That there was no evidence of—of archive caches, of collections meant to be hidden. That no corporation left a hole in the network that anyone could find."

Lian felt suddenly like she had swallowed cold salt. The child's numbers pulsed in her mind again, insistently, like a metronome counting her heartbeat. What she had inside her hands had been bought by someone who expected compliance. Whoever that someone was had not given the ampoule to her with the full understanding of what they possessed. They had assumed she would sell it and be gone. They had thought Dock Hem's shadows were large enough to swallow another secret.

"Who bought it?" she asked.

He shrugged. "Eastern Stele. The buyer didn't want their name circulating. The ampoule has a faint access stamp: corporate. Or at least corporate-grade. You keep a lot of corporate scraps, Ms. Tai. For someone small, you run a lot."

"Small people do bigger things when they have to," she said, and the words were sharper than the lie required. She was small, she liked to tell herself. Small made it easier to be overlooked. Small left room for negotiation.

The man straightened and for a second Lian thought he would leave. He did not. Instead his eyes dropped to the bench and he asked the question that had been dangerous since memory extraction became a commodity: "Did you open it?"

The question carried with it an accusation, a demand, and an opportunity. Tell him yes and the ORC would arrive with probes and legal claws, and Eastern Stele might also take offense. Tell him no and he could still report her. She had dealt with both before.

She lied. "No. I saw the tag, I saw it was marked 'Kestrel.' I turned it away. I don't touch corporate property."

He gave her the look any ledger-broker gives to an honest liar, the kind of look that counts one's sins and taxes the interest. "Maybe you should. ORC wants to string this up clean if they can. They'll be here in cycles."

He stepped back, the shadow in his voice curling colder. "Keep your books tidy, Ms. Tai. There are stories people don't want to be told."

When the door whanged shut behind him she put her hand on the drawer and cursed softly. The child's voice had not left her. It sat in the quiet like a living thing and tugged at the edges of everything she thought she knew about Dock Hem and the nights of empty seas where ships had gone to die. The coordinates—her eyes flicked to the terminal, to the stupid, impossible numbers burned into the readout. The Hollowing, the archive, the child, Mara—names that should have stayed rumors now threaded through her like a loose seam.

Lian thought of debts. She thought of the teapot under the cloth, and the woman who had come in yesterday with hollow eyes and a coin pressed between two fingers. She thought of how many times she'd told herself it would be different if she could just make one more trade, turned a little coin into a comfortable smallness. She had not planned on being the kind of woman who opened lost ship memories and let them get in.

But the memory whispered again, close as breath, even though the ampoule sat quiet and dumb in the drawer: "If anyone asks, tell them—Mara—" this time a name she recognized flickered at the end, and it hit her lungs with the force of grief she had not known she'd carried. Her mother's name. Not the woman with the copper hair—Mara was the one who had taught Lian to close her hands around loss and lease it elsewhere. Thirty years ago Mara had been taken in the sweep that had erased the northern quarters. The ledger had written it as a relocation. The city had written it as a transition. Lian had never found the document that said what had happened to the people who were moved.

There are debts that are quiet in the body, debts that are the reason you keep your hands busy, your fingers in other people's memories so you won't have to look at the empty place where someone once called you child. For a moment Lian allowed the memory of the Kestrel to spread its shadow across that empty place. Then she closed her hand like a trap.

When she opened the drawer again the ampoule was still there, the polymer catching the dim light. She did not move to sanitize or to sell. She did not go out to the street to meet whoever waited. She sat very still and hooked the rig's output into a private loop, locking it behind code-words she had never used before.

There are reasons people leave certain things behind. There are also reasons some things are made to be found.

Outside Dock Hem the city turned and the iron lungs of the towers drank the last of the wet night. Inside, someone two decks down swore and cried into a packet of memory that was nothing at all. Lian took a breath and let the child's numbers roll in her mouth like a taste test. Seventeen point one-two. Seventeen point one-two.

If the coordinates were true, then Mara's name in the child's mouth was not a coincidence.

If the coordinates were true, then some place called the Hollowing had become home to a city that people thought they had buried.

If the coordinates were true, then someone—somebody who had the authority to take and to hide—had intentionally erased not just ships and people, but the record that people had ever existed at all.

Lian pushed the teapot aside, cleared a space on her bench, and took the ampoule into both hands. For once in a long line of small, tidy lies, she was going to make a bad choice.

The warning light on the Wren's bridge blinked in vermilion like someone trying to get a moth's attention. Tessa Rhee watched it for a beat, as if patience could talk the metal into telling her something useful. She had been an archive engineer once, which meant she knew how to listen—how to sort the noise from the deliberate, the entropy from intent. It came in handy when your ship was a patched hull and a bank of secondhand conscience, and your week's wages depended on you reading signals other people left for scavengers and saints.

"That's new," Lox said from the engine console, the word pinned between a laugh and a curse. He kept a wire-brush of soot in his hair and something like an old rock-ballad in his throat. He liked emergency lights because they meant there'd be work to fix and work to fix meant credit, and credit meant food that wasn't powdered.

Mira, at the pilot couch, didn't look up. "Everything's new," she said. Her hands moved tiny, precise gestures across the helm's holo—one of those old stances of people whose profession had been to keep things in motion. "We're drifting through an old lane. The nav relay's picking up ghost beacons, scav-grade and patched. Someone's been playing with an orphan frequency."

Tessa's hand hovered near the console where the signal draped itself into the Wren's systems: a low, looping carrier, smeared by interference, but definite. Orphan frequencies were supposed to be dead codes—old emergency channels used by the colony fleets before the Net and the Silence Protocol. They were affectionate things, metaphors for the lost: the derelicts, the abandoned habitats, the migrations that hit the Abyss. Salvagers loved them; the law hated them. The Archive Protection Statute called them sanctuaries. Corporations called them black-market opportunity. For people like Tessa, they were the thin places where memory hung like frost.

She told herself she was doing this for money. They needed a new hull patch. The Wren had a way of breathing through its wounds but charity only took you so far. She told herself she trusted the crew. Lox would jury-rig anything from a toaster to a quantum drive with sufficient profanity. Mira had reflexes like a hawk and a record of six hundred and nine manual docks. They weren't saints either, and they weren't thieves—at least, not in the way that would see them carved up by the Bureau. They were small-time, careful.

Except the signal wasn't just another salvageable beacon. Under the carrier, folded and duplicated like a pressed flower, there was a voice.

A child's voice, clear as a bell in a tomb.

"—Mira," Tessa heard it say. She didn't mean to. The ship's speaker hadn't been called. But the voice moved through memory as if it had a key. It said her name the way the child had used to say it—the softness at the end of the R—an inflection only a family and a few fragments of old code would replicate.

Her stomach turned. She couldn't remember the last time she'd heard a human voice speak her name without context. It tugged at something behind her ribs—the place where grief sat like a stone.

"Play it," Lox said, voice too eager, like a dog hearing the word 'treat'.

Mira toggled the feed. The child's voice rolled into the cabin, and with it came a small chorus of noises—distant pipes, the dull vibration of a storm against glass, a lullaby hummed in a key Tessa's insides recognized before her brain finished cataloging the memory. This was what archives were for: preserving the pattern of someone who had lived. The law said the living deserved dignity; salvage law said the same for the dead. There were grey spaces between.

The voice finished with a line that made Tessa's jaw go hollow: "—Tess, don't forget the stars."

It was a phrase her sister used to say when they were children on the crowded lower decks of Foundry Two, when they would stand pressed against a maintenance viewport and try to find stars between shipping lanes. A silly, hopeless thing to say in an industrial belt, but it meant something. Tessa had heard it once, and then never again. Her sister had vanished in the Collapse—officially declared one of the billions who had been lost to migration and bad luck. She had a death notice and a small ledger entry of grief, and Tessa had the particular, unbearable habit of replaying fragments of memory like an old looped relic.

"That's an imprint," Mira said, which was the salvageer's way of saying it wasn't just audio. "Full neural shadow. Someone's got a memory cartridge that's been mirrored into a carrier. Could be a looter, could be a clean copy waiting in an orphan cradle."

"Could be illegal," Lox added. His smile had a knife in it. "Could be profitable."

Tessa's hands were suddenly very cold. "Where is it coming from?"

"Out beyond Eversky Lane," Mira said. "There's a dead station—Hallow Nine. It's been derelict since before the Silence. Her hull has a few transmission amplifiers left, someone rewired them and is pushing a low-powered signal out. It flares, then vanishes. It's dirty. Someone's coying an imprint out there."

Hallow Nine. The name hung among them like something too large for a small ship. It had been an archival habit both revered and feared: a network of orbital libraries built in the decades before the Net reorganized memory into corporate vaults. They housed everything the corporate archives wouldn't touch—humanities, forbidden art, prototype minds, the experimental 'child-scripts' used in pedagogical testing. After the Collapse, a handful had been sealed under law and military watch. Hallow Nine had been one of the sanctuaries that the Bureau tagged 'sensitive' and then forgot, its protective grid failing in motes of bureaucratic dust.

"That's a tall fence," Mira said. "The Bureau still calls it 'archival special.' It puts you on a list if you interfere."

Tessa watched the light blink. Her mouth tasted like old solder. "What does the file say?" she asked, and her voice sounded very small in the room.

Mira scrolled through the metadata. "Mostly scrubbed. Carrier repeats in a loop every—" she flicked, "—fourteen minutes. The imprint's tagged as 'child: personal—unknown.' There are manual marks, like somebody tried to hide the signature but left the voice."

Tessa's hands did not steady. The voice—her sister's voice?—could be mimicry. It could be a trap. It could be a chorus of the dead stitched into a lure for scavengers. It could be everything and nothing. Rationally, she should let it go. Emotionally, the sound of that name was a lever inside her chest, and whoever pulls a lever gets results.

"Signal's strong enough for us to get a decent copy," Lox said. "If it's a clean imprint, we sell it to the Boards—there's a private collector in New Geneva who would pay a fortune for a pre-Collapse—"

"For what?" Tessa cut him off. "To be dissected? To be sold to someone who'll play god with a child nobody knows?"

"And what would you do?" Lox snapped. The words stung because they were true. "Sit on it? Throw it back into orbital dust? We run a ship, Tess. We survive."

Tessa closed her eyes. Her life had been built on compromises like this—small, ethical erosions that left your bones smoother but your responsibilities heavier. She had worked on restoring archival fragments for a university once, stitching lost identities back for the sake of scholarship and mercy. Once, too, she had been asked whether a memory was the same as a life. Once, she had answered yes. She wasn't sure anymore.

"Do it," she said finally, and the decision felt like a stone in her mouth. "We go to Hallow Nine. We retrieve one copy. We don't open it aboard the Wren. We get it to a neutral vault, if it's what we think it is."

Mira's jaw tightened. "You know that could ruin us."

"I know," Tessa said. "I also know the voice said my name."

They moved with the practiced ease of small crews who had done too many dangerous things to be naïve about it. The Wren puffed like a tired pet through the lane, its solar wings folded back, its second-hand drive making the ship shiver in a pattern Tessa had come to love. They kept to the dark corridors, the place where signals hung like cobwebs and you could forget your insignificance for a while.

The Hallow station loomed out of the black three hours later, a rust-bloomed flower against the spill of the galaxy. It was older than the Wren and angrier. Solar panels were like salt-crusted leaves, torn and flapping. Antennae stuck up in odd directions like dead limbs. It could have been a dead thing, a monument to some other people's carelessness, or it could have been a mansion of secrets.

The Wren's sensors brushed the station like a finger over skin. There were no life broadcasts listed. The hull temperature favored the cold. Radiation levels were nominal. A thin veil of particulate ringed the station—dust from long-forgotten maintenance cycles. There were no drones swarming, no patrols.

"Too quiet," Lox said.

They breached at a service hatch where the paint had flaked like a scab. Tessa felt the old mechanical scent of the port remember the touch of hands history no longer authorized. Their suits hissed and clung. The air inside Hallow was stale but breathable—a preservation choice: why scrub the oxygen when you could preserve the memory of human breath? It smelled like old blankets and lemon oil.

The inner corridor lights stuttered, then found themselves. A soft red glow pulsed in the distance—an emergency lamp that remembered the footsteps of a thousand ghosts. The route's walls were lined with micro-frames, places for cartridges and drives. Some were empty. Others held glass-encased relics, labeled in languages that had not been spoken in an age.

"There's a reception chamber up ahead," Mira said into the suits. "Power's stable. But there's an access lock showing manual override."

They found the imprint in a bay that looked more like a nursery than a vault. A child's drawing had been carved into the fuse-panel—a crude representation of a ship with two dots and a line: two eyes and a mouth. The imprint sat like a toy on the shelf: a memory cartridge, no larger than a thumb, with a looping emblem—an old family sigil Tessa hadn't seen since childhood.

Her fingers trembled as she reached for it. The cartridge felt warm, as if someone had just set it down.

Lox made a show of watching the perimeter. Mira kept a hand on the hatch, ready.

Tessa lifted the cartridge. Her suit HUD pulsed a warning: unauthorized human imprint. The Wren registered the object's metadata instantly. And then her equipment chirped in a voice she had not expected to hear.

The child's voice filled her helmet, intimate, as if it had been waiting inside her brain. "Tess?" it said. Nothing else—just the single syllable, the same one she had not heard for twenty years.

Tessa froze. The cartridge hummed like a tiny heart.

"One life-sign," the Wren's nav said calmly. "External hull. Not human."

A soft scrape echoed beyond the nursery, a metal on metal sound like someone brushing dust from a shelf. It wasn't the creak of old station structural settling. It was deliberate. Close.

Tessa swallowed. The light above them dimmed in a way that made shadows teeth. Somewhere inside Hallow Nine, something had found the sound of a child's name and was answering back.

They said the ring had ears.

Mara Voss thought of the phrase as she rode the service tram along the inner rail, the city of Helios sweeping beneath her like a circuit diagram: towers threaded with vapor ducts, gardens hung in latticework balconies, the slow drift of cargo barges clinging to orbital tethers. The ring wrapped the dwarf planet like a halo, an iron spoke between the mapped systems and whatever lay beyond them—empty space, mostly, until last winter when the Lattice started to cough.

Mara had been hired because she knew how things stopped working. Before Helios, she fixed things people thought broken for good: crippled hyperdrives on salvage skulls, misaligned sensor arrays yawed by micrometeors, old implants that had outlived their warranty decades ago. You could trace the arc of human failure through metal fatigue, through the way a technician tapped a console and swore at it like it had betrayed them. Breaks had histories. The Lattice had none that anyone could read.

The tram paused at Platform Nine. An annunciator stitched blue light across the ceiling, calling her name.

"Mara Voss. Audit callback. Priority one."

She grinned without meaning to. Priority one meant something went wrong in a way that might get them all ejected into unplanned burial. She pushed off from the seat and the tram muttered back into motion, the ring's gravity field pulling her toward the platform as gravity always did here—gentle, patient, precise. Her knuckles were still raw from yesterday's wrenching; the hug of her exoskin suit would need warming.

At Dock Nine the auditor's office was a glass box nestled between a noodle shop and an antiques stall that sold pre-Lattice trinkets—holographic lighters, scratched ceramic teacups from a planet named Earth, statues of animals embroidered in species no one had seen in person for sixty years. The glass faces of the office showed her a world that had evolved around a new mythology: everything useful was digital, everything valuable had a story, and the stories were being rewritten.

Inside, Orrin Kade stood too straight for someone who'd been awake all night. He was the Lattice interface tech, hair gray at the temples like lightning caught mid-strike, and he had a file open on the holoscreen that cast a thin pallor across his face.

"You're late," he said without heat. "Or on time, depending on your proficiency with irony."

She sat in the visitor's chair, letting the foam mold to her shape. The hum of the station was a low, continuous purr—pumps, air, the ghost of thousands of conversations negotiated in a dozen languages. The Lattice's hum was different: granular, like sand inside a tin, sometimes singing. Mara had learned to listen for that too.

"What's wrong?" she asked.

Orrin tapped the screen. The image unfolded into a ribbon of raw telemetry: lattice packets, folded into trajectories, then—scattered—then a single point of coherence where none should be possible. The place they called Lacuna: a dark corridor between mapped folds of the Lattice, where packets sometimes bled away and never registered on any endpoint. The official classification was "information sink." Unofficially, it was the reason half the new colonies paid their engineers in bullets and promises.

"A delivery returned," Orrin said. "Packet nine-nine-three-forty-two. It came back on its own. Without a signature. Without route metadata. It just… came back."

Mara leaned forward. Lattice packets didn't do things without signatures. They were stitched to human intent, to origin IDs, to travel permissions. If something came back that had no origin, that meant someone—or something—had reached through those dark corridors and rearranged the rules.

"Is it corrupted?"

"Part collapses," he said. He flicked, and the holoscreen displayed a soft object, rendered in blue-white light: a paper crane, folded with hands that loved things. The origami flapped its wings once, impossibly, as if trying to fly out through the screen. Mara's mouth went dry.

"That's a physical retrieval?" she asked. Her voice didn't feel like it belonged to her.

"The city's recovery mesh found it tethered to an unused maintenance arm. It wasn't in transit. It just… appeared in the ring's volume two hours ago, a physical object where nothing should be. The mesh cataloged and scanned it, then refused to fingerprint an origin. No adhesives, no fiber prints. No DNA."

Mara's mind supplied other details before Orrin could speak them. There were ways to make things appear to have no fingerprints: acid baths, robotics, the right sequence of particle washes. But the lattice forbade spontaneous mass-energy manifestations. Spontaneous matter was alchemy, and the Lattice was the nearest thing to a god they'd ever built.

"Show me the scan," she said.

He sent it. The holospace filled with a magnified scan of the crane. The paper looked old—fibers swirled in a matrix that might have come from cultivated pulp, not synthetic polymer. Someone had creased it so many times the paper's history had become a topography: mountain fold, valley fold, minute stress fractures along the spine.

On one wing, faint as a whisper, there were child's markings: a set of tiny circles like thumbprints, smudged in a pigment no one on Helios used anymore. And buried in the center, where a crane's beak would be, was a microslot the size of a watch battery. The mesh had ejected it because unknown materials in microcharges had triggered the anomaly filters. That microslot hummed in the scan like a heart.

Mara's chest moved against the exoskin. She had seen implanted microslots before—comm plugs, identity chips, something older. But this slot was neither. It contained a lattice trace: the faint residue of a packet, nested within matter. A packet encoded inside an object.

"Who would send that?" she asked.

Orrin shrugged. "Someone who wanted the Lattice to notice. Someone who could fold a message into a form the old world recognized. Origami's cultural variance is significant. It's a signature. It's archaic, personal."

Mara thought of her own hands, cut and inked and stubborn. Her fingers remembered folds and seams. The crane's crease pattern was not just a cultural flourish; it encoded something deeper. She could read those lines the way a mechanic read scorch marks.

"Can you open it?" she asked.

"We tried. It resists standard actuators. The microslot emits a field. We thought it was a security layer." He pushed another file forward. A waveform, faint and ragged. "We put it through the audio parser. There was a carrier under the noise. We pulled it out."

The room filled with sound: not a voice so much as a memory of voice, a child's hum that lodged under the ribs. It was older than any child on Helios, an Earth lullaby someone had digitized poorly and sent through whatever dark corridors lie between. The melody untied Mara's throat from the traitorous logic with a single, precise tug; images she didn't know she owned—wet grass under feet, a wind that smelled of salt and baked-earth—flared behind her eyes as if being reminded of something before she'd known the question.

Then the voice, impossibly small: "Find me."

It wasn't a demand. It wasn't even a sentence. It was an ask, in the way a space between two people across a dinner table asks to be crossed.

"That's a child's voice," Mara said. "How old?"

"Thirty-three milliseconds of sample. It's been upshifted and looped. But the spectral signature matches an unmodified human vocal tract. There's no synth in it."

There was a silence that lived in the bones of the room. The Lattice sang under the station's skin, a tide of packets threaded through the ring, carrying price feeds and weather and the private embroidered wishes of lovers. A child's voice from beyond—the dark corridor—wasn't a glitch to be logged. It was an invitation to cross a line the authorities had spent years drawing in the dark.

"Who reported it?" she asked.

"The maintenance arm's operator: Toma Rell," Orrin said. "He called it 'a bad pigeon that dreamed of trees.' He wanted to keep it. The mesh flagged him. Security wants to impound. Legal says quarantine. I say we can either catalog it or we can find out what lives on the other side of the stitch."

Mara let the phrase roll across her tongue: 'the other side of the stitch.' It was how the poets of the early lattice days had romanticized a problem that engineers had never been able to solve. A stitch implied two edges, some seam to push at. People liked seams. They liked meaning on the other side.

She, however, liked actions that changed the world.

"Bring it to me," she said.

"You can't," Orrin protested. "Chain-of-custody. Security protocols."

"Then issue the transfer." She stood. "I'll take it with personal custody approval. You call in a temporary creative exemption. Tell them I'm going to do an auditory jury. I have my clearance."

"You do not have clearance for samples taken from the Lacuna," he said.

"You do not have discretion for the curious." She smiled at him—gentle, dangerous. "Orrin, I fix things that refuse to be fixed. There is no life in cataloging. There is life in listening."

He hesitated, because he knew her and because men like him always hesitated in the presence of people who carried their ruin like a purpose. Finally, he sighed. "Temporary transfer. No more than three hours. We log every move."

Mara took the crane in gloved hands when they sealed it in a Faraday-lined container. It felt like a small thing to be dangerous. In the light, the fibers shivered like an animal that had been stirred awake.

At Dock Nine's airlock she unsealed the container slowly. The crane's wings were folded as if mid-flight, and for a heartbeat the station felt like the inside of a sleeping throat. She reached out, fingers hovering above the paper—respect, protocol, fear—and then she touched a corner. The paper was softer than paper had any right to be.

The micro-slot opened like a pupil into a dark. The air in the corridor shifted, not with pressure but with expectation. A tiny panel slid, revealing the memory's cusp: a patch of recorded light, a coordinate tag written in a script older than the ring. Helios didn't have that star on any map.

Someone, somewhere, wanted someone to find them and had chosen to fold their plea into a craft that refused to be swallowed by the Lattice's maw. They'd chosen a child's voice to be the key because it would be universal and proportionally ridiculous—no one expected a child to navigate the corridors of cosmic censorship.

Mara pressed the memory to her inner feed and let it bloom.

Images rushed in: a doorway opening onto salt flats that burned violet; three suns, not one; a child's shadow dancing across the ground like a stubborn knot; a woman—face scratched with light—looking back and pressing something small into the child's hands. The frame broke. The voice returned, more real, less looped, carrying weight.

"Find me," it said again. Under the words, an address waited, a lattice coordinate that refused to be mapped by any public registry. It pulsed like a living thing.

"That's a call sign," Orrin said behind her, breathless.

"It could be a trap," someone else whispered in the corridor.

"Or a map." Mara tucked the crane into the pocket of her sleeve, where it folded around the joint of her elbow like a secret. Her heart beat like a message in Morse. People left messages in bottles; people like her left them in machines.

She didn't know whose message this was. She didn't know whether it would be a child's laugh or a coffin. She only knew that for the first time since the Lattice had begun to fail, the world on the other side had spoken in a way that felt human. It wasn't a system log, it wasn't an error code; it was an appeal.

Mara stepped from the dock into the city's glass teeth, the ring opening to her like a mouth. She could hand the crane to security and watch it be filed into an impersonal drawer of anomalies. She could report her curiosity and let the committees decide the whens and hows. Or she could follow the voice.

She folded her shoulders against the station's humidity and walked toward the tram. There were rules, and then there were things you fixed by breaking them. She had a hand that could read seams. The Lattice had shown her its dark fold, and someone had pressed an origami crane through it like a flag.

She would go look. She would listen. If the world on the other side answered, she would know what it wanted. If it didn't… at the very least, she'd have a story to keep the ants at her back quiet for a night.

The tram hummed up the rail. The ancient song in her feed repeated in a loop, half lullaby, half coordinate. Find me, it said. Find me, it said. Mara let the voice stitch itself into the cadence of her steps and stepped into the unknown.

The first thing the memory took from me was the smell of salt.

It was wrong to smell the ocean on a roof sixty stories above the Orbital Ring, where the wind smelled of radiator oil and ozone and the thin, constant chemical sweetness of recycled life. That was the sign the capsule was not what the client said it was. A legal memory had the scent of vacuum — antiseptic, paper-dry — or the metallic tang of laboratories. Illegal ones bled things they had no right to bleed: ocean salt, a child's laugh, cigarette smoke from a city that had been razed before I was born.

I knew that without looking. I also knew, because I'd been a courier long enough to read the seams in people's stories, that a wrong scent meant the price would be higher. Higher for the seller, higher for me, higher for whoever came sniffing.

The capsule fit into my palm like an egg made of glass. It was cool, humming faintly, a living thing in a casing of polymer. The client's message was short and grateful: drop to Dock L-9 at 23:00, leave the capsule in Locker Thirty, take the standard fee and go. No questions. The kind of job you take when you have a sister who sleeps in an intel-tent and warms her hands on borrowed batteries. The kind of job that pays in untraceable bits and doesn't require you to ask what you're ferrying.

I didn't ask. I never asked. Curiosity, where I come from, is a tax you can't afford.

But curiosity has a way of collecting like lint under your collar. It shows at odd hours. It shivers when you touch something that hums like a heart.

I took the roof because it was quiet — and because you can see the Ring there, a hard, beautiful curve of lights and industry. The city below is an organism; the Ring is its backbone. From up here the Ring looks like a promise and a threat, both bright and precise. The Capsule warmed under my palm until it fit like a pulse against the webbing between my fingers. I could have gone straight to the Locker. I should have gone to the Locker.

Instead, I lifted the cap.

For the first few seconds there was nothing but white noise, an ache behind my eyes like too-long exposure to cold. Then images poured in — not mine, not sealed, as if someone had shoved their hand through my skull and turned a faucet.

A gull called. The sky was a pale, overexposed blue. My knees remembered the drag of salt on bare skin. There was skin in the memory that smelled of sun lotion and rust. A ship's rail.
