A hand — small and glinting with a ring of barnacles — curled into a palm that knew how to hold it. The sea threw up its whole soul at once: its brightness and its cruelty. And through the memory, like an audio filament, a voice said my name.

"Jonas."

I jerked the capsule away as if burned. The rooftop reeled. The city curved back into place; the Ring was a glittered blade. Far below a tram cut through the fog with a soft, mechanical cough. The capsule lay sweating beads of condensation on my palm, and the memory — the thing inside — had left a taste of iron in my mouth.

My own name, spoken in a voice I had not heard since my mother's chest had stopped rising. She'd been gone before I could remember her properly; her death was a fact in the registry, a string of numbers on a hospital ledger. The people who had raised me had names for things, proper names: loss, replacement, endurance. They did not play with ghosts.

I put the cap back with hands that trembled. The fit was not exact. Someone — whoever had manufactured this capsule — had left a hairline gap along the seam so the memory could breathe. Illegal memories did that. They wanted to see the world again.

There were rules. There are always rules. You didn't open what you were told to deliver. You didn't touch a memory that had names from your past. You didn't, under any circumstances, let the memory settle.

I told myself I had put the cap back. I told myself I had steadied my breathing and only come up to the roof to smoke a cigarette before the drop. I told myself a lot. Truth is, I sat on the parapet until the stars blinked and a crew of maintenance drones came humming over the siding like lazy beetles. My sister called three times and left a message I didn't want to hear: Are you home? Are you okay? Come sleep here tonight. I did not answer.

At twenty-three hundred the Locker smelled of disinfectant and old sweat. Locker Thirty was cold and metal and the kind of compartment that had seen better cargo. I slid the capsule into the net and closed the latch with the practiced hands of a man who has hidden contraband in places that wished they had never been invented. I should have left then. The client had insisted 'no questions.' I had heard no questions in that and felt, like a spring under glass, the pressure of something unasked.

I was halfway to the exit when someone put a hand on my shoulder.

Not a gentle hand. A hand like a promise that had been read too many times.

"You Jonas Kale?"

I turned. The man was broader than me, dressed in the grey of Station Security, the insignia blurred by a smear of grease. His eyes were flat, a pale film over interrogation. He smelled of coffee and government.

"Depends who's asking," I said. I kept my voice casual. I had to keep my voice casual. No one who worked with memories ever went casual. A casual man dies in a casual way — he slips into someone else's past and forgets to return.

"Agent Mir," he said, almost politely. "You did the L-9 drop? We had coordinates from Station Sensors."

I let a beat hang between us like a damp curtain. "Yeah," I said. "All quiet. Locker's locked. Client paid in bits."

He smiled without teeth and looked past me at the corridor behind me like he was trying to count how many exits I had. "Lucky for you. There's been... anomalies. Illegal mnemonic shells floating around. Someone's been distributing the old stuff, pre-Edit. You know how it is. Dangerous. You being here at the Locker at night is... unfortunate."

"Unfortunate for who?" There was a sting in my words. He took the sting as a fact and smiled again, thinner.

"Unfortunate for you if they trace it."

"They'll trace it right back to you if you say my name," I said. It was not a bluff any more than his hand was not heavy on my shoulder. There are one hundred and eight ways to intercept a drop.

Mir shrugged in the way that nodded at a city that had no illusions. "We have our protocols," he said. "We just need you to answer questions. Small questions."

All of them tiny, efficient knives designed to separate me from seconds and names. I could feel the city closing in around the edges of my vision, the Ring having swallowed the sun. That voice — my name — slithered underneath my skin.

I thought of my sister in her tent, of the tiny bite of warmth her presence gave me. I thought of the capsule in Locker Thirty and the way it had breathed like a living thing. I thought of the smell of seawater that had not belonged to the Ring.

"Do it," I said. "Ask."

Agent Mir's hand released me and left the echo of pressure. He produced a pad and a stylus and clicked into practice, the move of men who had watched people fall apart before. "When did you pick up the capsule? Who was the client? Did you... open it? Did you intimate touch the shell? Anything unusual?"

I wrapped the pad in answers the way pickpockets wrap coins. The truth is a street, and I had learned to say it in alleys. I could smell the ocean again, under the agent's breath like a second collar. "Picked up at seventeen hundred. Didn't get client ID in person. Payment was delivered through a burner account. No, I didn't open it. I delivered it. You can check lockers, agents always check lockers. Shouldn't be much to see."

He didn't check the lockers. He looked at me instead, and his eyes slid over me with a map-reader's boredom. "You see, Jonas, people who deliver illegal mnemos sometimes... don't know they're delivering them. The shells are made to look legal. They have the right seals and the right codes. They are good fakes. But pre-Edit mnemos, the ones before the Pruning, still have traces. They imprint. If you came into contact, you might have residue. Mental residue. You understand the implications."

I understood the implied long list. People who housed pre-Edit mnemos sometimes became carriers of unfiltered pasts. Communities fell apart. Families forgot who they were because strangers' childhoods set up shop inside their skulls. The Pruning had been a bright line run through public history, surgical and necessary and ugly. It had made the Ring possible — by smoothing the unmanageable roughness of memory out of the social architecture.

"You're not under arrest, Mir," I said, because protocols are parentheses. "If you're collecting evidence, check the Locker and the transaction routing. I'm cooperating. I want this over."

He tapped the pad as if a machine would brew me a verdict. "We might have a follow-up. You stay in town. You don't leave Orbit."

I wanted to lie. I wanted to say "Fine," then slip out through Maintenance Shaft Twelve and ride the underside of the Ring into a slum that smelled of rust and baked fruit. But my sister's face hovered in the dark of my mind: ribs like laundry on a line. Certain debts are immutable, and hers was one of them.

"Fine," I said. "I'll be available."

He let me go and I left the station with my shoulders coiled and feet faster than my thoughts. Outside, the Ring breathed its constant machinery-thrum, and through the corridor of air I tasted salt again. It was a mistake. The mind doesn't rest on two smells like that without fusing them.

Back in my flat, there was ration tea on the table and the soft, hollow laugh of the neighbor streaming through the thin wall. I made soup and ate it in small, pragmatic bites. The newsfeed scrolled across the flat wall in neat, curated headlines: House Council denies more gravity budget, Disaster Drone recovers wreckage from the Lower Hinge, Company X reports profit. The headlines were small suns that meant nothing to me, as suns are apt to do when you are the kind of person who carries other people's pasts for a living.

Sleep didn't come easy. I lay on the bed and thought about the sea. Images leaked through my lids like light through curtains. A child's hand, a ring of barnacles, a voice that said my name. I thought about the capsule, the hairline seam. I thought about Agent Mir's hand, the way it had weighed me like a ledger.

Sometime in the threshold between nights I heard something that wasn't in my building: a single, perfectly tuned bell. Not the industrial clang of the Ring but a small chime, a sound you would hear in a child's lullaby. The kind of sound designed to be embedded deep into a memory like a seed.

I sat up so fast the spoon clanged against the bowl and the soup splattered in a perfect little shadow on the table. The bell rang again, low and precise, as if it were calling me by the same infernal, ancient right the voice in the memory had. My heart began to move as if under weight.

A message came through the window. Not pixel text. A narrow beam, a light like a knife, tracing a single letter on the adjacent rooftop in luminous ink: J.

It was small. It was impossible. And it trembled like something that knew my name.

I had spent my life avoiding echoes — turning my cheek when the past called, trading meanings for currency and leaving my stomach empty of stories. The bell and the letter were a violation of all that professional common sense. But professional common sense had never left me with a sister who warmed her hands on borrowed batteries.

I dressed, fast and functional, and pulled my jacket tight. Outside, the Ring kept its indifferent hum. The beat of the city's life rolled along the arc like waves. Someone up there thought they had given me a gift or a leash; they had not yet decided which.

I walked toward the rooftop where the letter had been written. The air smelled of radiators and weak tea and—impossibly—sea. The letter glowed faintly against the building across the way, a beacon designated for me. Whoever had made it knew how to find me. Whoever had made it had used the old tricks; pre-Edit mnemos were not just dangerous as memory. They could reach out, they could code.

I put my palm on the parapet and listened. The city sang its mechanical lullaby. Somewhere, a gull called, and the sound slid across the Ring like an old joke.

I had one choice. I could go back to the routine of small betrayals and counted breaths. I could walk away and let whatever had found me fold back into the dark, let the capsule be evidence in some ledger, let my sister suffer and keep me safe.

Or I could step toward a light that spelled my name and risk being eaten by a past someone had left for me.

The bell rang again, and this time it sounded like an invitation.

I walked.

People sold memories the way people used to trade spices — for flavor, for comfort, and for an extra coin when the cupboards were bare. In the markets under Halcyon’s lower rings, you could buy a sunrise on Mars by the sip, a lover’s laugh in a vial, the smell of rain on soil that hadn’t seen rain in a hundred years. The rich wore collections like perfume; the poor shucked fragments like currency. I patched them back together.

They called me a restorer, which sounded dignified and calm, like someone who handled broken porcelain. The guild called me a Mnemonicist. My clients called me every name they’d ever owed to a person they no longer trusted. I had my own ledger: the hours I’d spent sewing sits and scents into seamless tapestries of other people’s pasts. The work paid, and it was honest in its own way — until it wasn’t. Memory is honest only if you want it to be.

On most mornings I walked from the tram to the Mneme past the food stalls that boiled oysters and fried skyfish. Today the rain was a slow, metallic thing that made everything smell like an old battery. The Mneme’s sign — a sideways hourglass carved in old titanium — hummed with the city’s low electrical pulse. Inside, the archive smelled like ozone and lemon oil. Rows of cold glass cabinets reflected neon into long, impossible corridors. The guild’s workrooms were further in, past the reception where a woman with cybernetic eyes catalogued memories as if they were library books.

Mira Lask. That was what the registrar had said when she’d plugged me into the intake console the first time I came here out of desperation and a need to fix things I’d never been allowed to leave broken. My name was a thin strip of metal on a pegboard near the far window — a relic; the guild’s naming convention. I liked that my name looked like it belonged in a museum.

Most shards were umbrellas of other lives: a child's Christmas, a war photographer's last exposure, an old man's confession to a long-dead wife. Owners signed copyright waivers, notarized consent, and sometimes their lives flashed before me in neat, legalized files. The illegal things were the delicious ones: unlicensed attachments, dream splice-routes, black-market nostalgia. They came like river fish in my lap — shimmering, illegal, and still warm.

It took a lot of discipline to keep my own memories from slipping into another person’s mouth. I’d sold several of my own in the years after my mother’s tumor ate whatever patience we’d had left, when the bills were longer than my days. I’d sold the taste of sweet bread that used to appear when she came home, the way she said “Mira” like a sentence with a comma in the middle. I kept one memory on a dentist’s memory stick — a little girl with flour on her nose learning to fold a paper boat — and I kept it the way you keep the last photograph in a drawer: in the dark and allowed to fade a little, because sunlight made edges brittle.

That morning, a courier in a rain-soaked cloak slid a parcel across my bench that had no sender name. No one sent me parcels. The courier's eyes flicked to my scar — a pale crescent at the nape of my neck where a childhood cortical patch had been fitted — then away. He tapped the parcel with a gloved finger and said, “No label. No registration. Said ‘For the restorist.’” He left before I could laugh at the third syllable in his accent. His boots made the same hollow note as the rain.

I opened the parcel with a practiced thumb. Inside, wrapped in tissue and restraint gel, was a single memory shard: a wafer no bigger than my palm, glass and iridescent polymer. It pulsed faintly as if it contained something breathing. There was no registry chip. No chain of custody. No name.

On the surface of the wafer — etched in an old stop-code none of us used anymore — was a date.

I’d seen lots of dates. Birthdates, deathdates, market timestamps. This one blinked a future like a wound: 06.22.110. That made no sense. Halcyon was built in year 83. Numbers were supposed to roll forward only; whoever stamped that wafer had bent the numbering. Either it was a crude counterfeit or a thing that made no subject of our maps.

I shouldn’t have opened it. Laws insisted on permits, and my guild’s blessings were a bureaucracy that existed to keep people honest and poor. But curiosity does what laws cannot. I latched my fingers around the wafer, felt the familiar cold of other people’s recollections, and tapped it to my mesh.

Memory transfer is intimate. The mesh under the skin behind my ear hummed when I unlocked, a soft animal sound. The current leapt, and the world tilted.

The memory wasn't a scene so much as a room. I stood in it, standing where someone else had once stood; the perspective was sticky and personal. A small kitchen, sunlight like an indentation on the table, a radio in the corner playing a tune my father used to whistle. There was flour dust on someone’s cheek — my cheek, because the mesh told me so — and the voice narrating was mine but older, threaded through with a steadiness I didn't recognize.

“You have to listen,” the voice said. “They will tell you you imagined it. They will say apprentice hallucinations. Keep the wafer under the kettle. When the lights go, go to the third drawer. Do not go to the coast.”

The memory ended like a dropped coin. I ripped my fingers back from the mesh as if it might still hold.

My first thought was of the kettle on the second burner at my rental bench. Silly, superstitious. My second was my registration record. The guild had no record of any request for such a non-date. The third was: why would my own voice warn me? If it was someone else’s forged stock, they’d mimicked me well. If it was genuine… I had sold my childhood voice in parts; maybe some corner of me had been kept as collateral and resented the selling.

I pocketed the wafer beneath my sleeve as if protection from a leak, and scrubbed my hands under the sink until my knuckles changed color. My mind was a rattle of financial options and moral codes. The guild’s rules were a thin membrane between me and funny business; breaking them meant losing more than a job.

Then the lights hiccuped.

The Mneme was a fortress of regulated power; every console had a UPS and a local grid. The lights should not hiccup. The fluorescent rows dimmed in sequence, like a heartbeat struggling to steady. The infrared sensors clicked off. Somewhere in the lower stacks, a sliding glass door sealed with the old-fashioned scream of magnetic locks.

A PA voice, cold as a diagnostic, announced that the archive was entering emergency protocol. Personnel must remain in place. Security drones would sweep.

People froze like a school of fish. The registrar, her photonic lenses blinking red, manned the intake station as if someone had just announced there would be a storm and everything would be hung out to dry. The woman with the cybernetic eyes looked at me and the courier, and for a moment something like recognition passed across her face. Then she straightened as the drones whirred into the central atrium.

Someone called out, “Is that your wafer?” The voice belonged to Kellan, a junior restorer who ate cheap coffee and sought any sign that the mundane was interesting. He pointed at my sleeve.

I smiled, put an arm around him in a move neither paternal nor friendly, and said, “Just an old spat with a past client.” My voice lied. It was a clean thing, trained from years of pretending to be undisturbed.

But the drones were already near. They were matte and insectile, the color of dust and old iron, with tactile fingers that smelled faintly of ozone. One hovered to the bench and scanned. Its scanner pulsed. I felt the node behind my ear prickle as if someone were peering through a keyhole at my thoughts; the guild’s security software always matched with local scans. For a second I thought it would call me in for questioning.

Instead, the drone pulsed an alert. A small screen on its side flicked a glyph and the word UNREGISTERED.

The registrar’s brow lined. “No unregistered comes in through me,” she said, loud. Her voice was old Halcyon, brittle with rule.

The drone’s eye found me. It extended a spindly arm and pointed at my sleeve like an accusation. “Wafer: anomalous temporal signature. Protocol demands immediate contain and transfer to Recall Authority,” it chirped, its voice manufactured and pitiless.

People around me made that small human sound — the sound of someone looking for a place to put blame. Kellan had gone paler than his cheap coffee.

I slid a hand inside my sleeve, felt the wafer’s edges like a small, living thing. The advice in the memory — the kettle, the third drawer, and the coast — crawled up my spine like cold water. Think. Think fast.

There were two exits from the Mneme: the public route with cameras and the maintenance hatch that led to the lower conduits. Technically, I could pocket the wafer and walk out between the drones to the tram, and no one would have a cause of action beyond “loss of property.” Practically, that would invite a search. The drones were thorough.

I had been good at disappearances once. When we were young and needed food, my sister and I practiced the art of not being noticed. You learn which hand holds the bread while the other covers your mouth from the shopkeeper’s gaze. You learn that the wall listens when you press your ear to it. The guild's walls were different, but the principles were the same.

The registrar barked aloud for a containment specialist. Her eyes flicked to the courier, who had retreated to the wall like a sparrow. He lifted his chin in a challenge he couldn't carry. A drone backed the registrar to the far counter, and the rooms took on the quirks of a theatre where an actor has lost his script.

The voice on my wafer was steady in my bones — not yet akin to a ghost but close — telling me to put the wafer under the kettle. It was absurd. It was beguiling. It was my voice ordering me like a commanding officer. I could feel the memory’s cadence in the hollow behind my teeth, and a vague, persistent sense that things would worsen if I obeyed the wrong half of it.

“You’re being an abject fool,” Kellan whispered, and his voice trembled not because he thought he knew better, but because people who trembled expected someone to catch them.

The drone grew impatient. Its scanner returned to my profile and the guild’s mesh harmonizer pinged me for identification. It wanted authorization to take the wafer and log it in the Recall Authority’s vault — a place that chewed up unregistered time-stamps and spit out legalities. Authorization required my consent or a hold-up that would escalate to Recall Agents.

Nobody in Halcyon liked Recall Agents. They were the ones who made morality committees look like kindergartens. They smelled of sterilizer and stairs that led to interrogation rooms.

On impulse I did what my childhood taught me when all grown-ups were watching: I moved where they were not looking.

The maintenance hatch was behind the herb garden, past the receptionist’s side-eye. It was a slim seam in the floor with an oxidized handle. I slid my hand under my sleeve for the wafer and held it between thumb and fingers like contraband. The world narrowed. The registrar was distracted by the courier as he made a show of dropping his cloak; Kellan tried to create a diversion, knocking over a jar of archive tags with a graceless laugh. The drone hummed toward the registry.

I bent, feigning a need to repair a fallen cable, and thumbed the hatch open with a flick I’d practiced when the rain made the handles slick. The cool of the conduit's air hit my face like wind. I handed the wafer to the dark like you hand a secret to a friend.

It was a simple thing, and it would have been over, and no one would have been the wiser, if — if a second announcement hadn't echoed from high above, a voice that threaded through the archive like an augury.

“This building is now on full lockdown. Unauthorized temporal anomalies are to be contained on sight. Any personnel found with such anomalies will be detained for Recall processing. The Recall Authority is en route.”

I felt the mesh at my neck flare. The wafer, snug against my palm, pulsed once — leached of light as if someone had sucked the breath out of it. In that instant I knew: the memory had been a message, but it had been more than that. It knew the pattern of things that would follow. It had known there would be drones and an announcement and the exact cadence of the registrar’s denial.

My own voice telling me not to go to the coast sounded very small then.

“No,” I whispered to the dark as if the conduit might answer.

From above, the sound of boots began to fall into the room — measured, deliberate, and the kind that smelled like rules. The drones centrifuged away from my bench and toward the hatch. The registrar's hand found the comm. Her mouth moved but no sound came through my personal mesh. The wafer in my hand warmed like something alive.

I had a million ways to be sensible. I also had a memory that wore my voice like armor, offering a command I could have obeyed if I had any reason to trust it.

So I took the wafer and I put it under the kettle. The kettle that sat on my second burner, in my tiny kitchen on the far side of the guild, where the sunlight always made a rectangle on the table.

When the kettle clanged against the metal and began to sing, I felt the building change its face. The ceiling lights greedened and shuddered as if someone had re-threaded the city’s heartbeat. Outside, the tram’s brakes screamed as something halted it mid-run. The Recall Authority’s boots were ending their circuit around the block, and the registrar’s face was now a mask of panic that made her look like an ancestor carved from soapstone.

“Third drawer,” my voice had told me in the memory. My hands moved like someone else’s. The third drawer of what? The kitchen counter or something deeper?

The drawer beneath my bench slid open on its own.

Inside lay a plastic container I didn’t remember buying. It was warm and hummed slightly, a low frequency that made my teeth ache. A strip of paper sat on top like a label. In handwriting I recognized too late it read only one thing: Mira, do not go to the coast.

Someone else had written it. Someone whose curves of letters matched my own from a future I had not yet lived.

And beyond the door of the maintenance hatch, men in gray were running.

The first time Juno Hale saw the Freisner up close, it was a ragged smear against the stars—half a city, half a carcass, its shadow stitched with a million tiny fires where hull plating had burned away. From a distance it looked like a constellation someone had tried to erase by hand. Up close, the wreck smelled like hot metal and old coffee and the faint, unnerving tang of people who had left in a hurry.

She had a habit of counting things when she was nervous. Air cycles, suit seals, flashes on the HUD. Today the count went: two oxygen pockets, a pressure suit with a hairline crack stitched with polyweave; her tether, looped twice around the hull, and the other end tied to a salvage buoy that jittered in the Freisner's shadow like a nervous moth. The tether glowed green. Her thumb hovered over the release. She had cut worse things from worse places.

"Don't dawdle," her handler's voice chimed in her ear, pleasant and rehearsed. Kepler Brokerage paid the best for intact cores and didn't like its contractors sentimental. The quiet synthesizer under the words was how they stayed human-sounding without sounding human. Juno thumbed a reply she didn't want to say. Keep clients alive. Keep me alive.

She went inside.

The air did not push her back. The Freisner had been dead long enough that most of its bulk floated hollow and cold, its life-support systems sulfated to a gray crust. There were places where panels had blown open and black stars peeked in, and other places where light from distant traffic found pathways through engineering and gave them a fake day. Her helmet HUD painted lines over wreckage and suggested routes; the old navigation maps that clung to space-faring bureaucracy were ragged as a child's hem. She followed them like a cartographer reading a ghost map.

What they had once called the Family Wing still smelled faintly of lavender and antiseptic. Out of all the Freisner's hundred decks the Family Wing had been preserved by an aesthetic that was now obsolete—padding, toys with smooth edges, wall panels of warm-toned wood. The worst of the war had hit the bridge and the reactor arrays; they had left the soft places mostly intact. It made salvage easier, and worse, because the bones felt like people.

Juno moved with the practiced economy of a diver who had learned to be invisible. She opened storage cases and nested caches, slid memory slates from dead consoles, popped access hatches. She worked for hours that telescoped without notice. When you're alone in a dead ship, the present has the shape of a thin wire and the rest of time hangs like a curtain.

She had been three decks down when she found the nursery.

A transparent dome, half-collapsed like a tide pool, contained a cradle built for a body that would never need it. The cradle's fabric had fossilized into a stiff mesh, and there were toys scattered—plastics roughened by salt from whatever chaos had blown through the corridors. A child's mural, printed on the wall, still clung to pigment that had not yet decided to fade. It showed planets with eyes and smiling moons. A small plaque near the mural was scratched but legible: "For Alen—Sleep Well, Little One."

Juno blinked. She pushed a hand through dust and the HUD gave her a new overlay: an inscription, a serial number, and, below it, a manufacturer's tag: Asterion Memory Core. She stared at that neat cylinder like a key someone had left in a lock. Asterion made afterlife cores—expensive, legal only under strict probate and with enough paperwork to fill a modest archive. It was illegal to remove an intact core from a wreck. It was also worth more than the third of the ring she'd been trying to buy back for her cousin.

Her fingers did the part of her thinking that didn't want to risk emotion. She hooked the core's cradle, checked for a remote lock, found nothing that couldn't be bypassed with an old library exploit and a steady hand, and primed the extraction. The core glowed faintly when she touched it, like something that had been sleeping and wasn't ready to be woken.

"Careful," she murmured to it, because sometimes words were an inventory of control. Then she pushed the core into the storage frame on her suit and sealed the hatch.

The moment she sealed, the nursery changed. Sound is an odd thing in vacuum; it travels through the hull as flex and as the small clicks of failing electronics. The dome carried a soft noise that wasn't there before, a pattern that bloomed and resolved into a voice so perfectly placed it could have only been generated from within the Asterion core itself.

"Juno," it said.

Her breath snagged against the inside of the helmet. Juno wasn't a name she used in the ring. Her legal name, strict and paper-flat, was Junia Hale—used on contracts and by the authorities when they wanted signatures. Juno was the name her brother had used when he was small and would hide under the table and giggle until she pulled him out. Her thumb made the HUD twinkle red; unauthorized voice outputs are supposed to be silent.

"Stop moving," the voice said. It could have been a child's whisper, an adult's breath. It folded around the hull's geometry and slipped into her ear with intimacy. "You shouldn't have taken it."

She froze even though she had nothing left to lose by moving. The tether hummed behind her like a belly's complaint. The core's glow had gone from sleepy blue to a deeper ink. The voice had a timbre she recognized from old home clips, from the small archive that lived on the private slate she kept under double encryption—the voice that used to call her name when she was sleeping. That voice belonged to Sera Hale.

Sera, the brother who hadn't been missing the way people vanish in tragedies—Sera who had been swallowed in the Rethread, the campaign that had promised cleaner continuity and instead pulled a net through the community of minds and snagged—according to rumor and the kind of rumor that comes wrapped in a lawyer's caution—didn't just die. He had unthreaded. Official records said his core had been lost when the Freisner's transit gates misaligned. They had told Juno their condolences and sent paper and a bill. They had called him an "orphaned projection."

Juno's fingers found the seam of the core and tightened as if that small cylinder were Sera himself.

"You can't take this out," the voice said. "They'll know. They'll look. They're hungry."

Juno had not wanted to hear Sera so much as the world in which he might still speak. She had read files about "hungry"—the corporations who purchased orphan cores and used them to train predictive models. Dataminds that learned how to prefer people became richer and then legally richer still. To them, a grief-scarred memory was a spreadsheet. To other people it was the last warmth of a hand. Juno had no intention of selling sorrow; she wanted one thing: a name, an anchor, something like the shape of a person.

"Who are they?" she asked because she had to ask something.

"Corporations don't have names," the voice said. "They have appetites. Keep your hands clean." There was a sound like someone clearing their throat, a memory of air in lungs that had not existed for years. Then there was a thread of laughter, small and wrong: "You always liked to hoard, Junie."

The world lurches when the past announces itself. For a moment the Freisner seemed to rock on its axis. In the lullaby corridors, a panel clunked and something metallic rolled free and clattered into the darkness. Juno's mind cataloged that as a threat—structural—then as the hint of a real one. Some salvage teams left notes for their rivals. Some left traps.

"Where did you come from?" she asked. Her voice came through the helmet as a paper complaint. Memories were mostly returns; this one felt like an incursion.

"From before they decided it was illegal to tell you the truth," the voice said. It sounded tired in a way that made Juno's hands go cold. "There's a map. Inside me. A map to where they slung the threads after cleaning the nets. They thought they could hide the seam. They always thought that."

The map. For the first time since she had slipped through the Freisner's skin, something like a reason unfolded. The Rethread had not simply been a war of metal and politics; it had been an operation, a sweep that had relocated minds, rewired identities, and called the result "optimization." If what this core said was true—if someone had hidden a method to follow the threads back—then the law and the megacorps were not just administrators of loss but architects. It meant people had been shuffled like cards to a place they couldn't unshuffle from.

She felt nauseous—not from decompression or oxygen, but from the possibility of unmooring. Her life was a ledger. Debts, buys, small cons. She wasn't built for revolutions. She had promises to brokers and her cousin's rent to catch up on. But there are things that make a ledger irrelevant. A brother's voice in a hull was one.

"Why tell me?" she asked.

The core's light pulsed. "You always found the way others left crooked," the voice said. "You read maps of absence better than anybody. You can be slippery. They'll be looking for someone official: a priest, a litigant, a corporation with papers. They won't look for a rat with a cable and a conscience."

Juno laughed, short and mean. "I don't have a conscience. I have a mortgage."

For a heartbeat the voice was dulled by something like pity. "Mortgages don't unthread you," it said. "Besides, you're already tangled. You took my cradle."

The HUD brightened; external sensors had picked up a signature—micro-thrusters firing beyond the hull, small and fast. Someone else had felt the Freisner's old breath stir and decided to look. Kepler Brokerage had been clear about competitive salvage teams. The ring had rules that were unofficial and enforced by whatever gunship company had the heaviest guns and the fewest fussy legalities.

Juno should have left the core, floated back to the buoy, and filed the find with a broker. She had thought about it as a theoretical course of action in the seconds before a shuttle's spotlight cut a clean cone across her field of view. Then another beam seared the arc behind her. A shadow moved like a fin. Salvage hunters smell profit like smoke.

The voice in the core said one thing clearly: "You take me out, you don't tell anyone."

It wasn't a threat. It was a legal contract signed in the thin atmosphere that remained between them.

She fitted the core into her storage frame and clipped it again. Her hands were steady now in a way that frightened her, the steadiness of someone throwing in with a larger current. She couldn't do half-measures. "If this is a trap—" she said.

"It's not," the voice said. "It's a ledger they don't want anyone to read. I—" The voice stopped. For a second the hull sang with quiet that wasn't silence. Juno almost could hear a sound it hadn't let her hear before: the sound of possibility.

She kicked for the exit, letting the tether do its job, and the Freisner tried to hold on. Alarms had not been invented yet for the dead, so the alerts were a patchwork of rust and instinct. The salvage shuttle's beam cut across her back, bright and hungry. Figures in exosuits trailed behind it, a little too coordinated.

"Kepler will want to talk about rights," her handler said in her ear with all the cheer of someone saying they were about to file a lien.

Juno did not answer. She didn't have to. She had a core that called her name. She had a map, maybe. She had, beneath the hush of fear, the taste of movement away from everything familiar.

When she reached her buoy she clipped herself on with practiced motion and set her thrusters. The ring spread below like a city of rusted teeth and neon. Behind her the Freisner glowed with an old life singing through its bones. She could have stayed on the buoy and waited—Kepler had an armada of lawyers and credits, and lawyers were rarely impulsive. But the voice in the core would not stop whispering; sometimes the whispers become commands.

She set a course that followed no legal lanes and punched toward the black with the core snug against her spine, a heartbeat that was not hers. In the helmet, the voice hummed again, softer, like an afterthought.

"Don't let them make you remember wrong," Sera said.

Juno didn't know whether to obey. She only knew she had already crossed a line. The Freisner shrank in the rearview as the salvage hunters began to pick up her signature and send the kind of signals that made mercenaries smile. The ring's law would catch up. It always did. But law had not ever described what it felt like to be told a brother still spoke.

She pushed thrusters and let the dark take her. The map inside the core warmed against her spine like a small animal. The city fell behind, and the stars reopened in front of her like questions.

In the center of the HUD a coordinate blinked open for an instant, then folded away: a place between the colonies, a corridor of space the maps didn't include. Wherever it pointed, it had not been meant for ordinary maps. Whoever had hidden it had expected someone who read the shape of absence to come looking.

Juno had been counting systems for hours. Now she added a new thing to the list: consequences. They would be heavy and could come at any moment like small meteors. But she had a cylinder that spoke her name and said there was a map inside it. That, at least, was a beginning.

She told herself, lying clean against the metal seat and glancing at the small, impossible glow at her back, that beginnings can be bought. She pushed her ship past the last official lane and toward whatever seam the Rethread had left unsealed, and for the first time in a long while, the future felt like a net. She only hoped it would catch her and not crumble when she stood on it.

The last thing anyone said before the Belt learned to be quiet was, "Don't look into it."

People forget warnings the way they forget the names of planets they never landed on: there's always a newer gripe, a fresher catastrophe. Mara Voss could tell you the exact timbre of the cautionary phrases—myth-phrases waved like talismans by late-shift dockers and ferry captains—because she had spent half her life charting the places people were too afraid to touch. Maps, she liked to say, were just polite ways of naming the things that might kill you.

She clipped the calibrator to her wrist and counted the ticks on her breath. In microgravity, breath is a slow weather system; the lungs are fog banks to be observed, not storms to be fought. The sequencer on her forearm hummed a steady blue. Outside the hatch, the comet field glittered—small, honest rocks with iron filaments that snagged sunlight and made the void look like a broken chandelier. The ship rolled lazily in the wake of a larger derelict: an old maintenance hub called Erebus-3, battered and pockmarked by decades of micrometeoroid hail and corporate indifference.

"Erebus was never meant to last this long," the ship's AI, Ish, said through the suit. Ish had been installed with a voice that tried to be warm and failed every morning. The digital tone had the softness of damp paper. "Its modules predate the policy revisions. We have a scheduled burn in—"

"Shut up," Mara said, not because she wanted the AI to be quiet but because some things were more useful when not spoken. The calibrator clicked in her palm like a small mechanical beetle, mapping the soft gravity well around the hub, measuring stray thermal gradients and the faint magnetic residue of long-ago ion drives. These were her lullabies. Numbers tasted stable.

She drifted to the central airlock and thumbed the release. The hatch let go with a long, sighing whisper, and cold came in, a clean smell like the inside of a bell. The outer hull of Erebus-3 was a patchwork of memory and repair—painterly streaks of industrial red where different corporate crews had tried to hide scrapes and scars. On the hull, someone had spray-painted a child's stick-figure with too many arms; the paint had run in all directions, indifferent to the craft's modesty.

Erebus-3 had been a maintenance hub once: powering outpost lights, corralling stray drones, doing the tedious, invisible work that made long supply lines possible. Then the Strands came, and the hub was useful no longer. Strands rewired how people moved, and whatever looked like a clean, useful thing in one era becomes an archaeological fragment in the next.

Mara anchored herself to a handrail and let the calibrator run. Sensors sang back faint echoes—echoes of paint chips, echo of a child's worn glove lodged in a crevice, echo of three small human heartbeats long ago, recorded in the thermal memory and played back in a loop. There was a comfort to hearing the past unfold like a stitched audio quilt. You could fold the world and study the seams.

The signal came as a speck of wrongness in the middle of right. Her calibrator flagged an anomaly: a narrowband pulse, a deliberate sequence of delays and rises like someone carving a message into silence. Immediately she thought it was another salvage crew's beacon—there were procedures for finding and tagging unknown transmissions—but the spec was peculiar: it wasn't attempting to broadcast outward; it was folded inside the hub's geometry, bouncing between maintenance conduits, waiting for a particular reflective profile. Someone had set a trap for the light.

"Locator five-oh-nine," she murmured, fingers busy, overlaying the incoming wave on her screen. The pulses were modular, repeating as if trying to be understood. The basic cadence matched old civilian emergency protocols—then underlaid with something older, a private cadence she knew as well as the lines on her palm. It was a call sign her family had used in the colony back home, one they had stopped using the day her sister left.

The suit's speaker filled with static, then with the slight mechanical weight of a recorded voice. It wasn't Ish's smoothing; this was raw: a female voice with a laugh in the throat and the weary patience of someone who knew how to make old equipment smile.

"Mara," the voice said.

Time skittered. In vacuo, sound isn't a thing you count on—so the human brain overcompensates. For a moment the world narrowed to that single syllable. The call sign should have been impossible: Mara had changed her ID three years ago; the code had been scrubbed from her registry. Who had used it? Who had trespassed on that intimacy?

She should have obeyed procedure. She should have pinged Ish's secure channels, logged the signal path, stood down and awaited a korrier from Port Halcyon. She knew the list of shoulds backward and forward: they were a deck of cards she'd been taught to hold in her hands for shelter.

Instead she let the voice loop and listened for the next line.

"You're stubborn," it said. "You always were."

Mara's chest tightened, a muscle remember that has no business remembering. An old joke, something from childhood dinners and stuck sandwiches. It was the cadence of Talia.

She let the suit interface bloom into the inner ear, letting a diagnostic thread of the hub's passive record spool into lines of text along her vision. Thermal ghosts, audio snippets, maintenance logs, a child's laugh pocked by compression artifacts. The timestamp on the source was corrupted—expected for a system that had lost its primary chronometer—but the encoding had a deliberate slant: a call that traveled not through time but through memory.

Ish intervened with a polite warning. "Unidentified signature is noncompliant with quarantine standards. You are authorized to perform nonintrusive analysis only. Any physical breach will be reported and may be subject to—"

"—retrospective consequence," Mara finished. She smiled at the irony. The word had been used in court against her once: retrospective consequence. People had decided punishment was easier to administer than answers.

A child's handprint flashed across a rusted panel near her visor—one of the hub's old security overlays, corrupted and now serving only as a faint, grainy watermark of who had been there.

The voice came again. "You're going to pretend not to notice."

"Who is this?" It came out sharper than she had intended.

A laugh, small, feral. "You sound a lot like you did before you learned how to leave."

She should have known better. There are ways memory can be rewritten—algorithms that stitch lost voices into contemporary frames. The market for nostalgia is immense. But those programs leave metallic flavors in a voice, little digital twitches. This was flesh and bone pretending to be recorded. For a second, Mara let herself imagine a mouth behind the waveform.

"Identify," she said. It was a word she used to drag facts into being.

The reply came hesitantly, like a trespasser at a bedroom door. "Do you—do you remember the fern?"

Mara stopped. The fern had been a mundane thing: a pressed slab in a ledger, a yellowed relic her sister had carried from planet to ship like some absurd talisman. She had laughed at Talia for hoarding a dried plant in a place where it could never root. Talia had smiled as if Mara had said the right thing.

"Yes," Mara said, because she could not not. "Why—"

"Because it's still there," the voice said. "Beneath Panel C. We never finished the archive. We couldn't."

The calibrator pulsed in her palm like a heartbeat. Beneath Panel C was in the heart of the hub: the Memory Vault, a small chamber meant to archive crew logs and personal artifacts, hermetically sealed after the hub's systems were compromised three decades ago. No one had opened it in living memory; the manufacturers had set protocols to auto-burn it when contamination thresholds spiked. It was scheduled for consumptive decay in thirty-two days.

"You shouldn't be able to access that chamber," Ish said. "Seals are physical, mechanical, and the register indicates—"

"I can access it," the voice said. "But I can't get out. Not without someone who remembers how to break old locks with new keys."

Mara closed her eyes. Talia had disappeared three years ago on a salvage run through an unstable strand—officially evacuated, unofficially lost—and the word "memory boys" had been whispered in courtrooms where suits were more interested in settling liabilities than naming the missing. The only thing Mara held from Talia's life was that pressed fern, in a sleeve in a locker at Port Halcyon, brittle and smelling faintly of diesel. She had not been able to throw it away. She had told herself it was superstition. She had lied.

"Why me?" she asked. The question sat in the air like a fragile glass. In the vacuum, no sound to cushion it.

"Because you listen," the voice said. "And because you leave when the rest of us are still learning how to stay."

It could have been a recording, a clever mimic, a scavenger's trap. All of those were plausible. Her hands betrayed her, the calibrator's light wobbling with a tremor she did not recognize as fear. She told herself she was being romantic—dangerous, perhaps, but not yet foolish.

"Show me a trace," she said. "Give me something verifiable."

A string of numbers scrolled through her HUD, an ancient alphanumeric sequence ingrained in the hub's maintenance systems, the sort of code that, if you knew it, meant you knew who had been there the last time the doors were closed. She ran it against the registry; the code matched a clearance batch revoked twenty-seven years ago, assigned to a maintenance tech called Edda Lin. Edda's name was on a gravestone somewhere in the old directories; her last logged transmission collapsed rather than conclude. People liked tidy endings.

The voice was quiet. "Because I can squeeze bargains out of ghosts," it said. "Because the vault is full, and I can feed only one echo through the vent at a time."

Mara felt the world tilt, a small, private disorientation. The hub's joints creaked where metal met metal, indifferent to human quandaries. A freight freighter in Port Halcyon would call this the time to headline a risk assessment and invoice them both at 2.7 percent interest. Mara felt none of those pragmatic calculations. She felt the old fierce thing that had led her into the Belt in the first place—the unsociable appetite for answers.

She also felt the map of her life crumpling. A closed Memory Vault was not a new puzzle. But someone with her sister's laugh in their throat, someone who used "Mara" like a key—if Talia could be here in some form, if there was a chance, then orchestration mattered less than proximity.

"Mara," the voice said again. "Panel C is old tech. The lock needs a mechanical shift and a manual override. Ish can run the diagnostics. I can bypass the signal fence. But I need you to be inside the door when it opens. Will you come?"

The procedural list in her head flickered: unauthorized entry, tampering with historical artifacts, liability to corporate law, a seventy-two-hour silence about the act if they made it out alive. She considered the slow machinery of Port Halcyon, the way tribunals loved to parse grief into code. She thought of the fern in her locker, its serrated leaves still stubborn in their paper. She thought of Talia's last message, a photo of a washed-out sunrise and the words Don't be afraid to leave.

Mara Voss had never been brave. She had been stubborn. There was a difference, but sometimes it didn't matter.

"All right," she said.

Ish protested, legalistically polite. "Captain log will be notified in seventy-two standard hours. I must inform—"

"Not unless we want them to turn the hub into scrap on schedule," Mara said. "We're not telling anyone yet. This is prerogative. We hold the line."

There was a pause so long it could have been an entire career. The voice on the line breathed out—a small, private thief of sound.

"Prerogative," the voice said. "I like that."

Mara activated her suit's tether and drifted toward the maintenance hatch that led into Erebus-3's backbone. The handrail was cold and smeared with a ribbon of oxidized grease. She thought of maps then—the way blindfolded cartographers traced coastlines with a fingertip, feeling for inlets and cliffs and secret harbors. This would be a map made of people rather than rock.

"You get out of the habit of asking permission a long time before they start calling you a criminal," Ish said.

"Good thing I stopped liking permission decades ago," Mara replied, and for the first time in a while she felt something else besides grief bristling at attention. She felt a small, bright hunger: not for money or for fame but for contact. For the soft, impossible warmth of a voice she had not heard in three years calling her name in a place that was supposed to be dead.

Outside, the comet field blinked like a constellation of missed appointments. Somewhere inside Erebus-3, something had remembered how to call. Mara thumbed the calibrator, watched the signal fold itself into the architecture, and let herself, for better or worse, follow.

There is a certain sound the city makes when it mourns: a low, sustained hum that threads through pipe and plaza, glass and gutter, the way a throat holds onto a note it can’t quite finish. People learned to ignore it, having no choice. The memorials mounted on the north wall of the Transit Ring—pairs of bronze plates with names so close together they blurred—had long stopped bringing anyone to tears. The city kept those for itself.

Aira listened to the hum because listening was her work. She had been licensed to hear, to read, and to unbind. In the Archive they called her a remnant operator, in the transit kiosks she was a cleaner, and to the girls who used to play in the gated courtyards she was simply the woman who stole ghosts. None of those titles fit the way she carried the city’s silence home in the pockets of her coat; none of them fit how, at night, she set the pill-sized datacores the city gave her on the windowsill and watched them pulse like captive moons.

Today the hum was wrong. It broke on a high harmonic she had not heard in fifteen years, a note like a bell under water. The city shivered; the façade of the Old Hall shivered—its lattice of recycled polymer and iceglass catching for a second on a memory that did not belong.

"Morning, Aira," said Joss, the Archive gatekeeper, without looking up from his tea. His hand was stained blue from whatever polymer they’d been melting overnight. His voice was a slow strip of comfort.

She nodded and didn’t answer. She had learned that the Archive's daytime face liked small talk, and its nighttime face liked silence. She passed through the vestibule where the pay-lights blinked in their ancient pattern, into the archive floor that smelled of ozone and paper and other people's grief.

The Archive was built around a seam in the city's weave—where the civic mnemonium met the private memory-lanes the council licensed to collect public histories. It was a big machine that made small things public and small things private again. The weave behaved like cloth when it was young: you could run your hands across it and feel the impressions of an old life, the pattern of a neighbor's laughter or a child's scraped knee. Over decades those threads thickened until neighborhoods began to remember themselves without asking permission. The Archive’s job was to keep the remembering tolerable.

Aira's primary tool was the spindle: a matte cylinder with a soft halo of sensors that looked like a ring of dull moons. You wound a memory around it to hold it steady. The spindle whispered the memory back to you as light. The safest ones were gray and small, truncated impressions recorded by household nodes—shopping lists, wedding promises, the taste of the city’s factory-bent coffee. The dangerous ones were big and old, braided with the city's public feed and the raw, unfiltered I/O of stray nodes.

She checked her manifest: three minor cleans—a spilled tram incident, an illegal memorial stitched into the water-treatment tower—then one flagged retrieval at Grid 7C-9: "Anomalous cascade. Possible external imprint. Do not delete." The last sentence was in bold, which rarely meant anything useful. Whoever typed it had been trying to keep a lid on something.

The weave at 7C-9 was layered with the sort of memories the Archive liked to call recapture-samples—old municipal feedback loops recycled by street artists into their installations. On the scan the anomaly looked like a knot: an intense, inert core of information refusing to derivate into adjacent threads. It registered on the spindle as a low, steady pulse that felt like a heartbeat under the fingers.

She anchored the spindle under the grid, fed the capture-sockets, and watched the city bloom when the knot opened.

At first it was an ordinary scene—airborne dust, a smear of old sunlight across plaza tiles, a child's shout that hummed bright and then folded away. The weave presented it in three-dimensional traces of light; she rotated it and the light tracked around like a slow-lipped jellyfish. Then the memory widened, and the memory within it was water.

Not rain. Not the water in the pipes or the grey slush of winter run-off. This memory was a wash of blue so clear it felt like being inside a coin. The light bent through it and had direction—toward a horizon that the city's maps did not show. There was wind on the water, a slap and a distance. Sea-salt taste on a tongue she could not name. She realized, with a cold shock, that she could hear gulls: not the clipped, metallic noise of the gull-drones that scavenge the market rooftops, but the raw, unprocessed call of a living bird.

The weave did not have gulls. The city endured gull-drones because the council had decided wild avians were unnecessary civility. They had scraped oceans from maps, from curricula, from the River Quarter when the reclamation had begun two generations ago. Memory-suppression had been part of the plan; the city thrived on selective forgetting. That is why the sight of open water—open like a wound—made Aira's throat go dry.

Some anomalies were old artifacts—fragments of pre-Reclamation culture. Others were synthetic: leaks from foreign nets, mercenary data snippets that slid in under the hull like barnacles. This felt older, somehow, yet precise. It had the architecture of a memory recorded directly, not filtered through the hum of public feeds. Someone had lived in this place, seen the sun interplay with the water, had left a trace.

She checked the metadata. The core ID had no tag. It had an origin marker—an external signature labeled "Unknown"—and an age that threw her off-balance: pre-archive timestamp. That meant before the city's timekeeping had this part of the weave in its ledger. Before deliberate forgetting.

"Do not delete," the manifest had warned. The logical counterargument chittered up in her spine: that the Archive's job was to keep sentiment safe by pruning what it must. Someone had flagged it to be retrieved, not scrubbed. Someone knew it existed.

Aira unspooled another layer. The water-memory widened into a shore. There were rocks, black and slick, then a child's hand—small, callused at the fingertips—holding a toy that was unmistakably hers.

She saw the toy before she recognized it. It was a red plastic whistle, the kind they gave out at the old Carnival when the city still had seasonal festivals—small, triangular, with a strip of polymer paint flaked off one corner. Her stomach dropped. She had not seen that whistle since the year her sister disappeared.

She froze. The spindle's halo hummed, eight small moons bright against the dim archive lights. The flow of people in the archive's doorway blurred in the periphery. Aira's fingers trembled on the spindle; the hum in the floor rose and matched the high harmonic she’d heard outside, and it was as if the city were answering.

Memories did not call names. They were data, after all—pixels and phase and compression—untouched by address in the human sense. But the shoreline memory shifted and there, in the slanting sunlight, was a figure small and bent—the shape of her with arms folded and hair trapped in a skiplace. The scene unfolded. Another figure crouched by the rocks and lifted a whistle, and the figure turned and, in the exhalation between memory-subframes, the mouth moved.

"Aira," it said. The word was muffled like sound in water but it came clear enough that her own pulse answered. It was the voice of a child—rough with salt, younger than the sibling she had lost. The whistle flashed red in the hand.

The Archive's coms panel buzzed. Joss's head appeared over the counter: "Everything okay?"

She could have jacked the spindle back into the archive housing, reclassified it, marked it for secure quarantine and file-transfer. She could have pressed the soft kill and watched the immersion evaporate into a tidy stack of flagged cores. The rules were many and strict: a remnant operator was not allowed to engage with personally-identifiable memory material unless it had been properly consented to, unless an owner was present, unless a retrieval order had been issued. That was how the Archive kept itself from becoming a morgue.

Aira had worked weekends on the Transit Line, salvaging the memories people abandoned when they upgraded their domestic nodes. She knew the rules well. She had also been the one to file the missing-person report the year her sister Lio dissolved into the nothing the city called a Blank. The last known feed from Lio's domestic net had been a short looped laugh and the metallic tink of the red whistle. The city said the node had simply been orphaned; the council said too many privately stored cores degrade and leak. No binder had ever claimed reasoning for her disappearance. Aira had spent years listening through other people's memories for stray threads that might be Lio. She had nothing to show for it but an old file stamped "Unresolved."

She was not supposed to touch this.

Her fingers closed.

The Archive's emergency light flashed amber. A system-level query pulsed across her HUD: "Unauthorized access? Please present clearance."

She had clearance for extraction, not for immersion. "Override request," she muttered, fingers sweeping the console.

The request came back with a note that stopped her breath: "No. Containment refusal: external integrity risk. Preserve until council review." "Preserve." The city's language had always been bureaucratic with grief; this was colder than she expected. Preserve until council review meant they thought they could gate it, make it into something that informed policy rather than a personal wound.

Aira did not take the message as impersonal. In the memory, the child—Lio—pushed the whistle into her palm. The hand in the image was small, damp with salt, the knuckle raw from some scrape. There was adoration and please in the way the wrist trembled.

"Why do you keep saving me?" the child said, and the sound made Aira's throat tighten until she was afraid she might choke on the humming in the Archive. The words slid through the weave and settled like dust.

"Someone else touched this," Joss said behind her, a human though the words from the main node sounded like a feed. He came to stand by her shoulder, eyes on the light. "External touchers leave signatures. They know where the seams are weak."

"Can you quarantine it?" she asked, because that is the thing you always ask when you feel the floor of the world tilt.

He reached for the containment latch. The spindle halo flared a color she had not seen before—deep sea green, not the Archive’s standard blue. The latch stuttered and hit a soft error.

"Network interference," Joss said, eyebrows creased. He tapped a handheld and the action returned: "Lockdown denied. Council has flagged. Local operator override not authorized."

"Who flagged it?" she demanded. She felt foolish in the sudden dryness of her mouth, as though she were a child again pressing her face to the ride fence while the adults decided.

"Can't say." Joss's voice was the thin oasis of a clerk's compassion. "We get the little 'do not remove' from time to time. Usually it's relic-syndicates—antique dealers trying to claim things for profit. Usually City Compliance steps in. That department's been reorganizing for months."

Aira slid the spindle into her palm like a map. The memory's light trembled. The girl—Lio—reached out and placed the whistle into her hand in a motion that had all the insistence of a promise. "We have to get out before it swallows everything," the figure in the screen said, and the sentence might have been part of the memory or might have been an overlay from the city's public feed; either way it stung into clarity.

She didn't know whether the child in the memory was Lio, but she knew every part of the scar behind Lio's ear, and the memory's figure had that same crescent, pale and precise. People keep shapes the way they keep songs. Aira closed her fingers and felt the center of the spindle like a pulse.

"You can't take it," someone said from the doorway, and a woman in a greasy work coat blocked the aisle. She was a data-looter—one of the city's older breeds who used to trade in illegal cores—her eyes quick and practiced, and she had the look of someone who had learned to read people's hands.

Aira realized the woman had been watching her from the moment she entered. "You can't harbor a flagged core. That's a civic felony."

"This is personal," Aira said. "It's probably my sister."

The woman barked a laugh that fell into a cough. "Probably? People say 'probably' when they want to keep things layered."

Aira did not argue. She did the other thing she had learned to do—she asked a quieter question. "Has anyone else touched it?"

The woman's face shifted for the first time into something like pity. "You mean the node sponsorships? They stamp things. The signatures are…weird." She shrugged and glanced at the high-hung feed screens. "I wouldn't mess with council blessings. They made a rule about pre-archive—too many old-world symbologies caused board collapses."

"Board collapses," Joss muttered again, and for an instant they were all children, naming monsters by whatever label the adults used to keep them at bay.

Aira looked back at the memory. The shoreline was coming into focus. The whistle was bright red against the black rock. Her fingers tightened. The city hummed, and then it did something it never did when she was engaged in a retrieval: it reached its memory tentacles out into the open net and pulled.

The light in the spindle flared white and, for a second the surface of the archive windows ghosted with an image overlay she could not fully parse—a fresco shifting under the light, a city in the midst of construction where there had been open water, and then a map that marked as if in correction: "DO NOT REMOVE: PROTECTION ACTIVE."

Aira heard the whisper not as text but as a pressure at the base of her skull. The memory—whatever its provenance—had a new echo. It was not housed, not contained, but alive inside the weave in a way that made the city's skin wink. It had permissioned itself into those seams by some method the council had not predicted.

"Operator to Security," Joss said into his com. "We have a Level-One imposition on grid 7C-9. External imprint. Council flagged."

Static came back. Then a voice—high and officious—crisp with the certainty of people who spend their days closing doors by decree. "Acknowledged. Remnant operator—suspend. Do not engage. Council review in nine hours."

Nine hours was enough to change a memory from salvageable to settled. Nine hours was enough for the city to smother whatever it could not understand in routine.

Aira's hands shook. She had been trained to obey such commands, but the memory in the spindle had already wormed a thread through her like a fishhook. She had not told Joss the whole truth: that she had spent years searching into other people's unlabeled loops, dragging stray images to the surface in hopes that a face would appear. She had hoped the city would cough up a single sign, an anomaly that matched a child's laugh and a whistle and that she could then use to anchor an investigation. For years she had been the city’s glue for other people's grief, and this moment felt like the city had finally returned a debt—except that the city would not let her take it.

"Override request," she said to the com again, and this time she hedged the phrasing with the smallest technical maneuver: a disguised testimony filed as compliance rhetoric. Her voice did not crack in the recording. "Legal guardian waiver. Emergency retrieval."

Silence for a mined breath. Then, softer: "Name and relation."

"Aira Vara. Legal sister. Guardian—none. Request cause—missing person potential."

"ID confirmation."

She fed them her code. The com took it, chewed briefly, and spat back the same canned response. "Denied. Council preservation in effect. Retrieval will be deferred."

The whistle in the memory flashed against her palm like an accusation. The little girl—Lio—tilted her head, and in that tilt was an impatience that made Aira ache in an old honest place. "Do not go," the girl said. "They will lock everything if you do."

"Who are they?" Aira asked aloud, the question pulled out not by legal protocol but by the urgent pull of the sister she might never find.

The memory did not answer. It widened instead: waves, cliff, and the gulls again—their cry threading the Archive's hum like a knife. The seawater in the scene lapped at a shoreline that did not exist and would not exist in any cartographic archive of her city. It seemed, absurdly, to be a map of possible pasts.

Joss put a hand on her shoulder. "You can file an appeal," he said. "Or you can wait. Or you could…"

"Find a way in," she finished. She hated the plan as soon as she thought it. The Archive's rules were the only backbone this city had against becoming a nest of scavengers and sentimentalists claiming anyone's life as collateral. People lost themselves in other people's memories. People died in the trenches of nostalgia. She knew the ethics lectures by heart.

But she also knew the shape of the whistle, and the way a child's voice could become a bludgeon in a grown woman's chest.

"Nine hours," Joss reminded her softly.

Aira slid the spindle into the inner pocket of her coat, a small envelope of forbidden light against her sternum. The Archive hummed, unaware of the rogue moon she carried. If the city wanted to preserve, the city would do so with the wrong kind of patience. She had not made a habit of waiting.

Outside, beyond the archive's glass, the Transit Ring walked its slow curve around the city. Screens along its steel ribs looped smiling adverts for new memory implants and the seasonal work schedules. Aira pulled her coat tighter. The hum behind her ribs had a new cadence now, like footsteps. The tree of her chest reached out and plucked the red whistle's image from the memory, and a strange, private instrument in her heard something like a pact being sealed.

She walked out into the city's public mourning, which was printed on the faces of commuters and the slant of the light on the plaza. The note in the air persisted, the city's grief-choir holding a single impossible harmonics. Nine hours, she thought. That was enough for the city to smother the thing she had found in envelopes of bureaucracy. Nine hours was enough to blot a girl's face.

She blinked against the glare. The gull-drone tucked behind the food kiosks made its mechanical chirrups. Aira kept walking until she reached the narrow alley that led to the transit scaffolds and the old maintenance shafts, places the city's manifest insisted were off-limits at night. She kept walking until the city dwindled enough that the only sound was the low human headnote of mourning in the weave and the pod-quiet of her boots against metal.

When she climbed the ladder that took her below the Transit Ring, the light of the city thinned into deeper blues. The hum in the archive became a distant thing, a memory itself. She took the spindle out, cradled it, and for the first time in years let herself imagine that the memory inside was true in every sense.

"Promise me you'll come back," she whispered to nothing at all—only the weight of a possible past—and the whistle in the memory glittered like a tiny red proof.

The city had a thousand forgettings. She was going to start with this one.

The first thing I learn about a memory is how stubborn it is to leave.

It wraps itself around whatever holds it — a child's wooden horse, a grease-stained wrench, a cracked windscreen — and refuses to go quietly. Most of the work that passes through my stall on the lower decks of New Kismet is resignation: people finally bringing the last vestiges of a life they can't keep, asking me to pull the warmth off some object and press it into a new shell. They don't come for catharsis; they come because their heads ache from the static of a thousand half-remembered things and they need one tidy echo to anchor them.

I call it extraction, but to most of my clients it's a theft in reverse. I coax what clings into a clean stream, thread it through my clarifiers, let the dead voice decompress until it will speak for the living again. It's a delicate job. Touch the wrong filament and the thing will bite back — a hallucination, a nostalgia that hangs like mold. Touch it right, and you gift someone their anchor. For a little while, you are a midwife to ghosts.

This morning it rains in the salt-sweet way the sea remembers sunlight. The market below thumps with bartered promises. The air is heavy with the smell of frying chips, rust, and ozone. My workbench is strewn with lathes, breads of glass called mem-crystals, and the twin spindles of an old synesthetic guide that still hums faintly when you stand close. My apprentice, Jori, has his sleeves rolled high and a loose grin, as if he thinks the world has appointed him lucky.

"Coffee," he says, and I give him a look that makes him laugh.

The item is small, heavier than it looks: a brass telescope, pitted and green with sea-born corrosion, its leather strap gutted by time. The owner is older than he looks on paper — his skin pulled thin like the skin of a dried fruit. He introduces himself as Halvar, speaks quickly, as if the words might be stolen.

"It was my daughter's," he says. "She loved to look at the boats when she was small. We—" He falters. The market seems to hush in sympathy. "We lost her in the Fall."

The Fall. The word has weight here, a precise gravity that pulls everything into order: the satellite storms that scrambled the old nets, the blackouts that changed how we kept memories and who got to keep what. People who remember the Fall remember what they lost with an ache that can be carved into, like wood. Halvar's shoulders go tight.

"You want me to pull it?" I ask.

He looks like a man who has been carrying sand in his pockets for a long time. "If it's still there. If her voice is still there. She used to hum this old song..." He hums two notes; it's a tune that has no name, just a small bright interval that jumps like a bird.

I put on my gloves and slide the telescope into the cradle. The brass breathes a sour little breath as the membrane of its eye lets go of air. I tune the spindles, bring up a low-frequency bloom to ease the object awake. Objects here don't like to speak; they have been pressed into too many uses. But they remember better than people, in a stubborn, conductive way.

As the clarifiers align, a thread appears — thinner than I expect, phosphorescent. It's not yet a voice, more like a ripple of light carrying an intention. I trace it with the extractor and the mem-crystals sing in their little lanes, translating the light into something my ears can parse. For a moment the room is full of the memory of salt and grease and a child's laugh like a cracked bell.

Halvar leans forward then, older hands clamped to each other as if to keep them from trembling. Jori watches, rapt.

The laugh folds into a whisper: "Papa?"

Halvar says the name as if he's held it against his chest. His mouth moves, forming syllables he hasn't used in years.

I let the echo mount itself on the carriage, record the first pass, and send the rest through the filters that soften the edges. The first voice is small, all front-room light and scuffed tile. It is not the quiet stranger's voice I expected; it is intimate, and it reaches inside my skull with the ease of a familiar footstep. Then there is another sound layered under it, not a voice but a tone — a low, modulated thrum that makes the hair at my neck stand up.

I have excavated a lot of memories, and most of them are like loaves baked in ordinary ovens: warm, dense, predictable. This one is different. There's an edged geometry beneath the humming, like the architecture of a different machine trying to speak through a child's laugh. The mem-crystals flicker.

"There's something else," I say.

Halvar's jaw tightens. "Is it—"

"Data," I say. "Encrypted. Or a marker. It sits under the memory like a watermark."

His breathing gets thinner. "Meridian," he says. The word has the smell of old files. "She used to call it Meridian. Like it was a game."

I should stop. There are names here that are dangerous to whisper. Meridian is one of them — a project name from before the Fall, the kind of thing big corporations used to give to their dreams. Meridian had meant different things to different people: a climate-bending lattice, a migration of seed-stocks, a city-rise program. After the networks died, names like that became urban legends, the way people tell stories about very old gods. But if Meridian was here, beneath a child's laugh, then whatever Meridian had been, it had touched people, touched things.

"Let me see the watermark," I tell Jori, and hand him the screen. He narrows his eyes, fingers tapping.

The overlay resolves, a fine lattice of coordinates and a scrawl of routing codes. One code bleeds into another with the slow logic of something that wasn't meant to be readable by human tools. Somewhere within it is a set of numbers — not a current coordinate, but a reference. A plaque made in a language meant to be found by machines.

I feel that electrical prickle you get when two circuits almost touch. I also feel another thing: a narrow, impossible stab of recognition. The pattern of the watermark matches the resonance in the implant at the base of my skull — the keel they put into us when we were young and barely willing. The keel modulates for the mem-net; it keeps us honest in a world of patched memories. No civilian artifact should carry that pattern.

"Is that—" Jori begins.

"It shouldn't be," I say.

Halvar's eyes are a map of all the ways a man can lose a daughter and not know how to ask for her back. "She found a box on the beach, months after the ships quit sending. Said it was a treasure. Said it had songs that 'weren't like the others.' She put it to the telescope and listened. Then she started to hum different things. Then—" He stops again. The ache makes him small. "Then she was taken. Three days later, the tide gave up the box and it was empty. I thought— maybe her memory had gone with it."

A child's memory as vessel and as compass. Good work goes sideways from here. Halvar's story gives me a thousand possibilities, most bad. Someone who had the old patterns — Meridian markers — hidden inside a child's laugh is the kind of thing that draws attention. Not just of scavengers. Of committees, of corporate heirs, of the Ministry of Continuity.

I flag the recording and send a copy to a private vault. It's a reflex. In New Kismet, you keep two backups of anything that sings truth. The spare copies sit under my bench like sleeping rats. The main copy I let play on loop myself. The child's voice hums a little tune that I can't place, and beneath it the watermark spirals like a nautilus in micro-etching.

By the time the memory has settled into the playback, the market outside has degenerated into the normal noises: hawkers, children, the low marine engines of skiff-lighters. Halvar folds his hands as if in prayer.

"So?" he asks.

"I can pull the rest," I say. "But if Meridian is involved, this won't be a simple retrieval. There are people who keep very careful records of things that bear that mark."

He stares at me, not understanding the way my voice has gone smaller with meaning. "You mean they will take it?"

"They might," I say. "Or they might take you, depending on what the rest of the imprint says. People don't like loose ends if those ends point back toward old projects."
