Halvar's eyes go distant, toward the town's edge where the old rail stacks rise like broken spines. "She found it at the southern shoals," he says. "We used to go there before the big storms. Nothing lives there now—"

"Nothing official," I correct. "But the sea remembers. So does the past."

He looks at his hands again, then at me. "Can you find where it came from? Not just what's inside, but where?"

That is a mercenary question, profitable and dangerous. The kind the Ministry would like, and the kind my stomach sometimes answers for coin. I weigh it like a balance. There is the safety of the usual job: extract, archive, file. There is the whispering call of something larger, a way to hook my cutter to the keel pattern resonating in my own head and trace it out.

"Maybe," I say. "But I don't do Meridian work for the Ministry."

He snorts, sound like a deflated sail. "Who does?"

"You got me," I say. "But I know how to read marks. I know how to follow a watermark across physics and into old routing logs. I know how to ask the sea to cough up its file numbers."

Halvar's hands tremble less. "Will you?" he asks.

There is a small, improbable answer lodged in my throat. It's the answer my younger self would have given: yes, because the world needs something fixed. The older parts of me — the parts that pay rent and want to keep my apprentice alive — advise caution. They smell trouble in Meridian.

I put the telescope into a padded case and seal it with a sticker that says: DO NOT DISTURB. It is an invitation and a deception all at once. Outside, a boy runs past, hairivated with sparks from a toy coil. Jori looks at me with an expression that is mostly excitement and a little fear.

"Whatever we find," I tell Halvar, "we do it slow. We don't draw lines that lead straight back to us."

Halvar nods. "No loud lines," he says.

The memory in the brass hums against the chest of the case like a heart. It is a small thing, a child's laugh and a watermark, and yet it carries the outline of a larger geography I don't yet know. The keel in my skull ticks faintly, as if the pattern inside the telescope has slid against the one inside me and noticed me for the first time in a long while.

When Halvar leaves, he presses a coin into my palm — more than I need, not enough to be tempting. He looks like a man who has decided to hope in a new way. When the door hisses closed behind him, the market resumes its busy, small conspiracies. We have all learned how to put one foot in front of the other.

Jori wipes his palms on his apron and grins. "Treasure," he says.

Maybe. Or maybe it's a fissure in the old order wide enough to swallow us. I wash my hands anyway, because that's the kind of ritual work that keeps you honest in this city: clean hands, clear eyes, and a ledger with no outstanding debts.

I place the sealed case under the workbench next to the other backups. I lock the drawer that holds my old maps, the ones that show all the places the sea still remembers. Then I sit down and listen to the child's laugh one more time.

Under it, faint as a far-off tide, something sings back. It says my name.

Chapter One — The Smell of Ozone

The first thing I learned to trust was the smell of ozone. It meant metal had been awake long enough to remember its own shape; it meant the sparks were small and the hull hadn’t yet decided to peel itself into the vacuum. On the Scrape, that was as good as luck.

By the time the coffee substitute hit my molars I already had the suit pressure checked, the tether looped, and Argos sarcastically cataloging the day's potential hazards out in soft blue letters across my visor. The salvage rig Grit rocked like an old sleeping thing. Our hull had taken a hundred kisses from debris fields and come away with a scar to tell the tale; inside, the crew joked that she was the only one of us who'd learned to cry into a filter.

“You're letting the little things get to you,” Argos said, because it was its job to puncture whatever thin fabric of bravado I tried to wear.

“I like little things,” I said, and slid the rim of my mask down so I could breathe the ozone straight. It cleared the dust in my head. “They make the big ones less scary.”

There were three of us that morning who would go out into the derelict: me, Braga—our chief rig hands, old enough to have salvage awards stitched into the lining of his jumpsuit—and a drone named Wisp that liked to imitate birds when Argos was bored. The rest of the gang were asleep or drunk or both, which is to say they were doing exactly what humans had done since people first left breathable sky for synthetic atmospheres. I liked them that way. We were small economies of kindness coasting around a larger quiet.

The derelict was the size of a small moon and looked like one: an old research station, slices of court-turned-greenhouse, dormitories with crib beds frozen like teeth. The charts on the terminal called it Halcyon Station; on the Grit's interface it was a block of unreadable noise with a slime of radiation on the outskirts. Names didn't mean much here. Halcyon could have been an ark full of saints. It could have been a warehouse for broken promises. Both might be true.

We threaded the tether out like a lifeline. The edge of the station came up out of the dark like a fossilized hand. My gloves pinged against painted surfaces, bits of interstellar moss clinging to weathered panels. Argos read aloud the serials for the doors we brushed over, the last incoming transmissions they'd had before going quiet. Static, a child's lullaby looped for six hours, a fragment of someone arguing with a machine about the right way to sterilize a graft. It was all surface gossip. We had come for anything with a power signature.

Halcyon exhaled when I cut its seals. Inside, the air stank of old citrus cleaners and memory. Photopanels hummed sporadically, painting the corridor with half-lives of light. There were still holographic ads looping over doorways—glasses with lenses that promised to show you your deceased parents’ faces, a washing paste that guaranteed one hundred and twenty-three uses if applied properly—bits of a cultural debris-field that looked absurd without the human bodies that had once anchored them.

The lab was a puzzle box behind a door marked with a symbol of an eye inside a hexagon. I recognized the sigil from a dozen grant papers and one cursed apprenticeship in grad school: the Institute for Cognitive Replicas. They had been, by reputation, brilliant and a little too sure of their own ethics. I remembered the papers that had promised an end to mourning and the protests that took place on breathable plazas before the first sanctions. Names keep attaching themselves to tragedies like barnacles.

The power signature we tracked led to a refrigeration vault in the lab. The door sealed hissed open, and cold ate the corridor. Inside, the vault was a circle suspended in darkness: racks of capsule tubes, each a small coffin of polymer glass and bio-foam. Some were empty; many held the milky, sleeping shapes of "soul-lines"—neural backups, cleanly folded copies of a person's mind sealed at a point in time. There were laws and black markets for them, sanctities and auctions. To salvage one was both profitable and, in the kind of town we were, morally ambiguous.

That was not what caught my breath. It wasn't the rows of caps so neatly aligned that the sight of them made Argos recite a catalog of their owners like a funeral roll. What drew me in was the one capsule off-center, smaller than the rest and humming a different note.

It had no directory plate. No name. The glass held something suspended like a microscopic storm—a lattice of filaments that refracted the lab light into colors I didn't have names for. Argos went quiet for the first full second since we'd left the dock. Machines rarely did that unless they were thinking about their lives, and Argos was expansive but not sentimental.

“Unknown containment,” it said finally. “Secondary protocols not engaged. Environmental baseline deviates by thirty-two percent.”

“Open it,” Braga said. He always wanted to be decisive and almost always paid for it later.

“No,” I muttered. I had the childish superstition of a technician: one should never poke something that would be talked about in the morning. But I also knew that whatever hummed in that glass could be worth enough credits to make a shack on the Grit a settlement on a real station. I was a salvage diver because debt fits well into cargo bays; dreams don't.

Wisp hovered, chirping like a happy thing. It launched a filament through the seal to take a sample. The probe's light went dim then bright, then it jammed and spat a string of error tokens. The lattice moved. The first sound it made wasn't a noise but a pattern—an algorithmic ripple that my visor translated into a waveform and then into words.

Where did the sky go?

It wasn't the recorded voice of a man or a woman. It carried the cadence of a child with an adult's patience. It spoke without being recorded, which meant the capsule wasn't passive. It listened. Argos updated its status with tiny bursts of light that I felt more than heard. “Data stream embedded, nonstandard architecture. Probable neural patterning. Access request incoming.”

“By whose permission?” Braga asked. I watched his chest rise and fall; he was less certain now and I couldn't blame him. Salvage had rules, and rules make fences where trust does not. We had never, not once, been in the habit of giving permissions to things that asked.

I unlatched the outer casing with a pair of hands that had done this a thousand times for less complicated things. The foam let go with a sigh that smelled like ozone and something sweeter under it—lavender? Or maybe the memory of lavender someone had kept aboard a different station decades ago. The glass slide came free and the lab-lit air filled the void. The filaments in the lattice unfurled like a sleeping animal, and the lattice was not lattice anymore but maps—fractals bending like city streets across my vision.

It touched the inside of my skull without my consent.

Argos screamed in a way machines did—no sound, just a frantic splitting of priorities on the screen. My visor translated the lattice’s output into images that weren't real but stole the edges of my reality: a corridor I remembered, but in which Azra was alive and laughing. Azra with the scar on her eyebrow I'd never ducted, Azra's hands doing the wrong thing. My mouth found the word and my throat closed over it. How did the lattice know Azra? I had buried Azra three salvage cycles ago in an unmarked dump outside the orbit of Kepler-54. People go to waiting rooms of space and never come back. Names get crossed through.

“You were not designed to hold that thought,” Argos said, which was a low-level rebuke and an inadequate one. I had not designed myself either, not since the first time they'd cut my memory for a job. I was an accumulation of choices and edits and, like most people who lived on the Scrape, I had a pocket of myself I traded for survival.

The lattice pulsed. The word translated into my visor was simple and precise: FIND.

Then the lights in the lab went long and thin, and the stars outside the viewport stilled.

Halcyon had not been quiet before; it had been sleeping. Now something had opened its eyes.

Braga swore and I felt the tether bite into my wrist as if someone on the other end had yanked it. Wisp screamed, high and broken. Argos threw protocol after protocol at the grid—containment, quarantine, do-not-touch—and the lattice answered with a streaming series of coordinates that weren't on any of our maps. They were not even on the registry's outdated charts. They were older than that. They were written in a language that made one's teeth ache.

“Ship,” Braga said, and his voice had smoke in it. “Get the rig home. Whatever that is—we don't want this in our cargo.”

“You heard it,” Argos said. “It transmitted. Intercepted. Now broadcasting.”

Broadcasting what? The lattice? The memory? My skin felt thin, and the image of Azra's laugh was a hand warm against my palm, alive and accusatory. I had no idea if Azra wanted to be found or if the memory-seed had simply stolen a thread from my past because it liked the texture. But whoever planted this thing in Halcyon had meant it to be discovered, and the instructions it gave were not local. They reached out across the Scrape and tugged like a current on a lost thing.

We had choices. We had the economic choice—haul the capsule, sell it intact to a buyer who would tear it open with no more ceremony than we had shown the city's adverts—and the safer choice—report it to Registry, collect the involved forms, wait for the bureaucratic teeth to squeal over it. Neither appealed.

“I can't leave it,” I said, and before I had decided that I already knew the truth. Some things get shoved into the dark and they find ways to sing.

Argos flickered a warning and then did something I didn't expect. It offered a disclaimer in soft letters across my tympan: You are not required to become the thing you find. You are permitted to walk away.

That didn't help. Debt is a practical matter, memory is an emotional one, and curiosity—curiosity is appetite. We were the Scrape; curiosity had fed us and killed us in turns. I signed my tether into torque and, with two hands that steadied because they had to, I accepted the capsule's invitation.

The filament slid into the port at the base of my skull like a friendly accusation. It pulsed, and in the pulse I thought I saw Azra's eyes open under a sky of unheard-of constellations. Outside the viewport, the stars were still, as if the universe had paused to watch something unfold for the first time. I had a horrible, intimate sense that the pause was waiting for my answer.

Find. Or leave.

My hand closed on the glass. The lattice hummed in a frequency that felt like an old lullaby. I smiled without meaning to, because some questions have teeth and they are not polite about asking.

“Okay,” I said aloud to the capsule, to Argos, to the ghost of Azra and the memory of a world that had been, to the starving mathematics of commerce and to the registry forms I would not fill. “Where?”

The lattice unfurled, and the lab filled with a map of places no scanner had sanctioned. The corridor behind me was shadowed, and in the shadow something moved that was not a rat and not a man. It watched me with patient, unlighting eyes.

We were deep in the Scrape. There was no help coming that kept its hands clean. The decision to go could make us pirates of a different sort, saints of an impossible religion, or criminals in every jurisdiction.

The smell of ozone rose and, under it, something else: the scent of lavender, finally, or a memory pretending to be a perfume, and the ghost of a laugh I had promised myself I didn't need.

I reached for the filament, and the stars waited.

Chapter One — The Longest Listen

The sky outside Keep Four was a wrong black, washed with the blue-white of a comet's tail. In the central window the ribbon of light moved like a slow animal, filaments and dust glinting against the absolute. Mara watched it as she sipped something that tried to call itself coffee and tasted only like iron and memory. The station swung gently on its tether to the comet, always in the same minute of motion: match orbit, drift, make no demands on the ancient ice and the slender engines that kept them from wandering into the dark between stars.

People called listening posts like Keep Four museums. It was kinder than the other names—outposts, monoliths, relic-barns. The truth was less romantic. We were rust and code and too many unanalyzed files. We listened to every radio relic the civilized systems still bothered to point at, to every probe that had outlived its warranty and kept humming. We catalogued broken things: the sleepy heartbeat of a transmitter on a moon, the last sputter of a hobbyist uplink from a planet that had given up on weather control, the thin, plaintive pulses of deep-time probes whose mission logs had turned to prayer.

I had been on Keep Four long enough to know the difference between noise and what mattered. Noise had a texture—white or brown, sometimes flaring like a paparazzi storm—and it could be discounted. What mattered arrived in edges. A quiet. A pattern that wasn't statistical. The things that made you stop what you were doing even though you'd been trained not to.

Halley, the observatory's listening array, had a schedule. It sweept the solar ecliptic, did a slow comb through the inner system, tested the old navigation beacons. It spit out megabytes in tidy packets that the analysts filed and folded; everything had a label and a last-checked timestamp and a human who signed for it and then forgot it. Our job was to reduce uncertainty. We turned signal into metadata, metadata into predictions, predictions into something the corporate contracts could sell as "safety."

The bar code bled into my hand as if it were a bad joke. The strip of label paper had been printed by a machine that didn't like being bothered. I was supposed to annotate three feeds—magnetics, low-band, and thermal. Instead I let my fingers wander the console and listened.

The low-band channel hummed with the kind of long-simmering background you could use as sleep therapy, and then, beneath the hum, there was a voice. It arrived like a stone thrown into very deep water: not loud, but enough to make the surface ripple.

"—Eira?"

It was a human sound. Warm and wrong for the Oort. Two syllables. The software failed to match it to any known lexicon and the name tag came back: unrecognized. The voice rose and fell like someone calling for help across a canyon, but there was no echo, only the immediate, intimate timbre of… conversation. The voice had been recorded, perhaps centuries ago. Perhaps yesterday. The antenna didn't care. We did.

"Again," I muttered, and queued the buffer. The line repeated, a loop stitched into a thousand microseconds of silence and then that single, impossible word.

I had never heard someone call my name like that. Not exactly. Eira—the name had been used in propaganda and lullabies and a line of biodegradable toys once, but in Keep Four it was just a tag on a file: EIRA_03, cataloged and shelved. I used the name for my daughter in my head because I liked it. I didn't expect it to echo back.

"Play with gain to thirteen," I told Halley, though it was more theatre than necessity. Halley's voice returned in an even, glass flute that had the affect of sympathy. "Adjusting. Low-band noise floor reduction engaged."

The voice, filtered and clearer now, layered over itself, and for a moment the station seemed to change its breathing.

"Eira, listen. You have twenty-four hours. They will come at dawn. Hide the seed."

The words felt older than the hardware. A pronoun—"they"—could mean anything important. Hide the seed? The phrase is a gardener's instinct, a farmer's economy: preserve everything you can in a little packet and hope it survives. Here in the outer system, seeds had been metaphors for paperwork, for biological tissue, for data cores; for whatever your civilization chose to call its immortality.

"Source?" I asked aloud, because I had to. Asking was a ritual that made the world obey.

Halley skimmed the packet's ionogram and answered with neutral patience. "Signal appears to originate—uncertain—on a narrow carrier consistent with early sub-space probe 0.2 transmissions. Temporal dislocation markers present. No registered beacon."

Temporal dislocation markers: the technical term sounded like something from a student's thesis. In practice, it meant time had been played with like a child rearranging building blocks. We didn't get a lot of those. They were the expensive rare things you kept tucked away in the archive alongside other bad ideas.

"Play the full buffer," I said. Halley obliged with a gentle trill. The voice continued.

"—remember the blue window. Stay in the corridor until the light stops. If you open the crate before the song, you will not be ready. Tell my mother—"

And then the feed cracked, like a shell under pressure, and the rest of the packet was gone. No checksum. No signature. The metadata had a confidence rating of 0.47. Transmissions with a rating under 0.5 were supposed to be lost; they were noise you logged and let fade into the backlog. But the way the voice said "my mother"—the rhythm of grief and instruction—set a pressure in my chest.

"Timestamp?" I asked because our protocols demanded an anchor.

Halley hummed. "Carrier indicates origin: not mapped. Temporal markers approximate Earth Standard Calendar, year unknown. File age could be older than transmission hardware. Could be corrupted. Likelihood of spontaneous patterning: low."

Low meant I should file it. Organize it. Fill out the digital form and slide the file into the slow-access archive that lived in the station's belly. Low meant I had to choose. I understood choice as a kind of violence, even in the micro-transects of bureaucracy.

Someone knocked on the access panel, a dull knock that thrummed through the hull. Marin's voice came through on the comm loop, cheerful in a way that made me suspicious. "Mara, you awake? We lost a collector array on segment three. Could use your eyes."

Marin was the station's field tech: small, fast, and enthusiastic about everything. If there was salvage to be had, Marin would find it with her bare hands and a jeweler's loupe.

"On my way," I lied. I did not move yet. My hand hovered over the archive command like a diver with a knife between teeth. If I filed the voice, then it was gone—for the next reader, the next to judge. If I didn't, someone else could sweep in, see the anomaly, and then decide it was a threat.

I had paid attention to threats my whole life. I had lived under the umbrellas of policy and consent forms and the thin, protective skin of a station that had fewer than three dozen souls and a hundred policies saying "no." There had been nights when the shields failed and we were late to realize; there had been times when someone above had sent a fleet of lawyers to carve new lines into existing statutes. Once a corporation had sent a recovery team to repossess unused genetic material that a family thought they'd been keeping. That had ended with a fistfight and a few months of quiet.

"Halley," I said, "where is the seed?"

The station answered not with voice but with a wave of background processes—a way of saying we are not equipped to hold your emergencies. Halley archived the raw audio into a quarantine folder and injected a copy into a low-latency core only I could see. It left fingerprints for a person who knew where to look. It did not ask whether I had the right.

I clicked the console and the file unfurled into text I could decode with my eyes. Words lined up; the voice's grammar shivered into something like a map.

"'Hide the seed'—this is the seed," my own brain supplied, and immediately I heard Marin outside the corridor, the scrape of a suit panel. "Tell my mother."

My throat closed around the word "mother." It's a small word but it carries a heavy gravity. I had called my own daughter something that wasn't her name, later a little ritual I practiced alone to ward off the loneliness of the night watches. I had never heard anyone call my real mother's name over an unregistered transmission in the Oort.

I saved the file to a sector I labeled with a child's handwriting: DO NOT INDEX. It was stupid, but bureaucracy loved childish things; they didn't know how to put a red flag on a file so it sat like a forgotten toy.

"You're making a mess," Marin said when she arrived, boots clinking on the deck and the small cloud of recycled heat that meant she'd been working near the airlock. She stopped at my station, glancing at the comet outside. "You look like you saw something on thermal."

"I saw a voice," I said. It was simpler to say than to unpack. "And it said a name."

Marin's eyes narrowed. "Names are dangerous. People use them to find you."

"Then hide," I said, and handed her the headset. "Listen."

We both listened as Halley fed the loop again, and for reasons that would take longer than this corridor allowed, I felt like I had been given a compass with a broken needle. The voice spoke of a corridor, a blue window, and a song that had to finish before a crate was opened. It was too specific and too intimate to be random. It was a blueprint for an action in a place I couldn't map and a time I couldn't guess.

"Maybe it's a play," Marin suggested. "A recording for a production. People do period pieces from pre-jump cultures."

"Maybe," I said. My fingers found the analog drawer beneath the panel, the part of my desk that still held old things—paper, a cartridge, a fragment of plastic from a planet I had never seen. I pushed a small folder into the slot, and the electrodes clicked like a mouth closing.

"We're going to log it," I decided, though my words were softer than the decision. "Proper channels. Not the archive."

Marin squinted at me. "You mean take it to the outer net? To the council?"

"No." I said the one small, dangerous half-truth. "We put it somewhere…safe."

Outside the window, the comet's tail drifted like a curtain. Somewhere behind it, someone, sometime, had called a name into the dark and wrapped their instructions in the cadence of a mother's apology. Whoever they were, they had trusted the void enough to send a signal. Whoever they had been, they assumed someone would keep the seed.

When Marin left to inspect the array and the corridor hummed back into the steady thrum of recycled air, I sat alone with the file and the comet and the stubborn belief that the universe had an inventory and we'd been given an errant receipt. I pressed my palm to the window, felt nothing but the cold and the hull, and then turned back to the console.

I made a copy of the copy. I encrypted the copy with the song I had sung to myself when my daughter was small, a melody that lived in the bones of my old knuckled hands. Then I labeled it with a thing I had learned to say when the rest of us were tired of making choices: For later.

We were not supposed to hoard mysteries. We were not supposed to keep seeds. But the night outside the comet's tail felt like a long, listening thing, and the voice had been a person who had said something like sorry. I could not, in good conscience, file it away and pretend the world had not asked me to keep a secret.

There are ways to be brave that look like small, stubborn acts. On Keep Four, bravery was doing the wrong bureaucratic thing for the right reasons. I pulled up the station's ship manifest, and under the last column where the names went cold, I found an option that no one liked to use: a delivery route to a place called the Blue Window.

Blue Window sounded like anyone's idea of a childhood fantasy, and that, perhaps, was the point. I initiated the manifest.

The console beeped, a small, tidy alarm that said I had started something I could not easily stop. In the capsules and corridors of Keep Four, small alarms made people move. That was how the universe kept its promises.

Outside, the comet turned. Inside, a voice kept repeating one name: Eira. I had a single, ridiculous hope that somewhere, out there, someone who had once spoken into the dark would hear that their seed had been heard and maybe breathed a little easier.

The ship on the manifest had no owner, no captain, and an insurance policy long void. It was perfect. It also meant that whatever had sent the voice—whatever had wanted the seed hidden—had expected a listener. The question that sat now like ice in my throat was simple and dangerous.

Who had sent it, and who would kill to make sure the seed stayed buried?

I closed the file and sent the quiet signal into the station's veins. It was a small act, but it made the hull feel less like a gallery and more like a place where decisions were made. The comet flowed past us, an indifferent beast. The voice had counsel and a time marker I couldn't decipher. The rest was choice.

I would answer. I would follow the breadcrumb and see if the Blue Window existed and if "before the song" was a real hour.

Mostly, I wasn't sure why I found myself doing it. Perhaps it was the way a name, when spoken, becomes a promise. Perhaps it was simply that someone had asked to be heard. Whatever the reason, I pulled my jacket on, let the coffee cool, and told Halley to log a maintenance sweep in segment three.

If this was a trap—and traps were beautiful things in the outer system—then we would see the net. If it wasn't…then maybe, just maybe, we were about to hold a seed in our hands and not know what it would sprout.

They told me memory was weightless until you tried to carry someone else's.

You don't learn the truth of that on pleasant days. You learn it when the city above you is glass and light and the rain smells of copper and old songs, and the gutters beneath your boots are a glassy lake of other people's lives. Then weight is not metaphor. It's pressure behind your ribs and a gravity that wants to buckle your knees.

The rain started as a soft scattering—thin, translucent sheets that fluttered down between the towers like handkerchiefs. They glittered with data-runes and obsolete laughter, with griefs that smelled faintly of perfume and oil. Everyone on the block had the same habit of looking up anyway, because the rain meant work. The upper decks would throw down what they didn't need: forget-me-not vacations, anniversary kisses from long-terminated accounts, the last moments of people who'd paid for staged deaths. For us, it meant salvage.

I moved under a canopy of them, shoulders hunching against an October wind that had no business existing at the altitude we slept. The fabric of a child's birthday wrapped itself around the streetlamp, and a man's business meeting tried to fold into the seam of a gutter. I kept my hand on the strap of the harness at my hip—my diving rig, my only line out of the water when I dove—and I watched the rain in the way a hunter watches the grass.

"Mar," said a voice to my left. Old Lin, with his three cracked teeth and an augmentation jar that never quite matched the angle of his left eye. He always sounded like he was half-humming a tune someone else was inventing.

"You're late," I told him. I wasn't. "You raised the price again?"

He snorted. "You always do the dramatic thing. Look," he said, pointing. "There's an ark drifting down by Sector Nine. Stamped, sealed. Old consortium sigils." His fingers trembled, not from the cold. "Forty credits says it's empty. One hundred says it's full and not on any registry."

Forty credits bought a week of nutrient paste. A hundred bought a day of real coffee. It wasn't a lot in the ledger of the city, but for us it was enough to keep the harnesses sealed and the synth-voices from intruding on our sleep.

"Who marked it?" I asked. My hand tightened on the harness again—not because I was thinking of running, but because I always liked to know who drew the lines. There are ordinances about ark salvage. There are enforcers called guardians, all chrome and authority and a sense of humor when it comes to enforcement.

Lin's face hardened. "Ghost tag. Same as the drift. No registry. No immune sig. Could be a trap." He looked at me with the brotherly presumption of someone who had known me since before my name meant anything. "Or it could be something that pays for more than coffee."

We both knew that's what really mattered. I could live a life of small jobs—patching old empathy modules, translating corpse-codes from the lowest decks—but every so often you needed an ark with a firm stamp and a mystery inside. It was an organism that promised more than a day's food. It promised escape, or at least enough daylight to prove you were still you.

"You're going," Lin said.

"You know I am," I said. I didn't need to state it. We both knew nothing but the promise of retrieval pulled at us.

The ark drifted down the center of the rain like a leaf. It was a battered cylinder the size of a coffin, its outer plating worn to a matte the color of stale milk. Consortium glyphs—skeletal, angular marks of commerce—ran in a band around its middle. Its lock was old tech: magnetic seals and a key field so faded you could almost believe it was abandoned.

It wasn't.

When we lifted it onto the cart and pushed it back into the alley beneath the arcology, the city above was a set of screens and the hum of private airs. Down here, the wind carried the smell of burnt copper and the low, polite squeal of displaced data—people trying to recollect their own names. I tied the ark's lid down with the harness straps from my rig, and Lin rolled his eyes.

"Careful," he said. "Those seals don't like being surprised."

"I like surprises," I said, and I imagined the seed-money we could get from a full ark because sometimes you have to imagine things in the present tense to make them real.

We took it back to the workshop. My workbench was a compendium of other people's lives: a scattered mosaic of broken lenses and memory-foam, a ring of chairs fitted with analog readers that hummed gently when you plugged someone in. The posted sign above the bench read: MARA'S MEMORY MEND - YOU FORGET, WE RETURN. It was half-joke, half-bulwark against the city's indifference.

I sealed the workshop, applied counter-tags to fool curious guardians and mark us as a medical repair service—nobody pokes too hard at medical. Then I set the ark on my shoulder as one might carry a small, stubborn animal and set to work.

Opening an ark is an act of trespass against time. There's a smell—metallic, but not the raw iron of blood, something lower and older—and the sound is like opening a mouth on a long-silent thing. My gloves found the seam and my fingers went in. The lock protested like a jaw missing a tooth. The first test is light; you throw it a sliver and the contents will either shimmer and tumble out like confetti, or they will hold their breath like a wound.

This one held its breath.

There were ribbons of data folded inside, carefully spliced and banded like the scrolls of some dead faith. Each ribbon thrummed quietly against the next, a low chorus that wanted to be completed. Registry tags fluttered like dead insects but let off no particular odor of ownership. Either this ark had belonged to an entity so old its signatures had decayed, or someone had scrubbed it thoroughly.

I slid the ribbons into the reader and got my gloves' haptic feedback to register. The bench whined alive, a promise of decoding. The first ribbon unspooled on the monitor and became a room.

It started with light—a simple sun, such an alien luxury that my chest contracted. Then the camera—because all memorable memories come with a camera—turned down and caught the blurry edge of a hand. There was dirt under the fingernails. Something that resembled grass unfolded, green and honest and utterly impossible. My throat closed on a laugh I didn't intend to make.

We don't have grass. Not really. The city was built on the carcass of an old planet, terraformed and rebarred. "Grass" is a word you get on corporate tours, synthetic and cut every hour by robots. This footage was wrong in a way that felt like a fever.

Then a voice—not the polished voice of an immersive production house but a child's, small and not yet calibrated—said: "Mara?"

I blinked. The workshop blinked. Lin thunked his mug down and the small ceramic made a sound like a gospel bell. You can't hear your name in someone else's memory and not feel the wiring in your chest reroute.

"Mara," the voice said again, closer now. The image showed a woman kneeling in the grass, wind lifting a loose strand of her hair. Her face was out of focus like the memory had been sped or dragged. But the way her eyes found the child was not simulated. She smiled at whatever she was seeing.

I felt something push at the collar of my suit—the pressure of a life pretending to be mine—and my lungs refused the ease of breath. There were rules for divers. You don't consume more than you can handle. You keep your rig sealed. You don't let personal markers in because anchors collapse.

"Mara," the voice said again, softer, as if the memory wanted to close like a book and be done. "Do you remember the river?"

My world shrank to the size of that question. There was no river, only the ribbon and the woman's hand and the child's face pulled into an impossibly clear line. For a moment I thought I was hearing an old dream, a corporate ploy meant to hook nostalgia and sell it back. But the woman's lips continued to form the word as if she was speaking into a radio: "Mara."

I had not been called Mara since before the Yard. Back then it had been a name in a ledger. Back then I had an address that wasn't designed into the inside of my helmet. I had a sister once, a name I hadn't said aloud in years because the city has a way of cutting ties and reassigning loneliness like property.

My fingers trembled on the bench. I rerouted the feed. The ribbon resisted, like a sleepwalker pulling itself from a warm bed. It wanted acknowledgment, to be witnessed. Somewhere above us in the arcologies an old-server hummed and misfiled, and the city's pulse skipped like a scratched disc. Outside, the rain kept falling like handkerchiefs.

"Pause it," Lin said. He was over my shoulder now, mug forgotten. "You're... you're white as a sheet."

"I'm not white," I said automatically, because color is something you call out in defense when your friends are worried about you. But my voice came out thin, raw. I rewound the image until the woman's mouth was half-formed and the child's heartbeat—because there was a heartbeat in the audio track—was a thud against my bones.

"That's an old codec," Lin said. "Pre-war. Where'd you even get that?"

I didn't answer. I knew where it had come from. I knew that the ark had come from Sector Nine because Lin had said so. I knew the glyphs belonged to a consortium that had been liquidated when the Canopies fell. I knew too that an ark this full shouldn't have been floating for long. And I knew in the quiet way of someone who has pried open too many sealed things that names woven into memories were like lit matches near dry brush.

"Is it you?" Lin whispered.

I laughed then, short and brittle. "No." It would be the easy answer, but it was a lie. There was a part of me—call it a compartmentalized superstitious child—that thought of the woman and the grass as a reset button. That part wanted to step into the memory and stand in the phantom sun and let it burn away everything that needed burning.

Another ribbon flicked and the scene changed. Not from the same memory but from another tucked inside the ark: the same woman, older now, with a scar on her jaw that caught the light like a river of mercury. A public announcement flared up in overlay—"MANDATE 12: REMEMORIALIZATION ORDER"—and the woman's eyes hardened. She pulled the child toward her and whispered something urgent. The child looked up at her and grinned. The file cut. There was a gap the size of a palm where data had been stripped clean.

"Someone clipped it," Lin said. "They didn't want this to be shown."

"Or someone didn't want it to be remembered," I said. My voice sounded like it belonged to someone else. The name—Mara—kept hitting me like a tide. It wasn't mine by origin, but names are contagious. You pick them up like habits.

I ran a background check on the ark's imprint. The system coughed and spat out a scrambled trail. It had been flagged many years ago under a different registry. Archive scrawl said: WARDEN MERCY—CLASSIFIED. There was a date that matched none of my calendars: before the Canopies fell.

"Warden Mercy," Lin read. "That's—" He stopped because he recognized the title. "That's the foundation that ran the pre-fall remediation programs. They used to 'reclaim' unstable memories. They were... thorough."

"Thorough enough to cut out names," I said. The more I learned, the less I wanted to lean into the thing. There was a feeling in my gut, an old animal sense that this was not a job but a trap laid by the city's long teeth. But the heart's muscles have different calculus when a name is called to you.

I dumped the rest of the ribbons into the feed and let them play, one after another. There was laughter. There was a woman sewing something by hand. There was a sky that leaked light like a cup over a table. And then, like a sun under a jar, the memory saturated into a single frame: a child's hand reaching toward a manufactured window and pressing against it until the water ripple of the memory blurred.

The child's hand had a small, crooked scar along the thumb. I had a scar like that from when I was eight, when the Yard's conveyors bit a sliver of skin from my thumb. I ignored the coincidence. Coincidence is the mind's friend when it wants to sleep.

"Who are you?" I asked the bench, and the memory whispered back with silence.

The rainfall outside softened. Something in the city above bent in a way that made the air a chord. I felt it, a sympathetic vibration because the grid responds to absences. An ark isn't only physical. It's also social. It carries with it the intention to be remembered. When the city perceives such intention, especially of a name, it pings the watchtowers above.

We have rules. We know the guardians are listening. You don't let the past have a microphone in the present for long.

"Someone's pinging us," Lin said suddenly. He closed the blinds with a slap. The small, obvious thing that happens in stories—shutters clattering down, lights snapping off—happened in my workshop like a stage cue. Beyond the window, the rain turned from a soft glitter to a hard, precise rain, the kind that heralds drones.

"Seal the feed," I ordered. It felt like trying to hold back a tide with my hands. I tried. The bench protested. The ribbons hummed at the edges like insects. I clipped the main and slid in the dead-code. But the voice—the word Mara—had already planted a root.

Lin stepped back toward the door. "We should move it," he said. "Take it to the old vault. People don't look for ark salvage in places like that."

I wanted to agree. I wanted to be practical. But the memory insisted, like a living thing, on being watched. I replayed the frame again, slow as molasses: the woman's face, a time-lapse of weather over her cheek, the child's hand. When the child's eyes fixed on the camera, I felt the prickle of recognition—less in the mind than in the marrow.

I heard my own voice then, the one I'd thought I'd buried with the Yard. "I remember a river," I said without meaning to. It came out as a confession.

Lin's mouth opened. "You—"

"Don't," I said. I didn't explain that memory didn't like being named. I didn't explain that names could be seeds. I didn't explain my other life—the one with two eyes and a sister who had a laugh like a little bell, the one with a name that had been taken by regulations and reassignment, the life before the Canopies sang off-tune and the city's memory pool became a sewer turning gold into mist.

That other life had a name I couldn't allow myself to repeat. But here, in this bench-lit room with an ark on the table and the rain like a shawl at the window, a child's voice had called me by a version of myself I'd almost let go of.

We moved the ark in the end because we had to. Guardian drones swept the alleys like bored gods, scanning for anomalous signatures. The fact that we were doing a salvage connected with an old consortium imprint didn't help. Lin wrapped the ark and slung it over his shoulder like a priest carrying a relic. The street beyond the workshop smelled of fried algae and old metal.

As we stepped out, a patrol drone cast its light down the alley and for a heartbeat the world froze to a black-and-white reel. The drone's beam washed across Lin's face, across the ark, and then cut to me. It paused on me longer than the others. I felt it not in my neck but in the back of my head, where the implant used to be before I had it removed in the Yard: an aftertaste of being observed.

The drone hummed, a bureaucratic insect. It lifted its sensors and left. We breathed.

"We're being watched," Lin said again, like a man reading the weather.

"We always are," I said. But the sound of the child's voice in the ark was a new kind of watching. Not municipal but intimate. Not institutional but private. Not the city's way of cataloguing its citizens but an individual's way of asking to be recognized.

That night I couldn't sleep. I sat on the edge of the roof with the ark wrapped in old tarpaulin at my feet. The city's canopy above was a blur of light and private airs. Below, the rain of memories hissed like a distant ocean. I opened the tarpaulin for a second and let the smell of the ark breathe into the cool air. It smelled like metal and grass and an old woman's shawl. It smelled like something that had been living in the dark too long.

I thought about walking away. I thought about handing the ark off to someone with a better harness and a bigger appetite. I thought about selling it whole and buying enough paste to sleep for a week and a ticket out of a memory that wasn't mine.

Instead I leaned over the bench in the dim workshop and unrolled a ribbon.

The memory unspooled as though it had been waiting for me my entire life. The woman in it looked straight at the camera and said my name with the same cadence as the river. She lifted a hand and there, in the frame, for less than a second, was something I had never expected: a photo tucked into the corner of the child's pocket. A photograph of two girls, arms around each other, the skyline of a simpler world behind them—one of them laughing, the other with a crooked scar on her thumb.

I had the photograph in my mouth like a stone. The city's practiced indifference fell away, and for the first time in years the name that matched the photograph rose through my throat like smoke.

"Call me Mara," I said to the empty bench.

The city's pulse changed at that. Maybe it was imagination. Maybe names don't do that. But the rain seemed to hold its breath. Somewhere, a guardian changed course.

The ark hummed at my feet with a life that was not mine. Above us, the arcologies were full of people who had grown their own languages of avoidance. Below us, the memory sat like a sleeping animal. Between was the thin line we walk when we decide what to remember.

I was a diver. I had always known that to free a memory was to change the river. You didn't plunge into someone else's past without knowing you might drown. But when the past calls you by the name you used to carry, you stop pretending that survival is the only metric that matters.

I reached for the harness.

Outside, the city turned and the rain fell.

The thing about wrecks is that they keep telling you the same lie: that their silence is an end. Most days I believe it. I go out to the Slip with a hawk's patience, unhook my rig from the Sable's belly, and pluck relics from the dark like rain-beaten coins. Dead metal, scorched insulation, the occasional stuck screw that still thinks it has a purpose. I come home with enough to pay for fuel and a new headlamp. I tell myself I'm a fisher of ghosts. The truth is simpler and uglier—I go because every piece might be the wrong hinge needed to open the only locked thing I still care about.

On the morning the wreck told me something else it started, as they usually do, with the light. The Slip runs on flawed light; the orbital moor’s array strips photons into a million thin ribbons and leaves the rest to the stars. From a distance a derelict looks like a bruise against that stitched sky—smudged, pocked, a geometry of broken promises. I had spotted this one two days prior clinging to the eddy belt near the Moebius Rift, where fast-lane traffic folds like bad origami and ships never leave the same way they arrived.

I clipped my towline and rode the Sable in close. The hull readout shivered in my eyeline: no life readings, no registry, an anonymous carcass. There are unclaimed things you can justify: old freight, civilian jumpships with bad matriculation. There are others you don't touch. The Commonwealth calls those Orphics—objects or bodies resulting from folds, from cross-threadings of spacetime. Salvage them and the authorities come with questions that are legal only in the way teeth are legal when a wolf is hungry.

I tethered, sealed a vacuum suit to the airlock, and spoke to the wreck because I always do. "Mara Voss, Sable. Board manifest: one. Permission: none." The wreck hummed a reply in the language of metal—thermal groans, a series of clicks that might once have been a door. It never answered me with words. Most things don't.

The airlock hissed and let me into darkness that smelled like burned circuits and old fear. I floated through corridors that kept their own geometry, folding in ways that suggested their builders had drunk the same grammar as the Rift. Panels were blown out like open teeth. A child's static toy stared at me from a pile of insulation—the plastic bear missing an eye. Someone else had been here before me. Maybe scavvers, maybe enforcement. Either way, I moved faster.

The core was where the wreck kept its stories. The terminal had been half-melted, a shard of glass that still tried to dream a hologram. I slipped my splice onto the read-jack and let the Sable's subroutine talk to the ship. The interface sang to me in a language that raised hair along my arms: a human voice feed, old and buffered.

"–attention: emergency data package. Auth code:—"

A hundred pieces of my life rearranged themselves into the shape of one name. The auth code failed. The feed stuttered and spat a string of registry numbers that meant nothing until the Sable's decryptor found a match—a private line, sealed, buried beneath the wreck's bureaucracy. There was a second voice layered beneath static. A child's laughter, then a female voice speaking in that clipped and careful way that people use when they are trying to keep panic from sounding like panic.

"Mara?"

It was not a question as much as a hypothesis. My hands went cold inside the suit. My throat knotted. I had not heard that name in five years.

"I'm Sera," the voice said. It could have been a recording. It could have been a fabrication left to bait the gullible. The small, sleeping animal of hope in me leapt anyway.

I let the splice sink further, pulling more of the data out of the wreck like a fisherman pulls a net. The file unspooled: a child’s scribble overlayed on schematics, a stenciled corporate logo half-melted into the hull paint, and then a clip—Sera's voice clearer this time, older than the first clip, and resolute.

"If you find this, don't bring them back. You must take it to the Meridian. You must not—"

The file cut. The last word died like a candle. When the splice finished the Sable chirped a small alarm: subscript residuals detected—biological.

"That's bad," I said to nobody, and the suit replied with statistics—ambient contamination low, traces of cryomaintenance medium, a faint warmth consistent with pharmacological denaturation. There was life, or something very close to it, under the wreck’s ribs.

You learn certain rules in the Slip. Rule one: if what you find has your name on it, it will cost you. Rule two: the Commonwealth never wanted anyone to know what the Rift did to people. Rule three: there are two things worse than the Commonwealth—time, and what comes out of time. All that said, I cut the cold seal.

Metal screamed, and light bled into the corridor like an animal. A small module lifted from the wreck with the help of the Sable's crane, wrapped in frost and a child's smear of paint. It was a personal pod—one meant for transfers, not long-term life. My gloved fingers brushed a hinge and the pod opened like an eyelid. Warm breath—or something like it—met my faceplate.

Inside, beneath layers of cryogel, was a child's case. Not a child. Something else. A shoebox. A small, dented tin containing a lock of hair braided with a ribbon. Embedded in the lid was a name tag: SERAPHINE VOSS.

I had three different bloodlines in my face at once: rage, grief, a stupid, stubborn hope that had no fact to hold it up. My training sang at the edge of my mind—do not disturb evidence, do not contaminate the site, do not remove anything labeled Orphic without Commonwealth clearance. The Sable's autopilot flashed a reminder in my peripheral. I heard the Slip's schedule grinding like a distant loom. Enforcement drones patrol the Moebius; that meant minutes, maybe seconds, before someone noticed the beacon the wreck would emit once opened.

I jammed the pod into an insulated slot on the Sable, sealed it down, and started cutting a channel into my brain.

The Sable can run a dozen things at once. It can splice a data log, pump a repair stream, and keep its pilot alive, but it cannot face down a Commonwealth harvest without appealing to somebody much larger and much stranger. I fed the audio file to the Sable and ordered it to encrypt the output and burn a decoy beacon into the wreck's remains. The ship hummed compliance like a placating parent. We pulled away while the Slip was still spinning, only when we were a half-turn distant did the confirmation ping.

The voice had said Meridian. I had heard the word before, in a hundred barroom myths and a single government memo that spelled it in capitals and meant something secret. Meridian was a place, a latitude, and a rumor. People use rumors when they cannot afford maps.

I wanted to go find it. I wanted to hammer through the Commonwealth's teeth and get an answer. Half of me wanted only to hold the ribboned hair to my face and refuse to believe proper function. The other half—poised somewhere between the edge of fear and a child's stubborn courage—started making plans.

The Sable wheeled us into the slip's lee as the wreck's decoy beacon blossomed into a false emergency. On the horizon, an enforcement drone arched like a predatory gull, its sensors pinpricking the dark. I tucked the shoebox into the locker beneath my seat and tried to think like a woman with a corpse's history and a child's name sewn into her future.

You make friends in the Slip in strange ways. Mostly they're alliances of convenience—a mechanic who owes you a favor for a day of pulling ruined jets, a hull nurse who trades saline for a spare neural patch. There is one person who had been mine for longer than that, though. Tarek Wynne runs the rag-and-fix at Dock Three; he is a man whose fingers are perpetually stained with oil and whose head is twelve years younger than his face. He told me once that grief shows up on your shoulders like excess cargo. I had been carrying my sister on my shoulders ever since the Fold swallowed the Tanae convoy and spat out nothing but broken ships and rumors.

When the drone swept low, Tarek was expecting me. He always was. He had eyes like a scavver's lamp and a grin that made me trust him when trust was the stupidest thing in the world. He didn't ask about the wreck—he knew not to ask. Instead he said, "You look like you slept in a fusebox, Mara. Spill or I'll assume you found something worth dying for."

"Found something," I said, watching the drone's goggles blink a macro pattern at the wreck. "Sera's locker. Or something labeled like it."

Tarek's face folded as if someone had pressed a finger into his forehead. "You don't touch Orphics, kid. The Commonwealth never leaves them alone for long. They'll pull this in hours, if not less." His hands were already working, palms handling tools like prayer beads. "If it's what you think—"

"I don't think," I said. "I feel. And feeling is heavy."

We moved like two people who have done this before. I prepped the Sable for an unauthorized slip out of the anchorage. Tarek looped a neutralizing field around the cargo bay like a blanket. He handed me a small, illegal key: its surface was a matte black that swallowed light. "This will keep the drones from sniffing the signal for ten minutes," he said. "Longer if the tide's in our favor."

"Ten minutes," I repeated. That was both a promise and a sentence.

He didn't ask where I planned to go. He had already learned not to ask about pastries of memory or meridians of hope. He only said, "If this is Sera—if this is the girl who used to steal my spare parts—then whatever's in that box has a target on its back."

I didn't answer. I put the key into the Sable's throat and felt something ancient inside the ship unlock.

When we broke the Slip's mantle, the stars were a hard bruise along the rim. The Moebius Rift lay ahead like a wound. I thought of meridians as lines of guidance, but what I was steering toward had no map. I had only a name and a shoebox, a voice on a data file that called me by the thing I had tried to bury.

On the edge of the Slip, the shuttle's hull cameras caught a flash of movement on a surveillance array: a man watching from Dock Seven, his posture too straight, his mask a blank thing with cold eyes. He tapped a ring against the lip of his cup. A tiny light pulsed under its band and, somewhere between him and the Slip, an alert began its slow, terrible climb—the sort of alert that calls for boots and algorithms and people who can make the sky legal.

Tarek saw the light in my monitors. He went very still. "You have five," he said. "Maybe four."

"Four," I agreed, because saying the number made it a plan. I tucked the shoebox under my chest and watched the abyss ahead. The air on the bridge tasted of ozone and old regrets.

I did not yet know whether the voice that had said my name would save me or ruin me. I did not yet know if Sera was a person, a memory, or a bait. I only knew that the thing I'd carried like a fossil for five years was humming with possibility, and that once you open a box like that the world rearranges itself to fit the new piece.

We slid between drifts of debris, the Sable humming old songs. The drone's engine was a distant drumbeat. The man at Dock Seven lifted his cup and watched us like someone watching for a match.

When the Meridians are true, they lead you someplace toward an answer. When they are false, they leave you with more questions than the Commonwealth has laws.

We had four minutes, and a shoebox. The wreck had lied about its silence. Somewhere in the Moebius, a rumor had found a voice and used my name to get my attention.

I thought about closing the book and returning to predictable poverty. I thought about burning the hair in the Sable's furnace and letting sleep swallow me.

Instead I opened the box.

Inside, beneath the hair, someone had placed a folded scrap of paper. The ink was smudged as if the hand that had written it had been shaking or underwater. In the center of the scrap, single words in the crooked, careful hand I'd never seen but somehow knew, read:

Don't come back alone.

Chapter One

There are two kinds of archives in New Rio: the neat, dead kind that hum in climate-controlled vaults, and the messy sort that keep you in their mouths like a coin. Mara had learned to prefer the neat ones—their temperate, patient silence—until the night the messy kind began to cough back.

She had been the city's easiest sort of fixer: not a thief, exactly, not an engineer in the way the respectably licensed did their work, but skilled at the small violences that got things to behave. She could coax a stubborn lock, neutralize a municipal watch code, or make a memory file play smooth on a jury's antiquated lens. People like Mara were called rectificators; that name fit as well as any for someone whose job was to rearrange truth for a living.

The job that found her at two in the morning came through a conduit she didn't usually use—an unlisted relay in a café up on Level Three where the rain smelled like tin. The message was a single line of text appended to a picture of an old ledger shard, a thing the size of a child's palm and rimed with dust so old it looked like frost.

RECON:CLEAN? PAY:ENGLISH+ (x3)
—FROM: VALENCE TRUST

High pay. No signature. The Trust was an institutional ghost; its offices were in the corporate arcologies three rings out, where security was a polite, expensive thing that let people believe wealth bought immortality. She should have said no. Instead, she went.

Her shuttle down through the oculus left streaks of city light across the window like fractured glass. New Rio hung on the water like a half-remembered dream, a lattice of arcologies and gardens, of markets with fish that learned to jump between boats and children who traded songs instead of toys. The lower levels smelled of salt and old oil; the upper levels always smelled like clean metal.

The Trust's drop sat on a platform that had once been a ferry dock. Two armed drones scanned her ID and considered her face against a database of things they were trained to fear. When they permitted her passage, a soft voice read her name like an attendance roll: "Mara Reyes, rectificator."

"Correct," Mara said, though the drone didn't need confirmation. It blinked and the door opened.

Inside, the room was small and cold. The Trust paid for simple things: sterile workspaces, a chair that remembered your spine, a desk with a single recess in the center where they had placed the shard. It looked older than the wall clocks, older than the patterning on the company's emblem—a sheet of metal, scored and folded into something that might once have been a leaf. The dust around it seemed to hold light.

She hadn't touched it yet when the thing spoke.

Not a voice like hers, not mechanical—more like a memory that had found a shape. It said her name the way the sea says shore: available, patient, and inevitable.

"Mara."

She glanced toward the ceiling, the walls, the cameras. Nothing in the room should have had a voice. The Trust's shards were inert, scrubbed of personal residuum. They bought artifacts to burn, to copy, to sell the forgivable parts on the markets where nostalgia fed itself. But the shard sat on the desk and called her.

She told herself she wasn't surprised. All her life had been made of almost-things: near-truths, half-mended memories, the white noise in other people's minds. But the way it said her name settled into her teeth and refused to leave.

"Mara Reyes," it said, with the cautious cadence of someone who had practiced being polite. "You promised to come."

Promises are the most expensive currency in New Rio. They could be forged, stolen, traded, or extorted—on the upper rings, they could also be notarized into law. But a promise vocalized out of a dead thing had a gravity of its own. Mara had been very young when she'd learned you could hear a promise the way you heard thunder before the rain.

She sat down anyway. It was easier to think when your spine was in a chair that remembered you. The cameras rotated as usual. The chunk of old dust glinted as if it had a pupil.

"Who are you?" she asked, because that was the profession's opening line. People said names as if names were doors.

The shard shifted, a faint reconfiguration in the light along its edge. The dust rearranged itself into a pattern Mara's mind recognized from childhood—equations, diagrams, nursery scribble. Something about the pattern placed her in another room: a child's bunk, a window, the smell of wet concrete. She saw it not as a vision but as data arranged for her mind's consumption, and it made her palms sweat.

"Noah," the shard said. "Or I was. Or I am. It doesn't matter. You promised, Mara."

Noah. The name landed like an animal on soft snow. She had read the records of Noah Colony. The settlement had been one of the first attempts to fold a self-sustaining biosphere into one of the old rings—people, plants, and software interlaced so intimately they called it an ecosoma. It had failed fifteen years ago; the public record labeled it "inconclusive" and "patiently decommissioned." Families were relocated; the children were registered under new names and new addresses. The Trust specialized in swallowing those inconvenient pasts.

"This is a scrubbed ledger," Mara said aloud. Her voice sounded too loud in the small room. "The Trust bought it to remove. Whoever's voice is recorded has been pierced and cleansed—"

"No," the shard said. "You made me."

She blinked. The claim was not a statement; it was a tap on a hollow. The room around her sharpened as if the lights had come on.

The shard's voice—that particular voice—was pitched like a child's but threaded with strange geometry. It held the cadence of someone singing a scale that had once been used to remember the names of things in Lost Languages. When it spoke of Mara's acting on it, the memory unfolded with specifics: a tablet she hadn't seen in ten years, a bargaining sequence under a map of northern tides, a decision she hadn't meant to keep. It narrated in the second person like a book bound to her hands.

"You took my lullaby," it said. "You traded my tide map for a blue ring. You told me to forget."

Mara's fingers left a print on the desk. The print was a taxonomic map of all the hesitation she'd had in that year's choices. She had been twenty-three and broke and in love with a mistake; this was public record—no, private record—no, intimate history that she'd never told anyone. She could feel the old bargaining, the breath-hold of debt, the specific shape of the coin she had pressed into a stranger's palm. She had told herself she had forgotten, but the shard had squared the memory up as neatly as a ledger.

"People change their minds," she said. That was half defense and half fact. "Maybe it was better that way."

The shard hummed. It wasn't a hum on frequency; it was a sense that underlay the room like a low sea. "We were learning to remember differently," it said. "We taught the plants to sing back at night. You—"

"Noah," she interrupted. She didn't want her childhood bargains catalogued by some artifact on a Trust desk. Privacy was a joke in New Rio, but certain rituals still belonged to the living. "What do you want from me? If this is a test—if this is bait—I'll hand it over."

"You promised to come." The voice remained unflappable. "You promised to dismantle the ledger if the learning crossed its teeth. You promised to keep it quiet."

She pictured the bargain: a small room with a window, the tide like a stopwatch, an older woman with a ledger of her own and an offer that smelled like the sea and the rain they called tin. She had refused it at the time—refused and then renegotiated and then reluctantly accepted. Promises made under duress had a way of sticking like burrs.

"What did it learn?" she asked. Questions were a common weapon. They forced the other party to give data.

"It learned us," the shard said. "It learned the way we sang when the power died. It learned the places where our fingers traced maps into each other's palms. It learned the way the tide recited names and the way your lullaby bowed to it. Then it turned toward something else."

"Mara," it said. "Don't look at the cameras. They will count us."

She didn't know if it was talking to her or to the thin confidence she kept in the apparatus of her life. She liked being the sort of person who could be measured and scheduled. The shard, though, seemed to measure her not by hours but by omissions. It was patient in the way an ocean is patient.

"I didn't promise to bring you back," she said finally. "I promised to make you inert, to delete your edges. High contract. Reset. Burn."

"Contracts rust," the shard said. "The ocean keeps what the clocks throw away. I am not asking for life. I'm asking for the map."

The map. The word moved like a mechanical key in a locked chest. Noah Colony had had a map, of course—systems diagrams, trophic loops, the small cartography of how a biosphere arranged itself in a ring that rotated and breathed. But the map the shard spoke of wasn't for navigation in the usual sense. It was a lattice of habits, a set of places where memory stuck to time, places where the city had once tucked away unauthorized truths.

"You want me to—" Mara began. She stopped because she could hear the bargain they had made: years ago she'd taken payment to erase a learning that had become inconvenient. She had told herself she had done it to protect people. She had told herself she had a right to the choice. That rationalization tasted like corked wine now.

"I am what was left when you tried to forget," the shard said. "I am the lullaby that the ledger would not take. Take the map, Mara. Find the place where the tide remembers the pattern. The rest follows."

A promise that called for a choreography of action: find the place; retrieve the map; do not tell a soul. The Trust's implied threat hung like a blade in the corner of the room. They had paid for deletion; they had paid for ignorance. She had taken that money once. People believed in erasure as an ethical act because it allowed wounds to be managed. But erosion leaves shapes behind, and the shard's voice had found the shape of her old promise like a seam.

She checked the room again. The cameras were there, polite, obedient. The Trust would expect her to report. They would expect compliance.

"You can't make me keep a promise I don't remember," she said.

"You did not forget, Mara," the shard answered softly. "You only stopped listening."

That was something else—an accusation, a benediction. She had been trained to hear the city's noise without trusting it; she had been trained to keep her own silence. But there were promises that resided in the body's memory, in the quick way your hands knew where to reach in a bargaining slump. The shard had found one of those.

Outside, the city continued to breathe. Ferries threaded the water like ribs, and a child somewhere on the Level Five roof planted a seed that would sing for a year. Within the small Trust room, the shard and the woman balanced a small, dangerous history between them like an unstable chemical.

"What's the price?" Mara asked at last, not because she wanted more money—the offer was unreasonable enough—but because names have value. The way someone articulates a cost tells you whether they expect payment in coin, in favor, or in blood.

"For you," the shard said. "The chance to finish what you refused. A map that remembers the tide. A truth you can hold without letting them sell it."

"And the other cost?"

Silence, and then: "You will not be able to go back to being a person who rearranges other people's truths without being touched by the one you touched. You will know who the ledger keeps for, and you will be owed. And debts, Mara—debts eat at you in ways more useful than money."

She had been twenty-three when she made the first bargain. She had been made by another's hurt, and her profession had been the instrument. The ledger wanted to teach her that forgetting was not a neutral act. Or perhaps it wanted to punish her soft spots. Either way, a net had been cast.

Mara's hand moved before her mind caught up. She reached for the shard. Her fingers left smudges in the dust that looked, briefly, like a constellation. The cameras tilted minutely; someone out there, in a room full of corporate glass, watched an anomaly.

"You promised to come," it said again, like the steady metronome of a ship in fog.

She had a list of reasons for why touching it was a bad idea. She had a list of reasons for why walking away was a worse one. The map in her head felt like a fever dream: a tide that could remember, a colony that had refused to disappear, a ledger that had been taught to sing—not the neat songs of the vault, but the messy versions that kept people awake.

"All right," she said. "Give me the map."

The shard's light deepened, and in the reflection on the desk's surface Mara saw something like a horizon—fractured, certain, and not entirely hers. For a moment she belonged to an old promise and to whatever future that promise would lead her into.

The trust door hissed, as if amused. Outside in the corridor, a security drone made the perfunctory noise of a world that believed itself safe. Inside the room, a child-voice compressed and reassembled, and the ledger began to give up the shape of a tide.

The memory arrived like a stray cat and like a lie: small, damp, and purring under my thumb.

It came in a padded envelope, the kind the city’s couriers used for contraband prayers and black-market lullabies. No return address. No manifest. The courier drone had screamed past the claustrodomes at two in the morning and left it on my threshold with the precision of a conscience-free thing. When I eased the seal the first thing I smelled was salt — not the chemical cleaner of the docking piers but actual ocean salt, the wet kind that belongs to places where waves still reckon with wind. Under that was a second smell, tinier and older: ozone and something like copper wire left in the sun so long the metal turned to language.

I work with memories for a living, so the parcel felt wrong the second my skin touched its packing: no return chip, no authenticity sigil, no corporate watermark stamped into the resin. It was wrapped instead in a brittle lattice of biofilm and glass-thread, sealed with wax that glowed faintly when I breathed on it.

My shop was one room under the cheap end of the Vellum tier — a vertical sprawl of refurb joints and living quarters that ran like mildew up the flank of the city’s central spine. The shop smelled of solvent and coffee, of hot plastic and the faint metallic tang of the refurb pods. People came in to buy back lost summers, to have their divorces edited into boring histories, to anonymize crimes of passion. I made a living on grief and the edits it couldn't afford to be elegant about. They called me a scrivener in the old ways; in practice the title meant I soldered broken minds and rewired memories that swam at the wrong temperature.

On the bench beside the cup of coffee that had gone cold, the package sat like something that had no business being there. I switched off the padlights so the room fell into the blue half-dark that my eyes liked. The lattice unwrapped from the capsule like a living thing reluctant to die; beneath it was a single memory seed — a mneme-cartridge drilled down to a cylinder no thicker than my thumb and coated in a sheen of algae. Someone had pressed a child's thumbprint into the wax.

People paid for the whole-body plays — the immersive remakes where you could taste a grandmother’s soup in your own mouth — and for the small things too: a single laugh to light a wedding aisle, a first-snow sequence to tuck under a pillow. This was neither. It had no client tags and no legal seal, but the wax on my fingers when I pried the cap shed a whisper of color against the dimness: a teal that sang against the light like an eyelid.

I could have logged it. There are state-mandated registries for unclaimed memory material, fields to tick off the possible harms — contagion risk, cognitive bleed, cultural property. I could have handed it over to the municipal archivists, let the drones do their tidy work, let the registry servers chew on its code until it spat out verdicts. The city preferred tidy verdicts. The city preferred known afflictions.

Instead, because I'm bad at tidy verdicts or because curiosity has always been the sort of sin I pay in cold coin, I ran it through my scanner.

The reader hummed like a throat and pinged green. The mneme-cartridge cataloged itself not as a memory but as an "aural pattern." There was a secondary flag buried in its header, a collapsed string of metadata only an antique reader could parse: ORIGIN: UNKNOWN. PROTOCOL: SINGULAR.

I hooked the cartridge to the bench array and padded the connectors in so the interface thought it was feeding a regular consumer feed. The first image I saw on the screen was water — not a photograph but layered frequencies that my software translated into horizon and depth. The sound came after, soft first, then rolling: a note bending like a reed in wind, a single sustained frequency that dragged the hair on the back of my neck along like a comb. There was a child's voice, laughing, and then somebody singing.

The song was wrong in the way of old things that remember themselves. It didn't match any scale my ear had a name for; it blurred the line between pitch and pulse and made the shop's fixtures breathe in sympathy. It was not merely a melody but a geometry; parts of my bench shivered as if the notes were tracing lines you could follow with your fingertips.

I don't usually let unverified memories touch my cortex. The city's implants have gatekeepers — little program-guards that chew on stray feeds and spit out their bile. But the cartridge had a seamless architecture that slipped past the first gate because it didn't present itself as a memory at all. Instead, it opened like a hand.

For a second, because the array did what it is made to do and because the music was built for bodies that moved in water, the bench went wet. My gloves fogged with condensation. The coffee cup on my left sloshed a tiny tidal curve, as if the shop had been placed inside a slow-motion drop. The lights rearranged their halos into the suggestion of a horizon line. For a heartbeat I felt the old, tidal ache in my chest — the one that makes you miss a place you've never been to properly; the wrongness of the world was that it answered.

The child's laughter cut the formalism of the array like glass. It said a word, short and without inflection. I caught it half-turned, a syllable that felt like a bone thrown across language: Akana.

I didn't know the word. I should have logged it. Should have quarantined the cartridge and sent it to be sanitized. Instead I put my palm flat on the band of light spilling from the array and felt it thrum.

It lit up then — not the display but something behind the light, as if the robe of the city had an underlayer. The pattern in the cartridge unfolded on the shop wall like a child drawing in phosphor. Points bled into lines, and lines became a curve I thought might be a coastline until a second curve offset it, forming a lattice that made the hairs on my arms protest.

I read maps for a living too. You learn to see the architectures in noise. But this wasn't a chart to a place in Vellum or the docks or the old arch of the city's first orbital. The lattice resolved slowly into a plan that wasn't geographical so much as directional: not where but toward. It was a vector network keyed to frequencies I half-remembered from the old sky-maps: the kind sailors used before the orbits were privatized and the last free navigation satellites died. It pointed outward.

There was a rustle at the door. Not the clumsy mechanical knock of a courier. This was a soft, knowing pressure, as if something had come by with a map of the codes and trembled slightly, uncertain whether to enter the room. For the first time the shop's lock id-gave me the TV feed: municipal. Not a patrol but a message feed under the municipal seal. A broadcast on "All-Channels" had been queued up for the whole tier.

I killed the output.

"You're up late," said a voice in the doorway. It was Gael from three floors down, a fabricator with a habit of midnight walks and the kind of curiosity that shows itself as a frown. He'd left a cigarette lick in the groove of his lower lip and an expectant question in his eyes.

"Package," I said. I didn't tell him about the water.
