The locket's image was intimate. It bore something the town's clippings never had: proof that two stories had met and eaten one another. My mother's history and Eleanor Ashby's disappearance had been folded into a piece of metal and thrown to the tides.

That night—forty-three days ago—my mother had given me a purse she said had belonged to a woman who "never finished anything." She had said the woman's name so softly I thought it was a joke. "Keep her safe," she had told me. I had laughed the kind of laugh that covers up worry and put the purse away. I had not expected the town to cough up anything like a ghost.

I stepped forward before I could talk myself out of it. "Where's the coroner?" I asked. My voice sounded small and decisive at the same time—like a stone thrown to see what ripples it would make.

"Two hours. They got crossing closures." Baird rubbed his knuckles together. "We'll need to tow the boat and bag the evidence. Get you to the station to take a statement."

The town closed in around me. Mr. Lang's flour dusted the air like the first snow, settling on coats and temple where gossip settles into the brain. The pair of women in the photograph smiled forever, and Eleanor's smile had something coy in it that belonged to secrets kept too long.

As they zipped the sailcloth back into a bundle for the coroner, I felt the locket as a weight in my palm like a leaden heart. It was small and ordinary and packed with consequences. When I turned it over I could just make out the letters again, E.A., their edges softened by tide and time.

"Whoever she was," Sheriff Baird said, "she didn't belong in the water tonight."

No, she didn't. But she belonged to Grayling Harbor—its tides, its docks, its people who kept histories in boxes and told stories over coffee until the edges had frayed. I had come back to town with a bruised suit of hopes and a camera. I had come for quiet, for the unexamined parts of small-town life to stay exactly that—unexamined. But the locket in my hand was an invitation. Some things, once pulled from the deep, demanded answers.

I slipped the photograph into my pocket as if it were contraband and not part of a stranger's mourning. The violet crumbled under my fingers like old promises. The harbor kept breathing in, exhaling fog that smelled of rope and diesel and long-decayed secrets. I said the town's name under my breath like a benediction: Grayling Harbor.

You can't look at a locket and not want to know what it's holding shut. I hadn't even meant to be a detective. But people—cities, towns, families—tend to notice the ones who look too long at the seams. They notice the ones who keep asking questions they think they're done answering.

I put the camera back over my shoulder and left the pier. Behind me, a portion of the town's hush was already unravelling. The tide would take the rest in its time. I walked home with the picture of two young women in my pocket, and when I reached the house where my mother's books were still stacked like small graves along the living-room wall, I set it on the table and did something I had not done since the funeral: I opened one of my mother's boxes.

There are a dozen ways to be dragged back into history, and all of them smell faintly of the sea. The locket's photograph was one. The other, I realized as I turned the first brittle page of an old notebook, was that my mother had known more than she had told me. Her handwriting slanted across the page—notes, names, a shorthand that read like a map.

At the bottom, in ink I recognized as hers, there was a line that made everything feel as though it had been on a hinge this entire time: Find E.A. before the harbor does.

Outside, the harbor breathed in another cold, low tide. Inside, a question sat in my chest like a seed. Some things never should surface. But some things, once lifted, set the rest of the town to drifting.

The morning the body washed up against the old stone of the harbor, it was still almost dark enough to call it night. A low bank of cloud had swallowed the east and the fog horn from the lighthouse down on Gull Point breathed slow and indifferent into the town. I had my hands shoved into the pockets of a thrift-store coat that once belonged to my father and the collar smelled faintly of his tobacco. For a moment I forgot where I was, which made it feel like every town in every memory: the endless edge of sea and sky, the soft thud of shoes on wet planks, the hush that comes when everyone is still sleeping and the ocean is doing its thinking.

I was opening the museum that morning—locking the front glass and mentally checking the placement of the model ships, the way the light hit the glass cases with the old compasses—when Tom Avery called my cell. Tom's voice is a two-note thing: always the same weather-beaten surprise. "Eliza? You down by the point?"

"It’s me, Tom," I said. "The museum's open in an hour."

"Not what I mean." He exhaled the word out of the receiver like a man blowing away a bad dream. "There's someone on the rocks."

By the time I reached the breakwater the tide had knuckled its way in close enough to lick the base of the lighthouse steps. The man lay half-turned on the slick boulders, and for a minute I thought he was one of the birds—so still, so absurdly small against the groove of sea and stone. Then Tom's hand came down on my shoulder and something cold sank into my chest. He’s been a deputy for fifteen years; his hands know how to be present where things have gone wrong.

"Don't move," he said to my town, and I understood the order was as much for me as for the man on the rocks.

It wasn't the face that stopped me—I've seen faces rearranged by time or grief or illness and sometimes the skin forgets how to hold in the person—but the ticket stub folded like a little flag in his fist. It was rain-sodden but still readable enough to give a name: PROMENADE THEATRE, OCTOBER 12, 9 PM. Someone had written, in a hurried hand that leaned like a row of trees, "Come alone."

Old paper has a way of holding onto time, of showing you the past has visited. I knew that stub because I'd found one like it in a box my father left behind two months after his funeral. I had thought it a trivial thing then—part of whatever life he'd taken apart in order to leave. His handwriting was a bad imitation of his smile: rounded letters with a stubborn tail. The "alone" on the stub in the man's hand was in the same slant.

"You see it?" Tom asked.

I did. The subconscious logs these small loops; the world is built of them. The stub in my hand and the stub in his pocket were the same arc of ink. He could be anyone, this man, but that handwriting was an accusation and a benediction. It was a ribbon tying me to a memory I had tried not to pull.

"Call Clara," I told Tom before I knew why I was telling him. Clara oversaw the prom night volunteer list at the theatre and knows everyone who works the light and sound like she knows her own bones. "And the coroner."

He nodded and moved with the slow diligence of someone who has practiced. We stood there—my gloved fingers finding the wet paper, his other hand on his radio—and a gull passed low and vengeful. The lighthouse fixed its halo out to sea.

The man’s coat had been heavy, like someone had dressed for a late storm and then forgotten the weather. A brass tag swung from a thin chain at his neck, bright against the sea-dark fabric. H7—stamped, not etched. Something about the tag set off another memory. Two months ago, in the tidy aftermath of my father's boxes, I found a small brass tag stitched into the lining of an old duffel. It had read the same: H7. I had laughed then—at the absurd notion that a tag stitched into cloth had any claim on the future. I had set it on the mantel among the other small things I couldn't place and told myself the rest of his things would sort themselves into a story later.

I never told anyone about the other stub. I had told fewer and fewer things as time had leveled my life into fewer, quieter shorelines.

"Name?" I asked the deputy because the answering of small questions felt like doing something useful.

Tom squinted up at the cliff where the houses began, the way a man checks the sky. "No ID on him. No wallet. No phone. We’ll call it a John Doe, pending." His jaw pushed forward. He didn't say what I heard: that a John Doe is a previous life wrapped tight and waiting for someone to open it.

We moved the way we always move in town in an emergency: snug, economical, with a hot center of gossip to stoke later. People started coming down the lane with towels and slippers and the cautious curiosity of neighbors who have always found it hard to ignore a spectacle at the edge of town. Mrs. Crandall from the bakery crossed herself and muttered something about the sea taking and leaving. A teenager with a camera phone in hand made the obligatory step-two: he recorded the scene and missed everything that mattered.

A boat pulled up as the coroner arrived. The tide that had carried the man in gently slurred away again, leaving him almost dry, like the sea had decided it couldn't keep the secret. They covered him with a sheet in the end because that's what you do, and the sheet is always the first lie. We all know how to cover something so that, for a while, it is no longer there.

Later, when Tom and I were on the docks in an aftertaste of officialness—notes made, a line put out that the area was closed, a request from his boss to keep it quiet until the town setter got ahead of the news—he asked about the tag.

"You said you found another tag?" he said in a voice that has learned how to hoard facts like currency.

"Yes." I had to tell someone, even if the telling would tilt the world into smaller angles. "My father's things. He had a duffel with a tag stitched inside the lining. H7."

Tom's face folded into a look like someone solving a crossword without the benefit of the printed clues. "You sure?"

"I put it on the mantle." I felt ridiculous and exposed. People in small towns have recesses where they keep their shame and their relics. I had a mantel of both.

He was quiet for a long time. In the distance, the prom in the theater would have been rehearsing mid-season pieces—if the ticket was genuine. I thought about all the nights my father didn't come home and the stories he'd told to cover where he'd been. I thought about the way he had liked to give things names, as if naming a trivial object made it less likely to betray him.

"It might be nothing," I said because not everything people call fate deserves the name. "It might be coincidence."

Tom tipped his head toward the lighthouse where someone had left a light on in the keeper's window. "Coincidences pile up in this town," he said. The truth in that sounded like a confession.

The coroner's van left, indifferently blinking its yellow lights. The town returned to itself in small increments; kids who had once dared each other to step on the rocks for the thrill went back to their lawns, their lives, their chores. The sea resumed its patient task of erasing footprints, as if to pretend it had not conspired with anyone.

I found myself walking away from the covered body toward the steps that led up to the museum. The glue that keeps a life in place is small things: a key left on a ring, a dent in the banister of the house you grew up. At the foot of the steps, half-buried in a puddle of last night's rain, something lay like an accidental blessing—a small brass key on a loop of frayed leather. It looked stupid and important at the same time, the sort of key you might imagine opening a box of postcards no one ever thought to look through. The tag attached to it read, in my father's hand, "H7—Do not open."

The handwriting was the same slanted thing I'd seen in the ticket stub. I picked the key up with only the most measured reluctance, the tug you give to a hidden seam before you decide whether to pull it open.

There are sounds that announce decisions: a drawer shutting, a boat's engine cutting. Mine was the hollow, insistent sound of footsteps on the museum's wooden floor as I went inside. I had imagined a dozen different wakes for that key—trivial, ceremonious, vindicating. I had not imagined it would be attached to a body on the rocks by morning.

I slid the key into my pocket and felt the shape of it press into my thigh like a small, hard truth. Someone had left clues that would have to be followed. I did not know yet whether I was dangerous to myself or necessary to the truth.

When I turned back toward the lighthouse, the light in the keeper's window had gone out. The town was awake now enough to begin to watch. We are all of us small sentinels until the sea decides what it wants to give up.

I told Tom I would stay in town for the day. I did not tell him why. I told myself I would only open the duffel once—just to see if the tags matched—and then I would go back to the business of running the museum. The way one tells a lie to be brave.

The hitch of anxiety in my chest was not so much fear as the recognition that some things were beginning to form that could not be ignored. The key in my pocket was a pin; I could feel the point of it in the soft tissue of my thoughts. The man on the rocks was a loose end on a very old rope.

Someone had come to tell me a story. The sea had been its messenger. All I had to do was answer.

The first shape of the morning was fog. It settled against the windows like wool, muffling the town into blurred edges and soft curses. From my bench at the back of the shop I could have been anywhere: a cramped boat cabin, a votive room in an old cathedral, a stage set just before the curtains rose. The smell of glue, old paper and boiled linseed put my pulse into a steady, domestic rhythm. For five years The Binding Room had been my small, precise universe—linen, thread, a press that liked to bite—until things started arriving that made the universe tilt.

The crate was the size of a small coffin and arrived at nine-thirty, bundled into the shop by a courier who had the sort of face that looked embarrassed to be in the world. He left it on the doormat without a word, like contraband, and stamped a delivery slip with a hand that trembled somewhere between apology and duty. On the top of the crate someone had painted a symbol in black—two S's that folded into each other like mirror-image serpents. I knew that symbol as well as I knew the scars on my fingertips: it had been on a plaster cast my mother kept on the mantle when I was a child, a small brass thing you could turn like a key. We called it her "bad luck coin" because she would slide it into the seams of books when she didn't want to lose them. She'd been gone eleven years. I had not touched any of her things.

There was a small label pinned to the crate with my name written in a hand that had the habit of sliding off its baseline. "For Clara Arden," it said, and beneath, "Handle with care. Open by hand."

People in town sent me things they wanted repairing. They also sent me secrets. I rubbed my thumbs over mine to steady them and set the crate on the workbench. The shop was a narrow room off the Market Street arcade, windows fogged with salt and time. Outside the gulls argued with one another like old relatives. Inside, the radiator grunted, the press waited with the patience of a hibernating animal, and my hands—hands raised on paste and patience—folded the crate open.

There was nothing garish inside. The air slipped out smelling of cedar and old daylight. At the top, cushioned in tissue, lay a small wooden box with brass corners and a lock the color of old coins. The S symbol had been branded into the lid. Under the box, wrapped in oilcloth, was a hardcover album—black cloth, cloth the color of night sky washed in dust. I set the album aside, fingers drawn to the box as if pulled by a current. The lock was rusted but not so badly that it resisted the wick of oil. When the key at last turned, the sound it made was less mechanical than theatrical: a small, obedient click followed by a sigh.

Inside the box was a single object, nestled in dark velvet—a coin. It was thin and coppered, about the size of a dime, and in the center it bore the same double-S I had seen three times in less than ten minutes. Someone had left it polished to a brassy tilt. It lay there as if waiting for me to remember something. My hand hovered over it and then closed.

There was a photograph tucked into the lining of the box, too—loose, soft at the corners. I drew it out. Black-and-white, glossy, a little curled from age. The front showed a child on a lap, a beach wall beyond them: the pier house at Marrow's End, weathered boards and a hand-painted sign that read "PIER HOUSE." The child was grinning with an arrogance that comes from not knowing what you are supposed to be afraid of. The child was me.

I didn't recognize the man in the photograph. He was younger than I was now and older than the memory that tumbled through me—those bright, inscrutable parents-of-my-very-young-child days one keeps like coins in pockets. His jaw was narrow, his eyes shadowed beneath a hat like a swimmer's shadow. He wore a coat that had a patch at the breast: the twin serpents curling into themselves. Someone had slid an inscription along the bottom edge in a fountain-pen scrawl a hundred hands had tried to imitate over the decades. It read, in a hand that trembled a little between warmth and resolve: For Clara, June 4, 1999 — Pier House.

My fingers tightened on the photograph. June 4th was my birthday.

I checked the date on the flaky calendar tacked above my workbench as if a sudden arithmetic could anchor me. June 4, twenty-twenty-five. The writing on the photograph had a present-tense certainty about it, the way a person underlined a sentence to make it true.

The bell above the door chimed: a hollow, wind-blown sound. I kept my eyes on the photograph and turned only after the sound finished. It was Ben, standing there in a raincoat that had seen better winters. Ben had long been my town's semi-retired whatever-you-needed: ex-fireman, occasional handyman, man who remembered everyone's crises and had the habit of carrying them as if they were his own. He smelled of coffee and salt. He had a newspaper tucked under his arm like a secret.

"You look like you've seen a ghost," he said by way of greeting. His lungs had the slow ache people get when they live by the sea.

"Something like that." I tucked the photograph back into the box and closed the lid, though the coin rested in my palm like a hot truth.

Ben didn’t push. He folded his hands in the front of his coat as if trying to force his fingers to orderliness. "They found a body this morning," he said then, like a man dropping an heirloom. He did not mean it in the dry local-news way; there was a weight to his voice I didn't like. "Pier House. Open water. Early tide. They say the coroner's still out there, and—"

"Who?" My voice came out small and accidental. The photograph on my workbench slipped like a pulse against the wood beneath my palm.

"Don't know the name yet." Ben glanced at the crate and followed my gaze to the S on the lid. His mouth opened and closed like a fish. "There was…there was a coin on the man's eyelid."

Time has a way of changing the scale of your fears. For a second all the small noises in the shop—the press's gasp, the clock's patient hands—shrank away. The coin in my closed fist felt suddenly heavier than copper. "A coin?" I echoed, as if saying the word might place it back into the realm of the sensible.

Ben didn't look well. Men who remembered the town's rough edges often left their faces soft with what they had seen. "They say it's like a ritual thing. The deputy—Hale—he thinks it's a mark. He said it's the first thing they noticed. Said it looked like…like a symbol. He mentioned the Pier House. He said the man was found on the beach, half-washed, no ID. He said the tide did him no favors." Ben let out a breath that might have been a laugh. "I come by to tell you because you used to go to the Pier House when you were small. Thought you should know."

There are conversations where the air rearranges itself so that you can stand in the same room but be in different decades. The photograph felt suddenly like evidence laid across my palms. "Was it the—" I stopped. The coin had an S. The photograph had an S. My mother had kept an S. The world liked such loops; my mind liked narratives.

"Yeah," Ben said softly. "They say the coin had that mark. Distinctive. He said the deputy wanted me to pass on the word, on the off-chance—" He lifted his eyebrows as if off-chances sometimes came with a warning. "There was…a date. People talking. And because you were part of the Pier House old story."

There were stories everyone in Marrow's End told in varying tones depending on whether they wanted to keep the children quiet or the older folk entertained. The Pier House had been a party shed and a boardinghouse and little else. It had hosted a hundred summers of laughter, and once, a decade before I could remember, a row had happened there that people still chewed over like surplus gum.

I felt the blood in my ears, a small, clinical pressure. My thumb brushed the edge of the coin. The metal hummed cold against my skin as if it had soaked itself in moonlight. "Who found him?"

"Local fisherman. Early. The tide pulled him up like a bad joke. Hale's there now. He said to tell you—" Ben hesitated. "Said if you had anything that might help. Old photos, maybe. He thought you might know more than the rest of us."

I looked at the black album I had set aside. It seemed suddenly like a ledger, a map with inked routes I'd forgotten I knew. I thought of my mother's hands folding pages, of the way she slid things between covers like little prayers. For years, when a photograph arrived for repair, I tried not to look too closely at the faces. Curiosity had its own taxonomy of trouble.

"Do you remember him?" Ben asked, nodding toward the photograph I had hidden by instinct.

His question took a breath out of me. The man in the photo had the same eyes my mother used to squint into the morning light with, the sort that suggested a person who could laugh and also keep a secret. I couldn't place him precisely, but I recognized the shape of a story: a stranger who had sat on my childhood lap once and then had not been asked to stay. Recognition came wrapped in absence.

"I don't remember him," I said. "Not really. I remember my mother and the pier and…a coin she kept. That's all."

Ben's face folded then, in a way that every aunt, neighbor and ex-priest in that town knew how to fold when they were about to offer something people had stopped asking for. "Hale said to tell you not to go down there alone anything," he said. "He sounded like he was used to telling people not to go poking about where they'd rather not. And he said—" Ben's eyes flicked to the crate, as if reading the brass mark like a page. "—he said if anything turns up with the coin, to call him right away."

The bell overhead chimed again, a lonesome note. Outside, the fog swallowed the storefronts into smudges of paint and breath. I imagined the beach, the pier's skeletoning posts, a man's body held by the sea and the town's small curiosity like a net. I imagined Hale with his coat collar up, the deputy's hat clinging to his skull like a barnacle. I imagined my mother with one hand on the plaster cast of a coin and the other on my shoulder, pressing directions into me that I hadn't yet learned to follow.

"All right," I said finally. The coin in my hand felt less like an object than a sentence strung across several voices. "I'll go to Hale. But not because of the coin. Because someone was found dead, and because the photograph—"

A packet fell from the corner of the box then, loose as an afterthought. I hadn't seen it at first. It landed on the bench and unfurled like an odd white flag: a note, paper the color of bone. My name was on it, in the same slanted hand as the inscription on the photograph. There were only three words.

Don't trust the lighthouse.

For a second the shop tilted. Lighthouses don't talk; they point. But the line was a message and a warning and some old small-town thing I had been avoiding for most of my life. I remembered how my mother had watched the lighthouse from the kitchen window, the glass fogging around the light like a swollen eye. I remembered not asking.

Ben exhaled, an unnecessary noise in a room newly full of meaning. "You okay?" he asked.

I folded the note in half and slid it into my pocket as if by tucking words into my jeans I could put them somewhere sensible. Outside, someone called "Mrs. Archer?" and the name drifted away. The gulls made a lot of noise, a washing of wings and throat.

"Yeah," I said. The coin felt heavy in my palm, the photograph tucked like a key under my arm. "I think I am. For now."

Ben took a step back, the way townspeople give space when they hand you a map no one asked for. "Hale's at the Pier House," he said. "He's got the whole street taped off. You going there?"

I looked at the box, at the coin with its pair of curling serpents, at the photograph with its inscription that had counted one more year into my life without asking my permission. The fog outside had thickened into a thing one could step into and disappear. The lighthouse beyond the roofs was a dark chunk on the skyline, its lamp unlit for the morning.

"For now," I repeated. Then I picked up my coat. The coin warmed my palm for the first time.

As I stepped out into the fog, the photograph pressed into the inside pocket of my jacket like a promise. The world around me muffled into grey; the town closed behind me like a book about to be opened. The pier waited like a wound, and I couldn't say I was not going to go look at it.

Someone somewhere in the noise of gulls and the thin, precise clack of my shoes on the arcade stones cleared a throat. The town inhaled, as if bracing. The next thing I knew, the bell at the door had chimed once more behind me, and at the edge of my hearing there was the faraway voice of Deputy Hale, methodical and close: "If you find anything, Mrs. Arden—anything at all—you call me."

I folded my hands over the coin one last time and felt its cold print against my palm. The fog swallowed my answer. I could not remember whether I spoke it aloud or only thought it, but either way the words fit the morning: "I will."

The box was the size of a shoebox and smelled faintly of salt and mothballs when I opened it, which is to say it smelled like the town: brine and old paper. It had arrived at the Greyhaven Historical Society the morning after a thunderstorm, wrapped in brown paper and without a return address. No invoice, no note—only a strip of packing tape stretched over the seam, the kind you use when you don't want anything to leak out or in.

I should have tossed it in the back room with the other oddments—old postmarks, a rusted button or two, the postcards people drop off when they clean out attics—but something about the tape made me peel my index finger along the glue as if looking for a seam in a map. Curiosity, which kept me awake nights cataloguing other people's lives, won. The tape came away cleanly. Inside, on top of shredded paper, lay a single sheet: a maritime chart of Greyhaven's harbor, yellowed at the edges and creased into thirds. A thin brown stain in the center had dried into the fibers like a fossil. Someone had folded the corner over and scrawled two words in ink so faded they were almost blue: "Look deeper."

People leave things at museums the way they leave keys on kitchen counters—a habit of displacement. They want someone else to witness the objects; to give them names and dates and context. My job, in a town of sixty-two streets and more secrets than proper nouns, was to make beans of those fragments. I had been doing it for eleven years—labeling, cross-referencing, sometimes lying when donors asked for a price—and for eleven years I had preferred the company of books to the company of people.

I had not expected the chart to be about me.

The stain sat almost at the center of the harbor, right where the harbor master's map showed a shallow sandbar and the note "danger" written in a hand that slanted left. There was a pencil arrow pointing from the stain to a tiny cluster of numbers: 42.17.12. I ran my finger along the faded contour lines, felt the texture like ridges under skin.

Someone had written more on the margin in a hurried, heavier hand: FOR L., and then a string of letters that might have been a name or a cipher—MORROW? MORROW. The idea of the word stuck in my mind the way sea foam clings to your boots after wading too close to the breaker. L. could be anyone. But my first thought, which isn't how I like to work, went to Luke.

I had not seen my brother, Luke Greeley, in fifteen years. He left town the summer after our mother died, with a duffel bag and a borrowed fishing license. He called twice in the first month—whiskey, static—and then the calls stopped. The sheriff's office logged him as "left voluntarily" and the newspapers printed a short notice that summer was gone sooner than expected and that the harbor looked emptier without his boat. People said he would show up when the tide shifted. People are comforting.

People are also wrong.

I set the chart on the long work table in the front room of the Historical Society, where the light comes in angled and patient, where the dust motes are inclined like congregants waiting for a sermon. Around me, the exhibits stood like a village—glass cases full of fishing hooks, a weathered sign that still proclaimed "HARBOR INN—EST. 1890," a photograph of the town's only lighthouse, painted white until the paint seemed to be bleached into memory. On a whim I pulled the ledger from the shelf under the table and set it beside the chart. Logan's ledger. The donor list. Names, dates, addresses—little silos of life.

I had not planned to think about Luke when I came to work that morning. I had planned, as always, to index. To do what archivists do: give each thing a taxonomy, a place. But the chart had a gravity I should have resisted. For one thing, it was accurate in a way that old romantic trinkets are not; the coordinates matched the town's current charts. For another, someone had torn a thin strip from the lower corner as if extracting a sample. Whoever sent it wanted something returned—or wanted someone to find something they had hidden.

I went to the back room to fetch the magnifier and the small lamp with the blue glass that makes old ink look honest. The back room smells like glue and cold, the windows frosted with condensation in winter and the fine grit of summer by May. I knelt on the floor between the stacks where no sunlight reaches and laid the chart over a sheet of conservation paper. The stain, when viewed through the lens, had a pattern—like a spatter someone would see and call ruined, but there were scabs and darker flecks within the brown. Blood oxidizes over time and can look like ink. I am trained, quietly, to notice such things. I am not a coroner, though I have catalogued enough death to be intimate with its residues.

The words FOR L. were heavier through the magnifier. It could be L. for Luke, or L. for anyone with a name that starts there: Lila, Lawrence, Lark. Morrow, if that was Morrow, was a surname that had brushed the edges of Greyhaven for generations—the Morrow estate, the Morrow mills on the inlet—but the family had died out or moved away during the oil boom. If someone had scrawled Morrow in the margin, it could be a direction or a derision.

The bell over the front door chimed—three short jangles—the kind of bell that announces newcomers and how they carry themselves. I tucked the chart back into the box and slid the lid shut, folding the paper over as if to preserve the secret, though I knew whatever shelter the box offered would be short-lived. The bell again. Then the soft scrape of shoes on the threshold.

"Morning, Evie." Sheriff Tom Calloway's voice is broad as a coastline.

"Tom." I called back, keeping my voice level. He came in carrying a wet cap and a face that had been prematurely wind-creased. "Thought the museum was closed this morning."

"Well, I thought someone might be in here," he said. His eyes lingered on the box by omission, the way people look at things they do not know how to name. Tom has been sheriff twice as long as I've been cataloguing. He is the sort of man who sees what falls between the lines and then makes a file for it. "There was a storm out back last night. A pile of seaweed nearly took the bridge. Old man Peters called me at two."

"Did he say anything interesting?" I lifted a hand from the counter to the brim of my hat, a gesture of the town's long habit of minute exchanges.

"Only that the tide brought something in." He rubbed his jaw. His left hand had a nick on the knuckle, which I have watched scar over with the patience of one who observes patterns. "Said he'd seen a small skiff on the rocks and thought maybe a fisherman lost his boat, but the Coast Guard said nothing was missing. Nothing registered." He sighed as though that was the category into which most of Greyhaven's small catastrophes fell. "You mind if I look around?"

"Do you want a formal list, or do you want to wander like a man with a headache?" I teased. We both know the town's jokes.

"Coffee," he said instead, smiling. "And whatever it is you have that smells like old paper and mystery. I'm hungrier than I am suspicious."

I made the coffee because it's easier to hand someone a hot cup than an accusation. We sipped in companionable silence. The Historical Society, for all the ghosts in its display cases, has a small kitchen that has the barest of comforts—two mugs, a kettle, a jar of loose tea where people leave notes on envelopes like prayers. We watched through the front window as the town opened itself like a hand: Mrs. Alvarez wheeled her cart down Main, the high school cheerleaders shuffled past in navy and silver, the harbor breathed.

When Tom left, he took his coffee and his unease with him. He had not seen the chart in the box. No one had, but me. I made a list on a scrap of ruled paper—Date received, condition, items—but left the space for "donor" empty. Anonymous things like to be anonymous until they're not.

I walked the harbor after leaving the Historical Society, because you go where your questions might cast shadows. It was low tide, the mudflats exposed like old skin, and the gulls argued like small relatives over the unclaimed. The shoreline had not changed much since I was a child; the lighthouse still leaned a fraction, the rope lockers were still salt-burned, and the old pier creaked in a way that had names for every oak plank. A fisherman I knew, Hank Dyer, tipped his hat. He had a boat named Mercy, which was ironical in a town where the sea owes you nothing.

"Found anything interesting?" Hank asked. He meant gossip. He was a man who spent most of his day looking for silver. I thought of the chart in the box and how, like most things, it wanted company.

"An anonymous gift," I said.

"Always the best kind," he said. "Usually cheaper, too."

There are parts of Greyhaven people don't talk about anymore. The bay on the far side of the shoal—Cartwright's Cove—used to have a reputation. It is the kind of place that breeds stories: fishermen who cut deals with the tide, a mid-century family that lost its daughter to an accident and never recovered. Before the harbor modernized, before the Coast Guard built the new station, Cartwright's Cove had been where lads from town got into trouble and where, sometimes, they came back different.

I thought of scribbles in margins and of the stain on the chart and of the way someone had folded the corner just so. I had not planned to go looking, but I had also not planned on the bell at the door or Tom's visit, and those are the small events that add up to a decision: curiosity, obligation, grief, maybe a thwarted urge toward gathering the loose ends.

When I reached the pier, an old man sat on the edge, his boots swinging over slow water. He looked like someone we should all have learned from and had not. He watched me approach without surprise. His hands were stained the color of the tide.

"Morning, Evelyn." He nodded. "You look like you've swallowed a map."

"Maybe I have," I said. He smiled in a way that was almost apologetic.

"Careful with those," he said. "Maps remember where things went."

He called himself Peters, though everyone calls him Old Man Peters, and he has been on the rocks longer than the lighthouse has had a keeper. He knows every groove in the harbor. He had called the sheriff the night before. He had seen something out there that didn't fit his ledger of usual misfits.

"The tide washed in something that smelled like copper," Peters said. "Not money copper. Blood copper." He spat a careful mouthful over his shoulder. "Thought I'd seen everything."

"You call the sheriff?" I asked.

"Aye. But Tom's got more than he can tally." He looked at me with the kind of pity that has room for amusement. "You too, Evie? You don't look like the sort to hang about a mystery."

"Neither the mystery nor the town are particular," I said. "They tend to hang around you if you listen."

I could tell him what I had found, but I didn't. The chart was still sitting on my desk at the Historical Society, folded like a thing asleep. I could have left it there, filed under "uncatalogued," a paper that might sit on a shelf and accumulate dust and another generation's curiosity. Or I could follow the arc of the handwriting, follow the stain to a sandbar and ask questions of people who prefer to shape the past into stories that don't hurt.

I don't like storms much. I like what they do in the dark: purify the air and leave a smell of retribution. I don't like being pulled by tides that have opinions about where things belong. But sometimes, when a map arrives in a box and someone has scrawled FOR L. in a margin, you realize that you have already been named into someone else's story.

On my walk back to the Historical Society I passed the lighthouse. Someone had nailed the new signboard to the gate: FOR SALE. The letters were stark against the salt-gray wood. On the horizon, a low bank of cloud gathered—an old syntax of weather that the sailors call "the promise line." It promised rain, and it promised a tide that would reveal more than shells.

I turned the key in the door and set the chart on my desk, smoothing the edges until the crease looked less like a wound. Then I made a list. Item: Chart, anonymous donation. Condition: stained. Assigned to: Evie Price. Note: Follow-up—Cartwright's Cove? Call Tom. Call Peters.

I checked the ledger and under D for donors, the column awaited. I left it blank and wrote a new entry at the bottom, in my careful archivist hand: Received—an uninvited clue. Date: today. Time: the morning after the storm. Signature: E.L. Price.

It is a foolish thing to put your signature on a beginning. It is also the first step in declaring yourself responsible. I realized, with a small particular hush in my chest, that I had signed on to a story in which my brother's name might be a place and a casualty. The smell of salt and mothballs settled somewhere in my throat. I turned off the lamp, locked the door, and as I walked the road home with a map folded under my arm like a sleeping thing, the town's lights swung behind me like fireflies and the harbor exhaled, collections of secrets waiting to be sorted.

When my key clicked in the lock at home, there was a car idling down the street. A single headlight glanced off the wet pavement. Whoever it was pulled away before I could see a face. The engine's hum dwindled into the night like someone closing a book mid-sentence.

The chart fit into my coat pocket like a cold hand. I told myself I was only bringing it home to examine it by lamplight. I told myself I was doing my job. The truth is simpler: when something looks as if it has been left for you, some part of you recognizes the handwriting of fate. Some other part of you—a part with a name and a memory and a brother who didn't answer his phone—knows that the tide will not be the only thing picking at the shore.

I set the kettle on. The house smelled like lemon oil and old photographs. I spread the chart out on my kitchen table and stared at the stain until it orbited the room with a rumor of meaning. Look deeper, it had said.

Outside, the town settled into the hush of the coming rain. The map, folded on my table, seemed to hunch closer to the night.

Chapter One

The sea has a memory of its own, and on mornings like this it insists on being heard. It unspools itself along Holloway’s breakwater in a steady, patient way—the wind rolling through the gulls like a low conversation, the tide licking at the harbour stones. When I first came back, after a decade of getting my hands dirty in other people's histories, I thought the sound would be a comfort. Now it is an undercurrent, a metronome I never quite learned to tune out.

My workroom smells like paper. There is another smell layered over it—a mineral tang from the sea, and the faint ghost of glue and lemon oil. The desk lamp throws a small pool of light over the ledger I'm stitching. In daylight the town looks like it's been painted with watercolors; under the lamp everything is raw and granular. I like the intimacy of it. When you repair book spines you become part keeper of confidences. Edges reveal little private lives: a child's crayon margin here, a pressed pebble there. You learn to read a book like a person.

This ledger is local: Holloway Registry, 1938–1947. The binding is buckram, the pages foxed where hands were damp with brine. I work with tweezers and waxed linen thread, my fingertips steady because the past does not forgive clumsiness. I have a routine—steam out the folds, consolidate the tears, make a new guard for the spine. It is method and patience and, on the best days, a kind of grace.

Halfway through the fourth signature, my fingers pause on something thinner, less honest than the ledger's birth certificate entries and grain shipments. A corner of an envelope is lodged in the gutter, its flap torn open, the paper softened by time. Whoever slipped it in had folded it smaller than the page, as if hiding something from the books themselves.

I fish it out with the tip of my scalpel. The envelope is unmarked except for a single smear of salt and a faint thumbprint pressed like a dried seed. Inside is a Polaroid—one of those cheap square ones, its white border browned—and a scrap of paper no larger than a matchbook page. The photograph is of the old clocktower on Mill Street, the one that hasn't kept time since the wind took its hands in 1979. Someone stood on the quay, back to the camera, and looked up at the face. It could be anyone; the figure is only a silhouette against a lilac sky. But the scrap is written in a hand I know well enough to name without thinking.

Maeve— it says, and the ink is not old enough to be a relic but not new enough to be a joke. The handwriting has my leftward tilt, the small loop on the y that my mother always corrected. My shoulders tighten around a memory that is not mine yet feels like a bruise: a summer night, paper lanterns on the pier, the clock striking something that was not time. My mouth goes dry.

"Do you always catch treasures in every shipment, or is today special?" Etta's voice floats from the stacks. She is the museum's trustee and the kind of woman who calls everyone 'dear' in all conditions. Her cardigan is piled with brooches like drowned shipwrecks. She understands the town's quiet better than anyone, and she assumes you do too.

"Someone hid this in fifty years’ worth of property taxes," I tell her. I fold the scrap back into the envelope and lay the photograph face down on the bench. It looks small and ordinary beside the ledger, but ordinary things are often heavy.

Etta squints at the envelope. "Holloway loves its mysteries," she says. "And its paperwork. Maybe the two are the same thing."

If she says 'mystery' with a smile, it is because all of Holloway's secrets are partly hers. I nod, and we both pretend the act of acknowledging won't pull anything taut.

My phone buzzes; the display reads 'Unknown'. I answer it out of habit.

"Ms. Quinn?" A man's voice, low and wind-rubbed. Jonas Reed. I haven't heard his voice in months and it carries the raw winter edge he's always had, like glass on stone. He used to stand in the shadow of the clocktower with me and pretend that the clock kept secrets we could not. He is the chief detective now, and the town has given him a uniform that's slightly too big for his bones.

"Jonas." The name is a small thing, hard to swallow. "Is everything—"

"Where are you right now?"

I tell him. He asks me to stay there. That is the kind of request that sits in a different register, like an overture that crescendos into something serious. He says, "I need you at the quay. There's been—"

He doesn't finish the sentence. I know enough of the constabulary's grammar that an unfinished sentence means someone is dead, or nearly so, and something about the body has made it messy beyond the town's appetite. My chest unclenches with the kind of dread you practice against but never truly master.

"I'll be there in ten," I say. I tell Etta I'm going out. She raises an eyebrow but hands me my coat without asking, which is the Holloway way: people mind your business until it becomes their business.

Outside, the wind is acting as if it owns the place. It throws my scarf against my jaw; the gulls are louder, disruptive as an accusation. The quay smells of engines and winter fish. On the far edge of the pier a crowd has formed like a small, reluctant island—neighbors pressed together, their faces pale under knit hats. Jonas meets me at the breakwater. He is bigger than the town remembers and smaller than his badge suggests. For the first second our eyes find each other and then do the predictable, awful thing men who once loved each other do: they measure distance.

"Maeve," he says without a question. He doesn't offer condolence. He never was good at those.

"What happened?" I ask.

He jerks his chin toward the mouth of the harbour. "They pulled him out of the marsh at dawn. Local fisherman—Gus—found him when the tide turned. No wallet. No ID. Name's not in the system." His breath fogs in the cold. He hands me a plastic evidence bag. Inside is a scrap of paper, crumpled soft and spattered with old mud. On it, in my handwriting, are three words.

Don't look for me.

The bag is warm because someone has held it for a while. My fingers tremble as if the tremor can be accounted for by the cold. Jonas watches me like an examiner, like someone waiting to see if a mark will open.

"I know that hand," I say. If I sound certain, it is only because certainty is easier to hold than the other thing—memory, that unreliable meter. Jonas nods, and the small stoicism on his face is a landscape I used to draw upon.

"Maeve, we found a photograph in his jacket. He had it folded in his shirt pocket—waterlogged, but the emulsion held. It's a child's photo." He turns away for a second, and I can read the decision under his skin: whether to bring me closer or keep me distant. "We need you to look at it."

I follow him down the pier. The crowd parts like it's my duty to pass. The body is not there—there are tarpaulins and talk and a cordon of tape that says 'POLICE LINE DO NOT CROSS' with the casual cruelty of a county fair. The air smells now of iron and salt and the bright soap of antiseptic. Gus, the fisherman, stands with his cap in his hands like an accused man at a parish. The ambulance lights have drained the morning of color.

Jonas hands me the photograph with gloved hands, an odd formality by now. It's a portrait from the seventies, the kind with a blurred edge and a gloss that refuses to lie flat. A girl sits on a wicker chair, hair cropped in a bob, sunburned freckles across the bridge of her nose. A small charm bracelet loops her wrist—tiny shells cast in bronze—and her knees are scabbed where she fell from the pier. For the first few seconds I see only a child's face: the tilt of the chin, the overgrown front tooth. Then something like a tide turns inside me.

The girl's mouth is supposed to be empty because mine once was. I came home missing a tooth, the only souvenir I kept of that summer. On the back of the photograph, in a hand I can no longer pretend not to know, someone has written: Forgive me, Maeve.

It is my mother's hand—no other hand could curve into that particular mercy of a capital F. My throat makes a small, surprised sound. Etta's cardigan is suddenly loud against the far wall. Jonas's jaw tightens.

"How did he—" I begin.

"That's what we're trying to figure out." His voice has narrowed into the small space where disbelief lives. "Whoever he is, this photograph was with him when they pulled him out. The pocket was stitched with—" He searches for the word and then finds it. "—care. Like someone put it there and wanted it to stay."

My mind moves slow and fast at once. The photograph is older than any of my recent decisions. It is a relic of a summer that was cut clean by a police siren and then shelved to gather dust. Every story I have told myself about that night sits on a shelf that suddenly looks suspiciously like a lie.

"Do you remember the clock stopping that summer?" Jonas asks. It is a small question, one meant to tie the old town myth to shifting facts—the clock famously stopped at two thirteen a.m., a preserved mystery as much as a broken gear. The stop was never explained. My sister, Lila, had gone missing on a night like that. So, of course I remember. Of course I remember.

"The clock stopped at 2:13," I say. My voice returns as an echo in a long tunnel. "We thought the whole town had gone to sleep."

Jonas holds the photograph between us like a third presence. "Gus said he found a shoe too—small, like a child's. He couldn't get close enough with the tide. We dredged at low and found a scrap, something folded into the ledger by the old registry shed. Your name was written on it."

The ledger. My hands go back to where the envelope had been, even though the ledger is six blocks away under my lamp, safe and patient. The world narrows into tracks: the ledger, the envelope, the photograph, the mud. They link like rusted chain.

"Someone put my handwriting on his person," I say. The accusation is not wholly mine, and it is not wholly Jonas's. It is a claim being made against the town's long history of forgetting.

"Whoever he is," Jonas says quietly, and there is the steady cruelty of his profession, "he wanted you—or he wanted someone who knew you—to find him."

The gulls call like judgment. I fold my coat tighter around me because the wind has moved into my bones. My head is a room with windows flung open to a memory I have been avoiding all these years. The image of my sister's wrist—bracelet of tiny shells glinting in the salt light—slides into place like a click.

"Was there anything else with him?" I ask.

Jonas shakes his head, then draws in a breath so long it seems to steal time from the sea. "Only this."

He hands me a shredded slip of paper, the same one from the ledger, the same one that read Don't look for me. It sits like a prophecy. On the back of the photograph, the three words sit like an apology offered by a ghost.

Forgive me, Maeve.

The syllables are a pinprick. They puncture the mock-safety of the present and spill cool, old blood into the light. I feel, for the first time in a long while, the shape of what the town has kept hidden. Not just a body. Not just a summer. A ledger of small betrayals stitched into the margins.

"Who else knows about this photograph?" I ask, though I already know the answer. Everyone, at one time or another, knew someone who owned a piece of us. Holloway is compact. It keeps nothing very far from its shore for long.

"No one we can ask yet. Gus is at the pier, and the coroner's coming," Jonas says. "Maeve—" He stops, and the old intimacy shutters between us. "If you think of anything, anything at all, you call me."

I want to tell him the broken parts of my memory—the fragments of a lantern, the taste of salt on a tongue too young to know fear—but memory isn't a ledger you can mend with thread. It is a glass jar that has lost its lid. You put the pieces together and hope they hold.

Instead, I fold the photograph back into my palm, feeling the impression my mother's handwriting leaves on the paper, like a shallow grave. Holloway is a town that remembers everything in tiny, inconvenient ways. It has a habit of throwing the past up like flotsam until someone comes to fetch it.

"Jonas," I say, and the name tastes right. "Keep me posted."

He watches me walk away as if he's measuring whether I will keep myself intact. I feel inadequate to the task of being myself. On the walk back the town closes around me: the shuttered bakery, the tobacconist with its hand-lettered sign, the clocktower, motionless and patient. There are footprints in the sand like a child's, leading nowhere and everywhere at once.

Back at the workroom the lamp waits. The ledger lies where I left it, and when I slide my hand under the lamp the room seems to hold its breath. I place the photograph on the bench and lay my palm over the handwriting as if pressing it back into time might still it.

Forgive me, Maeve.

The words are a place I cannot go without taking someone with me. My fingers find the envelope again and, beneath the ledger, my thumb grazes something else—an old, browned ribbon tied in a knot I recognize. It is the same ribbon that used to bind the shells on Lila's bracelet. My breath stops. The ribbon smells faintly of the sea and of a summer that ended too fast.

Outside, the gulls keep up their low, relentless conversation. Inside, I have the photograph and the scrap of paper and a town that will not be put away again. Somewhere in the marsh a tide is pulling at the bottom of things, and the wind is asking questions that were better left unasked.

I sit down and begin to stitch. The ledger is patient. The past is not.

The morning the sea gave me a body, the fog had the town in its teeth. It sat low and hungry over Port Harrow, swallowing the pier lights and muffling the gulls until everything sounded as if it were happening under water. I walked into it like walking into the past: slowly, with my hands in my coat pockets and my jaw set against the cold.

I hadn't meant to come down to the jetty. My week had been full of forms and prescriptions and the small, flat talk of a hospital room; my father had taken a tumble, had a bruise on his ribs and a head full of questions he saved for the quietest hours. I needed air. I needed the place where, as a teenager, I had learned to throw rocks and not look back. Port Harrow was the same neat collection of storefronts and salted porches, the same leaning sign for the diner, but the town had its own way of aging: softer edges, fewer secrets. I liked to believe that until I pulled aside the yellow tape and saw a shape on the rocks.

They had cordoned off the jetty at the far end with tape that flapped like a bright wound. A couple of cruisers were parked at awkward angles, their engines idling. Men in dark coats moved with the calm, efficient choreography of people who performed grief professionally. I should have turned back then. I almost did. Instead, something harder than curiosity threaded through me — recognition, maybe, or habit. I had been running toward this part of myself for years without knowing it. I stepped over a patch of wet rope and let the cold salt air hit my face.

The body was lying half on the slick stones, half in the shallows where the sea lapped and withdrew in a slow, indifferent rhythm. It was a woman, mid to late thirties, hair matted with silt. Her coat was dark and expensive enough to suggest she belonged to someone who mattered in town or kept track of what mattered. There was no blood on her face; the skin was grey with the bluish undertone that comes from cold and from something else. The coroner — because the coroner had to be here, because death requires paperwork even on a foggy Tuesday — crouched by the body with a notepad, cigarette forgotten between two fingers. He looked up when I approached.

"Nell?" he said. It was more statement than question. The world that gathers police to a scene is small. Everyone knows someone who knows someone. "You shouldn't be here."

I took off my gloves. The air felt thin; my breath came in small white bursts. "What do we have?"

He thumbed his lips as if unsure how to talk about what was happening while it was happening. "Unidentified. Female. Cause unknown. Time of death unknown. You need to step back."

I stepped closer anyway. I had been a detective once, and that muscle still flexed under my skin even though I had promised myself, and everyone else, I wouldn't let it. Part of me had left Port Harrow and never looked back; another part had stayed behind to check on the things that didn't fit. The things that kept you awake.

The woman’s hands lay folded on her chest. Tucked under her gloved fingers, like something left for a casual ceremonial, was a single playing card. I knew — before I was even given the luxury of a formal look, before the coroner said anything or the officer asked me to move along — what card it would be. A memory, sharp and involuntary, slid through me: a laminated table, a file drawer, a card with a small, crooked heart stamped in the corner. For ten years we had called the phantom who left those cards the "Queen of Hearts." Ten years we had not caught a thing but a trail of faces and folded paper. Ten years I had not worn a badge.

I knelt. The rocks were slick and bitter with seaweed; the smell of brine filled my sinuses. I craned my neck to see the card without touching anything. The card was bright against the grey, the queen's face looking absurdly cheerful amid seaweed and wet wool. Red hearts cut across the paper like a wound. Whoever had placed it had done it with care; it was not shoved into a pocket, not flung with rage. She had been covered with a sign.

"Step back, Nell," the coroner said. His voice had a pleading edge. "We need to keep a perimeter. You know this. We don't want contamination."

"I know contamination," I said. The words tasted like dust. "But I also know the Queen's card."

He closed his eyes for a beat. When he opened them, there was something like old friendship in the look and something like despair. "I thought we were done with that," he said. "I thought you —"

"I know what I thought," I said. "We both thought a lot of things."

Detective Miles Carter appeared then, as inevitable as tide. He had been leaning against his cruiser, collar turned up, a cigarette burning down to the filter. He looked the same — too tall for the town, a jaw that had been kind to him in his youth and kept being kind in the way only faces can. He had been my partner on the Queen of Hearts case at the end: when we were younger and our belief in pattern outweighed our belief in rest. We had stopped courting the same things at some point; he stayed, I left. There is a metabolism to small towns' resentments. The air was taut between us.

"You okay to be here, Nell?" he asked, but he wasn't asking for my permission. He was stating a boundary.

"Okay?" I echoed. "I didn't come for permission. Who is she?"

"Unknown for now." He tilted his chin to the coroner. "Coroner says hold off until we have a tech team." He looked back at me. "You should go home, Nell. You know how this looks."

I had not brought my uniform, nor any intention of walking into that old life. But recognition is not a thing that you can choose not to have. I watched him watch the body, watched him look and not see certain small details because the human brain is an efficient animal and Miles's brain was protecting something. Something fragile. He had left the detective work to others for a reason: the present had teeth.

The coroner reached down, careful with his notepad, and slid a pair of latex gloves over his hands. He plucked the card from under the dead woman's fingers as if it might combust. Hands moved; someone photographed. There was a low hum of radios and the metallic click of cameras. The town performed its rituals.

I stepped away, but not far enough. My feet found a patch of craggy stone behind the cruisers where the fog was less absolute. I folded my arms around myself and let the cold wash over me. I felt an old itch of a problem waking up: that peculiar way a past pattern insists on reasserting itself. The Queen of Hearts had been a symbol, then a signature, then a ghost. We had found her cards on doorknobs, under pillows, pinned to bulletin boards with neat little ribbons. She had been seen by people who swore they couldn't have been. We had found people who'd been touched and left changed. We had never found her.

"Why would she come back here?" I asked, because once you know a regularity you want to name it. The fog swallowed my words as if it had a vote.

Miles looked at me then. "Because she likes the sea?" he offered, and for a second the joke landed like a stone. He pressed his cigarette to the heel of his shoe and stubbed it out. Up close I could see the line at his right eyebrow where a scar had flattened something that once might have been a laugh.

"You know how it looks, Nell," he said. "You burned your badge for a reason. We don't need your—"

"My badge?" I interrupted. "You wore yours till it rusted. Don't pretend you didn't use to knock on doors at midnight because you liked the adrenaline of finding a truth."

For a moment we were only two people who had once fit neatly into each other's silences. Then we were the past and the present slamming into each other. He cuffed the brim of his hat and said nothing for a beat, which was his way of deciding how dangerous it was to be honest. "We need to get a positive ID," he said finally. "We need a tech team, a canvass. No press. No —"

I thought of the Queen's cards pinned to the sheriff's corkboard; of late nights at the precinct, the smell of stale coffee; of a face in grainy CCTV footage that was only a face by the grace of our need to see one. I thought of the way my hands remembered fingerprints and the smell of different kinds of fear. It was ridiculous, and it was me. Part of me had left that life because the weight of other people's secrets had felt like an open wire against my skin. Part of me wanted nothing more than to piece it back together.

"Who is she?" I asked again, softer. There was a childishness in it, as if I wanted the answer to be simple. The coroner, who had been circling his notepad like a moth, looked up.

"Not yet," he said. "But whatever reputation this town thinks it has — it's about to get interesting."

He used a different word than I would have picked. Interesting in a place that measured seasons by boat festivals and the opening of the lobster shacks had a certain quiet monstrousness. Port Harrow's idea of excitement was usually a new shipment of scallops. A body on the rocks with a Queen card altered the town's calculus.

I wandered closer while the others did their formalities. The woman's face was turned to the sky; her mouth hung open as if she might say something and then found the air insufficient. Her fingers were pale and slender. Around her wrist a thin bracelet caught the weak light, a string of small sea-glass beads threaded on a cord. Something in the way it was clasped — not a factory clasp but a loop, a knot tied with a practiced hand — made me think of summer camp and secrets kept in pockets and little girls trading treasures. That small object, more than the card, tugged at a part of me that shouldn't have been tugged. It made this closer than it should be.

I felt a hand on my shoulder, gentle but assertive. "Enough, Nell," Miles said. His voice had lost its casualness. He was no longer my partner or my old friend. He was an officer of the law.

And yet my hand was already in my pocket. The habit was ridiculous — it had been years — but my fingers curled around something I kept for emergencies: a small brass compass my father had given me when I turned nineteen and decided I was leaving Port Harrow for good. I pressed the metal smooth with my thumb. The needle quivered, useless under the sky that read like a grayed-out photograph.

I had told myself once, the night I handed in my badge, that I would stay away from cases that wanted me. I had carried that promise like a talisman. Now, with damp stones under my boots and a queen's face grinning in the river light, the promise felt thin.

The coroner zipped up his jacket and moved back. Someone had placed a canvas over the woman's face. The card was bagged. Names would be run, families would be called, and the town would fill with the polite, efficient nervousness that follows death. I felt the old compulsion coiling in my bones, and with it, an answering whisper of dread.

"Do me a favor?" I asked Miles before I knew I would. "If it is her — if it's connected — tell me first."

He blinked. The night we stopped chasing ghosts together still lived under his skin. "Nell," he said. The word was short and yet the weight of the last ten years hung in the space between it sounded.

"I know how this looks," I said. "And I know why you say no. But some part of me thinks this was left for me."

He looked at me for a long time as if he was mapping old loyalties. Then he sighed, which was a surrender layered over another. "If it is, I'll tell you first," he said. "But don't get in the way. We do this by the book."

I didn't tell him that I no longer believed in the book. I only nodded, like a student returning to a classroom she had once failed.

As the techs swarmed and the tape flapped and the fog settled back over the town like a benediction, I stepped away from the yellow perimeter and let my feet take me back over the pier. My compass was warm against my palm. Somewhere, a gull cried. The Queen of Hearts had not sent a postcard. She had come with her signature pinned like a pin to someone's chest.

The thought made the skin along my arms prickle: this was no longer a rumor in the file room. It was a call.

When I reached the road, the diner was pulling its chairs out from under the tables; the coffee would be hot and the town's small talk would be cheap and thick as syrup. The day would fold into itself in the practiced way these places know. People would put their lives back together with the same careless threads. But someone had placed a queen in the tide, and the town would not be the same after.

I walked away with my hands in my pockets and a card I had not touched burning under my fingernails. In the pocket of my jacket, my father’s brass compass hummed like a small, disagreeable thought.

I had thought, for ten years, that I had left the Queen of Hearts in the past. Standing at the edge of the water, with the fog swallowing the harbor like a mouth, I understood that it had been waiting — patient as an animal — for the exact moment I thought I was safe.

The sea had been the color of old pewter that morning, flat and indifferent under a sky the color of unmade beds. Grayhaven wakes slow in October; the shops still smelled of last night's coffee and burnt toast, and the harbor looked as if the tide had forgotten to come back for its usual morning review. I was walking without meaning to — because routine is the safest thing left to me and because I had been awake all night thinking of other people's secrets — when I saw him.

At first I thought he was sleeping, slumped against the harbor's retaining wall, rain-dark hair plastered to his forehead. He lay with one arm over his face like a man trying to shade himself from the wrong kind of light. A gull rolled lazily in the wind and landed two feet away, cocked its head, and then decided he had seen better things.

I almost stepped around him. Almost told myself it wasn't my business. I've learned the difference between curiosity that saves you and curiosity that buries you deeper. But there was a small, absurd insistence that the dead have about them — a way they drag attention like a hook — and I crossed the cobbles and crouched.

His face was younger than I would have thought, maybe late thirties, maybe early forties. He had a scar like a comma at the outer edge of his left eyebrow and a bruise blooming on his neck. The rain had washed a ribbon of red out from under his shirt collar and the smell of him, up close, was a mixture of salt and something sweet and oily — cologne, too expensive for the harbor, as if he'd come from somewhere that charged more for things than grief does here.

He held something in his hand. I saw it before I saw the badge on his jacket: a small, battered locket on a chain, its brass dulled by years of hands. Someone's impulse had been to close it shut around the small photograph inside; the clasp was bent a little, as if it had been pried open once too often. The photograph — when I leaned closer, because you never stop being a reporter even when you pretend not to — was a child's face, a girl with freckles and a toothy smile. For a moment I couldn't breathe.

"June?"

The voice belonged to Chief Hargrove, who smelled of coffee and cold hands. He had that specific way of saying my name that made everything feel like an accusation wrapped in concern. He was already on the phone, flannel collar up against the wind. Behind him two uniformed officers stood awkwardly, like men who had been asked to play a role in a tragedy and had not yet learned their lines.

"Don't touch anything," he said. He didn't have to tell me twice. My fingers hovered over the locket; I withdrew them because a lifetime of rules about contamination and evidence has an odd way of outlasting fear.

"Who is he?" I asked.

"No ID on him," Hargrove said. "No wallet. No phone. Came in with the tide, or maybe somebody brought him down. No witnesses yet, except some early-morning jogger who called it in, said she saw him, thought he was sleeping."

"Looks like an accident?"

He looked at me like he'd known me long enough to read the answer and still wanted me to make it official. "Nothing about that wall suggests he fell," he said. "Not likely. But I'm not forming hypotheses yet. Not when there's a dead man on the stones."

People in Grayhaven argue about everything — parking, politics, whether the pier should be restored or left to rot — but when there's a body the town becomes a place where you stop pretending you don't know people with secrets. I have spent enough of my life studying people who hide things to know what I'd already suspected: someone had brought him here to be seen.

When the medics lifted him onto the stretcher, the locket rolled free and slid across the cobbles with a sound that might as well have been a tiny bell. It stopped under my shoe.

"June," Hargrove said again, gentler now, like a man tackling the wrong loose end. "This is police business. You should go home."

There are many ways to leave a place without actually leaving it. I left for home but walked down to the bookstore instead, because running away from a problem usually means running toward something that feels like a life before you get to it. The bell over the door announced my arrival, but the shop was as it always was at that hour — a small, warm rectangle of light and paper in a town that likes to believe both are permanent.

People who have left things behind — husbands, houses, careers — learn to fill the spaces with other things. My life is full of paperbacks and dust and polite customers who like their mysteries solved in a weekend. It's safe here. Complicated things stay on the other side of the glass.

Except sometimes they don't.

I don't know what made me take the locket from my coat pocket when I reached for my chai. Maybe it was muscle memory; maybe it was something like guilt. The clasp gave with a sigh, and the tiny photograph stared up at me like an accusation. A small freckle on the left cheek, a scar at the hairline. Claire, my sister.

My hands went numb. She had been twelve when she left — two decades ago now, if you can believe it. She had left a jacket on the back of her bedroom door and a note that said, "I'm going to find something better than this," and the town had folded itself in on that little absence as if absence could be made neat. We were told there were leads, right away and again by the wayside; we were told the usual consolations — runaway, new life, age will soften. We were told almost everything except the truth. The police files had gone cold, public interest had moved on, and my parents had learned to breathe around a missing person as if grief were a draft in a room you don't quite notice until the window is open.

This locket belonged to us. It was mine once; I remember hiding it in the false bottom of a biscuit tin the night Claire tried to run away from a world that seemed to her too small. We had exchanged it as if we were handing each other a secret. I had carried it for a while, then given it back, because she was the type to collect small treasures. The back of the locket bore a single scratched initial I had always assumed was hers.

There is a particular taste to panic: metallic and sharp. It rose in my mouth and spread to my limbs. I sank onto a stool and set the locket on the counter like an accusation on a table.

I called Hargrove because there are some things you cannot un-know quietly. His voice on the other end was careful. "Bring it to the station," he said. "Don't touch anything else."

I told him I would. I told myself I would. But I knew, with the absurd clarity of a night that ends in daylight, that I would not hand it over without learning why a man I'd never seen before was carrying my sister's photograph like a talisman.

I went to the harbor first.

The place had turned into a cluster of moving bodies. Crime scene tape made the air look like a tightrope. The coroner's van was here, and a photographer, and neighbors standing in clusters, like birds, commenting at a distance. The reality of the body had become other people's work. I stood at the edge where they'd let us look and watched the creases in Hargrove's forehead deepen. He didn't want me here. He needed me to leave. But then — he never could hide his eyes when certain things happened — he could not pretend not to see I had the locket.

"June," he said as I approached, voice low. "You weren't supposed to be here."

"I wasn't supposed to leave a locket on the stones either," I said. "Who was he?"

He hesitated. "No ID. Clothes were expensive," he said. "A watch with the crest of Halberd & Crane. That's an old firm. He had a card, a thin folded paper with a name and a number. I'll have it catalogued. We have to assume nothing. But — you should go home, June."

There was a last thing he wanted to say, something lodged like a splinter in his mouth: the town was small, people knew each other, and if the dead had come to us, he worried about the living who were left behind and the ways in which the two could be entangled. It was the shape of a warning and he refused to finish it.

I walked back to the shop through a wind that did not feel like weather. My hands shook when I opened the back door. It had been latched when I'd left; when I pushed against it, it swung easily. The kettle on the stove had been left to cool; the kitchen smelled of old tea, and a smear of ink stained a piece of paper on the table.

A single line had been written in a hand I recognized like the shape of my own breath: Don't trust the mayor.

There are small practical truths about living in a town where everyone votes for the same names on the ballot or remembers the same scandal a hundred ways: rumors are currency, loyalties are inherited, and power is something that wears a suit and a smile. The mayor of Grayhaven was as much a fixture as the clocktower, and he had used the town's affection to his advantage in ways that were legal and not, depending on who you asked and how loudly they were asked.

I folded the paper with the fewest possible motions and slid it into my pocket. The locket clicked against the coin of the town, and I felt a motion inside me that is old and familiar: something that had been waiting, patient, for a shape to give itself to. Call it grief, or duty, or the stupid hope of a sister who remembers a face a child made and trusts her memory more than the silence that followed. Whatever it was, it left the harbor with me, a small weight like a decision.

Outside, the town of Grayhaven went about its morning as if nothing had happened. The gulls announced themselves. A man on a ladder fixed a string of lights. Somewhere a radio was announcing the weather. I stood on the threshold of my life and realized something I had not allowed myself to feel for years: that the disappearance had been a question mark placed on my chest, and now someone had set a period at its end by pressing a brass locket into a dead man's hand.

I did what any rational person would do next. I made coffee, because coffee is an instrument of focus and because keeping my hands busy seemed like a sensible temporary defense against the fact that a locket with my sister's face had been in a stranger's palm. I washed it in the sink and set it on a towel to dry. The photograph inside was fragile as old tissue. The girl's smile was mischievous and full of promise. Her name used to mean the future.

A car idled across the street and then left, tires hissing into the mist. A woman walked by the shop and looked at the window. She did not see me; she never does. The town has that way of not seeing what is right in front of it. It prefers its comfortable explanations.

I did not want to be dragged into another missing person's case. I did not want to pry open old wounds or disturb graves that had been neatly paved over with the town's good intentions. But the locket was a protest against forgetting, and somehow, in the way birthmarks and memories have a stubbornness to them, the world had contrived to hand me a clue that belonged to the past and to a man who would never tell me why he'd been carrying it.

There is a law in me I learned from always wanting to know: you follow the line until it ends or it takes you somewhere else. I set the locket back in my hand and felt the small photograph like a hunted thing. Outside, the harbor hummed. Inside, the shop held its breath. The piece of paper in my pocket was a single, scrawled line of warning. I put the kettle on, and then I sat down and began to write, because the first thing you do when the past and the present collide is to make a list. Names. Times. Questions with no answers yet.

When the phone rang, I did not pick it up for a full minute. The ringing was a slow insistence, like someone knocking from a room you had tried to lock. When I finally put the receiver to my ear, I heard Chief Hargrove's voice on the line, low and tight.

"June," he said. "You were right to keep the locket."

The sentence was small and ordinary and terrible all at once. Behind it, the harbor sighed, and the town continued to pretend that it could keep its secrets tidy if no one asked too hard. But someone — or something — had decided to make that impossible.

Chapter One
